nodes.title: ABN AMRO grievance mechanism
nodes.heading: 7.6.4 ABN AMRO grievance mechanism
nodes.start_phrase: ABN AMRO is committed to meeting the expectations set by the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs).
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines ABN AMRO’s grievance ecosystem aligned with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, explaining how potentially affected people and other stakeholders can raise concerns across the bank’s different roles. It highlights:

- Overall commitment: ABN AMRO acknowledges potential human rights impacts linked to its activities and provides multiple speak-up and complaint channels tailored to stakeholder groups.
- Lender role: 
  - ABN AMRO’s complaint channel—open to anyone, with emphasis on corporate clients and affected people.
  - Human Rights Remedy Mechanism—accessible to potentially affected people and/or their nominated representatives, and corporate clients.
- Service provider / procurer of goods and services:
  - ABN AMRO’s complaint channel—for individual and business clients.
  - International Framework Agreement (IFA)—for workers in ABN AMRO’s supply chain.
- Investment services provider:
  - ABN AMRO’s complaint channel—for clients using the bank’s investment services.
- Employer role:
  - Multiple internal channels for raising concerns, as detailed in the “Channels for own workforce to raise concerns” section of the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
  - Eligible users include employees and some third-party workers.

The section clarifies who can use each mechanism and positions these channels within the bank’s broader Pillar 3 Report 2024.

nodes.title: Consumers and end-users
nodes.heading: 7.6.5 Consumers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: Through our double materiality assessment, we have determined three material matters that relate to our consumers and end-users and reinforce our dedication to their overall well-being and inclusion.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines ABN AMRO’s approach to consumers and end-users, highlighting three material topics identified via a double materiality assessment: privacy, suitability of products and services, and social inclusion. It details the bank’s human rights commitment and due diligence aligned with the UN Guiding Principles, ILO Fundamental Principles, and OECD Guidelines, including engagement with consumers or their representatives, procedures to identify and manage potential negative impacts, and access to remedy through established complaints mechanisms; no human rights violations were reported to the bank’s knowledge. On privacy, the Personal Data Policy sets GDPR-based, bank-specific standards across the full data lifecycle and is reinforced by Binding Corporate Rules for cross-border data protection, including requirements for breach notifications, rights facilitation, and complaint handling via the Complaints Management Policy. For suitability and inclusion, the Product Approval and Review (PAR) Policy ensures products serve defined target markets in clients’ best interests, embed inclusivity and suitability, meet regulatory requirements, adapt to macroeconomic, social and sustainability changes, and align with Client Centricity Principles, ESG objectives, and the bank’s broader risk strategy and appetite.

nodes.title: Addressing human rights issues arising from our consumers’ activities

nodes.start_phrase: We are dedicated to respecting the human rights of all people that can be affected by our operations and those of our business relations.

- Privacy policy framework: Personal Data Policy grounded in GDPR and ABN AMRO-specific sub-principles; implements Binding Corporate Rules for cross-border data protection; covers the full data lifecycle; requires breach notifications, facilitation of data subject rights, and linkage to the Complaints Management Policy.

nodes.title: Product Approval and Review Policy
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.3.1 Product Approval and Review Policy
nodes.start_phrase: ABN AMRO's Product Approval and Review (PAR) Policy is designed to ensure that our products and services serve the best interests of clients and are offered to a defined target market, while considering all relevant risks for clients, the bank and external stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Consumers and end-users, with three material topics from a double materiality assessment—privacy, suitability of products and services, and social inclusion.
- Human rights: Commitment to UNGPs, ILO core principles, and OECD Guidelines; human rights due diligence with stakeholder engagement; access to remedy via complaints mechanisms; internal collaboration to detect risks; no human rights violations reported.
- Privacy governance: Personal Data Policy aligned with GDPR and ABN AMRO’s Binding Corporate Rules; lifecycle controls for personal data; breach notification, data subject rights facilitation, and complaints handling.
- Product and client safeguards:
  - Product Approval and Review (PAR) Policy ensures target-market fit, inclusivity, suitability, regulatory compliance, and adaptation to macro/social/sustainability changes; aligns with Client Centricity and ESG; Executive Board accountable; GRC oversight.
  - Duty of Care & Client Centricity Policy sets bank-wide framework for managing Duty of Care risk and embedding it into the ERM cycle; overseen by the Management Body and Senior Management.
  - Client Categorisation, Suitability and Appropriateness Policy defines client classification and when to perform suitability/appropriateness checks for investment services; Compliance oversight.
  - Complaints Management Policy standardizes complaint handling, roles, timelines, root-cause analysis, and regulatory adherence; Legal’s Complaints Management department owns and oversees the process.
- Scope and hierarchy: Policies apply globally to ABN AMRO Bank N.V. and controlled entities; stricter local requirements take precedence; deviations governed by the Policy on Policies.
- Privacy engagement and incident response: Primarily reactive channels for breaches, complaints, and GDPR rights requests; internal notification within 24 hours and regulatory notification within 72 hours; multiple reporting channels for consumers; clients generally informed; issues resolved through the grievance mechanism.

nodes.title: Duty of Care and Client Centricity Policy
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.3.2 Duty of Care and Client Centricity Policy
nodes.start_phrase: The Duty of Care and Client Centricity (DoC & CC) Policy, introduced in June 2024, establishes our approach to managing Duty of Care (DoC) Risk and prioritising clients’ interests across all areas of ABN AMRO.
nodes.summary:
- Governance: The Executive Board (ExBo) has ultimate accountability for product approvals and an effective Product Approval and Review (PAR) process, with Group Risk Committee (GRC) oversight.
- Duty of Care and Client Centricity (DoC & CC) Policy (June 2024): Establishes the bank’s approach to DoC risk and client-first principles; defines scope and key concepts; sets bank-wide requirements to embed DoC risk into the ERM cycle; oversight by the Management Body and Senior Management under the ERM Policy.
- Client Categorisation, Suitability and Appropriateness Policy: Sets minimum standards for investment services and activities; defines client classification and when suitability/appropriateness assessments are required; Compliance holds an independent mandate to establish and review this policy.
- Complaints Management Policy: Provides a structured framework for complaint handling and registration; defines roles and responsibilities; sets timeliness and accuracy standards; requires analysis of root causes for continuous improvement; ensures compliance with relevant laws; the Complaints Management department within Legal independently develops, reviews, oversees, and owns the process.
- Applicability: All policies apply to ABN AMRO Bank N.V., its controlled subsidiaries, branches, and representative offices globally, across all roles and seniority; stricter local rules prevail; deviations require approval per the Policy on Policies.
- Privacy engagement: Focus on reactive channels for data breaches, privacy complaints, and GDPR rights requests; internal notification within 24 hours and regulatory notification within 72 hours for breaches; consumers can report via phone, email, or regulator; clients are generally informed even when not mandated; grievances handled through the bank’s complaints mechanism for timely resolution.

nodes.title: Client Categorisation, Suitability and Appropriateness Policy
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.3.3 Client Categorisation, Suitability and Appropriateness Policy
nodes.start_phrase: The Client Categorisation, Suitability and Appropriateness Policy establishes minimum standards for providing investment services, performing investment activities, and delivering ancillary services.
nodes.summary:
- Governance: ExBo holds ultimate accountability for product approvals and maintaining an effective PAR process, with GRC providing oversight.
- Duty of Care & Client Centricity Policy (introduced June 2024): Sets definitions and scope for DoC Risk and Client Centricity, outlines key DoC Risk management concepts, and embeds DoC Risk into the ERM cycle; oversight assigned to the Management Body and Senior Management under the ERM Policy.
- Client Categorisation, Suitability and Appropriateness Policy: Establishes minimum standards for investment services and activities, defines client classification, and sets when suitability/appropriateness assessments are required; Compliance has an independent mandate to establish and review this policy.
- Complaints Management Policy: Provides a framework for effective complaint handling and registration, defines roles/responsibilities, sets timeliness/accuracy standards, mandates root-cause analysis, and ensures compliance with relevant laws; the Complaints Management department within Legal independently develops, reviews, oversees, and owns the complaints process.
- Applicability: All referenced policies apply across ABN AMRO Bank N.V., its controlled subsidiaries, branches, and representative offices globally, for all locations, roles, and seniority levels; stricter local requirements prevail; deviations require approval and recording per the Policy on Policies.
- Privacy engagement: Primarily reactive channels addressing data breaches, privacy complaints, and GDPR rights requests; breach protocol includes internal notification within 24 hours and regulatory notification within 72 hours; consumers can report via phone, email, or regulator; clients are generally informed of relevant breaches; privacy issues are handled through the bank’s grievance/complaints process.

nodes.title: Complaints Management Policy
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.3.4 Complaints Management Policy
nodes.start_phrase: The Complaints Management Policy provides a structured approach to improving our products and services by ensuring effective complaint handling and registration.
nodes.summary:
- Governance: ExBo holds ultimate accountability for product approvals and an effective PAR process, with oversight by GRC.
- Duty of Care and Client Centricity (DoC & CC) Policy (June 2024): Bank-wide umbrella framework aligning with client-centric principles; defines DoC Risk and Client Centricity, outlines DoC risk management concepts, and embeds DoC Risk into the ERM cycle; oversight by the Management Body and Senior Management under the ERM Policy.
- Client Categorisation, Suitability and Appropriateness Policy: Sets minimum standards for investment services/activities and ancillary services; defines client classification and when suitability/appropriateness assessments are required; Compliance independently establishes and reviews the policy.
- Complaints Management Policy: Establishes structured complaint handling and registration with clear definitions, roles, timelines, and accuracy standards; mandates root-cause analysis and compliance with laws/regulations; Legal’s Complaints Management department independently develops, reviews, oversees, and owns the complaints process.
- Applicability and deviations: All policies apply to ABN AMRO Bank N.V., its controlled subsidiaries, branches, and representative offices globally, across all locations, roles, and seniority; stricter local requirements prevail; any deviations require approval and recording per the Policy on Policies.
- Privacy engagement: Focus on reactive channels for data breaches, privacy complaints, and GDPR rights requests; breach protocol requires internal notification within 24 hours and regulatory notification within 72 hours; consumers can report via phone, email, or regulator; clients are generally informed of relevant breaches; grievances mechanism aims for timely resolution of privacy issues.

nodes.title: Dialogue & engagement with consumers and end-users relating to suitability of products and services and social inclusion
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.5 Dialogue & engagement with consumers and end-users relating to suitability of products and services and social inclusion
nodes.start_phrase: In our daily interactions with clients, we actively seek feedback to continually refine our services.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines ABN AMRO’s ongoing dialogue with clients to ensure product and service suitability and promote social inclusion, using roundtables, surveys, client panels, and pilots (e.g., testing a new payment feature). It incorporates behavioral insights and external inputs, including research by the Customer Digital Engagement department and third-party researchers, as well as feedback from the Dutch consumers’ association Consumentenbond.
- The bank’s objective is to use client and stakeholder feedback to improve offerings, assess suitability through product approval reviews and scenario analyses, and integrate product-related complaints into a closed feedback loop to refine product features and target market definitions.
- Targeted engagement focuses on clients who may face barriers—women, culturally diverse groups, elderly clients, people under financial stress, individuals with disabilities, less digitally skilled clients, and youth. In 2024, efforts included consultations with clients with disabilities to enhance accessibility and focus groups, surveys, and interviews with culturally diverse clients and women.
- Grievance and remediation mechanisms include a multi-channel complaints process (website, chat, phone, app) with an initial response within five days, potential escalation to the Security and Integrity Management team, options to escalate externally to Kifid or Meldpunt Discriminatie after eight weeks, and internal reassessment routes.
- Effectiveness is measured via post-complaint surveys generating a journey Net Promoter Score (jNPS) and qualitative feedback. Insights feed a closed feedback loop, with dashboards available to product and client teams for direct follow-up and quarterly trend reporting by Complaints Management (Legal) to the Executive Board and other stakeholders.

nodes.title: Engagement with specific groups of consumers and end-users
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.6 Engagement with specific groups of consumers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: We focus on specific client groups who may face barriers, including women, clients from culturally diverse backgrounds, elderly clients, those facing financial stress, individuals with disabilities, clients less familiar with digital tools, and young people.
nodes.summary:
- The organization outlines a structured approach to dialogue and engagement with clients to improve product and service suitability and advance social inclusion.
- Feedback is gathered through roundtables, surveys, client panels, pilot programs (e.g., testing a new payment feature), and analysis of client behavior.
- Engagement methods vary by interaction type and seniority; the Customer Digital Engagement department and third-party researchers study digital experiences (e.g., online appointment booking), process accessibility, and sustainability expectations. External inputs (e.g., Consumentenbond) are also incorporated.
- Product suitability is governed via product approval reviews, scenario analyses, and integration of product-related complaints to refine features and target market definitions.
- Targeted engagement focuses on groups facing barriers: women, culturally diverse clients, elderly people, those under financial stress, people with disabilities, clients with low digital literacy, and youth. In 2024, activities included consultations with clients with physical disabilities and focus groups/surveys/interviews with culturally diverse clients and women.
- A comprehensive complaints and remediation system allows submissions via website, chat, phone, and app, covering issues such as accessibility, suitability, discrimination, and product use. Clients receive an initial response within five days, with possible escalation to the Security and Integrity Management team.
- If unresolved after eight weeks, clients can escalate externally to Kifid or Meldpunt Discriminatie; internal reassessment is available, with further escalation options if reassessment is declined.
- Complaints effectiveness is measured via surveys generating jNPS and qualitative insights; data feeds a closed feedback loop. Dashboards are accessible to relevant teams, and the Legal Complaints Management team reports quarterly on trends to the Executive Board and other stakeholders.
- Overall, the document emphasizes continuous improvement of accessibility, inclusivity, and client-centricity through proactive engagement and robust grievance mechanisms.

nodes.title: Grievance mechanisms and remediation channels for consumers and end-users
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.7 Grievance mechanisms and remediation channels for consumers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: Under ABN AMRO’s official complaints procedure, clients can submit complaints via the website, using our online chat facility, by calling or through the app.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines ABN AMRO’s approach to engaging consumers and end-users to ensure product suitability and promote social inclusion, using roundtables, surveys, client panels, pilots, and behavioral insights to refine offerings.
- It describes tailored engagement by function and seniority, including the Customer Digital Engagement department’s research (e.g., online appointment booking, process accessibility, sustainability expectations) and incorporation of external insights such as from Consumentenbond.
- Product suitability is continuously assessed through product approval reviews (including scenario analyses) and integration of product-related complaints to adjust features and target market definitions.
- The bank prioritizes engagement with potentially underserved groups—women, culturally diverse clients, elderly, financially stressed individuals, people with disabilities, clients with low digital literacy, and youth—via research, panels, focus groups, surveys, and interviews; 2024 efforts focused on culturally diverse clients, women, and people with disabilities.
- A comprehensive complaints mechanism allows submissions via web, chat, phone, or app, with a five-day initial response, potential escalation to the Security and Integrity Management team, reassessment options, and external recourse to Kifid or Meldpunt Discriminatie after eight weeks or if dissatisfied.
- Complaint handling effectiveness is monitored through jNPS and qualitative feedback, a complaints dashboard accessible to relevant teams, and quarterly trend reporting by Legal’s Complaints Management to the Executive Board, with complaints able to trigger PAR reviews and product/service adaptations.
- Supplier and intermediary arrangements require effective complaints handling aligned with ABN AMRO’s Supplier Code of Conduct; clients can access ABN AMRO’s complaints process directly, and the Whistleblower Policy protects clients and third parties, with complaints channels kept separate from whistleblowing.
- On privacy, the bank is strengthening foundations by expanding first-line responsibilities, implementing a privacy programme, enhancing privacy management, and improving privacy risk insights.
- For social inclusion, actions include researching barriers for culturally diverse customers, building employee awareness of unconscious bias, enhancing accessibility of products and services, and collaborating with other organizations; effectiveness is monitored through controls, testing, tools, and integration into key risk reports.

nodes.title: Our approach to consumers and end-users relating to privacy
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.8 Our approach to consumers and end-users relating to privacy
nodes.start_phrase: We take the following approach and actions to address impacts and risks on privacy, suitability of products and services and social inclusion:
nodes.summary:
- Complaints about products can trigger the PAR process to assess product suitability and accessibility, leading to adaptations where needed.
- Suppliers must operate effective, monitored complaints mechanisms aligned with ABN AMRO’s Supplier Code of Conduct; intermediaries are legally bound to ensure appropriate handling, and clients can access ABN AMRO’s complaints mechanism directly. Ultimately, ABN AMRO handles all product/service complaints.
- The Whistleblower Policy protects clients and third parties from retaliation; the complaints channel is separate from the whistleblowing channel.

Approach to consumers and end-users on privacy:
- Strengthening privacy foundations by expanding the first line of defence.
- Implementing a privacy programme.
- Further improving privacy management.
- Developing enhanced privacy risk management insights.

Approach to consumers and end-users on social inclusion:
- Minimising barriers to access via improved client due diligence and risk assessments.
- Researching barriers faced by culturally diverse customers.
- Building employee awareness of unconscious biases.
- Enhancing product and service accessibility.
- Collaborating with other organisations.
- Effectiveness is monitored through controls, testing, and tools, feeding into key risk reports and assessments.

Targets:
- No specific social risk targets in 2024.
- In 2025, exploring the feasibility and meaningfulness of setting such targets.

nodes.title: Our approach to consumers and end-users relating to social inclusion
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.9 Our approach to consumers and end-users relating to social inclusion
nodes.start_phrase: ABN AMRO strives to minimise negative impacts on access to financial products and services by improving client due diligence and risk assessments.
nodes.summary:
- Complaints about specific products can trigger ABN AMRO’s PAR process to assess product suitability and accessibility, with potential adaptations to products and services.
- Suppliers are expected to operate effective complaints mechanisms aligned with the Supplier Code of Conduct; intermediaries are legally bound to ensure proper handling of ABN AMRO-related complaints.
- Clients using intermediaries can still access ABN AMRO’s complaints mechanism, and ABN AMRO ultimately handles all product/service complaints.
- The Whistleblower Policy protects clients and third parties from retaliation; the complaints channel is distinct from the whistleblowing channel.
- Privacy approach focuses on: strengthening privacy foundations and first line of defence, implementing a privacy programme, improving privacy management, and enhancing privacy risk insights.
- Social inclusion approach aims to reduce barriers to financial access via improved client due diligence and risk assessments, including research on culturally diverse customers, employee bias awareness, accessibility enhancements, and collaborations.
- Effectiveness is monitored through controls, testing, and tools, with outcomes integrated into risk reports and assessments.
- Targets: No specific social risk targets in 2024; in 2025, ABN AMRO will explore the feasibility and value of setting such targets.

nodes.title: Targets related to consumers and end-users
nodes.heading: 7.6.5.10 Targets related to consumers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, ABN AMRO did not have specific targets for social risk topics.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines ABN AMRO’s complaint handling and client protection framework, and its approaches to privacy and social inclusion. Complaints about specific products can trigger the Product Approval and Review (PAR) process to reassess suitability and accessibility, with adaptations made as needed. Suppliers are expected to maintain effective complaint mechanisms per the Supplier Code of Conduct, while legal arrangements ensure intermediaries handle ABN AMRO-related complaints appropriately; clients can always access ABN AMRO’s own complaints channel, and the bank ultimately handles all product and service complaints. A separate Whistleblower Policy protects clients and third parties from retaliation, distinct from the complaints channel. On privacy, the bank focuses on strengthening first-line ownership, implementing a privacy program, improving privacy management, and enhancing privacy risk insights. On social inclusion, it seeks to reduce barriers to access through improved due diligence and risk assessments, research into challenges faced by culturally diverse customers, unconscious-bias awareness for employees, enhanced product/service accessibility, and external collaborations, with effectiveness monitored via controls, testing, and tools feeding into key risk reporting. The bank had no specific social risk targets in 2024 and plans to explore the feasibility and value of setting such targets in 2025.

nodes.title: Business conduct (Governance)
nodes.heading: 7.7 Business conduct (Governance)
nodes.start_phrase: We are subject to strict regulatory requirements, at both national and international level.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on business conduct and governance, emphasizing strict national and international regulatory requirements translated into internal policies with monitoring to ensure effectiveness, compliance, risk awareness and a culture of integrity.
- Materiality assessment identifies Client Integrity as a material topic, with vigilance required to safeguard the banking system.
- Client Integrity risk comprises six key types: Anti-Money Laundering (AML), Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC), Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT), Tax, Fraud and Sanctions.
- Stakeholders include clients, regulators, employees, shareholders and broader society; per the DMA, Client Integrity is material from a financial perspective.
- The compliance framework includes multiple Client Integrity-related policies:
  - Client Acceptance and Anti-Money Laundering (CAAML) Policy: measures to prevent/detect ML/FT and manage associated risks.
  - Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC) Policy: bank-wide framework to prevent involvement in bribery/corruption across clients, employees and third parties; includes client risk indicators (e.g., adverse media).
  - Tax Policy: global tax mandate, responsible tax behavior, strategy, risk appetite and control framework; defines when Group Tax involvement is mandatory.
  - Fraud Risk Policy: minimum standards for managing fraud risk (including first-party fraud) through prevention, detection and response; adaptive to evolving fraud threats.
  - Sanctions Policy: rules to prevent prohibited transactions and sanctions evasion, with requirements, consequences, escalation and reporting.
- Policies collectively reinforce legal compliance (e.g., Dutch Financial Supervision Act, AML/CTF Act, Sanctions Act 1977), industry best practices and positive culture to mitigate financial crime.
- All policies are accessible on the bank’s intranet; an AML, CTF and Sanctions Statement and the ABC Policy are publicly available.

nodes.title: Business conduct (Governance) - Introduction
nodes.heading: 7.7 Business conduct (Governance)
nodes.start_phrase: We are subject to strict regulatory requirements, at both national and international level.
nodes.summary:
Business conduct (Governance)
We are subject to strict regulatory requirements, at both national and international level. These requirements are 
translated into internal policies for which mechanisms are in place to monitor operational effectiveness and 
compliance. The mechanisms enhance risk awareness and effective risk management, fostering a culture of integrity. 
Through our materiality assessment of business conduct topics, our activities relating to Client Integrity are identified 
as material. We are aware that our role as a bank requires us to remain vigilant in order to safeguard the integrity of 
the banking system.

nodes.title: Client integrity
nodes.heading: 7.7.1 Client integrity
nodes.start_phrase: Client Integrity risk at ABN AMRO encompasses six key risk types: Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Bribery and Corruption, Combating the Financing of Terrorism, Tax, Fraud and Sanctions.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of business conduct and governance: the bank operates under strict national and international regulations, translated into internal policies with monitoring mechanisms to ensure operational effectiveness, compliance, risk awareness, and a culture of integrity.
- Materiality: Client Integrity is identified as a material topic (financial materiality per DMA). Key stakeholders include clients, regulators, employees, shareholders, and society.
- Client Integrity risk scope: six risk types—Anti-Money Laundering (AML), Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC), Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT), Tax, Fraud, and Sanctions.
- Policy framework:
  - Client Acceptance and Anti-Money Laundering (CAAML) Policy: sets measures to prevent/detect ML/FT and manage related risks.
  - Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC) Policy: addresses bribery/corruption risks across clients, employees, the organization, and third parties; includes risk indicators (e.g., adverse media).
  - Tax Policy: defines global tax mandate, responsible tax behavior, strategy, risk appetite, and control framework.
  - Fraud Risk Policy: establishes standards for preventing, detecting, and responding to fraud (including first-party fraud) within an adaptive framework.
  - Sanctions Policy: prevents prohibited/sanctions-evasive transactions; outlines rules, consequences, escalation, and reporting.
- Policy governance: policies apply globally to all entities; stricter local laws prevail. ABC Policy also covers employees and third parties. Policies are on the intranet; AML/CTF/Sanctions statement and ABC Policy are publicly available. Policy adherence and key controls are periodically monitored and tested.
- Training: employees are required to understand AML/CFT responsibilities; a dedicated Client Integrity training curriculum and ongoing training are provided.
- Regulatory remediation: following a 2021 settlement with the Netherlands Public Prosecution Service over AML shortcomings, the bank continues to enhance AML processes and systems, focusing on monitoring effectiveness and client due diligence. The Dutch Central Bank is monitoring progress and has identified shortcomings in event-driven reviews (updating client files), which may lead to enforcement; financial impact is uncertain and no provision has been recorded.
- Broader bribery and corruption stance: the bank works to strengthen internal policies, processes, and controls for employees and third parties; further details in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Governance risks with counterparties and clients: managed via non-financial risk management (fraud, third-party, outsourcing) and client sustainability assessments; related disclosures referenced elsewhere.
- Reporting and consequences: violations or suspicions related to ABC are reported internally and to regulators. Unacceptable corruption risks can result in rejecting prospective relationships or terminating existing ones.

nodes.title: Bribery and corruption
nodes.heading: 7.7.2 Bribery and corruption
nodes.start_phrase: ABN AMRO plays an important role in helping protect the wider financial system against bribery and corruption.
nodes.summary:
- ABN AMRO maintains global policies and control frameworks, with monitoring via policy adherence indicators and key controls; local laws prevail where stricter.
- The Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC) policy applies to all entities, employees, and relevant third parties acting on ABN AMRO’s behalf.
- Employees are required to understand AML/CFT responsibilities and escalation steps, supported by a comprehensive Client Integrity training curriculum for all staff.
- Following a 2021 settlement with the Netherlands Public Prosecution Service over AML shortcomings, ABN AMRO continues enhancing AML processes and systems.
- Current priorities include improving the effectiveness of transaction monitoring and the quality of client due diligence.
- The Dutch Central Bank (DNB) is engaged in ongoing supervision, has identified shortcomings in event-driven reviews (e.g., updating client files after changes), and may take enforcement action; financial impact is uncertain and unprovided.
- The bank strengthens anti-bribery and corruption controls for employees and third parties, aiming to ensure regulatory compliance and reduce risk; further details appear in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Non-financial risk management covers governance risks related to counterparties (fraud, third-party, outsourcing), while client-related governance risks are addressed through sustainability assessments and the Client Integrity framework.
- Violations or suspicions of ABC breaches by staff, third parties, or clients are reported internally and to regulators; unacceptable corruption risk can result in rejecting or terminating relationships.

nodes.title: Governance risk related to our counterparties
nodes.heading: 7.7.3 Governance risk related to our counterparties
nodes.start_phrase: Our non-financial risk management looks after governance risks relating to our counterparties, such as fraud, third party and outsourcing risk.
nodes.summary:
- ABN AMRO has global policies and control frameworks with policy adherence indicators and key controls to monitor and test effectiveness; stricter local laws prevail where applicable.
- The Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC) policy applies to all entities, employees, and relevant third parties acting on ABN AMRO’s behalf.
- Employees are required to understand AML/CTF responsibilities and escalation steps; a Client Integrity training curriculum complements ongoing mandatory training for all staff.
- Following a 2021 settlement with the Netherlands Public Prosecution Service over AML shortcomings, ABN AMRO is enhancing AML processes and systems to meet regulatory requirements.
- Current focus areas include improving the effectiveness of transaction monitoring and the quality of client due diligence.
- ABN AMRO maintains ongoing dialogue with the Dutch Central Bank (DNB), which monitors progress; DNB has identified shortcomings in event-driven reviews (e.g., timely updates to client files) that may lead to enforcement actions; no reliable estimate of financial impact and no provision recorded.
- The bank strengthens anti-bribery and corruption controls for employees and third parties, aiming to improve policies, processes, and compliance; further details are in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Non-financial risk management addresses governance risks related to counterparties (fraud, third-party, outsourcing), with client governance risks covered via sustainability assessments and the Client Integrity framework.
- Violations or suspicions related to the ABC policy are reported internally and to regulators; unacceptable corruption risk can result in rejecting prospects or terminating existing relationships.
- Additional references: EU ORA – Qualitative information on operational risk and the “Risk management of sustainability matters” section.

nodes.title: ESG1 - Banking book- Climate Change transition risk: Credit quality of exposures by sector, emissions and residual maturity
nodes.heading: 7.8 ESG1 - Banking book- Climate Change transition risk: Credit quality of exposures by sector, emissions and residual maturity
nodes.start_phrase: The table below shows the bank’s exposure to non-financial corporates in carbon-related sectors, as well the scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions of our counterparties.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Presents ESG1 disclosures on banking book climate transition risk for non-financial corporates, detailing credit quality, financed GHG emissions (counterparties’ scopes 1–3), and residual maturity by NACE sector/subsector. It also flags exposures to companies excluded from EU Paris‑aligned Benchmarks (PAB) and “environmentally sustainable (CCM)” exposures.
- Headline movements (31 Dec 2024 vs 30 Jun 2024):
  - Exposure to sectors that highly contribute to climate change decreased to EUR 46.7bn (from EUR 48.3bn).
  - Total reported book c. EUR 66.1bn, of which EUR 19.4bn to other sectors.
  - Financed emissions for corporate loans fell to about 20.6 MtCO2e (from 22.8 MtCO2e).
  - Within-sector increases in emissions mainly from mining and quarrying and real estate activities.
- Credit quality and sector mix (31 Dec 2024):
  - Detailed gross carrying amount, accumulated impairments, Stage 2 and non‑performing exposures across NACE A–H and L.
  - Large exposures in real estate (c. EUR 10.3bn), transportation and storage (c. EUR 8.6bn), wholesale/retail (c. EUR 8.5bn), manufacturing (c. EUR 6.9bn), agriculture (c. EUR 5.1bn), construction (c. EUR 2.7bn), and electricity/gas/steam (c. EUR 2.3bn).
  - Stage 2 and NPE metrics shown per sector; impairments presented as negative figures.
  - “Of which” breakdowns include exposures to PAB‑excluded companies and CCM‑eligible exposures.
- Emissions profile and maturity (31 Dec 2024):
  - Total financed emissions roughly 20.6 MtCO2e; share of emissions based on company‑specific reporting is disclosed by sector.
  - Major sector contributors: manufacturing (~6.1 Mt), agriculture (~5.0 Mt), transportation and storage (~4.8 Mt, predominantly water transport), electricity/gas (~0.8 Mt), wholesale/retail (~1.5 Mt), construction (~0.5 Mt), real estate (~0.2 Mt).
  - Residual maturity skewed short‑term: ~55.7bn ≤5 years, ~7.0bn >5–10 years, ~2.5bn >10–20 years, ~0.9bn >20 years; average weighted maturities by sector typically around 3–4 years (e.g., real estate ~4 years).
- Time‑series context:
  - Full sector tables shown for 31 Dec 2024, 30 Jun 2024, and 31 Dec 2023, allowing comparison of exposures, credit staging, impairments, financed emissions (including scope 3), coverage from company‑reported data, and maturity buckets over time.
- Methodology and data notes:
  - Data sources and methods are developing.
  - Identification of companies excluded from the EU PAB is based on revenue split per Article 12.1; due to limited reporting, NACE principal activity codes are used as a proxy (listed codes include B05.10, B05.20, B06.10, B06.20, B09.10, C19.20, C20.11, D35.11 with renewable exceptions, D35.21–D35.23).
  - For Article 12.2 DNSH screening, the CASY assessment tool is applied as a proxy.
  - Regulatory template inconsistency noted: Sector I (Accommodation and food service) is not classified as a high‑contributing sector under the regulation; therefore, related exposures are presented under “other sectors.”

nodes.title: ESG1 - Banking book- Climate Change transition risk: Credit quality of exposures by sector, emissions and residual maturity - Introduction
nodes.source_title: ESG1 - Banking book- Climate Change transition risk: Credit quality of exposures by sector, emissions and residual maturity
nodes.source_heading: ESG1 - Banking book- Climate Change transition risk: Credit quality of exposures by sector, emissions and residual maturity
nodes.heading: 7.8 ESG1 - Banking book- Climate Change transition risk: Credit quality of exposures by sector, emissions and residual maturity
nodes.start_phrase: The table below shows the bank’s exposure to non-financial corporates in carbon-related sectors, as well the scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions of our counterparties.
nodes.summary: ABN AMRO’s ESG1 “banking book – climate change transition risk” disclosure presents credit quality and financed emissions for non‑financial corporate exposures by NACE sector/subsector, covering gross carrying amounts, accumulated impairments/provisions, exposures to companies excluded from EU Paris‑aligned Benchmarks, environmentally sustainable (CCM) amounts, and Stage 2/non‑performing exposures, alongside financed GHG emissions (scope 1–3 and scope 3), the share based on company‑specific reporting, residual maturity buckets (≤5y, >5–10y, >10–20y, >20y) and average weighted maturity. As of 31 Dec 2024, exposure to sectors contributing to climate change fell to EUR 46.7bn (from EUR 48.3bn at 30 Jun 2024), with total portfolio gross carrying amount EUR 66.1bn (EUR 69.5bn at 30 Jun 2024; EUR 67.6bn at 31 Dec 2023). Financed emissions for corporate loans were ~20.6 MtCO2e at 31 Dec 2024 (22.8 MtCO2e at 30 Jun 2024; 21.6 MtCO2e at 31 Dec 2023), of which scope 3 totaled 12.3 MtCO2e (13.8 MtCO2e; 13.0 MtCO2e), with ~20–21% of the gross carrying amount linked to company‑specific emissions reporting and average weighted maturity ~3–4 years. The mining and quarrying and real estate sectors are cited as main contributors to increases in GHG emissions. The disclosure follows the EU Climate Benchmark Standards Regulation (EU 2020/1818) referencing NACE A–H and L, notes treatment of Sector I due to a template inconsistency, and references PAB exclusion criteria (Article 12.1(d–g), 12.2). Data sources and methodologies are still developing.

nodes.title: Companies excluded from the Paris Aligned Benchmark
nodes.heading: 7.8.1 Companies excluded from the Paris Aligned Benchmark
nodes.start_phrase: Under Article 12.1 of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/1818, the identification of companies excluded from EU Paris aligned benchmarks should be done on the basis of revenue split.
nodes.summary:
- Extract from ABN AMRO’s Pillar 3 Report 2024 showing financed GHG emissions and exposures by sector (NACE) as at 31 December 2023, aligned with the EU Climate Benchmark Standards Regulation (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/1818).
- Table contents per sector/subsector: financed GHG emissions (tCO2e), gross carrying amount, share of emissions based on company-specific reporting, maturity profile (≤5y, >5–10y, >10–20y, >20y) and average weighted maturity, with an “of which: Scope 3 financed emissions” indicator.
- Coverage focuses on sectors considered to highly contribute to climate change (NACE A–H and L), with detailed breakouts for:
  - D35 Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning (including D35.1 and D35.11 for electricity production, D35.2 gas manufacture/distribution, D35.3 steam/air conditioning).
  - E Water supply; sewerage; waste management and remediation.
  - F Construction and its subsectors (F.41 buildings, F.42 civil engineering, F.43 specialised activities).
  - G Wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles.
  - H Transportation and storage with subsectors H.49 land transport, H.50 water transport, H.51 air transport, H.52 warehousing and support activities, H.53 postal and courier.
  - L Real estate activities.
- Key figures highlighted:
  - Total financed emissions about 21.6 MtCO2e and gross carrying amount roughly 13.0 (units per table), with 21% of emissions based on company-reported data and an overall average weighted maturity of around 3 years.
  - Transportation and storage is the largest contributor, driven by water transport; other sizeable contributors include wholesale/retail trade, construction, and electric power generation/transmission/distribution. Real estate, water/waste activities, and gas/steam supply also contribute.
- Regulatory notes and methodology:
  - Footnote references to Recital 6 (sectors A–H and L) and Articles 12.1–12.2 of the Climate Benchmark Standards Regulation.
  - Sector I (Accommodation and food service activities) is not classified as a “highly contributing” sector under the Regulation; due to a template inconsistency, exposures to Sector I are included under “Exposures to other sectors.”
  - Identification of companies excluded from Paris-aligned benchmarks relies on revenue-split criteria; where unavailable, NACE principal activity codes are used (B05.10, B05.20, B06.10, B06.20, B09.10, C19.20, C20.11, D35.11 except renewables/specific renewable financing, D35.21, D35.22, D35.23).
  - For Article 12.2 DNSH screening, the CASY assessment tool is used as a proxy to detect significant harm relative to the EU Taxonomy’s environmental objectives.

nodes.title: Financed GHG emissions
nodes.heading: 7.8.2 Financed GHG emissions
nodes.start_phrase: The financed GHG emissions have been calculated according to the Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard for the Financial Industry (PCAF, December 2022).
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines how financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are calculated in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (December 2022), allocating emissions proportionally to the bank’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s value.
- It prioritizes client- or collateral-level data; where unavailable, it applies economic emission intensities relevant to each segment.
- It summarizes portfolio-specific data sources and methods:
  - Corporate loans (listed bonds and equity): ISS ESG and client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed NL): Statistics Netherlands (CBS) economic intensity.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed RoW): PCAF emission factor database.
  - Agriculture: sector-specific factor for dairy (RVO, International Dairy Federation, Hospers et al. 2022); CBS intensities for other subsectors.
  - Shipping: Poseidon Principles and third parties (e.g., DNV) and emissiefactoren.nl/KiM; client-reported for sea/coastal freight; intensities for inland and other subsectors; CBS/PCAF as fallback.
  - Oil and gas (upstream/midstream): Rystad Energy, company disclosures, IPCC factors; specific emissions via Rystad.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch government open data; client-reported emissions and average capacity factor estimates.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft emission factors by vehicle type.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF database; estimates by building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; estimates by building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Additional methodological notes:
  - For corporate clients not in ISS ESG, CBS and PCAF provide country/sector carbon intensities.
  - Renewable energy producers (solar, wind, hydro) are assigned zero scope 1 and 2 emissions; scope 3 uses client data or CBS/PCAF.
  - Shipping data are collected and validated at vessel level under Poseidon Principles; inland shipping uses external emission factors; CBS/PCAF used when gaps exist.
  - Oil and gas intensity metric is kg CO2e per barrel produced/distributed/transported; client disclosures are linked with Rystad production and intensity data to set baselines and targets.

nodes.title: Financed GHG emissions - Introduction
nodes.heading: 7.8.2 Financed GHG emissions
nodes.start_phrase: The financed GHG emissions have been calculated according to the Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard for the Financial Industry (PCAF, December 2022).
nodes.summary: Introduces the bank’s methodology for calculating financed GHG emissions under the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022), allocating absolute emissions proportional to the bank’s share of a counterparty’s value and prioritizing client/collateral-level data; where unavailable, economic emission intensities are applied. A table details segment-specific data sources and methods: ISS ESG and client reports for listed corporates; Statistics Netherlands (CBS) and PCAF emission factor database for non-listed corporates (Netherlands and rest of world); RVO and International Dairy Federation for agriculture (dairy-specific factors, economic intensities for other subsectors); Poseidon Principles, CO2emissiefactoren.nl, and KiM for shipping (client-reported for sea/coastal freight, economic intensities for inland/other); Rystad Energy and IPCC for oil & gas (upstream/midstream); BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, and overheid.nl for power generation (including average capacity factor estimates); TRACCS and CE Delft for road transport (vehicle-type factors); RVO and PCAF for commercial real estate (building type and energy label); and RVO, CBS, and BAG for residential mortgages (building type, floor area, energy label).

nodes.title: GHG emissions for corporate loans
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.1 GHG emissions for corporate loans
nodes.start_phrase: The ISS ESG database is used as the source for collecting GHG emissions for our corporate clients.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How ABN AMRO calculates and reports financed GHG emissions across its portfolios, aligned with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022).
- Methodology: Absolute emissions allocated proportional to the bank’s share of counterparty value; preference for client/collateral-level data; use of economic emission intensities when client data are unavailable.
- Data sources and methods by portfolio:
  - Corporate loans (listed bonds/equity): ISS ESG; client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed, Netherlands): Statistics Netherlands (CBS) economic intensities.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed, rest of world): PCAF emission factor database.
  - Agriculture: Sector-specific factor for dairy (RVO, International Dairy Federation, research by Hospers et al. 2022); CBS intensities for other subsectors.
  - Shipping loans: Poseidon Principles and collaboration with DNV for vessel-level data; emissiefactoren.nl and KiM for inland shipping; CBS/PCAF fallbacks.
  - Oil and gas (upstream/midstream): Rystad Energy data, company disclosures, and IPCC factors; client-level carbon intensity used.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch government open data; client-reported plus average capacity factor estimates.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft vehicle-type emission factors.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF; estimates based on building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; estimates based on building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Segment-specific treatments:
  - Corporate loans: ISS ESG as primary source; CBS/PCAF used when ISS coverage is missing; renewable power (solar, wind, hydro) assigned zero Scope 1 and 2; Scope 3 from client data or CBS/PCAF.
  - Agriculture: Dairy sector uses a tailored emission factor; other subsectors rely on CBS intensities.
  - Shipping: Sea/coastal freight uses Poseidon Principles/client-reported vessel data; inland shipping uses external emission factors; fallbacks to CBS/PCAF when needed.
  - Oil and gas: Portfolio intensity measured as kg CO2e per barrel produced/distributed/transported; combines client disclosures with Rystad production and intensity to establish baselines and targets.

nodes.title: GHG emissions for agriculture
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.2 GHG emissions for agriculture
nodes.start_phrase: For dairy farming, a combination of the research paper Hospers et al. (2022), RVO (via StatLine) and International Dairy Federation was used to calculate a sector-specific emission factor.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How ABN AMRO measures and reports financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022).
- Core approach:
  - Absolute financed emissions are proportional to ABN AMRO’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s total value.
  - Data hierarchy prioritizes client- or collateral-level emissions; if unavailable, applies country/sector economic emission intensities.
- Portfolio-specific sources and methods:
  - Corporate loans (listed bonds/equity): ISS ESG; client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed NL): Statistics Netherlands (CBS); economic emission intensity.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed RoW): PCAF emission factor database; economic emission intensity.
  - Agriculture: Dairy uses sector-specific factor (Hospers et al. 2022, RVO, International Dairy Federation); other sub-sectors use CBS intensities.
  - Shipping: Sea/coastal freight via Poseidon Principles and third-party data (e.g., DNV); inland shipping via KiM and emissiefactoren.nl; fallback to CBS/PCAF intensities.
  - Oil & Gas (upstream/midstream): Company disclosures linked with Rystad data; IPCC factors where possible; intensity measured as kg CO2e per barrel to set baselines and targets.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch government open databases; client-reported emissions with average capacity factor estimates when needed.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft; external emission factors per vehicle type.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF; estimates based on building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; estimates based on building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Additional rules:
  - Renewable power producers (solar, wind, hydro) are assigned zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions; Scope 3 uses client data or CBS/PCAF where unavailable.

nodes.title: GHG emissions for shipping loans
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.3 GHG emissions for shipping loans
nodes.start_phrase: The Poseidon Principles framework has been used as our main source for collecting GHG emissions at vessel level for the sea and coastal freight water transport portfolio.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are calculated and reported in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022), allocating absolute emissions proportional to the bank’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s value.
- Data hierarchy: Prioritizes client or collateral-level, client-reported data; where unavailable, applies country/sector economic emission intensities and emission factors relevant to each segment.
- Portfolio methodologies and sources:
  - Corporate loans, listed bonds and equity: ISS ESG; client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans, non-listed Netherlands: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) economic emission intensities.
  - Corporate loans, non-listed rest of world: PCAF emission factor database.
  - Agriculture: Sector-specific emission factor for dairy using Hospers et al. (2022), RVO, International Dairy Federation; other sub-sectors via CBS intensities.
  - Shipping loans: Poseidon Principles with vessel-level data; collaboration with DNV; KiM and emissiefactoren.nl for inland shipping; fallback to CBS/PCAF for gaps.
  - Oil and gas (upstream/midstream): Rystad Energy data, company disclosures, IPCC factors; carbon intensity metric in kg CO2e per barrel produced/distributed/transported; used for baseline and targets.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch open government data; client-reported emissions and capacity factor estimates.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft vehicle-type emission factors.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF; emissions estimated from building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; emissions estimated from building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Renewable energy handling: For solar, wind, and hydropower producers, scope 1 and 2 emissions set to zero; scope 3 based on client data or CBS/PCAF where unavailable.
- Overall approach: Combines multiple databases and sector-specific methodologies to estimate financed emissions consistently across asset classes.

nodes.title: GHG emissions for oil and gas - upstream and midstream
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.4 GHG emissions for oil and gas - upstream and midstream
nodes.start_phrase: For the ABN AMRO portfolio, the carbon intensity metric measures the kg of CO 2e emissions for each barrel of oil produced, distributed or transported by each client we finance.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and framework: Describes how financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are measured in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022), attributing absolute emissions proportionally to the bank’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s value.
- Data hierarchy and approach: Prioritizes client- or collateral-level data; otherwise applies economic/sectoral emission intensities. Summarizes key data sources and methods per portfolio segment.
- Portfolio methodologies and sources:
  - Corporate loans (listed, bonds, equity): ISS ESG client-reported emissions. For non-listed NL clients: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) intensities; Rest of world: PCAF emission factor database. Renewable power producers assigned zero scope 1–2; scope 3 from client data or CBS/PCAF.
  - Agriculture: Dairy farming uses a sector-specific factor (Hospers et al. 2022, RVO, International Dairy Federation). Other sub-sectors use CBS country/sector intensities.
  - Shipping: Sea/coastal freight uses Poseidon Principles and third-party validation (e.g., DNV) with vessel-level data; inland shipping uses KiM and emissiefactoren.nl. Fallback: CBS/PCAF.
  - Oil & gas (upstream/midstream): Carbon intensity in kg CO2e per barrel using Rystad Energy, company disclosures; IPCC factors for combustion; proxies where data is missing.
  - Power generation: Company disclosures, BP Energy Statistics 2022, Dutch government open data (overheid.nl), and internal databases; estimates used to close gaps (e.g., average capacity factors).
  - Road transport: Trucks measured in gCO2/tonne-km; vans in gCO2/vehicle-km (scope 1), with scope 2 from electricity use. TRACCS provides activity data and emission factors (UK, DE); CE Delft for NL. Passenger cars use external emission factors, average distances, and grid-intensity-based scope 2.
  - Commercial real estate: Scope 1–2 based on energy label and asset type with PCAF emission factors.
  - Residential mortgages: PCAF-aligned method using building type, floor area, and energy label; CBS energy consumption and emission factors; loan-level attribution by gross carrying amount to property value at origination.
- Scope 3 reporting: As of 31 Dec 2023, upstream scope 3 estimated via PCAF EEIO emission factors; lowest data quality score noted.
- Company-specific reporting coverage: Defined as the share of gross carrying amount calculated with PCAF data quality scores 1–3 (company-specific inputs).

nodes.title: ESG2 - Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Loans collateralised by immovable property - Energy efficiency of the collateral
nodes.heading: 7.9 ESG2 - Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Loans collateralised by immovable property - Energy efficiency of the collateral
nodes.start_phrase: Specifically for loans collateralised by residential immovable property, the amounts attributed to EPC labels in this report consist of EPC labels under the old regulation (NEN7120, prior to 1 January 2021) and new regulation (NTA8800) as provided by Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland (RVO).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: ESG2 disclosure on climate change transition risk for ABN AMRO’s banking book, focusing on the energy efficiency of collateral for loans secured by immovable property (residential and commercial) using EP scores (kWh/m²) and EPC labels.
- Methodology and data sources:
  - Residential EPC labels include both old regulation (NEN7120, pre-2021) and new regulation (NTA8800) as provided by RVO.
  - Only the new regulation EP score is “official” in EP score columns; old-regulation EP scores are treated as estimated.
  - EP score columns (B–G) combine official and estimated values; EPC label columns (H–N) include only official labels.
  - Exposures without an official EPC label are reported under “Without EPC label of collateral,” including buildings exempt from labels (e.g., monuments), assets under development/not yet registered, and cases where the label is unknown to the bank.
- Portfolio strategy and progress:
  - ABN AMRO targets lower portfolio emissions by increasing A and higher-than-A labels and reducing exposure to D–G labels.
  - From 30 June 2024 to 31 December 2024, official energy labels increased from 52% to 55%; 76% of the portfolio had a label of C or higher (vs 74% on 30 June 2024).
  - Growth in A and higher-than-A driven by new inflow (labels mandatory at sale/purchase) and migration from lower-than-A; new-build homes under the Building Decree have at least A+++.
- Key figures at 31 December 2024 (EU area):
  - Total gross carrying amount: EUR 185.95bn (Commercial: EUR 26.77bn; Residential: EUR 159.19bn).
  - EP score distribution concentrated in ≤200 kWh/m²: EUR 55.85bn (0–100) and EUR 91.67bn (>100–200).
  - A large share of EP scores are estimated: EUR 130.93bn of the EU-area total is based on estimated EP scores.
  - Official EPC labels (A includes >A): A EUR 44.92bn, B EUR 13.05bn, C EUR 18.87bn, D EUR 9.09bn, E EUR 6.06bn, F EUR 4.85bn, G EUR 4.93bn; “Without EPC label of collateral”: EUR 84.20bn.
- Non-EU exposures are minimal (EUR 0.18bn total at 31 December 2024).
- Repossessed collateral: none at 31 December 2024 (no exposures related to repossessed residential or commercial properties).
- Comparative context (30 June 2024 and 31 December 2023 tables provided): show stable EP score banding, rising share of official labels, and improving distribution toward higher energy efficiency over time.

nodes.title: ESG3 – Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Alignment metrics
nodes.heading: 7.10 ESG3 – Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Alignment metrics
nodes.start_phrase: T h i s t e m p l a t e a i m s t o c a p t u r e t h e b a n k ’ s a l i g n m e n t e f f o r t s w i t h r e s p e c t t o t h e o b j e c t i v e s o f t h e P a r i s A g r e e m e n t f o r a s e l e c t e d n u m b e r o f s e c t o r s .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Template ESG3 reports ABN AMRO’s banking book alignment with Paris Agreement objectives across selected sectors, mirroring the bank’s climate strategy and serving as a Pillar 3 complement to the Integrated Annual Report (IAR), which is the primary disclosure.
- Methodology and coverage:
  - Sector-based target setting prioritising carbon‑intensive sectors in line with NZBA; sectors and NACE codes reflect the most material parts of each value chain.
  - Counterparty scope difference: EBA template focuses on non-financial counterparties, while ABN AMRO’s climate strategy covers all counterparties. This creates discrepancies in gross carrying amounts versus the IAR, most notably in agriculture where much exposure is classified as households (outside this template), leading to lower reported emission intensity in Template 3 and even below the target.
  - Product scope: only products aligned with the climate strategy are included; debt securities and equity instruments are currently excluded but may be added if brought into scope in future.
- Scenario alignment: EBA prescribes IEA NZE2050 sector benchmarks; ABN AMRO applies sector‑specific scenarios for shipping, commercial real estate, and agriculture.
- Data and timing: Emissions intensities often use client‑reported data with a one‑year lag to ensure consistency.
- Sector highlights:
  - Power generation: Q4 2024 emissions intensity of 3.5 kgCO2/MWh, below the 2030 target; distance to IEA NZE2050 scenario is 0%.
  - Fossil fuel combustion – oil and gas upstream: 2024 commitments reduced to EUR 804 million, below the 2030 target; distance to NZE2050 is 0%.
  - Oil and gas upstream and midstream: new target first published in the 2024 IAR; target‑driving processes have begun; operational emissions intensity reported with a one‑year delay; methodology details in the IAR.
- Future updates: Additional sectors will be incorporated into the template as they enter the bank’s climate strategy scope.

nodes.title: Power generation
nodes.heading: 7.10.1 Power generation

nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Presents ESG3 Template 3 alignment metrics for ABN AMRO’s banking book, showing progress toward Paris Agreement objectives across selected, climate‑material sectors aligned with the bank’s climate strategy and primarily disclosed in the Integrated Annual Report (IAR).
- Approach: Sector-based target setting prioritising carbon‑intensive sectors per NZBA; focuses on the most material parts of each value chain. Sectors and NACE codes in Template 3 mirror those in the climate strategy.
- Scope differences: EBA template covers non‑financial counterparties, while ABN AMRO’s strategy covers all counterparties. This creates discrepancies in gross carrying amounts and intensities versus the IAR—most notably in agriculture, where a large household share is out of scope, lowering Template 3 intensities (even below target) relative to strategy targets based on full scope.
- Product coverage: Template 3 includes products aligned with the climate strategy; debt securities and equity instruments are currently excluded but may be added if brought into scope in future.
- Scenarios: Uses IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE2050) pathway as EBA benchmark; ABN AMRO applies sector‑specific scenarios for shipping, commercial real estate, and agriculture.
- Data and timing: Emissions intensities are derived from client‑reported data with a one‑year reporting lag for consistency.
- Sector metrics:
  - Power generation: Q4 2024 portfolio emissions intensity 3.5 kgCO2/MWh; below 2030 target; distance to IEA NZE2050 scenario 0%.
  - Fossil fuel combustion – oil and gas upstream: 2024 commitments EUR 804 million; below 2030 target; distance to NZE2050 0%.
  - Oil and gas upstream and midstream: Target to be first published in the 2024 IAR; target‑driving processes just initiated; operational intensity figures reported with a one‑year lag; methodology detailed in the IAR.

nodes.title: Oil and gas upstream
nodes.heading: 7.10.2 Oil and gas upstream

nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: The ESG3 template captures ABN AMRO’s sector-level alignment with the Paris Agreement for selected sectors, mirroring the bank’s climate strategy and primary disclosures in the Integrated Annual Report (IAR).
- Sector-based approach: Targets are set by sector, prioritizing carbon-intensive areas per NZBA guidance. Only the most material parts of each value chain are included, and sectors/NACE codes match those in the bank’s climate strategy.
- Counterparty scope differences: The EBA template covers non-financial counterparties, while ABN AMRO’s strategy includes all counterparties. This creates discrepancies between IAR and Pillar 3 figures, especially in agriculture where a large portion is classified as households (outside the template), leading to lower emission intensity in Template 3 and even below the target due to differing scopes.
- Product coverage: Only products within the current climate strategy are included; debt securities and equity instruments are excluded for now and will be added if brought into scope in future.
- Scenario alignment: The EBA prescribes the IEA NZE2050 pathway as the benchmark. ABN AMRO applies sector-specific scenarios for shipping, commercial real estate, and agriculture.
- Power generation: Emissions intensity is based on client-reported data with a one-year reporting lag. As of Q4 2024, intensity was 3.5 kgCO2/MWh, below the 2030 target; distance to the IEA NZE2050 scenario is 0%.
- Fossil fuel combustion – oil and gas upstream: 2024 commitments declined to EUR 804 million, below the 2030 target; distance to NZE2050 is 0%.
- Oil and gas upstream and midstream: Targeting begins with publication in the 2024 IAR; operational emission intensity reported with a one-year delay; methodology details are in the IAR.
- Future updates: Additional sectors will be incorporated into the template as they enter the scope of the climate strategy.

nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: ESG3 template reports ABN AMRO’s portfolio alignment with Paris Agreement objectives for selected, climate‑material sectors, aligned with the bank’s climate strategy as primarily disclosed in the Integrated Annual Report (IAR). Targets are set by sector, prioritizing carbon‑intensive activities per NZBA, and focusing on the most material parts of each value chain. Sectors and NACE codes shown mirror those in the bank’s climate strategy.
- Counterparty and product coverage: EBA Template 3 focuses on non‑financial counterparties, while ABN AMRO’s strategy covers all counterparties, creating discrepancies versus the IAR—most notably in agriculture, where a large share classified as households is excluded here, lowering reported emission intensity below the strategy target. Products included match the climate strategy; debt securities and equity instruments are currently out of scope but may be added in future.
- Scenario references: EBA requires IEA NZE2050 sectoral pathways. ABN AMRO uses sector‑specific scenarios for shipping, commercial real estate (CRE), and agriculture.
- Data timing: Several sector intensities are reported with a one‑year lag to ensure consistent client‑reported datasets.
- Power generation: Client‑reported data; Q4 2024 emissions intensity of 3.5 kgCO2/MWh, below the 2030 target; distance to IEA NZE2050 scenario is 0%.
- Fossil fuel combustion – oil and gas upstream: 2024 commitments reduced to EUR 804 million, well below the 2030 target; distance to NZE2050 is 0%. Upstream and midstream targets to be first published in the 2024 IAR; methodologies and operational intensity figures use a one‑year lag.
- Automotive:
  - Trucks and vans (asset‑based financing lease portfolio): Trucks intensity 79.8 gCO2/tkm; 31% distance to NZE2050. Vans intensity 218.6 gCO2/vkm; 55% distance to NZE2050.
  - Passenger cars (direct lease and ALFAM consumer loans): Target first published in 2024 IAR; processes initiated; figures use 31 Dec 2023 as base year; methodology in IAR.
- Maritime transport:
  - Deep sea shipping: Uses verified Poseidon Principles data with a one‑year lag. In 2024 adopted DNV 1.5°C trajectory (Scenario 10); alignment delta −2%; target is full alignment with DNV 1.5°C.
  - Inland freight water: Q4 2024 intensity 25.1 gCO2/tkm (improved from 26.6 in Q2). Metric based on average by ship size. Due to lack of a dedicated benchmark, the IEA freight and shipping benchmark (aggregating maritime and trucking) is applied, implying a low baseline.
- Agriculture: Baseline and 2030 targets use Dutch national averages. Pillar 3 counterparty scope excludes household exposures, reducing financed emissions and showing an alignment metric lower than the bank’s target.
- Commercial real estate (CRE): Q4 2024 intensity 58.2 kgCO2/m2 (down from 61.9 in Q2), driven by a higher share of A‑or‑better energy labels and fewer D–G labels.
- Forward scope changes: Additional sectors/products added to the bank’s climate strategy will be incorporated into Template 3 in future reporting.

- Automotive
  - Trucks and vans: Targets based on the asset-based financing lease portfolio. Reported financed emissions intensity is 79.8 gCO2/tkm for trucks (31% above NZE 2050 trajectory) and 218.6 gCO2/vkm for vans (55% above NZE 2050).
  - Passenger cars: Target covers the asset-based financing direct lease portfolio and the ALFAM consumer loan portfolio. First target publication in the 2024 Integrated Annual Report; base year is 31 December 2023; further methodology provided in the Integrated Annual Report.

- Maritime transport
  - Deep sea shipping: Uses verified data from the Poseidon Principles with a one-year reporting lag. In 2024, adopted the DNV 1.5°C trajectory (Scenario 10) as Poseidon trajectories are not fully 1.5°C-aligned. 2024 alignment delta is -2%; target is full alignment with DNV 1.5°C.
  - Inland freight water (inland shipping): Q4 2024 emissions intensity is 25.1 gCO2/tkm, down from 26.6 in Q2 2024. Metric based on average intensity by ship size. Due to lack of a recognized benchmark, uses the IEA freight and shipping benchmark, which yields a relatively low baseline.

- Agriculture
  - Baseline and 2030 targets derived from Dutch national averages. Pillar 3 counterparty scope excludes household clients, affecting financed emissions calculations and producing an alignment metric below the target.

- Commercial real estate
  - Q4 2024 portfolio emissions intensity is 58.2 kgCO2/m2, a slight decrease from 61.9 kgCO2/m2 in Q2 2024. Improvement driven by a higher share of collateral with energy labels A or better and a lower share with labels D–G.

nodes.title: Agriculture
nodes.heading: 7.10.8 Agriculture
nodes.start_phrase: The agriculture portfolio utilised Dutch national averages to calculate the baseline and anticipated targets for 2030.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Excerpts from ABN AMRO’s Pillar 3 Report 2024 outlining climate targets, methodologies, and current performance for high‑emitting portfolios across transport, agriculture, and commercial real estate.

- Automotive
  - Trucks and vans (asset-based financing lease portfolio): 
    - Trucks financed emissions intensity: 79.8 gCO2/tkm; 31% above NZE 2050 pathway.
    - Vans financed emissions intensity: 218.6 gCO2/vkm; 55% above NZE 2050 pathway.
  - Passenger cars (asset-based direct lease + ALFAM consumer loans):
    - Target first published in the 2024 Integrated Annual Report; active management just starting.
    - Base year: 31 December 2023; methodology details in the Integrated Annual Report.

- Maritime transport
  - Deep sea shipping:
    - Uses Poseidon Principles verified data with a one‑year reporting lag.
    - Adopted DNV 1.5°C trajectory (Scenario 10) in 2024 as PP trajectories aren’t fully 1.5°C‑aligned.
    - 2024 alignment delta: -2%; target is full alignment with DNV 1.5°C trajectory.
  - Inland freight water:
    - Q4 2024 intensity: 25.1 gCO2/tkm (down from 26.6 in Q2).
    - Metric based on average intensity by ship size; benchmarked to IEA freight and shipping (noting a relatively low baseline due to aggregated maritime + trucking data).

- Agriculture
  - Baseline and 2030 targets derived from Dutch national averages.
  - Pillar 3 scope excludes household counterparties, lowering reported financed emissions and driving an alignment metric below the target.

- Commercial real estate
  - Q4 2024 portfolio intensity: 58.2 kgCO2/m2 (improved from 61.9 in Q2).
