nodes.heading: 3.4.2.5.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group, operating in a context of continuous evolution and transformation, continues its initiative to digitalise customer interactions by expanding the range of products, services and access channels offered and improving access to banking services and products for less digitalised stakeholder categories, ensuring a smoother and more satisfying experience for all customers, regardless of their degree of familiarity with digital technologies, with the ultimate aim of optimising the customer experience.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on inclusive, non-discriminatory corporate communication aligned with EU Directive 2006/54/EC and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Guidelines cover inclusive language, diverse and respectful imagery, clear and accessible channels, and event organization with gender balance and accessible venues. Effectiveness is monitored via feedback and consumer involvement; no quantitative targets set under “freedom of expression.”

- Strategy to improve access to products and services through digitalization, ensuring a smooth experience for all customers, including less digitally skilled stakeholders. The Group Directive on ICT Governance and Strategy defines an IT strategy focused on operational excellence, customer reach “anytime, any device,” and protection of information assets, aligned with Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013. Policy applies across the Group and is available on the corporate intranet.

- Actions to enhance alternative distribution channels and inclusion:
  - ATM and e-money: Ongoing ATM migration (completion by 2025) to boost security and compatibility; extended audio guide functionality for visually impaired users across debit/credit cards; expansion of Apple Pay and Google Pay to Parent Company and Widiba customers.
  - Internet banking: Continued optimization of the multi-channel platform, enhanced protection tools, expanded online services, improved branch–online integration, and rollout of paperless processes to save time and reduce paper use. Commitment to accessibility with assistive technologies, periodic usability checks, and support from specialized providers/associations. Open banking enhancements planned (payment cancellation, bulk payments) and efforts to reduce friction in third-party payment authorizations.

- Governance and oversight: While no measurable quantitative targets are set for digital access, effectiveness is monitored by the Body with Strategic Supervision Function (OFSS), which annually assesses the adequacy, functionality, and reliability of the information system and services.

  - Establishing processes and rules to protect customers in line with regulatory requirements.
  - Setting commercial marketing plans (strategy, objectives, pricing, products, promotions, communications).
  - Overseeing customer relationship management.

- Special attention to vulnerable customers: promoting access to banking, informed credit use, and prevention of over-indebtedness.
- Creation of sustainable, inclusive products and services addressing basic financial needs to support social welfare.

  - Prohibition on relationships and transactions involving controversial/banned weapons (nuclear, biological, chemical, cluster bombs, depleted uranium, landmines).

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.6.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: Meeting customer needs is a fundamental condition for the Group in conducting its business activities and an inescapable requirement in maintaining and improving a relationship of trust with customers.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on responsible business practices centered on transparent, continuous, and non-discriminatory customer communications, meeting customer needs, and maintaining trust.
- Strong focus on social inclusion: facilitating access to banking, promoting informed credit use, preventing over-indebtedness, and tailoring sustainable products for vulnerable customers and broader society.
- ESG and human rights commitments embedded in the Sustainability and ESG Guideline, including exclusion and enhanced due diligence for high social impact sectors:
  - Armaments: exclusions aligned with Law 185/90 and bans on controversial weapons; no dealings with sanctioned/embargoed countries or severe human rights violators.
  - Tobacco: due diligence based on corruption/media risk, state ownership, and tobacco-derived revenues (including pharmaceutical tobacco).
  - Gambling: extended due diligence for online platforms, gambling halls, machinery, and marketing.
- Robust policy framework with defined scopes, Board-level approvals, Compliance pre-validation, and alignment with external regulations/standards (e.g., GDPR, MiFID II, EBA Guidelines, IDD, IVASS, EBA/EIOPA rules):
  - Group Policy on Commercial Policies.
  - Group Products Policy (conception, acquisition, control; Board and risk committee involvement).
  - Rules for ESG qualification of investment products to prevent greenwashing (SFDR compliance).
  - Governance and Control of Customer Banking Products (end-to-end product lifecycle, target market, RAF impact, delisting).
  - Governance and Control of Customer Financial Products (MiFID II product governance).
  - Distribution of Protection Insurance Products and Supplementary Pension Schemes (IDD/IVASS-aligned).
  - Sustainability and ESG Policy (community impact: digital inclusion, disaster support, regional and female entrepreneurship, anti-usury).
- Governance, oversight, and review cadence: strategic policies reviewed at least triennially; risk policies annually; involvement of the Board, Risk Management Committee, Risk & Sustainability Committee, and the Investment and Product Steering Committee.
- Product design actions grounded in customer intelligence and regulatory/sustainability compliance: assessing suitability/appropriateness, pricing within usury rules, precise target market definition, and system/process impact analysis.
- Social inclusion products and initiatives:
  - MPS Mio Futuro Account and Free Savings Service for under-18s (financial inclusion and education under parental oversight).
  - First Home Fund–guaranteed mortgages via Consap for primary residences, including young couples, single parents with minors, low-income tenants, and under-35s with non-standard contracts.
  - Participation in SACE Garanzia Futuro to finance company growth, infrastructure, supply chains, communities, and female entrepreneurship.
  - Sustainability Linked Loans with ESG covenants tied to pricing; 27 loans with social covenants totaling EUR 188.5 million in 2024.
  - Anti-usury financing via partnerships (e.g., Fondazione Toscana per la prevenzione dell’usura Onlus, Adiconsum), totaling about EUR 1.7 million in 2024.
- Attention to stakeholder interests through formal engagement processes; policy availability on the corporate intranet and selected overviews on the corporate website.

nodes.start_phrase: As part of the wider process of designing its products and services, the Group ensures that product characteristics are determined taking into account the findings of customer intelligence analyses.
nodes.summary:
- The Group embeds customer intelligence in product and service design, using behavioral segmentation, MiFID profiles, portfolio analyses, demand assessment, and feedback from customer interactions.
- Product governance ensures: assessment of investment product risk for suitability/appropriateness; pricing aligned with regulations (including anti-usury) and internal policies; clear target-customer definitions; adherence to Group directives on product governance and target market; and compliance with sustainability requirements across risk, business effectiveness, tools/processes, IT impacts, and regulations.

nodes.start_phrase: To prevent and combat usury, the Group has established specific financing, particularly in this area, with pilot agreements in place with “Fondazione Toscana per la prevenzione dell’usura Onlus” and Adiconsum.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the Group’s product governance and design process, driven by customer intelligence (behavioural segmentation, MiFID profiles, portfolio analyses, interaction feedback) and ensuring target-market definition, adequacy/appropriateness checks, compliant pricing (incl. usury rules), and alignment with internal product governance and sustainability requirements across risk, operations, IT, and regulation.

  - MPS Mio Futuro Account and Free Savings Service: new bundled current account for under-18s (from 16 Dec 2024) to foster financial inclusion and savings education under parental oversight.
  - First Home Fund–guaranteed mortgages: up to 100% LTV for main-home purchase/renovation, prioritizing eligible groups (young couples with at least one ≤35 years, single parents with minors, social-housing tenants, and under-35s with non-standard contracts).
  - SACE “Garanzia Futuro”: participation to finance company growth, infrastructure, supply chains, local communities, and women’s entrepreneurship.
  - Sustainability-Linked Loans: ESG covenant-based pricing improvements; 27 loans with social covenants disbursed in 2024 totaling EUR 188.5 million.
  - Anti-usury funding: pilot agreements with Fondazione Toscana per la prevenzione dell’usura Onlus and Adiconsum; about EUR 1.7 million disbursed in 2024.
- Supports regional development and entrepreneurship:
  - “Resto al Sud” incentives for new businesses in Southern Italy and selected areas; financing up to 100% of costs, max EUR 50,000 per applicant; EUR 5.8 million disbursed in 2024.
- Provides disaster-relief finance:
  - CDP-funded subsidised loans for those affected by the 2012 Emilia-Romagna and 2016 Central Italy earthquakes; 2024 concessional loans for areas hit by September events (Emilia-Romagna); instalment suspensions in declared emergency zones.
- Adopts protocols and credit programs for SMEs and innovation:
  - Agreement with Sviluppo Campania for the “FONDO ROTATIVO PMI” (FRI Campania) using ERDF funds to ease SME credit access and competitiveness.
  - Support for Tuscan SMEs via interest-rate reductions under an EIB-backed scheme.
  - Adherence to the Sustainable Growth Fund’s “Smart Specialisation” measure for strategic industrial R&D, with focus on less developed regions.
- Mitigates rising interest-rate impacts on households and firms:
  - Renegotiation of floating-rate mortgages (per Law 197/22) for customers with ISEE ≤ EUR 40,000.
  - Mortgage payment suspension under the Gasparrini law for qualifying hardship cases (unemployment, work suspension/reduction, death, or severe disability).
  - Advance payment product for TFS/TFR to support civil servants awaiting INPS settlement.

nodes.title: Resto al Sud
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.6.2.1.6 Resto al Sud
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has released products dedicated to businesses with registered office in the southern regions of Italy.
nodes.summary:
- The bank offers targeted products for southern Italy and other designated areas, notably MPS Resto al Sud, an Invitalia-managed incentive promoted by the Minister for Territorial Cohesion to finance up to 100% of new business costs (max EUR 50,000 per applicant) across Southern regions, central Italy earthquake zones, smaller islands, and marine/lagoon/lake areas of central and northern Italy; EUR 5.8 million was disbursed in 2024.
- Support for natural disaster recovery includes CDP-funded subsidised loans still active for the 2012 Emilia-Romagna and 2016 Central Italy earthquakes; in 2024, additional favourable loans were offered to companies affected by September events in Emilia-Romagna, along with initiatives to suspend loan instalments in emergency areas per regional provisions and bank measures.
- Participation in regional/EU-backed instruments: agreement with Sviluppo Campania for the FRI Campania ERDF-funded revolving fund to provide SMEs with credit on favourable terms for competitiveness, technology adoption, innovation, and restructuring; support for Tuscan SMEs via interest rate reductions on bank loans under an EIB facility.
- Adherence to the national “Smart Specialisation” measure under the Sustainable Growth Fund to finance industrial research and experimental development aligned with Italy’s Smart Specialisation Strategy, with a focus on less developed regions (Basilicata, Calabria, Campania, Molise, Puglia, Sardinia, Sicily).
- Measures to ease rising interest rate impacts in 2024: renegotiation of floating-rate mortgages under Law 197/22 for customers with ISEE up to EUR 40,000; mortgage instalment suspension under the Gasparrini law for defined hardship cases (unemployment, work suspension/reduction, death, severe disability/invalidity ≥80%); activation of a TFS-TFR advance product for civil servants awaiting INPS settlements.

nodes.title: Natural disasters
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.6.2.1.7 Natural disasters
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has established a series of CDP-funded subsidised loans to support those affected by natural disasters.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena initiatives supporting businesses and households, with a focus on Southern Italy, disaster-affected areas, and measures to mitigate rising interest rates.
- MPS Resto al Sud: targeted incentive managed with Invitalia and promoted by the Minister for Territorial Cohesion and the Mezzogiorno, supporting new businesses in Southern regions, central Italy quake areas, smaller islands, and marine/lagoon/lake areas in central and northern Italy; covers up to 100% of costs, max EUR 50,000 per applicant; EUR 5.8 million disbursed in 2024.
- Natural disaster support: CDP-funded subsidised loans still active for those affected by the 2012 Emilia-Romagna and 2016 Central Italy earthquakes; in 2024, additional favourable loans for companies in areas hit by September events in Emilia-Romagna; suspension of loan instalments in emergency areas via regional provisions and Bank initiatives.
- Adoption of protocols and credit instruments:
  - Agreement with Sviluppo Campania for the FRI Campania revolving fund (ERDF) to give Campania SMEs access to credit on favourable terms for competitiveness, technology adoption, innovation, and restructuring.
  - Support for Tuscan SMEs through interest rate reductions on bank loans under an EIB-backed measure.
  - Adherence to the “Smart Specialisation” measure under the Sustainable Growth Fund to back strategic industrial research and experimental development aligned with Italy’s national smart specialisation strategy, prioritising less developed regions (Basilicata, Calabria, Campania, Molise, Puglia, Sardinia, Sicily).
- 2024 measures to help households and businesses manage higher interest rates:
  - Renegotiation of floating-rate mortgages under Law 197/22 for customers with ISEE up to EUR 40,000.
  - Mortgage payment suspension under the Gasparrini law for cases of unemployment, employment termination, work suspension (≥30 consecutive days), hours reduction (≥20% for ≥30 days), death, or severe disability/civil invalidity (≥80%).
  - Product enabling advance payment of TFS-TFR for civil servants awaiting settlement from INPS.
- Clarification of the Smart Specialisation Strategy’s goal to align national and regional priorities, avoid duplication, and build new value chains from R&D to innovative products, key technologies, and sustainable jobs.

nodes.title: Adoption of Protocols, Products and Credit Pools
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.6.2.1.8 Adoption of Protocols, Products and Credit Pools
nodes.start_phrase: The Parent Company is a party to the Agreement governing the relationship between Sviluppo Campania and the Lending Bank for the operation of the financial instrument “FONDO ROTATIVO PMI” (FRI Campania).
nodes.summary:
- Targeted financing for regional development and new enterprises:
  - MPS Resto al Sud incentive for startups and new businesses in Southern Italy, Central Italy earthquake areas, smaller islands, and marine/lagoon/lake areas of Central and Northern Italy; covers up to 100% of costs, max EUR 50,000 per applicant; EUR 5.8 million disbursed in 2024.

- Support for populations and businesses hit by natural disasters:
  - CDP-funded subsidised loans still active for the 2012 Emilia-Romagna and 2016 Central Italy earthquakes, focused on damage to property, production plants, and services.
  - New 2024 loans with favourable conditions for companies in Emilia-Romagna affected by September events.
  - Suspension of loan instalments in areas under a state of emergency, based on regional provisions and Bank initiatives.

- Adoption of regional and national credit programmes:
  - Participation in FRI Campania (ERDF-backed revolving fund) to improve SME access to credit for competitiveness, technology adoption, innovation, and restructuring.
  - Support for Tuscan SMEs through interest rate reductions on bank loans within an EIB framework.
  - Adherence to the Sustainable Growth Fund’s “Smart Specialisation” measure, supporting strategic industrial research and experimental development, with focus on less developed regions (Basilicata, Calabria, Campania, Molise, Puglia, Sardinia, Sicily).

- Measures to mitigate rising interest rates for households and businesses:
  - Renegotiation of floating-rate mortgages under Law 197/22, prioritising customers with ISEE up to EUR 40,000.
  - Mortgage payment suspension via the Gasparrini law for cases of unemployment, work suspension (≥30 consecutive working days), working-hours reduction (≥20% for ≥30 consecutive days), death, or certified severe disability/civil invalidity (≥80%).
  - Advance payment product for TFS-TFR to support civil servants awaiting INPS settlements.

- Financial education initiatives:
  - Weekly “Flash Mercati” webinars for Private and Retail networks (~45 sessions in 2024), plus ad hoc digital/in-person briefings.
  - Monthly 45-minute webinars for the Companies network on markets and specialised services (Liquidity Management and Coverage).
  - “Digital B2B” interactive webinars for Wealth Management specialists and the Private/Family Office networks.
  - Nationwide info-training: three editions of “Le Giornate del Private Banking” (~140 employees each) and 19 one-hour sessions for the Private and Family Office network on key economic-financial topics.

- Strategic objective on financial inclusion (2024–2027):
  - Financial inclusion elevated as a strategic priority, with emphasis on customer relationships, community ties, and education.
  - Focus on retail customers aged 18–35 to enhance financial planning and resilience.
  - Target to raise penetration of savings and pension products in this segment by 1.2 percentage points, from 6.2% to 7.4% by 2027.
  - Levers: targeted commercial outreach, dedicated pricing for facilitated access, and financial education.
  - Ongoing monitoring via internal age-segmented data and annual public reporting, tracking penetration and initiative effectiveness.

- ESG-related investment and issuance targets (2024–2028 Business Plan):
  - Aim for ESG-purpose disbursements to reach 30% of total annual disbursements by 2028.
  - Target at least 25% of annual and period aggregate bond issuance to be green and social bonds.

nodes.heading: 3.4.3 Consumer and end-user involvement processes
nodes.start_phrase: The management of material impacts entails that the Group should have its own employee engagement processes in place to take their views into account.
nodes.summary:
- Customer-centric commitment: The Group’s Code of Ethics prioritizes customer satisfaction through transparency, innovation, and personalization, placing customers at the center of commercial strategies and monitoring satisfaction and loyalty targets.
- Active listening and omnichannel engagement: Continuous collection of feedback and proposals from customers and stakeholders; delivery of a personalized, accessible banking experience via an omnichannel model combining digital tools and qualified assistance.

- Banca Widiba specifics: Continuous customer rating and comment system (1–5 scores with suggestions); 2024 average of ~16,000 comments/month, 97.2% positive; feedback systematically analyzed to enhance offerings and service quality.
- Negative impact remediation and dispute channels: Structured, uniform dispute management across the Group (including Widiba) covering:
  - Complaints to Supervisory Authorities, mediation (Legislative Decree 28/2010), assisted negotiation (Legislative Decree 132/2014).
  - Access to Financial Banking Arbitrator (ABF) and Financial Disputes Arbitrator (ACF) for unresolved or late-handled issues.

  - Applications: Written requests/reports of logistical, relational, or commercial nature from customers or non-customers.
  - Complaints: Verbal objections about services or contractual/pre-contractual matters, relational issues with staff, objections via web/social, and media/journalist inquiries on products/services or inefficiencies.
- Complaints management process:
  - Transparency and accessibility via website, contract documents, branches/specialist centers.
  - Submission methods: In-branch delivery, postal mail, online form, email/certified email to the Complaints Function.
  - Operational oversight by the Complaints and Mediation Department.
  - Procedure steps: Receipt and transmission; registration in the GRB application; investigation with branches or competent functions; independent decision-making; accounting and settlement when customer reimbursement is due.

nodes.title: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise concerns
nodes.heading: 3.4.4 Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise concerns
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the processes to manage material negative impacts on customers and end users, the Group has processes in place to remedy and manage concerns expressed by customers.
nodes.summary:
- Section outlines the Group’s processes for remediating negative customer impacts and the channels available for consumers and end-users to raise concerns, within a structured, uniform dispute management framework tailored to each business (including Banca Widiba).
- Recognized dispute avenues include complaints to Supervisory Authorities, mediation (Legislative Decree 28/2010), assisted negotiation (Legislative Decree 132/2014), and escalation to the Financial Banking Arbitrator (ABF) for banking/financial services and the Financial Disputes Arbitrator (ACF) for investment services and collective asset management when complaints are unresolved or overdue.
- Consumer communication types are distinguished as:
  - Applications: written requests or reports of a logistical, relational, or commercial nature from customers or non-customers.
  - Complaints: verbal objections related to bank services or contractual/pre-contractual relations; verbal issues concerning staff conduct; objections via web/social channels about products/services; and media/journalist requests for clarification or remarks.
- The Group promotes transparent and accessible grievance channels via its website, contractual documentation, and direct communications at branches and specialist centres.
- Submission channels include in-person delivery at branches/specialised centres, postal mail, an online form on the institutional website, standard email, and certified email to the Complaints Function.
- Operational oversight of complaints, ABF/ACF appeals, mediation, and assisted negotiations is centralized in the Complaints and Mediation Department.
- Complaint handling process steps: receipt and forwarding to the department; registration in the Complaints Management application (GRB); investigation with the relevant branch or specialist function; independent decision-making; and accounting/settlement where compensation to the customer is due.

nodes.title: Complaints management
nodes.heading: 3.4.4.1 Complaints management
nodes.start_phrase: The Group seeks maximum transparency and accessibility of grievance channels, actively informing consumers of their existence through its institutional website, contractual documentation and direct communication at branches and specialist centres.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: How the Group manages, remediates, and tracks customer and end‑user concerns and negative impacts, within its sustainability and governance framework.

- Dispute pathways: Internal grievance handling and external resolution routes, including complaints to Supervisory Authorities, mediation (Legislative Decrees 28/2010 and 132/2014), and recourse to the Financial Banking Arbitrator (ABF) and Financial Disputes Arbitrator (ACF).

- Channels and definitions: Formalized processes for:
  - Applications/requests from customers and non‑customers (mainly logistical/relational/commercial).
  - Complaints, including verbal objections about services or pre‑contractual issues, relational issues with staff, web/social media objections, and media/journalist requests.

- Accessibility of grievance channels: Multiple submission methods—branch delivery, mail, online form, and email/PEC—communicated via website, contracts, and in‑branch notices.

- Governance and process ownership: The Complaints and Mediation Department oversees end‑to‑end monitoring, including ABF/ACF appeals, mediation, and assisted negotiation; operates independently from marketing to avoid conflicts of interest.

- Complaint handling workflow: Receipt, registration in dedicated systems (GRB/CRM), investigation with business support, independent decision‑making, and settlement/accounting when due; multi‑level (I/II/III) escalation with standardized ticket taxonomy and defined outcome categories (sustained/partially accepted/not sustained) and customer feedback steps.

- Regulatory response timeframes: Maximum times to reply—60 days (banking/financial/investment services), 45 days (insurance brokerage), 30 days for CIS Code of Conduct matters (with specific GDPR‑based exceptions/possible extensions), and 15 business days (payment services).

- Confidentiality and non‑retaliation: Protection for individuals using complaint mechanisms; commitment to transparency, fairness, and clear guidance so customers can exercise their rights.

- Monitoring and reporting: Quantitative/qualitative tracking of processing times, upheld/partially upheld/rejected rates, and ABF/ACF outcomes; annual public report on complaint handling per Bank of Italy provisions; issues and risks escalated to relevant functions, including Compliance and Risk.

- Stakeholder involvement: No direct customer involvement in procedure design/review; effectiveness gauged via indicators such as repeat complaints and ABF/ACF filings, alongside internal KPIs.

- Banca Widiba specifics: Customer Care via Mediacenter and advisors; formal complaint submission by mail/email/advisor with required identification and case details; a “Complaints Register” aligning with Group standards using ABI classification to census and monitor all complaints, including verbal, web/social, and media‑initiated objections.

- Human rights and customer protection: Commitment to trust, transparency, fairness, integrity, and respect; adherence to internal rules, external codes/agreements, contracts, and applicable laws/regulations across all geographies and activities.

nodes.title: Protecting the human rights of consumers and end users
nodes.heading: 3.4.5 Protecting the human rights of consumers and end users
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the significance identified in the Double Materiality Analysis of issues related to consumers and end users, the Group is committed to developing relationships of trust and mutual and lasting satisfaction with customers, marked by va- lues of transparency and fairness.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Group’s complaints and mediation framework, noting no formal stakeholder involvement in procedure design or review, but systematic tracking of effectiveness via customer complaints, appeals (ABF/ACF), complaint reiterations, and outcomes as proxies for satisfaction.
- Details quantitative and qualitative monitoring of the Complaints and Mediation Department, including adherence to processing times and effectiveness metrics (upheld/partially upheld/rejected complaints, and arbitration decisions by outcome).
- Confirms annual public reporting on complaint handling in line with the Bank of Italy’s Supervisory Provisions on transparency and fairness, and highlights the department’s organizational independence from marketing to avoid conflicts of interest.
- Outlines Banca Widiba’s specific grievance-handling pathway: initial recourse to Customer Care via Mediacenter or the customer’s advisor; if unresolved, formal written complaints via mail, email (reclami@widipec.it), or delivery through the advisor, with required contents (identification, relationship details, contact, issue description, supporting documents).
- Introduces the “Complaints Register” to standardize complaint management with Group procedures, enable early resolution, classify cases per ABI standards, and ensure ongoing monitoring.
- Defines what constitutes a complaint, including verbal objections on services/contractual relations, written objections via web channels (chat, social media), and clarification requests from journalists/newspapers.
- Sets out commitments to protect the human rights of consumers and end users: transparency, fairness, compliance with internal/external rules and laws, counterparty due diligence to avoid links to illegal or harmful activities, and adherence to the UN Global Compact and UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Specifies minimum sustainability criteria and exclusions: no financing where evidence of human rights or labor violations, fraud, money laundering, corruption, terrorism financing, or involvement with controversial/internationally banned weapons; no support for transactions involving sanctioned/embargoed countries, armed conflict contexts, or governments committing serious human rights violations.
- Introduces Governance Information – Business Conduct (ESRS G1): scope includes impacts, risks, opportunities; preventive/mitigative policies and actions; targets and metrics to assess effectiveness.
- Highlights governance mechanisms: a Board-approved Code of Ethics integrated with the 231 Compliance Programme; dissemination to subsidiaries/partners; monitoring via internal controls; and the presence on governing bodies of members with specialized expertise in business conduct and Legislative Decree 231/2001.
- Summarizes impacts, risks, and opportunities: strong safeguards for corporate culture, whistleblower protection, and anti-corruption training; recognition of evolving risks (e.g., IT security breaches); potential opportunities (enhanced stakeholder trust); and material positive impacts from practices that foster culture, protect whistleblowers, and prevent corruption.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity
nodes.heading: 4.1.3.2 Cybersecurity
nodes.start_phrase: IT security is one of the fundamental pillars of the Group’s culture, which is committed to ensuring the resilience, robustness and responsiveness of its digital system.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: Governance policies and actions within the Group’s Sustainability Reporting, centered on the Code of Ethics and Cybersecurity/Logical Security Governance, plus related training and implementation measures.
- Code of Ethics:
  - Objectives: define standards of good conduct; inform employees of required behavior; support implementation of Group sustainability policies; align Group objectives with civil society interests.
  - Scope: addressed to the entire corporate population across all geographies and value chain stages; stated as applicable to all customers.
  - Governance and validation: approved by the Bank’s Board of Directors; implementation ensured via the internal control system.
  - Commitments and references: adherence to internal rules and procedures; external codes and agreements (including international); contractual, legal, and regulatory obligations in each operating context.
  - Availability: published in the Sustainability section of the corporate website.
- Cybersecurity and Logical Security Governance:
  - IT security positioned as a fundamental pillar to ensure resilience, robustness, and responsiveness of digital systems.
  - Group Directive/Policy defines and implements an Information Security Management System (ISMS) to protect data and information across their lifecycle and all company activities.
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance:
    - Defines organizational model, principles, and responsibilities for Logical Security Governance and sets a medium/long-term strategic direction.
    - Scope: applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies.
    - Validation and implementation: adopted by Group companies through top management resolutions, with adaptation to company size/characteristics; governance centralized in the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implementation guided by Information Security and IT functions.
    - Standards: managed in line with internal rules and external standards, notably ISO/IEC 2700x series.
    - Availability: overview available in the Sustainability section of the corporate website.
- Actions and training:
  - Mandatory, structured compliance training for all employees, updated with regulatory/procedural changes; enrollment campaigns, monthly monitoring, reminders; courses require passing a final test.
  - Multidimensional training model to strengthen risk culture, integrated with Model 231/01, assigning relevance levels to material topics.
  - ISMS established with cooperation across all corporate structures and Group companies to protect Group and customer information assets; additional cybersecurity actions referenced under “Privacy” in the Consumers and End Users chapter.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 4.1.3.4 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The internal control system, which is a fundamental element of the overall and ordinary governance system of the Group, ensures compliance with the Code of Ethics.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on 2024 training coverage across the Group on “231-relevant” compliance topics and anti-corruption, showing near-universal participation (generally 99–100%).
- Headline figures: 16,433 Group employees trained on 231-relevant topics (99%); 16,159 trained on anti-corruption (99%).
- Detailed breakdowns by role and geography:
  - Executives, CEOs and direct reports, middle managers, and employees, with regional splits (Northeast, Northwest, South Central, Islands) all at 99–100% coverage.
  - Function-specific participation and coverage for key C-level areas (Audit, Compliance, Finance, HR, Lending, Operations, Risk, Safety & Security, Legal) and Commercial divisions (Enterprises & Private, Retail, Large Corporate & Investment Banking), with most at 99–100% and a noted 97% for HR.
- Governance objectives: the internal control system underpins Code of Ethics compliance; each function manages and monitors risks, including non-compliance risks.
- Control Functions and Internal Audit: verify regular operations, track risk evolution, and assess the adequacy, functionality, and reliability of the organizational and internal control system.
- Information security: defined roles and responsibilities to ensure separation of duties; an ISMS with security frameworks and indicators for guidance, control, and monitoring; active coordination with authorities and industry associations for alignment and information sharing.
- Whistleblower protection: a formal internal reporting system and Group Directive enable employees and qualified external parties to report fraud, business irregularities, and violations of banking rules and EU law; employees are expected to uphold high ethical standards and report concerns.
- Policy specifics:
  - Scope: all personnel of the Parent Company and Group companies (including Banca Widiba and Monte Paschi Fiduciaria).
  - Oversight: Board of Directors approves the internal reporting system; Board of Statutory Auditors supervises it.
  - Compliance references: Directive 2013/36/EU, Italian Legislative Decree 72/2015, Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and Directive 2019/1937/EU.
  - Availability: policy accessible in the Sustainability section of the Group’s corporate website.

nodes.title: Protection of whistleblowers
nodes.heading: 4.1.4 Protection of whistleblowers
nodes.start_phrase: The issue related to the protection of whistleblowers are dealt with in this paragraph.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the Group’s Information Security Management System (ISMS), which defines security frameworks, indicators, and monitoring mechanisms for protection and safeguard measures, and maintains ongoing coordination with authorities and industry associations for alignment and information sharing.
- Presents the Group’s approach to whistleblower protection, including an internal reporting system for employees and qualified external parties to report fraud, business irregularities, and violations of banking rules and EU law, governed by the Group Directive on Internal Violation Reporting Systems.
- Emphasizes employee responsibility to uphold ethical standards and report violations that could negatively impact the Group, customers, employees, or the community, with stakeholder interests considered through the Stakeholder Engagement process.
- Describes the Group Policy on managing whistleblowing systems: addresses actual/potential non-compliance, including breaches of equal opportunity, fairness, and inclusion principles in the Code of Ethics, and violations of EU and internal/external regulations.
- Defines scope across the Parent Company and Group companies (including Banca Widiba and Monte Paschi Fiduciaria), with implementation notifications to designated internal units (Corporate Reporting, Staff CAE and Government Audit Subsidiaries, Organisation Partner, Organisation Function).
- Details governance: the Group’s Board of Directors provides strategic supervision and approves the internal reporting system; the Bank’s Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the entire reporting framework.
- Notes compliance with external standards and regulations: EU Directive 2013/36/EU, its transposition into Italian law (Legislative Decree 72/2015), Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and EU Directive 2019/1937.
- Indicates public availability of the policy in the Sustainability section of the Group’s corporate website.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 4.1.4.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: With regard to reports of violations received through the Whistleblowing channel, the Group has set up an internal system, defi- ning a procedure for the management of reports that employees and qualified external parties may make in relation to events of fraud, as well as irregularities in the conduct of business or violations of the rules governing banking activity and of European Union law.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Group’s Information Security Management System (ISMS), which sets security frameworks and indicators to guide, control and monitor protection measures, and maintains ongoing coordination with authorities and industry associations for alignment and information sharing.
- Details the whistleblower protection framework, governed by the Group Directive on Internal Violation Reporting Systems, emphasizing ethical conduct, stakeholder considerations, and clear procedures for reporting violations of laws, regulations, internal rules, and EU law.
- Outlines the Group Policy on the management of whistleblowing systems: applies to all personnel of the Parent Company and Group companies (including Banca Widiba and Monte Paschi Fiduciaria); implementation notifications to designated corporate functions; strategic oversight by the Board of Directors and system-wide supervision by the Board of Statutory Auditors; compliance with Directive 2013/36/EU, Legislative Decree 72/2015, Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and Directive 2019/1937/EU; policy available on the corporate website.
- Specifies reporting channels and eligibility: a dedicated internet-accessible IT platform and a telephone line; reporters can include employees, suppliers, consultants, former employees, candidates, shareholders, and persons with administrative, management, or control roles.
- Explains case handling: the Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports; acknowledges receipt within 7 days and provides feedback within 3 months; produces Special Investigation Reports and, where responsibilities are found, follows publication requirements.
- Affirms protections: confidentiality of whistleblowers and reported individuals, protection against retaliation or discrimination for good-faith reports, and penalties for breaches of confidentiality, retaliatory acts, or obstruction.
- Clarifies governance and objectives: the Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the entire system; a Head of Internal Reporting Systems (within Internal Audit) ensures process integrity and reports annually to the Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director responsible for internal control and risk management; no quantitative targets set.
- Introduces the anti-corruption framework addressing active and passive corruption and the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing: internal procedures and conduct guidelines for all staff; a rule document providing prevention guidelines that complement the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures for signatory powers, expenditure cycle, and supplier relations.
- Notes the scope of reportable matters includes administrative, accounting, tax, AML/CFT, market abuse, investment services irregularities, and data privacy violations.

nodes.start_phrase: Through the dedicated IT platform, which can also be accessed via the internet by “qualified external persons”, or orally via a dedicated telephone service, staff and qualified external persons can report negligent, unlawful, irregular or improper cir- cumstances and conduct relating to their work - which they suspect or have become aware of in the course of their duties.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines the Group’s whistleblowing framework and anti-corruption governance. It describes a dedicated IT and phone reporting system accessible to employees and qualified external parties (including suppliers, consultants, former and prospective staff, shareholders, and individuals with administrative, management, or control roles) to report suspected negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct. Reportable matters include administrative and accounting/tax irregularities, AML/CTF violations, market abuse, investment service irregularities, and data privacy breaches. The Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports, acknowledges receipt within seven days, provides follow-up within three months, and issues Special Investigation Reports, including publication when required. The Group guarantees confidentiality and protects whistleblowers from retaliation or discrimination, with penalties for breaches or obstruction. Oversight is provided by the Board of Statutory Auditors, while the Head of Internal Reporting Systems ensures process integrity and reports annually to key governance bodies; no quantitative targets are set. The section also covers active and passive corruption, including AML/CTF, and details policies promoting transparency, accountability, and integrity through anti-corruption procedures and a guideline document that complements the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures governing signatory powers, the expenditure cycle, and supplier relationships.

nodes.heading: 4.1.4.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The supervisory role over the entire system is guaranteed by the Board of Statutory Auditors of the Parent Company.
nodes.summary:
- Whistleblowing framework: Accessible IT platform and dedicated phone line for employees and qualified external parties to report negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct related to work.
- Eligible reporters: Employees; suppliers, contractors, consultants; former staff (information gained during employment); job candidates (information from selection process); shareholders; individuals with administrative, management, or control roles.
- Reportable issues include: Administrative, accounting, and tax irregularities; violations related to anti–money laundering and counter–terrorist financing; market abuse (insider trading, manipulation); irregularities in investment services; data privacy violations.
- Investigation process: Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports, confirms receipt within 7 days, and provides follow-up within 3 months; prepares Special Investigation Reports and discloses per applicable standards when responsibilities are found.
- Protections: Strict confidentiality for whistleblowers and reported persons; prohibition of retaliation or discriminatory actions; penalties for breaching confidentiality, retaliation, or obstructing reports.
- Governance and oversight: Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the system; Head of Internal Reporting Systems (within Internal Audit) ensures proper operation and reports annually to key governance bodies (Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director overseeing internal control and risk management); no quantitative targets set.
- Anti-corruption and financial crime: Coverage of active and passive corruption, money laundering, and terrorist financing.
- Policies and controls: Group promotes transparency, accountability, and integrity; has issued a rule document with guidelines for preventing corruption, complementing the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures governing signatory powers, the expenditure cycle, and supplier relationships, alongside staff procedures and training.

nodes.title: Active and passive corruption
nodes.heading: 4.1.5 Active and passive corruption
nodes.start_phrase: This paragraph covers active and passive corruption issues, including the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing, are covered in this paragraph.
nodes.summary:
- Whistleblowing system and channels: dedicated IT platform (also for qualified external persons) and a telephone line for reporting negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct encountered in work contexts.
- Eligible reporters: internal personnel and qualified external parties, including suppliers, self-employed workers, freelancers/consultants, former employees (for information acquired during employment), job candidates (for information acquired during selection), shareholders, and individuals with administrative, management, or control roles.
- Scope of reports: includes administrative, accounting and tax irregularities, AML/CFT violations, market abuse (insider trading, manipulation), irregularities in investment services, and data privacy breaches.
- Handling of reports: the Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives reports, conducts preliminary checks and investigations, acknowledges receipt within 7 days, and provides follow-up feedback within 3 months.
- Outcomes and documentation: Special Investigation Reports summarize findings; if employee responsibilities are identified, reports are prepared and published per applicable standards.
- Whistleblower protections: safeguards against retaliation, discrimination, or unfair treatment; confidentiality of the report and personal data is ensured; penalties apply for breaching confidentiality, retaliating, or obstructing reports.
- Governance and oversight: Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the system; a Head of Internal Reporting Systems (in Internal Audit) ensures proper operation and annually reports to the Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director responsible for internal control and risk management. No quantitative targets are set for whistleblower protection.
- Anti-corruption framework: addresses active and passive corruption, including AML and counter-terrorist financing; promotes transparency, accountability, and integrity in dealings with public administrations and external staff.
- Policies and controls: a rule document provides guidelines for preventing corruptive events, complementing the Group’s anti-corruption policy through the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures governing signatory powers, the expenditure cycle, and supplier relations; staff receive internal anti-corruption procedures and training.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group promotes the principles of transparency, accountability and integrity in its relations with public administrations and external staff by adopting internal anti-corruption procedures and courses of action for all personnel.
nodes.summary:
- Whistleblowing system: Accessible via a dedicated IT platform (including for qualified external persons) and a telephone line to report negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct related to work. Eligible reporters include employees, suppliers, self-employed workers, consultants, former employees (for information acquired during employment), job candidates (for information acquired during selection), shareholders, and those with administrative, management, or control roles. Covered issues include administrative/accounting/tax irregularities, AML/CFT violations, market abuse, investment services irregularities, and data privacy breaches.
- Reporting process and protections: The Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports, acknowledges receipt within 7 days, and provides follow-up within 3 months. Findings are documented in Special Investigation Reports. The Group guarantees confidentiality, protects whistleblowers from retaliation or discrimination, and imposes penalties for breaching confidentiality, retaliatory acts, or obstructing reports.
- Governance and objectives: The Board of Statutory Auditors supervises the system. A Head of Internal Reporting Systems within Internal Audit oversees process execution and submits an annual report to the Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director responsible for internal control and risk management. No quantitative targets are set for whistleblowing.
- Anti-corruption and AML/CFT policies: The Group adopts a zero-tolerance approach to active and passive corruption, including AML/CFT. Key documents include the Group Anti-Corruption Policy and the Group Policy on Combating Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, both approved by the Board of Directors and available on the corporate website. Policies apply to all Group personnel and entities acting on the Group’s behalf, with control activities assigned to Corporate Control Functions. Policies align with national and EU laws and international standards and commitments (Italian Civil and Criminal Codes, OECD, UN, G20, Transparency International, Wolfsberg Group, UN Global Compact, UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking) and consider stakeholder interests via the stakeholder engagement process.
- Actions and risk management: The Group conducts periodic self-assessments of corruption risk, at least biennially identifies high-risk areas, and strengthens processes with preventive controls. Violations may trigger disciplinary measures up to termination. Sensitive areas include supplier appointments, joint ventures/M&A, gifts and entertainment, events and sponsorships, hiring, credit disbursement, expenditure cycle, consultancy, subsidised finance/public service transactions, political contributions, donations, membership fees, non-profit activities, and management of public services.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The Group operates in line with its values and with a sense of responsibility towards society by applying “zero tolerance” towards any corrupt practice (direct or indirect, public or private, external or within the organisation, instigated, attemp- ted, committed), to ensure that its staff and all persons working for it comply with anti-corruption regulations, adopting all measures necessary to prevent and effectively counter the risk.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Governance, policies, actions, controls, training, and oversight related to anti-corruption and the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing (AML/CTF) within Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena Group, as part of its Sustainability Reporting.
- Policy framework:
  - Group Anti-Corruption Policy: Sets principles and conduct rules for all employees and third parties acting for the Group; approved by the Board; control activities assigned to Corporate Control Functions; aligned with UN Global Compact, UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking, and guidance from OECD, UN, G20, Transparency International, and the Wolfsberg Group; available on the corporate website.
  - Group AML/CTF Policy: Defines the Group’s global AML/CTF approach for the Parent Company and all subsidiaries; Board approves the policy and annual AML report (including ML/TF risk self-assessment and activity plan); aligned with national, EU, and international standards; available on the corporate website.
- Stakeholders: Policy design considers interests identified through the Group’s Stakeholder Engagement process.
- Zero tolerance and disciplinary regime: The Group applies zero tolerance to all forms of corruption (public/private, internal/external, direct/indirect) and foresees disciplinary actions up to termination for violations.
- Risk assessment and scope:
  - Periodic self-assessments of corruption risks across all business processes; biennial identification of high-risk areas (e.g., suppliers, JVs/M&A, gifts/entertainment, events/sponsorships, hiring, credit disbursement, procurement, consultancy, subsidised finance, political contributions/donations/memberships/non-profit, management of public services).
  - Latest 2024 assessment found potential risks across structures but no need for additional measures beyond existing safeguards.
  - Explicit prohibition of political contributions and heightened controls in dealings with Public Administration.
- Anti-corruption program and training:
  - Ongoing risk self-assessments by functions and employee awareness/training.
  - Training content updated by the Training function with Compliance validation upon regulatory/procedural changes or audit findings.
  - Specialized training for Internal Audit’s Fraud Audit staff (including international certification paths such as CFE).
  - Board induction for subsidiaries on administrative liability and Group 231 Models.
- AML/CTF controls:
  - Identification of applicable regulations, impact assessment, and updates to internal rules.
  - IT systems for risk management, due diligence, data retention, continuous customer/transaction monitoring, detection of potentially suspicious activity, and reporting to the Financial Information unit.
  - Ongoing assessment of risk management processes and internal control adequacy.
  - Mandatory AML/CTF training for all employees.
- Roles and responsibilities:
  - Compliance Function: Identifies corruption-risk processes and evaluates safeguards; coordinates rule application and training; provides advisory support; partners with HR on info-training programs.
  - 2024 Compliance Plan: Approved 6 Feb 2024; 797 audits executed vs 692 planned; 758 conformity opinions and 649 validation opinions issued.
  - Internal Audit: Performs third-level controls within the Internal Control System.
  - AML Function (Parent Company) and Chief Risk Officer’s department (Group level): Monitor AML/CTF risks; CRO reports directly to the Board and centralizes duties for Italian subsidiaries.
- Targets: The Group ensures prevention of active and passive corruption (including AML/CTF) but has not set quantitative targets.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: On 6 February 2024, the Bank’s Board of Directors resolved on the programme of activities and controls (2024 Compliance Plan), which the Compliance function undertook to complete during the 2024 financial year.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Anti-corruption, anti–money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CTF) governance, controls, training, and metrics within the Group’s 2024 Sustainability Reporting.
- Risk assessment and policy: Corruption risks are assessed across all business processes; 2024 results found potential risks everywhere but deemed current safeguards adequate. Strict prohibition on political contributions or any support to political causes, with heightened focus on interactions with Public Administration.
- Anti-corruption program: Periodic risk self-assessments by functions; employee training and awareness plans. Training content is updated by the Training function under Compliance validation when regulations/procedures change or audits reveal gaps.
- Specialized training: Internal Audit’s Fraud Audit team receives targeted training (including “training pills” and structured courses) and may pursue international certifications (e.g., CFE). Subsidiary Boards receive induction on entities’ administrative liability and the Group’s Model 231 framework.
- AML/CTF controls: Ongoing regulatory scanning and internal framework updates; IT procedures for risk management, due diligence, recordkeeping, continuous monitoring, suspicious activity detection, and FIU reporting; periodic assessments of risk management and internal controls; AML/CTF training for all employees.
- Governance and responsibilities: Compliance Function identifies corruption-risk processes, assesses safeguards, coordinates rule application and training, advises on anti-corruption, and supports HR with info-training. Internal Audit performs third-level controls. The Parent Company’s AML function monitors AML/CTF risks; at Group level, the Chief Risk Officer (reporting to the Board) centrally oversees these duties for Italian subsidiaries. Corporate bodies are involved with defined roles per the Internal Control System. No quantitative prevention targets are set.
- 2024 Compliance Plan execution: Approved on 6 Feb 2024. Of 692 planned audits, 797 were performed; 758 conformity opinions and 649 validation opinions on internal regulations were issued.
- Training metrics (2024): 100% of Parent Company staff are enrolled due to universal exposure to corruption risk. Training recipients included 16,321 workers in functions at risk (out of 16,439 total), 155 executive managers, and 7 members of administrative/management/supervisory bodies. Delivery included classroom (e.g., 19.0 hours for functions at risk; 5.0 for administrative bodies) and computer-based training (e.g., 12,227.0 hours for functions at risk; 116.3 for executives; 2.0 for administrative bodies). Topics covered definitions, policies, and suspicion/detection procedures. Training frequency generally once per year where required.
- Outcomes: No confirmed incidents of corruption involving the workforce in 2024, and no legal/regulatory non-compliance cases resulting in penalties (monetary or non-monetary).

  - Administrative, management and supervisory bodies: 155 recipients.

  - Training frequency: annual where required.
- Training content: definition of corruption, relevant policies, and suspicion/detection procedures.
- Outcomes: In 2024 there were no legal or regulatory non-compliance cases, no penalties, and no confirmed instances of corruption involving the workforce.

nodes.title: Training on the fight against corruption and bribery
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.1 Training on the fight against corruption and bribery
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the periodic activities carried out by the Group in order to identify the main areas considered to be “at risk of corruption”, within which the mapping of functions at risk carried out by the Compliance function takes place, potentially all corporate structures are exposed to “corruption risk”.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and controls: The Group’s Internal Control System and Corporate Bodies have clearly defined roles to mitigate business-conduct risks, including corruption and bribery, with effectiveness monitored through specific metrics.
- Anti-corruption training: All Parent Company staff are considered potentially exposed to corruption risk and are enrolled 100% in the anti-corruption training campaign. Training covers definitions of corruption, internal policies, and suspicion/detection procedures, is required annually, and is delivered via classroom and computer-based modules.
  - Participation and hours (2024): Functions at risk trained total about 16,3k people; executives 155; administrative/management/supervisory bodies 7. Training hours: functions at risk 12,246; executives 116.3; administrative/management/supervisory bodies 7. Delivery included approximately 19 classroom hours for functions at risk and 5 for administrative/management/supervisory bodies, with the remainder via e-learning.
- Incidents and compliance (2024): No cases of legal/regulatory non-compliance (monetary or non-monetary) and no confirmed instances of corruption involving the workforce.
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures (KPIs for credit institutions):
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) at 31 Dec 2024: turnover-based 1.06% (vs 0.50% in 2023), capex-based 1.15% (vs 0.53% in 2023). Total GAR assets: EUR 94,586 million (vs EUR 94,254 million in 2023).
  - Data limitations: GAR depends on counterparties’ published non-financial data; exposures to entities outside NFRD scope are excluded, reducing the numerator.
- Methodology:
  - KPIs aligned with Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178. GAR = taxonomy-aligned exposures over total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers).
  - Counterparties under NFRD: For exposures where use of proceeds is not known, taxonomy eligibility/alignment is weighted by counterparties’ reported turnover and capex KPIs across the six environmental objectives, using an external data provider. Following EC FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024), entities whose parent companies are subject to NFRD are included. Where use of proceeds is known, no eligible/aligned exposures were identified under the screening criteria.
  - Guaranteed household loans: Only loans secured by residential real estate considered eligible. Loans for building renovations and motor vehicles excluded due to insufficient data to identify “green loans.” Alignment applies technical criteria differentiating buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. For pre-2020 buildings not holding EPC class A, alignment may be met if in the top 15% of national/regional building stock for primary energy demand, using studies by private entities.

nodes.start_phrase: The tables below show the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852)57.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Annex of the 2024 Sustainability Report outlining credit institutions’ KPIs required under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation and its Disclosures Delegated Act.
- Purpose: Enhance transparency on sustainability and support the low‑carbon transition by reporting eligibility and alignment of activities with the EU Taxonomy, focused on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- Scope and data dependency: GAR relies on counterparties’ non-financial disclosures; entities outside the NFRD scope are excluded, which constrains the ratio.
- Reported results (31 Dec 2024): turnover-based GAR 1.06% (vs 0.50% in 2023); capex-based GAR 1.15% (vs 0.53% in 2023); total GAR assets EUR 94,586 million (vs EUR 94,254 million in 2023).
- Methodological framework: Based on Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; GAR defined as exposures to taxonomy-aligned assets over total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals).
- Key methodological choices:
  - Counterparties under NFRD and those not obliged to publish NFI: where use of proceeds is unknown, exposures are weighted by counterparties’ published turnover and CapEx KPIs across the six environmental objectives; where use of proceeds is known, no eligible/aligned exposures per Delegated Regulation 2021/2139. Following EC FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024), counterparties whose parent companies are subject to NFRD are included (change vs 2023).
  - Guaranteed household loans: only residential real estate–secured loans considered eligible; renovation and motor vehicle loans excluded due to lack of “green loan” identification. Alignment applies technical screening criteria distinguishing buildings pre/post 31 Dec 2020; for pre‑2020 buildings lacking class‑A EPC, 2024 assessment uses the top 15% primary energy performance criterion based on private studies (not used in prior year).
- Cross-reference: Full regulatory framework discussed in the report’s Environmental Information section.

nodes.title: Key performance indicators (kpi) of credit institutions
nodes.heading: 5.1 Key performance indicators (kpi) of credit institutions
nodes.start_phrase: The tables below show the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852)57.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Annex of the 2024 Sustainability Report detailing Article 8 EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2020/852 and Delegated Reg. 2021/2178) disclosure requirements for credit institutions, focused on reporting eligibility and alignment KPIs to enhance transparency and support the low‑carbon transition.
- Core KPI reported: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) defined as exposures to taxonomy‑aligned assets divided by total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals).
- 2024 results and comparatives: Turnover‑based GAR 1.06% (0.50% in 2023); CapEx‑based GAR 1.15% (0.53% in 2023); total GAR assets EUR 94,586 million (EUR 94,254 million in 2023). GAR is constrained by counterparty disclosures; entities outside NFRD are excluded, reflecting data gaps.
- Methodological framework: Based on Annex V of Delegated Reg. 2021/2178 and technical screening criteria in Delegated Reg. 2021/2139; uses counterparties’ published Taxonomy KPIs for the six environmental objectives.
- Key methodological choices:
  - Financial undertakings and entities not obliged to publish NFI: For exposures with unknown use of proceeds (as per external data provider), weighting is based on counterparties’ turnover and CapEx Taxonomy KPIs from their non‑financial statements. No eligible/aligned exposures are recognized where the use of proceeds is known, per 2021/2139. Scope of NFRD counterparties expanded in 2024 to include entities whose parent companies are subject to NFRD, per European Commission FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024).
  - Guaranteed household loans: Only loans secured by residential real estate are considered eligible; building renovation and motor vehicle loans are excluded due to lack of “green loan” identification. Alignment assessment distinguishes buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. For pre‑2020 buildings not meeting EPC class A, alignment can be met via the “top 15%” primary energy performance criterion, now supported by private studies (not available in the prior year).
- Cross‑reference: Points to the Environmental Information section for a fuller regulatory discussion of Article 8 Taxonomy disclosures.

nodes.start_phrase: The tables below show the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852)57.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Annex section of a 2024 Sustainability Report outlining credit institutions’ KPIs under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation and its Disclosures Delegated Act.
- Purpose: Explain disclosure obligations starting in 2023 for Taxonomy eligibility and alignment, enhancing transparency and supporting the low‑carbon transition.
- Key metric: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) defined as exposures to taxonomy‑aligned assets divided by total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals).
- 2024 results: Turnover‑based GAR 1.06% (vs 0.50% in 2023); CapEx‑based GAR 1.15% (vs 0.53% in 2023); total GAR assets EUR 94,586 million (vs EUR 94,254 million in 2023).
- Data dependency: GAR calculation relies on counterparties’ reported Taxonomy KPIs; entities outside NFRD scope are excluded, affecting the ratio.
- Methodology basis: Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 and technical screening criteria in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139; application reflects European Commission FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024).
- Methodological choices:
  - For financial undertakings and entities not obliged to publish non‑financial information: when use of proceeds is unknown, exposures are weighted by counterparties’ turnover and CapEx KPIs across the six environmental objectives; no eligible/aligned exposures recognized where use of proceeds is known per screening criteria. NFRD perimeter broadened to include entities whose parents are subject to NFRD.
  - Guaranteed household loans: only loans secured by residential real estate considered eligible; building renovation loans and motor vehicle loans excluded due to insufficient green‑loan identification. Alignment applies screening criteria distinguishing buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020; for pre‑2020 assets not EPC class A, alignment may be met if in the top 15% of national/regional building stock for primary energy needs, supported by private studies (newly available in 2024).
- Cross‑reference: Points to a broader discussion of Article 8 disclosures in the Environmental Information section.

nodes.title: Methodology
nodes.heading: 5.1.2 Methodology
nodes.start_phrase: The main methodological choices adopted by the Group on the basis of current regulations are outlined below.
nodes.summary:
- Context and purpose: Part of the Sustainability Reporting section detailing Article 8 EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2020/852) disclosures for credit institutions. From 2023, financial firms must report eligibility and alignment KPIs to enhance transparency and support the low‑carbon transition. Scope follows the NFRD (2014/95/EU).

- Key metrics reported (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Turnover-based Green Asset Ratio (GAR): 1.06% (0.50% at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Capex-based GAR: 1.15% (0.53% at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Total GAR assets (denominator): EUR 94,586 million (EUR 94,254 million at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Note: GAR depends on counterparties’ disclosed data; exposures to entities outside NFRD scope are excluded, which impacts the ratio.

- Methodological framework:
  - KPIs per Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178.
  - GAR defined as exposures to taxonomy‑aligned assets divided by total covered assets (gross carrying amount of total assets excluding trading book exposures and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers).

- Key methodological decisions:
  - Financial undertakings and entities not obliged to publish non-financial information:
    - Where use of proceeds is unknown (assessed with an external provider), exposures are weighted by counterparties’ reported Taxonomy turnover and CapEx KPIs across the six environmental objectives.
    - Where use of proceeds is known, no taxonomy-eligible and aligned exposures were identified under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139.
    - Following European Commission FAQs (21 Dec 2023 and Nov 2024), NFRD counterparties now also include entities whose parent companies are subject to NFRD, expanding scope versus 2023.
  - Guaranteed household loans:
    - Eligibility limited to loans secured by residential real estate.
    - Building renovations and motor vehicle purchases excluded due to insufficient data to tag “green loans.”
    - Alignment screening applies criteria for buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. For pre‑2020 buildings lacking EPC class A, the Group used the “top 15%” primary energy performance criterion based on private studies (new in 2024).
  - Flows: Defined as gross new exposures; only positive flows are counted (no netting of repayments or sales).
  - Assets under management (AuM): KPI calculated as the share of equity and debt issued by NFRD‑subject companies within total AuM equity and debt.

- Comparability note: Templates as of 31 Dec 2023 are disclosed, but year‑on‑year comparisons are not fully homogeneous due to 2024 scope changes (notably inclusion of entities with NFRD‑subject parent companies).

- Gas and Nuclear templates: In line with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 (amending 2021/2139), the Group reports eligibility, alignment, and non‑eligibility for gas and nuclear activities. These templates cover only non‑financial companies that disclosed the relevant KPIs in their 2023 reporting.

nodes.title: Gas & Nuclear templates
nodes.heading: 5.1.3 Gas & Nuclear templates
nodes.start_phrase: In line with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 of 9 March 2022 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, the Group publishes templates for the alignment, eligibility and non-eligibility of gas and nuclear activities.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory basis and methodology: Disclosures prepared under EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, with “flows” defined as new exposures at gross book value (only positive flows), and an Assets Under Management ratio limited to securities issued by companies subject to mandatory NFRD. Templates are referenced to 31 Dec 2023; 2024 scope changes make year-on-year comparisons non-homogeneous.
- Gas & Nuclear disclosures: In line with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214, publication of templates on eligibility, alignment, and non-eligibility of gas and nuclear activities, limited to non-financial companies that reported the relevant KPIs in 2023.
- Key KPIs for credit institutions (Annex VI):
  - Main KPI Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – stock:
    - 2024: Environmentally sustainable assets €997m (Turnover) and €1,089m (Capex); % KPI 1.05% (Turnover) and 1.15% (Capex); coverage over total assets 75.77%; assets excluded from numerator 44.96% and from denominator 24.23%.
    - 2023: €467m (Turnover) and €496m (Capex); % KPI 0.50% and 0.53%; coverage 75.52%; excluded from numerator 49.52% and from denominator 24.48%.
  - Additional KPI GAR – flows:
    - 2024: €587m (Turnover) and €1,055m (Capex); % KPI 0.62% and 1.12%; coverage over total assets 6.54%.
    - 2023: €141m (Turnover) and €151m (Capex); % KPI 0.15% and 0.16%.
  - Trading book and fee/commission income: not applicable/blank. Financial guarantees and AUM show small aligned portions (e.g., 2024 FG 1.06% Turnover, 2.75% Capex; AUM 3.45% Turnover, 7.24% Capex).
- Detailed GAR stock breakdowns (2024 and 2023) by:
  - Counterparty type (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households), product (loans and advances, debt securities, equity), and environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO).
  - Classification of aligned activities into use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling.
  - Households, especially residential mortgage loans, represent the bulk of taxonomy-eligible exposure (2024: €30.354bn eligible; €867m aligned).
  - Non-financial undertakings contribute to aligned amounts; financial undertakings show limited alignment; insurance negligible.
- Scope of assets in GAR:
  - Numerator exclusions captured (but included in denominator): SMEs/NFCs not subject to NFRD, non-EU counterparties not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank, cash and cash-like, and other assets.
  - Total GAR assets and assets not covered for GAR provided; the latter include central governments, central banks, and trading book exposures.
- Off-balance sheet exposures (to undertakings subject to NFRD): Reported aligned amounts for financial guarantees and AUM, with debt/equity splits.

- Includes off‑balance sheet exposures for undertakings subject to NFRD (financial guarantees and assets under management), with “of which” breakdowns for debt and equity and their taxonomy eligibility/alignment.

nodes.summary:
- Extract from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Annual Report – Sustainability Reporting, focused on Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosure.
- Presents GAR sector information for the stock of taxonomy‑aligned exposures using two KPIs:
  - Turnover-based alignment.
  - Capex-based alignment (partial table shown).
- Granular breakdown by sector at NACE Rev. 2, 4‑digit code level, with line‑by‑line figures across numerous industries (manufacturing, energy and utilities, waste and remediation, construction and civil engineering, transport and logistics, telecoms and data services, real estate, business services, and other services).
- Discloses, in EUR million, for each sector and counterparty category:
  - Gross carrying amount.
  - “Of which environmentally sustainable” amounts under EU Taxonomy objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), plus a total across all objectives.
- Counterparty segmentation distinguishes:

- Methodological notes specify:

  - Joint exposures are classified by the borrower most relevant/decisive for granting the exposure.
