nodes.title: Measuring the impacts and dependencies of the financed activities on biodiversity (La Banque Postale)
nodes.heading: Measuring the impacts and dependencies of the financed activities on biodiversity (La Banque Postale)
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale measures the impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities of its activity in relation to nature throughout its value chain to understand its relationship with living things.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s biodiversity and ecosystems action plans within its Sustainable Performance/Environmental Information, acknowledging it currently has no dedicated sustainable land or agriculture policy but plans to develop one.
- Frameworks and approach: Early adopter of TNFD (Sept 2023); applies the TNFD LEAP process (Locate, Evaluate, Assess, Prepare) and the Global Biodiversity Score (GBS) from CDC Biodiversité to measure impacts, dependencies, risks, and opportunities across the value chain as a basis for a science-based roadmap to protect and restore biodiversity.
- Portfolio coverage and methods: Conducted an in-depth nature-related analysis on 39% of its financing portfolio (residential and commercial real estate, commercial, corporates, public sector and social economy). Combined “Locate” and “Evaluate” phases with sector-specific qualitative grids for priority sectors: real estate; food and beverage manufacturing; transport and warehousing; energy production and distribution; health and pharmaceuticals.
- Key findings on impacts and risks:
  - Corporate and public/social portfolios’ impacts mainly occur upstream in financed companies’ supply chains.
  - Terrestrial impacts largely from land use and climate change; freshwater impacts from pollution and wetland conversion.
  - High-impact activities in sensitive areas face elevated transition risk; nature-based activities in degraded areas face significant physical risk.
  - Identified top contributing companies to inform potential engagement policies.
- Dependencies on ecosystem services:
  - 62% of the Corporate portfolio technical reserves finance activities critically dependent on at least one ecosystem service; most exposed sectors: real estate, telecommunications, construction.
  - Most common dependencies: water-related services (surface and groundwater); highest dependency: soil stabilisation and erosion control.
- Measurement limitations and next steps:
  - Current exclusions: retail banking direct reserves (ex-real estate), equity securities, sovereign exposures (sovereign bonds, Banque de France technical reserves, centralized passbook savings) due to limited methodologies/data.
  - Measurements rely mainly on financial data; plans to enhance accuracy with physical, pressure-specific indicators (including climate change) for better management.
- Policies and governance landscape:
  - Group references include CDC Biodiversity and Water policies, Group Deforestation & Ecosystem Conversion policy, La Banque Postale’s Financing & Investment Charter, LBP AM Biodiversity policy, and CNP Assurances due diligence on principal adverse impacts.
  - Targeted material negative impacts and biodiversity erosion vectors include: land-use change, overexploitation, climate change, pollution, invasive species, species status, ecosystem condition (e.g., land degradation, desertification, soil sealing), and ecosystem services (e.g., pesticides).
- Financing biodiversity outcomes (Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund):
  - Supports biodiversity credits measurement and generation with CDC Biodiversité at the Cros du Mouton site (Var); funded two voluntary restoration/rewilding units in 2024 (€99,600 excl. tax).
  - Backs WWF France Nature Impact (payments for ecosystem services) to preserve, restore, and sustainably manage high-biodiversity forests in mainland France.
  - Ensures decarbonisation projects deliver biodiversity co-benefits (species diversity in reforestation, protection of water points, agroforestry and reforestation practices).
- Subsidiary actions (CNP Assurances):
  - Integrates biodiversity into ESG filters for listed equities and bonds, assessing disruption of fragile areas, biodiversity programs, land use, resource controversies, water dependency and discharge treatment.
  - “Green Works” charter for real estate mandates biodiversity protection in construction and operations: ecosystem respect, low-impact materials, waste and water reduction, plant- and biodiversity-promoting technical solutions, circular economy (reuse), and ecosystem services in buildings/green spaces.
  - Applies sustainable management principles to 54,986 hectares of owned forests via Société Forestière de la Caisse des Dépôts.

nodes.title: Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund (La Banque Postale)
nodes.heading: Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund (La Banque Postale)
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale relies on the “Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund” (see Section 2.2.1.9 “Internal carbon price”) to finance beneficial national and international projects to protect and restore biodiversity.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on La Banque Postale’s environmental strategy and biodiversity management within its 2024 Universal Registration Document.
- Implementation of a TNFD LEAP-based analysis on 39% of the financing portfolio (real estate, commercial, corporates, public sector and social economy), using the Global Biodiversity Score to quantify impacts and dependencies.
- Combined “Locate” and “Evaluate” phases plus sector-specific qualitative grids for five priority sectors: real estate; food and beverage manufacturing; transport and warehousing; energy production and distribution; health and pharmaceuticals.
- Key findings:
  - Most portfolio impacts arise upstream in financed companies’ value chains (linked to purchases).
  - Terrestrial impacts are primarily driven by land use and climate change; freshwater impacts by pollution and wetland conversion.
  - Identification of major contributing companies to inform potential engagement policies.
- Nature-related risk assessment:
  - High-impact activities in sensitive areas face elevated transition risks.
  - Nature-based activities in degraded areas face significant physical risks.
- Dependency analysis:
  - 62% of Corporate portfolio technical reserves fund activities critically dependent on at least one ecosystem service (notably real estate, telecoms, construction).
  - Most widespread dependencies are water-related services; strongest dependency is on soil stabilisation and erosion control.
- Measurement limitations and improvements:
  - Exclusions: retail banking direct reserves (excluding real estate), equity securities, sovereign exposures due to methodological/data gaps.
  - Current reliance on financial data; plan to collect physical indicators for each biodiversity pressure, including climate change.
- Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund:
  - Finances biodiversity protection/restoration projects, including CDC Biodiversité’s biodiversity credits pilot at Cros du Mouton (two restoration units purchased for €99,600).
  - Supports WWF France’s PES-based Nature Impact initiative for high-biodiversity forests in mainland France.
  - Ensures decarbonisation projects deliver biodiversity co-benefits (species diversity, water protection, agroforestry/reforestation).
- Subsidiary actions (CNP Assurances):
  - Integrates biodiversity into ESG filters for listed equities and bonds (considering land use, fragile areas, resource controversies, water dependency/discharges).
  - “Green Works” charter for real estate to protect ecosystems, use low-impact materials, reduce waste/water, promote biodiversity, circular economy, and ecosystem services.
  - Sustainable management of 54,986 hectares of owned forests via Société Forestière de la Caisse des Dépôts.

nodes.title: Actions of La Banque Postale Group subsidiaries
nodes.heading: Actions of La Banque Postale Group subsidiaries
nodes.start_phrase: CNP Assurances includes biodiversity in the ESG filters of listed equities and bonds.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: La Banque Postale analyzed nature-related impacts, dependencies, risks, and opportunities on 39% of its financing portfolio using the TNFD LEAP framework and the Global Biodiversity Score (GBS). Sector-specific qualitative grids complemented quantitative footprints for five priority sectors: real estate; food and beverage manufacturing; transport and warehousing; energy production and distribution; health and pharmaceuticals.

- Key findings and risk assessment:
  - Impacts in corporate and public/social economy portfolios are mainly in upstream value chains (supplier purchases).
  - Terrestrial impacts are driven by land use and climate change; freshwater impacts by pollution and wetland conversion.
  - High-impact activities in sensitive areas face elevated transition risks; nature-based activities in degraded areas face significant physical risks.
  - Dependencies: 62% of Corporate portfolio technical reserves finance activities critically dependent on at least one ecosystem service (notably real estate, telecoms, construction). Widespread dependency on water-related services; highest on soil stabilization and erosion control.
  - Identification of main company contributors informs engagement policies.

- Measurement limits and data needs:
  - Exclusions due to methodology/data gaps: retail banking direct reserves (excluding real estate), equity securities, sovereign exposures (sovereign bonds, Banque de France technical reserves, centralized passbook savings).
  - Current measurements rely largely on financial data; plan to add physical, pressure-specific indicators (including climate) tailored to LBP’s financing.

- Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund:
  - Finances biodiversity protection/restoration and decarbonization projects with biodiversity co-benefits.
  - 2024 actions: support for biodiversity credit generation/measurement with CDC Biodiversité at Cros du Mouton (Var); purchase of two voluntary restoration/rewilding units (€99,600 excl. tax).
  - Supports WWF France’s Nature Impact (payments for ecosystem services) for high-biodiversity forests in mainland France; promotes species diversity, water point preservation, agroforestry, and reforestation.

- Subsidiary actions:
  - CNP Assurances:
    - Integrates biodiversity in ESG filters for listed equities/bonds, addressing land use, fragile area disruption, resource controversies, water dependency/discharges.
    - “Green Works” charter for real estate to protect ecosystems, favor low-impact materials, reduce waste/water use, and promote biodiversity/circularity; sustainable management of 54,986 ha of forests.
    - Shareholder engagement embeds biodiversity; 2024: topic in 31% of direct dialogues (five companies).
    - Measures portfolio dependency on ecosystem services via BIA-GBS (covers 98% of directly held equities/bonds).
    - Participates in the 2024 “biodiversity marketplace initiative” with 11 institutional investors to advance methodologies and biodiversity goals.
  - LBP AM:
    - Conducts engagements on sustainable proteins, water, deforestation, pesticides, pollution; monitors portfolio biodiversity footprint.
    - SRI Analysis and Research team (10 people) and specialized data providers; launched a cross-sector Biodiversity rating in 2023.
  - Louvre Banque Privée:
    - Since 2024, measures biodiversity footprint with BIA-GBS; redesigning methodology to integrate UCITS.
    - Uses footprint to pinpoint pressures and main contributors and to guide company dialogues; invested in data and expanded ESG team (five officers).
    - Since Jan 1, 2023, all mandates must include biodiversity considerations.

- Internal awareness and practices:
  - Group-wide biodiversity e-learning available since February 2022.
  - No reliance on biodiversity offsets; focus on impact reduction and preservation via the Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund.
  - Nature-based solutions: investment in WWF France’s Nature Impact for forest preservation/restoration; local/indigenous knowledge not yet integrated.

- Targets and progress:
  - CNP Assurances: commit to measure biodiversity across entire forest portfolio by end-2025 (92% inventoried via IBP method by end-2024); allocate 3% of woodland to older/natural growth areas by end-2025.
  - LBP will consider quantified impact-reduction targets following 2023–2024 assessments, contingent on improved measurement accuracy, methodologies, and higher-quality data.

nodes.title: Employee awareness
nodes.heading: Employee awareness
nodes.start_phrase: The Group is raising its teams’ awareness of biodiversity issues, primarily by way of a biodiversity e-learning module which has been available to all employees since February 2022.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Environmental information) focusing on biodiversity strategy, actions, measurement, engagement, and targets across Group entities.

- Shareholder engagement and policy integration:
  - CNP Assurances has embedded biodiversity into its shareholder engagement, holding direct dialogues with companies (31% of 2024 conversations) to drive ambitious biodiversity action and disclosure of biodiversity-related risks.
  - It participates with 10 other institutional investors in a 2024 “biodiversity marketplace initiative” to develop robust methodologies for integrating biodiversity into financial management and to support international biodiversity goals.
  - LBP AM runs engagement campaigns on sustainable proteins, water, deforestation, pesticide use, and pollution; it aims to raise awareness, promote best practices, and monitors portfolio biodiversity footprints.

- Measurement, tools, and data:
  - CNP Assurances assesses portfolio company dependencies on ecosystem services using BIA-GBS, covering 98% of its directly held equity and bond portfolios.
  - LBP AM’s 10-person SRI Analysis and Research team, supported by specialized data providers, developed a cross-sector Biodiversity rating in 2023.
  - Louvre Banque Privée began measuring its biodiversity footprint with BIA-GBS in 2024, is redesigning its methodology to include UCITS, and uses results to identify main pressures and contributors and to initiate company dialogues. It has expanded ESG resources (five ESG officers) and subscribed to dedicated data services.
  - Since January 1, 2023, all Louvre Banque Privée management mandates incorporate biodiversity considerations in investment policies.

- Internal awareness and capacity building:
  - Group-wide biodiversity e-learning module available to all employees since February 2022.

- Offsets, nature-based solutions, and local knowledge:
  - La Banque Postale does not use biodiversity offsets; it prioritizes reducing its environmental footprint and preserving biodiversity, including financing projects via the Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund.
  - It invests in WWF France’s Nature Impact initiative, a nature-based solution fund for protecting, restoring, and sustainably managing forests in mainland France to deliver biodiversity protection and carbon sequestration.
  - Local and indigenous knowledge has not yet been integrated into its biodiversity actions.

- Targets and results:
  - CNP Assurances SA and its French subsidiaries target full biodiversity measurement of their forest portfolio by end-2025 (92% inventoried by end-2024 using the IBP method) and commit to allocate 3% of woodland to older and natural growth areas by end-2025.
  - Following 2023–2024 assessments of impacts, dependencies, risks, and opportunities, La Banque Postale will work toward quantified biodiversity impact-reduction targets, contingent on improved measurement accuracy, target-setting methodologies, and higher-quality data.

- Reference: A glossary of CSR terms is available (page 808).

nodes.title: Targets and results related to biodiversity and ecosystems

- Stewardship and market initiatives
  - CNP Assurances has embedded biodiversity into its shareholder engagement, discussing the topic with five companies in 2024 (31% of direct dialogues), encouraging ambitious corporate actions and disclosure on biodiversity risks.
  - CNP Assurances measures portfolio companies’ dependencies on ecosystem services using the BIA-GBS methodology, covering 98% of directly held equity and bond portfolios; participates with 10 other institutional investors in the 2024 “biodiversity marketplace initiative” to advance methodologies and investor practices.
  - LBP AM runs collaborative engagement on sustainable proteins, water, deforestation, pesticides, and pollution; monitors portfolio biodiversity footprint; uses a 10-person SRI research team and specialized data providers; launched a cross-sector Biodiversity rating in 2023.
  - Louvre Banque Privée began measuring its biodiversity footprint in 2024 with BIA-GBS, is redesigning methodology to integrate UCITS, and will use results to identify main pressures/contributors and engage companies on action plans. It has increased data resources and expanded its discretionary management ESG team to five officers. Since 1 Jan 2023, all management mandates include biodiversity considerations.

- Internal awareness, offsets, and nature-based solutions
  - Group-wide employee awareness via a biodiversity e-learning module available since February 2022.
  - No use of biodiversity offsets; the Group prioritizes footprint reduction and biodiversity preservation, notably via the Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund.
  - Investment in WWF France’s Nature Impact initiative (a Nature-based Solution) targeting forest preservation, restoration, and sustainable management in mainland France.
  - Local and indigenous knowledge has not yet been integrated into biodiversity actions.

- Targets and progress on forests and impact-setting
  - CNP Assurances SA and French subsidiaries: measure biodiversity across the entire forest portfolio by end-2025 (92% of the area inventoried with the CNPF IBP method by end-2024) and allocate 3% of woodland to older/natural growth by end-2025.
  - Following 2023–2024 assessment of impacts, dependencies, risks, and opportunities, La Banque Postale plans to set quantified impact-reduction targets as methodologies, data quality, and measurement accuracy improve.

- Biodiversity footprint indicators
  - La Banque Postale (four portfolios, 39% of financing portfolio) uses Global Biodiversity Score (MSA.sq.km):
    - Cumulative static impacts at 31/12/2023: 4,180 MSA.sq.km (land), 65 MSA.sq.km (aquatic).
    - Periodic (dynamic) change in 2023: +55 MSA.sq.km for land.
  - CNP Assurances (BIA-GBS™, end-2024) covers 99% of directly held equity and corporate bonds (100% relative to provider coverage). Footprint per € thousand invested (MSA.sq.m):
    - Aquatic: static 3.51; dynamic 0.05.
    - Land: static 48.65; dynamic 2.85.
  - LBP AM: at end-2023, 70% of assets (convertible, corporate and sovereign bonds, equities) covered by a biodiversity footprint of 58 MSA.PPB per € billion invested.

- Pollution management (material in financed activities, not in own operations)
  - Pollution recognized as one of five major biodiversity pressures (IPBES) and addressed within biodiversity policies.
  - Responsible Financing and Investment Charter excludes companies deriving >20% of revenue from pesticide manufacture/sales.
  - CNP Assurances’ 2021–2025 sustainable forest management charter: herbicides/fungicides prohibited; insecticides limited to health emergencies, with training and methodologies to support this.
  - Pollution factors included in ESG ratings for listed assets.
  - LBP AM actions: pesticides exclusion; engagement with pig farms and fertilizer producers on soil pollution/chemical use; engagement with salmon/shrimp farmers on aquaculture nutrient deposits; commitments on plastics circularity; GREaT rating model covers pollution.
  - Under CSRD and TNFD, La Banque Postale conducted deeper analyses with GBS to map dependencies on 21 ecosystem services and assess land and freshwater biodiversity impacts across IPBES pressures, including pollution.

  - CNP Assurances uses the BIA‑GBS tool; end of 2024 coverage: 99% of directly held equities and corporate bonds (effectively 100% per data provider coverage). Footprint per € thousand invested (MSA.sq.m):

nodes.start_phrase: In addition to the double materiality analysis carried out as part of the CSRD, as part of the TNFD, La Banque Postale SA has also conducted a more in-depth study of the impacts and dependencies related to biodiversity using the Global Biodiversity Score (GBS), a tool developed by CDC Biodiversité.
nodes.summary:
- Measurement of biodiversity footprint across investment and financing portfolios:
  - La Banque Postale: Assesses 39% of its financing portfolio using the Global Biodiversity Score (GBS) in MSA.sq.km; cumulative static impacts at 31/12/2023 are 4,180 MSA.sq.km (land) and 65 MSA.sq.km (aquatic); 2023 shows a +55 MSA.sq.km change for land.
  - CNP Assurances: Uses BIA-GBS™, covering 99% of directly held equities and corporate bonds (effectively 100% per data provider). Footprint per €1,000 invested—Aquatic: static 3.51 MSA.sq.m; dynamic 0.05 MSA.sq.m. Land: static 48.65 MSA.sq.m; dynamic 2.85 MSA.sq.m.
  - LBP AM: 70% of assets (convertible, corporate and sovereign bonds, equities) covered; footprint measured at 58 MSA.PPB per € billion invested.

- Pollution materiality and governance:
  - Pollution deemed non-material for own operations but material in financed activities; addressed via responsible financing and investment policies.
  - Exclusion of companies with >20% revenue from manufacturing/selling agricultural pesticides.
  - Forestry management charter (CNP Assurances) bans herbicides/fungicides and limits insecticides to health emergencies; training and methodologies to meet targets.
  - Pollution considerations integrated into ESG ratings and LBP AM’s GREaT rating model.

- Policies, action plans, and engagements to prevent/reduce pollution:
  - TNFD-aligned portfolio analysis using GBS to assess dependencies on ecosystem services and impacts across IPBES pressures (including pollution); findings published in the 2023 Climate and Nature Report and to inform a Nature Transition plan.
  - CNP Assurances applies ESG filters (Pollution/Waste) and a “Green Works” Charter for real estate to limit construction-phase pollution, select low-impact materials, reduce waste, and manage asbestos/lead.
  - LBP AM implements a pesticides exclusion policy and active engagements:
    - Agriculture: engage pig farming and fertilizer producers on soil pollution and chemical use; require plans to reduce pesticide use by 2030 (aligned with Kunming-Montreal Target 7 and EU Farm to Fork), phase out highly hazardous pesticides by 2030, disclose pesticide-free product shares, consumer communication, and transparent influence policies.
    - Aquaculture: engage salmon/shrimp farmers on sustainable practices and nutrient-related pollution.
    - Plastics/circularity: commitments sought from agri-food companies.
    - Water: require regular impact analyses, site- and substance-specific reduction targets, disclosure of indicators, remediation plans for incidents, and mapping/protection plans for activities near critical freshwater/sensitive aquatic ecosystems.
  - Louvre Banque Privée: improves management of SFDR PAI indicators and integrates pollution into issuer/asset manager engagement.

- Targets and next steps:
  - Following 2023–2024 impact/dependency/risk assessments, pollution impact-reduction targets will be progressively set, contingent on improved measurement accuracy, methodologies, and higher-quality data.

nodes.title: targets and results related to the prevention and reduction of pollution
nodes.heading: 2.2.3.3 targets and results related to the prevention and reduction of pollution
nodes.start_phrase: Following the exercise to measure impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities conducted in 2023-2024, impact reduction targets will be gradually established.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale Group’s CSR environmental measures on pollution prevention and water/marine resources, primarily across financed activities and real estate.
- ESG integration on pollution: CNP Assurances applies ESG filters to listed equities/bonds, including “Pollution/Waste” criteria (air/soil pollution, toxic emissions, e-waste, packaging).
- Real estate “Green Works” Charter: ecosystem protection during construction, low-impact materials, waste reduction, control of odours/VOCs, and compliance on asbestos/lead; measures to limit site-adjacent pollution.
- Soil pollution expectations (LBP AM): 
  - Pesticide use/production reduction plans by 2030 aligned with Kunming-Montreal Target 7 and EU Farm to Fork.
  - Phase-out of highly hazardous pesticides by 2030.
  - Reporting on pesticide-free production, clear consumer information, awareness actions.
  - Publication of an influence policy on plant protection products with transparent advocacy practices.
- Water pollution expectations (LBP AM for financed companies): 
  - Regular assessment of impacts on local surface/groundwater.
  - Action plans with site- and substance-specific discharge/pollution reduction targets, prioritizing high water-stress sites.
  - Publication of monitoring indicators.
  - Remediation/restoration/rewilding plans after incidents.
  - Mapping and protection plans for activities near critical freshwater/sensitive aquatic biodiversity ecosystems.
- Louvre Banque Privée: strengthens quantitative management of SFDR PAI indicators to identify high-impact entities and integrates pollution into engagement.
- Targets/results on pollution: Following 2023–2024 impact/dependency/risk/opportunity assessments, impact-reduction targets will be phased in as measurement accuracy, methodologies, and data quality improve.
- Water and marine resources policy (2024): Adoption of Caisse des Dépôts water policy addressing scarcity, water quality/infrastructure, flooding/soil sealing; aims to support:
  - 10% national water consumption reduction by 2030.
  - Preservation of 100% of drinking water catchments by 2027 (EU Water Framework Directive).
  - Three pillars: understand impacts/risks; adopt water-saving; preserve water quality/infrastructure. Implementation begins 2025 under GRMC oversight.
- Water-related commitments:
  - By end-2025: water footprint/dependency assessment.
  - By end-2027: initial estimate of aquatic pollution from operations and financed/invested entities; assessment of portfolio exposure to drought/water stress (France, overseas, and relevant international).
- Financing portfolio measures on water:
  - By end-2025: integrate water-saving target and local water-stress levels into ESG analysis.
  - In high-stress areas: require alignment with best-practice water consumption to avoid worsening scarcity.
  - Deploy financing tools for efficient water management; loans to sanitation services/water agencies to improve water quality.
  - Exclude financing/investment in companies with >20% revenue from pesticide manufacture/sales.
- Oceans: no dedicated policy yet; to be developed with Caisse des Dépôts in 2025 ahead of the UN Ocean Conference (UNOC) in Nice.

nodes.title: Preserving water and marine resources [E3]
nodes.heading: 2.2.4 Preserving water and marine resources [E3]
nodes.start_phrase: The “Water” topic is not included in the scope of La Banque Postale’s own operations.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: In La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (CSR, Environmental information 2.2.4), water is addressed primarily through financed activities (downstream value chain), not the Bank’s own operations.
- Policy framework: In 2024, the Group adopted Caisse des Dépôts’ water policy, targeting three challenges—scarcity of water resources, water quality and related infrastructure, and flooding/soil sealing—aiming to support France’s 10% water-use reduction by 2030 and preserve 100% of drinking water catchments by 2027 in line with the EU Water Framework Directive.
- Governance and rollout: The Group Risk Management Committee oversees implementation; the policy is structured around commitments, targets, and indicators, with first actions starting in 2025.
- Pillar 1—Understand impacts and risks: Commitments include producing a water footprint/dependency assessment by end-2025; estimating aquatic pollution from operations and financed entities by end-2027; and assessing portfolio exposure to drought/water stress (France, overseas territories, and relevant international exposures) by end-2027.
- Pillar 2—Water saving (sobriety): Support stakeholders in reducing consumption and modernizing water/sanitation networks; deploy financing tools for efficient water management. For financing portfolios: integrate water-saving targets and local water stress into ESG analysis by end-2025; ensure projects in high-stress areas align with best sector practices to avoid worsening shortages; expand dedicated water-efficiency financing.
- Pillar 3—Preserve water quality and infrastructure: Reduce ecosystem impacts, prioritize nature-based solutions, and support rewilding/restoration. Targets include combating aquatic pollution, ensuring proper water cycle functioning, and protecting wetlands. Portfolio rules: exclude financing/investment in companies with over 20% of revenue from pesticide manufacture/sales; provide loans that improve water quality via public sanitation services or water agencies.
- Marine/oceans policy: No specific sustainable oceans and seas policy yet; development planned with Caisse des Dépôts in 2025, ahead of the UN Ocean Conference (UNOC) in Nice, June 2025.

nodes.title: Policies related to water and marine resources
nodes.heading: 2.2.4.1 Policies related to water and marine resources
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, La Banque Postale Group, as a subsidiary, adopted the Caisse des Dépôts Group’s water policy to address the three major challenges it faces:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and materiality: Water is not a material topic for La Banque Postale’s direct operations but is material in its financed activities (downstream value chain). Resource use/circular economy is material through waste for both own operations and financed activities.

- Water policy (adopted 2024 from Caisse des Dépôts):
  - Key challenges: scarcity of water, water quality and infrastructure, flooding/soil sealing.
  - Pillars: understand impacts/risks; drive water savings; preserve water quality and infrastructure.
  - Governance: Group Risk Management Committee oversees; first implementation steps in 2025.

- Water-related commitments:
  - By end-2025: produce a water footprint or dependency assessment.
  - By end-2027: estimate aquatic pollution from operations/financed counterparties; assess portfolios’ exposure to drought/water stress (France, overseas, international as relevant).
  - Contribute to France’s 10% water-use reduction by 2030 via financing, ESG integration (by 2025 include water-saving and local water-stress in ESG analysis), and tools for efficient water management; ensure projects in high-stress areas align with best practices.
  - Preserve ecosystems: combat aquatic pollution, support the water cycle, avoid wetland damage; exclude financing/investment in companies with >20% revenue from pesticides; provide loans improving water quality (e.g., sanitation services, water agencies).
  - Marine/ocean policy: none yet; to be developed with Caisse des Dépôts in 2025 ahead of UNOC 2025.

- Action plans and tools:
  - Water as an indicator in the Impact Weighting Factor (with WWF France).
  - Green loans for local authorities’ water/sanitation; bridging loans tied to water-agency subsidies (leak reduction, reuse); Climate & Biodiversity Impact Fund supports water consumption reductions.
  - Subsidiaries: CNP Assurances’ real-estate “Green Works” (limit consumption, ensure quality); LBP AM in CERES Valuing Water; Louvre Banque Privée enhances PAI monitoring (emissions to water).

- Water risk mapping:
  - 2024 financing location analysis: ~65% of financed areas have at least two high-risk criteria (biodiversity importance, ecological integrity, water stress).
  - Priority areas: Île-de-France (significant potential building land, average risk) and parts of South-East France (very high risk).
  - Next steps: define actions to limit impacts. CNP Assurances to map portfolio assets in high/very high water-stress areas by 2027, and its sites/real estate by 2026; LBP AM engages companies to map abstraction sites and assess local impacts.

- Targets/results:
  - Following 2023–2024 impact/dependency/risk/opportunity assessment, quantified impact-reduction targets will be set progressively.

- Circular economy policy (2024):
  - Scope: La Banque Postale SA and main subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, LBP Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve, Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
  - Aim: reduce at source and optimize use and end-of-life of resources by 2030, using a life-cycle approach; applies to operational activities.
  - Governance: validated/monitored by the Sustainability Department; financing/investment considered but without specific targets; policy and targets shared internally and externally on request.

nodes.title: Action plans related to water and marine resources
nodes.heading: 2.2.4.2 Action plans related to water and marine resources
nodes.start_phrase: Water is one of the environmental indicators under the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF), an impact scoring tool developed by La Banque Postale in partnership with WWF France to guide financing and investment strategies (for more information on the IWF, see focus point: The Impact Weighting Factor (IWF)).
nodes.summary:
- Focus on water and marine resource management within La Banque Postale’s sustainability strategy, using the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF) developed with WWF France to guide financing and investment decisions.
- Deployment of water-focused financing tools:
  - “Green loans” for local authorities targeting sustainable water and sanitation investments (small water cycle).
  - Bridging loans to pre-finance water agency subsidies (supply security, leak reduction, treated wastewater reuse).
  - Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund supporting projects to reduce water consumption.
- Subsidiary initiatives:
  - CNP Assurances’ Green Works Charter to limit water use and ensure water quality in directly owned real estate.
  - LBP AM’s participation in CERES’s Valuing Water initiative to promote water resource protection.
  - Louvre Banque Privée’s enhanced monitoring of SFDR PAIs, including emissions to water.
- Water risk mapping and prioritization:
  - Analysis of financed activities’ locations identified sensitive areas, with ~65% of financed areas meeting at least two high-risk criteria (biodiversity significance, ecological integrity, or water stress).
  - Priority geographies: Île-de-France (significant potential building land, average overall risk) and parts of South-East France (very high overall risk).
  - Next steps include defining concrete actions to limit impacts in water-risk areas.
- Commitments and timelines:
  - CNP Assurances to map portfolio assets in high/extremely high water-stress areas by end-2027, and its sites/real estate by end-2026 (France and internationally).
  - LBP AM engaging investee companies to map abstraction sites, identify high-stress areas, and assess local impacts, with targeted engagements for highest-risk firms.
- Targets and results:
  - Following 2023–2024 impact/risk assessment, La Banque Postale will progressively set quantified impact-reduction targets for water and marine resources.
- Circular economy policy (2024):
  - New Resources and Circular Economy policy covering La Banque Postale SA and key subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, La Banque Postale Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve, Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
  - Commitment to reduce at source and optimize resource use and end-of-life by 2030, integrating waste management within a life-cycle approach.
  - Policy applies to operational activities; financing and investment activities were considered but have no specific targets or commitments.
  - Governance by the Sustainability Department, with targets and policy communicated internally and available externally on request.

nodes.title: Policies related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.1 Policies related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, La Banque Postale implemented a Resources and Circular Economy policy whose scope includes La Banque Postale SA as well as its main subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, La Banque Postale Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve and Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).

- Focus on water and marine resources:

- Water risk mapping and priorities:
  - 2024 analysis identified financed activities in sensitive areas using criteria including water stress; about 65% of financed areas have at least two high-risk criteria.
  - Priority locations: Île-de-France (significant potential building land, medium overall risk) and parts of South-East France (very high overall risk).

- Circular economy strategy:
  - 2024 Resources and Circular Economy policy covering La Banque Postale SA and main subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, LBP Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve, Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
  - Commitment to reduce at source and optimize resource use and end-of-life by 2030, with a life-cycle approach and subsidiary-specific roadmaps.

- Action plans for resource use and waste:
  - Reduce consumption and waste:

nodes.title: Action plans related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.2 Action plans related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: The main actions deployed under the Resources and Circular Economy policy include:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and policy: La Banque Postale’s environmental/CSR approach includes a Group-wide Resources and Circular Economy policy, translated into subsidiary-specific roadmaps based on operational needs and resource use.
- Eco-design and materials: All products placed on the market (notably bank cards) follow an eco-design approach prioritizing recycled inputs, recyclability of plastics/cardboard/IT equipment, and promotion of renewable resources. Procurement supports systematic use of recycled materials for paper/cardboard, plastics, and WEEE.
- CIB perimeter: No waste management policy currently applies to Corporate & Investment Banking due to the absence of robust methodologies to measure resource footprints. Group-level work (with La Poste Group) is underway to establish footprints and reduction pathways, which should enable better integration of waste impacts in CIB in the future.
- Action plans to reduce resource use and waste:
  - Plastics: Identify highest-consuming suppliers, deploy plans to reduce plastic supply, embed materials criteria in tenders, and raise awareness among specifiers/buyers.
  - Paper/cardboard: Map waste origins across activities, add dedicated procurement criteria, and raise awareness of alternatives.
  - Electrical/electronic equipment (IT): Review allocation/management policies, optimize allocation processes, and train employees on responsible use.
- End-of-life optimization:
  - Waste management: Assess volumes and types across sites; implement supplier progress plans; favor reuse and recycling while avoiding incineration and landfill; train employees on sorting and recovery.
  - Bank cards: Reduce undelivered cards, organize recovery of non-delivered products, and consider extending card validity to limit renewals.
  - Reuse: Strengthen supplier requirements for WEEE reuse, set up internal/external donation channels, conduct LCAs, and train specifiers on reuse methods.
- Governance and implementation: Actions are consolidated in an annual roadmap shared across entities and adapted to each operational scope. The Sustainability Department leads execution; efforts focus on human-resource prioritization and influencer awareness. No specific budget allocations were attached to these roadmaps.
- Exclusions: No waste management roadmaps exist for the credit and investment portfolio.
- Waste handling: Contracts apply the waste treatment hierarchy, systematically considering reuse before recycling. Most waste is processed by operators committed to 100% recycling (e.g., Recygo, Les Joyeux Recycleurs).

nodes.title: Targets and results related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.3 Targets and results related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: A number of operational targets have been set and are managed annually by the Sustainability Department.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Sustainable performance and environmental information, specifically strengthening the circular economy across La Banque Postale Group.
- Strategy and governance: Establish a Group-wide donation hierarchy and internal/external donation rules to enhance materials circularity; Sustainability Department leads, with quarterly steering committees and annual target reviews; subsidiaries have dedicated quarterly monitoring.
- Stakeholder engagement: Collaboration with institutional actors (e.g., CITEO) to track Extended Producer Responsibility; employee awareness initiatives; supplier engagement via annual reviews and progress plans; internal sustainability experts coordinate actions.
- CNP Assurances integration: Circular economy and resource use embedded in ESG filters for listed equities and bonds, assessing waste and circularity across design/production/use; in real estate, a “Green Works” Charter promotes deconstruction, reuse/recovery, and materials from redeployment channels; management companies handle associated risks case by case.
- 2030 operational targets (base year 2023) for entities under the Resources and Circular Economy policy:
  - Reduce plastic waste by 50% and paper/cardboard waste by 30%.
  - Sort and recover 100% of non-plastic waste on sites, prioritizing recycling.
  - Ensure 100% of plastic waste generated is recyclable, reusable, or compostable.
  - Reduce WEEE volumes by 30% vs. 2021 and keep WEEE recovery rates above 85%.
  - Maintain at least a 50% “second life” rate (one-third reuse, two-thirds redeployment).
  - Apply eco-design to 100% of products put into circulation.
  - Collect 30% of expired bank cards; recover 100% of collected expired cards.
  - Recover 100% of undistributed bank cards (NPL).
- Target-setting process: Developed by the Sustainability Department with Purchasing and Marketing; roadmaps monitored quarterly; annual performance assessment follows data collection.
- Scope notes: Subsidiaries e Zyness, Sofiap, and 115K have no specific targets due to size and limited materiality.
- Portfolio scope: No waste management targets set for the loan and investment portfolio.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.3.1 Targets
nodes.start_phrase: A number of operational targets have been set and are managed annually by the Sustainability Department.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s Resources and Circular Economy policy within its 2024 Universal Registration Document, covering governance, targets to 2030, eco-design and procurement practices, waste management approach, and performance metrics.
- Governance and engagement:
  - Strengthens circular economy via a shared donation hierarchy and specific internal/external donation rules.
  - Works with institutional actors (e.g., CITEO) to monitor Extended Producer Responsibility and coordinates ecosystem actions.
  - Engages all employees through awareness initiatives; involves suppliers via annual reviews and progress plans.
  - CNP Assurances integrates resource/circular-economy criteria into ESG filters for listed assets and applies a “Green Works” Charter in real estate (deconstruction, reuse/recovery, priority for redeployed materials), with risk management by asset managers.
- Targets to 2030 (base year 2023; set by the Sustainability Department; monitored quarterly; annual assessments):
  - Reduce plastic waste by 50% and paper/cardboard by 30%.
  - Sort and recover 100% of site-generated waste (excluding plastic), prioritizing recycling.
  - Ensure 100% of plastic waste is recyclable, reusable, or compostable.
  - Reduce WEEE by 30% vs 2021 and maintain recovery rates above 85%.
  - Achieve a minimum 50% “second life” rate (one-third reuse, two-thirds redeployment).
  - Apply eco-design to 100% of products put into circulation.
  - Collect 30% of expired bank cards; recover 100% of expired and 100% of undistributed cards.
  - Note: No waste-management targets for loan and investment portfolios.
- Eco-design and procurement:
  - All offers/services pass an internal ESG project grid assessing resource use and waste.
  - Purchasing embeds circularity, especially for IT: repairability indices, spare parts availability, take-back of replaced/EOL equipment, and robust redeployment/recycling/destruction channels.
- Waste management approach:
  - Prioritizes reduction at source and follows the European waste hierarchy (recycling, then material recovery, then energy recovery).
  - Voluntary, mission-driven policy exceeding regulatory requirements.
- Key metrics and results:
  - Total waste generated: 1,435 tonnes.
  - Waste diverted from disposal: 1,325 tonnes; waste sent for disposal: 110 tonnes.
  - Non-recycled waste: 253 tonnes (17.6% of total).
  - WEEE: 575 tonnes; classified as hazardous waste under EU Directive 2008/98/EC. No radioactive waste.
  - 36 tonnes of electrical/electronic equipment reused.
  - Main streams: office paper; WEEE (batteries, bulbs, phones, computers), containing rare metals, aluminum, plastics.
- Reporting:
  - Centralized by DEC teams using service-provider data; estimates used for some multi-tenant sites based on employee counts.
- Additional:
  - Targets mapped to circular economy levers (eco-design, circular material use, minimization of primary raw materials, sustainable sourcing, waste management).

nodes.title: Metrics
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.3.2 Metrics
nodes.start_phrase: The waste generated mainly covers three specific streams: paper/cardboard, WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) and non-hazardous industrial waste, in connection with the bancassurance activities of our various entities.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Environmental information). References a glossary of CSR terms (p. 808).

- Waste management scope and priorities:
  - Main waste streams: paper/cardboard, WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment), and non-hazardous industrial waste linked to bancassurance activities.
  - Priority on reuse and recycling, especially for paper, cardboard, and glass.
  - Non-recycled waste (including reuse and energy recovery where recycling is unavailable or constrained by contracts) represents 17.6% of total waste.

- WEEE specifics and circular practices:
  - La Banque Postale mainly generates paper and WEEE; WEEE includes batteries, light bulbs, telephones, and IT equipment (computers, printers, cartridges) containing rare metals, aluminum, and plastics.
  - All WEEE is treated as hazardous waste per Directive 2008/98/EC Annex III; all hazardous waste at the bank is WEEE; no radioactive waste produced.
  - 36 tonnes of electrical and electronic equipment were reused.
  - A Resources footprint study (La Poste Group scope) will provide an exhaustive material composition of WEEE.

- Governance and reporting methodology:
  - Waste data reporting and circular economy implementation are centralized by DEC teams for La Banque Postale and subsidiaries.
  - Data based on service providers’ feedback; where unavailable (e.g., multi-occupant sites where the bank is a minority), estimates are used based on total volumes and headcount.

- Quantitative waste metrics (tonnes):
  - Total waste generated: 1,435.
  - Waste diverted from disposal: 1,325.
    - Hazardous waste diverted: preparation for reuse 1; recycling 471; other recovery 0.
    - Non-hazardous waste diverted: preparation for reuse 0; recycling 711; other recovery 142.
  - Waste for disposal: 110.
    - Hazardous waste for disposal: incineration 72; landfill 17; other disposal 13.
    - Non-hazardous waste for disposal: incineration 0.005; landfill 8; other 0.
  - Non-recycled waste: 253 (17.6%).
  - Total WEEE (entity-specific): 575.
  - Total hazardous waste: 575; radioactive waste: 0.

- European Green Taxonomy (EUTax) background and implementation:
  - Regulation (EU) 2020/852 defines sustainable activities via substantial contribution criteria to at least one environmental objective, DNSH to the others, and Minimum Social Safeguards.
  - Six objectives: climate change mitigation; climate change adaptation; sustainable use/protection of water and marine resources; transition to a circular economy; pollution prevention and control; protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
  - Article 8 requires disclosure of how activities align with environmentally sustainable economic activities.
  - Technical criteria set by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 (climate objectives) and 2023/2486 (other four objectives).
  - Integration into the bank’s business model: green loan and green bond frameworks reviewed; front-office equipped to help customers meet green criteria.
  - Reporting scope and roadmap: alignment published for the first two objectives; remaining four considered non-material for current portfolios—analysis to be pursued next year subject to data availability.
  - Acknowledges uncertainties in interpretation and data gaps; future publications will refine disclosures.
  - Notes EC FAQ published on 8 Nov 2024; timing prevented incorporation this year; process under review to integrate at next reporting date.

nodes.title: Background and regulatory requirements of the European Green Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.1 Background and regulatory requirements of the European Green Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: The European Green Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 dated 18 June 2020 defines sustainable economic activities by establishing substantial contribution technical criteria (CCS), for at least one of the environmental and Do No Significant Harm (DNSH) targets and five other targets.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: La Banque Postale’s Universal Registration Document outlines how the European Green Taxonomy applies to the Bank’s activities, focusing on environmental information and sustainable performance.
- EU Green Taxonomy framework: Explains Regulation (EU) 2020/852, defining sustainable activities through substantial contribution criteria, Do No Significant Harm (DNSH), and Minimum Social Safeguards (MSS). Notes Article 8 disclosure obligations and the technical screening criteria set by Delegated Regulations 2021/2139 (climate objectives) and 2023/2486 (the other four environmental objectives). Lists the six environmental objectives (climate mitigation, climate adaptation, water/marine, circular economy, pollution prevention, biodiversity/ecosystems).
- Implementation at the Bank: Integration of the Taxonomy into the business model, including updates to green loan and green bond frameworks and front-office enablement to help clients meet green criteria.
- Reporting perimeter and timing: The Bank currently discloses eligibility/alignment for the first two objectives (climate mitigation and adaptation). It deems the remaining four objectives non-material for current portfolios but plans best-efforts analysis from next year. Acknowledges interpretation and data limitations; cites the EC FAQ of 8 Nov 2024 that could not be incorporated this cycle and will be addressed in future reporting.
- Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology:
  - Definition: GAR measures the share of Taxonomy-aligned assets in total assets; key KPI under the Taxonomy.
  - Denominator (covered assets): Total assets minus sovereign, central bank, supranational exposures, and trading book.
  - Numerator scope: Applies technical criteria to selected products/counterparties; excludes certain items only from the numerator (e.g., companies not subject to the NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans), ensuring eligibility/alignment ratios are inherently below 100%.
  - Eligibility boundaries: Only activities with defined technical criteria are eligible; some sectors (e.g., farming) are currently out of scope.
  - Alignment rules: Specialized/project financing that meets criteria is treated as aligned; general-purpose loans rely on counterparties’ published alignment ratios. Each asset can align to only one environmental objective to avoid double counting.
  - Stepwise calculation flow: Total assets → covered assets (after exclusions) → assets analyzed for eligibility → Taxonomy-eligible assets (after removing non-eligible portions) → Taxonomy-aligned assets (after removing non-aligned portions), based on project- or counterparty-level indicators.
- Disclosures: Results of the analyses and required qualitative information are provided, with a commitment to refine future publications as data quality and regulatory guidance improve.

nodes.title: Alignment analysis principles
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.2 Alignment analysis principles
nodes.start_phrase: The GAR is the ratio of Green Taxonomy-aligned assets to total assets, and is the Taxonomy’s key performance indicator.
nodes.summary:
- Source and context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Environmental information) detailing EU Green Taxonomy alignment analysis and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology and results.
- GAR definition and purpose: GAR measures the share of total assets aligned with the EU Green Taxonomy; it is the Taxonomy’s key KPI identifying investments in sustainable economic activities.
- Scope and calculation principles:
  - Denominator (covered assets): Total assets excluding exposures to sovereigns, central banks, supranationals, and the trading book.
  - Numerator: Assets meeting Taxonomy technical screening criteria among selected products/counterparties.
  - Scope differences: Certain exposures (e.g., companies not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, some interbank loans) are excluded from the numerator or from eligibility analysis, ensuring eligible/aligned ratios are always below 100% (e.g., an SME wind farm loan cannot enter the numerator if the SME is outside NFRD scope).
  - Eligibility constraints: Only activities with specified technical criteria can be assessed; some (e.g., farming) are not yet Taxonomy-eligible.
  - Alignment rules: Specialized (project) financing aligned when it meets criteria; general purpose financing included based on counterparties’ published alignment ratios; each asset is aligned to only one environmental objective to avoid double counting.
- Process flow: Total assets → Covered assets → Assets analyzed for eligibility → Taxonomy‑eligible assets → Taxonomy‑aligned assets.
- Four-stage Taxonomy assessment:
  1) Eligibility (activity listed in the Taxonomy),
  2) Substantial contribution (to one of six environmental objectives),
  3) DNSH (no significant harm to the other five objectives),
  4) MSS (minimum social safeguards).
- Mandatory vs voluntary GAR:
  - Mandatory GAR: Asset-by-asset assessment without estimates, per regulation.
  - Voluntary GAR: Supplementary indicator with estimates and a slightly broader scope; includes special purpose SME green loans excluded from mandatory GAR; complemented by Pillar III ESG Table 10 on green products not in GAR.
- Portfolio-specific application principles:
  - Households – Real estate:
    - Mandatory: Uses actual energy use data and a physical risk model aligned with Pillar III ESG (for DNSH); MSS presumed met for French financing.
    - Voluntary: Uses estimated energy use from external data provider with the same risk model; MSS presumed met.
  - Other household loans (e.g., motor vehicles, home renovation): Included in eligibility per regulations where applicable, but generally excluded from alignment if treated as general purpose financing.
  - Corporates:
    - Special purpose financing: Mandatory uses actual client data; voluntary may use estimates or partial analysis (e.g., only substantial contribution).
    - General purpose financing: Mandatory collects alignment ratios published by NFRD-reporting counterparties.
- Methodology governance: Despite unresolved interpretive issues in the texts, the Bank developed an internal reference framework to operationalize the Taxonomy’s technical screening criteria.
- Reported outcome: As of 31 December 2024, the regulatory GAR is 5.7% (€10.3bn) based on turnover, mainly from energy‑efficient household real estate financing aligned with climate change mitigation; includes some general purpose financing where counterparties publish alignment indicators; level is stable versus 5.5% (31 Dec 2023) and 5.9% (30 Jun 2024).

nodes.title: Alignment indicators
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.3 Alignment indicators
nodes.start_phrase: At 31 December 2024, the Bank’s regulatory green asset ratio was 5.7% (€10.3 billion) based on turnover.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Environmental information on La Banque Postale’s Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and EU Taxonomy alignment within the 2024 Universal Registration Document, including methodology, portfolio treatment rules, key indicators, results, data limitations, and reporting format.
- Taxonomy methodology:
  - Four-stage analysis: eligibility; substantial contribution to environmental objectives; Do No Significant Harm (DNSH); Minimum Social Safeguards (MSS).
  - Bank-developed reference framework to operationalize technical screening criteria, addressing unresolved methodological interpretations.
- Mandatory vs. voluntary GAR:
  - Mandatory GAR: asset-by-asset assessment without estimates; includes general purpose lending when counterparties publish alignment ratios (per regulation).
  - Voluntary GAR: broader scope using estimates; includes certain SME special purpose green loans excluded from the mandatory GAR because SMEs are outside NFRD scope; supplemented by Pillar III ESG Table 10 for green products not in GAR.
- Portfolio-based alignment principles:
  - Households (real estate): mandatory uses actual energy use and a physical risk model aligned with Pillar III ESG; MSS presumed met in France. Voluntary uses estimated energy data with the same DNSH model and MSS presumption.
  - Other retail (vehicle loans since 1 Jan 2022, home renovation): eligible base per regulation but excluded from alignment calculations as general purpose financing.
  - Corporates:
    - Special purpose financing: mandatory uses customer’s actual data; voluntary may use estimates (e.g., energy performance diagnostics) or partial substantial contribution-only analysis.
    - General purpose financing: relies on alignment ratios published by NFRD counterparties.
- Key 2024 alignment indicators (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Regulatory GAR: 5.7% (€10.3bn) based on turnover, mainly household real estate aligned to climate change mitigation. Stable vs. 5.5% (Dec 2023) and 5.9% (June 2024).
  - Voluntary GAR: 8.0% (€14.2bn), of which 2.3% is the voluntary component.
  - Off-balance sheet: 0.0% for financial guarantees; 3.0% for assets under management at LBP AM.
  - Additional KPIs: a flow GAR figure is provided (1.7%; value shown as 679 in the template), plus template-based disclosures on KPI coverage and assets excluded from GAR numerator/denominator.
  - Trading book and fee/commission KPIs only apply from 2026.
- Data constraints and improvements:
  - GAR reflects limited availability of reliable alignment data for existing portfolios (notably technical reserves), unlike new production where data are obtained at origination.

  - Disclosures follow Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; exposures shown twice using counterparties’ turnover and then CapEx alignment ratios; other exposures treated consistently.

nodes.title: Alignment indicators - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.3 Alignment indicators
nodes.start_phrase: At 31 December 2024, the Bank’s regulatory green asset ratio was 5.7% (€10.3 billion) based on turnover.
nodes.summary: Overview of La Banque Postale’s EU Taxonomy alignment metrics and methodology: at 31 Dec 2024 the regulatory Green Asset Ratio (GAR) was 5.7% (€10.3bn) based on turnover, mainly from energy‑efficient household real estate financing aligned to the climate change mitigation objective; some general purpose financing is included where counterparties’ alignment indicators exist. This is broadly stable versus 5.5% (31 Dec 2023) and 5.9% (30 Jun 2024). The Taxonomy assessment follows four stages: eligibility, substantial contribution, Do No Significant Harm (DNSH), and minimum social safeguards (MSS). Data limitations on existing technical reserves constrained alignment determinations, while new production data are captured at issuance; enhanced data collection is underway for real estate, asset, and project finance and integrated with broader ESG initiatives (Impact Weighting Factor, low‑carbon pathway, Equator Principles). Voluntary (non‑regulatory) GAR is 8.0% (€14.2bn; 2.3% voluntary component). Off‑balance sheet alignment ratios are 0.0% for financial guarantees and 3.0% for assets under management at LBP AM. Required Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 tables are presented, with exposures shown twice using counterparties’ turnover then CapEx alignment ratios; Green Taxonomy/Pillar III ESG Tables 6–8 are published once in the Green Taxonomy format, with insurance/asset management details in Section 2.5.1.7.

nodes.title: Employee Remuneration policy
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.2.3 Employee Remuneration policy
nodes.start_phrase: Remuneration policies aim to prevent and mitigate the negative impacts of the Group regarding a potential deterioration in remuneration levels, the number of jobs or the type of contract for employees.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: The excerpt outlines La Banque Postale Group’s social policies aimed at enhancing quality of life at work, safeguarding health and safety, developing employee skills, ensuring fair remuneration, and promoting diversity and inclusion across the Group and its subsidiaries.

- Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions (QWLWC):
  - Implemented by HR for La Banque Postale’s Economic and Social Unit (UES); aligned with French Labour Code and sector agreements.
  - Objectives: global QWLWC approach covering work content (workload regulation), prevention and health (physical/mental), work relations and work-life balance, and tackling information overload.
  - Method: multidisciplinary primary risk prevention—indicator-based analysis, co-building with stakeholders, broad involvement, continuous improvement, action monitoring.
  - Focus on good work relationships throughout careers; onboarding as a cultural alignment lever.
  - 2023 QWLWC agreement signed with three representative unions; published on intranet; annual commission monitors implementation.
  - CNP Assurances has a parallel QWLWC agreement and international D&I governance.

- Employee Skills Policy:
  - Training policy supports the Strategic Plan via skills development plans for all Group employees.
  - Covers onboarding, support during transformations, continuous learning, and mandatory/regulatory training (e.g., banking standards, GDPR, RGAA).
  - Skills plan co-built with business lines and HR; validated and shared across departments.
  - HR core missions: recruitment/onboarding, skills assessment, career path management, professional development, potential development.
  - Four HR principles: co-constructed career management; cross-entity mobility (La Banque Postale, financial services, La Poste Network, La Poste Group); talent recruitment; managerial development.

- Remuneration Policy:
  - Approved by Executive and Supervisory Boards; implemented by HR; based on performance recognition, fairness, transparency.
  - Aims: fair pay reflecting expertise, tenure, market and internal equity; gender pay equality; recognition of long-term individual/collective performance; alignment with long-term goals; career development to foster commitment.
  - Published on intranet; compliant with labor law and collective agreements.
  - Subsidiaries tailor policies to local/sector regulations.
  - CNP Assurances’ policy aligns with strategic, financial and non-financial objectives, ensures fairness and gender equality; each subsidiary drafts its own policy with HR oversight.
  - Louvre Banque Privée has remuneration and professional equality agreements.

- Health and Safety:
  - 2024 prevention plan validated by the Health, Safety and Working Conditions Commission (HSWCC):
    - Continue/adapt occupational risk assessments specific to La Banque Postale.
    - Analyze lost-time accidents using the “5 Whys” method.
    - Implement workstation adjustments recommended by occupational health.
    - Raise awareness of road safety risks.
  - QWLWC collective agreement integrated into UES development strategy; complements prior agreements (diversity, remote work).
  - Subsidiary measures: CNP’s QWLWC agreement; Louvre Banque Privée safety booklet; Louvre Banque Privée Immobilier Conseil DUERP.
  - Strengthened prevention via multidisciplinary impact assessments for transformation projects; three national HSWC committees held in 2023 plus monitoring of the “Réussir Ensemble” agreement.

- Diversity and Inclusion (D&I):
  - Policy renewed every three years via social agreement; implemented by HR for all UES employees; shared internally and externally.
  - Five pillars: Disability (RQTH recruitment and recognition), Generations (youth entry, older worker retention, intergenerational diversity), Parity (gender equality and governance parity, anti-sexism), LGBT+ inclusion, Social/Ethnic origins (fairness across the employee lifecycle).
  - Built with experts, charities, HR, and employees.
  - Covers all legally defined discrimination grounds (26 to date), including sex, gender, age, and disability.
