Cat.15) 161,913 (2024); total market‑based footprint 22,633,887 (2022), 24,376,841 (2023), 26,943,867 (2024, +11%). Scope 3 Cat.15 is disclosed only where methodologies exist; emissions for insurance‑associated activities, assets under management (EUR 34.7bn at 31/12/2024) and local public sector entities (EUR 18bn at 31/12/2024) are not disclosed; insurance emissions are preliminarily deemed insignificant but uncertain.

nodes.title: Financed emissions
nodes.heading: 2.2.1. Financed emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius calculates its financed emissions in accordance with the methodology of PCAF.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt is from Belfius Bank’s 2024 Annual Report Sustainability Statement, focusing on climate targets, carbon accounting, and emissions performance.
- Belfius is developing science-based targets for financed and investment emissions, prioritizing the most material, climate-sensitive sectors and portfolio segments; validation is expected in 2025, with a structured transition plan aligned to Strategy 2030 to follow. No significant Capex/Opex is currently allocated to implementation.
- Overall carbon footprint (market-based) rose 11% from 24.38 MtCO2e in 2023 to 26.94 MtCO2e in 2024, driven by financed emissions.
- Financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15, incl. sovereign) increased 11% to 26.78 MtCO2e in 2024.
- Operational emissions fell 7% to 163.8 ktCO2e in 2024: Scope 1 down 12% (1.9 kt), Scope 2 market-based down 28% (0.06 kt), and Scope 3 (excl. Cat. 15) down 7% (161.9 kt).
- Financed emissions are calculated per PCAF across seven asset classes (mortgages; business and corporate loans; commercial real estate; equity and bonds; motor vehicle loans; project finance; sovereign debt) and include financial leasing; these cover 63% of total loans and investments. Data quality scores are around 4.7–5.0.
- 2024 in-scope portfolio (excl. sovereign): €87.1bn carrying amount; 5.72 MtCO2e Scope 1&2 and 18.07 MtCO2e Scope 3; intensity 66 tCO2e/M€.
- Sovereign debt is reported separately to avoid double counting; Belfius applies the PCAF production-based approach (aligned with UNFCCC). 2024 sovereign emissions: 2.919 MtCO2e including LULUCF and 2.993 MtCO2e excluding LULUCF, on €10.5bn exposure.
- Certain categories are excluded due to lacking established methodologies: insurance-associated emissions, assets under management (AUM), and local public sector entities. Belfius will monitor methodology developments. Reference values: AUM €34.7bn and local public sector loans/investments €18bn (as of 31 Dec 2024). Insurance-associated emissions are preliminarily deemed insignificant but not disclosed due to uncertainty.
- The section transitions to “Operational emissions” (2.2.2), noting that material impacts and risks identified via the DMA will follow.

nodes.title: Operational emissions
nodes.heading: 2.2.2. Operational emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As a result of the DMA, the following Impacts and Risks have been identified as material:
nodes.summary:
- Financed emissions overview (2023–2024): Detailed PCAF-based inventory across asset classes (mortgages, business and corporate loans, commercial real estate, equity and bonds, financial lease, motor vehicle loans, project finance). Year-over-year shifts include:
  - Mortgages: scope 1&2 emissions down (1,297 to 1,211 kt CO2e) with stable data quality (5.00).
  - Business and corporate loans: scope 1&2 up (2,221 to 2,353 kt), scope 3 up (14,717 to 16,933 kt), intensity stable at 80 tCO2e/M€ (quality 4.38).
  - Commercial real estate: slight scope 1&2 increase (633 to 655 kt), intensity ~99 tCO2e/M€ (quality 5.00).
  - Equity and bonds: scope 1&2 down (1,165 to 1,064 kt), scope 3 up slightly (1,067 to 1,134 kt), intensity ~319 tCO2e/M€ (quality ~4.34).
  - Motor vehicle loans: scope 1&2 roughly flat (268 to 267 kt) with improving intensity (180 to 168 tCO2e/M€).
  - Project finance: near-zero reported emissions.
  - Totals: In-scope scope 1&2 slightly down (5,752 to 5,721 kt), scope 3 up (15,784 to 18,067 kt); overall intensity improves (68 to 66 tCO2e/M€); PCAF data quality score stable (~4.75).
- Sovereign debt emissions: Reported separately to avoid double counting. Methodology per PCAF with four options (production/consumption, with/without LULUCF). Belfius adopts production-based in line with UNFCCC. 2024 sovereign exposure increased (gross carrying amount 10,472 M€), production emissions 2,919 kt CO2e including LULUCF and 2,993 kt excluding LULUCF (up from 2023). Grand total including sovereign debt rises to 8,713 kt (scope 1&2) and 18,067 kt (scope 3); data quality score ~4.78.
- Operational climate IROs: Material impacts/risks identified include own GHG footprint, role in energy transition, and physical/operational risks if adaptation investments lag.
- Operational emissions results (excluding financed emissions): Full scope 1, 2, and 3 accounting with category detail and data-quality ratings.
  - Scope 1: Down 12% YoY to 1,873 tCO2e; heating lower, company car emissions lower, refrigerants up sharply.
  - Scope 2 (market-based): Down 29% to 56 tCO2e; location-based electricity shown separately.
  - Scope 3 operational (market-based): Down 7% to 161,914 tCO2e. Upstream dominated by capital goods; minor changes across commuting, business travel, waste. Downstream (excl. financed) down 14%, with leased assets the largest share.
  - Total operational footprint down ~8% YoY (market-based 163,844 tCO2e; location-based 167,218 tCO2e).
- Energy consumption and mix: Total energy use decreased (21,664 to 20,294 MWh). Renewables share increased from 61% to 65% via green electricity; fossil share declined; nuclear roughly stable at ~1%.
- GHG emissions intensity: 2024 intensity 8.3 kgCO2e per euro of net revenue (both market- and location-based), calculated including scope 3 category 15; net revenue €3.259bn.
- Targets and governance for own operations:
  - Targets approved by governance bodies; implementation overseen by the Own Operations Desk with technical oversight by a Climate Technical Decision Committee (ESG and risk/data leaders).
  - SBTi-aligned methodology using 1.5°C scenarios where available; 2022 baseline; primary horizon 2030 with future milestones toward 2050.
  - Covers buildings management, fleet and employee transport, and Belfius Auto Lease client activities.
  - Belfius not excluded from EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks eligibility based on revenue sources.
  - Quantification of decarbonisation levers to be finalized in 2025.

nodes.title: Operational emissions - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.2.2. Operational emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As a result of the DMA, the following Impacts and Risks have been identified as material:
nodes.summary: This section outlines Belfius Bank’s material operational climate impacts and risks from its DMA, including contributing GHG emissions, participation in the energy transition, and the risk from not investing in adaptation infrastructure and technology, all within its own operations. It defines the operational footprint as scopes 1, 2 and 3 (excluding financed emissions) and provides 2022–2024 emissions by scope and category with 2024 data quality. In 2024, total operational footprint was 163,844 tCO2e market-based (-8% YoY; location-based 167,218), with Scope 1 at 1,873 tCO2e (-12%; heating 1,212, company cars 486, refrigerants up to 176), Scope 2 market-based at 56 tCO2e (-29%; location-based electricity 1,545, -8%), and Scope 3 operational at 161,914 tCO2e (-7%; upstream 97,631, downstream 64,301). Key 2024 Scope 3 categories include capital goods 86,712, employee commuting 3,504, business travel 630, downstream leased assets 55,169, franchises 8,362, waste 48; categories 9–10 are non-existent. Reported 2024 data quality: Scope 1 84%, Scope 2 13%, Scope 3 62%. Energy use in 2024 totaled 20,294 MWh with 65% renewable (all green electricity), 34% fossil, 1% nuclear. GHG emissions intensity was 8.3 kgCO2e/€ based on net revenue €3,259,288,443 and includes Scope 3 category 15.

nodes.title: Targets on operational emissions
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.1. Targets on operational emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius climate targets are developed first on emissions for which Belfius fully controls.
nodes.summary:
- Presents Belfius Bank’s 2023–2024 operational energy mix and consumption: total energy use fell from 21,664 MWh to 20,294 MWh; renewables’ share rose from 61% to 65%; fossil energy declined (38% to 34%); nuclear steady at 1%; biofuels/biogas at 0; green electricity consumption reached 96.3% of total electricity in 2024.
- Discloses 2024 GHG emissions intensity at 8.3 kgCO2e per euro of net revenue (location- and market-based identical), with Scope 3 category 15 included; net revenue used: €3.259bn.
- Explains governance and methodology for operational emissions targets: Board/JMC approval; Own Operations Desk monitors; Climate Technical Decision Committee advises on methods; targets aligned to SBTi using primarily a 1.5°C pathway; 2022 set as the baseline year; main targets aim for 2030, with further milestones to come; indicates alignment with EU Paris-aligned Benchmark exclusions on fossil revenue.
- Details decarbonization targets:
  - Absolute reduction: −42% by 2030 across Scope 1 (buildings, company cars) and key Scope 3 categories (upstream energy, waste, business travel, employee commuting, franchises). 2022 baseline 23,583 tCO2e; 2024 at 14,924 tCO2e.
  - Intensity targets: leased car fleet −50% gCO2e/km by 2030 (driven by electrification/fuel switching, supported by Belgian incentives); leased real estate −64.7% kgCO2e/m² by 2030 (data and control depend on tenants).
  - Renewable electricity: 100% by 2025 for head/regional offices, salaried agencies, Crefius, Elantis; two buildings still on grey contracts in 2024.
- Notes 2024 progress drivers: accelerated electrification of the fleet and switching franchises to green electricity.
- Outlines three-pillar action plan for own operations:
  - Responsible building management (Scopes 1, 2, and 3 for leased/franchise assets): energy efficiency, renewable energy procurement/production, climate adaptation, waste reduction, responsible water management.
  - Green mobility (Scopes 1 & 3): employee fleet, commuting, business travel, and sustainable leasing offers.
  - Sustainable IT (Scope 3): lower tech footprint, extend device lifecycles, refurbish/donate, awareness campaigns (e.g., digital clean-up), and e-learning on climate.
- Lists concrete building actions: monitoring optimization; relocation to a more efficient Crefius building; nanogrids in salaried agencies; solar panels at Elantis; planned heat pump at Rogier Tower; EPC analyses; franchise emissions reduction offers (DVV); platform to automate tenant emissions data for leased assets.
- Describes climate adaptation and resilience: annual assessment of physical climate risks to critical assets (e.g., data center), redundancy and continuity measures to mitigate extreme events.
- Confirms ongoing waste management measures to prevent waste, increase recycling, and ensure responsible disposal.

nodes.title: Belfius’ targets
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.2. Belfius’ targets
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius aims to reduce its own emissions by setting emission reduction targets.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Belfius’ operational emissions-reduction targets and actions, use of carbon credits, and treatment of climate and environmental risks.
- Three-pillar plan to cut own emissions:
  - Responsible building management (scopes 1, 2, and scope 3 for buildings leased by Belfius Insurance): energy efficiency and renewable energy, climate adaptation, waste reduction, and water stewardship.
  - Green mobility (scopes 1 and 3): employee commuting, company fleet, and sustainable mobility offerings via Belfius Auto Lease.
  - Sustainable IT (scope 3): lower tech footprint, extend device lifecycles, refurbish/donate equipment, awareness and training, eco-design/coding.
- Buildings and energy:
  - Target 100% certified green electricity in all owned buildings and operations by end-2025; increase onsite renewables.
  - Most sites on green electricity; actions include energy monitoring optimization, moving to a more efficient building, nanogrids in branches, solar panels; planned heat pump at HQ, EPC analyses, better tenant data collection.
  - Climate adaptation via annual physical risk/threat analysis, multi-site critical activity execution, and resilient technologies.
- Waste and water:
  - Paperless policy and digitization; waste sorting and recycling across sites; new eco-friendly catering (vegetarian options), replacing paper cups with reusable cups by March 2025, targets for composting/biogas and eliminating single-use plastics.
  - 2024 waste roughly stable vs 2023; residual waste up, paper/cardboard down, recycled and biowaste up; e-waste excluded due to leasing.
  - Centralized water monitoring; nanogrids for local offices by 2025; telework has reduced water use since 2019.
- Green mobility (employees and leasing):
  - Telework and mobility incentives reduce commuting emissions; public transport fully reimbursed; active mobility allowances; parking fees discourage solo car use.
  - Fleet policy: since May 2023 only BEVs can be ordered; early 2025 fleet ~29% BEV, 34% hybrid; full fleet decarbonization by end-2029. Dynamic EV catalogue and options for shared/rental cars; plan to offer second-life leasing in 2026; 1,502 home chargers installed.
  - Federal mobility budget: ~50% of eligible employees opted in after one year; extended to Belfius Insurance in 2024.
  - Belfius Auto Lease: target -50% average CO2 per car-year by 2025 vs 2022 via electrification and MaaS; partnerships for charging (CenEnergy), mobility app/payment/budget platform (Skipr) with CO2 reporting; bike leasing via Cyclis.
  - Business travel: small share; 6% drop 2024 vs 2023 due to fewer long-haul flights.
- Sustainable IT:
  - Technology ~0.022% of total emissions; measurement complex and influenced by business choices and AI.
  - 2024 actions: ESG KPIs for tech leaders, laptop lifespan extended from 3 to 4 years, 1,500+ devices refurbished for schools, climate e-learning for staff; eco-design/coding handbook created, to be developed/tested in 2025.
- Carbon credits:
  - Voluntary purchase to cover emissions under highest direct control (excluding Auto Lease, financed emissions, DVV franchises); disclosed but not counted as footprint reductions.
  - Credits canceled: 44,600 tCO2e (2023) and 30,500 (2024); 100% reduction projects, 100% Gold Standard; no EU origin or corresponding adjustments.
  - Monitoring market integrity (e.g., ICVCM); all past credits canceled; future focus shifts from carbon credits to carbon removal credits.
- Climate and environmental risks:
  - C&E risks identified as top risks for Belfius, consistent with WEF assessments; long-term climate risk seen as most significant.
  - Belfius applies a holistic approach that integrates social impacts alongside financial effects of climate and environmental factors.

nodes.title: Carbon credits
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.3. Carbon credits
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to emissions avoidance and reduction efforts, Belfius purchases carbon credits equivalent to the emissions on which Belfius has the highest direct control, namely own operations excluding emissions from Belfius Auto Lease activities, financed emissions, and DVV franchises.
nodes.summary:
- Device lifecycle and circularity: laptop lifespan extended from 3 to 4 years; over 1,500 older devices refurbished and donated to schools; company-wide e-learning launched on climate change basics and Belfius’ role in the transition; eco-design and eco-coding best-practice handbook created, to be further developed and tested in 2025.
- Carbon credits policy: voluntary purchases cover emissions under direct operational control (excluding Auto Lease, financed emissions, and DVV franchises); credits do not affect the reported footprint and are disclosed separately. Cancellations totaled 44,600 tCO2e in 2023 and 30,500 tCO2e in 2024, all from reduction projects, 0% removals, 100% Gold Standard, 0% EU, 0% with corresponding adjustments. Projects are in developing countries; Belfius monitors ICVCM guidance; all past credits have been cancelled; future focus shifts from offsets to carbon removal credits.
- Climate and environmental risks: climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, and resource depletion recognized as significant, long-term economic risks; C&E risks identified among Belfius’ top risks, aligning with WEF assessments; commitment to a holistic approach that also considers social consequences.

nodes.title: Climate and environmental risks
nodes.heading: 2.3. Climate and environmental risks
nodes.start_phrase: There is no doubt that climate change and environmental degradation (including biodiversity loss, pollution, and natural resources depletion) will have a significant and lasting impact on economic growth and prosperity.
nodes.summary:
- IT and employee engagement actions:
  - Extended laptop lifecycle from 3 to 4 years.
  - Refurbished 1,500+ older devices for donation to schools.
  - Rolled out an all-staff e-learning on causes/consequences of global warming and Belfius’s transition role.
  - Created a best-practice handbook on eco-design and eco-coding, to be further developed and tested in 2025.

- Carbon credits approach and disclosures:
  - Purchases cover own operations under direct control (excluding Belfius Auto Lease, financed emissions, DVV franchises); credits do not reduce the reported footprint and are disclosed separately.
  - Cancellations: 44,600 tCO2eq in 2023 and 30,500 tCO2eq in 2024; 100% from reduction (not removal) projects; 100% Gold Standard; 0% EU projects; 0% with corresponding adjustments.
  - Focus on Gold Standard-certified projects in developing countries; monitoring ICVCM and other guidance to strengthen policy.
  - All purchased credits have been cancelled; no stock held. Future shift from carbon credits to carbon removal credits.

- Climate and environmental (C&E) risk framing:
  - C&E risks identified as top risks, consistent with WEF assessments; long-term climate change seen as most significant global risk.
  - Social impacts are considered alongside climate, with a holistic approach to financial and societal consequences.

- Climate risk assessment methodology and use:
  - Regular assessments to identify risk drivers, assess vulnerability across assets/portfolios/insurance/activities, flag material physical and transition risks, and estimate potential impacts on profitability, solvency, and liquidity.
  - Flexible, phased-in approach given immature methodologies/data; no precise financial impact figures yet.
  - Physical risks: acute (storms, floods, fires, heatwaves) and chronic (sea-level rise, water stress, biodiversity loss).
  - Transition risks: policy, technology, market, legal, reputational.
  - Analysis spans the 5-year strategic horizon and longer terms.

- Integration into strategy and risk management:
  - Outputs guide credit and underwriting attention points, data collection priorities, ESG strategy development, enhancement of climate stress test scenarios, and additional mitigation measures/action plans.
  - Recognition that C&E risks affect Belfius mainly indirectly via financing, but also directly through own assets, insurance coverages, operations, continuity, and reputation.

- Next steps in resilience analysis:
  - Separate financial resilience assessments for Belfius Bank and Belfius Insurance, with a group-wide operational resilience analysis to follow.

nodes.title: Climate and environmental risks - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.3. Climate and environmental risks
nodes.start_phrase: There is no doubt that climate change and environmental degradation (including biodiversity loss, pollution, and natural resources depletion) will have a significant and lasting impact on economic growth and prosperity.
nodes.summary: Introductory overview of Belfius Bank’s approach to climate and environmental (C&E) risks, identifying them as top risks aligned with WEF 2023–2024 reports; defines physical risks (acute weather/natural disasters; chronic shifts like sea-level rise, water stress, biodiversity loss) and transition risks (policy, technological, market, legal, reputational), assessed separately over a 5-year strategic horizon and longer terms. Describes a flexible, phased-in climate risk assessment program to identify risk drivers across activities, portfolios, geographies; evaluate vulnerability of assets, portfolios and insurance coverages; flag material exposures; and, where possible, quantify impacts on profitability, solvency and liquidity, noting current data/methodology limitations preclude precise figures. Emphasizes integration of social considerations, and use of results to inform credit and underwriting focus for vulnerable sectors, prioritize data collection for high transition-risk counterparties, refine ESG strategy, enhance climate stress tests with deep dives, and design mitigation measures and action plans. Notes C&E risks affect Belfius mainly indirectly via financing, but also directly through own assets, insurance, operations, continuity and reputation; subsequent sections cover financial (2.3.1) and operational (2.3.2) resilience analyses.

nodes.title: Financial resilience analysis
nodes.heading: 2.3.1. Financial resilience analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The climate resilience assessments for financial risk cover the downstream value chain and differ per entity/activity.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Belfius’ climate and environmental (C&E) risk assessment framework aimed at identifying risk drivers, assessing portfolio and asset vulnerabilities, flagging material exposures, and quantifying potential financial impacts where possible.
- It adopts a phased, flexible approach due to immature methodologies and data gaps; precise financial impact figures are not yet provided.
- Both physical risks (acute events like storms, floods, fires; chronic changes like sea-level rise, water stress, biodiversity loss) and transition risks (policy, technology, market, legal, reputational) are defined and assessed separately.
- Time horizons include the 5-year strategic planning window and longer-term horizons, reflecting the expectation of rising C&E risks over time.
- Risk identification and assessment inform strategy and risk management, enabling monitoring and mitigation to ensure short-, medium-, and long-term resilience.
- Outputs are used to refine credit analysis in vulnerable sectors, prioritize data collection for higher transition-risk exposures, inform ESG strategy, enhance climate stress scenarios with deep dives, and identify mitigation measures and action plans.
- C&E risks affect Belfius mainly indirectly through financing activities, but also directly via own assets, insurance coverages, operations, business continuity, and reputation.
- The report distinguishes financial resilience (section 2.3.1) and group-wide operational resilience (section 2.3.2); financial resilience analyses cover the downstream value chain and differ by entity/activity (Belfius Bank vs. Belfius Insurance).
- Overall conclusion to date: while material, C&E risks do not currently pose a significant threat to profitability, solvency, or liquidity under the assessed scenarios; resilience is supported by a climate-aware strategy, robust risk framework, strong balance sheet, and reinsurance.
- Assessment approach: a two-step process—(1) high-level qualitative/quantitative materiality assessment; (2) deep dives and climate stress testing for material exposures to test resilience, capital adequacy, and adherence to risk appetite.
- Methodologies are aligned with UNEP FI, TCFD, supervisory guidance (ECB, EIOPA), and insights from NGFS, IEA, academia, and market best practices.
- For Belfius Bank, portfolio-level assessments by prudential risk category (credit, strategic/business, operational, market, liquidity) translate generic transmission channels (property damage, business disruption, income loss, higher costs/investments, lower profitability/asset values, inflation/productivity effects) into Belfius-specific financial impacts.
- Supplementary measures include portfolio climate stress tests on credit risk and counterparty-level ESG scoring via an in-house methodology.
- Forthcoming sections detail methodology and scenario use (2.3.1.1.1), results (2.3.1.1.2), disclosures on assets at material risk (2.3.1.1.3), and mitigation actions (2.3.1.1.4); the process flow runs from risk identification to materiality assessment to quantitative stress testing.

nodes.title: Financial resilience analysis - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.3.1. Financial resilience analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The climate resilience assessments for financial risk cover the downstream value chain and differ per entity/activity.
nodes.summary: Introduction to Belfius’ financial resilience analysis of climate and environmental (C&E) risks across the downstream value chain, with separate assessments for Belfius Bank (section 2.3.1.1) and Belfius Insurance (section 2.3.1.2). Overall conclusion: while C&E risks are material, they currently do not pose a significant threat to profitability, solvency, or liquidity under the assessed scenarios. Belfius applies a two-step approach: an initial high-level materiality assessment using qualitative and quantitative data, followed—where risks are material—by deep-dive analyses and/or climate stress tests to evaluate financial impact, internal capital adequacy under severe but plausible scenarios, and adherence to risk appetite limits. Resilience is supported by a climate-aware strategy, robust balance sheet, and reinsurance program. Analyses draw on UNEP FI, TCFD, supervisory guidance (ECB, EOPIA), market best practices, academia, and organizations such as NGFS and IEA.

nodes.title: Financial Resilience analysis for Belfius Bank
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1. Financial Resilience analysis for Belfius Bank
nodes.start_phrase: The financial resilience analysis describes the resilience of Belfius Bank’s strategy and business model in relation to climate change.
nodes.summary:
- Key conclusion: Climate and environmental (C&E) risks are considered material for Belfius but, under assessed scenarios, do not currently pose a significant threat to profitability, solvency, or liquidity.
- Strategic stance: Belfius expects to remain resilient and grow through a climate-aware strategy, robust risk management, strong balance sheet structure, and reinsurance program amid the transition to a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy.
- Assessment approach: Two-step process—(1) high-level, qualitative and quantitative materiality assessment to identify risk drivers and potential financial impacts; (2) deep dives and climate stress tests for material portfolios to quantify impacts, test resilience, and check alignment with risk appetite and internal capital adequacy.
- Standards and inputs: Uses UNEP FI, TCFD, supervisory guidance (ECB, EIOPA), best market practices, academic/scientific research, and insights from NGFS and IEA.
- Financial resilience analysis scope:
  - Portfolio-level assessments across prudential risk categories (credit, strategic/business, operational, market, liquidity) translating generic economic impacts (e.g., property damage, business disruption, income loss, higher costs/investments, lower profitability/asset values, inflation, productivity changes) into Belfius-specific financial impacts.
  - Climate stress tests focused on credit risk for selected portfolios.
  - Counterparty-level ESG assessment via an in-house ESG Score methodology.
  - Linked sections: methodology (2.3.1.1.1), results (2.3.1.1.2), disclosures on assets at material risk (2.3.1.1.3), and mitigation actions (2.3.1.1.4).
- Challenges and stance: Recognizes complexity of multi-channel C&E risk transmission and market data limitations; applies a flexible, phased approach and awaits further regulatory guidance.
- CERMA methodology (materiality assessment):
  - Conducted in 2023 with external climate and internal banking experts; covers short (to 2026), medium (2026–2030), and long term (2050); applied to the consolidated scope.
  - Reviewed at least biennially; not repeated in 2024 due to no material portfolio or hazard changes; scheduled for 2025.
  - Steps: qualitative identification of material risk drivers at portfolio level, followed by quantitative methods where relevant to find risk pockets and estimate potential financial impacts.
- Scenario design:
  - Transition risk: Belgian CORE-95 scenario (federal pathway to climate neutrality by 2050 with ~95% emissions reduction vs. 1990 and ~5% negative emissions), implying high transition risks.
  - Physical risk: RCP 8.5 “hot house” scenario (insufficient global mitigation, severe physical impacts including sea-level rise), used as a worst-case physical risk lens.
  - Additional targeted sensitivity analyses for specific risk dimensions.
- Forthcoming disclosures: Shares of assets exposed to material physical or transition risks and the bank’s mitigation measures are addressed in subsequent sections.

nodes.start_phrase: The financial resilience analysis describes the resilience of Belfius Bank’s strategy and business model in relation to climate change.
nodes.summary: Introduction to Belfius Bank’s climate and environmental (C&E) financial resilience analysis, outlining a three-part approach: (1) portfolio-level high‑level materiality assessments across prudential risk categories (credit, strategic and business, operational, market, liquidity) to identify sensitive portfolios and translate generic economic impacts into Belfius-specific financial impacts based on exposures, maturities, and risk profiles; (2) climate stress tests simulating the evolution of credit risk in selected portfolios under prominent C&E risk drivers; and (3) counterparty-level ESG assessments via an in-house methodology producing an ESG Score. Key risk drivers and transmission channels include property damage, business disruption, income loss, higher costs/investments, lower profitability/asset values, and macro effects such as price increases and labor productivity declines. The CERMA flow (risk identification → materiality assessment → stress testing) underpins the process. References: methodology (2.3.1.1.1), results (2.3.1.1.2), disclosures on the share of assets at material physical or transition risks (2.3.1.1.3), and mitigation actions (2.3.1.1.4). The bank notes data limitations, cross-risk complexities, and a flexible, gradual approach pending further regulatory guidance.

nodes.title: Scope and methodology of assessments
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1.1 Scope and methodology of assessments
nodes.start_phrase: The potential impact of C&E risks on Belfius Bank’s risk profile was assessed in 2023 with the support of external climate experts and internal banking experts.
nodes.summary:
- Belfius Bank highlights that climate and environmental (C&E) risks affect multiple financial risk categories via diverse drivers and transmission channels, making assessment challenging amid limited market data; the bank adopts a flexible, gradual approach and anticipates further regulatory guidance.
- Scope and methodology center on the Climate and Environmental Risks Materiality Assessment (CERMA), performed in 2023 with external climate and internal banking experts to gauge impacts across micro/macro channels and time horizons: short (to 2026), medium (2026–2030), and long term (2050). The assessment covers the consolidated bank, is reviewed at least biennially, was not repeated in 2024 due to no material changes, and is planned for 2025.
- CERMA process: initial qualitative portfolio-level materiality screening (considering time horizons, risk drivers, risk dimensions, and vulnerability clusters), followed by quantitative analyses where feasible to identify risk pockets and estimate high-level financial impacts.
- Scenario framework:
  - Belgian CORE-95 transition scenario: aligned with Belgium’s path to climate neutrality by 2050 (≈95% emissions reduction vs. 1990 plus ≈5% negative emissions), implying high transition risks due to the ambition level.
  - RCP 8.5 “hot house world” scenario: assumes insufficient global policy action, leading to severe physical risks and irreversible impacts; used as a worst-case for physical risk assessment.
- Additional targeted scenarios and sensitivity analyses are applied to the most material risk drivers and specific risk dimensions. Detailed assessments per risk category follow in subsequent chapters; non-financial risk is addressed separately in the non-financial resilience analysis (section 2.3.2).

nodes.title: Climate and environmental risks materiality assessment (CERMA)
nodes.heading: a. Climate and environmental risks materiality assessment (CERMA)
nodes.start_phrase: The potential impact of C&E risks on Belfius Bank’s risk profile was assessed in 2023 with the support of external climate experts and internal banking experts.
nodes.summary:
- Context and approach: Belfius Bank outlines the challenges of assessing climate and environmental (C&E) risks given data gaps and multi-channel transmission across financial risks. It adopts a flexible, gradual approach and expects further regulatory guidance.
- Scope and methodology (CERMA): A bank-wide Climate and Environmental Risks Materiality Assessment was performed in 2023 with internal and external experts, covering short (to 2026), medium (2026–2030), and long-term (to 2050) horizons. It will be reviewed at least biennially; not repeated in 2024 due to no material changes and scheduled for 2025. The process combines a qualitative portfolio-level materiality screen (by time horizon, risk drivers, risk dimensions, vulnerability clusters) followed by quantitative analysis where relevant.
- Core scenarios used:
  - Belgian CORE-95 transition scenario: ambitious pathway to climate neutrality by 2050 (95% emissions reduction vs. 1990 plus 5% negative emissions), implying high transition risks.
  - RCP 8.5 “hot house” scenario: insufficient global policy action leading to severe physical risks and irreversible impacts; used as a worst-case for physical risk.
  - Additional targeted sensitivity scenarios were applied to specific risk dimensions.
- Risk categories and assessment types:
  - Credit risk (enterprises & entrepreneurs): exposure-based and scenario-driven sensitivity analyses on loans and investment portfolios.
  - Credit risk (individuals): scenario-driven sensitivity on the mortgage portfolio.
  - Market risk: scenario-driven sensitivity on the trading book.
  - Liquidity risk: scenario-driven sensitivity on liquidity, buffers, and funding access/costs.
  - Strategic and business risk: expert-based risk cartography (competitive position, strategy, partnerships, governance).
  - Non-financial risk: expert-based risk cartography (own assets, operations, third parties); details in section 2.3.2.
- Credit risk detail:
  - Non-retail portfolios: sector-level, bottom-up analysis in Belgium-focused geographies, combining exposure analysis with sensitivity tests on sample counterparties and dynamic extrapolation across short, medium, and long terms.
  - Mortgage portfolio: scenario analysis of transition (renovation mandates/regulation) and physical (flood) risks. Stresses applied to:
    - PD via required renovation investments relative to borrower capacity.
    - LGD via collateral value haircuts for poor energy performance and flood exposure.
- Strategic and business risk detail: Qualitative assessment of vulnerabilities in competitive positioning, strategy design/implementation, partnerships, and governance; evaluates potential loss of customers, market share, and revenues due to external shifts and Belfius’ actions/commitments.
- Market risk detail: Recognition that C&E risks can trigger valuation shocks, higher volatility, and correlation breakdowns. Scenarios include:
  1) rising carbon prices; 2) Belgium–EU inflation differentials from uneven transition progress; 3) physical events affecting FX; 4) impacts on equity price/dividend volatility; 5) effects on corporate and sovereign bond values via credit and correlation trading spreads.
- Liquidity risk detail: Scenario-driven analysis of potential net cash outflows and buffer depletion transmitted through deposits, loans, credit/liquidity line drawdowns, and funding access/costs. Scenarios cover: 1) renovation costs affecting deposits/loans/credit lines; 2) C&E-related reputational impacts on loan production and deposits; 3) financing repairs after adverse physical events; 4) tighter collateral eligibility and higher haircuts reducing market funding and liquidity buffers.
- Climate stress testing for credit risk: Development of simulation tools and standalone climate stress tests, including a cashflow simulation model to quantify transition risk impacts on non-retail customers and investees.

nodes.title: Climate stress test for credit risk
nodes.heading: b. Climate stress test for credit risk
nodes.start_phrase: In order to better grasp the transmission channels of climate risks and quantify their potential impacts on the evolution of the risk profile of its loan and investment portfolios,
nodes.summary: This section of Belfius Bank’s 2024 Sustainability Statement outlines how climate and environmental (C&E) risks are assessed across key risk types and portfolios. It begins by noting potential losses of customers, market share, and revenues from shifts in the business environment and from inadequate climate actions. For market risk, it describes channels through which C&E risks can trigger asset price shocks, higher volatility, and correlation breakdowns, and defines five scenario analyses covering carbon price shocks, BE/EU inflation differentials, FX impacts from physical events, equity volatility via dividends/prices, and spread impacts on corporate/sovereign bonds (including correlation trading). For liquidity risk, it explains how C&E drivers could cause net cash outflows and strain liquidity buffers and tests four scenarios: renovation costs affecting deposits/loans/credit lines, C&E-related reputational effects on business volumes, funding reconstruction after physical events, and tighter collateral eligibility with higher haircuts. It details climate stress testing for credit risk: a cash-flow simulation tool for non-retail portfolios assessing transition risks over short, medium, and long horizons, focused on transition-sensitive sectors (Manufacturing, Energy, Construction, Commercial Real Estate) and UK Water & Gas bonds, under NGFS-derived Current Policies (low transition risk) and Net Zero (high transition risk) scenarios; and a mortgage tool projecting asset values and borrower creditworthiness under transition (EPC ratings, energy prices, renovation pace) and physical (Belgian flood maps with value haircuts) risks, aligned with NGFS pathways and emphasizing impacts to 2030 across Realistic Base Case, Net Zero, and Delayed Transition scenarios. Finally, it introduces an ESG Score for non-retail clients with turnover above €10 million to gauge sustainability performance and Belfius’s exposure to ESG risk drivers, independent of credit ratings and aggregating seven metrics into a single score.

nodes.title: ESG score
nodes.heading: C. ESG score
nodes.start_phrase: To objectively assess the ESG profile of non -retail clients, Belfius Bank has also developed an ESG Score, for corporates with more than 10 million turnover.
nodes.summary:
- The report outlines Belfius Bank’s climate risk assessment for (mid)corporates using a cash flow simulation tool that projects impacts from transition factors (e.g., higher CO2 and energy costs, green capex) across three horizons: short term (to 2026), medium term (2026–2030), and long term (2050).
- Initial analysis targets the most transition‑sensitive sectors based on exposure and CERMA results: Manufacturing, Energy, Construction, and Commercial Real Estate, plus UK Water & Gas for long‑dated run‑off bond portfolios. About 10 representative companies per sector were individually assessed.
- Two NGFS‑derived transition scenarios are applied: Current Policies (lower transition risk, policy status quo) and Net Zero (higher transition risk, ambitious policies to achieve carbon neutrality).

- For mortgage portfolios, a dedicated tool assesses:
  - Transition risks via EPC ratings, energy prices, and renovation pace under three scenarios aligned to NGFS pathways: Realistic Base Case (early, gradually stricter policies), Net Zero (rapid market shift over next five years), and Delayed Transition (policy delay, limited change to 2030).
  - Physical risks via flood exposure in Belgium, geolocating collateral to regional flood maps and applying value haircuts for medium–high risk zones. Simulations emphasize short–medium term impacts to 2030.

- Belfius developed an ESG Score for non‑retail corporates (>€10m turnover), independent of credit ratings, to assess client ESG performance and related bank risk exposure. It aggregates seven dimensions: client consciousness, exposure to ESG risks, ESG maturity, risk mitigation, overall performance, benchmark position, and forward‑looking plans.
  - Inputs are gathered through a client questionnaire, fostering dialogue on practices, challenges, and support needs.
  - Key Risk Indicators (KRIs), aligned with EBA practices, combine quantitative (e.g., CO2 emissions, energy use) and qualitative measures (e.g., policies, transition plans, targets, trends), with expert‑set weights and sector‑specific benchmarks. The model will be iteratively improved.
  - By 31/12/2024, approximately 400 companies/groups were scored; similar internal frameworks exist for Financial Institutions and Sovereigns.

- Risk identification and assessment conclude that climate and environmental (C&E) risks are material, but potential financial impacts for Belfius are manageable even long term, considering current and planned mitigations.
  - From an initial set of 46 risk drivers (33 physical, 13 transition) based on EU Taxonomy, UNEP FI, and TCFD, Belfius prioritized 17 physical and 13 transition risk drivers for deeper analysis, focused mainly on Belgium. The selection and methodologies will be refined as data and best practices evolve.
  - The section transitions into a detailed discussion of physical risks (A1 Physical risks).

  - Physical risks: a 1–5 scale with definitions for acute (CDP-based), future likelihood (IPCC-based), and chronic hazards (expert assessment), indicating when critical thresholds may be permanently exceeded.
  - Transition risks: a 1–5 scale tied to policy/regulation status and sectoral sensitivity to market/technology/reputation shifts.
- Notes three time horizons (short to 2026, medium 2026–2030, long to 2050) and an expectation of increasing C&E risks over longer horizons, especially physical risks; emphasizes dependency on transition policies and adaptation measures and the need for regular updates as data and methodologies improve.

nodes.title: Assessment of the impact of selected C&E risks
nodes.heading: b. Assessment of the impact of selected C&E risks
nodes.start_phrase: The results of the CERMA are presented in the table below.
nodes.summary:
- Part of Belfius Bank’s 2024 Annual Report (Management Report – Sustainability Statement) outlining climate and environmental (C&E) risk assessment and management.
- Defines a five-level sector sensitivity and likelihood scale (Very Low to Very High) linked to policy/regulation and market/technology/reputation drivers, with corresponding organizational response status (from “Not in discussion” to “Already in place and about to be strengthened”).
- Considers three time horizons (short to 2026, medium 2026–2030, long to 2050) and notes rising C&E risks over longer horizons, especially physical risks; underscores dependence on the pace and scale of transition policies and adaptation; commits to regularly revising drivers and transmission channels.
- Presents results of the Climate & Environmental Risk Materiality Assessment (CERMA) as a relative ranking; even the most material impacts are viewed as manageable since current/future mitigations are not yet factored in.
- Materiality by risk type:
  - Credit Risk: Significant. Transition policies, carbon pricing, and technology shifts could pressure revenues and costs in climate-sensitive sectors, triggering rating downgrades, higher cost of risk and RWAs; impact monitored via CET1 ratio.
  - Strategic & Business Risk: Moderate. Falling behind peers on sustainable products/strategy or negative market perceptions could lead to customer loss, profitability impacts, and a riskier client mix.
  - Non-Financial Risk: Moderate. Physical risks may disrupt Belfius and third parties; execution risks peak mid-term; long-term product/service substitution expected; legal and reputational risks may affect investors and talent.
  - Market Risk: Limited. Small exposures, short liquidity horizons, and hedging reduce potential asset devaluations and P&L impacts.
  - Liquidity Risk: Limited. Possible deposit outflows and liquidity buffer use would likely be gradual and manageable.
- Overall expectation that financial impacts remain limited, even long term, with gradual manifestation allowing proactive management to preserve a sound balance sheet and earnings capacity.
- Mitigation and strategy: ongoing and planned actions to support the Belgian transition, manage portfolio composition to reduce C&E exposure, and engage counterparties on transition pathways and physical risk adaptation; prioritization of higher-risk sectors for deeper analysis; further details referenced in the mitigation actions section.
- Next section signposts: climate resilience analysis on credit risk for non-retail portfolios, with sector-by-sector exposure review and risk driver importance (graph referenced).

The table rates Credit Risk as Significant, driven by policy/regulatory changes, carbon pricing and technology shifts affecting climate‑sensitive sectors, with impacts measured on the CET1 ratio via higher cost of risk and risk‑weighted assets; Strategic and Business Risk as Moderate due to potential lags in sustainable products, strategy misalignment, or unmet commitments leading to customer loss and riskier portfolios; Non‑Financial Risk as Moderate from physical disruptions to Belfius and third parties, medium‑term execution risks, long‑term product substitution, and legal/reputational effects on investors and talent; Market Risk as Limited owing to low exposures, short liquidity horizons, and hedging; and Liquidity Risk as Limited since potential deposit outflows would be gradual. nodes.title: Climate resilience analysis on credit risk
nodes.heading: B1 Climate resilience analysis on credit risk
nodes.start_phrase: The exposure analysis of CERMA looked at each sector individually.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from Belfius Bank’s 2024 Management Report – Sustainability Statement detailing climate and environmental (C&E) risk materiality, impacts, and mitigation, with a focus on credit resilience (CERMA analysis).

- Risk materiality by type:
  - Credit risk – Significant: Transition policies, carbon pricing, technology shifts and higher input costs could weaken client risk profiles, trigger downgrades, raise cost of risk and RWAs; impact tracked via CET1.
  - Strategic and business risk – Moderate: Lagging on sustainable offerings, misaligned strategy, or perceived failure to meet commitments could erode customers and profitability and elevate portfolio risk.
  - Non-financial risk – Moderate: Physical risks to operations and third parties; execution risk peaking mid-term; long-term substitution to low-emission products; legal and reputational risks affecting investors and talent.
  - Market risk – Limited: Small exposures, short liquidity horizons, and hedging capacity reduce valuation and P&L impacts.
  - Liquidity risk – Limited: Potential outflows and buffer depletion expected to be gradual and manageable.

- Overall conclusion: Despite possible credit quality deterioration from C&E risks, financial impacts on Belfius Bank are expected to remain limited even long term; impacts are gradual, allowing management actions to preserve a low-risk balance sheet and earnings capacity.

- Mitigation and strategy: Ongoing and planned actions include supporting Belgium’s transition, optimizing portfolio composition to reduce C&E exposure, engaging counterparties on transition pathways and physical risk adaptation, and deepening sector analyses per CERMA; further detail referenced in section 2.3.1.1.4.

- CERMA non-retail credit portfolios:
  - Transition risk is the dominant driver due to policy alignment, technological substitution, carbon pricing, rising raw material costs, and stricter EPC regulations prompting renovations.
  - Physical risks are material long term, especially without effective policies; key perils in Belfius’s markets include floods, heavy precipitation, heatwaves, temperature change, drought/water stress, and storms.
  - Sectoral credit risk outlook (short-, medium-, long-term):
    - Highest long-term attention: Residential Real Estate; Building & Construction; Manufacturing; Public sector.
    - Other materially affected: Commercial Real Estate (partly mitigated by efficient new builds, stronger collateral/provisioning/RAF limits/credit criteria and monitoring), Water & Waste (notably water utilities; partial insurance mitigants), Agriculture (high sensitivity; indirect/second-round effects despite low direct exposure).
    - Expected to remain moderate: Power generation (high renewables share, strong credit quality), Health (public support), Road transport (mitigation/adaptation via Belfius Auto Lease), Sovereigns (mainly European).
    - Limited impact due to small exposures: Energy, Air transport, Sea transport.

- CERMA mortgage portfolios:
  - Flood risk: Very limited share of mortgages secured by properties in medium/high-risk flood zones.
  - Transition risk: Properties with poor EPC labels present asset value and borrower affordability risks, especially under accelerated transition.
  - Socio-economic lens: Roughly 20% of customers may struggle to finance energy renovations (indicative, data-limited); Belfius plans a combined social and climate approach to support vulnerable households.

- Next section teaser: Begins analysis of transition risk drivers on strategic and business risk (details not included in the excerpt).

nodes.title: Climate resilience analysis on strategic and business risk
nodes.heading: B2 Climate resilience analysis on strategic and business risk
nodes.start_phrase: The results of the materiality assessment highlight the expected impact of following transition risk drivers on strategic and business risks.
nodes.summary:
- Sectoral climate risk assessment for Belfius Bank’s credit portfolio:
  - Residential Real Estate and Building & Construction: substantially material exposures facing both transition risk (notably EPC regulations) and physical risk.
  - Manufacturing: significant transition risk from technology shifts and resource constraints.
  - Public sector: direct and indirect climate impacts with methodological and data challenges for assessment.
  - Longer-term sensitive sectors: 
    - Commercial Real Estate: high sensitivity but mitigated by energy-efficient development exposure, stronger collateral/provisioning, new risk limits, and tighter credit acceptance/monitoring.
    - Water & Waste: high physical risk exposure, partly mitigated by credit insurance.
    - Agriculture: low direct exposure but very high sector sensitivity may create indirect and second-round effects.
  - Expected moderate credit risk impacts: Power generation (renewables and high credit quality), Health services (public protection), Road transport (mitigation by Belfius Auto Lease), and Sovereigns (mainly European exposure).
  - Limited impact anticipated for Energy and Air/Sea transport due to small exposures.

- Mortgage portfolio (CERMA) findings:
  - Flood risk exposure in medium/high-risk zones is very limited.
  - Transition risk: mortgages on properties with poor EPC labels are potential risk pockets for collateral value and borrower affordability, particularly under accelerated transition.
  - Socio-economic screening suggests about 20% of customers may struggle to finance energy renovations; Belfius plans a combined social and climate approach to support vulnerable households.

- Strategic and business risk:
  - Key transition risk drivers: market disruption (risk to revenues if ESG product demand unmet), policy and regulation (risk if reporting/prudential requirements not met), and reputation (financing activities and support for transition).
  - Timing: short-term effects from market disruption and regulation, rising medium/long term including technology-related risks.
  - Physical risks: moderate impact expected from acute events (floods, droughts, storms) via client financial stress and potential strategy adjustments; possible disruption to strategic partnerships; impacts expected from the medium term.
  - Governance and data: strong emphasis on integrating ESG into governance and investing in data collection/management/reporting for effective oversight.
  - Overall materiality on strategic/business risks assessed as moderate due to ongoing initiatives and governance integration.

- Market risk:
  - Overall limited materiality of climate and environmental risks given a small trading book and short liquidity horizons.
  - Potential limited effects on credit spreads (counterparty downgrades from transition/physical risks) and FX volatility (uneven country responses to physical events).

- Liquidity risk:
  - Largest potential impacts stem from transition risk on deposits via regulatory changes and market disruption (e.g., renovation-related outflows, reputational effects), expected to phase in over time.
  - Market funding and costs may be affected progressively by factors like higher ECB repo haircuts and tighter green bond criteria.
  - Physical risks could cause abrupt liquidity shocks, though not observed to date; long-term funding impacts expected to be moderate and manageable as events are dispersed over time.

nodes.title: Climate resilience analysis on market risk
nodes.heading: B3 Climate resilience analysis on market risk
nodes.start_phrase: The results of the climate scenarios suggest that the materiality of the C&E risks on the market risk dimension is limited, compared to other, more classic, market risk parameters.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Belfius Bank’s Sustainability Statement detailing climate and environmental (C&E) risk assessments across strategic/business, market, and liquidity risk dimensions.
- Strategic and business risks:
  - Key transition risk drivers: market disruption if ESG product demand isn’t met; policy and regulation risks from reporting/prudential obligations; reputation risk tied to financing activities and transition support; technology-driven risks.
  - Timing: short-term impacts from market disruption and regulation, increasing through medium/long term, including reputation and technology risks.
  - Physical risks: expected moderate impact from acute events (floods, droughts, storms), potentially causing client financial strain, profitability pressure, strategy adjustments, and disruptions to strategic partnerships, with impacts materializing from the medium term.
  - Governance and data: emphasis on embedding ESG in governance and investing in data collection/management/reporting for effective board oversight.
  - Overall materiality: moderate, supported by ongoing initiatives, monitoring, product/process adjustments, and ESG-integrated governance.
- Market risk:
  - Overall limited materiality of C&E risks due to a small trading book and short liquidity horizons.
  - Potential limited effects on credit spreads (issuer downgrades from transition/physical exposures) and FX volatility (real exchange rate shocks from unequal country responses to physical events).
- Liquidity risk:
  - Largest potential impact from transition risks on deposits, triggered by regulatory changes and market disruption, leading to phased/gradual outflows (e.g., renovation financing, reputational effects).
  - Regulatory/market changes may raise funding costs (e.g., higher ECB repo haircuts from 2026, tighter green bond criteria), with changes expected to be progressive, allowing adaptation and issuance of ESG-compliant securities.
  - Physical risks could cause abrupt liquidity shocks, though not observed to date; long-term market funding impacts expected to be moderate and manageable.

nodes.title: Climate resilience analysis on liquidity risk
nodes.heading: B4 Climate resilience analysis on liquidity risk
nodes.start_phrase: Results of the analysis indicate that the largest potential impact on the liquidity position of Belfius Bank could come from the impact of C&E transition risk drivers on deposits.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on climate and environmental (C&E) risks within Belfius Bank’s 2024 Sustainability Statement, covering strategic/business, market, liquidity, and credit risk dimensions, plus asset identification.
- Strategic and business risks:
  - Market disruption risk if the bank fails to meet rising demand for ESG products.
  - Policy and regulation risk tied to reporting and prudential requirements.
  - Reputation risk from financing choices and level of transition support.
  - Physical risks (floods, droughts, storms) expected to moderately impact clients and profitability from the medium term, including effects on strategic partnerships.
  - Emphasis on integrating ESG into governance and investing in data for oversight; overall C&E risk materiality rated moderate due to ongoing initiatives and governance adjustments.
- Market risk:
  - Limited materiality of C&E risks given small trading book and short liquidity horizons.
  - Potential limited impacts on credit spreads (via counterparty downgrades) and FX volatility (from uneven country responses to physical events).
- Liquidity risk:
  - Largest potential impact via deposits due to transition drivers: regulatory changes and market disruption causing phased or gradual outflows (e.g., renovations, reputational effects).
  - Possible increases in market funding costs (e.g., higher ECB repo haircuts from 2026, tighter green bond criteria), expected to phase in progressively.
  - Physical risks could cause abrupt shocks, though not observed yet; long-term impact on market funding considered moderate and manageable.
- Credit risk climate stress testing:
  - Non-retail portfolios (Energy, Manufacturing, Commercial Real Estate, Legacy run-off: UK Water/Gas) under a Net Zero scenario:
    - Direct costs hit chemicals and generators; indirect costs affect steel, CRE development, water utilities.
    - Capex pressures for transmitters and water utilities; demand affects gas; pricing affects CRE development.
    - Key drivers: corporate investments and energy prices; CO2 costs partly mitigated by emissions reductions; high sectoral sensitivity; results preliminary pending better data.
  - Mortgages:
    - PD and LTV are scenario-dependent; Net Zero may temporarily raise capital needs and cost of risk around 2030.
    - Delayed transition is riskier with a pronounced 2030 peak and heavy 2030–2040 shock as renovations accelerate; lack of early action leads to disruptive catch-up.
    - Misalignment with EPC targets could hurt volumes/margins and slow stock improvement, risking exclusion of vulnerable borrower segments.
- Identification of assets at material risk:
  - Assets with material physical and transition risk identified in the banking book using CERMA and stress tests.
  - Portfolio is >95% Belgian; data gaps persist, so a top-down sectoral approach and proxy methods are used; disclosures to improve as data/methods evolve.
  - Quantification currently focuses on corporate/business loans and mortgages.
  - Disclosures as of 31/12/2024, broadly aligned with Pillar 3 ESG.
  - Average weighted maturity: banking book 7.02 years; high climate-contributing sectors 6.48 years.

nodes.title: Climate stress testing for credit risk
nodes.heading: C. Climate stress testing for credit risk
nodes.start_phrase: The climate stress test exercise explored further the potential financial impact on the 4 most transition -sensitive sectors that were identified based on (1) the CERMA transition risks (MT - 2030) and (2) the exposures within Belfius Bank’s portfolio, i.e. Energy, Manufacturing, Commercial Real Estate – and Legacy Run -off (UK Water and UK Gas ).
nodes.summary:
- The section reports on Belfius Bank’s climate stress testing for credit risk, focusing on transition-sensitive, non-retail sectors and mortgage portfolios.
- For non-retail credit portfolios, four sectors were prioritized based on CERMA (MT‑2030) transition risks and portfolio exposure: Energy, Manufacturing, Commercial Real Estate, and Legacy Run-off (UK Water and UK Gas). Analysis under a Net Zero scenario finds:
  - Direct cost pressures in chemical and power generation.
  - Indirect cost pressures in steel, commercial real estate development, and water utilities.
  - Significant capex needs for electricity transmission and water utilities.
  - Revenue effects: demand risk for gas; pricing risk for commercial real estate development.
  - Key risk drivers are corporate investment decisions and energy price evolution; rising CO2-related costs may be offset over time by emissions reductions, but sensitivities are highly sector-specific. Results are preliminary and will be refined with better data.
- For mortgage portfolios, findings align with CERMA:
  - PD and LTV outcomes are scenario-dependent.
  - Net Zero scenarios could temporarily increase capital requirements and cost of risk around 2030.
  - The delayed transition scenario is riskiest, with a peak in 2030 and a heavy 2030–2040 shock due to a sudden surge in renovations, highlighting risks of postponing short-term improvements.
  - Misalignment with EPC targets could hurt volumes and margins, slow overall portfolio energy performance improvement, and leave vulnerable borrower segments underserved, raising social concerns.
- Identification of assets at material physical and transition risk leverages CERMA and stress test outcomes, focusing on Belgium (over 95% of exposures). Given data limitations, the bank applies a top-down sectoral approach, prioritizes areas with better data, and develops proxy methodologies. ESG disclosures will evolve as data and best practices improve.
- Current quantification centers on business/corporate loans and mortgage loans. Disclosures reference 31/12/2024 and are largely aligned with Pillar 3 ESG requirements. The average weighted maturity of the banking book is 7.02 years, and 6.48 years for sectors that highly contribute to climate change.

nodes.title: Identification of assets at material risk
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1.3 . Identification of assets at material risk
nodes.start_phrase: Based on the outcome of the CERMA and the Climate Stress Tests , Belfius Bank identified assets at material physical and transition risk within its banking book.
nodes.summary:
- Climate stress testing for non-retail credit portfolios focuses on four transition-sensitive sectors identified via CERMA (MT-2030) and Belfius’ exposures: Energy, Manufacturing, Commercial Real Estate, and Legacy Run-off (UK Water and UK Gas). Under a Net Zero scenario, direct costs weigh on chemicals and generators; indirect costs on steel, CRE development, and water utilities; Capex pressures transmitters and water utilities; demand affects gas; pricing affects CRE development. Key risk drivers are corporate investments and energy prices; CO2 costs may be mitigated by emissions reductions. Results are preliminary and data-dependent.
- Climate stress testing for mortgage portfolios shows PD and LTV are scenario-sensitive. Net Zero may temporarily raise capital needs and cost of risk around 2030. A delayed transition is riskier, with a significant shock in 2030–2040 due to accelerated renovations, highlighting the downside of postponing improvements. Misalignment with EPC targets could hurt volumes/margins, slow overall mortgage stock improvement, and risk excluding borrowers with lower refurbishment capacity.
- Identification of assets at material risk (physical and transition) is based on CERMA and stress tests, with focus on Belgian exposures (>95%). Due to data gaps, Belfius applies top-down sectoral screening and proxy methods; disclosures will evolve as data and methodologies improve. Quantification currently targets business/corporate loans and mortgages. Reference date is 31/12/2024, largely aligned with Pillar 3 ESG disclosures.
- Asset maturities: banking book average weighted maturity is 7.02 years; high climate-contributing sectors 6.48 years; residential property loans sensitive to climate events 15.6 years; commercial property loans 5.5 years.
- Physical risk assessment centers on flood risk (acute) in Belgium. Method maps collateral locations to regional fluvial, pluvial, and coastal flood maps (harmonized across regions), allocates exposure across multiple collaterals by value, and notes potential volatility from six-year map updates and future forward-looking scenarios. Residual risk is mitigated by widespread flood insurance (≈90% of households) and mortgage insurance requirements; past floods (e.g., July 2021) had limited financial impact on Belfius.
- Reported figures for assets at material physical risk (before mitigation): EUR 1,370m (2.27%) in 2023 and EUR 1,622m (2.58%) in 2024; gross carrying amount: EUR 60,351m (2023) and EUR 62,747m (2024). Share of loans vulnerable to flood risk remains stable.
- Certain datapoints are not disclosed (chronic physical risk, net revenues at material physical risk, locations of significant assets) due to insufficient data and immature methodologies; a phase-in approach is planned.
- Transition risk monitoring: since 2022, Belfius tracks the share of climate-sensitive exposures within its banking book, including relative to total loans and loans to non-financial corporates.

nodes.title: Assets at material physical risk
nodes.heading: a. Assets at material physical risk
nodes.start_phrase: The most prominent physical risk driver in Belgium is flood (acute physical risk).
nodes.summary:
- Focus on climate-related risk exposures in Belfius Bank’s 2024 Sustainability Statement, with emphasis on physical and transition risks tied to loans collateralized by immovable property.
- Average weighted maturity of climate-sensitive mortgage collateral: 15.6 years for residential and 5.5 years for commercial loans.
- Physical risk emphasis on flood risk in Belgium (acute risk). Methodology maps collateral locations to regional fluvial, pluvial, and coastal flood-risk maps (EU Flood Directive 2007/60/EC), harmonizes differing hazard/probability levels, and allocates exposure across multiple collaterals by collateral value. Periodic six-year map updates and potential forward-looking/adverse scenario integration may introduce volatility in figures.
- Reported figures reflect gross risk before mitigation. Residual risk expected to be much lower due to high flood insurance penetration (~90%) among Belgian households and mandatory home insurance for Belfius mortgage borrowers. Historic events (e.g., July 2021 floods > EUR 2bn insured losses) had limited bank impact: very few payment moratoria, no provisions, and no lasting decline in collateral values.
- Stability noted in the share of loans vulnerable to flood risk over time.
- Quantitative disclosures:
  - Assets at material physical risk before mitigation: EUR 1,370m (2.27%) in 2023; EUR 1,622m (2.58%) in 2024.
  - Gross carrying amount of relevant loan book: EUR 60,351m (2023); EUR 62,747m (2024).
- Non-disclosures: no reporting on assets at chronic physical risk, net revenues at material physical risk, or locations of significant at-risk assets due to data and methodological limitations; phased disclosure planned for future reports.
- Transition risk (B1) introduction: since 2022, Belfius monitors the share of climate-sensitive exposures within its banking book, benchmarking against total loans and loans to non-financial corporations.

nodes.title: Assets at material transition risk
nodes.heading: b. Assets at material transition risk
nodes.start_phrase: Since 2022, Belfius Bank monitors the share of climate sensitive exposures within its banking book (by comparing the amount of those loans against the total amount of its loans and the amount of its loans to non -financial corporations).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Belfius Bank’s assessment and disclosure of climate-related risks within its loan portfolio as part of the 2024 Sustainability Statement, with emphasis on physical flood risk in Belgium and initial monitoring of transition risk.
- Loan maturities sensitive to climate impacts: residential real estate–backed loans average 15.6 years; commercial real estate–backed loans average 5.5 years.
- Physical risk driver: Flooding (acute risk) identified as the most prominent in Belgium.
- Methodology for identifying assets at material physical risk:
  - Mapping collateral locations (residential and commercial) to regional fluvial, pluvial, and coastal flood risk maps under the EU Flood Directive (2007/60/EC).
  - Harmonizing differing regional hazard/probability levels.
  - Allocating exposure proportionally when multiple properties secure a loan.
  - Note on potential volatility due to six-year map review cycles and future forward-looking/adverse scenario integration.
- Risk figures (gross, before mitigation):
  - 2023: EUR 1,370m at material physical risk (2.27% of EUR 60,351m gross carrying amount).
  - 2024: EUR 1,622m at material physical risk (2.58% of EUR 62,747m gross carrying amount).
  - Share of loans vulnerable to flood risk remains stable over time.
- Mitigation and expected impact:
  - Around 90% of Belgian households are insured against floods; flood insurance is mandatory for Belfius mortgage borrowers.
  - Historical events (e.g., July 2021 floods) had limited financial impact on the bank: few payment moratoria, no provisions, no lasting decline in collateral values.
  - Residual risk expected to be much lower than gross figures.
- Disclosure scope and limitations:
  - Not disclosing data on assets at chronic physical risk, percentage of net revenues at material physical risk, or locations of significant assets due to data gaps and immature methodologies.
  - Commitment to a phased-in approach with gradual future disclosure.
- Transition risk:
  - Since 2022, Belfius monitors climate-sensitive exposures in its banking book, benchmarking them against total loans and loans to non-financial corporations, focusing on loans and advances to business and corporate counterparties.

nodes.title: Loans and advances to business and corporate counterparties

nodes.start_phrase: Since 2022, Belfius Bank monitors the share of climate sensitive exposures within its banking book (by comparing the amount of those loans against the total amount of its loans and the amount of its loans to non -financial corporations).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Belfius Bank’s assessment and disclosure of climate-related physical and transition risks in its 2024 Sustainability Statement, with methodologies, coverage, and key metrics for 2023–2024.

- Loan maturities of climate‑sensitive collateral:
  - Residential property: average weighted maturity 15.6 years.
  - Commercial property: average weighted maturity 5.5 years.

- Physical risk (flood as the main Belgian acute risk):
  - Method: Map collateral locations to regional fluvial, pluvial, and coastal flood risk maps (per EU Floods Directive), harmonize hazard/probability levels, and allocate exposure across multiple collaterals by value.
  - Volatility caveat: Regional maps are reviewed every 6 years; forward‑looking/adverse scenarios may change figures.
  - Results (gross risk, pre‑mitigation) for loans collateralized by immovable properties:
    - 2023: EUR 1,370m (2.27%) on a gross carrying amount of EUR 60,351m.
    - 2024: EUR 1,622m (2.58%) on a gross carrying amount of EUR 62,747m.
  - Mitigation context: Residual risk expected to be low; ~90% of Belgian households insured against floods; flood insurance required for Belfius mortgages; past major floods (July 2021) had negligible credit impact.
  - Non‑disclosures: No current disclosure of chronic physical risk assets, net revenues at material physical risk, or locations of significant assets; phased approach planned as data/methods mature.

- Transition risk B1 (corporate and business loans):
  - Scope/method: Top‑down mapping of counterparties’ principal activity to NACE; sectors A–H and L treated as high climate impact per ESRS; acknowledges limitations and ongoing bottom‑up refinement using ESG scores.
  - Climate‑sensitive loans as share of total loans: 23% (stable vs. 2023: 23%, 2022: 22%).
  - Monitoring of exposures to companies excluded from EU Paris‑aligned benchmarks (per Climate Benchmark Standards Regulation revenue/intensity thresholds for coal, oil, gas, high‑intensity power, and “significant harm”):
    - Classification via NACE and external revenue breakdowns; conservative approach where data absent.
  - Results (gross risk, pre‑mitigation) – Banking book:
    - 2023: EUR 1,512m (3.29%) on a gross carrying amount of EUR 45,938m.
    - 2024: EUR 1,502m (3.11%) on a gross carrying amount of EUR 48,286m.

- Transition risk B2 (loans collateralized by immovable property – EPC focus):
  - Residential EPC data coverage: 40.8% based on collected certificates; 43.3% estimated via third‑party proxy (address, type, year, surface); 15.9% unknown. New/under‑construction buildings not auto‑bucketed without EPC but expected to be highly efficient due to legal standards.
  - Commercial EPC data coverage: Much lower; proxies not used due to immature/less reliable methods.
  - Risk definition: Mortgages with LTV > 80% and poor energy efficiency (>400 kWh/m²) deemed at material transition risk.
  - Result: 3.82% of the mortgage portfolio (EUR 42,428m total) currently considered risky.

nodes.title: Climate Risk Assessment
nodes.heading: a. Climate Risk Assessment
nodes.start_phrase: Generally speaking, the climate risk assessment is fully updated at least once a year.
nodes.summary:
- Belfius monitors a quarterly ESG and climate risk dashboard covering: climate‑sensitive and fossil fuel exposures in loan and investment portfolios; mortgage collateral energy efficiency (EPC distribution and average energy intensity); flood risk exposure for collateral across mortgage, business and corporate loans; average ESG scores of rated corporates; shares of customers and suppliers with very low ESG scores; progress on ESG data collection and the ESG Action Plan; and key operational events (losses, litigation, penalties).
- The bank aligns with major international standards: International Bill of Human Rights, UN Global Compact, and OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.
- It supports the Paris Agreement and the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and publishes policies on human rights and responsible investment to ensure transparency and inclusive stakeholder engagement on ESG.
- A dedicated Financial Resilience analysis for Belfius Insurance assesses climate risks via an annual (or more frequent, if needed) climate risk assessment supplemented by a climate stress test.
- The analysis is structured across sections: methodology and assessment, results of risk identification and assessment, disclosure of asset exposures to transition and physical risks, and mitigation actions.
- Scope covers all asset and liability categories (non-life, life & health) and operations, with risk levels evaluated in the short term (0–3 years) and long run (beyond 10 years).
- Transition risks are treated as time‑constant across horizons, while physical risks are expected to worsen; scenarios used are NGFS “disorderly” (transition) and “hot house” (physical).
- The assessment follows a two‑step process: a high‑level qualitative/quantitative screening, then deeper analysis where risks appear material; confirmed material risks prompt additional mitigation measures and action plans.
- A standardized risk score (very high/high/medium/low) combines three metrics: exposure, hazard/event likelihood or severity, and vulnerability; data are both quantitative and qualitative, with expert judgment applied.
- Effort on vulnerability analysis is proportionate to exposure and hazard levels; if both are low/medium, detailed vulnerability analysis may be unnecessary.
- A climate stress test complements the assessment to verify the insurer’s resilience under a severe but plausible climate scenario.

nodes.title: Climate Stress Test

- Outlines the stress-test storyline: catastrophic Northern Europe storms and floods trigger abrupt EU transition policies penalizing GHG emitters, causing a disorderly transition, profitability hits (especially for carbon-intensive firms), higher energy and input costs, equity market declines, wider credit spreads, prolonged structural economic strain, deteriorating public finances, and rising reinsurance costs; shocks are sourced from supervisory scenarios and internal calibrations.

nodes.title: Results of risk identification and assessment
