nodes.title: - 2024 Sustainability Strategy - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.3 2021 - 2024 Sustainability Strategy
nodes.summary: This introduction outlines Caixa’s national 2024 Sustainability Strategy and the assessment of the 2021–2024 cycle, detailing an evolving, cross-functional plan to integrate ESG and lead sustainable financing in Portugal, including transition to a low‑carbon economy and social impact financing. The strategy is built on five pillars: Sustainable and Inclusive Financing, Climate Risk Management, Equity/Digital/Financial Inclusion, Transparent Governance Models, and Disclosure of Sustainability Information. It delivered 231 actions—covering sustainable product development, climate transition plans, employee training, and strengthened internal ESG policies—and established five targets monitored annually. The section also describes the institution’s strategic investment plan aligned with the 2021–2024 Strategic Plan and shareholder vision, totaling approximately €241 million in 2024, including about €78 million for the new head office deed. Investments prioritize technology and digital leadership, customer relationship improvements, and financing innovation and corporate technological development, with roughly €65 million in 2024 dedicated to digital transformation (expanding digital customers, remote operations, online contracting, app evolution, and open banking) to enhance service and efficiency.

nodes.title: Material Topics and Main Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) Impacted.
nodes.heading: 4.3.1 Material Topics and Main Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) Impacted.
nodes.start_phrase: To support the development of the Sustainability Strategy, a materiality analysis was conducted in 2021 based on a dialogue process with nine stakeholder groups, which allowed for understanding their expectations and concerns regarding Caixa's ESG performance.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines a 2021 materiality analysis based on dialogue with nine stakeholder groups, identifying nine ESG topics relevant to Caixa’s internal and external stakeholders.
- Maps each material topic to the most relevant Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and targets.
- Positions the SDGs as a core framework guiding Caixa’s strategy, with defined quantitative and qualitative goals to focus impact where the bank can contribute most.
- Describes implementation of the Sustainability Strategy through a bank-wide, dynamic action plan aligned with the 2021–2024 Strategic Plan, comprising 37 macro-initiatives and 231 actions.
- Highlights progress under the “Sustainable and Inclusive Funding” pillar, noting completion of key initiatives: creating an ESG-responsible financial product framework; issuing Green/Social/Sustainability-linked bonds; advising clients on sustainable debt; developing ESG products and financing lines aligned with the EU Taxonomy; establishing a Caixa-specific green/brown activity framework aligned with the Taxonomy; and integrating ESG performance analysis across all assets under management.

nodes.title: Implementing the Sustainability Strategy
nodes.heading: 4.3.2 Implementing the Sustainability Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: In this context, and to achieve this, Caixa has implemented a dynamic action plan that cuts across all areas of the Bank, with the aim of executing the 2021 - 2024 Strategic Plan.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and alignment: Caixa uses the UN Sustainable Development Goals as the strategic compass for its sustainability agenda, setting quantitative and qualitative targets to maximize impact.

- Strategy execution (2021–2024): A cross-bank action plan with 37 macro-initiatives and 231 actions reached a 96% overall completion rate in the final year of the cycle.

- Pillars and progress
  - Sustainable and Inclusive Funding (100%): Full delivery of ESG-aligned products, green/social/sustainability-linked bond frameworks and issuances, taxonomy-aligned product development, ESG integration in assets under management, and a Sustainable Financing Policy.
  - Climate Risk Management (89%): Strong progress with remaining actions focused on supplier ESG integration, biodiversity/offset collaborations, and financed emissions targets for priority sectors; carbon neutrality transition rollout ongoing.
  - Equality, Diversity, and Financial/Digital Inclusion (94%): Broad delivery on inclusion, gender equality, community support; pending items include full dematerialization of asset subscriptions, expanded health and well-being programs, and rollout of ESG e-learning.
  - Governance Models (100%): Policies, governance structures, leadership balance, and engagement practices fully established, including a climate and environmental risk policy and asset manager engagement policy.
  - Sustainability Information Disclosure (100%): Best-practice reporting, ESG ratings engagement, stakeholder materiality, double materiality adoption, and responsible ESG communication fully implemented.

- Key achievements by pillar
  - Sustainable finance:
    - First Sustainable Finance Framework (aligned with ICMA Green/Social/Sustainability principles).
    - ESG bond issuances: €500m senior preferred for green/social objectives; two green bonds totaling €800m for energy-efficient residential mortgages.
    - Dedicated financing lines for ESG upgrades, decarbonization, circular economy, EV/hybrid leasing, and InvestEU green investments.
    - Asset management: deeper ESG integration; multi-asset SRI fund reclassified to SFDR Article 9; recognition in The Banker’s Sustainable Banking Revenues 2023 (63rd globally, 5th Iberia).
  - Climate risk:
    - First Portuguese bank (2021) with an ESG rating model for clients across sectors.
    - Carbon Neutrality and Climate Risk Management Transition Plan with 2030 GHG targets and client engagement for portfolio alignment.
    - ISO 14001 Environmental Management System certification maintained at HQ.
    - Full implementation of ECB climate/environmental risk expectations, including a comprehensive external context scan feeding materiality.
    - Strong performance in ECB climate risk stress test and EU-wide EBA stress test (2023): CET1 at 17.97% in adverse scenario; 3rd lowest capital depletion among 70 banks, 1st among ECB-supervised peers.
  - Inclusion and community:
    - Caixa Social Awards (3 editions): 106 projects, >€2.2m funding; first social impact report for the 5th edition (2023).
    - Caixa Mais Mundo scholarships (4 editions): 1,130 students, €1.35m.
    - Volunteering and donations: 16,000+ furniture items and 1,565 IT devices donated.
    - “Sou Cidadão” program: 298 identity documents issued for homeless individuals to enable access to services.
    - Equality Plan launched; talent programs (High Flyers, Top Performers); broad ESG e-learning (climate risks, DEI, sustainable finance).
  - Governance:
    - 15 Sustainability Committee meetings over the cycle; refreshed Corporate Sustainability Policy and group ESG expansion plan.
    - Corporate Climate Risk Management Policy published; remuneration policies for governing bodies and employees updated to embed ESG criteria.
  - Disclosure and ratings:
    - Allocation and Impact Reports for sustainable debt (2021, 2023, 2024).
    - TCFD-aligned reporting.
    - ESG ratings and recognitions: Sustainalytics improved from 21.3 (2021) to 13.4 (2025, low risk; top 10% of banks); CDP Climate Change 2024: B; MSCI ESG: A; FT Europe Climate Leaders (2021–2024); Moody’s V.E: 52/100.

- Reporting basis (CSRD/ESRS):
  - First year reporting under CSRD framework; phase-in exemptions applied for certain indicators (to be reported by 2025/2027 per regulation).
  - Limited year-on-year comparatives due to the new framework; no material information withheld for sensitivity reasons.
  - Consolidated reporting scope aligned with financial statements across the Caixa Group (commercial banking, asset management, investment banking, venture capital), excluding low-materiality real estate holding entities.

nodes.title: Sustainability Statement
nodes.heading: 4.4 Sustainability Statement
nodes.start_phrase:
The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) aims to ensure that companies disclose 
sustai nability information that is reliable, comparable, and relevant for stakeholders to assess the non -
financial performance of companies.
nodes.summary:
- Reports on sustainable finance efforts, including publication of the second Allocation and Impact Report for sustainable debt in 2024 and information on projects financed.
- Aligns climate-related disclosures with TCFD to provide clear, consistent reporting on climate risks and impacts.
- Demonstrates ESG performance through external ratings and indices: steady improvement in Sustainalytics’ ESG Risk Rating from 2021–2025 (reaching 13.4 in 2025, placing CGD among the top 10% of banks), CDP Climate Change 2024 score B (02/2025), MSCI ESG Rating A (06/2024), inclusion in the Financial Times Europe Climate Leaders 2024 (also 2021–2023), and Moody’s V.E 52/100 (01/2024).
- Explains the basis of preparation under the CSRD/ESRS: first year reporting under the new framework (not yet transposed nationally), limited year-on-year comparability for most indicators, and no material changes beyond those stemming from CSRD/ESRS implementation.
- Uses CSRD phase-in exemptions, with some indicators deferred to 2025 and 2027; where ESRS lacks specific standards for material topics, discloses own indicators or uses GRI.
- Addresses confidentiality: acknowledges right to withhold sensitive information but reports that no such withholding was necessary; no exemptions used for imminent facts or ongoing negotiations.
- Defines reporting scope: consolidated Caixa Group (Commercial Banking, Asset Management, Investment Banking, Venture Capital); excludes specific disclosures for low-materiality entities (Caixa Imobiliário, Imobiliária Caixa Geral, Imobci, and Caixa Participações, SGPS); overall consolidation aligned with the financial statements except for these noted entities.

nodes.title: General disclosures
nodes.heading: 4.4.1 General disclosures
nodes.start_phrase:
The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) aims to ensure that companies disclose 
sustai nability information that is reliable, comparable, and relevant for stakeholders to assess the non -
financial performance of companies.
nodes.summary:
- ESG reporting and performance: Published 2024 Allocation and Impact Report for sustainable debt; aligned disclosures with TCFD; notable improvement in ESG ratings (Sustainalytics from 21.3 in 2021 to 13.4 in 2025; MSCI ESG Rating A; CDP Climate Change B; inclusion in FT Europe Climate Leaders; Moody’s V.E 52/100).
- Basis of preparation under CSRD/ESRS: First year applying CSRD; phase-in and comparatives largely not provided; consolidated group scope (commercial banking, asset management, investment banking, venture capital); methodology updates to Scope 3 (added category 15 for group entities; ceased reporting categories 5 and 6); information aligned with supervisory expectations and UTAM requirements; use of GRI/own indicators where ESRS not specific; no external validation beyond assurance provider; selective disclosure exemptions considered but not used.
- Strategy and alignment: Sustainability embedded as a core strategic vector in 2021–2024 plan; five sustainability action areas (financing, climate risk, inclusion, governance, disclosure); target of €1.5bn cumulative ESG financing in Portugal; commitment to enhance reporting quality in 2025–2028 cycle.
- Business model and value chain: Universal bank leadership in Portugal; strong 2024 performance (net income €1.735bn; turnover €165bn), growth in loans/deposits, market leadership in several lines; expanding digital/mobile customers; ESG-linked products and preferential pricing; broad international footprint; clear upstream (investors, suppliers) and downstream (customers, communities) value chain mapping; Sustainability Committee with cross-functional participation.
- Double materiality process: Structured CSRD/ESRS 2-aligned approach; defined time horizons; extensive stakeholder engagement (14 groups, 2,301 survey responses plus interviews); internal expert input; evaluation using severity/probability/magnitude/irreversibility and heat maps; periodic review plan and integration into strategy and risk models.
- Material topics and ESRS scope: Material per ESRS E1, S1, S3, S4, G1; topics include climate change, community support, human resources management, customer relations, digital transformation and innovation, corporate governance, ethics/conduct/compliance, sustainable financing and investment, risk management, privacy/data protection. ESRS E2–E5 and S2 deemed not material.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - Impacts: Negative—portfolio and value chain GHG emissions; Positive—talent attraction/retention, community development, responsible marketing, ESG financing/investment.
  - Risks: Physical and transition climate risks (including failure to meet GHG targets), HR turnover/talent shortages, evolving compliance risks.
  - Opportunities: Portfolio decarbonisation; HR development/wellbeing; responsible product alignment; digital/AI to enhance efficiency and CX; stronger ESG disclosure; new ESG products; integrating ESG in risk models; enhanced privacy/data protection.
- Due diligence and controls: ESRS-mapped due diligence activities (governance integration, stakeholder dialogue, impact assessment, mitigation, monitoring/communication); sustainability reporting risks and controls being formalized and embedded via the Sustainability Committee.
- Governance for sustainability: State-owned public limited company with Anglo-Saxon model (Board, Executive Committee, Audit Committee, SROC); Governance and Risk Committees overseeing sustainability and climate/environmental risks; CRO accountable for ESG risks; Corporate Support Department leading strategy and coordination across entities; local Sustainability Officers; strong board diversity, suitability, and training programs; Sustainability Committee (chaired by CEO) supervises strategy execution and climate/finance initiatives.
- Remuneration and ESG: Executive variable pay tied to multi-dimensional KPIs including ESG; Employee Remuneration Policy embeds sustainability, risk appetite, non-discrimination, and anti–mis-selling principles; Balanced Scorecard includes corporate ESG KPI (12.5% weight) based on Sustainalytics, CDP, MSCI; variable pay deferred over 5 years via instruments; commercial incentives aligned with risk appetite.
- Stakeholder engagement: Ongoing multi-channel engagement with customers, employees, investors, regulators, suppliers, and community; 2024 double materiality consultation integrated into governance decisions and next strategic cycle.
- Climate change (ESRS E1): Climate integrated into strategy and prudential risk categories; identified negative impact (portfolio GHGs), key risks (physical, failure to meet targets, transition), and opportunity (portfolio decarbonisation); alignment with ECB climate/environmental risk expectations and EBA ESG risk guidelines.

nodes.title: Environmental information
nodes.heading: 4.4.2 Environmental information
nodes.start_phrase: As a leading financial institution in Portugal, Caixa has robustly integrated climate challenges into its overall strategy and risk management model, in response to the expectations of the supervisor and regulator in these matters.
nodes.summary:
- Climate change integration: Caixa embeds climate considerations into strategy, governance, and risk management, aligning with ECB/EBA expectations and EU/Portugal decarbonization goals. Climate risks are treated as cross-cutting drivers of traditional prudential risks.

- Double materiality IROs: Identifies negative impacts from portfolio GHG emissions; risks from physical and transition drivers and potential target shortfalls; and opportunities via portfolio decarbonization.

- Policies and governance: Adoption of Climate & Environmental Risk Management Policy, Sustainability Policy, a 2050 Carbon Neutrality Transition Plan, and an Environmental Management System (EMS) governance model. Group-wide action plan to meet ECB’s 13 expectations and EBA ESG risk guidelines.

- Risk assessment and scenarios: Annual climate/environmental materiality assessment using short-, medium-, and long-term horizons; BES scan of macro, regulatory, tech, social, and geopolitical trends; NGFS scenario use—Net-Zero 2050 as central for transition risks, Current Policies for physical risks, with sensitivity to Delayed Transition.

- Transition plan and targets: NZBA commitment to net-zero by 2050; SBTi-based 2030 targets for own operations (Scope 1+2: -42% vs 2021) and priority sectors (electricity generation, commercial real estate, cement). Pillar III prudential targets set for 2026 and distances to IEA NZE 2050 2030 goals across electricity, fossil fuels, cement, and aviation.

- Implementation and monitoring: Climate strategy monitoring manual with KPIs/KRIs; no use of carbon credits or internal carbon pricing. 2024 progress reported by sector (e.g., significant intensity reductions in electricity generation project finance and commercial real estate; mixed results in corporate electricity and cement).

- Financed emissions accounting: First full Scope 3 estimate across 15 categories shows 99.5% in category 15 (investments). PCAF-based financed emissions calculated by sector for Portugal and other entities; 36% primary data quality.

- Environmental management and operations: 10 years EMS certification at HQ; new HQ under construction targeting BREEAM Excellent and Passive House (considering LEED/WELL for fit-out), with projected energy use/emission reductions. €122m invested in 2024 and €118m planned for sustainability-related capex. Asset management ESG initiatives (NZAM, Climate Action 100+) and launch of Caixa ESG Awards. Subsidiaries implement solar PV and fleet electrification.

- EU Taxonomy disclosures: Methodology for eligibility/alignment across counterparties and households; constraints due to data availability; application of DNSH through risk practices. Reported GAR of 4.0%, with households (mortgages/vehicles) the main contributor; improvement vs 2023 driven by better corporate data coverage and refined mortgage analysis. Ongoing plans to enhance ESG data collection and expand taxonomy-aligned products (e.g., Caixa ESG Credit Line).

- Social information – own workforce (ESRS S1): HR management anchored in respect, equity, inclusion, and well-being. IROs highlight job creation benefits, turnover risk, and opportunities in talent attraction/retention, career development, and psychosocial support. Key policies include Recruitment & Selection, Mobility, and Training & Talent Development, with a 2024 Training Plan aligned to strategic skills and regulatory requirements.

nodes.title: Social information
nodes.heading: 4.4.3 Social information
nodes.start_phrase: For Caixa, the existence of a management system focused on human resources and on a responsible leadership should involve all of the company's hierarchical levels, promoting the creation of an environment of respect, equity and inclusion, allowing the deve lopment and well -being of its employees.
nodes.summary:
- Scope of the excerpt: Social information covering ESRS S1 (Own workforce), ESRS S3 (Affected communities), ESRS S4 (Consumers and end-users), and the opening of ESRS G1 (Business conduct/Corporate Governance).

- Human Resources Management (ESRS S1):
  - Double materiality IROs: positive job creation; risk of high turnover; opportunities in talent attraction/retention, career development, psychosocial support, and work-life balance.
  - Policies: Recruitment & Selection (merit-based, global scope), Mobility (as a retention and development lever), Training Plan 2024, Training & Talent Development Policy, BNU Macau Career Path, Work Organisation Model (in-person/hybrid/telework), Equality Plan and DEI Policy, Human Rights Commitment, Anti-harassment Code. Executive Committee oversees implementation.
  - Talent attraction initiatives and results: Geração Caixa internship (5,415 applicants; 172 trainees in 2024; 374 hires since inception), expanded Mentoring to all new or newly appointed staff, university Open Days (250 students), Summer Academy (42 interns), job fairs and career days in PT/Macau.
  - Talent retention: Merit & Excellence Awards (337 total awardees; 60 in 2025 edition), robust internal mobility (2017–2024 avg. 18%; 2024: 1,181 moves, 19% rate).
  - Training and development: €3.7m invested in 2024 (+26% YoY); structured onboarding (“100% Caixa”), Talent Management (6,378 hours for High Flyers/Top Performers), support for Executive MBAs (54 employees, rising), Learning Hub (lifelong learning incl. ESG, health), leadership programmes (8,500 hours), “Upgrade” for front line (1,437 participants; 35,000 hours), 75% staff with at least one international certification, Board PEP on ESG, GenAI pilot planned for 2025, BNU Macau delivered 20,614 hours.
  - 1st Group Sustainability Week: alignment and capacity building across 8 geographies; 545 participants; 2,800 training hours; streamed to 8 countries.
  - Occupational health, wellbeing, and work-life balance: Employee Support Programme (575 supported), Health & Wellbeing partnerships, birthday leave, telework support for parents/caregivers, hybrid work (14% uptake), socially focused mobility, Life Balance talks, corporate volunteering, extra vacation day (55+ with 30Y service), extended maternity leave at BNU Macau (to 90 days), Healthy Enterprise participation.
  - DEI: four pillars (equality/equity, culture/diversity, generations/knowledge, inclusion); risks managed via communication/training, on-the-job knowledge sharing, equitable career management; Equality Plan updated annually (2025 edition live); maturity index 92% (+2pp), with progress on women’s promotions, zero harassment cases, and health/wellbeing initiatives; 2025 priorities: more women in management, deeper internal DEI literacy, family–work reconciliation, and external visibility.
  - Targets/metrics: active monitoring via Sustainability Committee; training investment disclosed; 2025–2028 HR targets to be set.

- Community Support (ESRS S3):
  - Strategy and governance: material positive impact through social/environmental/economic development of communities; embedded in Sustainability Strategy pillars; Sustainability Committee (quarterly) monitors; policies include Sustainability Policy (support to communities; alignment with PRB, NZBA, WEPs, UNGC, SDGs, etc.) and Corporate Volunteering Policy; Human Rights Commitment statement.
  - Third-sector support: Caixa Social Awards (2024: 44 projects; €1,006,630; 365 apps; nationwide; cumulative since 2019: 180 projects; >€3.7m); volunteer evaluators; impact reporting; award ceremony.
  - Corporate Volunteering: 827 employee volunteers; >2,254 hours; >47 institutions; Week of Active Citizenship; Group-wide action on International Volunteering Day.
  - Goods Donation Programme: 2,098 furniture items and 271 IT units donated to >48 institutions.
  - Group Christmas Campaign: €281,583 donated to 43 institutions; volunteer actions across six geographies; collections, blood drives, solidarity events.
  - Education initiatives: Caixa IU Programme (€10.1m to 120+ HEIs; tailored banking and 360+ prizes/grants); Caixa Mais Mundo Awards (€600k; 480 awards/scholarships in 2024; six editions: 1,410 students; €1.6m total); EPIS scholarships and youth inclusion projects; BNU Macau scholarships and training support; BCI’s support to Girl Move Academy (women’s leadership in Mozambique).
  - Vulnerable citizens: “Sou Cidadão” IDs for homeless (2024: 106; since 2019: 397; €15,365); Caixa Blood Donor Group (14,929 registered; 3,167 successful donations supporting ~9,501 patients; activity up vs. 2023); refugee student support (APGES: two master’s scholarships; Nexus: two Afghan MBA students); Timor “Natal ba Povu” (gifts and supplies for children).
  - Culture: Culturgest (115,000 in-person; >140,000 online; accessible pricing; EU projects Common Stories and Europe Beyond Access II; improved physical accessibility); Caixa Cultura Programme (7 projects; €100,000); Caixa Alfama Festival; Caixa Fado Festival in Angola.
  - Targets/metrics: 2021–2024 community investment target €40m; achieved €59.9m total (2024: €18.9m); diverse project-level KPIs; new 2025–2028 targets in development.

- Customer Relations (ESRS S4):
  - Material topics: positive impact from responsible marketing/sales (informed decisions); opportunity to keep adapting offer to needs; attention to data privacy, clear information, and financial literacy.
  - Governance and policies: Executive Board for Products oversees launches, compliance, and feedback; Product Governance & Approval Policy; Customer Complaints & Suggestions regulation; Quality Policy; Human Rights commitment referenced.
  - Customer experience and service improvements (2024 capex €17.6m): integrated CX/complaints/process quality under one area; new in-branch service system; migration to virtual tellers; instant debit card issuance and PIN recovery via digital; sensitive-process alerts; streamlined heirs certification, data updates, account closure, mortgage renegotiations; enhanced corporate lending platform and systems; stronger contact centre; bolstered fraud prevention.
  - Group initiatives: BNU Macau launched Google Pay; 69% rate service as excellent/good; BNU Timor launched a full-service mobile branch (BNU Móvel) to expand access; Banco Comercial do Atlântico deployed “Nha Bex” remote ticketing to cut wait times.
  - Market offer oversight: 66 products approved in 2024; Sustainability team consults to mitigate greenwashing; monthly tactical review of offer vs. regulation, competitors, and feedback; no identified customer harm events due to product/service features.
  - Financial literacy: Saldo Positivo portal (6m visits; 8.6m views; ~500k monthly visitors; 27–30 articles/month; 136k Facebook followers) covering ESG, budgeting, taxation, digital topics, and more.
  - Complaints management: ISO 9001-certified process; strong monitoring/reporting; Dec-2024 complaints volume 31% lower YoY; average response time under 4 working days; top issues: service (9%), fraud (5%), heirs certification (5%); process reorganisation and automation addressed pain points; BNU Macau complaints down ~6% with behavioural training.
  - Ongoing engagement: “Encontros Fora da Caixa” monthly events engage regional business and stakeholders.

- Governance (ESRS G1 – opening):
  - Emphasises the importance of a robust governance model for transparency, ESG integration across the organisation, effective disclosure, and stakeholder engagement.

nodes.title: Governance information
nodes.heading: 4.4.4 Governance information
nodes.start_phrase: In the financial sector, the existence of a robust governance model plays a key role in promoting transparency, especially with regard to the cross -cutting integration of the ESG strategic vision within the Bank and the respective disclosure of its perform ance to stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Customer focus and metrics:
  - Monitoring of complaints, customer experience, and satisfaction to guide improvements.
  - 2024 closed with 31% fewer complaints versus 2023 and positive evolution in customer experience metrics.
  - 2025–2028 Sustainability Strategic Plan will define corporate customer‑relations targets and metrics.
  - Continuous improvement via suggestion intake, top‑management reviews, and CO‑Complaints’ support for website FAQs, safety guidance, and multi‑channel contact (information requests, complaints, suggestions, compliments).

- Corporate governance for ESG reporting (ESRS G1 – Business conduct):
  - Emphasis on robust governance to ensure transparent, accurate, and stakeholder‑aligned ESG disclosure.
  - Double materiality analysis identified the opportunity to disclose ESG information aligned with best practices/benchmarks.
  - ESG embedded in strategic pillars (2021–2024 Strategic Plan and Sustainability Strategy).
  - Governance overseen by the Sustainability Committee (chaired by the CEO; meets at least quarterly).
  - Reporting frameworks: continued use of GRI and TCFD; began reporting under ESRS in 2024 to align with CSRD.

- Policies and internal regulations underpinning ESG disclosure:
  - Code of Conduct (truthful, clear, objective information as a core value).
  - Sustainability Policy (responsible communication and compliance).
  - Internal Regulation on the Management Report and Accounts (transparent non‑financial disclosure enabling peer comparison).
  - Internal Corporate Regulation on Executive Boards and Committees (formalizes the Sustainability Committee’s role).

- 2024 actions and oversight:
  - Board/committee supervision of ESG performance and non‑financial reporting.
  - Approvals/publications: 2023 Management Report and Accounts; updated TCFD report; sustainable debt Allocation & Impact Report; Social Impact Assessment for Caixa Social Awards; CSRD adaptation and IRO approval.
  - Identified reporting challenges: ESRS data collection strengthening, regulatory coexistence/timing, and CSRD familiarity across geographies; development of support tools and controls.
  - Alignment with supervisor expectations (ECB, Bank of Portugal, EBA), including Market Discipline (Pillar 3) disclosures and response to ECB climate/environmental risk guidance.
  - Internal control system based on the three‑lines model; Internal Audit integrates sustainability (governance, data controls, reporting compliance, EMS, climate stress testing) and plans expanded ESG audits.
  - Stakeholder engagement: 2024 consultation of 14 stakeholder groups across 8 countries, yielding 2,301 responses.
  - Internal capacity building: CSRD/Double Materiality workshop during Sustainability Week; Permanent Education Programme on integrating ESG into banking processes for top management.

- Targets and metrics for governance:
  - Sustainability Committee scheduled quarterly and held four sessions in 2024 covering Sustainability Report, EU Taxonomy, CSRD, and Allocation & Impact Report.

- Ethics, conduct, and compliance (ESRS G1 – Business conduct):
  - Material risk: non‑compliance with ESG regulations.
  - Code of Conduct and its Management Model (initiatives, annual indicators, and continuous improvement).
  - Anti‑corruption framework: Policy and Plan for Prevention of Corruption and Related Offences; conflicts‑of‑interest policy; gifts & hospitality policy; Internal Reporting System for Irregular Practices (SCIPI) with confidentiality and broad reportable scope (market abuse, AML/CFT, prudential rules, governance, etc.).
  - Corruption risk management via division‑level risk identification, mitigation measures, and annual implementation reports (2023, 2024, 2025 cycles).
  - Fraud prevention and management framework with monitoring, alerts, and coordinated responses.
  - Compliance function roles: advisory/second line; dedicated mailbox for cultural/ethics concerns; SCIPI for whistleblowing; investigations coordinated among Compliance, People Management, and Internal Audit.
  - Group compliance model: local Compliance Officers functionally reporting to Head of Compliance; Entity Compliance Monitoring & Reporting Model; ongoing risk assessments, deficiency remediation with deadlines/owners, and corporate regulation transposition with HoC approval.

- 2024 ethics/compliance initiatives and training:
  - Code of Conduct minor update adding social media conduct; APEE “Creating Value with Values” award recognizing ethical practices.
  - Internal communications marking UN International Anti‑Corruption Day.
  - Training for Group Compliance Officers (opinions methodology, compliance testing) and broad staff training across ESG, climate risk, cybersecurity, GDPR, governance, product marketing, and conduct.
  - Mandatory onboarding and biennial Code of Conduct training; by 2024, 76% of Board members completed Ethics & Conduct course.
  - SCIPI regulation updated (May 2024) and procedures re‑communicated.
  - Active fraud monitoring, analysis of incidents, and publication of alerts/recommendations.

- Ethics/compliance targets and performance:
  - 2024 external monitoring by Inspectorate‑General of Finance yielded an excellent rating on anti‑corruption and whistleblower regime compliance.
  - New metrics implemented for the Code of Conduct Management Model; annual results reported to top governance.
  - Monthly reporting to MENAC (from July 2024) on compliance status and corrective actions.
  - Ongoing Compliance Testing Programme per Bank of Portugal Notice 3/2020, informing targeted compliance visits.
  - 2025 plan to review the Corruption Prevention Plan and further update the Code of Conduct.

- Lead‑in to sustainable finance:
  - Introduction to the Sustainable Financing and Investment section referencing the Paris Agreement and EU sustainable finance policies and regulations as drivers for transition finance.

nodes.title: Other material topics
nodes.heading: 4.4.5 Other material topics
nodes.summary:
- Ethics, compliance, and anti-corruption: Caixa operates under a Code of Conduct and a Code of Conduct Management Model with annually assessed indicators. In 2024 it received an “excellent” rating from the Inspectorate-General of Finance for compliance with Portugal’s anti-corruption and whistleblower regimes. Since July 2024, Caixa submits monthly compliance reports to MENAC. A risk-based Compliance Testing Programme identifies issues and can trigger compliance visits. In 2025, Caixa will review its Corruption Prevention Plan and update the Code of Conduct.

- Sustainable financing and investment:
  - Strategy and governance: Aligned with EU climate policy (Paris Agreement, EU Green Deal, Action Plan for Sustainable Finance); overseen by the Sustainability Committee. Policies include the Sustainable Financing and Energy Transition Policy, Sustainable Finance Framework, Exclusion and Sectoral Limitation Principles, SRI and Engagement policies for asset management and pensions, and due diligence disclosures.
  - Impacts/opportunities: Positive societal impact via capital allocation; market differentiation through sustainable products; integration of ESG in fund selection; business growth tied to the low‑carbon transition.
  - 2024 actions and results:
    - Sustainable debt impact: 2nd Allocation & Impact Report—€2.2bn allocated; 9,475 SMEs in disadvantaged areas supported (impacting 30,876 jobs); 43,085 tCO2 avoided; proceeds linked to SDGs 7, 8, 9, 11. Three sustainable issues since 2021 totaling €1.3bn.
    - Capital markets: Caixa BI led 21 sustainable debt deals (e.g., EDP €750m green, Fidelidade €500m RT1 green, REN €300m green, GALP €200m solar, Greenvolt €100m green via retail).
    - Asset management: Two funds upgraded from SFDR Art. 8 to Art. 9; 93.1% of funds classified Art. 8/9 (>€6.3bn). Pensions integrated ESG across €874.9m; open funds Art. 8 total €118.9m.
    - ESG product offer: Launched Caixa ESG credit line (including real estate subline). New InvestEU lines with BPF for sustainable mobility and sustainable investment. International network launched green/ESG products (Angola ESG car leasing; BNU Macau Eco-Car; Mozambique Eco-Environmental line; Cape Verde renewable energy credit; Timor green lines; France green loans).
    - Exclusions/limitations: No financing of child/forced labor; restrictions on projects with negative environmental impacts or high natural-resource strain; sector rules to mitigate socio-environmental risk.
    - EU funds support: Enhanced PT2030 portal and partnerships for application support and preferential financing conditions.
  - Targets: 2021–2024 ESG financing target of €1.5bn exceeded—€2.37bn achieved. New 2025–2028 sustainable finance targets to be set.

- Digital transformation and innovation:
  - Focus areas: Data analytics/big data, AI/automation, process dematerialisation, new channels and platforms. Led by the Digital Banking Division and Analytical Intelligence Centre reporting to the Executive Committee.
  - 2024 initiatives:
    - AI Digital Assistant in Caixadirecta app: ~6 million conversations (+3% YoY), >245k unblocks (+16%), >235k balance/movement queries (+18%), >100k transactions; expanded to personal loan initiation.
    - Metaverse launch: Virtual, immersive engagement zones for corporate, youth, ESG, brand heritage, and culture.
    - Digital Talks: Ongoing internal program on digital trends and change mindset.
    - Branch dematerialisation: >11 million documents digitised; 84% digital signature usage.
    - CIAM rollout: Replaced matrix cards with app-based strong authentication, improving UX, security, and eliminating plastic issuance.
    - AI in CRM: Next Best Action/Offer integrated with Salesforce to personalise engagement and improve conversion/retention.
  - Metrics: 2.4 million active digital customers in 2024. New 2025–2028 digital KPIs to be defined.

- Risk management (with ESG integration):
  - Governance and framework: CRO-led, multi-committee oversight; risk taxonomy elevates climate & environmental (C&E) risk to Level 1 with subcategories (transition, physical, biodiversity/other environmental). Key policies: Risk Appetite, Risk Taxonomy, C&E Risk Policy, Credit Risk Policy, Healthy Origination Guidelines, Exclusion Principles.
  - 2024 initiatives:
    - C&E materiality assessment (June and December 2024): Quantitative, scenario-based, covering 92% of Group assets (97% national). Transition risk deemed material (notably for corporate credit and real estate exposures); physical risk costs material for acute events; biodiversity and social risks assessed as non-material at Group level. Post-model climate adjustments to credit impairments of ~€84m.
    - Climate stress tests: Integrated into ICAAP, budget, recovery planning, and transition plan; PD/LGD sensitivities by sector, EPC class, and physical risk geography.
    - ESG Rating Model: Upgraded March 2024 (adds water and waste indicators); portfolio exposure largely “Good” (55%) and “Satisfactory” (39%) at Dec 2023; won a national sustainability award. Added geolocated physical risk simulator; ESG Rating reports made available to corporate clients.
    - Credit risk enhancements: Extra due diligence for carbon‑intensive sectors (per Reg. EU 2022/2453), inclusion of physical risk mitigants (prevention/BCP/insurance, guarantees), and updated origination guidelines. Prudent mortgage LTV maintained.
    - Venture capital: Strengthened ESG due diligence for direct and fund investments.
    - Asset management ESG integration: Exclusions, best‑in‑class, engagement; internal CXA Sustainability Rating; monitoring Principal Adverse Impacts (SFDR).
  - Risk appetite metrics tracked: Revenue share from high‑GHG sectors; exposure to low EPC collateral (<=E); share of non‑financials with “Weak” ESG; biodiversity‑sensitive exposures. New 2025–2028 risk targets to be developed.

- Privacy and information protection:
  - Policy framework: Updated Personal Data Protection and Privacy Policy (Dec 2024), internal GDPR regulation, SNI governance with DPOffice review, Global Cybersecurity Policy aligned to ISO/NIST/DORA, Information Classification Policy, and Incident Response Policy.
  - Governance: Executive Board for Business Continuity, Operational Risk, and Internal Control (CDCRC) met 18 times in 2024; DPO and DPOffice empowered; Emergency Data Protection Team manages breaches.
  - 2024 actions: Bank‑wide e‑learning on personal data breaches; onboarding sessions; Group-wide DPO plenary; internal awareness for Data Protection Day; ongoing customer security alerts and targeted fraud communications; active handling of data subject rights and regulatory monitoring; participation in GDPR anniversary panel; IS/IT employee event; privacy by design/default in strategic projects.
  - International subsidiaries: BNU Macau annual cybersecurity and data protection training (462 employees + 25 new); new customer card control features. Banco Interatlântico instituted incident mailbox, monthly CISO meetings, and mandatory security training.
  - Metrics: 34 confirmed customer privacy breach cases in 2024. New 2025–2028 privacy targets to be set.

- Workforce indicator (annex): 2024 headcount—10,817 employees (6,468 female; 4,349 male).

nodes.summary:
- Privacy and information security initiatives (Group level):

- Annex A – Sustainability indicators (workforce and HR):
  - Workforce profile (2024): total 10,817 employees (Male 4,349; Female 6,468); average headcount 10,864.
  - Employees by country: Portugal 5,704; Mozambique 2,775; other geographies totaling 2,338 (notably China 485, France 554, Cape Verde 567, Angola 501, BNU Timor 140, etc.).
  - Contract types (2024): permanent 10,614; temporary 203; non‑guaranteed hours 4; methodology notes on definitions and data sources (HR system).
  - Talent attraction/retention: 645 exits; turnover 5.96% (vs. 8.30% in 2023); definitions of turnover and exits.
  - Self‑employed/contingent workers (Portugal): 1,139 FTE supplied by employment agencies.
  - Training and development (Portugal): 99% received performance/career reviews; average 89 training hours per employee; methodology for calculating participation and hours.

- Energy consumption (Group):
  - Direct energy in infrastructures: diesel and natural gas with totals reported by entity (group total c. 3,614 MWh).
  - Fleet fuels: diesel, petrol, LPG (group total c. 10,994 MWh), with note that EV charging is included in electricity use.
  - Electricity: group consumption 66,176 MWh (−6% YoY), detailed by entity.
  - Renewable generation: thermal 726 MWh and PV 22 MWh (total 748 MWh, −25% YoY).
  - Electricity from nuclear sources: 1,179 MWh (France and Macau contributions).
  - Methodology highlights: supplier mix, guarantees of origin, grid/location vs. market‑based factors, and estimation approach for nuclear shares.

- Greenhouse gas emissions (Group and Portugal scopes):
  - Scope 1: 3,996 tCO2 (↑11% YoY); breakdown includes stationary fuels, mobile fuels, and fugitive refrigerants.
  - Scope 2: market‑based 5,778 tCO2 (↓39% YoY); location‑based 10,533 tCO2 (↓4% YoY).
  - Scope 3 Category 15 – Investments: 3,381,894 tCO2 (↑4% YoY), with portfolio breakdown (business loans, CRE, residential mortgages, project finance, vehicle loans, other geographies).
  - Total emissions (Scopes 1–3): market‑based 3,391,668 tCO2; location‑based 3,396,424 tCO2.
  - GHG intensity per net revenue improved ~−15.7% (both location‑ and market‑based).
  - Notes: some entities lack data for market‑based electricity; reporting boundaries and targets for own operations (Scope 1 and 2 location‑based) referenced.

- Methodologies and assumptions (measurement and accounting):
  - Energy and fuels: conversion and emission factors by geography and fuel (APA, IEA, GHG Protocol); approaches for estimating reimbursed fuel; hybrid/EV considerations.
  - Fugitive emissions: gases and GWPs used (e.g., R134a, R410A, SF6) with sources.
  - Electricity emissions: supplier‑specific factors (e.g., Iberdrola 100% renewable), regional grid factors across entities (IEA, EDF, CEM Macau, EDA, EEM).
  - Financed emissions (PCAF):
    - Business loans: PCAF options 2a/3a/3b with data hierarchy, sector factors, and use of public disclosures; proxies for non‑Portugal entities based on energy consumption and grid factors.
    - Project finance (power generation): option 2b using production and technology‑specific factors (ERSE).
    - Commercial and residential mortgages: options 2a/2b; use of property valuation, area, energy labels, and PCAF European Building Emission Factor Database; proxies using price per m² where necessary in other geographies.
    - Vehicle loans: options 3a/3b; conservative 100% allocation until payoff; factors by vehicle/fuel, distances (NIR2023), electric vehicle method (kWh/km × IEA factor); 2024 methodological enhancement enabling vehicle counts; DEFRA proxies for selected group entities.
  - Clear definitions for indicators, scopes, calculation bases, and data sources throughout.

nodes.title: Annex B - ESRS table (European Sustainability Reporting Standards)
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.2. Annex B - ESRS table (European Sustainability Reporting Standards)
nodes.start_phrase: List of ESRS Disclosure Requirements met in the preparation of the sustainability statement following the outcome of the materiality assessment
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Annex B compiles the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) disclosure requirements that Caixa has met based on its materiality assessment, cross-referencing each item to the relevant chapters/pages of the sustainability statement. It also maps ESRS datapoints that derive from other EU legislation and indicates their materiality status. Annex C summarizes Article 8 Taxonomy Regulation KPIs for credit institutions.

- ESRS 2 General disclosures covered:
  - Basis for preparation (including disclosures for specific circumstances and due diligence statement).
  - Governance: roles of administrative, management and supervisory bodies; sustainability topics addressed by these bodies; integration of sustainability performance into incentives; risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting.
  - Strategy and business model: market position, value chain, stakeholder interests and views, material impacts/risks/opportunities (IRO) and their interaction with strategy; processes for identifying and assessing material IROs; list of ESRS requirements covered.

- Climate change (ESRS E1) disclosures:
  - Transition plan for climate change mitigation; processes for identifying and assessing climate-related IROs.
  - Policies, actions, resources and targets for mitigation and adaptation.
  - Energy consumption and mix; gross Scope 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions; GHG removals/carbon credits; internal carbon pricing.
  - References to detailed metrics in Annex A (Sustainability Indicators).

- Social disclosures:
  - Own workforce (ESRS S1): material IROs, policies, actions/effectiveness, workforce characteristics (employees and non-employees), training and skills metrics.
  - Affected communities (ESRS S3): material IROs, policies, actions/effectiveness, targets.
  - Consumers and end-users (ESRS S4): material IROs, policies, actions/effectiveness, targets.

- Governance/Business conduct (ESRS G1):
  - Governance body roles relating to business conduct.
  - Corporate culture and business conduct policies.

- Cross-regulatory datapoint mapping:
  - A detailed matrix links ESRS disclosure requirements and specific datapoints to related EU frameworks (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law), with page references and flags for material, non-material, phased-in, or not applicable.
  - Items include governance diversity and independence, due diligence statements, exposure to sensitive sectors (fossil fuels, chemicals, controversial weapons, tobacco), climate targets and metrics (GHG emissions, intensity, physical/transition risk), environmental topics beyond climate (pollution, water, biodiversity, circularity/waste), human rights and labor-related indicators across S1–S4, and anti-corruption datapoints.

- Annex references:
  - Annex A contains the underlying sustainability indicators (e.g., energy, GHGs, workforce metrics).
  - Internal chapter references point to materiality assessment, governance model, sustainability strategy, climate and social topic sections.

- Annex C – Taxonomy Regulation (Article 8) KPIs for credit institutions:
  - Presents the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock and flow with monetary amounts, coverage over total assets, and the shares of assets excluded from GAR numerator and denominator per Annex V rules.
  - Additional KPIs for trading book (n/a), financial guarantees (monetary amount disclosed), assets under management (0%), and fees/commissions income (n/a).
  - Notes the use of turnover- and CapEx-based KPIs of counterparties and the extent of asset coverage/exclusions.

nodes.summary:
- Annex C presents EU Taxonomy Regulation (Article 8) disclosure tables for a credit institution as at December 2024, focused on required KPIs and the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- Table 1 summarises KPIs:
  - Main KPI: GAR (stock) with reported amount and percentages (coverage over total assets, and shares of assets excluded from numerator and denominator under Article 7 and Annex V).
  - Additional KPIs: GAR (flow) with amounts and exclusions; Trading book (where applicable); Financial guarantees; Assets under management; Fees and commissions income from non‑lending and AuM services. Some items are marked n/a where not applicable.
- Table 2 details assets used to calculate the GAR, with a granular breakdown by:
  - Counterparty type: financial undertakings (credit institutions, investment firms, management companies, insurance), non‑financial undertakings, households, and local governments (where relevant).
  - Instrument type: loans and advances, debt securities (including use‑of‑proceeds instruments), and equity instruments.
  - Taxonomy tags: use of proceeds, transitional, enabling activities.
  - Environmental objectives columns (taxonomy‑eligible and taxonomy‑aligned): climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WTR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PPC), biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - Specific household exposures: residential mortgage loans, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans.
- The tables identify:
  - Assets covered in both numerator and denominator of the GAR.
  - Assets excluded from the numerator but included in the denominator (e.g., SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD, non‑EU counterparties not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on‑demand interbank loans, cash and other assets).
  - Assets not covered for GAR calculation (e.g., exposures to central governments/supranationals, central banks, trading book).
- Totals and reconciliations are provided: Total GAR assets, assets not covered for GAR, and total assets.
- Off‑balance sheet and other disclosures:
  - Financial guarantees with taxonomy‑eligible versus taxonomy‑aligned splits across environmental objectives, shown for current period (T) and prior period (T‑1).
  - Assets under management with similar taxonomy eligibility/alignment breakdowns; equity/debt composition where relevant.
- All figures are presented in millions of EUR, with side‑by‑side reference dates T and T‑1 for comparability.

nodes.summary: Annex C, Table 1 summarizes the KPIs credit institutions must disclose under Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation (reference date December 2024), including the main KPI Green Asset Ratio (GAR, stock) with a reported value of 2,515,387,100.88 and accompanying coverage over total assets and percentages of assets excluded from the GAR numerator and denominator (per Article 7(1)–(3) and Annex V Sections 1.1.2 and 1.2.4). It also lists additional KPIs: GAR (flow) at 1,050,823,359.76 with coverage/exclusion percentages provided, trading book (applicable for institutions not meeting CRR Article 94(1) or 325a(1) conditions), financial guarantees at 75,267,758.92 (2% coverage), assets under management (0%), and fees and commissions income from services other than lending and AuM (n/a). Footnotes clarify KPI coverage as a share of total assets, indicate that KPIs can be based on counterparties’ Turnover or CapEx, and specify applicability conditions and scope of fee/commission disclosures.

nodes.start_phrase: GAR - Covered assets in both numerator and denominator
nodes.summary:
- The extract presents detailed EU Taxonomy reporting focused on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- Table 2 – Assets for the calculation of GAR:
  - Scope and structure:
    - Covered assets included in both numerator and denominator, split by counterparty type (financial undertakings, credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households).
    - Instrument breakdown: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds), equity instruments.
    - Flags for Use of Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
    - Environmental objective columns: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
    - “Of which” lines for taxonomy-relevant sectors (taxonomy-eligible) and taxonomy-aligned portions.
    - Comparative view for Reference Date T and T-1, with values in millions of euros.
  - Key portfolio segments highlighted:
    - Financial undertakings (including credit institutions and investment firms) with detailed split by loans, debt securities, and equity.
    - Non-financial undertakings with notable use-of-proceeds and enabling activity amounts.
    - Households, dominated by loans collateralised by residential property, and explicit sub-categories for building renovation loans and motor vehicle loans.
    - Local governments financing lines shown as zero.
  - Exclusions and denominator-only items:
    - Assets excluded from the GAR numerator but included in the denominator: SMEs and non-financial corporates not subject to NFRD, non-EU counterparties without NFRD obligations, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, cash and cash-related assets, and other assets (e.g., goodwill, commodities).
  - Totals:
    - Total GAR assets (for both T and T-1), assets not covered for GAR (central governments and supranationals, central banks, trading book), and overall total assets.
- Off-balance-sheet and ancillary disclosures:
  - “Posições em risco extrapatrimoniais” (off-balance-sheet exposures), notably financial guarantees with taxonomy-eligible/aligned splits for T and T-1.
  - Assets under management (AUM), including “of which equity instruments,” with taxonomy-eligible/aligned details.
- Table 3 – GAR sector information:
  - Sectoral breakdown by NACE (including 4-digit codes and labels) of gross carrying amounts and the portion environmentally sustainable (primarily CCM).
  - Examples listed for Agriculture, forestry and fishing (A) and Mining and quarrying (B) subsectors, largely showing zeros, and an aggregate sectoral view.
- Presentation notes:
  - Bilingual elements (English and Portuguese) and consistent unit reporting in millions of euros.
  - Emphasis on taxonomy eligibility versus alignment across objectives and activity types, and comparison between current and prior reference dates.

nodes.title: GAR sector information
nodes.heading: Table 3 – GAR sector information
nodes.summary: This section provides comprehensive EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures across NACE sectors A–S, combining Table 2 asset coverage and Table 3 sectoral breakdown. Table 2 details assets in the numerator and denominator by counterparty type (financial and non-financial undertakings, households, etc.) and instrument (loans and advances, debt securities including use of proceeds, equity), flags transitional and enabling activities, maps to environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO), presents “of which” taxonomy-eligible and aligned amounts, lists exclusions included only in the denominator (e.g., SMEs/non-EU without NFRD, derivatives, cash, other assets), and shows totals and items not covered, all with T vs T-1 comparisons in millions of euros. Key segments include financial undertakings, non-financial corporates with use-of-proceeds and enabling activity amounts, and households (residential mortgages, building renovation and motor vehicle loans), with local government financing reported as zero. Off-balance-sheet exposures (notably financial guarantees) and assets under management, including equity, are also disclosed with eligible/aligned splits for T and T-1. Table 3 provides a NACE 4-digit sectoral view of gross carrying amounts and environmentally sustainable portions (primarily CCM), with examples such as Agriculture and Mining often showing zeros, plus an aggregate sector view, presented bilingually (English/Portuguese).

nodes.heading: Table 3 – GAR sector information
nodes.summary:
- The extract presents detailed EU Taxonomy reporting focused on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- Table 2 – Assets for the calculation of GAR:
  - Scope and structure:
    - Covered assets included in both numerator and denominator, split by counterparty type (financial undertakings, credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households).
    - Instrument breakdown: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds), equity instruments.
    - Flags for Use of Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
    - Environmental objective columns: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
    - “Of which” lines for taxonomy-relevant sectors (taxonomy-eligible) and taxonomy-aligned portions.
    - Comparative view for Reference Date T and T-1, with values in millions of euros.
  - Key portfolio segments highlighted:
    - Financial undertakings (including credit institutions and investment firms) with detailed split by loans, debt securities, and equity.
    - Non-financial undertakings with notable use-of-proceeds and enabling activity amounts.
    - Households, dominated by loans collateralised by residential property, and explicit sub-categories for building renovation loans and motor vehicle loans.
    - Local governments financing lines shown as zero.
  - Exclusions and denominator-only items:
    - Assets excluded from the GAR numerator but included in the denominator: SMEs and non-financial corporates not subject to NFRD, non-EU counterparties without NFRD obligations, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, cash and cash-related assets, and other assets (e.g., goodwill, commodities).
  - Totals:
    - Total GAR assets (for both T and T-1), assets not covered for GAR (central governments and supranationals, central banks, trading book), and overall total assets.
- Off-balance-sheet and ancillary disclosures:
  - “Posições em risco extrapatrimoniais” (off-balance-sheet exposures), notably financial guarantees with taxonomy-eligible/aligned splits for T and T-1.
  - Assets under management (AUM), including “of which equity instruments,” with taxonomy-eligible/aligned details.
- Table 3 – GAR sector information:
  - Sectoral breakdown by NACE (including 4-digit codes and labels) of gross carrying amounts and the portion environmentally sustainable (primarily CCM).
  - Examples listed for Agriculture, forestry and fishing (A) and Mining and quarrying (B) subsectors, largely showing zeros, and an aggregate sectoral view.
- Presentation notes:
  - Bilingual elements (English and Portuguese) and consistent unit reporting in millions of euros.
  - Emphasis on taxonomy eligibility versus alignment across objectives and activity types, and comparison between current and prior reference dates.

nodes.summary:
- Presents Table 4 and Table 5 with the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI stock for Turnover and Capex.
- Reports, for both numerator and denominator, the coverage of assets considered in the GAR, including the proportion of total assets covered and totals for “Loans and advances, debt securities and equity instruments not HfT eligible for GAR calculation.”
- Provides a granular EU Taxonomy breakdown by:
  - Environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - Taxonomy status: taxonomy-eligible (“towards taxonomy-relevant sectors”) vs. taxonomy-aligned (“environmentally sustainable”).
  - Activity flags: Use-of-Proceeds (UoP), transitional, and enabling activities.
- Disaggregates exposures by instrument and counterparty:
  - Instruments: loans and advances, debt securities (including UoP instruments), and equity instruments.
  - Counterparties: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households.
- Includes detailed retail/real estate categories within households:
  - Loans collateralised by residential immovable property, building renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans.
- Covers public sector and other items:
  - Local government financing, housing financing, other local government financing, and collateral obtained (residential and commercial immovable property).
- Presents figures for two disclosure reference dates (current period T and prior period T-1) to enable year-on-year comparison of eligibility, alignment, enabling/transitional shares, and overall asset coverage.
- High-level signals from the data:
  - A large share of covered assets relates to households, notably residential real estate; building renovation and motor vehicle loans are highlighted as taxonomy-relevant subsegments.
  - Exposures to non-financial undertakings (particularly via debt securities) show notable taxonomy-eligible shares; taxonomy-aligned shares are generally low across many segments.
  - Overall GAR coverage of total assets is reported (around the high-50% range), with detailed percentage contributions by objective, instrument, and counterparty.

nodes.start_phrase: The CaixaBank Group continues focusing on improving the information it discloses on sustainability, which is in line with its aim of being the leader in sustainability in Europe.
nodes.summary: This excerpt outlines the Sustainability Information section of the 2024 Management Report, structured around the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). It covers the basis for preparation, sustainability governance, strategy and business model, and a materiality analysis. The environmental pillar focuses on climate change (including processes to identify and assess climate-related impacts, risks and opportunities) and EU Green Taxonomy alignment. The social pillar addresses the own workforce, affected communities, and customers. The governance pillar details corporate culture and conduct, mechanisms to detect and investigate illicit behavior, anti-corruption and bribery measures, political influence and lobbying, supplier relationship management, payment practices, and tax transparency. Additional sections span sustainable finance (ESG risk management, sustainable business, responsible investment, ESG indices/ratings, memberships and alliances) and cybersecurity.

nodes.title: ESRS 2-General Introduction
nodes.heading: ESRS 2-General Introduction
nodes.start_phrase:
The CaixaBank Group continues focusing on improving the 
information it discloses on sustainability, which is in line with its 
aim of being the leader in sustainability in Europe.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines CaixaBank Group’s 2024 Management Report section on Sustainability Information, structured for the first time under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) to meet Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) requirements alongside Spain’s Law 11/2018. It details the report’s basis for preparation, sustainability governance, strategy and business model, and a materiality analysis. The content spans:

- Environment: climate change (E1) and alignment with the EU Green Taxonomy.
- Social: own workforce, affected communities, and customers.
- Governance: processes to identify and assess climate-related impacts, risks and opportunities; corporate culture and conduct policies; mechanisms to detect and investigate illicit behaviour; anti-corruption and anti-bribery measures; political influence and lobbying; supplier relationship management; payment practices; and tax transparency.
- Sustainable finance: sustainability/ESG risk management, sustainable business activities, responsible investment, ESG indices and ratings, and memberships/alliances.
- Cybersecurity.

The introduction emphasizes enhanced transparency and continuity with prior frameworks (GRI, SASB, TCFD, IIRC) to aid comparability with 2023 reporting. It also notes inclusion of additional disclosures responsive to rating agencies, analysts, and other stakeholders.

nodes.start_phrase:
The contents of this report address the material
