nodes.title: Locked-in emissions
nodes.heading: 1.6.4.3.1 Locked-in emissions
nodes.start_phrase: In relation to the locked-in emissions from its financing or investment activity, CaixaBank has carried out a qualitative assessment where no locked-in emissions subsequent to 2050 and related to financial products and assets from carbon intensive sectors have been detected.
nodes.summary:
- Explains PCAF’s data quality scoring system for financed emissions (1 = highest quality, verified company data; 5 = lowest quality, sectoral estimates using PCAF factors).
- Presents 2024 data quality scores by asset class (e.g., mortgages, commercial real estate, corporate fixed income, equity, vehicles, corporate finance, sovereign debt), distinguishing Scope 1+2 and Scope 3; notes that sovereign debt reporting here covers only Scope 1.
- States that 32.5% of 2024 financed absolute emissions (Scopes 1, 2, and 3) were calculated using the best possible data quality (score 1).
- Provides a reference to the PCAF Global GHG Accounting & Reporting Standard.
- Describes CaixaBank’s qualitative assessment of “locked-in” emissions from financing/investment, finding no locked-in emissions beyond 2050 related to carbon-intensive sectors at this time.
- Commits to revisiting the locked-in emissions analysis as counterparties begin reporting under ESRS; if material, CaixaBank will develop a plan to quantify and manage them.
- Outlines existing controls to limit post-2050 locked-in emissions: 
  - Sustainability principles and policies (coal phase-out; limits on new oil and gas risks).
  - Decarbonisation target levers (gradual reduction of exposure to carbon-intensive activities and derisking counterparties not committed to transition).

nodes.title: Financed footprint insurance business
nodes.heading: 1.6.4.4 Financed footprint insurance business
nodes.start_phrase: By calculating the carbon footprint of the corporate investments portfolio of the Group's insurance activity, a specific monitoring of the exposure to carbon-intensive sectors and its evolution can be carried out.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines how the Group measures the financed carbon footprint of its insurance business’s corporate investment portfolio to monitor exposure to carbon‑intensive sectors and track its evolution over time.
- It applies the PCAF financed emissions methodology, using aggregated data from investee companies; ESG information is sourced from external providers based on companies’ public disclosures.
- The analysis focuses on understanding the portfolio’s contribution to overall emissions and assessing progress against specific climate commitments.
- Scope and perimeter: financed carbon footprint reported under Scope 3, Category 15 (Investments) for the insurance perimeter; the NZAOA perimeter covers corporate assets within the insurance portfolio.
- Reported metrics include financed emissions of 29,545 tCO2e and an intensity metric per €M invested based on investees’ Scopes 1 and 2, showing a 24% reduction versus 2023.
- Context: part of the Management Report 2024.

nodes.title: Environmental Management Plan
nodes.heading: 1.6.5 Environmental Management Plan
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank has a direct environmental impact due to the use of natural resources.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines CaixaBank’s 2022–2024 Environmental Management Plan, designed to reduce the Group’s direct environmental impact through innovation and efficiency across its operations and value chain. It covers governance, targets, scope, actions, and outcomes, highlighting completion of all plan objectives by 2024.

Key elements:
- Scope and governance: Plan applied across 172 Group subsidiaries (covering 99.4% of employees); CaixaBank Wealth Management Luxembourg added to the perimeter in 2024.
- Action framework: 8 lines of action, 27 initiatives, and 200+ projects focused on:
  1) Group-level environmental governance
  2) Carbon footprint mitigation
  3) Green procurement and contracts
  4) Environmentalisation of non-financial product sales
  5) Circular economy
  6) Sustainable mobility
  7) Efficiency improvements
  8) Renewal/extension of voluntary environmental certifications
- Targets and boundaries: Quantitative annual targets aligned with climate strategy; Group-wide coverage for scopes 1 and 2, carbon neutrality, 100% renewable electricity, and certifications; scope 3 (operational) and paper reduction limited to CaixaBank, S.A.; specific baseline nuances for cooling gases and corporate travel.
- 2024 performance vs 2021 baseline:
  - Scope 1: target -15%; achieved -32%
  - Scope 2 (market-based): target -100%; achieved -100%
  - Scope 3 (operational): target -18%; achieved -34%
  - Global CO2 emissions: target -19%; achieved -36%
  - Carbon neutrality: 100% (offsetting scopes 1, 2, and 3.6 corporate travel via voluntary market)
  - Renewable electricity: 100% consumption sustained
  - Paper consumption: target -15%; achieved -33%
  - Energy efficiency savings: target -10%; achieved -28%
  - Environmental certifications in main buildings: +4 vs 2021 baseline (expansion including BPI buildings)
Overall, the document confirms that CaixaBank met or exceeded its environmental targets by 2024, significantly cutting emissions across all scopes, achieving full renewable electricity use, maintaining carbon neutrality, and advancing circularity, procurement, and certification efforts.

Target scope focuses on reducing the impact of the activity.

nodes.title: 2022-2024 Environmental management plan
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1 2022-2024 Environmental management plan
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, CaixaBank successfully completed its 2022-2024 Environmental Management Plan , meeting al the objectives set in terms of reducing its carbon footprint in the three scopes defined by the greenhouse gases protocol.
nodes.summary:
- CaixaBank successfully completed its 2022–2024 Environmental Management Plan, meeting or exceeding all objectives to reduce its carbon footprint across Scopes 1, 2, and 3 (as defined by the GHG Protocol).
- Achievements vs 2021 baseline by 2024:
  - Scope 1: -32% (target -15%).
  - Scope 2 (market-based): -100% (target -100%; 100% renewable electricity maintained throughout 2022–2024).
  - Scope 3 (operational perimeter): -34% (target -18%).
  - Global CO2 emissions: -36% (target -19%).
  - Paper consumption: -33% (target -15%).
  - Energy savings: -28% (target -10%).
  - Carbon Neutral status: 100% of Scopes 1, 2, and 3.6 (corporate travel) emissions offset each year via voluntary market credits.
- The plan was structured around 8 lines of action and a carbon footprint mitigation strategy with three phases: calculation, reduction, and offsetting, driving energy efficiency, technological upgrades, and best practices across buildings and operations.
- Carbon footprint calculation follows the GHG Protocol (WRI/WBCSD) and the Scope 3 Corporate Value Chain Standard.
- Scope coverage:
  - Scope 1: direct emissions from building combustion, fleet fuels, and refrigerants.
  - Scope 2: indirect emissions from purchased electricity.
  - Scope 3: selected indirect categories—3.1 Purchased goods and services, 3.2 Capital goods, 3.3 Fuel- and energy-related activities, 3.6 Corporate travel—treated as material for the Group’s operational footprint.
- While Scope 3 category 15 (Investments) represents ~99% of total Scope 3 emissions (financed emissions), the plan focuses operational reductions on categories 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, and 3.6, based on a 2022 materiality analysis covering 16 subsidiaries (98% of Group assets); conclusions were reaffirmed in 2024, with an updated study planned in 2025 using 2024 data.
- For assessing 2022–2024 targets, the operational carbon footprint uses the pre-materiality perimeter; specific baselines include:
  - Scope 1 refrigerants: 2019–2021 average.
  - Scope 3 corporate travel: 2019 (pre-COVID).
- Environmental certifications in main buildings expanded in line with targets (2 in 2022, 3 in 2023, 4 in 2024), with baseline adjustments due to property changes (sale of Castellana 51 and additions of BPI-certified buildings).
- The Environmental Management perimeter covers 99.4% of employees; Group-wide targets apply to Scopes 1 and 2, carbon neutrality, renewable electricity, and certifications, while Scope 3 (operational) and paper reduction targets apply to CaixaBank, S.A.

nodes.title: 2022-2024 Environmental management plan - Introduction
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1 2022-2024 Environmental management plan
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, CaixaBank successfully completed its 2022-2024 Environmental Management Plan , meeting al the objectives set in terms of reducing its carbon footprint in the three scopes defined by the greenhouse gases protocol.
nodes.summary: CaixaBank’s 2022–2024 Environmental Management Plan was completed in 2024 with all objectives met, delivering carbon footprint reductions across the three GHG Protocol scopes and other operational impacts. The plan set annual quantitative targets focused on direct impacts and tracked via a 2022–2024 targets vs. actuals table, covering: Scope 1, Scope 2 (market-based), Scope 3 (operational), global CO2, carbon neutrality, 100% renewable electricity, paper reduction, energy efficiency, and environmental certifications. 2024 results vs. the 2021 baseline include: Scope 1 −32%, Scope 2 −100%, Scope 3 (operational) −34%, global CO2 −36%, energy consumption −28%, paper consumption −33%, with 100% renewable electricity and 100% offsetting of scopes 1, 2 and 3.6 (corporate travel) via voluntary market credits. Scope coverage notes: scopes 1–2, carbon neutrality, 100% renewable electricity, and certifications apply to the Group (including 16 subsidiaries); Scope 3 (operational) and paper reduction apply to CaixaBank, S.A.; Scope 1 cooling gases use a 2019–2021 average baseline; corporate travel uses 2019 as baseline for CaixaBank, S.A. Environmental certifications targets were achieved (4 vs. 2021 baseline), with the baseline later adjusted to 10 due to the sale of Castellana 51 and additions of BPI buildings. The plan was based on eight lines of action, with 2024 actions advancing each target.

nodes.title: Carbon footprint mitigation strategy
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.1 Carbon footprint mitigation strategy
nodes.start_phrase: The carbon footprint mitigation strategy is one of the Environmental Management Plan's lines of action.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines CaixaBank’s 2022–2024 Environmental Management Plan, highlighting 2024 progress on one of its eight lines of action: the carbon footprint mitigation strategy. The strategy follows three phases—calculation, reduction, and offsetting—and drives actions such as energy-efficiency upgrades in buildings, technological improvements, and best practices. Carbon footprint calculations follow the GHG Protocol (WRI/WBCSD) and the Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard. Scope 1 includes combustion in own facilities, fleet fuel, and refrigerants; Scope 2 covers purchased electricity; Scope 3 includes multiple indirect categories. A 2022 materiality analysis across 16 group companies (98% of assets) determined that Scope 3 category 15 (Investments/financed emissions) accounts for 99% of Scope 3. Excluding this, categories 3.1 Purchased goods and services, 3.2 Capital goods, 3.3 Fuel and energy-related activities, and 3.6 Corporate travel were deemed material and used to define a new perimeter for operational footprint calculations. However, progress against the 2022–2024 targets must be assessed using the pre-analysis (old) perimeter set from the 2021 baseline. An internal 2024 review confirmed the continued relevance of the 2022 materiality conclusions, with a new study planned for 2025 using 2024 data. The Environmental Management perimeter covers 99.4% of employees.

nodes.title: Calculating the Carbon Footprint
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.1.1 Calculating the Carbon Footprint
nodes.start_phrase: The CaixaBank Group calculates its carbon footprint with a view to identifying areas of action and setting up an action plan with initiatives designed to reduce it.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the 2022–2024 Environmental Management Plan, built on eight lines of action, and reports 2024 progress with emphasis on the carbon footprint mitigation strategy.
- Describes the mitigation strategy’s focus on calculation, reduction, and offsetting, supported by concrete measures such as energy efficiency in buildings, technological upgrades, and best practices.
- Details the carbon footprint calculation across:
  - Scope 1: direct emissions (building combustion, vehicle fuel, refrigerants)
  - Scope 2: indirect emissions from purchased electricity
  - Scope 3: other indirect emissions, with emphasis on material categories
- Highlights Scope 3 materiality:
  - Category 15 “Investments” (financed emissions) represents ~99% of Scope 3 and is addressed separately (“Calculation of financed CO2 emissions”).
  - Excluding category 15, a 2022 materiality analysis identified categories 3.1 Purchased goods and services, 3.2 Capital goods, 3.3 Fuel and energy-related activities, and 3.6 Corporate travel as material for operational management.
- Explains boundary setting:
  - The 2022 analysis (covering 16 Group companies, 98% of assets) defined a new perimeter for the operational carbon footprint including only material categories.
  - Progress against 2022–2024 reduction targets is assessed using the pre-2022 (old) perimeter on which those targets were set.
  - The Environmental Management perimeter covers 99.4% of employees.
- Confirms governance and updates:
  - A 2024 internal review validated the continued relevance of the 2022 materiality conclusions.
  - A new materiality study will be conducted in 2025 using 2024 data.
- States the methodological basis: GHG Protocol standards (WRI/WBCSD) for Scopes 1–3, with Scope 3 aligned to the Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard.

nodes.title: Calculating the Carbon Footprint - Introduction
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.1.1 Calculating the Carbon Footprint
nodes.start_phrase: The CaixaBank Group calculates its carbon footprint with a view to identifying areas of action and setting up an action plan with initiatives designed to reduce it.
nodes.summary: Introduction to CaixaBank Group’s carbon footprint calculation, outlining Scope 1 (direct emissions from building combustion, vehicle fuel, refrigerants), Scope 2 (purchased electricity), and Scope 3 (other indirect) per the GHG Protocol (WRI/WBCSD) and the Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard. It highlights that Scope 3 category 15 “Investments” (financed emissions) accounts for 99% of Scope 3, while a 2022 materiality analysis across 16 companies covering 98% of Group assets identified 3.1 Purchased goods and services, 3.2 Capital goods, 3.3 Fuel and energy-related activities, and 3.6 Corporate travel as material when excluding Investments, defining a new operational footprint perimeter. The 2022–2024 Environmental Management Plan reduction targets were set using the pre-materiality scope, so target assessment uses the old perimeter. A 2024 review confirmed the 2022 conclusions; the materiality study will be repeated in 2025 with 2024 data. The Environmental Management perimeter covers 99.4% of employees.

nodes.title: Scope 1 and 2
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.1.1.1 Scope 1 and 2
nodes.start_phrase: The emission factors used to calculate the footprint of scopes 1 and 2 have been obtained from the Carbon footprint, offsetting and absorption projects registry of June 2024 for Spain.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the methodology for calculating Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions.
- Emission factors: Spain uses the June 2024 Carbon footprint, offsetting and absorption projects registry; Portugal and Luxembourg use IPCC Fifth Assessment Report GWP values.
- Scope 1 coverage: facility fuels (Gas Oil C, propane, natural gas), vehicle fleet fuel, and cooling/refrigerant gases.
- Scope 1 data quality: primarily actual data; exceptions include:
  - Gas Oil C for territorial branches estimated from purchased amounts and the average fuel price published by IDEA.
  - Vehicle fuel use estimated from odometer readings and theoretical consumption by vehicle model.
- Scope 2 accounting: market-based approach with 0 emissions when backed by 100% renewable certificates or suppliers with a 100% renewable mix.
- Energy consumption reporting in kWh; mostly sourced from invoices, with remaining data estimated via software using monthly average consumption and pro‑rata values per supply point over the past three years.
- Extract from the Management Report 2024 (p. 299).

nodes.title: Scope 3
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.1.1.2 Scope 3
nodes.start_phrase: The methodology presented below in relation to the calculation of material categories of scope 3 according to the materiality analysis of scope 3 categories (ä see section “Materiality analysis of Scope 3 categories ”), except for category 3.15, which is presented in section ä “Calculation of financed C O2 emissions ”.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Methodology and results for Scope 3 emissions, aligned with a materiality analysis of categories; category 3.15 (Investments) is treated separately in a dedicated section.
- Categories 3.1 (Purchased goods and services) and 3.2 (Capital goods): 2024 method uses 100% of operating expenses and investments as the base, excluding emissions already counted in other scopes and non-emitting spend (e.g., taxes, fees).
- Data sources and factors: Supplier invoices are multiplied by supplier-specific emission intensities (supplier carbon footprint/turnover) gathered via CaixaBank’s carbon footprint survey (to suppliers with turnover > €0.5M) and public disclosures; if unavailable, sector emission factors from PCAF are used.
- 2024 methodology enhancements:
  - Coverage expanded to 100% of suppliers (vs. 80% previously).
  - PCAF intensities adopted as the conversion fallback.
  - Updated supplier questionnaire to obtain specific emission factors.
  - In 2024, 15% (3.1) and 24% (3.2) of emissions were calculated using supplier-specific factors; the 2025–2027 Environmental Management Plan targets increasing these shares via supplier engagement.
- Backcasted results: 2021–2023 Scope 3.1 and 3.2 emissions recalculated with the new method, applying filters to remove double counting and non-emitting spend, prioritizing supplier data and complemented by PCAF:
  - 3.1 (tCO2e): 2023: 158,001 → 229,493; 2022: 128,006 → 237,891; 2021: 146,724 → 235,307.
  - 3.2 (tCO2e): 2023: 46,756 → 90,016; 2022: 60,811 → 100,634; 2021: 45,842 → 101,065.
- Category 3.3 (Fuels and energy-related activities): Includes well-to-tank (WTT) and transmission & distribution (T&D) losses; Scope 1 fuels multiplied by DEFRA WTT factors; Scope 2 electricity multiplied by IEA factors for WTT and T&D.
- Category 3.6 (Business travel): Calculated with DEFRA factors using actual mileage by mode (air, rail, rental, company cars) and hotel nights; no estimates used due to complete actual data.
- 2024 environmental performance snapshot vs. 2023:
  - Scope 1 gross emissions: 7.28 ktCO2e (−13.55%).
  - Scope 2 gross emissions (location-based): 23.05 ktCO2e (−21.57%); market-based: 0.
  - Scope 3 total gross emissions: 82,164.57 ktCO2e (−7.32%), with category 15 (Investments) dominating and decreasing to 81,838.05 ktCO2e (−7.33%). Reported 2024 values include: 3.1 Purchased goods and services 229.49 kt; 3.2 Capital goods 72.70 kt; 3.3 Fuels and energy-related activities 5.12 kt; 3.6 Corporate travel 12.45 kt.
- Governance and targets context:
  - 2024 reduction targets were set using a previous carbon footprint perimeter.
  - Scope 3.6 historical data adjusted due to reclassification of certain flights from medium- to short-haul (<1,000 km).
  - Decarbonization targets published under NZBA (lending sectors) and NZAOA (insurance corporate portfolio); sovereign debt excluded; baseline years detailed elsewhere.
  - Notes: Some operational data involve estimates if unavailable at reporting close; for value-chain entities with different reporting periods, the latest available annual data are used.

nodes.title: Breakdown of operational emissions from scope 1, 2, and 3 by gas type for 2024 (T CO2 eq)
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.2 Breakdown of operational emissions from scope 1, 2, and 3 by gas type for 2024 (T CO2 eq)

nodes.summary:
- Presents CaixaBank’s 2024 operational emissions breakdown by greenhouse gas (CO2, CH4, N2O, HFC) for CaixaBank S.A. and the Group, alongside 2023 comparatives.
- Details Scope 1 sources: fixed combustion (heating oil, natural gas, propane), mobile combustion (leased vehicles), and refrigerant gas leakage—highlighting HFC-related emissions from refrigerants.
- Provides the operational carbon footprint across Scopes 1, 2, and 3 for 2024, 2023, 2022, and 2021, with:
  - Scope 2 reported via location-based method for all years and market-based figures where available; no self-consumption electricity.
  - Scope 3 category breakdowns: 3.1 Purchased goods and services (OPEX), 3.2 Capital goods (CAPEX), 3.3 Fuel- and energy-related activities (upstream and transmission/distribution), and 3.6 Business travel (air, rail, cars, hotels).
- Includes totals by scope, overall totals (market- and location-based), and intensity metrics per employee for each year.

nodes.title: Reduction of CO Emissions2
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3 Reduction of CO Emissions2
nodes.start_phrase: With the aim of helping to reduce the Group's Carbon Footprint emissions, several initiatives have been implemented at the Group level.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Group-wide initiatives to reduce the carbon footprint, especially Scope 2 emissions, through the Environmental Management Plan’s seventh line of action on energy efficiency.
- Building and branch efficiency measures: LED lighting replacements, more efficient HVAC units, motion sensors and automatic light-off systems, timed switches, and upgraded computer equipment.
- Data centers: Two Data Processing Centres hold LEED certifications (one silver, one gold).
- Renewable electricity strategy: 100% of electricity consumption sourced from certified renewables, secured via PPAs (113.88 GWh/year, ~52% of total) and Guarantees of Origin (218.05 GWh/year).
- Fuel switch: In 2024, four diesel tanks were removed from branches by replacing existing air-conditioning equipment with heat pumps.
- Energy consumption results: 2024 Group energy use decreased 27.87% versus 2023 (-31.86% for CaixaBank, S.A.), driven by efficiency measures, merger synergies, and compliance with Spain’s Royal Decree-Law 14/2022 on energy saving.
- Monitoring and analytics: A centralized energy analytics platform aggregates data from building controls and meters to prioritize investments and implement best practices (optimized lighting/HVAC schedules, temperature setpoints, and equipment operation).
- Operational coverage and scale: 2,865 branches monitored; 1,093 branches remotely managed; 42 buildings monitored and/or remotely managed.
- Scope and applicability: Measures apply to Group companies covered by the Environmental Management Plan, representing 99.4% of CaixaBank Group employees.
- Headline metric: 100% of electricity consumed in 2024 was from certified renewable sources.

nodes.title: Reduction of CO Emissions2 - Introduction
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3 Reduction of CO Emissions2

With the aim of helping to reduce the Group's Carbon Footprint emissions, several initiatives have been implemented at the Group level.

nodes.title: Promotion of energy efficiency.
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.1 1. Promotion of energy efficiency.
nodes.start_phrase: The promotion of energy efficiency is the seventh line of action in the Environmental Management Plan.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Group-wide initiatives to reduce the carbon footprint, especially Scope 2 emissions, through energy efficiency (line 7 of the Environmental Management Plan). The Plan covers Group companies representing 99.4% of employees.
- Energy efficiency in buildings/branches: LED retrofits, higher-efficiency HVAC replacements, motion sensors and automatic light-off systems, time-regulated switches, and upgraded computer equipment. In 2024, four diesel tanks were removed and replaced by heat pump systems.
- Data centers: Two Data Processing Centres hold LEED certifications (one Silver, one Gold).
- Renewable electricity strategy: 100% of electricity consumption in 2024 from certified renewable sources, secured via:
  - PPAs totaling 113.88 GWh/year (about 52% of total purchase).
  - Guarantees of Origin (GdO) totaling 218.05 GWh/year, certifying 100% of electricity purchased.
- Monitoring and analytics: An energy analytics platform aggregates consumption data from offices and buildings (via control/monitoring software and meter records) to prioritize investments and apply best practices—optimized lighting and HVAC schedules, temperature setpoints, and equipment operation.
- 2024 results: Group energy consumption fell 27.87% versus 2023 (-31.86% at CaixaBank, S.A.), driven by savings measures, merger synergies, and compliance with Spain’s Royal Decree-Law 14/2022, alongside climate and lighting factors.
- Operational reach of monitoring: 2,865 branches monitored, 1,093 branches remotely managed, and 42 buildings monitored and/or remotely managed.
- Overall: 100% renewable electricity consumption achieved in 2024.

nodes.title: Promotion of energy efficiency. - Introduction
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.1 1. Promotion of energy efficiency.
nodes.start_phrase: The promotion of energy efficiency is the seventh line of action in the Environmental Management Plan.
nodes.summary: This section outlines CaixaBank’s seventh Environmental Management Plan action line to promote energy efficiency and reduce Scope 2 carbon footprint emissions, detailing branch/building measures (LED retrofits, higher‑efficiency HVAC, motion sensors, timed switches, IT equipment renewal) and the 2024 removal of four diesel tanks in favor of heat pumps. Both Data Processing Centres hold LEED certifications (silver and gold). The electricity strategy ensures 100% certified renewable power, via PPAs totaling 113.88 GWh/year (52% of total) and GdO certificates totaling 218.05 GWh/year (stated as 100% of total). In 2024, Group energy consumption fell 27.87% vs. 2023 (‑31.86% at CaixaBank, S.A.), attributed to savings measures, merger synergies, and effects of Royal Decree‑Law 14/2022. The Monitoring project’s energy analytics platform supports investment prioritization and operational optimization, covering 2,865 monitored branches, 1,093 remotely managed branches, and 42 monitored/remotely managed buildings. The plan applies to Group companies representing 99.4% of employees and confirms 100% renewable electricity in 2024.

nodes.title: Consumption and mix of energy sources
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.1.1 Consumption and mix of energy sources
nodes.start_phrase: The data on the energy consumption and mix for the CaixaBank Group in 2024 and 2023 are as follows:
nodes.summary:
- Presents CaixaBank Group’s 2024 and 2023 energy consumption and mix, highlighting a strong reliance on purchased renewable electricity and minimal fossil fuel use.
- Key figures:
  - Total energy consumption: 237,509 MWh (2024) vs 253,726 MWh (2023).
  - Fossil fuel consumption: 19,460 MWh (2024) vs 20,253 MWh (2023); 8.19% of total (2024) vs 7.98% (2023).
  - Renewable energy consumption (purchased electricity, heat, steam, cooling): 218,049 MWh (2024) vs 233,472 MWh (2023); 91.81% of total (2024) vs 92.02% (2023).
  - No coal, nuclear, or renewable fuels consumed; no purchased energy from fossil fuel sources; no self-generated renewable energy used as fuel.
- Electric power consumption performance:
  - 27.87% reduction in Group electricity use versus 2021.
  - Electricity consumption per employee: 6.09 MWh (2021), 5.88 (2022), 5.25 (2023), 4.83 (2024), showing continuous improvement.
- Energy efficiency investments in 2024:
  - €22 million CAPEX and €1.9 million OPEX for energy upgrades (reported under Financial Statements notes 19 and 37).
- On-site renewable generation:
  - Solar installation in Valencia (20 kW) generated 23 MWh in 2024; energy fed into the grid, not self-consumed.
- Scope: Includes CaixaBank, S.A., VidaCaixa, and BPI.

nodes.title: Boost in sustainable mobility
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.2 2. Boost in sustainable mobility
nodes.start_phrase: This corresponds to the fifth action line of the Environmental Management Plan.
nodes.summary: The document outlines CaixaBank’s “Boost in sustainable mobility” initiative, a key pillar of its Environmental Management Plan. It reports the 2023 creation of a cross-functional Sustainable Mobility Group to reduce emissions from corporate travel and describes a 360-degree Sustainable Mobility Plan that addresses internal corporate travel and external mobility by employees, customers, and suppliers. Implemented measures include expanding remote work and digital customer interactions to cut journeys; installing EV charging points and bicycle parking at corporate sites; downsizing the vehicle fleet and shifting to hybrids; using electric scooters for last‑mile deliveries; embedding environmental criteria in events and business trips; and conducting 2024 employee awareness campaigns on travel-related emissions. The plan’s scope targets four stakeholder groups: Company (embed policy and governance for fleet, travel, and events), Employees (enable low-impact commuting and reduce travel needs), Suppliers (cut pollution-related emissions and drive decarbonization), and Customers (offer sustainable mobility solutions, notably in electromobility).

nodes.title: Environmentalisation of procurement and contracts
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.3 3. Environmentalisation of procurement and contracts
nodes.start_phrase: By incorporating environmental criteria into the purchase of products and contracting of services, we extend our commitment to the suppliers and encourage them to adopt measures that minimise their activities' environmental impact.
nodes.summary:
- Embedding environmental criteria in procurement and service contracts to drive supplier adoption of practices that reduce environmental impact.
- 2024 enhancements to the Environmental Procurement Plan: creation of new green procurement/contracting sheets and inclusion of environmental compliance checks in supplier audits.
- Introduction of a mandatory Carbon Footprint questionnaire for key suppliers to quantify purchasing/contracting impacts and inform targets to reduce indirect (Scope 3) emissions.
- Waste and circular economy commitments aimed at cutting Scope 3 emissions, including:
  - Selective waste collection and recycling across facilities.
  - Authorized waste management in corporate buildings; cafeterias free of single-use plastics.
  - Branch network use of municipal selective collection for non-hazardous waste; authorized management of hazardous waste (bulbs, cooling gases, e-waste, toner).
  - Staff awareness campaigns to reduce waste generation.
  - Collection and recycling of obsolete cards; 100% of cards sold made from recycled PVC and biodegradable material.
  - ReUtilízame program facilitating donation of surplus materials to NGOs (2024: 66,597 items donated, 52 companies participating, 292 NGOs benefited).
  - Reported waste data informing the carbon footprint, showing declines from 2021 to 2024 in toner cartridges (42 t to 28 t) and IT support waste (1,262 t to 414 t).

nodes.title: Waste and commitment to the circular economy
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.4 Waste and commitment to the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank considers good waste management to be essential, as well as the transition from linear consumption practices to circular consumption, with the aim of minimising its Scope 3 emissions in the Carbon Footprint.
nodes.summary:
- Environmentalisation of procurement and contracts: CaixaBank embeds environmental criteria into purchasing and service contracts to drive supplier environmental performance. In 2024 it expanded the Environmental Procurement Plan with new green procurement/contracting sheets and began integrating compliance checks into supplier audits. A mandatory Carbon Footprint questionnaire for key suppliers was introduced to improve data on indirect (Scope 3) impacts and inform emission-reduction targets.

- Waste and circular economy commitments: To cut Scope 3 emissions, the bank advances selective waste collection and recycling, uses authorised waste managers at corporate buildings, and operates cafeterias without single-use plastics. Across branches, non-hazardous waste uses municipal selective collection; hazardous waste (bulbs, cooling gases, e-waste, toner) is handled by authorised managers. Ongoing staff awareness campaigns, collection of obsolete cards for recycling, and a shift to 100% recycled PVC and biodegradable materials for sold cards are highlighted. The ReUtilízame program facilitates donations of surplus materials to NGOs (open to customers); in 2024, 66,597 items were donated by 52 companies, benefiting 292 NGOs. Waste data feed into CaixaBank S.A.’s carbon footprint, with reductions from 2021 to 2024: toner cartridges from 42 t to 28 t and IT support waste from 1,262 t to 414 t.

nodes.title: Paper
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.5 Paper
nodes.start_phrase: In recent years, several initiatives at Group level have been implemented to reduce paper consumption1:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Resource efficiency measures and performance on paper and water across the Group, with quantitative data for CaixaBank, S.A.
- Paper management:
  - Group-wide digitisation enables 100% digital signatures; ATMs support envelope-free deposits and screen-only receipts; invoicing is fully electronic.
  - Printer fleet reduced and centralised to multifunction devices with user ID controls.
  - Strong shift to sustainable materials: 93.3% recycled paper usage; publications on FSC/PEFC-certified paper.
  - Notable reductions vs 2021: 40% less paper for customer communications; 32.75% less A4 paper in corporate buildings and branches.
  - Performance (A4, CaixaBank S.A.): 1,246 t (2021) → 815 t (2022) → 902 t (2023) → 838 t (2024); paper per employee: 0.03 (2021) → 0.02 (2022–2024).
- Water management:
  - Water use is primarily sanitary and not reusable; efficiency measures include interrupted-flow taps, low-capacity dual-flush cisterns.
  - Technology upgrades in key buildings: Data Processing Centres use free cooling (no water); Barcelona HQ replaced evaporative towers with adiabatic towers to cut water use.
  - Performance (CaixaBank S.A.): 506,848 m3 (2021) → 398,206 m3 (2022) → 421,769 m3 (2023) → 409,676 m3 (2024), a 19.2% reduction vs 2021; water per employee: 11.89 → 10.84 → 11.69 → 11.21.

nodes.title: Water
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.6 Water
nodes.start_phrase: The water we use comes from the supply network, and its use is mainly for sanitary purposes, which does not allow its reuse and which is why its significance as an environmental vector is relative.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Summary of CaixaBank Group’s resource-efficiency measures, with quantitative results reported for CaixaBank, S.A.; focus on paper and water reduction.
- Paper:
  - Key initiatives: end-to-end digital signatures; fully electronic invoicing; ATMs enable envelope-free deposits and on-screen info/no receipt; centralized multifunction printers with user ID; preference for recycled paper (93.3% of consumption); publications on FSC/PEFC-certified paper.
  - Impact vs 2021: 40% reduction in paper for customer communications; 32.75% reduction in A4 paper in corporate buildings and branches.
  - Results: A4 paper consumption (tonnes) 2021–2024 = 1,246; 815; 902; 838. Per-employee consumption stable at ~0.02–0.03 t (0.03; 0.02; 0.02; 0.02).
- Water:
  - Context: Water sourced from the supply network, mainly for sanitary use (limited reuse potential).
  - Efficiency measures: interrupted-flow taps; smaller, dual-flush cisterns; free-cooling in Data Processing Centres (no water use); adiabatic cooling towers in the Barcelona corporate centre (lower water use).
  - Results: 2024 consumption 409,676 m3, a 19.2% reduction vs 2021. Annual consumption (m3) 2021–2024 = 506,848; 398,206; 421,769; 409,676. Per-employee (m3) = 11.89; 10.84; 11.69; 11.21.

nodes.title: Renewal and extension of certifications
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.7 4. Renewal and extension of certifications
nodes.start_phrase: This corresponds to the eighth action line of the Environmental Management Plan.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on renewing and expanding environmental certifications as the eighth action line of the Environmental Management Plan.
- Emissions reduction pursued through efficiency measures, indicator monitoring, and implementing an Energy and Environmental Management System aligned with ISO 14001, ISO 50001, and the European EMAS regulation.
- Certification status at CaixaBank S.A.: 5 buildings certified under ISO 14001, 2 under ISO 50001, and 1 under EMAS; all branches in Catalonia hold the Environmental Quality Mark.
- Approximately 30% of the workforce operates in certified buildings or offices.
- Group-wide certifications: CaixaBank Facilities Management and CaixaBank Tech have ISO 14001-certified Environmental Management Systems.
- In 2023, BPI added one more ISO 14001-certified center, reaching a total of 4 certified buildings.

nodes.title: Offsetting CO2 emissions
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.4 Offsetting CO2 emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the Environmental Management Plan, the CaixaBank Group has undertaken to neutralise the carbon footprint (Carbon Neutral) of its own activity for Scope 1, 2 and for category 3.6 corporate travel of Scope 3.
nodes.summary:
- Commitment and scope: CaixaBank targets carbon neutrality for Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 category 3.6 (corporate travel), prioritizing emission reductions first and offsetting only the residual.
- Offsetting approach in 2024: Shift to 100% GHG removal projects (no reduction projects), with 19,736 tCO2e offset at a cost of €447,168. Carbon credits are used only for neutralization and are not counted toward the reported footprint or reduction targets; no credits are banked for future years nor contracted beyond the current year.
- Offset project mix and standards: 
  - 50% Spain (Ourense, Galicia) reforestation under MITECO, Vintage 2023.
  - 40% Uruguay (Montes del Este) forest project under VCS, Vintage 2019.
  - 10% Mexico (Quintana Roo) forest project under CAR, Vintage 2022+.
  - 50% of credits within the EU; no corresponding adjustments under Paris Agreement Article 6.
- Year-on-year view: 2024 removals 100% vs. 75% in 2023; standards split in 2024—MITECO 50%, VCS 40%, CAR 10%.
- Own absorption projects: Two CaixaBank-led reforestations (Montserrat, Barcelona; Ejulve, Teruel) validated by MITECO; permanence risk managed via a guarantee fund. These nature-based projects provide environmental co-benefits and play a primarily symbolic role in demonstrating commitment.
- Value chain engagement: Not directly involved in removal/storage with value-chain agents; 2024 supplier questionnaire added questions on carbon footprint compensation efforts.
- Environmental Management Plan 2025–2027: Continues focus on impact mitigation, measurement, and reduction via six action lines:
  1) Climate change: 100% renewable energy (supplier + PPAs) and internal carbon pricing.
  2) Sustainable procurement: Supplier engagement on footprints and targets; maintain/extend the Environmental Plan for Procurement and Contracts.
  3) Circular economy: Donation program (ReÚtilizame) and reuse of plastic from obsolete bank cards.
  4) Sustainable mobility: Reduce corporate fleet; expand EV charging and carsharing; awareness to cut travel emissions.
  5) Efficiency: HVAC replacement; branch automation, LED, efficient climate control, operational best practices; digitization to reduce paper/toner/cards; review documentary management.
  6) Certifications: Extend ISO 14001 scope and increase number of events certified as sustainable.

nodes.title: Environmental Management Plan 2025-2027
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.2 Environmental Management Plan 2025-2027
nodes.start_phrase: This new Environmental Management Plan maintains the main lines of action followed by the previous plan, focusing on mitigating the environmental impact of the Group's activities, measuring its impact through the calculation of the carbon footprint, and prioritising its reduction through initiatives related to efficiency, the circular economy, engagement with the value chain, sustainable mobility, and the implementation of new certifications.
nodes.summary:
- CaixaBank runs two in-house CO2 absorption (reforestation) projects in Montserrat (Barcelona) and Ejulve (Teruel), which it has promoted, financed, and managed.
- Both projects are registered and validated by Spain’s MITECO; permanence risk is managed via a guarantee fund, and absorption is calculated per MITECO Climate Change Office methodology.
- The forests function as natural carbon sinks and deliver co-benefits (soil protection, erosion and landslide prevention, biodiversity), serving as nature-based solutions; their carbon impact is modest and primarily symbolic of CaixaBank’s local environmental commitment.
- CaixaBank is not currently involved in GHG removal/storage projects with value-chain partners, but in 2024 added supplier questionnaire items on carbon footprint compensation to identify supplier efforts.
- The Environmental Management Plan 2025–2027 continues the prior strategy: measure and reduce the operational carbon footprint and environmental impacts through efficiency, circular economy, value-chain engagement, sustainable mobility, and certifications.
- Six action lines and key initiatives:
  1) Climate change: 100% renewable energy (including PPA) and internal carbon pricing.
  2) Greener procurement/contracts: supplier engagement on carbon footprint and targets; extend the Environmental Plan for Procurement and Contracts.
  3) Circular economy: ReÚtilizame donation program (IT, furniture); reuse plastic from obsolete bank cards.
  4) Sustainable mobility: smaller corporate fleet; more EV charging and carsharing; travel-emissions awareness.
  5) Efficiency: replace HVAC; branch automation, LEDs, efficient climate control, operational best practices; digitisation to cut paper/toner/cards; review documentary management.
  6) Certifications: extend ISO 14001 scope and sustainable events.
- Emissions-reduction approach is based on internal criteria tailored to CaixaBank’s operations rather than external climate scenarios; targets address impacts from the Double Materiality Study, focusing on reducing the internal and operational carbon footprint.
- Quantitative targets (baseline 2024) for CaixaBank and the Group:
  - Scope 1 reductions: by 2025/26/27/2030 = -9%/-12%/-16%/-22% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7%/-10% (Group).
  - Scope 2 (market method): 0 tCO2 each year (reflecting 100% renewable electricity).
  - Scope 2 (location method) reductions: -5%/-8%/-10%/-15% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7.5%/-11% (Group).
  - Scope 1+2 reductions (market method): -9%/-12%/-16%/-22% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7%/-10% (Group).
  - Scope 1+2 reductions (location method): -6%/-9%/-11%/-16% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7.5%/-11% (Group).
  - Offsetting: 100% of Scopes 1, 2, and corporate travel (Scope 3.6) annually.
  - Renewable electricity consumption: 100% annually.
  - Electricity savings: -5%/-8%/-10%/-15% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7.5%/-11% (Group).
- Scope 1 and 2 targets cover 100% of the operational footprint perimeter; the Sustainability Committee monitors these targets.

nodes.title: Green taxonomy
nodes.heading: Green taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: In 2020, the European Parliament and the EU Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2020/852, hereinafter the Taxonomy Regulation , which establishes uniform and common criteria in the European Union to determine if an economic activity can be considered environmentally sustainable.
nodes.summary:
- Introduces the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and its purpose: harmonized criteria to assess whether economic activities are environmentally sustainable.
- Lists the six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation and adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems. Notes the 2023 extension of activities and remaining objectives.
- Explains alignment requirements: activities must meet technical screening criteria, Do No Significant Harm (DNSH), and minimum social safeguards.
- Describes transparency and disclosure obligations under Article 8: firms subject to NFRD must report eligibility and alignment; financial companies had a one‑year deferral. With CSRD from 2025, scope expands to large unlisted, listed SMEs, and certain non‑EU entities. Notes EC FAQs published in Dec 2023 for KPI guidance.
- Outlines phased disclosure timeline (2021–2025): eligibility and alignment for climate objectives first, then other objectives; KPIs include Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and Green Investment Ratio (GIR); separate disclosures for nuclear and gas.
- Defines eligibility vs alignment and the key ratios:
  - Eligibility ratio: share of assets/investments fitting Taxonomy activity descriptions.
  - GAR (banking and insurance assets) and GIR (asset management, pension plans, EPSV): share aligned with Taxonomy among “assets/investments covered.”
- Details calculation methodologies and exclusions:
  - Banking Group (prudential perimeter CRR/CRD IV): denominator excludes sovereigns/supranationals/central banks and trading book; numerator further excludes non‑NFRD companies, derivatives (hedging), cash/interbank, and certain other assets. Alignment requires meeting technical criteria, DNSH, and minimum safeguards.
  - Insurance Group and Pension Plans/EPSV: analogous coverage, exclusions, and alignment tests.
  - Mandatory reporting is based primarily on counterparties’ own KPIs (turnover and CapEx).
- Discloses exposure reporting to nuclear energy and fossil gas per Delegated Regulations (EU) 2022/1214, 2021/2139, and 2021/2178.
- Notes data sources, limitations, and interpretation:
  - Reliance on counterparties’ disclosures; supplementary ESG data via MSCI; conservative approach where data is missing (treated as not eligible/aligned).
  - Complexity and interpretive uncertainty around technical criteria, DNSH, and minimum safeguards; significant use of professional judgment.
  - GAR’s representativeness is affected by balance sheet composition, especially exposures to non‑NFRD entities (e.g., SMEs, non‑EU), which depress the ratio.
- Clarifies reporting scope and valuation:
  - Taxonomy prepared on a prudential basis; differences vs accounting consolidation (e.g., equity method for certain entities under prudential rules).
  - Financial assets at amortized cost are valued at gross carrying amount for Taxonomy templates.
- Presents 2024 results and insights:
  - Banking Group: GAR 3.05% (turnover KPI) and 3.93% (CapEx KPI). Eligibility ratios are higher than alignment due to exclusions and data gaps. Methodology update increased 2024 GAR versus 2023 by revising DNSH assessment for retail mortgages using the bank’s Pillar 3 physical risk methodology; households are not subject to minimum social safeguards. Aligned mortgage portfolio reached €7,471m at 31 Dec 2024; on a comparable basis, 2023 GAR would have been 2.30% instead of 1.05%. Expanded collection of Energy Efficiency Certificates and inclusion of certain exposures where counterparties fall under Accounting Directive Articles 19a/29a.
  - Insurance business (VidaCaixa): GAR 3.33% (turnover) and 4.94% (CapEx). Increase driven by classifying certain green bonds as aligned (use‑of‑proceeds consistent with Taxonomy) and greater availability of alignment data for NFRD financials; denominator mix affected by incorporating third‑party fund manager data.
  - Pension Plans and EPSV: GIR 2.48% (turnover) and 3.46% (CapEx).
- Provides additional conglomerate KPIs (banking + insurance): weighted average KPI 3.10% (turnover) and 4.12% (CapEx), based on ordinary income weights.
- Concludes with outlook: ratios expected to rise as remaining objectives are included, counterparty data availability improves, and regulatory clarity increases; the Group will enhance disclosures on counterparties’ alignment as new requirements become applicable.

nodes.title: S-Social
nodes.heading: S-Social
nodes.start_phrase:
Employees are a key stakeholder group for CaixaBank, which is why the emphasis in the 2022-2024 Strategic Plan is on people as a fundamental driver, aiming to 
address the challenge of:
nodes.summary:
- CaixaBank’s 2022–2024 Strategic Plan prioritizes people, aiming to be the preferred employer and attract top talent.
- The Personnel Master Plan focused on: approachable, non-hierarchical leadership; a collaborative, empowered, agile culture; diversity, inclusion, and equal opportunity; proactive development and training on critical skills; a differentiated employee value proposition; and shifting to a data-driven culture.
- 2024 outcomes: plan successfully concluded with improved team culture and leadership; Total Culture Favourability up 2% in the Engagement Survey.
- Diversity and equity: women in leadership reached 43.4% (above target); adjusted gender pay gap below 1%.
- Development model transformation: “Development by Skills” consolidated; full workforce assessed on hard and soft skills; targeted hard-skill training and soft-skill self-learning via People Skills.
- Stronger employee value proposition across Business Partners, PeopleXperience, and Healthy Organisation; eNPS rose by 18 points.
- Data-driven HR progress: 10 People Analytics use cases implemented, exceeding targets.

nodes.title: S1-Own workforce
nodes.heading: S1-Own workforce
nodes.start_phrase:
Employees are a key stakeholder group for CaixaBank, which is why the emphasis in the 2022-2024 Strategic Plan is on people as a fundamental driver, aiming to 
address the challenge of:
nodes.summary:
- Strategic people agenda and 2022-2024 results:
  - Employees positioned as a core driver of the bank’s strategy.
  - Personnel Master Plan completed with measurable progress in culture and approachable leadership; Engagement Survey favourability up 2%, eNPS up 18 points.
  - Diversity gains: women in leadership roles reached 43.4% (target exceeded); adjusted gender pay gap below 1%.
  - Shift to a data-driven HR model with 10 People Analytics use cases delivered.
  - Development by Skills model consolidated to assess and develop hard and soft skills across the workforce.

- Workforce profile and evolution:
  - Total staff 46,014 (+2.6% YoY): Spain 41,304; Portugal 4,426; Others 284.
  - Gender split: 56.1% women, 43.9% men; average age 46.8; average tenure 18.7 years.
  - New hires 2,116; headcount growth driven by technical roles and network staffing.

- 2025-2027 Strategic Plan (people priorities):
  - Ambition to be the best company to work for.
  - Lines of action: attract/retain top talent (employer brand, 360° engagement model, wellbeing), accelerate transformation of existing talent (skills planning, AI, agility, project management, upskilling/reskilling), strengthen a culture of proximity, agility and collaboration under the AHEAD leadership model.
  - Generational balance: ~3,000 young hires planned; target under-35s at 11.4% by 2027.

- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI):
  - Comprehensive framework via the Equality Plan and Wengage programme (gender, generational, functional/disability, LGTBI, cultural diversity), with governance through internal Diversity Committee and External Advisory Committee.
  - Gender: promotion of female leadership (Impulsa Plan, mentoring), unbiased recruitment, pay equity analysis; recognitions include Bloomberg GEI and multiple DEI awards/certifications.
  - Pay equity: adjusted gender pay gap 1.0% Group (0.9% Spain; 2.0% Portugal); gross pay gap down to 14% overall; continued actions to narrow gaps by 2027.
  - Functional diversity: formal inclusion policy, workplace adaptations, targeted hiring partnerships; employees with disabilities up to 650 (1.4%).
  - LGTBI and cultural diversity: guidance, awareness campaigns, new cultural diversity action plan.

- Talent development and training:
  - Development by Skills model: unified skills architecture, Skills Review and AHEAD Review assessments, tailored upskilling/reskilling plans; PeopleSkills platform launched to manage skills and recommend training.
  - Leadership development under AHEAD model with 360° reviews and targeted programmes; coaching and mentoring embedded.
  - Training scale: 2.99 million hours; €15.4m invested; 100% of staff trained; 92.5% online; 65.9 hours/employee; satisfaction 4.1/5.
  - Regulatory certifications (LCCI, IDD, MiFID II) and a robust Sustainability Training Plan.

- Working conditions, labour rights and collective bargaining:
  - Strong compliance with labour standards; constructive social dialogue.
  - New 2024–2026 sector agreement: cumulative 11% wage table increase (5%/3%/3%), €1,000 lump-sum, extra personal day, removal of entry level XIV.
  - Coverage: 99.8% under collective bargaining; 97.6% represented by worker representatives.
  - Job stability: 99.6% permanent contracts; goal to maintain ~100%.
  - Human rights commitments (no forced/child labour; non-discrimination; accessible reporting channels).

- Compensation and benefits:
  - Revised General Remuneration Policy (2024): meritocratic, competitive, non-discriminatory, aligned with long-term value and ESG risk mitigation.
  - Variable pay integrates ESG metrics for all staff (customer quality NPS mix; sustainable finance mobilisation), with disclosed targets and achievements.
  - Extensive benefits: pension plan contributions (€179m), insurance (€21m), enhanced employee loans, flexible remuneration (Compensa+), entry-level pay above local minimums (Spain 1.2x; Portugal 1.5x); total compensation ratio (highest paid vs median) of 62.
  - Employee pension plan (PC30): top market performance (8.67% in 2024), PRI 5-star governance rating, NZAOA member, strong long-term returns.

- Work-life balance and flexibility:
  - EFR (Flexible and Responsible Company) certification at Excellence Level A renewed; aim to maintain.
  - Enhanced leave and reduced-hours provisions (parental, disability-related, care responsibilities), economic supports for families, and aids for training and loans.
  - Digital disconnection protocol (no comms 7pm–8am; meeting curfews).
  - Remote work model (up to 30%/20% depending on area); 71.5% adoption among eligible staff.

- Health, safety and wellbeing:
  - Occupational Health and Safety Policy and prevention system; 2024 accident frequency index 1.50; severity 0.14; manageable absenteeism 3.8%.
  - Healthy Organisation strategy with AENOR certification and TOP Wellbeing recognition.
  - Broad wellbeing initiatives: Wellbeing Week, expanded psychological support, emotional wellbeing programmes.

- Employee engagement and dialogue:
  - Structured active listening ecosystem: biennial Engagement Study (2024: 83% participation; 69% favourability), interim Radars, lifecycle touchpoints (e.g., post-parental leave).
  - 2027 favourability target 72%, with action plans addressing workload, mobility, and customer service pressures.
  - “Nosotros Plan” with >150 initiatives across customer service, processes, and people management.
  - Business Partner model for proximity HR support; PeopleNow social intranet as a bidirectional communication and culture platform.

nodes.title: S3-Communities affected
nodes.heading: S3-Communities affected
nodes.start_phrase:
Social commitment is one of CaixaBank's main assets 
and differential values, which has been integrated into 
its activity, but goes beyond it, through solutions 
that meet the needs of people and social projects 
that improve their wellbeing.
nodes.summary:
- Theme and commitment: CaixaBank embeds social action into its core activity to drive positive change, prioritising a fair, inclusive society. It focuses on amplifying “la Caixa” Foundation programmes, building partnerships, delivering tailored social banking for vulnerable groups, addressing urgent social challenges, and fostering solidarity through extensive volunteering.

- Policy and governance framework: Actions are guided by the Principles of Action on Sustainability (integral, responsible, and sustainable action; unrivalled service; economic efficiency; long-term vision; innovation), complemented by the Sustainability Master Plan, Code of Ethics, and Human Rights Principles. The approach aligns with international standards and the UN SDGs.

- Community engagement: Ongoing, structured dialogue with “la Caixa” Foundation, major NGOs (e.g., Red Cross, ONCE), territorial social action managers, and social entities via regular meetings and focus groups informs priorities. Effectiveness is reviewed with partners and through monthly internal monitoring of community investments.

- 2024 scale and focus: €7.2M provided directly by CaixaBank and €75.2M channelled from “la Caixa” Foundation and customers. Interventions tackled illness/disability, poverty, labour integration, multiculturalism and social exclusion, senior care, education, basic needs, and environment. CaixaBank was named Global Finance’s “World’s Best Bank for its support of Society 2024.”

- Key programmes with “la Caixa” Foundation:
  - Decentralised Social Action: ~€25M directed through the branch network to thousands of local projects and entities, heavily supporting illness/disability, multiculturalism/exclusion, poverty, seniors, and employment.
  - Solidarity formulas: 62 agreements mobilising €0.52M from companies and individuals to complement local projects.
  - “Ningún Hogar Sin Alimentos”: €1.7M raised (including €1.0M from the Foundation), providing 1,548 tonnes of food to 54 food banks.

- Partnerships with regional foundations:
  - Social calls: €1.03M supporting 228 projects (vulnerable groups, seniors, quality of life).
  - Environmental call with Fundación Montemadrid: €0.12M for 14 biodiversity/circular economy projects.
  - Sociocultural initiatives with 11 territorial foundations: €1.62M for courses, workshops, and cultural/charitable actions.

- Other collaborations and own programmes:
  - Youth congresses (Fundación Lo Que De Verdad Importa and Relife): 13,895 attendees on values and addiction prevention.
  - Tree of Dreams: 34,136 beneficiaries (including a pilot for isolated seniors); customer and employee gift sponsorships.
  - Full of Life (seniors): €0.16M for workshops in health, personal development, and digital skills across 301 towns.
  - Land of Opportunities (rural depopulation): €0.63M; 1,966 entrepreneurs supported and 168 winning projects to create jobs and retain population.
  - ReUtilízame (circular economy): 66,597 donated items from 52 companies to 292 social entities.

- Support to the third social sector:
  - Donation platform (branches and digital): €48.64M raised for 2,783 causes and 2,311 entities, including €22.8M for the Valencia flooding emergency and extensive volunteer mobilisation.

- Volunteering:
  - Open to employees, customers, and society; structured into strategic, local, and emergency actions, with a new Volunteering Campus for training.
  - 2024 outcomes: 20,201 volunteers, 29,935 activities, 433,514 beneficiaries, 2,509 collaborating entities.
  - Social Month: 16,580 volunteers, 2,749 activities; 37% of CaixaBank Group staff participated.
  - Activity mix: 68% accompaniment, 28% education, 2% environment, 1% digitalisation, 1% other.
  - “Everyone’s Project”: €756,000 donated to 150 projects nominated by employee volunteers.

- BPI (Portugal) social commitment with “la Caixa” Foundation:
  - Social programmes: BPI “la Caixa” Awards (€5.1M; 133 projects; 18,096 beneficiaries) across disability, inclusion, seniors, and childhood.
  - PROMOVE: €5.2M for 18 pilot and 11 R&D mobilising projects in inland regional development.
  - Decentralised social initiative (ISD): €1.9M; 330 projects; ~70,000 direct beneficiaries.
  - Research and health: €7.7M for 9 projects (neurodegenerative, oncological, cardiovascular, infectious diseases, enabling technologies).
  - Culture and science: support to museums, theatres, orchestras, and travelling exhibitions.
  - Education and grants: 4 postgraduate-abroad, 5 doctoral, and 3 post-doctoral scholarships.
  - Volunteering: 4th BPI Volunteering Week; 208 initiatives; 2,100 volunteers; 17,000 beneficiaries; 9,300 hours.

nodes.title: S4-Customers
nodes.heading: S4-Customers
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank works to increase customer satisfaction and enhance the customer experience by implementing various communication channels and experience measurement models.
nodes.summary:
- Strategic focus on customers: CaixaBank prioritizes satisfaction, multi‑channel engagement, and experience measurement, with commitments to transparency, anti‑greenwashing, inclusion, entrepreneurship, financial education, and rigorous data protection. Double Materiality IROs highlight opportunities in new channels and education and risks in greenwashing and data loss. Client base: 20.3 million (18.5M Spain; 1.8M Portugal).
- Respect for human rights: Access to services, integrating social/environmental risks in decisions, avoiding financing tied to serious human rights violations, and safeguarding confidentiality and privacy, as set out in the Group’s Human Rights Principles.
- Customer experience model: “Listen–Understand–Act” with AI‑driven insights, continuous NPS tracking (relational, transactional, digital) linked to remuneration, and 2025–2027 goal to rank No. 1 in digital satisfaction. 2024 activity included >6M survey responses, 4M+ relational surveys, 37.6M transactional surveys, and real‑time “Close the Loop” remediation plus a Customer Service Improvement Plan (MAC). NPS and experience indicators improved across segments.
- Transparent and responsible marketing: Updated Corporate Commercial Communication Policy (Dec‑2024) mandates legality, clarity, balance, objectivity, and transparency; participation in Autocontrol pre‑clearance. Large volumes of campaigns reviewed with most approved or approved with modifications. Broad employee certification base (MiFID, LCCI, IDD).
- Responsible lending and clear contracts: Policies align with Bank of Spain circular on responsible lending; solvency assessment prioritizes repayment capacity and fair treatment. “Transparent contract” project uses plain language and digital‑first design; 42 key contracts updated to improve clarity, trust, and legal certainty.
- Product governance and greenwashing prevention: Corporate Product Governance Policy (Nov‑2024) and dual committees (Product Strategy; Transparency) oversee product lifecycle; 2024: 23 sessions, 266 products analyzed, 6 initially rejected. Automated ESG product classification (SFDR Articles 8/9, PAIs, Taxonomy) and robust controls (Sustainable Financing Guide, specialist teams, monthly reviews) to avoid greenwashing.
- Customer service and complaints: Omni‑channel Contact Center (phone, web, email, chat, social) with NPS monitoring (66.6% in 2024) and expanded branch phone service. Dedicated senior line handled 1.04M calls. Total interactions: 10.25M (+33.75% YoY). Independent Customer Service Office (SAC) manages complaints, reports to governance bodies; 2024 complaint volumes increased, with improved timeliness and a significant share resolved in favor of claimants; detailed breakdowns by product/channel.
- ESG client engagement: ESG advisory for corporates/institutions; acted as ESG Coordinator in sustainable syndicated lending; new regional sustainability team for Company Banking and structured client support through governance, diagnosis, materiality, and strategy phases.
- Financial inclusion, accessibility, and proximity: Omnichannel accessibility roadmap aligned to EU Accessibility Act, with accessible design principles and specific solutions (Braille card, accessible POS, sign‑language pilot). High accessibility in branches (Spain 89%; Portugal 75%) and 100% accessible ATMs with visual, acoustic, tactile, and senior‑friendly features. Inclusive app/website (WCAG‑aligned, ILUNION‑audited). Largest physical network and commitment to rural presence: 3,570 branches in Spain, 1,403 rural branches, 28 mobile branches serving 1,294 towns (644k people; 70% seniors).
- Solutions for vulnerable groups: MicroBank drives inclusion via microcredits for families (low‑income thresholds), social‑impact loans, and programs like Proyecto Confianza. Protocols to prevent financial abuse of people with disabilities/elderly; basic payment accounts with fee exemptions for vulnerable customers (362,728). Senior support includes specialized advisors/lines, adapted ATMs, dedicated products (e.g., MyBox Senior), in‑person training, and AENOR certification as an organization committed to seniors.
- Equal treatment and non‑discrimination: Plan under Law 15/2022 identifies priority vulnerable groups and adds protocols for detection/reporting of abuse (cases referred to Prosecutor’s Office), autonomy‑preserving procedures for victims, and accessibility pilots (e.g., sign‑language).
- Support for social entities and social housing: Specific products for third‑sector organizations (19,416 accounts) and NGO affinity cards; roadmap to expand offerings. Social housing policy combines early, specialized care (Mortgage Customer Service) and participation in public programs (Government’s Social Housing Fund). 2024: 9,536 social‑rent contracts with adapted rents; ongoing “Impulsa” social support.
- Financial education and health: Comprehensive literacy plan for multiple audiences (shareholders, youth, vulnerable adults, people with intellectual disabilities, seniors, entrepreneurs), delivered via conferences, workshops, in‑branch sessions, and digital content (webinars, podcasts, videos). Notable initiatives include Shareholder Aula, youth programs via imagin and in schools, MicroBank Academy with Google, and sector‑specific training (e.g., catering).
- Employability and entrepreneurship: MicroBank financing supports entrepreneurs, self‑employed, social enterprises, agro generational renewal, and education (Skills & Education loans for students and schools with EIF). 2024 outcomes include businesses created, jobs supported, and sizable financing volumes; broad partner network of public/private entities and European institutions (EIB, EIF, CEB). Cumulative jobs since 2022 exceed targets; new 2025–2027 goal to improve employability for 150,000 people. CaixaBank Dualiza advances vocational training through grants, events, teacher/student programs, and research, benefiting tens of thousands.
- Privacy and personal data protection: Board‑led governance, Corporate Privacy Policy (updated 2024) covering ethical data/AI use, and two corporate committees (Privacy; PIA). Transparent client communications (policy updated semi‑annually, multiple rights channels, in‑app controls), structured consent capture, and rigorous records/DPIA methodology aligned with AEPD guidance. Centralized breach management with monthly oversight, integration with HR/disciplinary processes, and continuous training/awareness tied to variable pay. Ongoing monitoring of regulatory changes and reinforced cybersecurity to minimize data‑related risks.

nodes.title: G-Governance
nodes.heading: G-Governance
nodes.start_phrase: Good corporate governance is key to successfully fulfilling the purpose.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on good corporate governance as a foundation for strategy, daily decision-making, and stakeholder relationships, grounded in values of integrity, respect, honesty, transparency, and professional excellence.
- Strong compliance framework: adherence to strict national and international regulations translated into internal policies with monitoring of operational effectiveness and compliance.
- People-centric business conduct: transparency with customers, shareholders, and investors; robust AML/CFT measures; active prevention of corruption and bribery; no contracting of direct lobbying or interest representation services; strict personal data protection; extension of governance standards across the value chain.
- Speak-up culture: ensuring an open, safe environment for employees to raise concerns to enable early detection of conduct and behavioral breaches.
- High priority on combating bribery, corruption, and financial crime; AML/CFT recognized as a material issue due to sector risks.
- Commitment to transparency regarding any lobbying activities, despite their limited scope.
- Supplier stewardship: supporting suppliers to improve sustainability and align with CaixaBank’s objectives and values; enhanced ESG compliance through supplier audits.
- Process to identify and assess material impacts, risks, and opportunities in business conduct: annual Risk Assessment covering conduct and compliance risks in the corporate risk catalogue; integration into a Double Materiality Study alongside stakeholder expectations, market practices, the Code of Ethics, and market trends.
- Key risks identified: non-adaptation or non-compliance with ESG regulations; inadequate risk management (including conflicts of interest and alignment with risk appetite), potentially leading to penalties or loss of trust; non-compliance with AML/CFT, corruption, and bribery requirements; lack of transparency in relations with public institutions.
- Key impacts/opportunities identified: promotion of ethical culture with customers, suppliers, and other stakeholders; contribution to public finances through tax payments; increased supplier ESG compliance resulting from audits.

nodes.title: Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities related to climate change
nodes.heading: Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities related to climate change
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines CaixaBank Group’s annual process for identifying and assessing business conduct risks through a formal Risk Assessment aligned with its corporate risk catalogue. The results feed into a Double Materiality Study that also considers stakeholder expectations, market practices, the Code of Ethics, and market trends. Key risks identified include non-adaptation or non-compliance with ESG regulations, inadequate conflict-of-interest and risk management frameworks leading to penalties or reputational loss, breaches of AML/CFT and anti-corruption requirements, and insufficient transparency with public institutions. The document also highlights identified conduct-related impacts: fostering an ethical culture with customers, suppliers, and other stakeholders; contributing to public finances through tax payments; and enhancing supplier ESG compliance via audits.

nodes.title: Corporate culture and policies of corporate culture and business conduct
nodes.heading: Corporate culture and policies of corporate culture and business conduct
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank's corporate purpose is based on its mission and values, which are reflected in its corporate culture and aim to guarantee excellence in customer service.
nodes.summary:
- Corporate purpose, mission and values: CaixaBank’s purpose is to contribute to customers’ financial well‑being and society’s progress, anchored in values of quality, trust and social commitment. Culture expresses the organisation’s personality and guides behaviour to guarantee excellence in customer service.
- Behavioural framework: Expected behaviours grouped into three areas:
  - People, our priority: committed, close, responsible/demanding, honest/transparent.
  - Collaboration, our strength: teamwork and shared purpose.
  - Agility, our attitude: anticipation, speed, flexibility, innovation.
- Culture promotion and leadership: AHEAD Culture and Leadership Model and “Somos CaixaBank” programme to align behaviour with change and foster non‑hierarchical, transformative leadership.
  - Levers to embed culture: education (onboarding, leadership and trainer programmes), promotion/communication (intranet resources, Code of Ethics dissemination, welcome packs, recognition events), ambassadors (culture trainers, HRBPs), and an employee value proposition.
  - Culture evaluation: organisation‑wide Engagement, Culture and Leadership Study, focus groups, employee touchpoints, and managerial assessment (AHEAD Review).
- Code of Ethics: Highest internal standard, mandatory for all employees (commitment signed at onboarding) and extended to suppliers via the Supplier Code of Conduct.
  - Principles: compliance with laws, respect for people and environment, integrity, transparency, confidentiality, social responsibility, excellence/professionalism.
  - Compliance support: training, queries channel, Internal Reporting System/Whistleblower Channel, alerts/controls, and mechanisms to detect/investigate misconduct.
- Business conduct policy framework: Overview of key corporate policies and principles:
  - Internal Rules of Conduct in Securities Markets (IRC): rules on personal transactions, handling inside information, market abuse detection/reporting, conflicts of interest in investment services, and treasury share management.
  - Corporate Policy for the Internal Reporting System: governance, independence of Compliance, integrated channels (Whistleblower Channel), external reporting options, and good‑faith principle (aligned with Law 2/2023).
  - Corporate Criminal Compliance Policy: crime prevention and management model (prevention, detection, reaction, reporting, monitoring), overseen by the Corporate Crime Management Committee; obligations to report risks/non‑compliance, disciplinary system, and periodic review.
  - Corporate Anti‑Corruption Policy: zero tolerance of corruption (UN Global Compact Principle 10), detailed standards on:
    - Gifts: strict prohibitions (e.g., public officials, cash, procurement conflicts); cap generally under €200 and workplace acceptance criteria; institutional gifts handled with controls (e.g., charity raffles).
    - Giving gifts: only below €200 or from approved catalogues; none to public officials.
    - Hospitality: reasonable, business‑related, paid by CaixaBank; prohibited if intended to influence, from public officials, or tied to tenders the recipient can influence.
    - Political activity: no donations, no debt write‑offs; no direct lobbying (positions conveyed via associations).
    - Sponsorships and donations: governed by formal agreements and controls; donations channelled via “la Caixa” Foundation with safeguards.
    - Suppliers: required to uphold anti‑corruption standards (Supplier Code of Conduct).
  - Corporate Regulatory Compliance Policy: defines Compliance function objectives, governance and independence; reporting lines to the Risk Committee; ECB fit‑and‑proper criteria for the Chief Compliance Officer.
  - Corporate Conflict of Interest Policy: identification, prevention, management, disclosure and record‑keeping for real/potential conflicts across the Group.
  - AML/CFT and Sanctions Policy: Group‑wide framework and principles (risk assessment, due diligence, transaction monitoring/examination, suspicious activity reporting, sanctions screening/notifications, record retention, training, consolidated risk management).
  - Procurement, supplier conduct and tax transparency policies referenced within the framework.
- Measures to ensure compliance: Group‑wide training, communication and incentives to entrench conduct culture.
  - 2024 mandatory training with very high completion rates, including data protection, information security/fraud prevention, conduct and market risks, AML/CFT, and equality/harassment prevention; linkage of variable remuneration to completion and conduct targets expanded.
  - Targeted training for Management Committee and Board on data protection, security, conduct/market risks, and AML/CFT regulatory developments.
  - Communications and awareness: branch/area sessions, intranet news/FAQs/circulars, 244 awareness actions; 42,295 employees with training‑linked bonuses.

nodes.title: Mechanisms for detecting and investigating illicit behaviours
nodes.heading: Mechanisms for detecting and investigating illicit behaviours
nodes.start_phrase:
Integrity in the course of professional activities and compliance with 
internal regulations by all members of the organisation are the essential 
pillars of the activity provided by CaixaBank .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: CaixaBank’s integrity and compliance framework to detect, investigate, and correct illicit or improper conduct, supported by the compliance function, ethical channels, internal controls, and key indicator monitoring.
- Compliance Function: Independent second line of defence overseeing Conduct and Compliance and Legal & Regulatory risks; integrated into corporate risk management and internal governance; reports to the Board via the Global Risk Committee and to supervisory authorities (Bank of Spain, ECB, SEPBLAC, Treasury, CNMV); group-wide, coordinated model with functional dependence of subsidiaries and centralisation where needed; programme includes policies, planning, risk assessment, and remediation.
- Compliance model maturity: Maintenance of major certifications—UNE 19601 (criminal compliance), ISO 37001 (anti-bribery), ISO 37301 (compliance management). All 2024 monitoring audits completed successfully with no non‑conformities; certificates renewed on three‑year cycles with annual follow‑ups.
- Internal Information System (IIS): Group-wide whistleblowing/reporting framework aligned with Law 2/2023 for EU-law breaches and serious offences; principles include governance commitment, independence, integrated channels, option to use external authorities, and good faith.
- Whistleblower Channel: Accessible 24/7 to employees, directors, agents, suppliers, shareholders, former employees, and applicants; multiple submission routes; multilingual (ES, CA, EN, PT); guarantees confidentiality, anti‑retaliation, anonymity/non‑traceability, and rights of affected parties; partial outsourcing to an external expert to reinforce independence and objectivity.
- Promotion and training: Mandatory ethics and integrity training (linked to variable pay) and onboarding modules for new hires; intranet communications and a public website space on the channel; specialised training for channel managers (including a UPF postgraduate) and ongoing knowledge exchanges with the external expert.
- Investigation and resolution process: Standardised phases—reception, admissibility analysis (with external pre‑analysis within set timelines), assignment to Internal Audit (specialised handling for harassment cases with HR), evidence gathering, and resolution via the Incidents Committee; typical resolution within three months, extendable up to six.
- Whistleblower protection: Explicit prohibition of retaliation; confidentiality throughout; option for anonymity; preservation of presumption of innocence and right to be heard; HR involvement and potential mitigating measures (e.g., temporary relocation) where necessary.
- 2024 Whistleblowing Channel results: 101 reports received (85% employees; others from former employees, suppliers, collaborators). 46 accepted, 54 rejected, 1 pending.
