  - Strategy and principles: Conduct tax affairs to generate sustainable value while complying with laws and respecting the intent and spirit of tax legislation, social context, and the bank’s reputation; principles apply across all businesses, regions, and entities; align tax outcomes with the economic, regulatory, and commercial substance of activities, considering tax authorities’ perspectives; strict prohibition on aiding or abetting tax evasion (linked to Anti-Financial Crime framework).
  - Risk management and operations: Control framework to ensure material compliance, accurate filings, and timely payment; proactive, transparent, professional engagement with tax authorities; no tax advice to clients; new product approval embeds tax principles and assumes client compliance; expectation that third-party providers also comply; staffed with skilled professionals to maintain robust positions on the bank’s own tax matters.

nodes.title: Tax
nodes.heading: Tax
nodes.start_phrase:
The bank has clear principles of conduct and behavior as they relate to the bank’s tax affairs and a framework setting out 
roles and responsibilities among the various functions for defined tax types to ensure that the bank remains compliant with 
its tax o bligations.
nodes.summary:
- Tax governance and strategy:
  - Independent in-house Tax function, led by the Global Head of Tax reporting to the CFO; separate from business divisions.
  - Tax strategy and tax principles policy framework are defined with Management Board support and approved by the CFO and Management Board; published externally.
  - Core principles: generate sustainable value while complying with legal and regulatory requirements; respect the intent/spirit of tax laws and broader social/reputational considerations; consistent application across all regions and entities.
  - Zero tolerance for tax evasion; strict prohibition on aiding or abetting it (linked to Anti-Financial Crime policies).

- Tax risk management, operations, and stakeholder approach:
  - Control framework to ensure material compliance, accurate filings, timely payment, and proactive, transparent engagement with tax authorities.
  - The bank does not provide tax advice to clients; new product approval embeds tax compliance expectations for clients; similar expectations for third-party providers.
  - Ongoing monitoring of legislative changes; routine updates to policies and procedures.

- Key regulatory developments and impacts:
  - EU listing of Russia as non-cooperative jurisdiction (effective 2024) expected to have no material impact on the bank’s Russia operations.
  - OECD BEPS Pillar 2 (Global Anti-Base Erosion) 15% minimum tax: EU directive implemented and transposed into German MinStG; generally effective for tax years beginning after Dec 30, 2023; 2024 Pillar 2 reports/returns due June 2026. Deutsche Bank monitoring enactment status across countries and implications.

- Tax positioning and reporting:
  - Profits reported and taxed where generated; intercompany transactions on arm’s length basis per OECD transfer pricing.
  - No use of uncommercial artificial steps for tax benefits.
  - Country-by-country reporting derived from IFRS Group accounts but not directly reconcilable due to Bundesbank guidance (e.g., cross-border intragroup eliminations handled differently; intra-group dividends included in country results and often tax-exempt), which can affect jurisdictional effective tax rates.
  - 2024 totals: income tax expense €1.8 billion; income taxes paid €1.4 billion.
  - References provided to Notes on Income Taxes, Country-by-country reporting, and Shareholdings for further detail.

- Public policy and regulation governance:
  - Structured framework to manage regulatory change and policy engagement; supports informed strategic decisions and oversight of regulatory implementation.
  - Government & Public Affairs sits within Corporate & Strategy Affairs (CA&S); Global Head of CA&S reports to the CEO; ~19 FTE across Frankfurt, London, New York, Berlin, Brussels, Washington.
  - Close collaboration with the Regulatory & Exam Management Group (also in CA&S): principal contact with supervisors, manages exams, requests, documentation, findings, and closure.

- Public policy and regulatory strategy:
  - Systematic prioritization of regulatory risks; clear accountability for identifying changes, impact assessment, and ensuring compliance.
  - Sustainability regulations significantly shape strategy: EU Taxonomy, CSRD, SFDR, CSDDD, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, California GHG disclosure laws, Singapore Transition Taxonomy.
  - Support for transition to sustainable economies; advocacy for practical, comparable, and interoperable rules to improve usability of ESG disclosures.
  - Engagement with policymakers and stakeholders globally; provides thought leadership and client advisory aligned with the Global Hausbank strategy.
  - Acts as intermediary between clients and policymakers—communicating implementation challenges and clarifying regulatory intent to facilitate an effective, efficient sustainable transition.

nodes.title: Public policy and regulation
nodes.heading: Public policy and regulation
nodes.start_phrase:
Deutsche Bank has a clearly structured framework for managing the risk of regulatory change and enhancing its profile in 
policy and regulatory debates.
nodes.summary:
- Public policy and regulation framework and governance
  - Deutsche Bank’s structured framework to manage regulatory change, engage stakeholders, and oversee implementation of key regulatory initiatives.
  - Government & Public Affairs housed in Corporate & Strategy Affairs (~19 FTE across Frankfurt, London, New York, Berlin, Brussels, Washington), reporting to the Global Head of Corporate Affairs & Strategy, who reports to the CEO.
  - Close coordination with the Regulatory & Exam Management Group (principal contact for supervisors; exam management, findings, closure), also in Corporate & Strategy Affairs.

- Strategy and focus areas
  - Systematic prioritization of regulatory risks; clear accountability for identifying, assessing, and ensuring compliance.
  - Sustainability regulations shaping strategy: EU Taxonomy, CSRD, SFDR, CSDDD, German Supply Chain Act, California GHG disclosure laws, Singapore Transition Taxonomy.
  - Aim to harmonize global guidelines for comparability and transparency; act as intermediary between clients and policymakers to translate implementation challenges and regulatory intent.
  - Position papers aligned with the bank’s net‑zero strategy and Paris Agreement; emphasis on financing transition, including high‑emitting sectors with credible pathways.

- 2024 policy environment and regional priorities
  - Elections (EU Parliament, UK, US) slowed new policymaking for much of 2024, with sustainability focus picking up late in the year.
  - European Union: implementation of final Basel III, macroprudential framework review, MiFID revisions, settlement cycle work, securitization framework revisions; support for digital euro (ECB preparation and legislative framework); Instant Payments Regulation; Payment Services Directive review; call for a holistic, competitive EU payments vision; advocacy on financing Europe’s digital and sustainable transition via deeper capital markets; investor protection and Retail Investment Strategy; centrality of transition finance.
  - United Kingdom: continued financial services reforms post-government change; Listing Act changes (in force July 29, 2024), Prospectus Regime updates, Pensions Review input; secondary market focus (Wholesale Markets Review, MiFIR transparency); contribution to T+1 settlement taskforce; support for sector-specific transition plan guidance; engagement on digital gilts and broader digitalization.
  - United States: focus on prudential regulators’ Basel III “endgame” proposal raising capital for >$100bn banks; uncertainty on finalization and timing; exploration of liquidity requirement changes after March 2023 banking stress.

- Impact, risk, and opportunity management
  - Detection of regulatory developments via direct policymaker engagement, trade associations, and internal monitoring with daily updates.
  - Continuous engagement through full policy cycles; sharing insights with clients and gathering feedback on implementation hurdles to inform policymakers.
  - Advocacy for ESG‑effective, efficient rules that enable growth while respecting environmental and social needs; positioning Deutsche Bank as a sustainability leader.
  - Transition finance stance: need principle-based guidance tied to sectoral net‑zero roadmaps; make EU Taxonomy more workable; support with industrial policy.
  - CSDDD position: supportive but advocating risk-based, proportionate, low‑bureaucracy application; limit scope for financial services to loans to direct clients; highlight competitiveness concerns versus non‑covered markets.

- Advocacy governance, transparency, and memberships
  - Mission-driven Government & Public Affairs mandate to advocate for strong European banks, responsible capital markets growth, fair green transition, and payments/tech innovation.
  - Strict policies for regulator and policymaker interactions: Supervisory Authorities Engagement Policy (logging/recording), Representation of Interests Policy (German Federal Government, Parliament, EU institutions), U.S. lobbying and PAC rules.
  - Registrations: EU Transparency Register and German Federal/Bavaria/Baden‑Württemberg Lobbying Registers; disclosure of advocacy expenditures and adherence to codes of conduct.
  - No direct political donations per Group Policy; note of indirect political contributions by two non-financial trade associations in Germany (€36,254) without bank involvement.
  - Broad trade association participation (e.g., BdB, AFME, VdP, UK Finance, ISDA, SIFMA, IIF, ASIFMA); CEO Christian Sewing presides over BdB and EBF (until Feb 2025), advocating digital and sustainable transformation and Capital Markets Union.
  - Influence on regulation considered medium; impacts materialize over time; no specific advocacy KPIs—engagement aligned to mission and Global Hausbank strategy.

- Data protection (privacy) program
  - Commitment to protecting personal data under GDPR and similar laws, recognizing privacy as a fundamental social value.
  - Governance: Group Data Privacy as independent Second Line of Defense; sets principles, policies, and minimum control standards; local Data Protection Officers network; Chief Data Privacy Officer reports to the Chief Legal Officer (Management Board member).
  - Collaboration with Technology, Data and Innovation and Information Security on controls (e.g., encryption, access rights).
  - Strategy and execution: privacy embedded in culture and conduct; continuous enhancement of policies and controls, including AI initiatives.
  - 2024 actions: launch of a group-wide framework of key data protection principles; revision of the global data protection policy to strengthen roles/responsibilities; planned 2025 update to consolidate and add country specifics.
  - Ongoing regulatory monitoring, control implementation, advice on lawful processing (including third parties), employee training and awareness campaigns.
  - Industry engagement via BdB and EBF to align standards, share best practices, and reflect evolving regulatory expectations (e.g., standard privacy notices, T&Cs).

nodes.title: Data protection
nodes.heading: Data protection
nodes.start_phrase: In most countries Deutsche Bank conducts business there is a data protection (also referenced as “data privacy”) law.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and commitment: Deutsche Bank views data protection as a core social value and legal obligation, committing to GDPR and equivalent global laws grounded in human rights frameworks.
- Governance setup: Group Data Privacy operates as an independent Second Line of Defense, with the Chief Data Privacy Officer reporting to the Chief Legal Officer (Management Board). Local Data Protection Officers support country operations. The function collaborates closely with Technology, Data and Innovation and the Chief Security Office and participates in business forums and worker council matters.
- Policy and strategy: Data protection is embedded in culture and conduct. In 2024, the bank issued a group-wide framework of key data protection principles and revised its global policy to clarify responsibilities, with a 2025 update planned to consolidate country-specific requirements. Group Data Privacy acts as the SME for legal interpretation and continuous regulatory monitoring.
- Risk and control framework: Data protection is a material topic due to reputational, legal, operational, and trust risks. Minimum control standards require notification of new personal data processing (including AI), integration into new product approval and third-party risk management, and ongoing assurance testing. Coverage of vendor risk management was expanded in 2024; no major deficiencies were identified.
- Transparency and data subject rights: The bank mandates privacy notices for clients and employees, lawful consent mechanisms, and timely handling of data subject requests. Suppliers processing personal data must meet contractual data protection obligations; Group Data Privacy supports on individual requests and complaints.
- Regulatory developments monitored in 2024: Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework adequacy, amendments to Turkey’s PDPL, additional U.S. state privacy laws; ongoing monitoring of the UK DPDI Bill and EU digital and cybersecurity initiatives (e.g., ePrivacy).
- Training and awareness: Mandatory global data protection eLearning for all employees and eligible contractors was enhanced in 2024 to address new laws and AI-related risks; completion rate was 99.29% (vs. 99.96% in 2023). Ongoing awareness includes targeted trainings, newsletters, and joint initiatives with Information Security; non-compliance may lead to disciplinary action.
- Incident management and reporting: Group Data Privacy monitors potential personal data breaches and coordinates with the global security incident process, advising on regulatory notifications and informing affected individuals when required. No personal data breaches of material impact to individuals were observed in 2024.
- Reporting frameworks: The section aligns with ESRS (e.g., GOV-2, SBM-3, IRO-1/2, S1, S4) and GRI (404-2/FS4, 418-1) disclosures.
- Information security reference: Detailed information security governance, strategy, and risk management are provided in the Annual Report’s Risk Report under Risk and Capital Management.

nodes.title: Information security
nodes.heading: Information security
nodes.start_phrase: For information on information security at Deutsche Bank, please refer to the respective chapter in Deutsche Bank’s Annual Report, located within the Risk Report section under Risk and Capital Management.
nodes.summary:
- Data privacy oversight: Group Data Privacy continuously monitors potential personal data breaches, with established reporting pathways from business and infrastructure units defined in a global data protection guidance document. In 2024, no personal data breaches with material impact to individuals were observed.
- Incident response: In case of a breach, actions are coordinated through the global security incident management process; Group Data Privacy advises on regulatory steps, informs affected individuals if required, and notifies relevant data protection authorities.
- Information security reference: Readers are directed to the Risk Report section (Risk and Capital Management) of the Annual Report for comprehensive details on information security governance, strategy, and risk management. The section cites ESRS 2 GOV-2, ESRS 2 SBM-3, ESRS 2 MDR-P, ESRS 2 MDR-A, and GRI 404 2a.
- Independent auditor’s limited assurance report on the group sustainability statement (FY 2024): 
  - Scope: Assurance over the group sustainability statement included in the Combined Management Report, prepared under CSRD, EU Taxonomy Regulation Article 8, and German Commercial Code (HGB) requirements.
  - Conclusion: Nothing came to the auditors’ attention indicating non-compliance, in all material respects, with CSRD, EU Taxonomy Article 8, HGB, and ESRS. The materiality assessment process is consistent with the Double materiality statement; Article 8 disclosures are compliant.
  - Basis: Engagement conducted under ISAE 3000 (Revised); limited assurance provides a lower level of assurance than reasonable assurance.
  - Independence and quality management: The auditors affirm independence under European and German law; firm quality systems align with IDW QMS 1 and ISQM 1.

nodes.title: Additional information
nodes.heading: Additional information
nodes.start_phrase: We have performed a limited assurance engagement on the group sustainability statement of Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft, Frankfurt am Main (hereafter “Deutsche Bank“) for the fiscal year from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2024 included in the Combined Management Report section of Deutsche Bank’s Annual Report.
nodes.summary:
- Independent auditor’s limited assurance report on Deutsche Bank’s 2024 group sustainability statement included in the Combined Management Report.
- Scope and criteria: assessment against CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), EU Taxonomy Article 8 (Regulation (EU) 2020/852), German Commercial Code (HGB) §§289b–289e, 315b–315c, and ESRS; statement is combined with the parent company’s sustainability statement; uses criteria presented by the executive directors.
- Assurance conclusion: nothing came to the auditor’s attention indicating the statement is not prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the above requirements.
- Specific confirmations: no indications of material non-compliance with ESRS, including the consistency of the double materiality assessment process as described; and no indications of material non-compliance with EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures.
- Basis of work: engagement performed under ISAE 3000 (Revised); limited assurance procedures provide a lower level of assurance than reasonable assurance.
- Independence and quality: auditor independent under EU and German professional requirements; quality management in line with IDW QMS 1 (09.2022) and ISQM 1.
- Evidence: auditor believes sufficient and appropriate evidence was obtained; further details on responsibilities are referenced in a dedicated section.

nodes.title: Independent auditor’s limited assurance report on the group sustainability statement
nodes.heading: Independent auditor’s limited assurance report on the group sustainability statement
nodes.start_phrase:
We have performed a limited assurance engagement on the group sustainability statement of Deutsche Bank 
Aktiengesellschaft, Frankfurt am Main (hereafter “Deutsche Bank“) for the fiscal year from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 
2024 included in the Combined Management Report section of Deutsche Bank’s Annual Report.
nodes.summary:
- EY issued a limited assurance report on Deutsche Bank’s 2024 group sustainability statement, which is included in the Combined Management Report and combined with the parent company’s sustainability statement.
- Scope and criteria: Assurance against CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), EU Taxonomy Article 8 (Regulation (EU) 2020/852), and German Commercial Code sections 289b–289e and 315b–315c, with reference to the company’s elaborative criteria.
- Conclusion: Nothing came to the auditor’s attention indicating the statement is not prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with CSRD, EU Taxonomy Article 8, ESRS, and that the materiality assessment aligns with the description in the Double materiality statement section.
- Assurance basis: Engagement performed under ISAE 3000 (Revised); independence affirmed; quality management under IDW QMS 1 and ISQM 1; limited assurance provides a lower level of assurance than reasonable assurance.
- Management and oversight responsibilities: Executive directors are responsible for preparation, internal controls, materiality assessment, methods, estimates, and forward-looking information; the Supervisory Board oversees the preparation process.
- Inherent limitations: Ongoing interpretation uncertainties in CSRD and related requirements may affect legal conformity; such limitations also affect the assurance work.
- Auditor responsibilities and procedures: Understanding of the preparation and materiality processes; risk-based focus on potential misstatements (including higher risk in value chain data); evaluation of forward-looking assumptions; assessment of methods, estimates, presentation; analytical procedures and inquiries; assessment of EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment processes. Where value chain data are estimated per ESRS after reasonable efforts, auditors evaluate the estimation approach and reasonableness rather than determining the data themselves.
- Use and liability: Report intended for the company’s purposes only; not for third-party decision-making; liability to third parties disclaimed per General Engagement Terms (1 January 2024); no obligation to update the report after issuance unless required by law.
- Formalities: Report dated March 10, 2025, issued by EY GmbH & Co. KG, signed by two German Public Auditors.
- ESRS content index: Introduction to the list of ESRS disclosure requirements complied with, stating the Sustainability Statement’s comprehensive coverage based on a 2024 double materiality assessment and compliance with all listed ESRS requirements; index maps ESRS 1 and ESRS 2 (including GOV-1, GOV-2, BP-1, BP-2, and general disclosures) to chapters such as Governance, Supply chain management (including Asset Management), Own workforce, Client centricity, Anti-financial crime, and Anti-competitive behavior, with page references.

nodes.title: List of Disclosure Requirements complied with
nodes.heading: List of Disclosure Requirements complied with
nodes.start_phrase: Deutsche Bank’s Sustainability Statement provides a comprehensive disclosure of the material topics for its sustainability performance.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: An “Additional information” section of Deutsche Bank’s 2024 Annual Report that serves as a comprehensive ESRS content index. It states the Sustainability Statement is based on a 2024 double materiality assessment and complies with all applicable ESRS disclosure requirements.

- ESRS content index: A detailed mapping of each ESRS standard and disclosure requirement to the relevant Sustainability Statement chapter and page. It covers ESRS 1 (general requirements) and ESRS 2 (general disclosures) across:
  - Governance (roles of administrative/management/supervisory bodies, information flows, incentive schemes, due diligence, internal controls over sustainability reporting).
  - Identification and assessment of material impacts, risks and opportunities.
  - Strategy, business model, value chain, stakeholder interests and engagement.
  - Policies, actions/resources, metrics, and targets for all material topics.

- Topical standards and themes: Cross-references for disclosures on:
  - Climate change (ESRS E1) including the transition plan, policies, actions, targets, and financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15), plus Asset Management portfolio metrics/targets.
  - Governance (ESRS G1) including corporate culture, supplier management, anti-corruption/bribery (incidents and prevention/detection), political influence/lobbying, and payment practices.
  - Own workforce (ESRS S1) including policies, engagement and remediation channels, workforce management, working conditions (talent development, performance/reward, work-life balance), diversity/equity/inclusion (gender, age, ethnicity, disability), pay metrics, incidents/complaints, and targets.
  - Consumers and end-users (ESRS S4) including product responsibility, selling/marketing practices, client satisfaction, complaint management, and remediation channels.
  - Additional material topics: sustainable finance across divisions, ESG due diligence (incl. Equator Principles), supply chain management, client centricity, culture/integrity/conduct, anti-financial crime, anti-competitive behavior, tax, public policy and regulation, data protection, and information security.

- Regulatory linkages: A separate table identifies ESRS datapoints that derive from other EU legislation (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3 Article 449a, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law), with references and reporting locations. Items include board diversity/independence, due diligence statements, involvement in fossil fuels/chemicals/controversial weapons/tobacco, the 2050 climate-neutral transition plan, Paris-aligned Benchmark exclusions, GHG reduction targets, and energy consumption/intensity (not material).

nodes.title: Table of all the datapoints deriving from other EU legislation
nodes.heading: Table of all the datapoints deriving from other EU legislation
nodes.start_phrase:
The table below illustrates the datapoints in ESRS 2 and topical ESRS that derive from other EU legislation as required in 
ESRS 2 Appendix B.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: A comprehensive cross‑reference table required by ESRS 2 Appendix B that maps ESRS 2 and topical ESRS disclosure datapoints to corresponding requirements in other EU legislation and shows where Deutsche Bank reports them in its Sustainability Statement.
- Regulations mapped: SFDR (Annex I indicators), CRR Article 449a Pillar 3 climate/social risk templates (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453), the Benchmark Regulation delegated acts (EU) 2020/1816 and 2020/1818, and the EU Climate Law (Regulation (EU) 2021/1119).
- What the table provides for each datapoint: the ESRS reference, associated SFDR indicator numbers/tables, Pillar 3 templates/paragraphs, Benchmark/Climate Law clauses, the Sustainability Statement chapter title, and an explicit note on materiality/relevance (e.g., material, not material, not applicable, not relevant for 2024).
- Governance (ESRS 2 GOV): Board gender diversity and independence (linked to SFDR and Benchmark Reg.), and a due diligence statement (mapped to SFDR PAI), reported under Corporate Governance and ESG due diligence.
- Strategy/business model (ESRS 2 SBM-1): Involvement in fossil fuels, chemical production, controversial weapons, and tobacco tied to SFDR and Benchmark Reg.; most marked “Not applicable” for chapter placement.
- Climate (ESRS E1):  
  - Transition plan to 2050 and GHG targets mapped to EU Climate Law, SFDR, Benchmark Reg., and Pillar 3; reported under Sustainability Strategy/Climate change – Transition plan.  
  - GHG emissions (Scope 1–3): SFDR and Pillar 3 linkages; only Scope 3 Category 15 (financed emissions) is material (reported under Client portfolios – Metrics and targets), others not material.  
  - Energy consumption/mix/intensity mostly “Not material.”  
  - Physical risk exposure, asset location, and real estate energy efficiency templates flagged “Not relevant for 2024.”  
  - Climate‑related opportunities linked to Benchmark Reg., reported under Sustainable Finance.
- Pollution (ESRS E2), Water & Marine (ESRS E3), Biodiversity (ESRS E4), and Resource use/Circular economy (ESRS E5): Multiple SFDR indicators referenced (e.g., E‑PRTR emissions, water consumption/recycling, deforestation and oceans policies, non‑recycled and hazardous waste), largely assessed “Not material.”
- Own workforce (ESRS S1): Policies and due diligence on human rights/ILO conventions, anti‑trafficking, accident prevention, grievance mechanisms, diversity and pay equity, and incidents of discrimination; mapped to SFDR and Benchmark Reg.; reporting spread across workforce‑related chapters (DEI, work‑life balance, remediation channels). Several quantitative safety metrics noted “Not material.”
- Workers in the value chain (ESRS S2) and Affected communities (ESRS S3): Human rights policy commitments, due diligence, risks of child/forced labor, non‑respect of UNGPs/OECD, and incident reporting mapped to SFDR/Benchmark Reg.; most items “Not material.”
- Consumers and end‑users (ESRS S4): Policies, non‑respect of UNGPs/OECD, and incidents tied to SFDR/Benchmark Reg.; disclosures located in Client centricity (product responsibility, client satisfaction, complaint management).
- Business conduct (ESRS G1): Anti‑corruption (UN Convention), whistleblower protection, fines, and standards mapped to SFDR/Benchmark Reg.; reported under Anti‑financial crime and Culture, integrity and conduct.
- Overall: The table demonstrates regulatory alignment, traceability across EU frameworks, and Deutsche Bank’s materiality conclusions and reporting locations for each ESRS‑linked datapoint for the 2024 reporting year.

nodes.title: Preface
nodes.summary: An outline of the ING Group Annual Report 2024 Sustainability Statement, detailing: general information and basis for preparation; the business model, strategy, and sustainability governance; environmental topics including E1 Climate change (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; transition plan; policies, actions, and performance) and E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; nature strategy; policies, actions, and performance); coverage of the EU Taxonomy regulation; social topics including S1 Own workforce (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; strategy to unlock people’s full potential; policies, actions, and performance) and S4 Consumers and end-users (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; strategy for superior customer value; policies, actions, and performance); and governance through G1 Business conduct (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; policies, actions, and performance). It also shows where the Sustainability Statement sits within the broader annual report, alongside sections such as strategy, financial and risk management, leadership and governance, and financial statements.

nodes.title: General information
nodes.heading: 1 General information
nodes.start_phrase: This report represents our first Sustainability Statement in accordance with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), which we voluntary apply as the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) has not yet been transposed into Dutch law.
nodes.summary:
- First Sustainability Statement aligned with ESRS, applied voluntarily as CSRD is not yet transposed into Dutch law.
- Acknowledges market-wide challenges: data availability and reliability, lack of industry-specific guidance, and comparability issues.
- Basis for preparation: covers ING Groep N.V. and subsidiaries (ING Group) for the year ended 31 December 2024, consistent with financial statement consolidation.
- Prepared in line with ESRS and a double materiality assessment (DMA) following EFRAG guidance, covering own operations and the full value chain.
- DMA outcomes define material topics and related impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs), disclosed across Environment, Social, and Governance sections.
- Includes an EU Taxonomy summary in the Environment section and mandatory tables in the Appendix to the Executive Board report.
- Highlights uncertainties: new regulatory implementation, evolving guidance, no industry-specific standard, absence of comparative figures, and the need to embed sustainability into processes and internal controls.
- Data limitations and reliance on estimates: extensive use of external data vendors for emissions and ESG data; vendor processes generally unaudited; ING performs its own data quality reviews but notes residual risk of inaccuracies; plans to refine metrics as better data emerge (details per metric in the Appendix).
- Connectivity with financial statements: monetary amounts for financed emissions, intensity metrics, and transition/physical risks derived from the credit risk portfolio; some disclosures include uncommitted limits; reporting follows internal data standards.
- Transition risk provisioning updated via a management adjustment to capture expected credit losses in the current business lending portfolio.
- Provides navigation to broader report sections (strategy, governance, risk management, financial statements, and appendices).

nodes.title: Connectivity with financial statements
nodes.heading: 1.3 Connectivity with financial statements
nodes.start_phrase: The monetary amounts presented in the disclosures on financed emissions, emissions-intensity metrics, and on transition and physical risks are derived from the credit risk portfolio.
nodes.summary:
- First Sustainability Statement prepared in voluntary alignment with ESRS, as CSRD is not yet transposed into Dutch law; acknowledges market-wide challenges with data availability, reliability, relevance, and comparability.
- Basis for preparation covers ING Groep N.V. and subsidiaries consistent with financial statement consolidation; reporting is guided by a double materiality assessment (DMA) per ESRS and EFRAG guidance, spanning own operations and the full value chain; material topics and related impacts, risks, and opportunities are disclosed across Environment, Social, and Governance sections; EU Taxonomy summary appears in Environment with mandatory tables in the appendix.
- Uncertainties and estimations stem from first-time application, evolving guidance, lack of industry-specific standards, absence of comparatives, and the need to further embed sustainability into processes and controls; heavy reliance on external data vendors for emissions and ESG data, which are not generally audited; ING applies internal data quality checks but notes residual risks and expects refinements as data and practices mature; metric-specific details are in the appendix.
- Financial connectivity: monetary amounts for financed emissions, emissions intensity, and transition/physical risks are derived from the credit risk portfolio, sometimes extended with uncommitted limits; data adheres to internal standards for transparency; provisions methodology updated with a management adjustment to reflect medium- to long-term transition risks for high-emitting sectors; climate risk cannot yet be fully embedded in IFRS 9 ECL models due to limited empirical data; for mortgages, next step is collateral valuation differentiation by EPC label.

- Incorporation by reference is used to avoid duplication where ESRS requirements are already met elsewhere in the Annual Report, with a reference index mapping disclosures.

nodes.title: Business model and strategy
nodes.heading: 2 Business model and strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Our strategy is about growing the difference by providing superior value for our customers and putting sustainability at the heart of what we do.
nodes.summary:
- States ING’s strategy to “grow the difference” by delivering superior customer value with sustainability at the core.
- Explains the section’s purpose: to outline material impacts, risks and opportunities, how they link to the strategy and business model, and to provide insights into the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) methodology.
- Defines the value chain scope for the DMA, extending beyond financial consolidation to include own operations and upstream/downstream relationships; six value-chain segments are identified using internal data.
- Highlights the loan book as the primary channel of sustainability impact; assessments focus on tier 1 direct counterparties, with exceptions for S2 (workers in the value chain) and S4 (consumers/end-users) where tier 2 effects are considered.
- Clarifies that non-consolidated associates and joint ventures are treated as other business relationships within the DMA, while intercompany transactions are excluded.
- Maps key activities, products, services, and actors across the value chain:
  - Upstream: supplier, employee, and property management.
  - Own operations (Retail, Wholesale/Business, Private Banking): lending, payments and cash management, trade finance, deposits and savings, product development, marketing, and distribution of lending, insurance, investment and financial market products.
  - Treasury and investments: high-quality liquid assets, hedging, debt instruments, shareholder’s equity, and equity holdings/investee companies.
  - Downstream actors: large corporates (incl. financial institutions), sovereigns and agencies, SMEs and mid-corporates, self-employed/micro, private individuals, and private banking clients.
- Provides cross-references to related sections (“ING at a glance” and “Strategy, business model and value creation”) for further context.

nodes.title: Business model and strategy - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2 Business model and strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Our strategy is about growing the difference by providing superior value for our customers and putting sustainability at the heart of what we do.
nodes.summary:
Business model and strategy
Our strategy is about growing the difference by providing superior value for our customers and putting 
sustainability at the heart of what we do. With our business we provide services to our Retail  and Wholesale 
clients, worldwide.  For more information on our  operating environment and strategy, see sections ‘ ING at a 
glance ’ and  ‘Strategy, business model and value creation ’. This section provides an overview of our identified 
material impacts, risks and opportunities, how these interact with our strategy and business model, and 
insights into the methodology of our DMA.

nodes.title: Our value chain
nodes.heading: 2.1 Our value chain
nodes.start_phrase: With a view to comprehensively captur e impacts, risks and opportunities, the DMA has to focus on the most significant activities, services and products.
nodes.summary:
- Strategic focus: grow by delivering superior customer value with sustainability embedded at the core; services span Retail and Wholesale clients worldwide.
- Purpose of the section: overview of identified material impacts, risks and opportunities, how they link to strategy and the business model, and an explanation of the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) methodology; references to related report sections for broader context.
- Value chain approach: DMA targets the most significant activities, products and services; scope extends beyond financial-statement consolidation to include own operations and indirect upstream/downstream relationships; six value-chain segments identified using internal data.
- Key sustainability nexus: the loan book is the primary driver of sustainability impacts; assessments are mainly at tier‑1 direct counterparties (e.g., financed corporates, retail clients), with tier‑2 considered for S2 (workers in the value chain) and S4 (consumers/end-users).
- Boundary choices: non-consolidated associates and joint ventures are treated as other business relationships and included in the DMA; intercompany transactions are excluded.
- Mapped value chain activities: 
  - Wholesale/Business/Retail Banking and Private Individuals: lending, deposits/savings, daily banking, trade finance, capital markets advisory, trading book, mortgages, insurance, investment and wealth-management products; product development, marketing, and distribution.
  - Own operations: supplier management, employee management, property management.
  - Treasury and investments: High Quality Liquid Assets, hedging, debt instruments, shareholder equity, and equity holdings.
- Principal actors covered: suppliers, employees, large corporates (incl. financial institutions), sovereigns/sub-sovereigns/agencies, self-employed/micro firms, SMEs/mid-corporates, private individual and private banking clients, corporate clients, and investee companies.
- Report context: excerpt from ING Group Annual Report 2024, Business model and strategy section.

nodes.title: Our double materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 2.2 Our double materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: This is the first year that we have performed our double materiality assessment in accordance with ESRS, based on the six identified value chain segments.
nodes.summary:
- First ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment, transitioning from prior GRI-based approach; key change is adding financial materiality to impact materiality.
- Materiality definitions:
  - Impact materiality (inside-out): actual or potential positive/negative impacts on people and the environment from financed activities, ING’s own operations, products, services, and business relationships.
  - Financial materiality (outside-in): risks and opportunities from environmental and societal changes affecting ING, notably via climate and environmental risk management.
- Time horizons used: very short (<1 year), short (1–3 years), medium (3–5 years), long (>5 years and at least 10), with ESRS requiring some forward-looking disclosures.
- Scope and evaluation: DMA based on six value chain segments; covers sector-agnostic topics E1–E5 (climate, pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity/ecosystems, resource use/circular economy), S1–S4 (own workforce, workers in the value chain, affected communities, consumers/end-users), and G1 (business conduct), assessed for risk, opportunity, and double materiality with thresholds (Material, Important, Informative–Minimal).
- Outcomes: Despite methodology shift, topic-level results broadly consistent with prior year. S2 (Workers in the value chain) and S3 (Affected communities) not deemed material for ING’s value chains but still considered important.
- Salient human rights issues:
  - As lender to corporates: forced labour, child labour, land and resource-related community issues.
  - As procurer: occupational health and safety, modern slavery and forced labour.
  - Identification, management, and mitigation detailed in ING’s latest human rights report (ing.com).

nodes.title: Process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 2.3 Process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Via the double materiality assessment process, ING identifies impacts, risk s and opportunities across environmental, social and governance (ESG) sustainability matters, arising from its own operations or within the upstream or downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Explains ING’s process for identifying impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across its operations and value chain using a Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) aligned with ESRS.
- DMA governance and flow: Five-step approach—(1) identify activities and business relationships, (2) identify relevant sustainability matters, (3) execute the DMA, (4) validate results through stakeholder engagement, (5) obtain Management Board and Supervisory Board approval.
- Scoping methodology: Starts from balance sheet and P&L to pinpoint activities/assets subject to IROs; maps financial statement items to core business areas and portfolios; excludes portfolios with low likelihood of material IROs.
- Exposure classification: Categorizes assets and liabilities by characteristics such as loan/position maturity, counterparty type, product/service type, geography, industry, and collateral to understand where sustainability issues can materialize.
- Sustainability matters selection: Uses ESRS sector-agnostic inventory as the baseline for alignment and comparability; conducts market consultation and reviews past assessments to find entity-specific topics—none added; assesses topics across the full value chain, recognizing relevance varies by chain (details in the appendix).
- Assessment granularity: Evaluates all ESRS topics at sub-topic level; Social matters assessed at sub-sub-topic level; granularity set by internal and external data availability.
- Impact drivers: Defines and considers environmental (e.g., resource use, emissions), social (e.g., labor practices, human rights, equity, community health/safety), and governance (e.g., transparency, accountability, anti-corruption, compliance) drivers, with a forward-looking perspective.
- Risk drivers: Identifies ESG risks within existing risk categories, including transition and physical risks; accounts for forward-looking characteristics and dependencies on natural and human capital; links to broader ESG risk management.
- Opportunity drivers: Views opportunities as ESG-related conditions that can enhance the business model, strategy delivery, and value creation; prioritization aligned with publicly disclosed sustainability commitments.

nodes.title: Execution of the double materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 2.4 Execution of the double materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The DMA leverages on renowned external data sources , internal data, voluntary reports and other regulatory disclosures to assess the impact from ING’s own operations and upstream and downstream value chain .
nodes.summary:
- Explains how ING executes its Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) across its full value chain (own operations, upstream, downstream) using a “gross” approach that excludes mitigating actions.
- Identifies data foundations: renowned external sources, internal data, voluntary reports, and regulatory disclosures; combines quantitative and qualitative methods against predefined thresholds.
- Defines impact materiality via severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood across time horizons for both actual and potential positive/negative impacts.
- Defines financial materiality via magnitude and likelihood arising from impacts, dependencies, and context analyses; considers dependencies on natural, human, and social resources, business relationships, and reputation; supplements indicators with expert judgment.
- Details risk assessment: mirrors approach for negative impacts and dependencies; incorporates individual exposures and context; determines portfolio risk materiality as the maximum across dimensions; enhanced by internal data and scenario analyses.
- Details opportunity assessment: evaluates magnitude (financial and non-financial gains, e.g., cost savings) across “use of own resources” and “reliance on relationships” dimensions; likelihood tied to time horizon.
- Describes scoring framework: combined scores from 1 (minimal) to 5 (critical) using a conversion matrix of severity/magnitude versus likelihood; sustainability matters are material if rated “critical” or “significant.”
- References “Technical notes to the double materiality assessment” for further methodological details and value-chain-specific sustainability matters.

nodes.title: Validation of the outcome through stakeholders’ engagement
nodes.heading: 2.5 Validation of the outcome through stakeholders’ engagement
nodes.start_phrase: To validate the outcome of our double materiality assessment, we engaged with our key stakeholders.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines how ING validated the results of its double materiality assessment (DMA) through structured engagement with two stakeholder groups—affected stakeholders and users. It describes a standardized process of workshops, surveys, and in-depth interviews to review the DMA methodology, preliminary results, completeness, and different time horizons, with interview minutes confirmed to ensure accuracy. Where direct engagement was not feasible, proxies were used (e.g., NGOs for affected communities and nature; internal and public data for retail customers). Stakeholder feedback was evaluated systematically for recurrence, consistency, evidentiary support, and relevance, with references cross-checked and discussed with subject-matter experts. An example is provided where some stakeholders expected “Workers in the value chain (S2)” and “Affected communities (S3)” to be material; ING maintained their non-material status given limited portfolio exposure to high human-rights-risk sectors, while continuing to report on them as salient human rights issues. The text also details stakeholder-specific engagement channels and focus areas: employees (S1, G1), customers and investors (all ESRS topics), and society via NGOs and regulatory experts (E1–E5, S2–S4, and all ESRS topics for governments/regulators). Finally, it records governance approvals: methodology endorsed by the ESG Risk Committee and the DMA outcome approved by the management boards and Supervisory Board, following communication to internal stakeholders and value-chain owners.

nodes.title: Approval by the management boards and Supervisory Board
nodes.heading: 2.6 Approval by the management boards and Supervisory Board
nodes.start_phrase: The outcome of the DMA was communicated to all relevant stakeholders and value-chain segment owners.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Validate the double materiality assessment (DMA) outcomes and identified material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) with stakeholders, checking recognition and any missing topics.
- Stakeholder scope and methods: Two groups—affected stakeholders and users—engaged via sessions, surveys, and in-depth interviews. A standardized approach covered soundness, completeness, and different time horizons. Interview minutes were confirmed to ensure accurate interpretation.
- Use of proxies: NGOs represented affected communities and silent stakeholders such as nature and biodiversity; internal and public data represented private customers; ING experts covered supervisory/public/regulatory perspectives when direct engagement was not possible.
- Feedback evaluation: Inputs were analyzed for recurrence, consistency, strength, evidence, and relevance; patterns across groups were identified; fact-based substantiation was prioritized and cross-checked with credible sources and subject-matter experts.
- Example outcome: Despite some stakeholder expectations for Workers in the value chain (S2) and Affected communities (S3) to be material, ING maintained its DMA outcome due to limited exposure to human rights–vulnerable sectors, while continuing to report on these salient issues in the human rights report.
- Governance and approvals: DMA methodology approved by the ESG Risk Committee; outcomes approved by the management boards and the Supervisory Board, after communication to relevant stakeholders and value-chain owners.
- Engagement by stakeholder segment:
  - Our people: Direct workshops with employees; proxies via European/local works councils; feedback via surveys and interviews; focus on S1 and G1.
  - Our customers: Retail via proxies (customer complaints, consumer protection publications); Business and Wholesale via proxies (sessions with ING sector experts); focus on all ESRS topics.
  - Investors: Direct sessions with investors and associations; focus on all ESRS topics.
  - Society: Direct sessions with NGOs as proxies for nature, biodiversity, climate, and workers in the value chain; proxy sessions with ING regulatory/public affairs experts; focus on E1–E5, S2–S4, and all ESRS topics for governments and regulators.

nodes.title: Reporting on the material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 2.7 Reporting on the material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: For each material sustainability matter, ING reviewed the associated disclosure and application requirements included in the ESRSs.
nodes.summary:
- Describes ING’s approach to reporting material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities under ESRS for the 2024 Sustainability Statement.
- States that ING disclosed applicable mandatory, relevant, and material information, while omitting certain requirements not applicable in the initial years; details are in the Reference index.
- Explains integration of sustainability risk management and internal controls into ING’s ERM framework and three-lines-of-defence model to strengthen governance and align with financial and non-financial oversight.
- Notes that the CSRD sustainability statement preparation is aligned with ING’s annual integrated reporting process and governance.
- Acknowledges inherent risks of material misstatement (e.g., human error, third-party controls, fraud) and indicates mitigating measures have been implemented.
- Provides cross-references to the Risk management framework and the Reference index within the ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Internal controls over sustainability reporting
nodes.heading: 2.8 Internal controls over sustainability reporting
nodes.start_phrase: At ING we have integrated our sustainability-related risk management and internal controls into our existing Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and three-lines-of-defence model.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: ING reports on material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) in line with ESRS disclosure and application requirements. For the 2024 Sustainability Statement, ING includes applicable mandatory, relevant and material information, while omitting certain requirements not applicable in the first reporting years. A Reference index provides details.

- Governance and controls: Sustainability-related risk management and internal controls are integrated into ING’s Enterprise Risk Management framework and three-lines-of-defence model, aligned with the annual integrated reporting and CSRD governance. ING acknowledges risk of material misstatement (e.g., human error, third-party controls, fraud) and has implemented mitigating measures.

- IRO overview table: Presents where IROs arise across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), the time horizons (very short to long term), and which business models are affected (Private Individuals, Private Banking, Wholesale Banking, Business Banking).

- Environmental
  - Climate change (E1)
    - Negative impact: financing high-emitting sectors and non–energy-efficient properties.
    - Risks: potential (non)financial losses from transition risks (defaults, reduced collateral values) and physical risks (storms, floods, sea-level rise, temperature increases).
    - Opportunities: ING’s voluntary commitments to support clients’ climate transition.
    - Broadly spans the value chain, multiple time horizons; affects Private Individuals, Private Banking, Wholesale Banking, Business Banking.
  - Biodiversity (E4)
    - Negative impact: lending to clients whose operations cause irreversible harm to species.
    - Risks: reputational and financial losses tied to severity of impacts.
    - Primarily linked to Wholesale Banking.

- Social
  - Own workforce (S1)
    - Negative impacts: unrealistic workloads, gender inequality, pay gaps, inadequate prevention of violence and harassment—affecting wellbeing, especially for vulnerable groups.
    - Positive impacts: upskilling, new competencies, diverse teams.
    - Risks: reputational and turnover risks; risks related to disability inclusion and workplace accessibility.
    - Located in own operations; relevant across time horizons.
  - Consumers and end-users (S4)
    - Negative impacts: insufficient access to quality information, lack of social inclusion, inadequate privacy protection—potentially harming customer wellbeing.
    - Risks: financial losses, regulatory exposure, reputational harm.
    - Applies to Private Individuals and Private Banking; primarily downstream; spans multiple time horizons.

- Governance
  - Business conduct (G1)
    - Risks: financial loss, regulatory fines, and reputational damage from breaches of corporate culture, bribery and corruption, and failure to protect whistleblowers.
    - Located in own operations; relevant across time horizons.

nodes.title: Our sustainability governance
nodes.heading: 3 Our sustainability governance
nodes.start_phrase: At ING, we have integrated sustainability into our existing governance.
nodes.summary:
- ING integrates sustainability into its existing governance framework; detailed roles and composition of the Supervisory Board (SB), Executive Board (EB), and Management Board Banking (MBB) are covered elsewhere, while this section focuses on sustainability governance.
- Supervisory Board: An ad hoc ESG Committee created in 2022 became a permanent committee in 2024. It meets quarterly, includes at least one member from each other SB committee, and is combined with the Audit Committee when disclosure or control topics are on the agenda. Its remit covers ESG development and integration, strategy alignment, and ratification/adoption of key policies, including business conduct.
- Management Boards (EB and MBB): ESG is a regular, often weekly, agenda item tied to day-to-day management and long-term ESG strategy. ESG considerations are embedded across discussions, with frequent reviews and approvals of ESG-related and business conduct policies. Further details are in the boards’ charters on ing.com.
- Senior management governance:
  - ESG Risk Committee (ERC): Ensures execution of ESG risk matters from the SB, acts as a technical adviser, aligns functional and business issues, plans ESG risk priorities, and advises on approval of material ESG risk items.
  - Disclosure Committee: Composed of senior management, business, and risk representatives; advises the boards on disclosure obligations and reviews external presentations, including sustainability information, prior to public release.
- Business governance:
  - Wholesale Banking: The Sustainability Steering Committee (established 2022) assigns ownership, accountability, and resources; steers ESG KPIs; and sets the WB sustainability strategy, including sector targets and sector-based transition plans.
  - Retail Banking (Private Individuals, Business Banking, Private Banking): Governance via councils such as the Net Zero Housing Committee and Business Banking ESG Council to drive sustainable product development and lending portfolio progress toward climate goals; responsibilities cascade to experts and country teams. Country sustainability leads have a functional line to the global head of Sustainability to connect global and local efforts.

nodes.title: Climate change
nodes.heading: 4.1 Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: Our climate is changing due to the release of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions into the atmosphere.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines ING’s climate strategy, acknowledging climate change driven by GHG emissions and focusing on three priorities: reducing emissions to achieve net zero by 2050, scaling financing for new technologies and sustainable systems, and enabling people to participate in the transition. It details material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across Wholesale Banking, Business Banking, and Private Individuals (real estate), managed through a sector transition plan for carbon‑intensive sectors and complementary policies. On mitigation, it highlights negative impacts from lending to high‑emitting sectors and low‑efficiency properties (assessed using the EPBD), and transition risks such as technology and retrofit costs, carbon pricing, energy price changes, and EPBD IV implementation, plus potential compliance, legal, and reputational risks. Opportunities are linked to ING’s commitments to mobilise more transition finance, expand green funding, and grow renewable financing via its Terra approach. On adaptation, the document explains how physical risks from acute events (storms, floods) and chronic trends (sea‑level rise, higher temperatures) can raise defaults and non‑performing loans, and describes ING’s role in financing adaptations to reduce vulnerabilities for clients and communities.

nodes.title: Climate change - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.1 Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: Our climate is changing due to the release of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions into the atmosphere.
nodes.summary:
Climate change
Our climate is changing due to the release of greenhouse gas  (GHG) emissions into the atmosphere. Our 
climate action activities are focused on the three areas where we believe we can make the greatest impact: 
helping to drive down emissions to meet the global goal of net zero by 2050; building up the financing of the 
new technologies and sustainable systems of the future; and finding ways to enable people to play their part 
in the transition. For ING, climate adaptation is essential to reduce vulnerability against the physical impact 
of climate change. We work on reducing those risks by financing the required adaptation of our clients and 
communities . 
Identified  impacts, risks and opportuniti es

nodes.title: Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 4.1.1 Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: This section elaborates on the material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) associated with climate change, and how these factors interact with and influence ING’s strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and goals: ING addresses climate change by targeting three impact areas—reducing emissions to align with net zero by 2050, scaling finance for new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and enabling people to contribute to the transition—while emphasizing climate adaptation to lower vulnerability to physical climate impacts by financing client and community resilience measures.

- Material IROs and scope: Climate change mitigation and adaptation are deemed material across Wholesale Banking (WB), Business Banking (BB), and Private Individuals (PI) real estate lending. A sector transition plan prioritizes the most carbon‑intensive sectors and is complemented by policies and guidelines that manage negative impacts, risks, and create opportunities.

- Mitigation: 
  - Negative impacts: Emissions linked to lending in high‑emitting sectors; and, in real estate, properties with poor energy performance, assessed using the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD).
  - Risks (transition risk): For WB/BB, costs from adopting low‑carbon technologies and exposure to carbon pricing (including indirect emissions); for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV effects on customer income, repayment capacity, and renovation financing eligibility. Non‑compliance can lead to reputational, legal/regulatory, and financial consequences.
  - Opportunities: Growth aligned with public commitments—mobilizing more WB volumes for the transition, issuing green funding, and advancing the Terra approach via increased renewable financing.

- Adaptation:
  - Definition and linkage: Adjusting to actual/anticipated climate impacts; closely tied to managing physical risk.
  - Physical risks: Acute (storms, floods) and chronic (rising sea levels and temperatures) hazards that heighten default risk and non‑performing loans through multiple transmission channels, creating financial vulnerabilities for ING.

nodes.title: Climate change mitigation
nodes.heading: 4.1.2 Climate change mitigation
nodes.start_phrase: Climate change mitigation refers to the process of reducing GHG emissions and holding the increase in the global average temperature to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels, in line with the ambition of the Paris Agreement1.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: ING’s climate strategy centers on mitigating and adapting to climate change across Wholesale Banking, Business Banking, and Private Individuals (real estate lending), with a goal aligned to net zero by 2050.
- Three climate action pillars: 1) drive down emissions, 2) finance new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and 3) enable people to participate in the transition; adaptation financing is emphasized to reduce physical climate vulnerability.
- Management approach: A sector transition plan targets the most carbon‑intensive sectors, complemented by policies and guidelines that address negative impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Mitigation: Defined as reducing GHG emissions to limit warming to 1.5°C (Paris Agreement). Key negative impacts arise from lending to high‑emitting sectors and to real estate with poor energy performance (assessed against EPBD).
- Transition risks: For corporates, costs of new technologies/retrofits and carbon pricing on indirect emissions; for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV effects on income, payment behavior, and renovation financing eligibility; plus compliance risks (reputational, legal/regulatory, financial).
- Opportunities: Scaling climate transition financing via increased Wholesale Banking volumes mobilised, green funding frameworks, the Terra approach, and expanded renewable financing ambitions.
- Adaptation and physical risk: Defined as adjusting to actual/expected impacts; physical risks stem from acute events (storms, floods) and chronic trends (sea-level rise, temperature increases), raising default and non-performing loan risks through multiple transmission channels.
- Materiality: Climate mitigation and adaptation are material topics across ING’s key value chains and influence strategy and the business model.

nodes.title: Climate change adaptation
nodes.heading: 4.1.3 Climate change adaptation
nodes.start_phrase: Climate change adaptation refers to the process of adjusting to actual and anticipated climate change and its impacts.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and strategy: ING targets three climate action priorities—driving emissions down toward net zero by 2050, scaling financing for new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and enabling customers to participate in the transition—while prioritizing climate adaptation to reduce vulnerability to physical impacts by financing client and community resilience.
- Scope of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs): Climate change mitigation and adaptation are material across Wholesale Banking (WB), Business Banking (BB), and Private Individuals (PI; real estate lending). ING manages IROs via a sector transition plan for carbon‑intensive sectors, complemented by policies and guidelines that address both risks and opportunities.
- Mitigation—negative impacts: Lending to high‑emitting sectors and to low‑efficiency real estate increases GHG emissions and long‑term temperature rise risk; poor energy performance properties are high impact in the short/medium term and all non‑net‑zero properties in the long term (assessed via EPBD).
- Mitigation—risks: Transition risk for corporates arises from decarbonization costs (technology upgrades, retrofits, indirect supplier costs) and carbon pricing; for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV implementation may strain borrower income, payment behavior, and renovation financing eligibility. Non‑compliance may trigger reputational, legal, regulatory, and financial consequences.
- Mitigation—opportunities: ING aims to expand sustainable finance through increased WB mobilized volumes, green funding frameworks, the Terra approach, and renewable financing ambitions.
- Adaptation—physical risks: Acute events (storms, floods) and chronic shifts (sea level rise, temperature increases) can cause defaults and losses.
  - Residential real estate: Asset damage, devaluations, insurance availability constraints, and borrower income impairment after disasters.
  - Wholesale/Business Banking: Infrastructure damage, operational interruptions, cost increases, revenue declines, supply disruptions, higher insurance costs, and third‑party claims affect borrower profitability and repayment capacity.
  - Governments/sovereigns: Lower tax revenues and higher spending for disaster response/adaptation can raise borrowing costs and restrict market access.
- Financial effects and resilience:
  - Current effects: Climate risk not yet fully embedded in IFRS 9 ECL due to data gaps; 2024 steps include explicit climate risk drivers in provisioning. Physical risk effects are based on actual events (e.g., Spain provision for payment holidays after Valencia floods). Transition risk captured via a management adjustment to ECL for current corporate portfolios.
  - Anticipated effects: Disclosures aligned with phased‑in EBA Pillar III ESG templates—Template 5 (physical risk exposures) and Template 2 (real estate energy efficiency)—with scope and resilience analysis in the appendix.
  - Risk controls: For material physical risks, mandatory credit risk mitigations (insurance or alternatives), enhanced underwriting data on adaptation, controlled financing amounts, or asset rejection if unmitigated; real estate valuations must reflect jurisdiction‑specific hazards.
- View on transition risk and stranded assets: High‑emitting sector exposure does not automatically imply default; structured transition planning and robust risk management can enable viable transformation. A three‑year horizon is too short to attribute defaults solely to transition failure; classifying all high‑carbon exposures as stranded over longer horizons is overly conservative. Bottom‑up transition risk assessment remains challenging due to data and forecasting limits.
- Real estate transition uncertainty: EPBD IV transposition into national law is expected by May 2026, creating interim uncertainty in linking EPC/primary energy demand to transition risk; sector transition plans for commercial and residential real estate are in place.
- Overall coverage: ING considers mid‑term transition risk significantly addressed through its Terra approach, which covers most emissions‑intensive sectors in the WB loan book.

nodes.title: Financial effects and resilience of ING’s strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 4.1.4 Financial effects and resilience of ING’s strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: For the identified risks we have two approaches to determine our current financial effects, more explicitly for physical risk and transition risk.
nodes.summary:
- Physical risk impacts by segment:
  - Residential real estate: extreme events can cause write-offs, asset devaluations, early retirements, reduced insurance availability; borrower distress may impair loan servicing and renovation financing.
  - Wholesale/Business Banking: infrastructure damage, operational interruptions, higher costs, reduced demand, supply issues, facility damage, third-party claims, and rising insurance premiums can depress income and increase default risk.
  - Governments: lower tax revenues and higher spending from disaster response/adaptation may raise borrowing costs or restrict market access.

- Financial effects and resilience:
  - Two approaches to quantify climate impacts: event-based provisioning for physical risk and a management adjustment for transition-risk ECLs.
  - IFRS 9 ECL models cannot yet fully isolate climate risk due to limited data, though 2024 enhancements add climate-risk drivers.
  - Example: 2024 provision in Spain for payment holidays after severe floods in Valencia.
  - Disclosures follow phased EBA Pillar III ESG: Template 5 (physical risk exposures) and Template 2 (real estate energy efficiency).
  - Proactive risk management: mandatory mitigations (insurance/adaptation), enhanced underwriting data, controlled financing, or asset rejection; material hazards embedded in real estate valuations.

- Transition risk perspective:
  - Arises from policy, technology, and market shifts; high-emitting sectors face capex and indirect supplier costs, and potential demand decline.
  - Not all high-emitting sectors will default; caution against labeling all exposures as stranded, especially over short horizons; bottom-up assessments remain challenging.
  - Real estate efficiency upgrades are a component of transition risk, with regulatory uncertainty pending EPBD IV transposition (expected May 2026).
  - Mid-term transition risk largely addressed via the Terra approach across emissions-intense sectors.

- Climate stress testing:
  - ING’s climate stress-test extends existing ICAAP/EBA frameworks with overlays for transition and physical risks on corporate and mortgage credit portfolios.

- Opportunities and commitments:
  - Support clients’ sustainable transition through products and green funding.
  - Financial effects tracked via progress against public commitments (e.g., Terra transition plan for renewable power, mobilized volumes, green funding framework).

- Transition plan and Terra approach:
  - Sustainability is core to strategy; aim to steer the most carbon-intensive portfolio segments toward climate goals.
  - Terra measures client emission intensities against sector decarbonization pathways; upstream oil & gas steered on financial exposure.
  - Collection of Client Transition Plans in Wholesale Banking to deepen sector plans and guide client engagement, advisory, and financing.
  - Monitoring absolute financed emissions enables hotspot analyses and informs expansion of the Terra scope.

nodes.title: Our transition plan - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.1.5 Our transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: At ING, putting sustainability at the heart of what we do is one of the core pillars of our strategy.
nodes.summary:
Our transi tion plan
At ING, putting sustainability at the heart of what we do is one of the core pillars of our strategy. Climate 
change is one of the world's biggest challenges, threatening societies as we know them today. We want to 
play our part in the low-carbon transition that’s necessary to achieve a sustainable future. We aim to steer 
the most carbon-intensive parts of our portfolio towards meeting global climate goals and working with 
clients to achieve their own sustainability goals.
Our ambition is to help acce lerate the transition – because it matters to us as a bank, to our clients and to 
society. Our activities are focused on the areas where we believe we can make the greatest impact. For more 
information on our strategy, see ‘Sustainability at the heart ’.

nodes.title: Approach to the transition plan
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.1 Approach to the transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: With the Terra approach, ING measures the emission intensities of clients active in the most carbon-intensive sectors, except for upstream oil & gas which we steer on financial exposures .
nodes.summary:
- ING enhanced its climate stress-testing methodology for corporate and mortgage credit risk, building on ICAAP/EBA frameworks with overlays for transition and physical risks.
- It supports clients’ sustainable transition via product offerings and green funding, tracking progress against publicly disclosed commitments (e.g., Terra transition plan, green funding framework) rather than product-level financial effects.
- ING’s Terra transition plan aims to steer carbon‑intensive portfolios toward global climate goals and help clients meet their own sustainability targets.
- Terra approach: measures emission intensities in high‑emitting sectors (upstream oil & gas steered on financial exposure), benchmarks clients to sector decarbonization pathways, measures absolute financed emissions where available, and performs hotspot analyses to manage risks/opportunities.
- Sector transition plans: tailored, GFANZ‑aligned and NZBA‑compliant; currently cover 10 sectors (residential real estate under refinement; aluminium and dairy in development); forthcoming targets, performance, and stakeholder asks outlined in “Our Terra approach.”
- Governance: ING’s management boards approve and oversee the net‑zero commitment, transition planning, and Terra implementation.
- Integration and resources: climate embedded in business planning via Risk Appetite Statements and KPIs to direct lending toward sustainable activities; strong emphasis on data availability, quality, and tooling as critical enablers.
- Decision‑making in Wholesale Banking: mandatory Terra/climate questions in deal approvals; expanded 2024 data‑driven ESG risk assessments consider client alignment to science‑based pathways, CTP ambition, and financial capacity; high‑risk cases escalate to ESR; Climate Risk Appetite and sector metrics set; quarterly/annual climate alignment benchmarks support 2030 targets.
- Client engagement: inclusion‑first approach to help especially carbon‑intensive clients transition; ESG.X tool collects ~2,000 clients’ transition data; clients receive CTP scores (Advanced/Moderate/Low); 2024 use of CTPs to guide strategic engagement with toolkits and training; stricter credit terms or exit for clients unwilling or unable to progress.
