nodes.title: Our Terra approach
nodes.heading: 4.1.6 Our Terra approach
nodes.start_phrase: ING’s integrated climate approach considers how we can mitigate climate change through our lending activities as well as how climate change may adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines ING’s Terra approach, an integrated climate strategy within its lending activities that addresses both climate mitigation and climate-related risks to the bank. It is built on three principles—impact-based, climate science-based, and engagement-driven—and is executed through a portfolio- and sector-focused transition plan. ING measures progress of its most carbon-intensive clients against sectoral net‑zero pathways and assesses portfolio alignment to set decarbonisation targets and sector-specific actions to manage transition risk. Target setting and portfolio steering begin with financed-emissions hotspot analysis to prioritize high-emitting sectors, followed by selection of science-based scenarios. The approach concentrates on the most impactful parts of sector value chains, with targets developed using peer- and expert-backed methodologies that define which products are in scope. A referenced visual illustrates sector value-chain focus relative to global emissions, underscoring emphasis on high-emitting sectors. The text situates this within the Environment section of ING Group’s 2024 Annual Report and points to the Policies, actions and performance section for detailed risk identification and policies.

nodes.title: Our Terra approach - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.1.6 Our Terra approach
nodes.start_phrase: ING’s integrated climate approach considers how we can mitigate climate change through our lending activities as well as how climate change may adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary:
Our Terra approach  
ING’s integrated climate approach considers how we can mitigate climate change through our lending 
activities as well as how climate change may adversely impact our business. Our Terra approach is based on 
three main principles: (1) impact-based, (2) climate science-based, (3) engagement-driven. Our transition 
plan, guided by our Terra approach, is portfolio- and sector-focused. It measures how our most carbon-
intensive clients have progressed against their sector net-zero pathways, as well as the progress in net-zero 
alignment of our portfolio on a sector and portfolio level. This approach allows us to set decarbonisation 
targets and identify the corresponding actions for each sector to manage the transition risks of our balance 
sheet. For details about the process of identifying our transition risks and the corresponding policies, see the 
‘Policies, actions and performance ’ section.

nodes.title: Target setting and portfolio steering
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.1 Target setting and portfolio steering
nodes.start_phrase: We use financed emissions as a hotspot analysis to prioritise high-emitting sectors, after which we select the science-based scenario.
nodes.summary:
- Describes ING’s Terra approach as the bank’s integrated climate strategy for both mitigating climate change through lending and managing climate-related risks to its business.
- Outlines three guiding principles: impact-based, climate science-based, and engagement-driven.
- Explains a sector- and portfolio-focused transition plan that measures carbon‑intensive clients’ progress against sectoral net‑zero pathways and assesses portfolio alignment to net zero.
- States the approach enables setting sector-specific decarbonisation targets and defining actions to manage transition risks on the balance sheet.
- Details target-setting and portfolio steering: using financed emissions for hotspot analysis to prioritize high‑emitting sectors, selecting science-based scenarios, and focusing on the most impactful parts of value chains.
- Notes targets are based on methodologies developed with peers and experts, including defining which products are in scope.
- Emphasizes focus on high‑emitting sectors and value-chain segments with the greatest potential to reduce global emissions.
- References related policies and processes in the “Policies, actions and performance” section and situates the content within the Environment section of ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.2 Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the selection process, and to align our lending portfolio with net zero, we check whether there is an available International Energy Agency (IEA) NZE scenario or other relevant scientific 1.5°C scenarios from recognised institutions.
nodes.summary:
- Uses recognized 1.5°C scenarios—preferably IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE)—to set sector-specific net‑zero targets, always applying the most recent scenarios.
- Keeps reporting boundaries consistent between baseline and reporting years; sector coverage is defined by adopted methodologies and available scientific scenarios.
- Translates sector benchmark scenarios into convergence pathways for ING’s portfolio, with intermediary 2030 targets that align toward net zero by 2050.
- Calculates alignment metrics using latest available emissions data (generally 2023, from external providers) and financial data as of year-end 2024; for shipping and aviation, both emissions and financial data use year-end 2023 to align reporting periods.
- Does not use offsets—now or in future—for Terra targets; external data providers also exclude offsets when assessing clients’ climate performance.
- Notes that targets, baselines, methodologies, and approach may evolve due to international agreements, regulation, data quality/availability, pathway updates, public policy, and sector/client developments.
- Steers the loan portfolio primarily on emissions intensity or alignment delta by sector (exception: upstream oil & gas is steered on financial exposure).
- Explains why financed emissions are not used for steering: while useful for hotspot analysis, they rely on multiple assumptions and mainly drive divestment-based action; intensity metrics better support client engagement and real-economy transition.
- Clarifies that, in a hypothetical scenario with all assumptions fixed, financed emissions would move with intensity, but real-world variability makes intensity a more effective steering metric.
- Distinguishes between Terra intensity metrics and financed emissions: different product scopes and sector focus; Terra targets specific sectors and high-emitting clients, whereas financed emissions include on‑balance sheet term loans, revolvers, and leases per PCAF.
- References further detail in “Technical notes to the sector transition plan” and situates the content within the Environment section of ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement - Introduction
nodes.source_title: Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement
nodes.source_heading: Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.2 Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the selection process, and to align our lending portfolio with net zero, we check whether there is an available International Energy Agency (IEA) NZE scenario or other relevant scientific 1.5°C scenarios from recognised institutions.
nodes.summary: Introduces ING’s approach to scenario selection, target setting, and metrics measurement for aligning its lending portfolio with net zero, using the most recent IEA NZE or other recognized 1.5°C scientific scenarios to set sector-specific targets. Reporting boundaries keep emissions scopes consistent between baseline and reporting years, with sector coverage defined by adopted methodologies and scenarios. Benchmark scenarios are translated into sector convergence pathways that inform 2030 intermediary targets and converge to net zero by 2050. Alignment metrics are calculated using latest available emissions data (generally 2023) from external providers against ING’s year-end 2024 financial data; for shipping and aviation, both asset emissions and financial data are aligned to year-end 2023. Offsets are not used or planned in the Terra approach, and data providers also exclude client offsets. Commitments, targets, baselines, and methodologies may change due to international agreements, regulation, data quality/availability, pathway and methodology updates, public policy, and broader sectoral or societal developments.

nodes.title: We steer our portfolio based on emission intensity
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.2.1 We steer our portfolio based on emission intensity
nodes.start_phrase: When setting up the transition plans in scope of our Terra approach, we apply what we consider to be the best-fit methodology for each sector to measure and steer our loan book.
nodes.summary:
- Scenario basis: Targets are set using the most recent IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE) or other recognized 1.5°C scientific scenarios, selected per sector.
- Reporting boundaries: Emissions scopes and sector coverage are consistent between baseline and reporting years, defined by adopted methodologies and available scientific scenarios.
- Convergence pathways: Sector benchmark scenarios are translated into pathways that guide ING’s portfolio alignment, underpinning 2030 intermediary targets and convergence to net zero by 2050.
- Data and timing: Alignment metrics use the latest available emissions data (generally 2023) from external providers and year-end 2024 financial data; shipping and aviation require both emissions and financial data aligned to year-end 2023 due to methodology.
- No offsets: Offsets are not used to measure portfolio alignment or to achieve Terra targets; data providers also exclude offsets in clients’ climate performance.
- Change factors: Commitments, targets, and methodologies may evolve due to international agreements, regulation, data quality/availability, pathway updates, policy changes, and sector or societal developments.
- Steering approach: ING steers its portfolio primarily on emissions intensity or alignment deltas by sector (exception: upstream oil & gas steered on financial exposure), supporting client engagement and transition rather than divestment.
- Financed emissions vs intensity: Financed emissions aid hotspot analysis but are less effective for steering; intensity-based targets avoid heavy reliance on assumptions about future client emissions, valuations, and balance sheet composition.
- Scope differences: Terra intensity metrics cover specific sectors and high-emitting clients with tailored methodologies, while financed emissions (per PCAF) include on-balance lending products such as term loans, revolvers, and leases.

nodes.title: Difference between intensity metrics and financed emissions
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.2.2 Difference between intensity metrics and financed emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As a financial institution, we finance economic activities which we present as our outstandings.
nodes.summary:
- Describes how ING selects climate scenarios and sets targets to align its lending portfolio with net zero, prioritizing IEA NZE and other reputable 1.5°C pathways and using the most recent versions.
- Defines consistent reporting boundaries between baseline and reporting years, with sector coverage determined by adopted methodologies and available scientific scenarios.
- Translates sectoral benchmark scenarios into convergence pathways that set 2030 interim targets and aim for net zero by 2050.
- Calculates alignment metrics using latest available emissions data (generally 2023) against year-end 2024 financials; for shipping and aviation both emissions and financial data are aligned to year-end 2023 due to methodology requirements.
- States no use of carbon offsets—now or in future—for portfolio alignment; data providers also exclude offsets.
- Notes that commitments, targets, and methods may evolve due to changing international agreements, regulation, data quality/availability, policy, and sectoral or societal developments.
- Explains portfolio steering based on emissions intensity or alignment delta (except upstream oil & gas, which is steered on financial exposure), rather than absolute financed emissions.
- Justifies intensity-based steering as more suitable for a bank’s role in financing and client engagement; financed emissions are useful for hotspot analysis but less effective for active portfolio steering without divestment.
- Clarifies that converting intensity targets to financed emissions would require many assumptions; only in a hypothetical steady-state would financed emissions mirror intensity changes.
- Differentiates Terra intensity metrics from financed emissions: different product scopes and a focus on specific high-emitting sectors for Terra, while financed emissions include on-balance sheet term loans, revolvers, and leases per PCAF.

nodes.title: Our sector transition plans
nodes.heading: 4.1.7 Our sector transition plans
nodes.start_phrase: Our Terra toolbox, as shown below, is a summary of our approach per sector.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt outlines ING’s sector transition plans within its Terra approach, explaining that for each key sector it assesses observed challenges, actions needed from society, its performance, and ING’s own actions. Definitions and details are referenced in the Appendix to the Executive Board report.

- A “Terra toolbox” table summarizes, per sector, the in-scope portfolio exposure, methodology used, emissions scopes covered, financial products included, the decarbonization metric, the 2030 scenario/pathway, baseline year and values, 2024 portfolio metric, distance to the IEA 2030 convergence point, the 2030 target versus baseline, and a 1.5°C-aligned reference value for 2050 (where applicable). Notes clarify that negative “distance” values mean performance is already ahead of the 2030 pathway and that real estate uses a whole-building approach including occupant electricity.

- Sectors, methods, metrics, and selected highlights:
  - Power generation (€11.5bn): PACTA; Scope 1; kg CO2e/MWh; IEA NZA (WEO 2023). 2024 is 4% ahead of the IEA 2030 convergence; 2030 intensity target −78% vs baseline; 1.5°C reference −100% by 2040.
  - Oil & gas – Upstream (€1.0bn): PACTA Credit Application and PCAF; Scopes 1–3; outstanding amount and absolute emissions; IEA NZE (WEO 2023). Outstanding down 61% vs baseline; absolute emissions down 78%; 2030 targets −35% (exposure) and −50% (emissions); 1.5°C reference −100% by 2040.
  - Oil & gas – Mid-/Downstream (€7.4bn): Convergence approach; Scopes 1–2; kg CO2e/boe; IEA NZE (2023). Needs 31% reduction to 2030 convergence; 2030 target −24%; 1.5°C −100%.
  - Cement (€0.7bn): PACTA; Scopes 1–2; t CO2/t cement; IEA NZE (2023). 33% above 2030 path; 2030 target −29%; 1.5°C −97%.
  - Steel (€2.0bn): Sustainable STEEL Principles; Scopes 1–2 and part of 3; SSP alignment score and t CO2/t steel; IEA NZE (2021) and MPP Technology Moratorium. 2024 SSP alignment score 0.83 with target 0 by 2030; intensity path indicates a 32% gap to 2030.
  - Automotive (€4.0bn): PACTA; Scope 3 Cat.11; kg CO2/vkm; IEA NZE (2021). 45% above 2030 convergence; 2030 target −49%; 1.5°C −98%.
  - Aviation (€4.1bn): Pegasus Guidelines; Scope 1 and part of 3; g CO2e/RTK; MPP PRU 2023. 33% above 2030 convergence; 2030 target −19%; 1.5°C −100%.
  - Shipping (€8.6bn): Poseidon Principles; Scope 1; alignment delta vs DNV 1.5°C Initiative. 2024 alignment delta −7.6% (ahead of trajectory); target 0% by 2030 and 2050.
  - Commercial real estate (€26.2bn): PCAF/CRREM; Scopes 1–2; kg CO2e/m²; CRREM 1.5°C (IEA NZE-based). 131% above 2030 convergence; 2030 target −56%; 1.5°C −98%.
  - Residential real estate (€294.3bn): PCAF/CRREM; Scopes 1–2; kg CO2e/m²; CRREM 1.5°C. Metrics reported (baseline 2021 and 2024), with distance and targets not specified in this table.

- The section sits within ING Group’s Annual Report 2024 Sustainability Statement (Environment) and signals that subsequent sections provide sector-by-sector overviews of challenges, needed societal actions, ING’s performance, and planned actions.

nodes.title: Our sector transition plans - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.1.7 Our sector transition plans
nodes.start_phrase: Our Terra toolbox, as shown below, is a summary of our approach per sector.
nodes.summary: Introduction to ING’s sector transition plans presenting the Terra toolbox: a 2024 baseline/target table that summarizes, by sector, outstanding exposure in scope, methodologies (e.g., PACTA, PCAF, Sustainable STEEL Principles, Pegasus Guidelines, Poseidon Principles, CRREM), emissions scopes covered (1, 2, parts of 3), financial products (e.g., on-balance term loans, revolvers, guarantees, mortgages), decarbonization metrics (e.g., kg CO2e/MWh, kg CO2e/boe, t CO2/t cement or steel, kg CO2/vkm, g CO2e/RTK, alignment deltas, kg CO2e/m2), scenario/pathway references (IEA NZE/NZA WEO 2021/2023, MPP PRU 2023, DNV 1.5°C, CRREM 1.5°C), baseline years, current metric values, “Distance to IEA 2030 convergence” (where negative values mean ahead of the 2030 pathway), 2030 target vs baseline, and 1.5°C-aligned 2050 references (including -100% by 2040 for power and oil & gas upstream). Sector exposures include Residential real estate €294.3bn, Commercial real estate €26.2bn, Power €11.5bn, Shipping €8.6bn, Automotive €4.0bn, Aviation €4.1bn, Steel €2.0bn, Cement €0.7bn, Oil & Gas (Upstream €1.0bn; Mid-/Downstream €7.4bn). Examples: power generation shows progress ahead of the IEA 2030 point and a -78% 2030 target; automotive targets -49% by 2030; aviation shows a 33% remaining distance and a -19% 2030 target; shipping has a -7.6% alignment delta; commercial real estate targets -56% by 2030; oil & gas upstream tracks both outstanding amounts and absolute emissions with a 2040 phase-out. Real estate metrics follow CRREM’s whole building approach including occupants’ electricity. Subsequent sections detail sector challenges, required societal actions, ING’s performance, and its own actions; definitions are in the Appendix to the Executive Board report.

nodes.title: Power generation
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.1 Power generation
nodes.start_phrase: We expect the power-generation industry to maximise renewable energy and boost power-storage technology.
nodes.summary:
- Sector outlook: Emphasis on maximizing renewable power generation, accelerating power‑storage deployment (batteries, hydrogen) with incentives where needed, enabling carbon capture and storage on waste/biomass incineration to deliver negative emissions, and expanding/modernizing grids to meet rising demand, higher renewable volatility, and extreme weather.
- Emission intensity performance (Terra): Calculated using 2024 portfolio outstanding and 2023 emissions data; improved by 41% from 106 to 63 kg CO2e/MWh (2023 to 2024). 2024 in-scope outstanding: €11.5 billion. ING target: −78% vs 2018 by 2030; distance to 2030 IEA convergence: −4%.
- Steering methodology: ING steers the power portfolio via the Terra approach; financed emissions are reported but not used for sector steering. 2023 emissions data applied as 2024 data is not yet available.
- Financed emissions trend: Scope 1&2 increased by +693 kt CO2e to 11,103 kt; Scope 3 increased by +1,314 kt CO2e to 5,728 kt, driven by portfolio growth and higher drawdowns among some higher‑emitting clients.
- Coal policy and exposure: Since 2015, no financing of new coal‑fired power plants or thermal coal mines. Target set in 2017 to reduce coal‑fired plant financing to near zero by end‑2025. Outstanding to individual coal‑fired plants remains €77 million (legacy loans), with continued reduction efforts.
- Renewable financing commitments: Target tripled in 2023 to €7.5 billion annually by 2025 (from €2.5 billion set in 2022). In 2024, €7 billion of new renewable generation financing committed (mainly wind and solar).
- Transaction highlight: Over €900 million financing to Sosteneo Infrastructure Partners for 49% of Enel Libra Flexsys, comprising 23 battery energy storage projects (1.7 GW) and refurbishment of open-cycle CCGT plants (0.9 GW). Provides critical flexibility and reliability to the Italian grid; revenues contracted for 15 years via capacity agreements with Enel, backed by Terna S.p.A.

nodes.title: Oil & gas
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.2 Oil & gas
nodes.start_phrase: Oil & gas accounts for about 60 percent of all primary energy consumed worldwide1.
nodes.summary:
- Sets global context: Oil and gas provide ~60% of primary energy. In the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario, combustion of crude oil and natural gas for energy phases out; sustainable bio- and e‑fuels must reach 13% of total energy by 2030. Decarbonisation is required across the mid- and downstream value chain, prioritising methane leak reduction and leveraging carbon capture and storage (CCS).
- Explains ING’s Terra approach, targets and 2024 performance: outstandings to clients in Terra scope fell 13% to €1.001 billion (from €1.155 billion in 2023) due to portfolio composition changes and active steering toward 2030/2040 targets. Emissions intensity improved 1% to 19.1 kg CO2e/boe, calculated using 2022 emissions data pending 2023/2024 availability.
- Upstream oil & gas steering and financed emissions: portfolio is steered on measured outstandings and financed emissions. 2024 financed emissions declined to 702 kt CO2e (Scopes 1–2, down 867 kt) and 10,325 kt CO2e (Scope 3, down 13,343 kt), mainly from portfolio size reduction and lower exposure to higher emitters. Total financed emissions ~11 Mt CO2e; outstanding in scope ~€1.0 billion. Target: −35% vs 2019 by 2030; shown distance to 2030 IEA convergence metric −61%.
- Mid- and downstream oil & gas approach: sector is steered via Terra emissions intensity rather than financed emissions (different product scope/methodology). Using 2023 emissions data, financed emissions increased to 3,417 kt CO2e (Scopes 1–2, +537 kt) and 16,928 kt CO2e (Scope 3, +75 kt), driven by higher product drawdowns by some higher‑emitting clients. 2024 outstanding in scope ~€7.4 billion; CO2e intensity 19.1 kg CO2e/boe. Target: −24% vs 2022 by 2030; distance to 2030 IEA convergence metric 31%.
- Includes references to methodology and data sources: “Technical notes to the transition plan” and the “Financed emissions” table; cites IEA World Energy Outlook 2023. Visuals indicate convergence pathways versus the IEA NZE2050 scenario and ING’s 2030/2040 targets.

nodes.title: Oil & gas - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.2 Oil & gas
nodes.start_phrase: Oil & gas accounts for about 60 percent of all primary energy consumed worldwide1.
nodes.summary: Introduction to ING’s Oil & Gas portfolio and Terra steering in the context of IEA NZE2050: oil and gas supply for energy is expected to phase out, sustainable bio- and e-fuels must reach 13% of total energy by 2030, and sector decarbonisation focuses on mid-/downstream, methane leak reduction, and CCS. In 2024, Terra outstandings to clients fell 13% to €1,001m (from €1,155m), and mid-/downstream emissions intensity improved 1% to 19.1 kg CO2e/boe, calculated with 2024 outstandings and 2022 emissions data due to data unavailability. Upstream steering uses outstandings and financed emissions, which declined to 702 kt CO2e (scope 1+2, −867 kt) and 10,325 kt CO2e (scope 3, −13,343 kt) mainly from portfolio size cuts; mid-/downstream is steered via Terra intensity, while financed emissions based on 2023 data rose to 3,417 kt (scope 1+2, +537 kt) and 16,928 kt (scope 3, +75 kt) due to higher drawdowns. 2024 in-scope metrics include upstream €1.0bn outstandings with total financed emissions ~11 Mt CO2e and a 2030 target reduction vs 2019 of −35% (distance to 2030 IEA convergence −61%), and mid-/downstream €7.4bn outstandings with a 2030 target reduction vs 2022 of −24% (distance to 2030 IEA convergence 31%); methods are referenced in the Technical notes to the transition plan and the Financed emissions table.

nodes.title: The key highlights of our action plan for oil & gas
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.2.1 The key highlights of our action plan for oil & gas
nodes.start_phrase: In March 2022, we announced we would stop dedicated financing to new oil & gas fields (upstream).
nodes.summary:
- Summarizes ING’s action plan for oil and gas in the 2024 Annual Report (Environment section), outlining a staged tightening of financing policies and a pivot to low‑carbon solutions.
- Policy timeline:
  - March 2022: Stopped dedicated financing for new upstream oil and gas fields.
  - March 2023: Extended restrictions to midstream infrastructure that enables new field developments.
  - December 2023: Announced phaseout of financing for upstream oil and gas activities by 2040.
  - September 2024: Decided to cease new financing for new LNG export terminals after 2025, aligned with IEA WEO 2023 NZE2050.
- Commits to reduce combined traded oil and gas volumes in line with IEA pathways and to include Trade and Commodity Finance in the Terra approach.
- Continues supporting clients transitioning to “new energies” that displace fossil hydrocarbons and help decarbonize other sectors.
- Details three focus areas for the hydrocarbons & new energies team:
  - Sustainable fuels (e-fuels and biofuels such as hydrogen, ammonia, biomethane, SAF) produced from non-fossil feedstocks.
  - Recycled feedstock for plastics via chemical recycling (e.g., pyrolysis) to replace fossil-based inputs.
  - Carbon capture and storage (industrial CO2 capture with storage in depleted gas fields or aquifers).
- Includes context of the broader report structure (strategy, governance, sustainability, risk, and financial statements).

nodes.title: Beyond our energy sector transition plan
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.3 Beyond our energy sector transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: Our energy strategy, which applies to our total energy outstanding, focuses on the following committed actions:
nodes.summary:
- Outlines ING’s energy transition strategy with three headline commitments: end lending to individual coal‑fired power plants by 2025; phase out lending to clients with upstream oil & gas activities by 2040; and triple annual renewable power generation lending commitments to EUR 7.5 billion by 2025.
- Explains the Terra approach, which targets high‑emitting sectors within the Wholesale Banking lending book; excludes non‑lending products (e.g., Financial Markets and Transaction Services) that are not directly linked to clients’ business activities.
- Describes how outstandings are defined and reported (based on NAICS industry codes within ING’s credit risk portfolio) and provides a reconciliation between Terra scope and total energy outstandings managed by the Wholesale Banking sector team.
- Highlights 2024 portfolio dynamics: continued reduction of upstream oil & gas lending and growth in renewables driving expansion of the power portfolio. Total energy outstandings were EUR 43.0 billion in 2024 (vs. EUR 40.6 billion in 2023), including oil & gas EUR 17.1 billion and utilities & power EUR 25.9 billion, of which renewables EUR 12.5 billion (vs. EUR 9.7 billion in 2023).
- Introduces a new “integrated O&G” category (companies active across the full O&G value chain) to reduce volatility from prior revenue‑based allocation; reclassifies EUR 0.1 billion from upstream to mid‑ and downstream and updates comparatives. Integrated O&G is managed under mid‑ and downstream Terra targets; loans dedicated to upstream remain in upstream and are managed accordingly. Client activities are monitored via a client engagement approach.
- Addresses Trade & Commodity Finance (TCF): recognizes its importance to energy trade flows and the challenge of aligning short‑term trade finance with climate pathways. Reports co‑development of an emissions measurement methodology now finalized and under stakeholder review, targeted for Terra inclusion in 2025. Discloses TCF exposures: oil & gas limits EUR 28.2 billion (2024) vs. EUR 27.3 billion (2023); outstandings EUR 11.1 billion (2024) vs. EUR 12.4 billion (2023).
- Notes scope differences outside Terra, including Retail (Business Banking) outstandings, which are not steered via Terra.

nodes.title: Cement
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.4 Cement
nodes.start_phrase: For the cement industry to decarbonise, technology needs to be stimulated – such as low clinker cement, carbon capture and storage, alternative fuels and electric kilns, together with emerging technologies in material efficiency and cement recycling.
nodes.summary:
- Sector context: Decarbonising cement requires scaling low‑clinker cements, carbon capture and storage (CCS/CCUS), alternative fuels, electric kilns, and innovations in material efficiency and cement recycling. Global cooperation between advanced and developing economies is needed to strengthen climate policies and prevent carbon leakage.
- Methodology and data: Emission intensity under ING’s Terra approach is based on 2024 outstanding exposure for clients in scope combined with 2023 emissions data (2024 emissions not yet available). Methodological details are in the Technical notes to the transition plan.
- Portfolio performance (Terra): Cement portfolio emission intensity improved by 2%, from 0.701 t CO2/t cement (2023) to 0.688 t CO2/t cement (2024), driven by changes in portfolio composition and measured outstandings. ING’s 2030 target is 0.519 t CO2/t cement, representing a 29% reduction vs 2020, with a 33% distance to the 2030 IEA NZE convergence metric.
- Financed emissions: Calculated separately from Terra (different scope/method). Using 2023 data, financed emissions rose to 1,427 kt CO2e (scope 1 and 2, +195 kt) and 473 kt CO2e (scope 3, +98 kt), mainly due to increased drawdowns by some higher‑emitting clients and greater portfolio coverage.
- Strategy and actions: ING actively steers its cement portfolio through client engagement and tailored sustainable finance aligned with science‑based targets. Focus areas include supporting CCUS projects, recycling activities, and alternative fuels, alongside advisory on transition strategies and investment solutions.
- Transaction highlight (Cemex): In 2023, ING served as joint bookrunner and sole sustainability coordinator for Cemex’s $3 billion refinancing (a $2 billion RCF and $1 billion term loan). ING had advised on Cemex’s sustainability‑linked financing framework (updated in 2023) covering KPIs on scope 1 and 2 CO2 intensity per ton of cementitious product, clinker factor, and alternative fuels rate. Targets are SBTi‑validated for 1.5°C alignment, with a second‑party opinion from Sustainalytics confirming alignment with ICMA/LMA/LSTA/APLMA principles.
- Portfolio snapshot: €0.7 billion outstanding in scope (2024); CO2 intensity at 0.688 t CO2/t cement.

nodes.title: Steel
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.5 Steel
nodes.start_phrase: The steel industry is recognised as a hard-to-abate sector operating within a highly competitive wholesale market.
nodes.summary:
- Context and challenges: The steel industry is a hard-to-abate, highly competitive sector with long-lived assets. Achieving net zero requires clear, supportive regulation, abundant affordable green electricity, robust hydrogen infrastructure, and international coordination on carbon pricing and border adjustments to prevent carbon leakage. Knowledge from early movers should later support transitions in major markets like China and India.
- Terra targets and performance: Using 2024 outstanding exposure and 2023 emissions data, the Sustainable Steel Principles (SSP) Alignment score is 0.83. Portfolio emissions intensity improved by 1% from 1.95 to 1.93 t CO2 per t steel (2023–2024) but remains above the IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE) pathway due to portfolio composition and client outstandings. Methodology details are in the Technical notes to the transition plan.
- Green steel financing: Drawdowns by green steel clients rose to about 4% of in-scope financing in 2024. These projects plan to produce green iron and steel using renewable power and green hydrogen; as plants are still under construction, their climate performance is not yet included. The approach will be updated if SSP guidance evolves to include non-operational greenfield projects.
- Financed emissions: Used for disclosure (not portfolio steering) and based on 2023 data. Scope 1 and 2 financed emissions increased by 780 kt CO2e to 1,309 kt CO2e; Scope 3 decreased by 169 kt CO2e to 698 kt CO2e, mainly due to higher drawdowns to a few higher-emitting clients.
- Action plan: Restrict dedicated financing for liquid/crude steel projects to net-zero-ready retrofits and new mills. Proactively seek clients developing net-zero-ready mills and factor producers’ emissions intensity and credibility of transition plans into commercial decisions. Maintain active engagement with existing steelmakers, new entrants, and projects to track technological progress.
- Policy engagement: Ongoing senior-level advocacy with the European Commission to accelerate the European steel industry’s transition.
- Portfolio snapshot: €2.0 billion outstanding in scope (2024); SSP Alignment score 0.83; distance to 2030 IEA convergence metric 32%.

nodes.title: Automotive
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.6 Automotive
nodes.start_phrase: For the automotive industry to decarbonise, there is a need to continue to stimulate the shift to electric vehicles (EVs) by setting norms and phasing out internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEs), with the aim to gain scale in EV production, stimulate product range development, and reduce the relative total cost of ownership of EVs.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines decarbonisation priorities for the automotive sector: accelerate EV adoption through standards and ICE phase-outs; scale EV production to expand product range and lower total cost of ownership; invest in charging infrastructure; shift subsidies from fossil fuels to renewable power; build localized battery value chains; and enforce battery recycling and accountability for decarbonised manufacturing and mining.
- Terra targets and performance: emission intensity calculated using 2024 portfolio outstandings and 2023 emissions (2024 data not yet available). Portfolio CO2 intensity rose 2% from 0.143 to 0.146 kg CO2/vkm, driven by portfolio composition and outstandings; per-client electrification shares unchanged. Method details in Technical Notes to the Transition Plan.
- Financed emissions vs Terra: methodologies and scopes differ; Terra used for steering, financed emissions not used for sector steering. Using 2023 emissions data, financed emissions increased mainly due to portfolio growth: scope 1–2 to 90 kt CO2e (+66 kt) and scope 3 to 4,487 kt CO2e (+1,916 kt).
- Action plan: provide sustainability-linked loans/bonds, supply-chain finance, green loans/bonds, and German market instruments; support critical value-chain areas (traction batteries, charging infrastructure, circularity); create internal commercial incentives; prioritize new clients with high electrification and strong transition plans; advocate for stronger policies, standards, recycling, waste treatment, and data disclosure.
- Transaction highlight: ING supported Volkswagen Leasing GmbH’s first green bond issuance—three bonds totaling €2 billion under VW’s Green Finance Framework—supporting the MOBILITY2030 strategy and financing BEVs exclusively.
- Key metrics and targets: automotive portfolio outstanding in scope €4.0 billion (2024); CO2 intensity 0.146 kg CO2/vkm (2024); ING 2030 target is a 49% reduction vs 2020; current distance to 2030 IEA convergence metric is 45%; references the NZE2050 scenario and convergence pathway.

nodes.title: Aviation
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.7 Aviation
nodes.start_phrase: For the aviation industry to meet the net-zero targets, there is a need for more research into policy, regulatory and market trends to monitor developments in pricing schemes and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
nodes.summary:
- Focus on aviation’s path to net zero: calls for more research into policy, regulatory and market trends, monitoring pricing schemes and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and stronger engagement with governments and policymakers.
- Terra targets and performance: 2023 emission intensity is 844 g CO2e/RTK (baseline), calculated per Pegasus Guidelines and aligned to the Mission Possible Partnership Prudential Scenario (ING’s benchmark). Portfolio exposure to next‑generation aircraft reached 71% in 2023 (up from 62.5% in 2022 and 25% in 2019). Methodologies are detailed in the Technical notes to the transition plan.
- Financed emissions: Differ in scope and method from Terra; Terra is used for sector steering. Using 2023 data, financed emissions fell to 2,507 kt CO2e (scope 1 and 2, down 103 kt) and 1,338 kt CO2e (scope 3, down 227 kt), mainly due to decreased outstanding amounts in term loans, leases, and revolvers.
- Action plan highlights: Continue increasing the share of next‑generation aircraft in financing; engage leasing companies on emissions measurement, reporting, and target setting; work with the energy sector to finance SAF production capacity; support sustainable aviation enablers via IMPACT through research and stakeholder dialogue.
- Key metrics and targets: 2023 committed amounts in scope €4.1 billion; 2030 target intensity 681 g CO2e/RTK (−19% vs 2023 baseline); distance to the 2030 IEA convergence metric 33%.
- Document context: Environment section of the ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Shipping
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.8 Shipping
nodes.start_phrase: While there has been material progress in reducing shipping emissions in recent years, the scaling up of alternative low-carbon fuels is crucial for the industry to meet its net-zero target.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines ING’s approach to decarbonizing the shipping sector, emphasizing the need to scale alternative low‑carbon fuels and develop port-side supply chains, supported by upcoming IMO and EU regulations. It highlights growing orders for alternative fuel–capable vessels, the importance of retrofitting existing ships and energy-efficiency devices, and the need for additional shipyard capacity and financing. Green corridors are identified as key accelerators; ING is the only commercial bank in the Silk Alliance Green Corridor and leads its finance workstream, engaging with governments and ports.

On targets and performance, ING applies the DNV 1.5°C Initiative methodology (aligned with Poseidon Principles) for its Terra approach, reporting a debt‑weighted portfolio alignment delta of -7.6% for 2023 on €8.6 billion outstanding in scope, and updating targets to the DNV 1.5°C trajectory. It distinguishes Terra steering metrics from financed emissions, noting use of 2023 data (2024 not yet available). Financed emissions changed mainly due to portfolio composition: scope 1 and 2 rose by +233 kt CO2e to 2,577 kt CO2e, while scope 3 fell by -444 kt CO2e to 1,500 kt CO2e.

The action plan centers on proactive client engagement to accelerate transition plans, provision of financing solutions (including Export Credit Agency options) for energy-efficiency retrofits and alternative-fuel propulsion, and cross‑sector collaboration on alternative fuels and CCUS. ING partners with governments, development banks, and specialized institutions to enable green corridors and participates in key industry initiatives (Poseidon Principles, 1.5°C Initiative, UK Clean Maritime Council, NZBA, Silk Alliance) to steer the sector toward climate goals.

nodes.title: Commercial real estate
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.9 Commercial real estate
nodes.start_phrase: For the commercial real estate industry to decarbonise, norms and regulation on data measurement and disclosure are important, as data measurement is a precondition for managing CO2 emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasizes the need for industry-wide norms and regulation on data measurement and disclosure to enable decarbonisation in commercial real estate, noting current sustainability requirements are limited or voluntary, while national building standards increasingly include energy efficiency and circularity.
- Calls for a blend of subsidies, regulations, and norms to accelerate deployment of measures such as insulation, heat pumps, district heating, and smart meters, and to mitigate transition risks.
- Highlights the EU’s EPBD IV as a key driver to upgrade low-performing assets and improve transparency; acknowledges global decarbonisation remains a major challenge.
- Reports Terra performance: portfolio emission intensity rose 7.6% from 36.7 to 39.5 kg CO2e/m2 in 2024, mainly due to a newly validated model in Business Banking Real Estate Netherlands (RE BB NL), higher emission factors, and improved energy-label data quality (including more granular data for Wholesale Banking Real Estate, WB RE). Results combine WB RE and RE BB NL; methodologies detailed in Technical Notes to the Transition Plan.
- Clarifies methodology differences: Terra approach is used for steering, not financed emissions. Financed emissions increased to 464 kt CO2e (WB RE, Scope 1 and 2) and 236 kt CO2e (RE BB NL, Scope 1 and 2), driven by data-quality changes and higher emission factors.
- Portfolio metrics: €26.2 billion outstanding in scope (2024); CO2e intensity 39.5 kg CO2e/m2; 2030 target of -56% vs 2022 baseline; 131% distance to the 2030 IEA convergence metric; alignment assessed against the CRREM 1.5°C pathway.
- Action plan:
  - RE BB NL: all buildings to have energy label A by 2030; in 2024 obtained client transition plans; from 2025 these plans will inform credit approval.
  - WB RE: all new transactions benchmarked to the CRREM convergence pathway and must meet minimum sustainability standards or have a transition plan; existing book engages clients of non-sustainable assets to adopt cost- and carbon-efficient, adaptable transition plans.
- Ongoing advocacy with stakeholders on standardizing ESG data for real estate, evolving valuation standards to reflect climate transition risks, and aligning decarbonisation legislation.

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.10 Residential real estate
nodes.start_phrase: Residential real estate, also referred to as residential mortgages, is a substantial part of ING’s lending portfolio and is a relevant contributor to our financed emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on residential real estate mortgages as a major share of ING’s lending and a key source of financed emissions, with reductions targeted by promoting energy-efficient home purchases and enabling renovations.
- Emphasis on broader stakeholder roles: government acceleration of renewable energy, phasing out fossil fuels, and ambitious national renovation plans under EPBD IV; commitment to continued collaboration.
- 2024 portfolio emission intensity stable at 37.5 kg CO2e/m2 (vs. 2023) across Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, and Spain, reflecting decarbonization challenges and limitations from incomplete EPC data.
- Methodology aligned with PCAF: uses EPC labels for emission intensities; excludes non-residential; applies proxies where EPC data are missing; aims to expand EPC data collection; consistent cross-country approach with regional adjustments for data availability; technical details referenced in the transition plan notes.
- Distinction between metrics: Terra approach used for steering via emission intensities; financed emissions not used for sector steering.
- Financed emissions (scope 1 and 2) for the 10-country residential mortgage portfolio decreased by 116 kt CO2e to 5,918 kt CO2e, primarily due to lower updated emission factors; further details in the financed emissions table.
- Action plan highlights: sustainable mortgage offerings in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Romania, and Italy; renovation-support products (mortgage features/unsecured loans) in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Australia, and Romania.
- Customer enablement through digital tools in several markets; in the Netherlands, launch of ING Upgrader providing renovation options, cost-benefit estimates, and connections to service providers.
- 2024 portfolio snapshot: €294 billion outstanding in scope; tracked against the CRREM 1.5°C pathway with intensity at 37.5 kg CO2e/m2.

nodes.title: Financed emissions: to identify and analyse emissions hotspots
nodes.heading: 4.1.8 Financed emissions: to identify and analyse emissions hotspots
nodes.start_phrase: As a bank, we measure our absolute financed emissions associated (scope 1, 2 and 3) with our direct lending and investment activities, also known as absolute GHG scope 3 category 15 emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How the bank measures and analyzes absolute financed emissions (GHG Scope 3 Category 15) to identify emissions hotspots in its lending and investment portfolios, with an expanded table now including clients’ Scope 3 and a Terra sector breakdown.
- Scope definitions: Clarifies Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (indirect from purchased energy), and Scope 3 (all other value-chain emissions).
- Methodology and boundaries:
  - Uses 2023 emissions data for business lending due to 2024 unavailability; portfolio changes reflect outstandings and client financials (e.g., EVIC).
  - Commercial and residential real estate: only Scope 1 and 2 per GHG Protocol.
  - Business lending (Wholesale and Business Banking): Scopes 1–3 for leases, term loans, and revolvers, aligned with PCAF.
  - SMEs: Scope 3 generally unavailable; applies PCAF data quality score 5.
  - Biogenic emissions in the value chain excluded due to data limits.
  - Sovereign bonds and facilitated emissions from capital markets not measured as “not material” per double materiality assessment.
  - Commitment to report facilitated emissions by 2025 per NZBA; approach aligning with PCAF’s Capital Markets Standard (Dec 2023).
  - Further methodological detail in technical notes appendix.
- Results highlights:
  - With lending growth, portfolio Scope 1 and 2 financed emissions increased; Scope 3 financed emissions decreased.
  - Corporate bonds financed emissions affected by improved PCAF data quality (greater use of reported emissions).
  - Terra sector changes referenced in sector transition plan.
- Use of metrics: Financed emissions and intensity metrics are used together for hotspot identification and portfolio management.
- Factors affecting year-on-year comparability:
  - Portfolio size, industry mix/composition, client entries/exits.
  - Drawdown patterns and outstandings to each client.
  - Clients’ emission profiles and financial metrics (EVIC, balance sheet indicators).
  - FX movements and other data quality improvements.
- Context: Content appears in the Environment section of the ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Financed emissions: to identify and analyse emissions hotspots - Introduction
nodes.source_title: Financed emissions: to identify and analyse emissions hotspots
nodes.source_heading: Financed emissions: to identify and analyse emissions hotspots
nodes.heading: 4.1.8 Financed emissions: to identify and analyse emissions hotspots
nodes.start_phrase: As a bank, we measure our absolute financed emissions associated (scope 1, 2 and 3) with our direct lending and investment activities, also known as absolute GHG scope 3 category 15 emissions.
nodes.summary: Introduction to ING’s financed emissions methodology and scope for identifying portfolio hotspots: the bank measures absolute financed emissions (its Scope 3 Category 15 from lending and investments) across Scope 1, 2, and 3 of clients, expanding the 2024 table to include client Scope 3 and a breakdown for clients in Terra sectors. Definitions of scopes follow the GHG Protocol. Calculations use 2023 emissions data (2024 not yet available), with Scope 1–2 only for commercial and residential real estate (no Scope 3 per GHG Protocol), and Scope 1–3 for business lending (Wholesale and Business Banking covering leases, term loans, revolvers) in line with PCAF; SME Scope 3 is largely unavailable so PCAF data quality score 5 is applied across Business Banking. Biogenic emissions in the value chain are excluded due to data limits. Financed emissions for sovereign bonds and facilitated emissions from off-balance capital markets are not measured after a double materiality assessment; however, per NZBA, facilitated emissions will be reported from 2025 using PCAF’s 2023 Capital Markets standard. Portfolio results reflect multiple drivers (portfolio size/composition, drawdowns/outstandings, client EVIC and financials, FX, and data quality). With lending growth, Scope 1–2 financed emissions increased while Scope 3 decreased; corporate bond changes reflect improved PCAF data quality (use of reported emissions). Further sector changes are in the sector transition plan; technical details are in the appendix.

nodes.title: Financed emissions per asset class
nodes.heading: 4.1.8.1 Financed emissions per asset class
nodes.start_phrase: The greenhouse gas (GHG) financed emissions (scope 1, 2 and 3) have been incorporated in the tables below for the financial years 2024 and 2023.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Disclosure of ING’s financed greenhouse gas emissions (Scopes 1, 2 and 3) by asset class for FY2024, with a restated and comparable FY2023 table.
- Methodology and data: Emissions estimated using external sources (CDP, PCAF, S&P and sector-specific emission factors) and calculated under PCAF’s Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard. Clarifies that Pillar 3 ESG Template 1 covers a narrower scope (non-financial corporates in high‑climate‑impact and carbon-related sectors).
- Coverage and structure: 
  - Asset classes include Residential Mortgages, Commercial Real Estate (Wholesale Banking and Business Banking), Business Loans (Retail and Wholesale Banking), Equity Investments, and Corporate Bonds.
  - Wholesale Banking loans are further broken down into Terra sectors: Power; Upstream Oil & Gas; Mid- & Downstream Oil & Gas; Cement; Steel; Automotive; Aviation; Shipping.
  - For CRE WB/BB and WB sectors, results are split between clients in scope vs not in scope of ING’s Transition Plan under the Terra approach.
- Metrics reported per asset class and sector: 
  - Outstanding and measured outstanding (EUR billion).
  - Financed emissions (ktCO2e) for Scopes 1&2 and Scope 3.
  - PCAF data-quality scores.
  - Share of financed emissions attributable to clients in scope of the Terra Transition Plan.
  - Economic intensity (ktCO2e per EUR billion measured outstanding).
- FY2024 highlights (from the table):
  - Total lending in scope shows large absolute financed emissions, with Scope 3 materially exceeding Scopes 1&2.
  - Business Loans – Wholesale Banking contribute the largest share of financed emissions; sectoral details show high intensities for oil & gas (especially upstream) and notable contributions from power, cement, steel, aviation, shipping, and automotive.
  - Residential mortgages display comparatively lower economic intensity; CRE portfolios report high shares of emissions from clients in scope of the Terra approach.
  - Equity investments and corporate bonds are also reported with Scopes 1&2 and 3, including data quality and intensity.
- FY2023 comparability update: The 2023 table is revised to include Scope 3 and to break down Scopes 1&2 by Terra sectors, enabling like‑for‑like comparison with 2024.
- Observed year‑on‑year movements (from the tables): 
  - Overall Scopes 1&2 financed emissions for lending rise, while Scope 3 financed emissions decline versus 2023.
  - Notable reductions in upstream oil & gas emissions (particularly Scope 3) and in Scope 3 for retail and wholesale business loans; mixed changes across other sectors (e.g., power and some industrial sectors increase in Scopes 1&2).
- Footnotes clarify:
  - How the Terra share is calculated (emissions from clients in scope divided by total emissions of the asset class).
  - How economic intensity is calculated (emissions divided by measured outstanding).

nodes.title: Financed emissions 2023
nodes.heading: 4.1.8.2 Financed emissions 2023
nodes.start_phrase: We have updated the 2023 financed emissions table to make the 2024 values comparable.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Update the 2023 financed emissions table to ensure comparability with 2024 figures by (1) adding scope 3 emissions and (2) breaking down scope 1 and 2 emissions by sector within Terra’s scope.
- Coverage: Financed emissions for 2023 across asset classes with both scope 1&2 and scope 3, including:
  - Outstanding and measured outstanding (EUR bn)
  - Financed emissions (ktCO2e)
  - PCAF data quality scores
  - Share of financed emissions from clients in scope of ING’s Terra Transition Plan
  - Economic intensity (ktCO2e per EUR bn)
- Asset classes and segments:
  - Residential Real Estate (Mortgages)
  - Commercial Real Estate (Wholesale Banking and Retail/Business Banking), each split into clients in scope and not in scope of the Transition Plan, with high shares in scope (e.g., 86% WB, 80% BB).
  - Business Loans – Retail Banking (high scope 3 footprint and intensity; PCAF 5.0 for scope 1&2, 4.4 for scope 3)
  - Business Loans – Wholesale Banking with detailed Terra sector breakdown: Power, Upstream Oil & Gas, Mid- & Downstream Oil & Gas, Cement, Steel, Automotive, Aviation, Shipping, plus clients not in Terra scope. Sectoral data show very high scope 3 intensities in Oil & Gas.
  - Equity investments and Corporate bonds with both scope 1&2 and scope 3 reported.
- Totals (illustrative highlights):
  - Total Lending in scope: 57,288 ktCO2e (scope 1&2; PCAF 3.7) and 250,322 ktCO2e (scope 3; PCAF 3.9), with economic intensities around 935 ktCO2e/EUR bn for scope 3.
  - Equity investments: 78 ktCO2e (scope 1&2; PCAF 5.0) and 544 ktCO2e (scope 3; PCAF 4.3).
  - Corporate bonds: 263 ktCO2e (scope 1&2; PCAF 5.0) and 316 ktCO2e (scope 3; PCAF 2.4).
- Transition Plan scope shares:
  - CRE segments: majority of financed emissions from clients in scope (c. 80–86%).
  - Wholesale Business Loans: 54% (scope 1&2) and 29% (scope 3) attributed to clients in scope, with sector-level shares noted.
- Method notes:
  - Share of financed emissions in Transition Plan is calculated as the ratio of emissions from clients in scope to total emissions of the asset class.
  - Economic intensity is financed emissions divided by measured outstanding.
- Placement: Part of the Sustainability Statement (Environment) in ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Other information related to our transition plan
nodes.heading: 4.1.9 Other information related to our transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: Decarbonisation levers can be considered as both sector-wide levers, and the levers that are within ING’s control.
nodes.summary:
- Explains ING’s approach to decarbonisation levers, distinguishing sector-wide levers from those under ING’s control. Notes limited quantitative data availability until broader CSRD reporting begins (from 2025). Highlights ING-controlled levers via financing strategy aligned with the NZBA Transition Finance Guide: client engagement based on Client Transition Plan assessments (e.g., grow green finance, manage phase-out of misaligned clients), committed financing targets (e.g., renewables), and exclusions/restrictions in financing. States ongoing data collection to refine targets and quantify lever impacts.

- Addresses “locked-in” GHG emissions: while less directly applicable to a financial institution, ING recognizes client exposure to stranded assets. Cites Pillar 3 disclosure showing ~5-year average weighted maturity for financing to high climate-impact sectors, enabling regular portfolio review. Describes sector-specific transition plans and actions: ending new financing for new LNG export terminals after 2025 (per IEA guidance) and increasing exposure to next-generation aircraft in aviation. Uses Client Transition Plan assessments to guide engagement and identify potential lock-in risks at client level.

- Outlines disclosure related to EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks: summarizes exclusion criteria under the Climate Benchmark Standards Regulation (revenue from coal/oil/gas-related activities or significant harm to environmental objectives). Notes that exclusions are determined by benchmark administrators based on public data and estimation rules. States ING Groep N.V. does not meet revenue-based exclusion thresholds but lacks sufficient information to confirm whether it is excluded from any specific benchmark.

nodes.title: Policies, actions and performance
nodes.heading: 4.1.10 Policies, actions and performance
nodes.start_phrase: With our sector transition plan we focus on the most carbon-intensive sectors and steering them towards net zero, as described in the previous section.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on “Policies, actions and performance” supporting ING’s sector transition plan, which targets the most carbon‑intensive sectors while outlining broader measures to manage impacts, risks and opportunities.
- Distinction between managing negative impacts/risks (ESG Risk Policy) and pursuing opportunities (sustainable finance guidelines and green bond framework).

Policies, actions and performance
With our sector transition plan we focus on the most carbon-intensive sectors and steering them towards 
net zero, as described in the previous section. As a bank, we have more measures in place to manage our 
impacts, risks and opportunities. These actions are not part of our sector transition plan, but do present our 
strategic direction and are an integral part of how we do and manage our business. 
This next section includes the relevant policies and guidelines to address the material impacts, risks and 
opportunities and the related actions to execute those policies and guidelines. Where the Environmental, 
Social and Governance Risk Policy addresses our negative impacts and risks, our sustainable finance 
guidelines and green bond framework address our opportunities.

nodes.title: Retail Banking: Business Banking lending
nodes.heading: 4.1.10.1.1.2 Retail Banking: Business Banking lending
nodes.start_phrase: ING regularly reviews its business strategy and sets decarbonisation goals for sectors identified as major drivers of negative impact.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines ING’s approach to integrating climate and broader ESG considerations into lending across Retail (Business Banking) and Wholesale Banking.

Key points:
- Strategy and targets: ING regularly reviews its strategy and sets decarbonisation goals, focusing on high-impact sectors (including Terra sectors). It aligns lending and portfolio management with net‑zero transition objectives.
- Processes and controls: Sector-specific processes include targeted data collection (e.g., EPC data for income‑producing/commercial real estate), defined lending criteria, and ongoing monitoring to track progress and manage risks.
- Client engagement: ING engages clients with higher negative impacts to assess their emissions profiles, transition plans, and financial capacity to decarbonise, offering support to facilitate their transition.
- Risk appetite and mitigation: ING accepts transition-related risks consistent with its role in financing the net‑zero transition, while setting risk‑appetite limits, key risk indicators for physical risks, and additional acceptance criteria (notably in real estate). Mitigations include insurance for physical risks, integrating transition/physical risks into collateral valuation, and covenants requiring investments aligned with client transition plans.
- Wholesale Banking frameworks:
  - Climate Risk Appetite Statement: Client-level assessment of emissions, transition capacity, and plan quality; stricter limits and growth constraints for high-severity clients; metrics to manage exposure in highest‑emitting sectors in line with decarbonisation targets.
  - Sector lending policies and steering signals: Policies reference the ESG Risk Policy minimums; sector transition plans inform steering; criteria embed ESG factors, transmission channels, and acceptable mitigants.
  - ESG risk assessment tool: A new, integrated E‑S‑G approach embedded in credit granting (phased in during 2024, with enhancements in 2025). Five-step process from materiality screening to credit risk expert review, with escalation to the ESR desk for high-risk cases and potential binding advice.
- Data and infrastructure: Enhanced ESG data integration (internal/external), including centralized client location data and EPC labels for commercial real estate, enabling granular, data-driven decisions.
- Collateral valuation: Material climate and ESG risks are incorporated into initial valuation, ongoing monitoring, and re‑valuations for commercial real estate.

nodes.title: Wholesale Banking lending
nodes.heading: 4.1.10.1.1.3 Wholesale Banking lending
nodes.start_phrase: ING conducts regular reviews of its business strategy and sets decarboni sation objectives for Terra sectors identified as having a high negative impact.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines ING’s approach to integrating climate and broader ESG considerations into Retail (Business Banking) and Wholesale Banking lending. For Business Banking, ING sets sector-specific decarbonisation goals and supports them with data collection and controls (e.g., EPC data for income-producing real estate), dedicated lending criteria, regular monitoring, and targeted client engagement to support transitions. It manages transition and physical climate risks within a defined risk appetite through client-level assessments, exposure limits, key risk indicators, and additional acceptance criteria, and applies mitigants such as insurance, collateral valuation adjustments, and covenants tied to transition plans, underpinned by sector-tailored data procedures for active portfolio management. For Wholesale Banking, ING focuses on high-emitting Terra sectors with a Climate Risk Appetite Statement that differentiates client risk by emissions, financial capacity, and transition-plan quality, applying limits and growth constraints to high-severity clients and using a metric aligned with decarbonisation targets. Sector lending policies and steering signals embed minimum ESG requirements and transition-plan expectations. A new ESG risk-assessment tool—integrating Environmental, Social and Governance factors and the former ESR framework—was rolled out in 2024 (with 2025 enhancements), and embeds a five-step process: materiality screening, initial assessment, front-office qualitative review and mitigants with minimum-standards checks, ESR desk due diligence for high-risk cases (with binding advice), and credit risk review. Additional pillars include a business-driven client engagement strategy, enhanced ESG data infrastructure (integrating internal and external sources, including client location and EPC data), and incorporation of material climate risks into commercial real estate collateral valuation and monitoring.
