It details strengthened ESG governance, including transforming the Risks Committee into the Risks and Sustainability Committee, appointing a Chief Sustainability Officer with a dedicated governance area, and expanding the ESG Control Room in 2024 to support the Steering Committee. ESG is embedded in incentives via a dedicated KPI: 15% of the Managing Director/CEO’s annual variable pay and a Performance Share Plan with a composite ESG KPI weighted 40% Environmental, 40% Social, and 20% Governance. The Statement’s scope is defined by a double materiality assessment covering impacts, risks, and opportunities across the full value chain, with related policies, actions, targets, and metrics outlined.

nodes.title: E–Environmental
nodes.heading: 1.1 E–Environmental
nodes.start_phrase: The Group pursues its ongoing commitment to furthering the transition toward a sustainable economy by setting concrete and ambitious emission reduction targets.
nodes.summary:
- Executive summary of Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s ESG strategy, highlighting sustainability as integral to business strategy and value creation for stakeholders, with performance linked to the wellbeing of employees, customers, and communities.
- First Consolidated Sustainability Statement prepared under the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), included in the annual report alongside financials; disclosures organized per European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) across E, S, and G.
- Strengthened ESG governance: transformation of the Risks Committee into the Risks and Sustainability Committee; appointment of a Chief Sustainability Officer and dedicated governance area; expansion of the ESG Control Room in 2024 to support the Steering Committee.
- ESG embedded in incentives: a dedicated ESG KPI; 15% of the Managing Director/CEO’s annual variable pay tied to ESG; Performance Share Plan includes a composite ESG KPI weighted 40% Environmental, 40% Social, 20% Governance.
- Double materiality assessment used to identify key topics, covering impacts, risks, and opportunities across the full value chain; associated policies, actions, targets, and metrics defined.
- Environmental focus—Climate Change:
  - Own operations: target to cut Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 53% by 2030 vs. 2019; achieved a 35% reduction by end-2024. Plan to procure 100% renewable electricity by 2030 (93% in 2024). Additional levers include building energy efficiency measures (heat pumps, photovoltaics, monitoring systems) and electrification/hybridization of the vehicle fleet with charging infrastructure.
  - Financed emissions: net-zero by 2050 with 2030 portfolio targets for high-emitting sectors (oil & gas, automotive, power generation, residential and commercial real estate, primary agriculture, aluminium, cement, iron & steel) and full coal mining phase-out by 2025. Targets submitted to SBTi in 2024 and validated in January 2025.
  - Sectoral Transition Plan detailing strategic actions, including dedicated finance for emission-reducing initiatives (renewables, sustainable agriculture, electric mobility, carbon capture/storage, green hydrogen).

nodes.title: Climate Change
nodes.heading: 1.1.1 Climate Change
nodes.start_phrase: The Group pursues its ongoing commitment to furthering the transition toward a sustainable economy by setting concrete and ambitious emission reduction targets.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and reporting shift: Intesa Sanpaolo’s first Consolidated Sustainability Statement under the EU CSRD, structured per ESRS and integrated into the annual report alongside financials, emphasizing sustainability as inseparable from performance. Topics identified via double materiality across the full value chain.
- ESG governance and incentives: Expanded ESG governance (Risks Committee renamed Risks and Sustainability Committee; Chief Sustainability Officer and governance area; enlarged ESG Control Room in 2024). Executive incentives tied to ESG: 15% of CEO annual variable pay; Performance Share Plan ESG KPI split 40% Environmental, 40% Social, 20% Governance.
- Climate strategy (own operations): Target to cut scope 1 and 2 emissions by 53% by 2030 from 2019 (35% achieved by end-2024). 100% renewable electricity by 2030 (93% in 2024). Decarbonization levers include energy efficiency in buildings, heat pumps, PV, energy monitoring, and electrifying the vehicle fleet with charging infrastructure.
- Climate strategy (financed emissions): Net-zero by 2050 with 2030 sector targets (oil & gas, automotive, power generation, residential/commercial real estate, primary agriculture, aluminium, cement, iron & steel; coal mining full phase-out by 2025). Targets submitted to SBTi in 2024 and validated January 2025. Sectoral Transition Plan actions: dedicated green finance (renewables, sustainable agriculture, EVs, CCS, green hydrogen), expanded green real estate products and advisory; target €12bn Green Mortgages during the business plan (€9bn since 2022; €4.1bn in 2024); sustainability-linked loans.
- Risk management integration: ESG Risk Governance Guidelines embed ESG across credit, market, operational, liquidity, and reputational risks. Lending controls for high-emission sectors; specific rules for oil & gas and coal (phase-out of non-conventional oil & gas resources and coal mining by 2025). ESG/Climate Credit Framework applied at sector (heatmap/color-coding), counterparty (ESG scoring integrated into strategy and CRA), and transaction levels (sustainable lending classification).
- Sustainable supply chain: Mandatory ESG questionnaire for suppliers via the Group Supplier Portal from 2024; goal to map all active suppliers by end-2025 (86% progress by end-2024).
- Pollution, biodiversity, and circular economy: “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature” (prepared 2024, adopted Jan 2025) set exclusions, enhanced assessments, and monitoring for lending; promote biodiversity-positive finance. ESG counterparty scoring includes biodiversity, natural resources, and pollution. Financing solutions include S-Loan Progetti Green and SACE Green-backed loans.
- Circular economy: Ongoing strategic partnership with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and the Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center; €8bn earmarked for circular-economy lending aligned with the internal green/circular framework.
- Social—own workforce: Commitment to people development, human rights, diversity and inclusion; zero tolerance for forced or child labor; protection of physical and moral integrity of employees.

nodes.title: Pollution, Biodiversity and the Circular Economy
nodes.heading: 1.1.2 Pollution, Biodiversity and the Circular Economy
nodes.start_phrase: Alongside climate change, the Group is similarly devoting great effort to other material environmental topics, such as pollution, biodiversity and the circular economy.
nodes.summary:
- The Group’s sustainable finance offering has expanded, notably in real estate with Green Mortgages for high energy-efficiency properties and energy upgrades (12 billion euro target; 9 billion since 2022, including 4.1 billion in 2024).
- Additional financing tools include sustainability-linked loans with incentives tied to decarbonization and advisory services to help clients reduce emissions and craft decarbonization strategies.
- ESG Risk Governance Guidelines integrate ESG factors across credit, market, operational, liquidity, and reputational risks, with enhanced controls on high-emission sectors and a 2025 phase-out for non-conventional oil & gas and coal mining.
- An ESG/Climate Credit Framework operates on three levels: sector (color-coded heatmap to guide credit strategy), counterparty (ESG scoring embedded in strategies and credit risk appetite), and transaction (classification framework for sustainable lending).
- Supply chain oversight requires a mandatory ESG questionnaire for suppliers (from 2024) to map environmental and social profiles and drive improvements; goal to map all active suppliers by end-2025, with 86% completion by end-2024.
- Environmental focus extends to pollution, biodiversity, and circular economy:
  - “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature” (prepared 2024, adopted Jan 2025) apply across lending, wealth management/protection, and direct impacts, setting exclusion, heightened assessment, and monitoring criteria and promoting biodiversity-positive lending.
  - The ESG score for corporate customers factors in biodiversity, natural resources, and pollution.
  - Financing solutions include S-Loan Progetti Green and loans backed by SACE Green guarantees.
  - Circular economy promotion continues via partnership with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and the Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center, with 8 billion euro earmarked to support circular business models under the internal framework.
- Social (Own Workforce): strong commitments to investing in people, protecting human rights, diversity and inclusion, prohibiting forced and child labor, and safeguarding the physical and moral integrity of employees.

nodes.title: S–Social
nodes.heading: 1.2 S–Social
nodes.start_phrase: One of the overriding goals of the Group is to invest in its people and ensure their constant growth and satisfaction.
nodes.summary:
- Expansion of sustainable finance offerings:
  - Green mortgages for high energy-efficiency properties and retrofits; target of 12 billion euro under the business plan, with 9 billion since 2022 and 4.1 billion in 2024.
  - Sustainability-linked loans incentivizing decarbonization outcomes.
  - Advisory services to help clients measure, reduce emissions, and craft decarbonization strategies.
- ESG risk governance:
  - Group-wide ESG Risk Governance Guidelines integrating ESG materiality across credit, market, operational, liquidity, and reputational risks.
  - Heightened lending controls for high-emission sectors; specific rules for oil & gas and coal, with a 2025 phase-out for non-conventional oil & gas resources and coal mining.
  - ESG/Climate Credit Framework applied at three levels:
    - Sector: ESG Sectoral Strategy with color-coded heatmap to guide sector attractiveness and credit strategy.
    - Counterparty: ESG scoring integrated into credit strategies and risk appetite.
    - Transaction: Internal classification framework for sustainable lending/products.
- Supply chain ESG management:
  - Mandatory ESG questionnaire for suppliers via the Group Supplier Portal starting 2024 to assess environmental and social performance and set improvement plans.
  - Goal to map all active suppliers by end-2025; 86% completion by end-2024.
- Pollution, biodiversity, and circular economy:
  - “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature” prepared in 2024 and adopted January 2025, defining exclusions, heightened assessments, and risk monitoring for new projects/counterparties based on location, sector, and project type; includes criteria to promote biodiversity in new lending.
  - ESG customer scoring incorporates biodiversity, natural resource, and pollution factors.
  - Financing tools for ecological transition (e.g., S-Loan Progetti Green, SACE Green-backed loans).
  - Ongoing partnership with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation (since 2015) and support from Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center to embed circular-economy principles in lending; 8 billion euro earmarked for circular-economy initiatives per internal framework.
- Social (Own Workforce):
  - Commitment to investing in people, continuous development, and satisfaction.
  - Strong stance on human rights, diversity and inclusion, and respect for individual dignity.
  - Zero tolerance for forced or child labor; protection of employees’ physical and moral integrity.

nodes.title: Own Workforce
nodes.heading: 1.2.1 Own Workforce
nodes.start_phrase: One of the overriding goals of the Group is to invest in its people and ensure their constant growth and satisfaction.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on environmental and social sustainability within Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s operations, products, risk governance, and value chain.
- Climate and sustainable finance:
  - Expansion of green real estate lending (e.g., Green – Mutuo Domus, Orizzonte Impresa – Transizione Energetica) for high energy-efficiency properties and upgrades; target of 12 billion euro in Green Mortgages over the business plan; 9 billion since 2022, including 4.1 billion in 2024.
  - Introduction of sustainability-linked loans with incentives tied to decarbonisation performance.
  - Advisory services helping clients reduce emissions and craft decarbonisation strategies.
- ESG risk governance and lending:
  - ESG Risk Governance Guidelines based on materiality across credit, market, operational, liquidity, and reputational risks, embedded in risk management.
  - Enhanced lending controls for high-emission sectors; specific oil & gas and coal policies, with a 2025 phase-out for non-conventional oil & gas resources and coal mining.
  - ESG/Climate Credit Framework across:
    - Sector level: ESG sectoral strategy with colour-coded heatmap to guide credit strategy.
    - Counterparty level: ESG scoring integrated into credit strategies and credit risk appetite (CRA).
    - Transaction level: internal framework to classify sustainable lending and products.
- Supply chain ESG:
  - Strict ESG-based supplier screening and monitoring; mandatory ESG questionnaire for bidding via the Supplier Portal from 2024.
  - Goal to complete ESG mapping of all active suppliers by end-2025; 86% completion by end-2024.
- Pollution, biodiversity, and circular economy:
  - “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature” (prepared in 2024, adopted Jan 2025) covering lending, wealth management & protection, and direct impacts; include exclusion, heightened assessment, and risk monitoring criteria by location, sector, and project type; criteria to promote and protect biodiversity in new lending.
  - ESG customer scoring includes biodiversity, natural resources, and pollution components.
  - Financing solutions supporting ecological transition (e.g., S-Loan Progetti Green, SACE Green guarantees).
  - Ongoing strategic partnership with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and support from Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center; lending principles promoting circular business models; 8 billion euro earmarked for circular economy initiatives under the internal framework.
- Social (S) – Own workforce:
  - Commitment to human rights, protection of people, diversity, and inclusion.
  - Upskilling/reskilling aligned with the 2022–2025 Business Plan: 6,902 people trained by end-2024 in digital skills, change management, and sustainability.
  - DE&I Principles and gender-balance target (approx. 50/50) in new senior appointments; 2022–2024 achieved parity (25 male, 25 female appointments).
  - Initiatives for female talent development, disability inclusion (IT accessibility and awareness), and LGBTQ+ inclusion via ISPROUD community.
  - Mandatory training expanded and governed by internal rules for all employees.
  - Creation of job communities to build skills; target of 20,000 by 2025 exceeded with 36,775 participants in 2024.
  - “Future Leaders” programme to develop next-generation leaders; 975 participants toward a 1,000 target.
  - Enhanced health, safety, and wellbeing: workplace safety monitoring, health surveillance for ~50,000 people, and 24/7 counselling globally.
  - Work-life balance and welfare initiatives: company welfare plan, “Next Way of Working,” short working week, parenting support, and “Time Bank.”
- Social – Workers in the value chain:
  - Supplier ESG assessment system to ensure respect for workers’ rights and safe conditions; mandatory acknowledgment of key Group policies (Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Anti-corruption Guidelines, DE&I Principles, Model 231, General Conditions of Supply) for Supplier Portal registration.
  - ESG criteria embedded in loan approvals for corporate customers; exclusion of lending to companies/projects with materially adverse social impacts (e.g., forced or child labour).

nodes.title: Workers in the Value Chain
nodes.heading: 1.2.2 Workers in the Value Chain
nodes.start_phrase: In line with Group principles, an ESG assessment system has been introduced to check that suppliers respect workers’ rights and ensure safe working conditions, as well as their compliance with Group policies.
nodes.summary:
- Human capital development: Targeted upskilling and reskilling aligned to the 2022–2025 Business Plan; 6,902 people trained in digital skills, change management and sustainability; expanded mandatory training for all employees.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion: Board-approved DE&I Principles; gender-balance target (approx. 50/50) for senior appointments achieved over 2022–2024 with 25 men and 25 women; initiatives for female talent (job rotation, shadowing, training, empowerment); disability inclusion via accessible IT and awareness training; strengthened collaboration with ISPROUD (LGBTQ+ community).
- People development platforms: Creation of job communities with 36,775 people involved in 2024 (exceeding 20,000 target by 2025); “Future Leaders” program nearing its 1,000-person target with 975 participants to date.
- Health, safety and welfare: Enhanced workplace safety monitoring; health surveillance for around 50,000 people; 24/7 counselling service globally; work-life balance measures including a welfare plan, “Next Way of Working,” short working week, parenting support, and “Time Bank.”
- Workers in the value chain: ESG assessments for suppliers; mandatory adherence to Group policies (Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Anti-corruption, DE&I, Model 231, General Conditions of Supply); ESG criteria integrated into lending with exclusions for forced or child labor.
- Community impact: Strong social inclusion focus under a Chief Social Impact Officer; “Food and shelter for the needy” program executing 54.1 million interventions since plan start (17.3 million in 2024) via broad partner networks; initiatives for social housing and employability (e.g., Youth & Work); Charity Allowance provided ~€23 million to 814 non-profit projects in 2024; “Culture Project” to promote artistic heritage.
- Consumers and end-users: Emphasis on service quality, transparency and responsible sales; NPS tracking based on 657,000+ surveys in 2024; structured complaint management.
- Data protection and security: Advanced ML and analytics for threat detection; mandatory data protection training; establishment of a Chief Security Officer governance area covering cybersecurity, business continuity and physical security; 271 data breaches in 2024 (252 with no risk; 19 notified to authorities).
- Consumer safety: Participation in an ABI–OSSIF memorandum to prevent bank crime (fraud, robbery).
- Financial inclusion products: Offerings with social impact including Mutuo Giovani; Gamma Impact (Per Merito, mamma@work); Business Gemma loans and microcredit; personal and anti-usury mortgages; CRE.S.Co community development credit.
- Support for SME sustainability: ESG Workshops expanded to 16 in 2024, surpassing the 2025 target of 12.

nodes.title: Affected communities
nodes.heading: 1.2.3 Affected communities
nodes.start_phrase: The Group places great importance on projects that promote growth and social, educational, cultural and civic inclusion in the communities where it operates.
nodes.summary:
This section of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement outlines the Group’s social impact and customer-focused initiatives. It details a strong commitment to community inclusion and support, led by the new Chief Social Impact Officer governance area. A flagship “Food and shelter for the needy” programme—Italy’s largest private initiative of its kind—delivers food, beds, medicines, and clothing nationwide through broad partnerships, totaling 54.1 million interventions since the Business Plan began, including 17.3 million in 2024. Additional measures target fragile socio-economic groups through social housing (for students and families) and employability programs (e.g., Youth & Work). The Charity Allowance funded about €23 million for 814 non-profit projects in 2024, while the “Culture Project” advances local artistic and cultural heritage.

For consumers and end-users, the Group emphasizes responsible sales, service quality, and transparent complaint management. Customer satisfaction is tracked via NPS based on over 657,000 surveys in 2024. Data protection and security were strengthened through advanced machine learning threat detection, mandatory privacy training, and the creation of the Chief Security Officer governance area overseeing cybersecurity, business continuity, and physical security. In 2024, 271 data breaches occurred; 252 posed no risk and required no authority notification, while 19 were notified to data protection authorities. The Group also supports consumer health and safety via a memorandum with the Italian Banking Association and OSSIF to prevent bank crime. Financial inclusion is pursued through targeted products—Mutuo Giovani, Gamma Impact (Per Merito, mamma@work), Business Gemma loans and microcredit, personal and anti-usury mortgage loans, and CRE.S.Co. ESG Workshops for SMEs continued, reaching 16 total by 2024 and surpassing the original 2025 target.

nodes.title: Consumers and End-Users
nodes.heading: 1.2.4 Consumers and End-Users
nodes.start_phrase: The Group places a special focus on customer satisfaction and the promotion of responsible sales practices, adopting a strategy that combines service quality, transparency and continuous listening to consumers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on social impact and inclusion in communities where the Group operates, with a dedicated Chief Social Impact Officer governance area.
- Major Social Action Plan: “Food and shelter for the needy” — Italy’s largest private initiative distributing food, beds, medicines, and clothing via profit and non-profit partners; 54.1 million interventions since the Business Plan launch, including 17.3 million in 2024.
- Additional social initiatives: social housing for students and families; training and employment programs for vulnerable groups (e.g., Youth & Work); Charity Allowance of about €23 million funding 814 non-profit projects in 2024; “Culture Project” to promote artistic and cultural heritage with public/private partners.
- Customer focus: service quality, transparency, and structured complaints management; customer satisfaction measured via NPS with over 657,000 surveys in 2024.
- Cybersecurity and data protection: advanced machine learning and analytics for threat detection, mandatory data protection training; creation of a Chief Security Officer area overseeing cybersecurity, business continuity, and physical security.
- Data incidents in 2024: 271 customer-related data breaches; 252 assessed as posing no risk (no authority notification required); 19 notified to relevant data protection authorities.
- Consumer health and safety: partnership with the Italian Banking Association and OSSIF to prevent bank crime (fraud, robbery).
- Financial inclusion and support for the real economy: products with social impact such as Mutuo Giovani; Gamma Impact (Per Merito, mamma@work); Business Gemma loans and microcredit; personal and anti-usury mortgage loans; CRE.S.Co; ESG Workshops for SMEs with 16 held in 2024, exceeding the 2025 target.
- Governance: integrity, transparency, and accountability anchored in the Code of Ethics; zero tolerance of corruption aligned with UN Global Compact and implemented via Anti-corruption Guidelines and Model 231/2001.
- Whistleblowing: 24/7 system ensuring confidentiality and protection from retaliation, managed by the Chief Audit Officer; ESG-aligned supplier screening and monitoring; transparent institutional engagement with a ban on political party funding.

nodes.title: G–Governance
nodes.heading: 1.3 G–Governance
nodes.start_phrase: Business conduct in the Group is underpinned by a sound governance system built on the principles of integrity, transparency and accountability.
nodes.summary:
- Governance: Emphasis on integrity, transparency, and accountability via a formal Code of Ethics; zero tolerance for corruption through Anti-corruption Guidelines and a 231/2001 Organizational, Management and Control Model; a 24/7 whistleblowing system ensuring confidentiality and protection from retaliation managed by the Chief Audit Officer; ESG-based supplier screening and monitoring; transparent institutional relations and a ban on funding political parties.

- Reporting framework: Consolidated Sustainability Statement prepared by Intesa Sanpaolo Group under Italy’s Legislative Decree 125/2024 implementing the EU CSRD, aligned with ESRS (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772) and including EU Taxonomy Article 8 specifications; certification by the Manager responsible for financial reports together with the Managing Director and CEO.

- Assurance: Limited assurance performed by EY S.p.A., covering compliance with ESRS and EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures.

- Reporting boundary and methodology: Boundary based on consolidated financial statements; first-year, significance-based inclusion of subsidiaries considering business type and FTE; 62 companies representing 99% of Group total assets and FTE included; boundary deemed adequate with annual reassessment for potential expansion.

  - Upstream value chain (supply chain and procurement), focusing on risk management, including reputational risks where sustainability control tools are absent.
  - Downstream value chain (business processes and relationships, including financing and investment portfolios), focusing on impact management and risks linked to sector and country.
- Reporting on own operations includes policies, actions, goals, and metrics deemed relevant via the Group’s double materiality assessment, plus organization-specific disclosures.
- Entity-specific disclosures are identified and prepared per ESRS 1 Appendix A and referenced in the Content index; readers are directed to Double materiality assessment and topic chapters for further details.

nodes.title: Reporting boundary
nodes.heading: 2.1.2 Reporting boundary
nodes.start_phrase: The Consolidated Sustainability Statement covers the following three macro -areas:
nodes.summary:

Notes that Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni S.p.A. and Všeobecná Úverová Banka A.S., as issuers of publicly traded securities, must publish sub-consolidated sustainability statements under Legislative Decree 125/2024.
- Structures disclosure around three macro-areas: own operations; upstream value chain (supply chain and procurement, with emphasis on risk management and reputational risks linked to suppliers lacking sustainability controls); and downstream value chain (business processes/relationships, with focus on impact management and risks from financing/investment portfolios by sector or country).
- Covers policies, actions, goals, and metrics aligned to the Group’s double materiality assessment, and includes entity-specific disclosures where ESRS is not comprehensive, prepared per ESRS 1 Appendix A and referenced in the Content index.
- For the value chain, provides qualitative information on policies, actions, and targets, and quantitative information on GHG emissions and portfolio entity-specific metrics. Applies ESRS 1 transitional provisions by omitting certain first-year requirements while leveraging available internal and public information.
- States that no information was omitted on grounds of intellectual property, know-how, or sensitivity.
- Sets forward-looking time horizons consistent with other disclosures: medium term up to five years (aligned with the Business Plan) and long term five to 25 years (aligned with 2050 Net Zero commitments).
- Explains the use of estimates and indirect data for ESRS E1 – Climate change metrics, notably:
  - Scope 3 GHG emissions across upstream and downstream value chains (E1-6).
  - Physical climate risk quantification on portfolio exposures (E1-9), disclosed under transitional provisions and aligned with Pillar 3 where applicable.
- Describes data collection constraints in the value chain and “best effort” approaches when direct data are unavailable, using sector averages and proxies.
- Specifies methodological frameworks: GHG Protocol for Scope 3 value-chain emissions; PCAF for financed emissions; and Italian Banking Association sector guidelines, to enhance consistency and reduce inaccuracy risk.
- Notes ongoing efforts to improve data quality by engaging portfolio companies and suppliers and using specialized environmental data providers.
- Outlines the current methodology to assess physical climate risk: external tools to map hazards under long-term climate scenarios, high-granularity grids, and a synthetic physical risk indicator (SPRI) by location for counterparties’ sites and collateral, with exposure classification based on maturity and risk severity trends.

nodes.title: Time horizons
nodes.heading: 2.1.3 Time horizons
nodes.start_phrase: The Consolidated Sustainability Statement includes forward -looking information for which the Group decided to adopt a time horizon that is in line with that envisaged by other disclosure requirements, such as Pillar 3 or management disclosure.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and content: The statement covers value chain disclosures with qualitative information on policies, actions, and targets for upstream and downstream activities, and quantitative data on GHG emissions and portfolio-specific metrics for the downstream value chain.
- ESRS transitional provisions: The Group applied ESRS 1 transitional provisions, omitting certain first-year requirements while disclosing value chain policies/actions/targets using internal and public sources; no sensitive or IP-related information was omitted.
- Time horizons: Medium term defined as up to 5 years; long term as 5–25 years, aligned with the Business Plan and the Group’s 2050 Net Zero commitments.
- Use of estimates: Estimates used for Scope 3 GHG emissions (E1-6) and for quantifying physical climate risk on portfolio exposures (E1-9). Data collection across the value chain faces practical constraints; reasonable efforts were made, and proxies/sector averages were applied when direct data were unavailable.
- Methodologies and data sources: Scope 3 calculated using the GHG Protocol; financed emissions category using PCAF; Italian Banking Association sector guidelines also considered. Recognized standards are used to mitigate inaccuracy. The Group seeks to improve data quality through counterparty engagement and specialized data providers; detailed methods and the share of directly sourced data are referenced in ESRS E1 metrics.
- Physical risk assessment: Methodology under development. An external tool maps hazards via long-term climate scenarios on high-resolution grids and computes a Synthetic Physical Risk Indicator (SPRI) per location (offices, production sites, collateral properties). Exposures are classified as subject to physical risk based on exposure maturity and changes in risk severity. E1-9 is implemented under transitional provisions with equivalent information aligned to Pillar 3.

nodes.title: Use of estimates
nodes.heading: 2.1.4 Use of estimates
nodes.start_phrase: In preparing the Consolidated Sustainability Statement , the Intesa Sanpaolo Group used estimates and indirect sources to disclose the metrics of ESRS E1 – Climate change relating to:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and content: Describes value chain disclosures in the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, covering qualitative policies, actions, and targets for upstream and downstream activities, plus quantitative data on GHG emissions and portfolio-specific metrics (downstream).
- Use of ESRS transitional provisions: The Group applied ESRS 1 transitional options, omitting certain first-year, gradually introduced disclosure requirements, while disclosing value chain policies/actions/targets using available internal and public information. No sensitive IP or know-how was withheld.
- Time horizons: Forward-looking disclosures align with other frameworks (e.g., Pillar 3), defining medium term as up to 5 years and long term as 5–25 years, consistent with the Business Plan and the 2050 Net Zero commitment.
- Use of estimates: Estimates and indirect sources are used for ESRS E1 metrics, specifically Scope 3 GHG emissions (upstream and downstream) and the quantification of physical climate risk on portfolio exposures (E1-9).
- Data limitations and efforts: Notes variability in obtaining value chain data due to control, contracts, and counterparties’ reporting scope; the Group made reasonable efforts and used sector averages and proxies when direct data were unavailable.
- Methodological frameworks: Uses the GHG Protocol for Scope 3 calculations, PCAF for financed emissions, and considers Italian Banking Association sector guidelines; reliance on recognized standards aims to reduce inaccuracy, with continuous improvement via counterparty engagement and specialized data providers. Additional methodological details are referenced in ESRS E1 Metrics.
- Physical risk methodology: In development; employs an external tool to map long-term climate scenarios onto high-granularity grids, derive hazard indicators, and compute a Synthetic Physical Risk Indicator (SPRI) per location for client facilities and collateral. Exposures are classified as subject to physical risk based on exposure maturity and the trajectory of risk severity.
- References/notes: Clarifies ESRS definitions for medium and long term; indicates transitional handling of E1-9 with equivalent information also disclosed in Pillar 3.

nodes.title: Value chain
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.1 Value chain
nodes.start_phrase: In preparing the Consolidated Sustainability Statement , the Intesa Sanpaolo Group used estimates and indirect sources to disclose the metrics of ESRS E1 – Climate change relating to:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: The Consolidated Sustainability Statement covers upstream and downstream value chain topics, providing qualitative disclosures on policies, actions and targets, and quantitative data on GHG emissions and portfolio entity-specific metrics. No information on intellectual property, know-how or sensitive content was omitted.
- ESRS transitional provisions: The Group applied ESRS 1 transitional options, omitting certain newly introduced disclosure requirements in the first reporting year. Value chain disclosures relied on in-house and publicly available information.
- Time horizons: Forward-looking disclosures adopt a 5-year medium-term horizon and a 5–25 year long-term horizon, aligned with the Business Plan and the Group’s Net Zero 2050 commitments.
- Use of estimates – value chain: Estimates and indirect sources were used for ESRS E1 metrics, notably Scope 3 GHG emissions (E1-6) across the value chain and physical climate risk quantification on portfolio exposures (E1-9). Data challenges are acknowledged; reasonable efforts were made to collect value chain data, using sector averages and proxies when direct data were unavailable.
- Methodologies: Scope 3 estimations follow the GHG Protocol and PCAF (for financed emissions), with reference to Italian Banking Association sector guidelines. The Group seeks to improve data quality via engagement with portfolio companies and suppliers and through specialized data providers.
- Physical risk methodology: An external tool maps long-term climate scenarios to high-granularity grids to derive hazard indicators, producing a synthetic physical risk indicator (SPRI) for each geo-located asset (offices, production sites, collateral). Determination of exposure to physical risk considers exposure maturity and risk severity trends.
- Use of estimates – own operations: Estimates were also applied to energy consumption (E1-5), internal carbon pricing coverage (E1-8), and work-related accidents (S1-14). No additional assurance was performed beyond the independent auditors’ assurance on the Statement.
- Comparative information: This is the first report under ESRS (transitioned from GRI). Quantitative metrics are provided for 2024 only, per ESRS 1 transitional provisions.
- Incorporation by reference: Not used in 2024.
- Due diligence: The Group operates due diligence processes embedded in governance, strategy and business model to identify, assess and manage negative impacts across own operations and the value chain. Core elements include stakeholder engagement, impact identification/assessment, actions (E1–E5, S2, S3, G1), and tracking effectiveness. For climate (E1), monitoring hinges on portfolio-level targets; for other downstream impacts, quantitative targets are not yet set, but policies and actions are in place to manage material impacts.
- Strategy and business model highlights: The Group emphasizes sustainable, fee- and service-driven revenues, high efficiency and low risk, positioning as a leading Italian/European wealth management and protection company. Strong integration between product factories (asset management, life and non-life insurance) and commercial networks creates synergies. People are central to strategy, with a workforce of 93,539 (71,174 in Italy; 22,365 abroad), and ongoing initiatives for people development.

nodes.title: Own operations
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.2 Own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group used estimations also to calculate other metrics, such as E1 -5 (energy consumption), E1 -8 (portion of emissions covered by internal carbon pricing) and S1 -14 (work -related accidents).
nodes.summary:
- The Group used estimations for certain metrics: E1-5 (energy consumption), E1-8 (share of emissions under internal carbon pricing), and S1-14 (work-related accidents), with detailed methodologies referenced in ESRS E1 and ESRS S1 sections.

- Core due diligence elements include stakeholder engagement, impact identification and assessment, actions to address impacts, and tracking effectiveness, with cross-references to relevant ESRS topics (E1, E2, E4, E5, S2, S3, G1).
- For climate (ESRS E1), monitoring negative impacts hinges on portfolio-level targets; for other downstream issues, measurable quantitative targets are not yet adopted, though policies and actions provide control tools.
- Strategy and business model focus on sustainable revenue growth (fees/commissions and services), high efficiency, and a low risk profile, positioning the Group as a leading wealth management and protection company in Italy and Europe.
- Strong integration between product factories (asset management, life and non-life insurance) and commercial networks generates synergies, profitability, and flexibility in offerings.
- People are central to the strategy; the workforce totals 93,539 (71,174 in Italy and 22,365 abroad, with a notable presence in Central/Eastern Europe), with emphasis on ongoing development.

nodes.title: Comparative information
nodes.heading: 2.1.5 Comparative information
nodes.start_phrase: The Consolidated Sustainability Statement of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group is the first report drawn up in accordance with the ESRS, instead of the previous Consolidated Non -financial Statement prepared under the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) standards.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and methodology notes: Certain sustainability metrics are estimated, including E1-5 (energy consumption), E1-8 (share of emissions under internal carbon pricing), and S1-14 (work-related accidents). Methodologies and assumptions are detailed in ESRS E1 (Climate change) and ESRS S1 (Own workforce) sections.
- Assurance: No metrics received additional assurance beyond the independent auditors’ work on the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Reporting framework shift: This is Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s first Consolidated Sustainability Statement prepared under ESRS, transitioning from GRI. Quantitative metric disclosures are limited to 2024, leveraging ESRS transitional provisions (ESRS 1, par. 136).
- Incorporation by reference: Not used in 2024.
- Due diligence approach: The Group has embedded due diligence to identify and manage negative impacts from own operations and across the value chain, integrating actions into strategy, products, and business relationships.
- Mapping of due diligence elements to the Statement:
  - Embedding in governance/strategy/business model: covered in General disclosures (strategy, governance, double materiality).
  - Stakeholder engagement: addressed via the double materiality assessment.
  - Impact identification/assessment: through double materiality and materiality processes for E1 (Climate), E2 (Pollution), E4 (Biodiversity), E5 (Resource use/circular economy), S2 (Workers in the value chain), S3 (Affected communities), G1 (Business conduct).
  - Actions to address impacts: portfolio-level policies, targets, and actions across E1–E5, S2, S3, G1.
  - Tracking effectiveness and communication: focused on E1 with portfolio-level climate strategies.
- Targets status: For climate (E1), monitoring hinges on setting portfolio-level targets. For other downstream value chain matters, quantitative targets are not yet adopted; management relies on existing policies and control tools.
- Strategy and business model: Emphasis on sustainable, service-driven revenues (fees/commissions), high efficiency, and low risk, positioning the Group as a diversified wealth management and protection leader in Italy and Europe.
- Operating model: Strong integration between product factories (asset management, life and non-life insurance) and commercial networks to enhance profitability and flexible offerings.
- People focus and workforce: People are seen as the key enabler. As of 31 Dec 2024, workforce totals 93,539 (71,174 in Italy; 22,365 abroad, notably in Central/Eastern Europe), with a commitment to continuous development and growth.

nodes.title: Incorporation by reference
nodes.heading: 2.1.6 Incorporation by reference
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the Group did not avail of the incorporation by reference option.
nodes.summary:
- Explains that certain sustainability metrics were estimated: E1-5 (energy consumption), E1-8 (share of emissions under internal carbon pricing), and S1-14 (work-related accidents), with methodologies referenced to ESRS E1 and ESRS S1 sections.
- States that no metrics underwent additional assurance beyond the independent audit of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.

- Emphasizes people as a core asset; provides workforce figures as of 31 Dec 2024 (93,539 total: 71,174 in Italy; 22,365 abroad, with a significant presence in Central/Eastern Europe).

nodes.title: Statement on due diligence
nodes.heading: 2.1.7 Statement on due diligence
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group identified due diligence processes that enable the identification and management of the negative impacts arising from own operations or from the upstream and downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Use of estimates: Certain ESRS metrics were calculated using estimations—E1-5 (energy consumption), E1-8 (portion of emissions covered by internal carbon pricing), and S1-14 (work-related accidents)—with methodologies detailed in ESRS E1 (energy and GHG) and ESRS S1 (health and safety) sections.
- Assurance: No additional assurance was performed on individual metrics beyond the independent auditors’ assurance of the overall Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Comparative scope: This is the Group’s first report prepared under ESRS (transitioning from GRI); quantitative disclosures cover only 2024 in line with ESRS 1 transitional provisions (par. 136).
- Incorporation by reference: Not used in 2024.
- Due diligence framework: The Group has embedded due diligence across strategy and the business model to identify, assess, and address negative impacts in own operations and the value chain, engaging affected stakeholders. Core elements are mapped to Statement sections:
  - Embedding in governance/strategy/business model (General disclosures)
  - Stakeholder engagement and double materiality assessment
  - Identification and assessment of adverse impacts (materiality process across E1, E2, E4, E5, S2, S3, G1)
  - Actions to address impacts: portfolio-level policies, targets, and actions for climate (E1), pollution (E2), biodiversity (E4), resource use/circular economy (E5), workers in the value chain (S2), affected communities (S3), and business conduct (G1)
  - Tracking effectiveness and communication (notably under E1)
  - Note: Climate impact monitoring depends on defining portfolio-level targets; for other downstream topics, quantitative targets are not yet set, though policies and control tools are in place.
- Strategy and business model highlights: Focus on sustainable, fee- and service-based revenues, high efficiency, and low risk; a diversified, internationally present wealth management and protection model with leading positions in Italy and Europe. Strong integration between product factories (asset management, life and non-life insurance) and commercial networks drives synergies and commercial effectiveness.
- People focus: Employees are central to strategy; workforce totaled 93,539 at 31 Dec 2024 (71,174 in Italy; 22,365 abroad, with a notable presence in Central/Eastern Europe), with emphasis on continuous development and growth.

nodes.title: Strategy, business model and value chain
nodes.heading: 2.2 Strategy, business model and value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s business model combines the generation of sustainable revenues focused on increasing fee and commission and revenues from services, high efficiency and a low risk profile.
nodes.summary:
- The document is part of Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement, prepared under ESRS standards and focused on own operations, due diligence, and strategy.
- Metrics and estimates: Certain indicators rely on estimates (E1-5 energy consumption, E1-8 emissions covered by internal carbon pricing, S1-14 work-related accidents). Methodologies are detailed in ESRS E1 and S1 sections. No additional assurance was performed beyond the independent audit of the Statement.
- Comparative information and transition: This is the first ESRS-based report replacing the prior GRI framework. Quantitative metrics cover only 2024, applying ESRS 1 transitional provisions (par. 136).
- Incorporation by reference: Not used in 2024.
- Due diligence: The Group has embedded due diligence to identify, assess, and manage negative impacts from own operations and the value chain, including through products and business relationships. Core elements include:
  - Embedding in governance, strategy, and business model.
  - Stakeholder engagement.
  - Impact identification and assessment across E1/E2/E4/E5/S2/S3/G1.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 2.2.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s business model combines the generation of sustainable revenues focused on increasing fee and commission and revenues from services, high efficiency and a low risk profile.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement, covering “Own operations,” general disclosures, due diligence, and the strategy/business model/value chain.
- Metrics and assurance:
  - Some metrics use estimates: E1-5 (energy consumption), E1-8 (share of emissions under internal carbon pricing), S1-14 (work-related accidents), with methodologies referenced in ESRS E1 and ESRS S1 sections.
  - No additional assurance beyond the independent auditors’ assurance on the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Comparative framework:
  - First year reporting under ESRS (replacing GRI); quantitative disclosures cover 2024 only, applying ESRS 1 transitional provisions.
  - No use of incorporation by reference in 2024.
- Due diligence:
  - Group-wide processes identify and manage adverse impacts from own operations and the value chain; embedded in strategy and business model.
  - Table links core due diligence elements (governance, stakeholder engagement, impact identification, action, and tracking) to specific Statement sections across E1/E2/E4/E5/S2/S3/G1.
  - Monitoring: Climate impacts tracking depends on portfolio-level targets (E1). For other downstream impacts, quantitative targets are not yet set, but policies/actions and control tools are in place.
- Strategy:
  - Distinctive, diversified model focused on sustainable fee/service revenues, high efficiency, and low risk, positioning the Group as a wealth management and protection leader in Italy and Europe.
  - Strong integration between product factories (asset management, life/non-life insurance) and commercial networks.
  - People-centric approach: 93,539 employees (71,174 Italy; 22,365 abroad); extensive employee engagement (c. 58,000 contributors to the 2022–2025 Plan).
- 2022–2025 Business Plan pillars:
  - Structural risk reduction (Zero-NPL target, lower cost of risk).
  - Structural cost reduction via technology and operational efficiency (including Isybank digital bank).
  - Growth in fees/commissions through leadership in Wealth Management, Protection and Advisory.
  - Significant ESG commitment: global social impact leadership, climate focus, own-emissions reduction, and support for energy transition.
- ESG priorities and initiatives:
  - Social support (donations/in-kind, education and youth employability, local infrastructure/services, youth social housing, elderly care).
  - Financial inclusion (tailored products for vulnerable groups; social lending for students, working mothers, disaster-affected families, at-risk individuals/small businesses; non-profit sector offerings incl. crowdfunding; local initiatives via international subsidiaries).
  - Cultural commitment (Gallerie d’Italia and Progetto Cultura).
  - Innovation promotion via Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center (ISPIC).
  - Net-Zero acceleration in own operations and portfolios, renewable energy use, participation in Net-Zero alliances, reduction of financed emissions.
  - Customer transition support: sustainable lending (including green mortgages, real estate energy retrofits), circular economy financing (with Ellen MacArthur Foundation), ESG-aligned investments in asset management, dedicated ESG advisory (Fideuram), and ESG insurance solutions; proprietary ESG scoring for customers.
  - Linkage to UN SDGs (details in separate reporting).
- Business model and operations:
  - Core processes: financial resource management; provision of banking/investment/insurance services; multi-channel distribution (branches, online/mobile, ATMs) with strong digitalization; sales/marketing; after-sales care and satisfaction monitoring.
  - Divisions:
    - Banca dei Territori (retail/SMEs/non-profit; includes Isybank; industrial loans, leasing, factoring).
    - IMI Corporate & Investment Banking (commercial/transaction/investment banking, structured finance, capital markets; global network).
    - International Banks Division (commercial banking across CEE, MENA; with SEE and Danube HUBs and listed subsidiaries).
    - Wealth Management Divisions:
      - Private Banking (Fideuram – Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking; 6,814 private bankers).
      - Asset Management (Eurizon).
      - Insurance (Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni and Fideuram Vita).
- Enablers and governance:
  - Company management: policy, strategy, risk management, compliance.
  - Human resources: recruitment, training, welfare, wellbeing, digital skills development.
  - Technology: investment in digital platforms, AI, blockchain, data analytics; accelerated digitalization to improve efficiency and CX.
  - Procurement: acquisition of technology, software, consulting, real estate services to support operations.
- Funding model:
  - Primary sources include customer deposits, short-term wholesale (repos, CDs/CP), medium/long-term market issuances, interbank borrowing, and ECB refinancing operations.

nodes.title: Business model
nodes.heading: 2.2.2 Business model
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s activities contribute to the creation of value for its customers and include the main processes underlying the provision of banking and financial services:
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s business model, highlighting core processes: managing financial resources (liquidity and capital), providing a full suite of banking and investment services (accounts, loans, mortgages, advisory, private banking, portfolio management), distributing services through branches, digital and automated channels with strong digitalization focus, targeted sales/marketing, and robust after-sales customer care and satisfaction monitoring.
- It describes the Group’s six business divisions: Banca dei Territori (Italy retail/SME/non-profit, industrial loans, leasing, factoring, Isybank); IMI Corporate & Investment Banking (global CIB across 24 countries); International Banks (commercial banking in CEE, MENA, and a network including hubs in South-Eastern Europe and the Danube, plus banks in Albania, Hungary, Serbia, Egypt, Ukraine, Moldova); and Wealth Management divisions—Private Banking (Fideuram-Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking, 6,814 private bankers), Asset Management (Eurizon), and Insurance (Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni and Fideuram Vita).
- Governance and enabling areas ensure efficiency and quality: corporate management (policy, planning, risk, compliance), human resources (recruitment, training, welfare, well-being), technology (digital platforms, AI, blockchain, data analytics), and procurement (technology, software, consulting, real estate).
- The funding model combines customer deposits, short-term wholesale (repos, CDs/CP), medium/long-term market issuance, interbank loans, ECB refinancing, and equity. Financial soundness is maintained through liquidity management, interest rate risk control, regulatory capital, and risk tools to balance resources and lending, ensuring resilience in adverse conditions.
- Sector policies and exclusions: the Group does not directly operate in fossil fuel, chemical production, controversial weapons, or tobacco. Stringent internal rules govern ESG-sensitive exposures, including coal and Oil & Gas. Arms-sector rules prohibit any activity related to controversial or treaty-banned weapons and restrict military goods financing/trading to EU/NATO countries, with exceptional approvals required elsewhere; international subsidiaries need Parent Company authorization.
- The value chain is detailed:
  - Upstream (centralized sourcing): ICT (hardware, maintenance, licenses), real estate (leases, maintenance, cleaning), advertising/PR (communications, events, sponsorships), physical security (systems, equipment, services), office equipment and supplies, and insurance (employee benefits, property, liability).
  - Downstream (distribution): a multichannel model combining Italy’s extensive branch network (serving Retail, Business, Corporate, Private), digital branches, internet and mobile banking (including corporate/business remote connectivity), Isybank (fully digital complementary bank for younger/digital clients), an international network supporting local and cross-border needs, and specialized product factories (funds, insurance, pensions) that also distribute via third-party channels.

nodes.title: Value chain
nodes.heading: 2.2.3 Value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The Group's value chain consists of a set of activities carried out as part of interconnected processes, as detailed below.
nodes.summary:
- Financial soundness and funding: Emphasis on the role of own equity instruments in solvency and investor confidence. The Bank manages a sustainable balance between resources raised and lending through liquidity management, interest rate risk control, regulatory capital, and risk management tools.
- Sector exclusions and ESG policies: The Group does not operate directly in fossil fuel, chemicals production, controversial weapons, or tobacco. Strict internal exclusion criteria apply to ESG-sensitive sectors, including coal and Oil&Gas (details in ESRS E1 – Climate change). In armaments, the Group prohibits any banking/lending tied to controversial or treaty-banned weapons and limits activities related to military goods to EU/NATO countries or, outside these, to cases with extraordinary approval linked to intergovernmental programs with Italy.
- Value chain overview:
  - Upstream (procurement): Centralized sourcing for ICT (hardware, maintenance, licenses), real estate (leases, furnishings, maintenance, cleaning), advertising/PR, physical security (systems, equipment, services), office equipment/supplies, and insurance (employee benefits, property, liability).
  - Downstream (distribution): Multi-channel model combining Italy’s branch network, digital branches, Internet/Mobile Banking (including corporate/business remote services), Isybank (fully digital bank), an international network serving multiple markets, product factories (investments, insurance, pensions, also via third parties), and strategic partnerships.
- Customers and markets: Serves retail/households, SMEs, large corporates, institutions, and private banking clients. Customer base includes ~13.7 million in Italy retail/small business, ~7.4 million in international retail, ~19,000 corporate clients in Italy, and ~125,000 private/HNW clients. Footprint: ~3,000 branches in Italy; ~900 branches and 7.5 million customers abroad; corporate support network in 25 countries.
- 2024 performance highlights: Net income €8.7bn; cash dividends €6.1bn (about 40% to Italian households and foundations); €2.0bn share buyback planned for June 2025 (subject to approval) plus €1.7bn completed in Oct 2024; personnel expenses €7.2bn; direct and indirect taxes €5.3bn (+€0.7bn vs 2023); €69.8bn in medium/long-term loans (€43.4bn in Italy); ~144,000 businesses returned to performing since 2014 (3,100 in 2024).
- ESG results and commitments: Continued “Cibo e riparo per i bisognosi” program with €54.1m initiatives in 2022–2024, exceeding plan. Green loans to individuals totaled €9bn in 2022–2024 (€4.1bn in 2024). ESG asset management/insurance products reached ~76.4% penetration of total AuM. Net-Zero targets validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (Jan 27, 2025). Employer recognitions: Top Employer Europe 2025 and Top Employer Italy (fourth year), and #1 in LinkedIn Top Companies 2024 in Italy.
- Double materiality assessment: Conducted per ESRS requirements and EFRAG guidance, including FAQs, with stakeholder engagement. Assesses actual/potential positive and negative impacts on economy, environment, and people (including human rights), and identifies risks/opportunities with or expected to have material financial effects on the Group.

nodes.title: Performance
nodes.heading: 2.2.4 Performance
nodes.start_phrase: Thanks to its strong performance, the Intesa Sanpaolo Group can generate increasing and sustainable value for all its stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Intesa Sanpaolo’s distribution model centered on partnerships and service integration, enabling a full spectrum of financial solutions from simple retail products to complex services for sophisticated clients.
- Outlines customer segments and divisions:
  - Retail customers and households served mainly by Banca dei Territori (approx. 13.7 million) and International Banks Division (about 7.4 million).
  - Corporate customers (companies, financial institutions, public administration) within IMI Corporate & Investment Banking (19,000 in Italy).
  - Private banking for high-net-worth individuals via the Private Banking Division (approx. 125,000 clients).
- Details geographic footprint:
  - Strong domestic presence in Italy with about 3,000 branches.
  - International presence with roughly 900 branches and 7.5 million customers across 12 CEE and MENA countries, plus a corporate support network in 25 countries focused on regions of strong Italian business activity.
- Presents 2024 performance and stakeholder value creation:
  - Net income: 8.7 billion euro.
  - Shareholder returns: 6.1 billion euro in cash dividends (around 40% to Italian households and foundations), a 2 billion euro share buyback planned for June 2025, and a 1.7 billion euro buyback completed in October 2024.

- Highlights ESG progress aligned with the 2022–2025 Business Plan:

nodes.title: Double materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 2.3 Double materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: For the purposes of this Consolidated Sustainability Statement, the Group has preliminarily conducted an assessment of the main material sustainability matters (the “double materiality assessment”), considering the impacts (positive and negative, actual or potential) of its operations on the economy, the environment and people.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of distribution model: Intesa Sanpaolo leverages partnerships and service integration to broaden its distribution model and offer a full spectrum of financial solutions—from basic retail products to sophisticated services for advanced clients—serving retail customers/households, SMEs, large corporates, and institutions.

  - Private banking: around 125,000 high-net-worth clients with customized services.

- Geographic footprint: Strong presence in Italy (~3,000 branches); strategic international footprint with ~900 branches and 7.5 million customers across 12 CEE/MENA countries; specialized corporate support network in 25 countries, notably in MENA and markets with strong Italian business activity.

- 2024 performance highlights and stakeholder value:
  - Net income: €8.7bn; cash dividends: €6.1bn (about 40% to Italian households and foundations).
  - Share buybacks: €2bn planned for June 2025; €1.7bn completed in October 2024.
  - Personnel expenses: €7.2bn.
  - Taxes: €5.3bn paid to the public sector (+€0.7bn vs 2023).
  - Credit to the economy: €69.8bn in medium/long-term loans (€43.4bn in Italy).
  - Business support: ~144,000 businesses returned to performing status since 2014 (3,100 in 2024).

- ESG progress aligned with the 2022–2025 Plan:
  - Social inclusion: “Food and shelter for the needy” program with €54.1m in initiatives (2022–2024), exceeding plan targets.
  - Green transition: €9bn in new green loans to individuals (2022–2024), including €4.1bn in 2024.
