nodes.title: Double materiality assessment - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.3 Double materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: For the purposes of this Consolidated Sustainability Statement, the Group has preliminarily conducted an assessment of the main material sustainability matters (the “double materiality assessment”), considering the impacts (positive and negative, actual or potential) of its operations on the economy, the environment and people.
nodes.summary: Introduces the Group’s 2024 double materiality assessment for the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, outlining methodology and rationale: evaluation of positive and negative, actual and potential impacts of operations on the economy, environment, people, and human rights; identification of risks and opportunities with material financial effects; alignment with ESRS regulatory requirements, EFRAG’s IG 1 Materiality Assessment Implementation Guidance, and regulator FAQs; and execution within the Group’s business context through active stakeholder dialogue.

nodes.title: Methodology and rationales
nodes.heading: 2.3.1 Methodology and rationales
nodes.start_phrase: Compared to the 2023 report, which was prepared in accordance with the GRI Standards – Universal Standards (2021), in 2024, the Group’s double materiality assessment complied with the ESRS which introduce the concept of materiality and consider the impact of the Group’s operations (impact materiality) on internal and external stakeholders and the external risks and opportunities which have or may have material financial implications on the Group (financial materiality).
nodes.summary:
- Distribution model and partnerships: Intesa Sanpaolo leverages strategic partnerships to broaden product breadth, delivering solutions from basic retail services to complex offerings for sophisticated clients and integrating services across channels.
- Customer segments and scale: Clear delineation of retail (approx. 13.7m in Banca dei Territori, 7.4m in International Banks), corporate (about 19k clients in Italy within IMI CIB), and private/HNW (approx. 125k clients in the Private Banking Division).
- Geographic footprint: Strong domestic presence with ~3,000 branches in Italy; strategic international network with ~900 branches and 7.5m customers across 12 CEE/MENA countries; corporate support network in 25 countries, notably in MENA and markets active for Italian businesses.
- 2024 performance highlights: Net income of €8.7bn; cash dividends of €6.1bn (with significant flow to Italian households and foundations); a completed €1.7bn buyback in 2024 and an additional €2bn buyback planned for 2025 (subject to approval); personnel expenses of €7.2bn; €5.3bn in direct and indirect taxes (+€0.7bn vs 2023); €69.8bn in medium/long-term loans (€43.4bn in Italy); cumulative 144,000 businesses restored to performing status since 2014 (3,100 in 2024).
- ESG progress vs 2022–2025 Plan: Food and shelter program delivering €54.1m in initiatives (2022–2024), exceeding targets; €9bn of green loans to individuals since 2022 (€4.1bn in 2024); enhanced ESG product penetration at ~76.4% of AuM (Eurizon Article 8/9); Net-Zero targets validated by SBTi (Jan 2025); employer recognitions (Top Employer Europe 2025 and Italy) and #1 in LinkedIn Top Companies 2024 Italy.
- Double materiality assessment (ESRS-aligned): Methodology covers impact materiality (inside-out impacts across own operations and value chain, including human rights) and financial materiality (outside-in risks/opportunities with potential financial effects); identification and assessment of material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs).
- Assessment process: Stakeholder mapping and engagement; context analysis of positive/negative, actual/potential impacts; identification of IROs; internal ESRS-metric-based analysis with materiality thresholds aligned to risk management; aggregation of internal results and stakeholder input to derive material topics; consolidation and annual update of the process, responsive to regulatory changes.
- Contextualization: Assessment tailored to business lines, geographies, and counterparties/suppliers relevant to the Group’s activities.
- Stakeholder universe mapped: People (employees, unions), customers (including financially vulnerable individuals, SMEs, corporates, startups, consumer groups), shareholders/investors (small, foundations, institutional, sustainable), suppliers/partners (large/small, subcontractors), community and institutions (non-profits, trade associations, public bodies, regulators, media), and environmental stakeholders (environmental groups, scientific community, future generations).

nodes.title: Group’s stakeholder mapping
nodes.heading: 2.3.2 Group’s stakeholder mapping
nodes.start_phrase: Stakeholder engagement activities are carried out as part of the double materiality assessment.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the 2024 transition to an ESRS-compliant double materiality assessment from the 2023 GRI-based approach, defining impact (inside-out) and financial (outside-in) materiality and using them to identify and assess impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs).
- States that results drive both sustainability reporting and corporate strategy, with the process tailored to business lines, geographies, and types of suppliers/counterparties, and updated annually.
- Outlines the assessment macro-stages: stakeholder mapping; context analysis; IRO identification; IRO assessment via ESRS-aligned internal metrics and risk thresholds plus stakeholder engagement; aggregation into material sustainability matters; consolidation and sharing.
- Presents a comprehensive stakeholder map: People (employees, unions), Customers (retail incl. vulnerable households, SMEs, corporates, start-ups, consumer orgs), Shareholders/Investors (incl. SRI), Suppliers (large/small, partners, subcontractors), Environment (groups, future generations, scientific community), Community (NGOs/associations, regulators, public institutions, media).
- Describes engagement approach aligned with EFRAG guidance: leverage internal relationship owners for stakeholder management and conduct direct engagement (workshops, interviews, questionnaires).
- Details listening methods and key themes by stakeholder group:
  - Customers: environmental footprint reduction; responsible governance and value sharing; climate and circular-economy offerings; compliance and fairness; inclusive lending/social-impact products; service quality and satisfaction; digital innovation/multichannel; cybersecurity; sustainable investments/insurance; talent and skills; community and cultural support.
  - Environment/Community experts: climate change and biodiversity; evolving regulation (e.g., CSDR, ESRS) and organizational impacts; contribution to SDGs; ESG leadership and transparent communication; enablers/challenges for Business Plan (ESG focus); diversity and inclusion; innovation and customer needs; SME support; sustainability education for youth.
  - Shareholders/SRI investors: climate adaptation, biodiversity, natural resources, decarbonization; sustainable finance/investments; standard ESG policies; inclusion and diversity; employee well-being; development and digitalization; ESG integration in strategy; gender pay gap; workers’ rights and governance.
  - People (employees): customer-perceived image; employment protection in restructuring; youth recruitment; recognition, pride, merit, autonomy, pay; talent development/retention; training and growth; well-being and work-life balance; job satisfaction; performance assessment transparency; awareness of D&I policies; customer satisfaction drivers; ESG initiatives/products. Survey reached over 72,000 people.
  - Trade unions: employment protection amid digitalization; community support; financial inclusion; non-financial reporting; environmental issues and biodiversity; renewables and sustainable mobility for employees; youth unemployment in Southern regions; gender pay gap.
  - Suppliers: environmental topics, biodiversity, circular economy; labor protection, health and safety, diversity & inclusion, well-being across the supply chain; supplier relationship management.
- Notes compliance with Legislative Decree 125/2024: employee representatives engaged in the assessment and involved in Board approval of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Summarizes the context analysis informing IRO mapping, drawing on updated 2024 external sources: ESG indices (DJSI, Morningstar ESG, Euronext ESG, CDP 2023); global standards/reports (WEF Global Risks, OECD Guidelines, BSR, WBCSD, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights); EU regulations and directives referenced by ESRS (CSDDD 2024/1760, SFDR, CRR Pillar 3, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law); and sector-specific materials (SASB Materiality Map, S&P and Fitch research, OECD guidance for institutional investors).

nodes.title: Context analysis
nodes.heading: 2.3.3 Context analysis
nodes.start_phrase: In order to map IROs, the Group analysed the context in which it defines and implements its business activities and relationships.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of stakeholder engagement and key sustainability topics raised across shareholders/investors, employees, trade unions, and suppliers.
- Shareholders/ESG investors’ priorities: climate adaptation, biodiversity, natural resources, decarbonisation; sustainable finance; standard sustainability policies; diversity and inclusion; employee well-being; digitalisation; ESG integration in strategy; gender pay gap; workers’ rights and corporate governance.
- Employees (Italy and abroad) engagement via interviews and a large-scale survey (>72,000 people) on: customer perception of the Group, employment safeguards during restructuring, youth recruitment, recognition and compensation, talent development/retention, training and growth opportunities, well-being and work-life balance, job satisfaction, transparency of performance assessments, awareness of Group policies (e.g., D&I), customer satisfaction drivers, and ESG initiatives/products.
- Trade unions’ focus: employment protection amid digitalisation, community support, financial inclusion, non-financial reporting, environmental issues and biodiversity, ecological transition (renewables and sustainable mobility), youth unemployment in Southern regions, and gender pay gap.
- Suppliers’ concerns: environmental topics, biodiversity and circular economy; job protection, health and safety, D&I and well-being across the supply chain; and supplier relationship management.
- Compliance and governance: engagement of employee representatives under Legislative Decree 125/2024 in the double materiality assessment and their subsequent involvement in Board approval of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Context analysis underpinning IRO mapping draws on 2024-updated external standards and benchmarks (e.g., DJSI, Morningstar ESG, Euronext ESG, CDP, WEF Global Risks, OECD Guidelines, UNGPs, CSDDD/EU Directive 2024/1760, SFDR, CRR “Pillar 3”, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law), sector frameworks (SASB, S&P, Fitch, OECD guidance for institutional investors, MSCI ESG Materiality Map, GRI Sector Standards, Bank of Italy/ECB supervisory expectations, TCFD, PRB, IFRS), internal documents (Business Plan 2022–2025, Code of Ethics, prior Non-financial Statements, Financial Statements, governance communications), benchmarking peers, and stakeholder feedback.
- Double materiality scope covers own operations and the full upstream and downstream value chain.
- Identification of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) aligned to ESRS, considering how the Group’s operating model and strategic decisions create impacts and related financial effects.
- Illustrative IROs: ESG-weak exposures increasing credit/market risk via concentration; ESG programmes, donations and controls enhancing reputation and stakeholder trust; ESG criteria and strategies enabling product range expansion in line with sustainability goals.
- Materiality assessment methodology: formalised internally; combines internal analysis, interviews with operating structures, and stakeholder input; conducted simultaneously for impact and financial materiality.
- Impact materiality metrics and scoring: scale (severity), scope (breadth), irremediable character, and likelihood (for potential impacts), with scores assigned and averaged against pre-set thresholds.
- Tailored assessment for the value chain, identifying sectors most exposed to adverse impacts for each sustainability topic.
- Calculation rules: positive actual impacts = average of scale and scope; negative actual impacts = average of scale, scope, and irremediable character; potential impacts multiply likelihood by the relevant average (positive: scale+scope; negative: scale+scope+irremediable).

nodes.title: Identification of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 2.3.4 Identification of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The analyses conducted identified and assessed, for each ESRS, the Group's possible IROs, applied to own operations and the value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement detailing the Group’s approach to double materiality in line with ESRS.
- Sources used for the assessment:
  - External frameworks and expectations: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, MSCI ESG Industry Materiality Map, GRI Sector Standards, Bank of Italy and ECB supervisory expectations, TCFD recommendations (especially Climate-Related Risks, Opportunities, and Financial Impacts), Principles for Responsible Banking, and IFRS for sustainability reporting.
  - Internal sources: 2022–2025 Business Plan, Code of Ethics, prior three years’ Consolidated Non-financial Statements, Financial Statements, top management communications, Shareholders’ Meeting minutes, and company policies.
  - Sector benchmarking of Italian and international financial groups and stakeholder engagement feedback.
- Scope: Assessment covers own operations plus upstream and downstream value chain.
- IRO identification: For each ESRS topic, potential impacts, risks, and opportunities are identified across operations and the value chain; impact and financial materiality are assessed concurrently.
- Link between impacts and risks/opportunities:
  - Negative examples: Financing/investing in weak ESG sectors/countries may increase credit/market risks due to concentration in high-risk geographies or activities.
  - Positive examples: ESG initiatives, donations, programs, and controls can enhance brand and stakeholder trust; integrating ESG criteria into financing/investment can expand product offerings aligned with sustainability goals.
- Governance and methodology:
  - Materiality assessment aligned with ESRS metrics, validated via interviews with internal functions and stakeholder processes.
  - Methodology formalized in internal regulations.
- Impact assessment metrics and scoring:
  - Metrics: scale (severity), scope (reach), irremediable character (ability to remediate), and likelihood (for potential impacts, across time horizons).
  - Each impact receives a score; downstream analysis identifies counterparties/sectors most exposed to adverse impacts by sustainability issue.
- Materiality determination:
  - Materiality is defined by exceeding a threshold based on averaged metric scores.
  - Positive actual impacts: average of scale and scope.
  - Negative actual impacts: average of scale, scope, and irremediable character.
  - Potential positive impacts: likelihood multiplied by average of scale and scope.
  - Potential negative impacts: likelihood multiplied by average of scale, scope, and irremediable character.

nodes.title: Assessment of the materiality of IROs
nodes.heading: 2.3.5 Assessment of the materiality of IROs
nodes.start_phrase: The materiality of IROs was assessed by conducting an internal analysis based on metrics aligned with the ESRS requirements, discussed and consolidated through interviews with the Group's internal operating structures and, as described earlier, through a stakeholder management process.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: This section of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement explains the Group’s double materiality assessment under CSRD/ESRS, covering how it identifies, evaluates, prioritizes, and governs sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across own operations and the full value chain (upstream and downstream).

- Reference frameworks and inputs: The assessment integrates external standards and expectations (OECD Guidelines, MSCI ESG Materiality Map, GRI Sector Standards, Bank of Italy/ECB supervisory expectations, TCFD, Principles for Responsible Banking, IFRS for sustainability reporting, EFRAG IG 1) with internal sources (2022–2025 Business Plan, Code of Ethics, prior Non-financial Statements, Financial Statements, top management communications, Shareholders’ Meeting minutes, policies), peer benchmarking, and stakeholder engagement.

- Scope and identification of IROs: IROs are mapped for each ESRS topic across own operations and value chain. Impacts derive from the business model and strategy; risks/opportunities arise from those impacts, dependencies, and sustainability issues. Examples include:
  - Credit/market risks from exposure to sectors/countries with weak ESG profiles.
  - Reputation and trust benefits from ESG initiatives, donations, programs, and controls.
  - Product and customer expansion through ESG-aligned financing/investment criteria.

- Impact materiality methodology: Impacts are scored using ESRS-aligned metrics—scale, scope, irremediable character, and likelihood (for potential impacts)—with thresholds based on average scores. Potential positive/negative impacts incorporate likelihood in the materiality calculation. For potential human rights–related negative impacts, impact severity outweighs likelihood as required by ESRS. Downstream analysis reflects portfolio exposure by sector/country. Time horizons (short: 1 year; medium: up to 5 years; long: >5 years) are considered.

- Financial materiality methodology: Assessed in parallel with impact materiality and linked where relevant. Quantitative assessments leverage existing risk data/processes (e.g., ICAAP, stress scenarios, projections, prudential risk frameworks), inherent risk (pre-mitigation) exposures by sector/country and financial asset class, and potential operating losses/penalties tied to sustainability issues. Opportunities are aligned with budget and Business Plan targets for ESG products. Financial risk/opportunity metrics include magnitude, likelihood, and time horizon.

- Qualitative assessment: Complements quantitative work using internal policies, strategies, and initiatives, notably the 2022–2025 Business Plan.

- Governance and decision-making: The IRO map is consolidated via internal structures, validated through stakeholder management processes, and discussed with the Steering Committee and the Risks and Sustainability Committee, which support the Board of Directors’ approval.

- Material topics outcome: All ESRS macro-topics are deemed material except Water and Marine Resources. Not all sub-topics and sub-sub-topics are material. The section highlights materiality outcomes and boundaries for:
  - E1 Climate Change (mitigation, adaptation, energy),
  - E2 Pollution (air, soil, microplastics),
  - E4 Biodiversity and Ecosystems (direct drivers of biodiversity loss),
  - E5 Circular Economy (resource inflows/use, resource outflows in products/services, waste),
  across own operations, upstream, and downstream, with both impact and financial materiality considered.

nodes.title: Consolidating and sharing the list of sustainability matters material for the Group
nodes.heading: 2.3.6 Consolidating and sharing the list of sustainability matters material for the Group
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has a structured decision -making process designed to consolidate and verify material impacts, risks and opportunities.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines Intesa Sanpaolo’s approach to sustainability materiality and governance. It defines scenario time horizons for risk and planning (short: 1 year, medium: up to 5 years, long: over 5 years) and describes a structured process to identify, review, and consolidate impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) through a double materiality assessment aligned with CSRD/ESRS. All ESRS macro-topics are deemed material except Water and Marine Resources, though not every sub-topic/sub-sub-topic is material; materiality is mapped across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains for environmental (climate, energy, pollution, biodiversity, circular economy), social (own workforce, value chain workers, affected communities, consumers/end-users), and governance (business conduct, whistleblowing, lobbying, supplier practices, compliance/training) areas. The results were reviewed by internal functions, discussed with the Steering Committee and the Risks and Sustainability Committee, and support Board approval. The analysis confirms the resilience of the Group’s strategy and business model, with actions planned to mitigate ESG risks and capture opportunities over the long term. The governance section details the one-tier model with a Board of Directors and a Management Control Committee, roles of the Chair (non-executive) and the Managing Director/CEO, and four internal Board committees (Nomination, Remuneration, Risks and Sustainability, Related Parties). The Board has 19 directors (18 non-executive, 1 executive), appointed in April 2022 for three years, meeting suitability and independence requirements.

nodes.title: Governance structure
nodes.heading: 2.4 Governance structure
nodes.start_phrase: The Parent Company Intesa Sanpaolo has adopted the “one -tier” management and control model, whereby management and control duties are performed, respectively, by the Board of Directors and the Management Control Committee set up within it, both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: The Consolidated Sustainability Statement outlines the Group’s analysis of impacts, risks and opportunities informing its materiality assessment, confirming the resilience of Intesa Sanpaolo’s strategy and business model. ESG-related negative impacts are being managed through current and planned actions to mitigate risks, capture opportunities and support long‑term sustainability.

- Governance model: Intesa Sanpaolo adopts a one-tier system with management by the Board of Directors and control by the Management Control Committee within the Board, both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting. Detailed governance and remuneration information is available in dedicated reports on the Bank’s website.

- Board roles and responsibilities: 
  - The Board provides strategic guidance and supervision, deciding on significant corporate actions and transactions, with certain major decisions subject to shareholder approval.
  - The Chair is non-executive, oversees and organizes Board work, and does not perform management functions.
  - The Managing Director and CEO, also General Manager, oversees company management within powers aligned to the Board’s strategic guidelines.

- Control and advisory bodies:
  - Management Control Committee: five independent Directors, performing control functions and acting as the internal control and audit committee (Legislative Decree 39/2010).
  - Board committees: Nomination; Remuneration; Risks and Sustainability; Transactions with Related Parties.

- Board composition and suitability: As of 29 April 2022, the Board has 19 members (18 non-executive, 1 executive) appointed for a three-year term. Directors meet legal and bylaw suitability requirements, including independence of mind under banking rules.

- Business conduct materiality focus (G1): The Statement frames impacts, risks and financial/materiality outcomes across the value chain (own operations, upstream, downstream) for subtopics including:
  - Protection of whistleblowers
  - Political engagement and lobbying activities
  - Management of supplier relationships, including payment practices
  - Prevention and detection (e.g., training) and incident management

nodes.title: Role and composition of the administration, management and control bodies and of sustainability governance
nodes.heading: 2.4.1 Role and composition of the administration, management and control bodies and of sustainability governance
nodes.start_phrase: The Parent Company Intesa Sanpaolo has adopted the “one -tier” management and control model, whereby management and control duties are performed, respectively, by the Board of Directors and the Management Control Committee set up within it, both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting.
nodes.summary:
- The chapter introduces the impacts, risks and opportunities identified through analysis that informed the materiality assessment, confirming the resilience of the Group’s strategy and business model. It notes that potential negative ESG impacts are being managed through existing and planned actions aimed at risk mitigation, opportunity capture and long‑term sustainability.
- Governance structure: Intesa Sanpaolo adopts a one‑tier model in which the Board of Directors (management) and the Management Control Committee within it (control), both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting, perform oversight and control functions.
- Board of Directors: responsible for strategic guidance and major corporate decisions (ordinary and extraordinary), with certain significant matters submitted to the Shareholders’ Meeting. The Chair is non‑executive and oversees Board work without managerial functions. The Managing Director and CEO, also the General Manager, supervises management in line with Board directives.
- Management Control Committee: composed of five independent directors; performs control functions and acts as the internal control and audit committee pursuant to Legislative Decree 39/2010.
- Board committees: Nomination Committee; Remuneration Committee; Risks and Sustainability Committee; Committee for Transactions with Related Parties.
- Board composition: as of 29 April 2022, 19 directors elected for a three‑year term; 18 non‑executive and 1 executive (the MD/CEO). Directors meet suitability requirements, including independence of mind; further details on governance, diversity and remuneration are available in the Bank’s published reports.
- Governance materiality focus (G1 Business conduct): coverage of subtopics such as corporate culture, protection of whistleblowers, political engagement and lobbying, management of supplier relationships and payment practices, and prevention/detection including training and incidents. The content references assessment of positive/negative impacts and financial and impact materiality across own operations, upstream and downstream value chains.

nodes.title: Board of Directors: role and main characteristics
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.1 Board of Directors: role and main characteristics

nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines how identified impacts, risks and opportunities informed the materiality assessment, confirming the Group’s strategic and business-model resilience and the management of ESG risks through current and planned actions to mitigate risks, seize opportunities and support long-term sustainability.

nodes.title: Composition of the Board of Directors
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.2 Composition of the Board of Directors
nodes.start_phrase: The Ordinary Shareholders' Meeting of 29 April 2022 set the number of members of the Board of Directors at 19, appointing directors for the three -year term of office on the basis of the lists submitted by shareholders.
nodes.summary:
- Confirms the Group’s ESG materiality assessment, outlining key impacts, risks and opportunities; states the strategy and business model are resilient, with actions in place to mitigate ESG risks and capture opportunities.
- Describes the governance structure: a one-tier model with a Board of Directors and a Management Control Committee appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting; Chair is non-executive; the Managing Director/CEO is also General Manager and manages within the Board’s strategic guidelines.
- Lists Board committees and their roles/composition: Nomination, Remuneration, Risks and Sustainability, and Transactions with Related Parties; all have five non-executive members, majority independent, and are chaired by independent Directors; the Related Parties Committee is entirely independent.
- Details Board composition and independence: 19 Directors (18 non-executive, 1 executive); all meet suitability and independence of mind; 14 independent (74%); minority shareholders hold 5 seats (26%) and are represented across committees; no employee representatives; no recent similar roles in public administration among Directors.
- Highlights diversity and competence policies: commitment to diversity in experience, age, gender, and international orientation; legal gender quota (≥40%) met with 8 women (42%); strong female presence on committees (e.g., 80% on Related Parties Committee) and chairing of Risks & Sustainability and Nomination Committees; Board assesses its composition as adequate.
- Outlines Group-wide approach to appointing senior officers of subsidiaries, ensuring diverse, fit-for-purpose profiles aligned with each subsidiary’s activities and risks, informed by annual self-assessments.
- Notes professional qualifications: at least four Directors must be registered statutory auditors; currently 9 Directors (47%), including all Management Control Committee members, meet this.
- Presents the Board’s Skills Directory (2022–2024) and prevalence of key competencies among Directors: financial/ non-financial reporting literacy (95%), strategy (95%), governance (95%), financial markets (100%), banking products (89%), regulation (84%), internal controls (74%), risk management (79%), and information/digital technology (16%).
- Introduces Governance Topic G1: Business conduct, with sub-topics including whistleblower protection, political engagement and lobbying, supplier relationship and payment practices, and prevention/detection with training and incident management; considers impact and financial materiality across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains.

nodes.title: Competences and diversity
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.3 Competences and diversity
nodes.start_phrase: According to Intesa Sanpaolo's Articles of Association, the Board shall adopt the necessary measures to ensure that each Director, and the Board as a whole, have a continually adequate level of diversification,
nodes.summary:
- Governance structure and independence: The Board of Directors meets and exceeds independence requirements (14 independent directors, 74%). All committees consist of five non-executive members; most have a majority of independents, and the Related Parties Committee is entirely independent. All committees are chaired by independent directors.
- Minority representation: Minority shareholders hold 5 board seats (26%) and are present in all committees; they chair the Management Control Committee and the Related Parties Committee. No employee representatives sit on the Board. No director held comparable public administration roles in the two years prior to appointment.
- Diversity and composition: The Board pursues diversified composition in experience, age, gender, and international outlook. Shareholders were guided in 2022 to ensure broad gender and age diversity and comprehensive skills. Legal gender quota (at least two-fifths) is met: 8 women (42%) on the Board; strong female presence in committees and female chairs for the Risks and Sustainability Committee and the Nomination Committee. The Board deems its composition and committee balance adequate.
- Group-wide appointments: Senior officers of subsidiaries are appointed following uniform Group policies emphasizing diversity (age, gender, seniority, geography, international orientation) and alignment to each entity’s business and risk profile, informed by subsidiaries’ annual self-assessments.
- Professional qualifications: At least four directors must be registered statutory auditors with relevant experience; currently 9 directors (47%), including all members of the Management Control Committee, meet this criterion.
- Skills and expertise: A 2022–2024 “Skills Directory” defines the optimal competencies. High levels of very good/distinctive expertise are reported in financial statement analysis and strategic planning (95%), financial markets (100%), banking products (89%), regulations (84%), internal controls (74%), risk management (79%), banking business and sector strategies (95%), and socio-economic/market knowledge of operating geographies (74%). Only 16% report very strong IT/digital expertise. ESG knowledge is strong: 84% report very good/distinctive expertise and integration into strategy.
- External engagements: Several directors serve on boards of universities, foundations, and non-profits across culture, health, environment, poverty, circular economy, and nutrition. The chair of the Risks and Sustainability Committee also chairs the same committee in another listed company.
- Ongoing assessment and renewal: Following the 2022 renewal, the Board confirmed the adequacy and balance of its composition. Guidelines for the optimal qualitative-quantitative composition ahead of the April 2025 renewal are available on the Group website.
- Induction and training: Comprehensive onboarding and ongoing training are overseen by the Nomination Committee, tailored by initial and annual self-assessments, with options for individual requests. In 2024, 11 induction sessions covered ESG topics, risk data aggregation/reporting, Basel IV changes, new EBA AML Guidelines, and Digital Finance/MiCA. The Board rated the program very positively.
- Information access and oversight: Directors have a regularly updated electronic repository of governance documents, regulatory references, supervisory correspondence, and accounting positions. Corporate control functions provide periodic reports on activities, findings, and remediation proposals, including anti-corruption and AML matters.
- Next section header: Introduction to the allocation of ESG responsibilities across Intesa Sanpaolo’s bodies and structures (“Sustainability governance”).

nodes.title: Board induction
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.4 Board induction
nodes.start_phrase: The skills and expertise were subsequently strengthened and supplemented on the basis of training programmes as well as of intensive induction activities for both the new directors (onboarding) and the entire Board.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Board composition, expertise, and governance in Intesa Sanpaolo’s sustainability context.
- Directors’ competencies: 95% with strong banking and risk-management knowledge; 74% with knowledge of socio-economic/market dynamics; 84% declaring very good/distinctive ESG expertise and integration into strategy.
- Directors’ external roles include boards of major universities and non-profits (art, culture, health, environment, poverty, circular economy, nutrition); one director chairs the Risks and Sustainability Committee and holds the same role in another listed company.
- Post-2022 renewal assessment confirms diverse, well-balanced Board and Committees; guidelines for the optimal qualitative-quantitative Board composition ahead of April 2025 renewal are available on the Group website.
- Board induction and training: structured onboarding and ongoing programs led by the Chair with Nomination Committee support; content covers business areas, Group dynamics, risk management, regulatory/self-regulatory frameworks, and strategic topics; individualized training available.
- Annual Board self-assessment evaluates and refines induction quality and effectiveness.
- In 2024, 11 induction sessions addressed ESG, risk data aggregation/reporting, Basel IV changes, new EBA AML Guidelines, and Digital Finance/MiCA; feedback was extremely positive on scope, depth, and relevance.
- Board members have access to a regularly updated digital repository of governance documents, regulatory references, supervisory correspondence, and accounting positions.
- Corporate control functions provide periodic reports on checks, results, weaknesses, and remediation actions, including anti-corruption and AML coverage.
- Lead-in to sustainability governance section outlining ESG responsibilities of corporate bodies and structures per Articles of Association and internal regulations.

nodes.title: Sustainability governance
nodes.heading: 2.4.2 Sustainability governance
nodes.start_phrase: The main ESG responsibilities of Intesa Sanpaolo Bodies and Structures are specified below in line with the Articles of Association, the Bodies’ regulations and the Group’s internal regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Board composition and expertise
  - Directors possess strong banking, risk, and market knowledge; high self-declared ESG expertise (84% with very good/distinctive sustainability competence).
  - Many directors hold roles in universities, foundations, and non-profits; one director also chairs a Risks & Sustainability Committee in another listed company.
  - 2022 renewal confirmed diversified and adequate composition; guidelines for optimal qualitative-quantitative board composition ahead of April 2025 renewal are available.

- Induction and training
  - Ongoing onboarding and training plans defined after appointment and via annual self-assessment; directors can request tailored training.
  - In 2024, 11 induction sessions covered ESG topics, risk data aggregation/reporting, Basel IV changes, new EBA AML Guidelines, and Digital Finance/MiCA; feedback was highly positive.
  - Directors access updated governance and regulatory documents via a dedicated platform; control functions provide periodic reports, including on anti-corruption and AML.

- ESG governance roles and responsibilities
  - Board of Directors (supported by the Risks & Sustainability Committee) sets ESG strategies/policies, integrates ESG risks into the Risk Appetite Framework (RAF), approves materiality analysis and the Consolidated Sustainability Statement (CSS), and updates the Code of Ethics and DE&I policy. In 2024, 21 meetings (16 with ESG matters).
  - Risks & Sustainability Committee supports all ESG oversight, approves ESG-sensitive sector lists, oversees materiality for CSS, benchmarks against best practices/indices; 47 meetings in 2024 (23 with ESG), monitored CSS preparation, ESG KPIs for Budget 2024, NZBA sector targets, and climate risk processes.
  - Management Control Committee supervises Code of Ethics compliance; examines CSS under Legislative Decree 125/2024 before Board review; fulfills Control and Audit Committee duties (Legislative Decree 30/2019).
  - Managing Director and CEO governs sustainability performance, proposes ESG decisions, ensures risk process consistency, and jointly certifies financial and sustainability information.

- Internal governance structures for ESG
  - Steering Committee (Business Plan & ESG session) co-defines ESG strategy/policies, identifies material topics, pre-reviews CSS, and aligns tech development with ethical principles (AI/ML); met 26 times in 2024; reports quarterly to the Board.
  - Group Control Coordination and Non-Financial Risks Committee (Operational & Reputational Risk session), chaired by CRO, examines ESG risk profiles; reports quarterly to the Board.
  - CFO area prepares the CSS, tracks evolving regulation, and sets methodology.
  - Chief Sustainability Officer (CSO) area (established April 2024) drives ESG strategy, supports reporting and culture, fosters community development and innovation (startups, circular economy, ecosystems), and promotes heritage assets. Includes the Chief Social Impact Officer (CSIO) for social impact and direct environmental footprint mitigation.
  - ESG Control Room (strengthened in 2024) advises on ESG strategy, policies, KPIs/targets, voluntary commitments, reporting, integration into investments/credit, regulatory monitoring, and regulator requests. It reports to the Steering Committee and operates through:
    - ESG Coordination Panel (shares/monitors ESG goals across areas/divisions),
    - Sustainable Investments & Insurance Panel (oversees Wealth Management ESG initiatives),
    - Social Impact Panel (from 2025).
    - Sustainability Managers in each area/division monitor ESG topics, including subsidiaries.
  - CRO area develops the ESG risk framework, proposes RAF tolerances/limits/indicators for ESG and reputational risk, leads climate risk management, and issues the “Tableau de Bord of Risks” including ESG/reputational risk monitoring.

- ESG impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) in strategy and risk management
  - In 2024, the Board approved new sector targets supporting climate transition, new tools for community support, and key internal policies (RAF, reputational risk governance, conduct principles, DE&I).
  - Regular Board and Committee discussions on material IROs: reputational risk governance, climate/environmental risks, NZBA-aligned indirect GHG reduction targets, culture and social/environmental responsibility, DE&I, worker health and safety, community support and local development.
  - Ongoing KPI monitoring of ESG performance and Business Plan targets, reviewed by the Risks & Sustainability Committee.

- Incentive systems linked to sustainability
  - The CEO, as the sole executive director, is the only beneficiary of the annual Incentive System and the Long-Term Performance Share Plan; both integrate ESG metrics.
  - Annual Incentive System: scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs across Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; includes a cross-Group ESG KPI; weighted, deterministic payout with gateways, malus, and clawback; partly cash and partly shares with 5-year deferral.
  - Long-Term Incentive Plan: share-based, tied to Business Plan targets (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR) with de-multipliers for Composite ESG KPI and CET1 capital target; gateways, deferral (60% over five years), retention, malus, and clawback apply.
  - A cross-Group ESG KPI is also assigned to about 3,000 managers (10–15% weight).

nodes.title: Incentive systems linked to sustainability factors
nodes.heading: 2.4.3 Incentive systems linked to sustainability factors
nodes.start_phrase: The Managing Director and CEO is the only executive member of the Board of Directors and, therefore, is the only beneficiary of an annual Incentive System and a long -term Incentive Plan for the role of General Manager.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and oversight of ESG commitments:
  - Setting targets for reducing indirect greenhouse gas emissions aligned with private initiatives (e.g., Net Zero Banking Alliance).
  - Promoting corporate culture and social/environmental responsibility, diversity, equity and inclusion, worker health and safety, and community support/local development.
  - Monitoring Group ESG performance and main sustainability KPIs, with results and target progress assessed by the Risks and Sustainability Committee in Q1.

- Incentive systems linked to sustainability:
  - The Managing Director and CEO, as the sole executive director, is the only Board member with an annual Incentive System and a Long-Term Incentive Plan, both embedding sustainability metrics.

- Annual Incentive System:
  - Performance Scorecard combining financial and non-financial KPIs grouped under Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; qualitative strategic actions support Plan objectives.
  - A transversal ESG KPI assigned in 2024; each KPI carries a 10%–30% weight; annual accrual; deterministic calculation based on results.
  - Payout partly in cash and partly in shares; five-year deferral with ex-post malus; claw-back possible for five years post-payment.
  - Subject to gateway conditions, absence of compliance breaches, and corrective mechanisms.

- Long-Term Incentive Plan (PSP):
  - Granted to the CEO and ~3,100 managers; share awards tied to Business Plan targets: PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, and relative TSR.
  - De-multipliers: Composite ESG KPI (10%–20% reduction if 2022–2025 ESG targets missed) and Capital target (CET1 above RAF; 10% reduction per breach year, up to 40%).
  - 60% of any bonus deferred over five years; 60%–55% delivered in shares subject to retention; malus and claw-back apply; gateway and compliance checks required.

- Centrality of ESG in CEO pay:
  - ESG KPI included in the annual plan since 2021 (evolving from a prior Diversity & Inclusion KPI) and an ESG composite KPI acts as a de-multiplier in the PSP.
  - A cross-Group ESG KPI is also assigned to about 3,000 managers (weight 10% or 15%).
  - Additional details referenced in the Group’s remuneration policy and compensation report.
