nodes.title: Structure of the annual incentive system
nodes.heading: 2.4.3.1 Structure of the annual incentive system
nodes.start_phrase: The annual Incentive System49 is formalised through a Performance Scorecard with both financial and non -financial KPIs.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on governance and targets for ESG performance across the Group, including setting goals to progressively reduce indirect greenhouse gas emissions aligned with commitments such as the Net Zero Banking Alliance, promoting corporate culture and social/environmental responsibility, advancing diversity, equity and inclusion, ensuring worker health and safety, and supporting communities and local development.
- ESG performance oversight through monitoring of key sustainability KPIs and Business Plan targets, with results presented to the Risks and Sustainability Committee in the first quarter.
- Incentive systems linked to sustainability: the CEO, as the only executive director, is the sole beneficiary of an annual Incentive System and a Long-Term Incentive Plan; both integrate sustainability metrics.
- Annual Incentive System: performance scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs grouped into Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; qualitative strategic actions enable plan delivery. A cross-Group ESG KPI is assigned (2024), KPI weights range 10–30%, accrual is annual, and payouts are determined formulaically. Payments are split between cash and Intesa Sanpaolo shares, with a five-year deferral, malus on deferred tranches, and a five-year post-payment clawback; subject to gateway conditions and compliance checks.
- Long-Term Incentive Plan (Performance Share Plan): extended to about 3,100 managers including the CEO; share awards depend on Business Plan targets (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR). Two de-multipliers apply: a Composite ESG KPI (reduces vesting by 10–20% if 2022–2025 ESG targets are missed) and a Capital target tied to CET1 above RAF (10% reduction per breach year, up to 40%). Plan includes gateway/compliance checks, 60% deferral over five years, significant share delivery with retention, and malus/clawback provisions.
- Centrality of ESG in CEO pay: an annual ESG KPI (evolved from a prior Diversity & Inclusion KPI, in place since 2021) and an ESG composite de-multiplier in the LTI. A cross-Group ESG KPI is also assigned to roughly 3,000 managers (10–15% weight).

nodes.title: Structure of the Long-Term Incentive Plan
nodes.heading: 2.4.3.2 Structure of the Long-Term Incentive Plan
nodes.start_phrase: The CEO is also a beneficiary of the Long -Term Incentive Plan (PSP), which is also awarded to the remaining Management (around 3,100 beneficiaries).
nodes.summary:
- Outlines sustainability priorities: reducing indirect greenhouse gas emissions in line with private initiatives (e.g., Net Zero Banking Alliance), fostering a responsible corporate culture, advancing diversity, equity and inclusion, ensuring worker health and safety, and supporting communities and local areas.
- Describes ESG governance and oversight: ongoing control of Group ESG performance, monitoring key sustainability KPIs and Business Plan targets, and submission of results to the Risks and Sustainability Committee for assessment in Q1.
- Details incentive systems tied to sustainability for the Managing Director and CEO (the Board’s only executive), comprising an annual Incentive System and a Long-Term Incentive Plan (PSP), both embedding ESG criteria.
- Annual Incentive System: a performance scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs grouped under Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; qualitative strategic actions; a cross-Group ESG KPI; KPI weights of 10–30%; annual accrual; deterministic payout calculation subject to gateway conditions, compliance checks, and corrective mechanisms; payment in cash and shares with five-year deferral, malus and post-payment claw-back provisions.
- Long-Term Incentive Plan (PSP): for the CEO and ~3,100 managers; share-based awards contingent on Business Plan-aligned targets (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR); two de-multipliers—Composite ESG KPI (Environmental, Social, Governance) reducing vesting by 10–20% if Plan ESG targets are missed, and a CET1 capital target reducing vesting by 10% per year of breach (up to 40%); 60% of any bonus deferred over five years; majority delivered in shares with retention; gateway, malus, and claw-back apply.
- Emphasizes the centrality of ESG in CEO variable pay: a dedicated ESG KPI in the annual plan and an ESG composite de-multiplier in the PSP; a cross-Group ESG KPI also assigned to about 3,000 managers (10–15% weight).

nodes.title: The ESG Component in CEO Incentive Plans (Annual and Long-Term)
nodes.heading: 2.4.3.3 The ESG Component in CEO Incentive Plans (Annual and Long-Term)
nodes.start_phrase: With regard to the variable remuneration of the Managing Director and CEO, the ESG component is of central importance and is included both in the annual Incentive Plan through the provision of a specific KPI, and in the long -term Performance Share Plan in which an ESG composite KPI is envisaged that acts as a de -multiplier of any bonus earned.
nodes.summary:
- ESG governance priorities and targets: progressive reduction of indirect greenhouse gas emissions aligned with commitments (e.g., Net Zero Banking Alliance), promotion of a responsible corporate culture, diversity-equity-inclusion, worker health and safety, and community support. Ongoing monitoring of Group ESG KPIs and Business Plan targets, with results submitted to the Risks and Sustainability Committee in Q1.
- Incentive systems tied to sustainability: the CEO (sole executive director) is beneficiary of an annual incentive system and a long-term Performance Share Plan (PSP), both embedding sustainability metrics, subject to gateway conditions, compliance checks, malus and clawback.
- Annual incentive system: performance scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs grouped under Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability. Includes a transversal Group ESG KPI; KPI weights 10–30%; annual accrual; deterministic payout calculation; payment split between cash and shares with a five-year deferral, malus on deferred portions, and five-year post-payment clawback.
- Long-term PSP: extended to ~3,100 managers; awards shares based on Business Plan metrics (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR). Two de-multipliers reduce vesting for underperformance: (i) Composite ESG KPI (Environmental, Social, Governance sub-KPIs versus 2022–2025 Plan targets) and (ii) CET1 capital target relative to RAF. 60% of any bonus deferred over five years; significant portion in shares with retention.
- ESG components in incentives: 
  - Annual CEO ESG KPI (15% weight) with drivers covering: inclusion in sustainability indices; inclusive workplace and gender equity (hires and candidate pools for first managerial appointments); Group ESG initiatives (green/circular economy support, financed emissions targets in priority sectors, exposure reduction in ESG risk sectors, ESG Credit Framework completion); growth of Sustainable Investments (ESG share of AuM); youth orientation and employability.
  - PSP ESG composite KPI: Environmental—new loans for green/circular economy and Corporate/SME transition (40%); Social—successful re/up-skilling with reallocation to new roles (40%); Governance—women in new senior appointments at -1/-2 levels below CEO (20%).
- LECOIP 3.0 for Professionals in Italy: long-term plan based on certificates linked to Intesa Sanpaolo shares; includes the same ESG composite KPI; guarantees a minimum 4% return if KPI achieved; if not, the foregone amount is invested by the Bank in ESG projects aligned with those objectives.
- Governance and approvals: Shareholders’ Meeting approves annual and long-term plans on Board proposal supported by the Remuneration Committee; Risks and Sustainability Committee reviews alignment with current and prospective risks.
- Sustainability reporting controls: three lines of defense model—Level I line controls; Level II risk and compliance (Chief Compliance Officer and Chief Risk Officer areas); Level III Internal Audit assessing overall control and IT systems. A structured, risk-based control framework ensures the Consolidated Sustainability Statement’s compliance and quality across:
  - Planning: regulatory analysis, scope of consolidation definition, complete/accurate double materiality analysis.
  - Data collection/preparation: verification of data sources; formal systems and procedures to ensure completeness, accuracy, consistency, and comprehensiveness with contributor/validator checks.
  - Aggregation/finalization: validation outcomes review, metric checks, and harmonization of policies/actions/targets to meet regulatory and quality requirements.

nodes.title: Risk management and internal controls of sustainability reporting
nodes.heading: 2.4.4 Risk management and internal controls of sustainability reporting
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group adopts an internal control system based on three levels, in line with the legal and regulatory provisions in force.
nodes.summary:
- Executive remuneration and incentives linked to ESG:
  - CEO’s ESG KPI (15% weight) assessed on: presence in sustainability indices; initiatives for an inclusive workplace with divisional gender equity targets (in hiring and candidate pools for first-time managerial appointments); Group ESG initiatives (support for green/circular economy, targets to cut financed emissions in additional sectors, reduction of exposures in ESG risk sectors, completion of the ESG Credit Framework); growth of sustainable investments (ESG share of AuM); youth orientation and employability programs.
  - Long-term Performance Share Plan (PSP): composite ESG KPI used as a de-multiplier with sub-KPIs and weights:
    - Environmental (40%): new loans to green/circular economy and ecological transition, prioritizing Corporate/SME transition.
    - Social (40%): number of people completing re-/up-skilling with reallocation for re-skilling.
    - Governance (20%): share of women in new senior appointments at -1 and -2 levels below the CEO.
  - LECOIP 3.0 Plan (for Professionals in Italy): 45,629 participants (~63% of those entitled); certificates linked to Intesa Sanpaolo shares; same ESG composite KPI guarantees a 4% minimum return if achieved; if not achieved, the foregone amount is invested by the Bank in ESG projects aligned to the KPI’s objectives.
  - Governance of incentive systems: Annual Incentive System and PSP approved by the Shareholders’ Meeting upon Board proposal supported by the Remuneration Committee; Risks and Sustainability Committee reviews consistency with current and prospective risks.

- Risk management and internal controls for sustainability reporting:
  - Three lines of defense model:
    - Level I: line controls embedded in processes/IT and performed by operating/business structures.
    - Level II: risk and compliance controls separate from production, including Chief Compliance Officer (regulatory compliance) and Chief Risk Officer (risk management), with corresponding units in Group companies.
    - Level III: internal audit assessing completeness, adequacy, effectiveness, and reliability of the internal control and IT systems.
  - Structured, risk-based control framework for the Consolidated Sustainability Statement:
    - Planning: interpret applicable regulation, define scope of consolidation, verify completeness/accuracy of double materiality analysis.
    - Data collection/preparation: verify data sources; use formal systems/procedures to ensure completeness, accuracy, consistency, and comprehensiveness; contributor/validator checks.
    - Aggregation/finalization: verify validation outcomes, check metrics, harmonize policy/action/target information to meet regulatory and quality standards.
  - Manager responsible for preparing financial reports oversees compliance of the Statement with CSRD-adopted reporting standards; results reported to governance bodies.
  - Reporting: annual report to the Board on sustainability statement risk within the “Report on the internal control system for the financial reporting process”; periodic reports by corporate control functions.

- Environmental information (ESRS E1 – Climate change):
  - Double materiality approach:
    - Impact materiality (inside-out): effects on people and environment over short/medium/long term.
    - Financial materiality (outside-in): risks and opportunities affecting development, financial position/performance/cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital over varying time horizons.
  - Identification of climate-related impacts, risks, opportunities aligned with Group frameworks (Environmental and Energy Policy, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines, 2022–2025 Business Plan, Business Environment Scan, climate risk analyses), covering sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy; includes physical and transition risks.
  - Impact materiality methodology: interviews with internal units and external stakeholders; qualitative and quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
    - Own operations: positive material impacts on adaptation driven by internal policies and strategies targeting climate neutrality and energy efficiency.
    - Upstream supply chain: no material impacts identified given the Group’s service-based model; assessed via supplier ESG questionnaires.
    - Downstream value chain: both positive material impacts (through financing/investment criteria supporting clients’ mitigation/adaptation and energy reduction) and negative material impacts (due to portfolio exposures to high-emitting, high-risk sectors); references to commitments (UN Global Compact, NZBA) and internal policies (e.g., transition plans).
  - Financial materiality: dual quantitative/qualitative assessment across scopes.
  - Physical climate risk assessment: structured process distinguishing acute (e.g., heat waves, storms, floods, wildfires) and chronic (e.g., sea level rise) risks; further details continue beyond the excerpt.

nodes.title: Environmental information
nodes.heading: 3 Environmental information
nodes.start_phrase: Impacts, risks and opportunities within the scope of ESRS E1 – Climate Change were identified taking into consideration the specific features of the Group.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from the Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement under ESRS E1 – Climate change within Environmental information.
- Focus: Double materiality assessment covering impacts, risks, and opportunities related to climate change across three ESRS E1 sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy (all forms of production and consumption).
- Approach:
  - Double perspective:
    - Impact materiality (inside-out): effects on people and environment over short/medium/long term.
    - Financial materiality (outside-in): climate-related risks and opportunities affecting development, financial position, performance, cash flows, and access/cost of capital over various time horizons.
  - Reference framework and governance: Group policies and guidelines (Rules for Environmental and Energy Policy; Group Guidelines on ESG Risk Governance), 2022–2025 Business Plan, Business Environment Scan, materiality analysis of climate risks, and existing controls.
  - Inclusion of both transition and physical climate risks as required by ESRS E1.
- Methodology for impact materiality:
  - Criteria: scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood.
  - Evidence gathering: interviews with internal units and external stakeholders/experts.
  - Value chain scopes:
    - Own operations: evaluated against internal policies and initiatives for climate neutrality and energy efficiency.
    - Upstream: supplier ESG questionnaires and response analysis.
    - Downstream: portfolio analysis of exposures to high-GHG sectors and sectors exposed to physical/transition risks; review of external commitments (e.g., UN Global Compact, Net-Zero Banking Alliance) and internal financing/investment policies favoring counterparties with credible climate actions/transition plans.
- Impact materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts identified for climate adaptation due to adopted policies/strategies.
  - Upstream value chain: no material impacts identified given the Group’s primarily financial-services profile.
  - Downstream value chain: both material positive impacts (across mitigation, adaptation, energy) and material negative impacts due to exposures to high-risk/high-emission counterparties.
- Financial materiality:
  - Assessed using a combined quantitative and qualitative approach across own operations, upstream, and downstream scopes.
- Physical climate risk assessment:
  - Structured process initiated with identification of material climate hazards.
  - Differentiation between acute risks (e.g., heat waves, storms, floods, wildfires) and chronic risks (e.g., sea-level rise).

nodes.title: ESRS E1 – Climate change
nodes.heading: 3.1 ESRS E1 – Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: Impacts, risks and opportunities within the scope of ESRS E1 – Climate Change were identified taking into consideration the specific features of the Group.
nodes.summary:
- The section presents the Group’s ESRS E1 (Climate change) materiality assessment within its Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- It applies a double materiality lens: impact materiality (inside-out effects on people and environment) and financial materiality (outside-in risks and opportunities affecting performance, cash flows, and capital access over different time horizons).
- Identification and mapping of climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities are grounded in internal frameworks and governance (Environmental and Energy Policy Rules, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines), the 2022–2025 Business Plan, the Business Environment Scan, and climate risk materiality analyses, alongside established controls.
- Analysis is structured across ESRS E1 sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy (covering all energy production and consumption types), and distinguishes between physical and transition risks.
- Impact materiality methodology combines interviews with internal functions and external stakeholders with qualitative and quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood).
- Scope-specific impact findings:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts identified, particularly for climate adaptation, due to internal policies and efficiency/neutrality strategies.
  - Upstream value chain: no material impacts found, reflecting the Group’s primarily financial-services profile and supplier assessment via ESG questionnaires.
  - Downstream value chain: material positive impacts from financing and investment criteria supporting counterparties’ transition/adaptation and energy/emission reduction; material negative impacts also identified due to exposures to high-emitting sectors and those vulnerable to climate risks.
- Financial materiality is assessed through a combined quantitative and qualitative approach across the same scopes.
- For physical climate risks, the Group uses a structured identification and assessment process that differentiates acute hazards (e.g., heat waves, storms, floods, wildfires) from chronic hazards (e.g., sea-level rise), with further steps implied beyond the excerpt.

nodes.title: ESRS E1 – Climate change - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.1 ESRS E1 – Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: Impacts, risks and opportunities within the scope of ESRS E1 – Climate Change were identified taking into consideration the specific features of the Group.
nodes.summary:
ESRS E1 – Climate change  
 
Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities  
 
As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double 
materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:  
 
− impact materiality, which takes into account the Group's impacts with respect to external and internal stakeholders (people 
and the environment) in the short, medium or long term from an inside -out perspective;  
− financial materiality, which considers, from an outside -in perspective, sustainability topics that give rise to:  
o risks affecting, or potentially affecting, the development of the undertaking, its financial position, performance and cash 
flows, access to finance or cost of capital in the short, medium or long term;  
o opportunities that have, or may predictably have, a material financial impact on the Group in the short, medium or long 
term.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.1.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Impacts, risks and opportunities within the scope of ESRS E1 – Climate Change were identified taking into consideration the specific features of the Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framework: The Group’s ESRS E1 – Climate change disclosure is built on a double materiality assessment (impact and financial) across three sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy. It draws on internal policies and governance (Environmental and Energy Policy, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines, 2022–2025 Business Plan, Business Environment Scan), and assesses both transition and physical risks.

- Methodology for impact materiality:
  - Own operations: qualitative assessment via internal policies and initiatives tied to climate neutrality and energy efficiency.
  - Upstream value chain: ESG questionnaires and feedback analysis from suppliers.
  - Downstream value chain: portfolio analysis of exposures to high GHG-emitting sectors; review of external commitments (UNGC, NZBA) and internal financing/investment policies prioritizing counterparties with credible climate actions.
  - Outcomes: 
    - Own operations: material positive impacts on adaptation.
    - Upstream: no material impacts identified given the Group’s services profile.
    - Downstream: material positive impacts across all sub-topics from supportive criteria/strategies; material negative impacts due to exposure to high-risk sectors.

- Methodology for financial materiality:
  - Physical risk process: identify acute and chronic hazards (using IPCC SSP5-8.5 and regional projections), apply geospatial tools and climate models, assess exposure/sensitivity for own sites, analyse suppliers/counterparties’ vulnerabilities, and integrate into risk management.
  - Scenario use: NGFS climate projections; sovereign bond analysis via scenario-driven interest rate projections and yield curve shocks.
  - Risk focus by scope:
    - Own operations: operational and reputational risks from extreme weather-related disruptions.
    - Upstream: reputational risk if suppliers have weak resilience/BCP/DR plans.
    - Downstream: credit, market, liquidity, strategic, and reputational risks.
  - Material outcomes:
    - Physical risk: downstream credit and reputational risks are material in the medium to long term.
    - Transition risk: 
      - Own operations: operational and reputational risks if actions fall short of targets.
      - Upstream: operational/reputational risks where suppliers have weak GHG controls.
      - Downstream: credit, market, liquidity, and reputational risks; material (credit, market, reputational) in the medium to long term. Upstream reputational risk is also material.

- Energy sub-topic:
  - Upstream: reputational risk if suppliers lag on energy efficiency; material.
  - Downstream: credit and reputational risks from counterparties’ energy management inefficiencies affecting asset values; material.

- Opportunities assessment:
  - Adaptation: downstream opportunities identified but not financially material.
  - Mitigation (transition-related):
    - Own operations: material opportunities from emissions-reduction initiatives (Own Emissions Plan).
    - Downstream: material opportunities from expanding sustainable/Taxonomy-aligned products and financing for mitigation.
  - Energy (own operations): brand/positioning gains from energy efficiency targets not financially material beyond broader mitigation opportunities.

- Time horizons: all analyses consider short, medium, and long term, aligned with internal RAF, business plan projections, and risk simulations.

- Resilience assessment via Business Environment Scan (BES):
  - Integrates external trends into strategy: macroeconomic variables under three climate scenarios (Hot House World, Orderly Transition, Disorderly Transition), competitive landscape, regulatory and technology trends, social/demographic trends, and quantitative transition/physical risk impacts on exposures.
  - Produces an integrated view of how climate- and environment-related risks/opportunities may affect the business model over short, medium, and long terms.

nodes.title: Resilience Assessment
nodes.heading: 3.1.2 Resilience Assessment
nodes.start_phrase: Using an in -depth analysis of external factors such as global sustainability trends, changes in public policy and evolving stakeholder expectations, banks can accurately identify risks and opportunities that influence their operations and long -term strategy.
nodes.summary:
- Financial materiality of opportunities:
  - Climate adaptation opportunities identified only in the downstream value chain were deemed immaterial.
  - Climate mitigation–related opportunities are material across own operations and the downstream value chain, supported by existing initiatives (e.g., Group Own Emissions Plan), alignment with the EU Taxonomy, and commercial objectives.
  - Energy-sector opportunities tied to brand/positioning via energy-efficiency targets in own operations (outside broader mitigation initiatives) were assessed as not financially material.

- Resilience assessment via Business Environment Scan (BES):
  - Purpose: integrate climate and environmental considerations into strategic planning, informed by global trends, policy changes, and stakeholder expectations.
  - Scope: 14 business areas across retail, SMEs, large corporates (manufacturing, trade, construction, real estate, oil & gas, power generation, automotive), international banking, private banking, asset management, insurance, and Corporate Centre (including Treasury/ALM).
  - Variables analyzed: macroeconomic, competitive landscape, regulatory trends, technology trends, social/demographic trends, transition risk, and physical risk.
  - Scenarios/time horizons: NGFS-aligned scenarios (Hot House World, Orderly, Disorderly) with short term to 2027, medium term to 2030, long term to 2050; macro projections from Oxford Economics and NGFS.
  - Results:
    - Six areas show all variables at medium/high and at least one high impact: Residential Real Estate (Italy), SMEs (Italy), Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, and International Banks Division.
    - Expected impact timing: 30% short term, 60% medium term, 10% long term.
    - Dimension insights: macroeconomic impacts mainly medium term (energy prices affect Oil & Gas and Power Generation short and long term); competitive impacts short–medium term; regulatory impacts high for 13/14 areas in short–medium term (both risks and opportunities); technology impacts mainly medium term; social/demographic impacts more limited and area-dependent.

- Quantified portfolio risk findings:
  - Transition risk: limited short-term exposure rising over time; increasing exposure for SMEs and large corporates, notably in Power Generation and Oil & Gas; residential real estate faces medium/long-term regulatory impacts from emissions reductions.
  - Physical risk: long-term flood risk significant for residential properties; SMEs face moderate exposure (drought and wildfires); large corporates see significant long-term exposure to drought, wildfires, and floods.

- Follow-up actions informed by BES:
  - Ongoing monitoring of ESG regulation and participation in climate initiatives.
  - Integration of climate/ESG risks into credit processes and creditworthiness assessments; ESG sector mapping to NACE/ATECO.
  - NZBA-aligned sector targets to reduce financed emissions with monitored transition plans.
  - Implementation/monitoring of the Own Emissions Plan; business continuity and physical risk mitigation for facilities; energy-efficiency measures.

- Integration into incentive systems:
  - ESG/climate metrics embedded in variable remuneration for the CEO and workforce via the Annual Incentive System and Long-Term Performance Share Plan (PSP).
  - 2024 CEO Annual Incentive includes a 15% ESG KPI; PSP includes a composite ESG KPI acting as a 10–20% de-multiplier on vested shares.
  - 2024 outcome: ESG KPI contributed 16% of the CEO’s annual bonus.
  - Annual ESG KPI drivers: support for green/circular economy (ESG commitments progress, sectoral financed-emissions targets, reduced exposures in ESG risk sectors, completion of ESG Credit Framework) and growth in ESG investments as a share of AuM.
  - PSP environmental component emphasizes new credit to green/circular transition, especially for SMEs (40% weight).

nodes.title: Integration of sustainability performance into incentive systems
nodes.heading: 3.1.3 Integration of sustainability performance into incentive systems
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group is aware that it also has a significant social and environmental impact in the settings in which it conducts its business, choosing to act not only in the pursuit of profit, but also with the aim of creating long -term value for the Group, our people, customers, the community and the environment.
nodes.summary:
- Climate risk assessment: Transition risks for the Group’s portfolios are limited short term but rise over longer horizons, with SMEs and large corporates—especially in Power Generation and Oil & Gas—most exposed; residential real estate faces medium/long-term regulation-driven impacts. Physical risks intensify long term: floods for residential properties; drought and wildfires as main drivers for SMEs; drought, wildfire and flood risks material for large companies across sectors.
- Follow-up actions: Ongoing monitoring of ESG regulation; participation in climate initiatives; integration of climate/ESG risks into credit processes and creditworthiness; ESG sector mapping to NACE/ATECO; sector targets under NZBA to cut financed emissions and implement a sector transition plan; execution of the Own Emissions Plan; business continuity and physical site protection; energy efficiency measures.
- Strategic intent: Manage climate and environmental risks while pursuing sustainable growth by recognizing impacts, executing defined actions, and monitoring the operating context.
- ESG-linked remuneration: Climate and broader ESG performance embedded in variable pay for the CEO and workforce via the Annual Incentive System and the Performance Share Plan (PSP).
- CEO incentives: 2024 Annual Incentive includes a 15% ESG KPI; outcome led to 16% of bonus vesting. PSP uses a composite ESG KPI as a de-multiplier, reducing vested shares by 10–20% based on achievement; failure to meet the KPI cuts vesting accordingly.
- KPI design: Annual ESG KPI emphasizes support for green/circular economy via commitments, setting additional financed-emission reduction targets, reducing exposure in ESG-risk sectors, completing the ESG Credit Framework, and increasing ESG investments as a share of AuM. PSP environmental component focuses on new credit for green/circular transition, prioritizing corporate/SME transition (weight 40%).
- Operational climate strategy and governance: Code of Ethics promotes efficient resource use and climate, nature, and biodiversity protection, and backs green/circular economy. Environmental and Energy Policy aligns with Italian regulations (Leg. Decree 152/06 and 231/01), targets climate action, ESG risk management, impact prevention, resource efficiency, and responsible sourcing aligned with initiatives like the UN Global Compact.
- Roles, systems, and controls: Environmental Manager leads the Environment & Energy structure; operational oversight by Real Estate Management and Group Technology. Certified management systems (ISO 14001, ISO 50001) with periodic audits, checks on waste and energy versus building characteristics, and regulatory compliance reviews.
- Sustainable procurement: Green Banking Procurement Rules guide purchasing (energy, office materials, renovations, events) to optimize resources, cut CO2, and advance efficiency and circularity; overseen by the Environment & Energy head.
- Policy scope and transparency: Policies apply across all Group companies and are communicated internally (Intranet) and externally (website).
- Own Emissions Plan (SBTi 1.5°C-aligned): Target a 53% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 versus 2019 (−51,427 tCO2e from a 96,192 tCO2e baseline), reach carbon neutrality concurrently via high-quality offsets, and procure 100% renewable electricity. Coverage spans the full Group; the 2019 baseline is retained despite minor boundary changes (<1% additional impact).
- Decarbonization pathway methodology: Bottom-up process engaging multiple internal stakeholders to identify key levers, complemented by an integrated approach (top-down element implied beyond the excerpt).
- Additional note: No direct investments in carbon capture and storage; the Group holds EU ETS emission rights from proprietary trading activities.

nodes.title: Strategies to counter climate change in own operations
nodes.heading: 3.1.4 Strategies to counter climate change in own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group has developed and adopted a series of policies to monitor and address issues related to climate change and energy efficiency.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s operational strategies to mitigate and adapt to climate change, grounded in a Code of Ethics that promotes resource efficiency, combats climate change, protects biodiversity, and supports a green, circular economy.
- An Environmental and Energy Policy translates these values into actionable objectives: compliance with environmental laws (Legislative Decrees 152/06 and 231/01), climate change mitigation, ESG risk management, prevention of environmental impacts, efficient resource use, and ethical/sustainable supplier selection; it aligns with initiatives like the UN Global Compact.
- Governance and accountability are assigned to the Environmental Manager heading the Environment and Energy structure, with operational monitoring delegated to functions such as Real Estate Management and Group Technology.
- Dedicated environmental and energy functions oversee regulatory compliance, conduct periodic checks, inspections, and audits across sites, and monitor energy use against expected consumption considering building characteristics.
- The Group maintains ISO 14001 (environment) and ISO 50001 (energy) certified management systems, audited periodically by an international third party.
- Green Banking Procurement Rules guide sustainable purchasing (energy, office materials, renovations, events) with goals to optimize resources, cut CO2 emissions, drive efficiency, and foster circularity; responsibility rests with the head of the Environment and Energy structure.
- Policies are communicated to all relevant stakeholders via the corporate intranet and the public website and apply across the Parent Company and all subsidiaries.
- The Own Emissions Plan (launched in 2022 under the 2022–2025 Business Plan) follows SBTi 1.5°C criteria, targeting a 53% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 (–51.427 kt CO2e from a 2019 baseline of 96.192 kt CO2e) and carbon neutrality by 2030 via offsetting residual emissions with carbon credits; the Group aims for 100% purchased electricity from renewable sources.
- Targets are based on 2019 data, anticipated green certificate availability and PPAs through 2030; the scope covers the entire Group and remains unchanged, with new subsidiaries adding <1% CO2e impact and not altering the baseline.
- The emissions reduction pathway uses an integrated approach beginning with a bottom-up process engaging internal stakeholders (Real Estate, HR/People, Workers Benefits, branches, foreign companies) to identify key decarbonization levers; the text notes no direct investment in carbon capture/storage and mentions holding EU ETS emission rights from trading activities.

nodes.title: Policies to mitigate and adapt to climate change
nodes.heading: 3.1.4.1 Policies to mitigate and adapt to climate change
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group has developed and adopted a series of policies to monitor and address issues related to climate change and energy efficiency.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Strategies to counter climate change in Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s own operations, within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.

- Policy framework:
  - Code of Ethics promoting efficient, conscious resource use; combating climate change; protecting nature/biodiversity; supporting a sustainable, green, circular economy.
  - Environmental and Energy Policy aligned with Italian Environmental Code (Legislative Decree 152/06) and Model 231/01; objectives include climate change mitigation, ESG risk management, prevention of environmental impacts, efficient resource use, and responsible supplier selection; alignment with initiatives like the UN Global Compact.
  - Governance: Environmental Manager (head of Environment and Energy structure) accountable for implementation; operational monitoring delegated to specialized units such as Real Estate Management and Group Technology.

- Controls and management systems:
  - Environmental and energy functions conduct regulatory compliance audits, periodic checks, inspections, and site audits focused on waste and energy performance versus expected levels considering building characteristics.
  - ISO-certified management systems: ISO 14001 (environment) and ISO 50001 (energy), third-party certified and periodically audited.

- Sustainable procurement:
  - Green Banking Procurement Rules covering energy, office materials, sustainable renovations, and event organization; goals include resource optimization, sustainable purchasing, CO2 reduction, efficiency, and circularity.
  - Responsibility resides with the head of the Environment and Energy structure.

- Transparency and scope:
  - Policies accessible to internal stakeholders via the intranet and to external stakeholders via the official website.
  - Applicability across the Parent Company and all subsidiaries.

- Own Emissions Plan (per 2022–2025 Business Plan; SBTi 1.5°C-aligned):
  - Target: 53% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 vs. 2019 baseline (96,192 tCO2eq), equivalent to a reduction of 51,427 tCO2eq.
  - Carbon neutrality target by 2030 through offsetting residual emissions with carbon credits; aim for 100% purchased electricity from renewable sources (via green certificates and options such as PPAs).
  - Emissions calculation covers the entire Group; 2019 baseline retained despite subsequent inclusion of additional subsidiaries (collectively <1% of total CO2eq).
  - Note: As of 31 Dec 2024, the Group does not directly invest in GHG capture and storage; it holds EU ETS emission rights from proprietary trading.

- Decarbonization pathway definition:
  - Integrated approach combining methods, including a bottom-up process engaging multiple internal stakeholders (e.g., Real Estate Management, People Management & Development, Workers Benefits, branches, and foreign companies) to identify key levers.

nodes.title: Own Emissions Plan
nodes.heading: 3.1.4.2 Own Emissions Plan
nodes.start_phrase: In accordance with the "2022 -2025 Business Plan", in 2022 the Intesa Sanpaolo Group implemented a plan to reduce its own emissions, called "Own Emissions Plan", following the Science Based Target Initiative (SBTi) protocol that calls for keeping the global temperature increase below 1.5°C compared to pre -industrial levels, as envisaged by the Paris Agreement.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s strategies to mitigate and adapt to climate change within its own operations, governance structures, management systems, procurement rules, and progress toward emission-reduction targets.

- Policies and governance:
  - Code of Ethics promoting efficient resource use, climate action, biodiversity protection, and support for a green/circular economy.
  - Environmental and Energy Policy aligned with Italian legislation (Legislative Decrees 152/06 and 231/01), targeting climate change mitigation, ESG risk management, prevention of environmental impacts, resource efficiency, and responsible supplier selection; aligned with UN Global Compact principles.
  - Environmental Manager (Environment and Energy structure) accountable for implementation; operational monitoring delegated to Real Estate Management and Group Technology.

- Management systems and oversight:
  - ISO 14001 (environment) and ISO 50001 (energy) certified systems with periodic audits and site inspections focused on waste, energy consumption versus expected benchmarks, and compliance.
  - “Green Banking Procurement Rules” guiding sustainable procurement (energy, office materials, renovations, events), aiming at resource optimization, CO2 reduction, efficiency, and circularity; overseen by the head of Environment and Energy.

- Scope and transparency:
  - Policies apply to the Parent Company and all subsidiaries; communicated via intranet (internal) and website (external).

- Own Emissions Plan (aligned to SBTi 1.5°C):
  - Target: 53% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 vs. 2019 baseline (96.192 kt CO2eq) and carbon neutrality by 2030 via offsetting residual emissions; 100% purchased electricity from renewables by 2030.
  - Baseline year 2019 maintained despite boundary expansions; additional entities contribute <1% of total CO2eq.
  - Dual approach: bottom-up (stakeholder engagement across functions and geographies) and top-down (prioritization by abatement potential and cost).

- Decarbonization levers:
  1) Shift electricity procurement to renewables (entire Group).
  2) Reduce building energy use and fossil fuel dependence (Italy and selected foreign subsidiaries) via heat pumps, system retrofits, PV installations, and energy monitoring.
  3) Electrify company fleet and deploy charging infrastructure (Italy and selected foreign subsidiaries).

- 2024 key actions:
  - Renewable electricity: continued monitoring; Bank of Alexandria used I-RECs and a contract with Egypt’s NREA covering ~91% of Cairo-region electricity.
  - Buildings: heat pump rollouts and smart building monitoring in Italy; HVAC upgrades in Hungary (CIB), PV in Croatia (PBZ), LED and system upgrades in Slovakia (VUB).
  - Fleet: increased hybrid/electric vehicles and installation of charging stations at major sites.

- Resources and governance:
  - Implementation coordinated across corporate functions; funded through annual capital budget; OPEX/CAPEX impacts limited for the banking sector.
  - Plan updates shared with ESG Control Room and ESG Coordination Committee.

- Targets and progress (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Scope 1 and 2 emissions: -35% vs. 2019 (reduction of 34.256 kt CO2eq); on track for -53% by 2030.
  - Renewable electricity purchases: 92.8% (baseline 87.7%); target 100% by 2030.

- Additional note:
  - No direct investment in GHG capture/storage; holds CO2 emission rights (EU ETS) tied to proprietary trading by the IMI Corporate & Investment Banking Division.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets
nodes.heading: 3.1.4.3 Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets
nodes.start_phrase: In this context, as at 31 December 2024 the Group had already achieved a 35% reduction in emissions compared to the 2019 baseline ( 96.192 thousand t CO 2eq).
nodes.summary:
- Focus and approach: Describes Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s “Own Emissions Plan,” a top-down program prioritizing projects with the highest emissions abatement per cost. It uses three levers: (1) shifting electricity procurement to renewable sources; (2) cutting building energy use and fossil-fuel dependence via heat pumps, photovoltaic installations, and energy monitoring; (3) electrifying the company car fleet and deploying charging infrastructure.

- Scope of application: Lever 1 applies Group-wide; levers 2 and 3 apply in Italy and at foreign subsidiaries in Albania, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Ukraine, Serbia, Slovenia, Moldova, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Egypt, Romania, and Hungary.

- 2024 implementation highlights:
  - Renewable electricity: Ongoing monitoring confirms alignment with targets. Bank of Alexandria purchased I-RECs and signed with Egypt’s NREA to source renewable power for Cairo-area sites, covering about 91% of electricity needs.
  - Buildings: Heat pump replacements and smart building consumption monitoring in Italy; heat pump adoption and HVAC upgrades at CIB Bank (Hungary); photovoltaic system installation at PBZ (Croatia); LED lighting and electrical/HVAC upgrades at VUB (Slovakia).
  - Fleet: Increased share of electrified vehicles (full electric, plug-in hybrid, full hybrid) and reduced ICE vehicles; launch of charging station installations at major Group buildings.

- Execution and resourcing: Actions are coordinated across relevant corporate functions with costs and resources shared. Funding is provided via the annual capital budget; implementation leverages specialist skills, suitable technologies, and enabling regulation. OPEX and CAPEX impacts are limited for the Group’s sector. Plan updates are periodically reviewed in the ESG Control Room and ESG Coordination Committee.

- Targets and performance:
  - Scope 1 and 2 emissions: Baseline 96,192 tCO2eq (2019). As of 31 Dec 2024, emissions reduced by 35% (about 34,256 tCO2eq), on track for the 2030 target of -53%.
  - Renewable electricity: 87.7% (2019) to 92.8% (2024), target 100% by 2030.
  - Entity-specific disclosure (EU Regulation 2023/2772): percentage of purchased electricity from renewable sources is 92.8% at year-end 2024.
  - EU PAB note: The Group does not fall into any exclusion categories under EU Paris-Aligned Benchmark rules.

- Portfolio-level climate strategy and governance:
  - Policies and oversight: Guided by the Code of Ethics and approved by the Board of Directors with support from the Risks and Sustainability Committee. The Chief Risk Officer Governance Area maintains the “Guidelines for the Governance of ESG Risks,” covering climate mitigation and adaptation and the internal system for ESG and reputational risk management.
  - Applicability and standards: Guidelines apply across Group entities with local adaptation as needed; aligned with EU Sustainable Finance initiatives and international frameworks (UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, PRB, PRI, PSI, Equator Principles, NZBA).

- ESG risk governance process:
  - Identification: Defines ESG risk factors and transmission channels, including climate and physical risks, and integrates scenarios/stress testing.
  - Assessment and measurement: Determines exposures, notably through the ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process.
  - Monitoring and control: Tracks ESG KPIs within the Risk Appetite Framework.
  - Mitigation: Applies preventive and remedial actions, including responses to RAF breaches.
  - Communication: Provides ESG risk reporting and disclosures, including indicators that capture physical climate risks. The Clearing process screens credit proposals, supplier/third-party engagements, equity investments, and extraordinary transactions for ESG and reputational risks.

nodes.title: Strategy to combat climate change at portfolio level
nodes.heading: 3.1.5 Strategy to combat climate change at portfolio level
nodes.start_phrase: The Group adopts a series of policies to safeguard decarbonisation objectives at the portfolio level and to monitor climate adaptation issues, starting with the “Code of Ethics”, which, among its principles, envisages responsible management of indirect environmental impacts, for example committing to promoting services and products to foster the development of a low -emission economy.
nodes.summary:
- The Group provides an entity-specific disclosure under EU Regulation 2023/2772, reporting that 92.8% of purchased electricity came from renewable sources as of 31 December 2024.
- It notes that, like other financial institutions, the Group is not included in categories excluded from the EU Paris-aligned Benchmark (EU PAB).
- At the portfolio level, the Group’s climate strategy is guided by policies for decarbonisation and climate adaptation, anchored in the Code of Ethics, which promotes low‑emission products and services.
- Governance: the Board of Directors, supported by the Risks and Sustainability Committee, approves climate-related policies, including the Group Guidelines for the Governance of ESG Risks; the Chief Risk Officer area develops and maintains these guidelines and the internal ESG and reputational risk management system.
- The ESG guidelines emphasize monitoring and mitigating climate risks (including physical risks) via preventive regulation and sector-specific rules that can limit credit exposure in higher‑risk sectors; they apply across Group entities and are adapted for local regulations in the International Banks Division.
- The guidelines are aligned with EU sustainable finance developments (post-2018 Action Plan) and international frameworks and commitments, including UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, Principles for Responsible Banking, Principles for Responsible Investment, Principles for Sustainable Insurance, Equator Principles, and the Net‑Zero Banking Alliance.
- ESG risk governance process comprises five steps:
  - Identification of ESG risk factors and transmission channels (e.g., scenarios in stress testing).
  - Assessment and measurement of exposures (e.g., ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing).
  - Monitoring and control via ongoing tracking of ESG KPIs within the Risk Appetite Framework (RAF).
  - Mitigation through actions and strategies, including remedial measures for RAF breaches.
  - Communication via reporting and disclosures, including indicators that capture physical climate risks.
- The ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process screens for ESG and reputational risks in advance across credit proposals, supplier/third‑party selections for commercial agreements, equity investments, and extraordinary transactions.

nodes.title: ESG risk governance process
nodes.heading: 3.1.5.1.1 ESG risk governance process
nodes.start_phrase: The “Guidelines for the Governance of ESG Risks” outline the Group's ESG risk governance process (including on climate change adaptation issues), which consists of five steps:
nodes.summary:
- Entity-specific sustainability disclosure per Regulation (EU) 2023/2772: percentage of electricity purchased from renewable sources, at 92.8% as of 31 December 2024.
- Statement that the Group does not fall into any exclusion categories under the EU Paris-aligned Benchmark (EU PAB) legislation.
- Portfolio-level climate strategy focused on mitigation and adaptation, anchored in the Code of Ethics promoting low-emission products and services.
- Governance framework: Board of Directors (with the Risks and Sustainability Committee) approves climate/ESG policies; the Chief Risk Officer area develops and maintains ESG risk guidelines and systems, including reputational and ESG risk management.
- Group Guidelines for the Governance of ESG Risks: align with EU sustainable finance developments and international initiatives (UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, PRB, PRI, PSI, Equator Principles, NZBA); applied across Group entities with adaptations for local regulations.
- ESG risk governance process covering five steps: identification, assessment/measurement, monitoring/control, mitigation, and communication, including consideration of physical climate risks and integration into stress testing, RAF KPIs, remedial actions, and reporting.
- ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process: pre-transaction screening of ESG/reputational risks for credit, suppliers/third parties, equity investments, and extraordinary deals; two-tier review (line functions then expert assessment), advisory outcomes, and escalation if beyond risk appetite.
- Adoption and application of Equator Principles (EP IV) across relevant Group entities and geographies for project-related financing (advisory, project finance, project-related corporate loans, bridge loans, refinancing/acquisitions), including risk categorization, documentation requirements, and environmental/social clauses with compliance verification.
- Sector materiality assessment (Climate/ESG Materiality Assessment): identifies ESG/climate risk drivers, integrates forward-looking elements, and informs sector-level controls, strategies, and Risk Appetite Framework safeguards.
- Sensitive sectors approach: list of sectors with heightened ESG/reputational risk, with general exclusion criteria and sector-specific rules.
- General exclusions: no financing for activities negatively impacting UNESCO World Heritage Sites, Ramsar wetlands, and IUCN protected areas (categories I–VI).
- Sector-specific regulation example: Group-wide “Rules for Oil & Gas Operations” to support the energy transition, covering upstream, midstream, downstream, and trading activities.

nodes.title: Management of sustainability issues in sensitive sectors
nodes.heading: 3.1.5.2 Management of sustainability issues in sensitive sectors
nodes.start_phrase: At the portfolio level and with respect to the objectives of decarbonisation, the “ESG Risk Governance Guidelines” also outline an ESG risk governance model based on materiality assessments of ESG risk factors in relation to the various risk categories (credit risk, market risk, operational risk, liquidity risk and reputational risk) and their incorporation into the various risk management areas.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Intesa Sanpaolo’s ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process with two levels of review: a first-level assessment by frontline units and a second-level expert analysis, producing advisory opinions with risk ratings, mitigants, and escalation when outside risk appetite.
- Details adoption and implementation of the Equator Principles (EP IV) across the Group and applicable products (project finance/advisory, project-related corporate loans, bridge loans, refinancing/acquisitions), including three-tier risk categorization, required documentation, and inclusion/verification of environmental and social clauses in financing.
- Outlines the Group’s ESG Risk Governance Guidelines and Climate/ESG Materiality Assessment, integrating ESG/climate risks across credit, market, operational, liquidity, and reputational risks; driving sector-level controls, sector strategies, and safeguards within the Risk Appetite Framework.
- Defines sensitive sectors, general exclusions (no financing for projects impacting UNESCO World Heritage Sites, Ramsar wetlands, or IUCN I–VI protected areas), and sector-specific rules.
- Presents Oil & Gas sector rules covering upstream, midstream, downstream, and trading: no financing for new oil extraction sites or projects with negative impacts in critical areas (e.g., Arctic, Amazon Sacred Headwaters); exclusions and 2025 phase-out for unconventional resources; portfolio alignment via risk clearing, analysis of counterparties’ transition plans, and periodic measurement of financed emissions intensity; preference for counterparties credibly transitioning with lower CO2 profiles.
- Sets coal sector policies: support clients’ gradual coal phase-down, rigorous ESG assessment, and capped exposure; no increased exposure to power companies lacking decarbonization plans, exceeding 35% coal capacity by 2030, or planning new coal plants; Group-wide phase-out of coal mining exposures by 2025; applies to coal mining and coal-fired power generation.
- Establishes internal rules for classifying sustainable lending products and transactions under the Chief Risk Office Governance Area, defining activities for climate mitigation and adaptation (including enabling activities like data collection and early warning systems) addressing temperature, wind, water, and soil-related physical risks.
- Aligns sustainable lending classifications with Loan Market Association principles for Green, Social, and Sustainability-linked Loans; sets division-specific classification processes, including assessment of conventions/covenants/KPIs, and CRO Governance validation for consistency with the ESG risk framework.
- Confirms Group-wide applicability of policies across countries of operation and public availability of guidelines to internal and external stakeholders via intranet and the institutional website.

nodes.title: Internal classification of sustainable lending products and transactions
nodes.heading: 3.1.5.3 Internal classification of sustainable lending products and transactions
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group also has internal regulations for the classification of sustainable lending products and transactions, under the responsibility of the Chief Risk Office Governance Area.
nodes.summary:
- The Group’s exclusion and phase-out policies: no financing for new oil extraction or projects with negative impacts in critical areas (e.g., Arctic, Amazon Sacred Headwaters), and phase-out of unconventional fossil fuel exposures (shale/tight oil and gas, tar sands, coal bed methane) by 2025; application via ESG and reputational risk clearing, counterparty transition plan analysis, and periodic measurement of financed emissions intensity in Oil & Gas, prioritizing clients advancing decarbonization.
- Coal sector approach: support clients’ gradual reduction of coal in power generation through targeted financing and rigorous ESG assessment; cap overall exposure; no increases in exposure to companies lacking credible emissions-reduction strategies, exceeding 35% coal capacity beyond 2030, or planning new coal capacity; phase-out of coal mining exposures by 2025; rules apply Group-wide to coal mining and coal-fired power generation.
- Internal sustainable lending classification: Group-wide rules (under Chief Risk Office Governance) define environmentally sustainable activities—with criteria distinct from the EU Taxonomy—to promote mitigation and adaptation, including activities that reduce damages from adverse temperature, wind, water, and soil events and related enabling activities (e.g., data, early warning systems); alignment with Loan Market Association principles for Green, Social, and Sustainability-linked Loans; divisional processes assign sustainability attributes, validated for ESG risk consistency; guidelines accessible to internal and external stakeholders.
- Sectoral Transition Plan and targets: commitment to net-zero by 2050 with 2030 interim targets; participation in NZBA, NZAMI (via asset managers), NZAOA, and FIT; evolution from a 2022 High-Level Transition Plan to a 2023 Sectoral Transition Plan; sectoral targets set for Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, Coal Mining, Iron & Steel, Commercial Real Estate (revised in 2024 for a well-below-2°C pathway), and in 2024 for Cement, Aluminium, Residential Real Estate, and Agriculture–Primary Farming; no targets for Shipping and Aviation due to immateriality.
- Governance of target setting and reporting: targets developed by CSO Governance with CRO/CFO and business divisions, reviewed by ESG Control Room and Steering Committee, and approved by the Board (with Risks and Sustainability Committee); detailed disclosures in the annually published Climate Report; SBTi validation obtained January 2025; OPEX/CAPEX deemed limited in relevance for the Group’s activities.
- Client transition enablement: suite of products and incentives including a circular economy credit facility, green financing, sustainability-linked loans with discount/bonus mechanics, Green/Social/Sustainability bonds aligned to ICMA guidelines, and advisory support; 2024 initiatives in the IMI Corporate & Investment Banking Division to develop green products and EU Taxonomy-aligned financing frameworks.
- Monitoring: structured, five-iteration annual process to track progress toward targets, support year-end reporting, and enable final accounting.

nodes.title: Sectoral Plan
nodes.heading: 3.1.6 Sectoral Plan
nodes.start_phrase: Aware of the challenge posed by climate change, the Intesa Sanpaolo Group is committed to contributing to the achievement of global climate goals by supporting the transition to a low -carbon economy.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Sectoral Transition Plan within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, detailing its net-zero strategy, sector targets, governance, tools, and early sector plans (Agriculture and Aluminium).

- Net-zero commitment and memberships:
  - Target: Net-Zero by 2050 with interim 2030 targets embedded in the 2022–2025 Business Plan.
  - Alliances: NZBA (banking), NZAMI (asset managers), NZAOA and FIT (insurance); note NZAMI’s 2025 review and temporary suspension of tracking.
  - SBTi: Targets submitted in 2024 and validated in January 2025.

- Transition planning and sector targets:
  - Evolution from a 2022 high-level transition plan to a 2023 Sectoral Transition Plan.
  - 2030 targets set for: Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, Coal Mining (initial); Iron & Steel and Commercial Real Estate (2023, CRE target revised in 2024 to align with well-below-2°C); Cement, Aluminium, Residential Real Estate, and Agriculture – Primary Farming (2024).
  - No targets for Shipping and Aviation due to immaterial exposures/emissions.

- Governance and reporting:
  - Target setting led by the CSO Governance Area with CRO/CFO and business divisions; reviewed by ESG Control Room and Steering Committee; approved by the Board with the Risks and Sustainability Committee.
  - Targets and plans disclosed in the Consolidated Sustainability Statement and detailed annually in the Climate Report (reviewed by the Steering Committee, approved by the Board).
  - OPEX/CAPEX climate relevance limited given the bank’s business model.

- Execution levers and products to enable client transition:
  - Circular economy credit facility (developed with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation; not EU Taxonomy-screened).
  - Green financing; sustainability-linked financing with incentive mechanisms; Green/Social/Sustainability Bonds aligned with ICMA guidelines.
  - ESG advisory and development of Taxonomy-aligned products and frameworks in IMI Corporate & Investment Banking.
  - Strategic initiatives in 2024 to expand green products and Taxonomy-aligned financing.

- Monitoring and performance management:
  - Structured monitoring in five annual cycles comparing baseline, target, and benchmark curves by sector; corrective actions coordinated with business divisions; results reported under “Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets.”

- Sector-specific transition plan overviews:
  - Agriculture – Primary farming:
    - Context: Hard-to-decarbonize sector; >10% of EU GHG; Italy’s non-ETS sectors (incl. agriculture) target −43.7% by 2030 vs 2005.
    - Enablers: Low-emission fertilizers, cover/bioenergy crops, efficient livestock practices, sustainable food systems, forest management for removals and bioenergy.
    - Bank levers: Financing for low-emission clients with transition plans and innovative green solutions; products include Crescita Agri and S-Loan Green. 2024 initiatives with ACEA on water efficiency; agreements with Coldiretti and Consorzio Italiano Biogas to finance agricultural biomethane plants.
  - Aluminium:
    - Context: Critical to low-carbon transition but high-emission production (~270 Mt CO₂ in 2022); output up >3% (2020–2022); sector is hard-to-abate with <2% annual decarbonization vs ~4% needed under IEA NZE; requires near-zero technologies and expanded recycling.
    - Enablers: Inert anode technology, hydrogen use, and near-zero-emission electricity.
    - Bank levers: Increased financing to firms with Net-Zero-aligned transition plans; performance-based products; emphasis on secondary (recycled) aluminium; support for “green aluminium,” renewable energy sourcing, circular economy models, and enabling infrastructure.

nodes.title: Agriculture – Primary farming
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.1 Agriculture – Primary farming
nodes.start_phrase: − The agricultural sector is commonly defined as difficult to decarbonise in view of the emissions generated by its physical, chemical and biological processes, contributing to more than 10% of the EU's greenhouse gas emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Group’s monitoring process for climate targets, comparing reported performance to baselines, targets, and benchmark curves, and convening corrective meetings when deviations arise; points to the “Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets” section for progress details.
- Introduces Sector-Specific Transition Plans, outlining for each sector: market context, enabling factors, and Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s decarbonisation strategy and levers; cross-references portfolio-level climate objectives.
- Agriculture – Primary farming:
  - Market context: Agriculture is hard to decarbonise; responsible for >10% of EU GHG emissions; Italy’s non-ETS sectors must cut emissions 43.7% by 2030 vs 2005.
  - Enabling factors: Sustainable cropping (low-emission fertilisers, cover/bioenergy crops), efficient livestock management, sustainable food systems (plant proteins, waste reduction, responsible sourcing), and forest management for removals and renewable energy.
  - Group strategy/levers: Finance low-emission clients with credible transition plans and innovative green solutions; key products include Crescita Agri and S-Loan Green for sustainable agriculture, livestock, forestry, and restoration; 2024 initiatives with ACEA on water efficiency and agreements with Coldiretti and CIB to finance agricultural biomethane plants.
- Aluminium:
  - Market context: Critical to the low-carbon transition but highly CO₂-intensive (~270 Mt in 2022); production rising (>3% from 2020–2022); current decarbonisation pace (<2%/yr) lags IEA NZE needs (~4%/yr); calls for near‑zero technologies and enhanced recycling.
  - Enabling factors: Innovations such as inert anodes and the use of hydrogen or near‑zero‑emission electricity.
