nodes.title: Aluminium
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.2 Aluminium
nodes.start_phrase: − Aluminium is a crucial element in the transition to a low -carbon economy as it plays a key role in reducing emissions in various sectors, such as transport, construction and food and beverage packaging.
nodes.summary:
- Extract from Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement describing how the Group monitors decarbonisation targets and outlines sector-specific transition plans.
- Target monitoring approach: compares reported performance against baselines, targets, and benchmark curves for each sector; convenes meetings to address deviations and define corrective actions; points to the “Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets” section for progress details.
- Overview of sector-specific transition plans: for each sector, the document presents market context, enabling factors/technologies, and the Group’s decarbonisation strategy and financing levers; cross-referenced to the Climate Report and portfolio-level objectives.

Sector summaries and bank strategies:
- Agriculture – Primary farming:
  - Context: Hard-to-decarbonise sector; >10% of EU GHGs; Italy’s non-ETS sectors must cut emissions 43.7% by 2030 vs 2005.
  - Enablers: Sustainable cropping and fertilisers, livestock efficiency, sustainable food systems, forest management/carbon removals.
  - Bank levers: Finance low-emission clients with transition plans; support innovative green solutions (e.g., Crescita Agri, S-Loan Green). 2024 initiatives include ACEA collaboration on water efficiency and financing agricultural biomethane with Coldiretti and CIB.
- Aluminium:
  - Context: Essential for low-carbon economy but high emissions (~270 Mt CO2 in 2022); production growing; decarbonisation pace (<2%/yr) below IEA NZE (~4%/yr) needs.
  - Enablers: Inert anode technology, hydrogen, near‑zero‑emission electricity, expanded recycling.
  - Bank levers: Increased financing for Net‑Zero‑aligned firms; performance-based products; emphasis on secondary (recycled) aluminium; support “green aluminium,” renewable-powered operations, circular economy models, and transition infrastructure.
- Automotive:
  - Context: Significant emitter (cars ~16% and vans ~3% of EU emissions); EU targets: −55% CO2 by 2030 and zero-emission new vehicles by 2035; rapid EV share growth 2020–2023; emission cuts for new cars/vans; ongoing 2024 industry uncertainty.
  - Enablers: Government strategies and investments in charging infrastructure.
  - Bank levers: Finance advanced low-emission mobility (EVs, hydrogen, hybrids, batteries); support manufacturers and suppliers across the value chain; structure financing for the shift to electric mobility.
- Cement:
  - Context: Hard-to-abate; direct CO2 largely flat since 2018; needs ~4% annual carbon intensity reduction to 2030 under IEA NZE.
  - Enablers: Material efficiency, low‑carbon fuels, energy efficiency, and CCUS.
  - Bank levers: Finance clients with credible Net‑Zero commitments and innovation; support green cement, renewable integration, and CCUS deployment.
- Coal mining:
  - Policy: Lending rules set limits/exclusions for coal extraction and coal‑fired power; support client transitions away from coal toward renewables and gas.
  - Commitment: Phase out exposure to coal mining counterparties by 2025.

- The section includes references to external sources (e.g., European Commission, IEA, International Aluminium) supporting market context data.

nodes.title: Automotive
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.3 Automotive
nodes.start_phrase: − The automotive sector is one of the largest contributors to CO ₂ emissions: cars and vans respectively account for around 16% and 3% of EU emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Excerpt from Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement detailing sectoral decarbonisation context, enablers, and the Group’s strategic levers for Automotive, Cement, and Coal Mining.

- Automotive:
  - Market context: Significant emitter (cars ~16%, vans ~3% of EU CO2). EU targets: −55% CO2 by 2030 and zero-emission new vehicles by 2035. Rapid electrification (EV share nearly tripled 2020–2023); new car/vans emissions down 27%/10% (2019–2022). Ongoing 2024 uncertainty and competitive realignment.
  - Enablers: Government strategies and major investments in EV charging infrastructure in the EU and US to accelerate adoption.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo strategy: Finance and advise across the value chain (manufacturers, suppliers) to enable low-emission mobility (EVs, hydrogen, advanced hybrids, batteries). Provide dedicated products, partnerships, and tailored financing for the shift to electric mobility.

- Cement:
  - Market context: Hard-to-abate sector with carbon-intensive processes and high heat needs; direct CO2 emissions flat since 2018 amid rising demand. NZE pathway requires ~4% annual carbon-intensity reduction to 2030.
  - Enablers: Near-term measures (material efficiency, low-carbon kiln fuels, plant energy efficiency) and growing adoption of CCUS as a complementary solution.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo strategy: Prioritize financing for clients aligned with transition, assessed on published decarbonisation commitments; support firms with ambitious Net-Zero targets and innovative tech. Promote development of green cement, renewables integration, and CCUS.

- Coal mining:
  - Policy: Lending rules set limits/exclusions for coal extraction and coal-fired power; support clients reducing coal use and shifting to lower-carbon alternatives (renewables, gas).
  - Commitment: Full phase-out of exposure to coal mining counterparties by 2025.

nodes.title: Cement
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.4 Cement
nodes.start_phrase: − Cement is a “hard to abate” sector due to the use of carbon -intensive materials and the high temperatures required for production, and is characterised by still underdeveloped decarbonisation technologies.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement covering sectoral decarbonisation context, enablers, and Intesa Sanpaolo Group (ISG) strategies for Automotive, Cement, and Coal Mining.

- Automotive:
  - Market context: Cars and vans account for ~16% and ~3% of EU CO2 emissions; EU targets −55% CO2 by 2030 and zero-emission new vehicles by 2035. EV share in Europe nearly tripled from 2020 to 2023; 2019–2022 emissions fell 27% for new cars and 10% for new vans; 2024 marked by uncertainty and market readjustment.
  - Enablers: US/EU investment in public charging infrastructure to accelerate EV adoption.
  - ISG strategy: Finance and advise across the value chain to enable low-emission mobility (EVs, hydrogen, advanced hybrids, batteries); provide dedicated financial products, partnerships, and support clients’ investment plans for electric mobility.

- Cement:
  - Market context: Hard-to-abate sector with carbon-intensive processes; direct emissions flat since 2018 amid rising demand; NZE pathway requires ~4% annual carbon-intensity reduction to 2030.
  - Enablers: Near-term measures (material efficiency, low-carbon kiln fuels, energy efficiency) and scaling of CCUS.
  - ISG strategy: Prioritise financing for transition-aligned clients with credible, ambitious Net-Zero plans and innovative tech; support sector solutions including green cement, renewable integration, and CCUS.

- Coal mining:
  - Policy: ISG lending rules set limits/exclusions for coal extraction and coal-fired power; support clients reducing coal reliance and shifting to lower-carbon alternatives (renewables, gas).
  - Commitment: Full phase-out of exposure to coal mining counterparties by 2025.

nodes.title: Coal mining
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.5 Coal mining
nodes.start_phrase: − The Intesa Sanpaolo Group's "Rules for lending operations in the coal sector" (for more information on the subject, see the section on policies on climate change mitigation and adaptation) define the limits and exclusion criteria for the lending operations in the segments of coal extraction and coal -fired power plants, supporting customers in their efforts to reduce their use of coal for the production of energy and encouraging the transition towards low carbon -intensity alternatives, such as renewable sources and gas.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and structure: Excerpt from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement covering sector-specific market context, enabling factors, and Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s (ISG) decarbonisation strategies for Automotive, Cement, Coal Mining, Iron & Steel, Oil & Gas, and Power Generation.
- Automotive:
  - Market context: Cars and vans account for ~16% and ~3% of EU CO2; EU targets −55% by 2030 and zero-emission new vehicles by 2035; EV market share in Europe nearly tripled 2020–2023; 2019–2022 new car emissions −27%, vans −10%; 2024 marked by uncertainty and competitive realignment.
  - Enablers: US/EU investments in public charging infrastructure to accelerate EV adoption.
  - ISG levers: Finance and advisory across the value chain (OEMs to suppliers); support investments in EVs, hydrogen, hybrids, and batteries; structure financing for transition to electric mobility.
- Cement:
  - Market context: Hard-to-abate due to process emissions and high-temperature kilns; direct CO2 flat since 2018; needs ~4% annual carbon-intensity reduction to 2030 to align with 1.5°C.
  - Enablers: Material efficiency, low-carbon fuels, plant energy efficiency, and growing CCUS deployment.
  - ISG levers: Prioritise financing for clients with credible, ambitious Net-Zero plans; back solutions such as Green Cement, renewable integration, and CCUS.
- Coal mining:
  - Policy stance: Lending rules with limits and exclusions for coal extraction and coal-fired power; support clients reducing coal use and shifting to lower-carbon alternatives (renewables and gas).
  - Commitment: Phase-out of exposure to coal mining by 2025.
- Iron & Steel:
  - Market context: Sector responsible for about 25% of global CO2; emissions stabilised but require ~25% intensity reduction by 2030 to align with NZE; decarbonisation spurred by regulation and sustainable investment.
  - Enablers: Strong corporate targets, international collaborations (e.g., First Movers Coalition), and technologies including hydrogen-based steelmaking, electric arc furnaces, renewables, and CCS.
  - ISG levers: Support counterparties with Net-Zero targets; finance decarbonisation projects (e.g., hydrogen steel); engage clients on Net-Zero strategies with tailored financing for efficiency, renewables, and innovation.
- Oil & Gas:
  - Market context: ~15% of global energy-related emissions, with methane a major share; ~$600bn in global investments needed by 2030; oil demand expected to stabilise near 106 mb/d by decade’s end due to EVs, efficiency, and renewables.
  - Enablers: Government support (incl. for developing countries), company pledges to cut emissions (esp. methane), and technologies such as CCUS and biorefineries (notably for SAF).
  - ISG levers: Provide sustainability-linked, green and transition financing, green bonds, transition project finance, and advisory; tighten sector policies, bringing forward phase-out of exposures to unconventional oil & gas to 2025 (updated June 2024).
- Power Generation:
  - Market context: Central to Net-Zero; renewables-driven growth essential; electricity expected to reach ~50% of global energy consumption by 2050; key technologies include solar, wind, nuclear, EVs, heat pumps, and hydrogen.

nodes.title: Iron & Steel
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.6 Iron & Steel
nodes.start_phrase: − The steel sector, responsible for about 25% of global CO ₂ emissions, plays a crucial role in climate change mitigation.
nodes.summary:
This section of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement covers the Group’s view and actions across three high‑impact sectors—Iron & Steel, Oil & Gas, and Power Generation—structured around market context, enabling factors, and Intesa Sanpaolo’s decarbonisation levers.

Iron & Steel
- Market context: Steel accounts for about 25% of global CO₂ emissions; while emissions have stabilised, a ~25% drop in emissions intensity by 2030 is needed for Net‑Zero alignment. Progress is driven by tighter regulation, sustainable investments, and decarbonisation technologies.
- Enablers: International regulatory frameworks, global collaborations (e.g., First Movers Coalition), corporate targets, and technologies including hydrogen-based steelmaking, electric arc furnaces, greater use of renewables, and CCS.
- Group strategy: Support clients with Net‑Zero‑aligned targets; finance decarbonisation (e.g., hydrogen steel); engage customers with tailored financing to boost energy efficiency, renewables integration, and green innovation.

Oil & Gas
- Market context: Sector contributes nearly 15% of energy‑related emissions, with methane a priority for reduction; requires $600bn investment by 2030. Oil demand expected to stabilise around 106 mb/d by decade end due to EVs, efficiency, and renewables.
- Enablers: Government support (incl. for developing countries), company pledges to cut methane and expand renewables, and technologies such as CCUS and biorefineries (notably for SAF).
- Group strategy: Provide sustainability‑linked/green/transition financing and advisory; apply stricter sector policies, including an accelerated phase‑out of exposures to unconventional oil & gas by 2025.

Power Generation
- Market context: Central to Net‑Zero, propelled by rapid growth in renewables; electricity must expand to ~50% of global energy consumption by 2050. Key technologies: solar, wind, nuclear, EVs, heat pumps, and hydrogen.

nodes.title: Oil & Gas
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.7 Oil & Gas
nodes.start_phrase: − Oil & Gas operations contribute almost 15% of global energy -related emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Excerpt from Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement covering sectors 6–8 (Iron & Steel, Oil & Gas, Power Generation), structured around market context, enabling factors, and the Group’s decarbonisation strategy.

- Iron & Steel:
  - Market context: Sector accounts for about 25% of global CO₂ emissions; despite recent stabilisation, a ~25% drop in emissions intensity by 2030 is needed. Declines driven by stricter regulation, sustainable investment, and decarbonisation tech.
  - Enablers: International regulatory frameworks, global collaborations (e.g., First Movers Coalition), corporate emission‑reduction targets, and technologies such as hydrogen‑based steelmaking, electric arc furnaces, greater use of renewables, and CCS.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo actions: Support clients with Net‑Zero‑aligned targets; finance decarbonisation (e.g., hydrogen steel); engage customers with tailored financing for energy efficiency, renewable integration, and green innovation.

- Oil & Gas:
  - Market context: Operations contribute nearly 15% of energy‑related emissions; methane reduction is critical alongside electrification and low‑emission hydrogen. ~$600bn investment needed by 2030. Oil demand expected to stabilise around 106 mb/d by decade’s end due to EV adoption, efficiency gains, and renewables.
  - Enablers: Government support for emission cuts, company pledges (especially methane), and key technologies including CCUS and biorefineries for SAF.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo actions: Provide sustainability‑linked, green and transition financing, green bonds, transition project finance, and advisory; apply stricter sector policies with limits/exclusions; bring forward phase‑out of exposures to unconventional oil & gas to 2025 (per June 2024 policy update).

- Power Generation:
  - Market context: Central to Net‑Zero; rapid expansion of renewables and electrification needed, with electricity expected to reach ~50% of global energy consumption by 2050. Key technologies: solar, wind, nuclear, electric vehicles, heat pumps, and hydrogen.

nodes.title: Power Generation
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.8 Power Generation
nodes.start_phrase: − Power generation is a sector at the heart of the transition to Net -Zero emissions and is driven by significant growth in renewables.
nodes.summary:
- This partial document is a sector-by-sector snapshot from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement outlining market context, enabling factors, and Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s decarbonisation strategy for Iron & Steel, Oil & Gas, Power Generation, and Real Estate.

- Iron & Steel (Section 6)
  - Market context: Sector accounts for ~25% of global CO2 emissions; intensity must drop ~25% by 2030; stabilization driven by regulation and sustainable investment, with decarbonisation technologies gaining traction.
  - Enablers: International frameworks, global collaborations (e.g., First Movers Coalition), corporate targets, and technologies such as hydrogen-based steel, electric arc furnaces, renewables, and CCS.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo actions: Prioritizes financing clients with Net-Zero–aligned targets; funds decarbonisation projects (e.g., hydrogen steel); engages clients with tailored financing for energy efficiency, renewable integration, and green innovation.

- Oil & Gas (Section 7)
  - Market context: ~15% of global energy-related emissions; methane reduction is pivotal alongside electrification and low-emission hydrogen; ~$600bn in investments needed by 2030; oil demand expected to stabilize around 106 mb/d by decade’s end due to EVs, efficiency, and renewables.
  - Enablers: Government support, company pledges (especially on methane), and technologies like CCUS, biorefineries, and SAF for hard-to-abate sectors.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo actions: Provides sustainability-linked, green and transition finance, bonds, and project finance plus advisory; applies stricter sector policies and exclusions; accelerates phase-out of unconventional oil & gas exposures to 2025 (e.g., shale/tight, oil sands, coal bed methane).

- Power Generation (Section 8)
  - Market context: Central to Net-Zero; rapid growth in renewables needed to meet electrification goals (electricity to reach ~50% of global energy consumption by 2050); key technologies include solar, wind, nuclear, EVs, heat pumps, hydrogen.
  - Enablers: Renewable capacity to reach ~2.7x 2022 levels by 2030; rising renewable electricity use across transport, industry, and buildings; EU RED targets at least 42.5% renewables in total energy by 2030.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo actions: Early sector targets; two pillars—(1) active financial support for PV, on/offshore wind, BESS, green hydrogen, and CCUS; (2) multi-stakeholder engagement via M&A advisory, MDB collaborations, and PPPs.

- Real Estate – Commercial and Residential (Section 9)
  - Market context: EU buildings emit ~36% of CO2 and consume ~40% of energy; low renovation rate (~1%/yr); EPBD aims for -60% building emissions by 2030 and a zero-emission stock by 2050; emissions down 34% since 2005 but off-track for targets.
  - Enablers: Electrification, renewables, efficient materials/designs (e.g., aerogels, daylight/ventilation), supportive regulation and incentives, and grid decarbonisation.
  - Intesa Sanpaolo actions—Commercial:
    - “Orizzonte Impresa – Transizione Energetica” program with favorable loans tied to energy performance; S-Loan Green Projects for top certifications (e.g., LEED Gold, energy class A/B).
    - Strategic consulting (e.g., with Enel X, Regalgrid, Deloitte) for Renewable Energy Communities and tender advisory via the “Incent Now” platform.
    - Additional tools: bank assignment of tax deductions for eligible works and Rent Foryou solutions (IoT, software, AI for energy management; solar panels).
  - Intesa Sanpaolo actions—Residential:
    - Dedicated financing for buying, building, or retrofitting energy-efficient homes (min. class B), including windows/boilers replacement and PV, supported by incentives and advisory.
  - Note: Target achievement depends heavily on government policies for grid decarbonisation; cross-referenced to “Climate Change Actions and Resources at the Portfolio Level.”

nodes.title: Real Estate (Commercial and Residential)
nodes.heading: 3.1.6.1.9 Real Estate (Commercial and Residential)
nodes.start_phrase: − The building sector accounts for a significant share of global energy consumption and emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Context and enabling factors for decarbonisation:
  - Rapid global scale-up of renewables: capacity expected to reach 2.7x 2022 levels by 2030; renewables’ electricity in end-use sectors to ~20% by 2030 (from 13% in 2023).
  - EU policy push: Renewable Energy Directive target of at least 42.5% renewables in total energy by 2030.
  - Buildings’ impact in the EU: 36% of emissions, 40% of energy use; slow 1% annual renovation rate; EPBD aims for −60% building emissions by 2030 and net-zero building stock by 2050.

- Intesa Sanpaolo Group decarbonisation strategy:
  - Power Generation:
    - Active financing for solar PV, onshore/offshore wind, battery storage, green hydrogen, and CCUS.
    - Multistakeholder engagement via M&A advisory, partnerships with MDBs, and support for PPPs.
  - Commercial Real Estate:
    - “Orizzonte Impresa – Transizione Energetica” with targeted products and services.
    - Loans with favorable terms linked to energy efficiency and certifications (e.g., S-Loan Green Projects, LEED Gold, energy class A/B).
    - Consulting and partnerships (Enel X, Regalgrid, Deloitte), support for Renewable Energy Communities, and “Incent Now” platform for public tenders.
    - Additional tools for retrofits, energy efficiency, seismic upgrades, including tax credit assignment to the bank (per Italy’s “Rilancio Decree”); Rent Foryou solutions for IoT/AI energy management and solar.
  - Residential Real Estate:
    - Dedicated financing for purchase, construction, and energy-efficiency upgrades (minimum class B), with incentives and advisory.
    - Both CRE and RRE progress depend strongly on government policies for grid decarbonisation.

- Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets:
  - 2030 targets set for priority, high-emitting NZBA sectors; Board-approved.
  - Timelines: Oil & Gas and Coal mining from 2021 (coal phase-out by 2025); other sectors from 2022.
  - Methodology aligned with UNEP FI climate target-setting guidelines, SBTi Financial Sector Guidance, PCAF, and IEA NZE 2050 scenarios; Paris Agreement temperature alignment (except residential real estate target note).
  - Scope of financial activities: medium- to long-term lending (plus short-term for Oil & Gas), HTC bonds for Oil & Gas, and banking book equity where material.
  - SME treatment: unaffiliated sole proprietorship SMEs generally excluded due to data gaps; Agriculture includes SMEs with turnover > €10m; CRE includes corporate SMEs (not retail SMEs); RRE includes private retail only.
  - Sector boundaries and value chain focus to avoid double counting (per NACE), including:
    - Agriculture: primary farming operators.
    - Aluminium: aluminium producers.
    - Automotive: light vehicle production only (no components).
    - Cement: cement and clinker producers.
    - Iron & Steel: crude steel producers (excludes mining/finishing).
    - Oil & Gas: upstream and integrated operators (excludes refineries/pipelines/downstream).
    - Power Generation: generation and integrated operators (excludes T&D).
    - CRE and RRE: emissions from building use in Italy.
  - Emissions scopes by sector:
    - Agriculture, Aluminium, Cement, Iron & Steel, Power Generation: Scope 1–2.
    - Oil & Gas: Scope 1–3.
    - Automotive: Scope 3 Well-to-Wheel.
    - Commercial and Residential Real Estate: Scope 1–3.

- References and linkage:
  - Data sources include IEA, EEA, and EU EPBD.
  - Cross-reference to “Climate Change Actions and Resources at the Portfolio Level” for further detail.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets
nodes.heading: 3.1.7 Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets
nodes.start_phrase: The aforementioned sectors for which 2030 emission reduction targets have been set, approved by the Bank's Board of Directors, were identified based on a materiality criterion from among the most emission -intensive sectors envisaged by NZBA.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of section: Intesa Sanpaolo’s 2030 greenhouse gas emission reduction targets for high-emitting sectors, aligned with Paris Agreement temperature goals and a net-zero economy by 2050, within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.

- Governance and timeline:
  - Targets approved by the Board and set for sectors prioritized by materiality among NZBA high-emission sectors.
  - Application from 2021 for Oil & Gas and Coal Mining (coal phase-out by 2025), and from 2022 for other sectors.
  - 2023 methodological updates for Power Generation and Automotive to align with SBTi; Automotive target revised, Power Generation target unchanged.
  - Annual monitoring and disclosure of physical/economic intensity and absolute emissions (no absolute GHG cap set for 2024).

- Methodological framework:
  - Based on UNEP-FI Guidelines (Apr 2021), SBTi Financial Sector Guidance v1.1 (Aug 2022), and PCAF standards; science-based scenarios such as IEA Net Zero 2050.
  - Sectoral Decarbonisation Approach (SDA) used across sectors with intensity metrics (financed emissions over financed output; revenue intensity for Agriculture).
  - Avoidance of double counting through defined value-chain segment boundaries per sector.
  - Residential Real Estate target is an exception to Paris alignment note; CRE/RRE targets depend significantly on grid decarbonization policies.

- Perimeter of activities/data scope:
  - Included: medium- to long-term financing (plus short-term for Oil & Gas), Hold-To-Collect bonds for Oil & Gas, and banking book equity if material.
  - SME treatment: exclude unaffiliated sole proprietorship SMEs due to data limitations; include corporate SMEs in CRE (per SBTi), and include Agriculture SME corporates with turnover >€10m; RRE includes only private retail exposures.

- Sector boundaries and emission scopes considered:
  - Agriculture – Primary Farming (operational primary farming; Scopes 1–2).
  - Aluminium (producers; Scopes 1–2).
  - Automotive (light vehicle production only; Scope 3 WTW).
  - Cement (cement/clinker; Scopes 1–2).
  - Iron & Steel (crude steel producers; Scopes 1–2).
  - Oil & Gas (upstream and full-chain operators excluding refineries/pipelines/downstream; Scopes 1–3).
  - Power Generation (generation and integrated; Scopes 1–2).
  - Commercial and Residential Real Estate (use-phase building emissions in Italy; Scopes 1–3).

- Intensity metrics by sector:
  - Agriculture: tCO2eq/€MM (revenue intensity).
  - Aluminium: tCO2eq/t aluminium.
  - Automotive: gCO2eq/vkm.
  - Cement: tCO2eq/t cement.
  - Iron & Steel: tCO2/t steel.
  - Oil & Gas: gCO2eq/MJ.
  - Power Generation: kgCO2eq/MWh.
  - CRE/RRE: kgCO2eq/m2.

- Targets and 2024 progress (baseline → 2024 → 2030 target):
  - Agriculture: 721 → 675 → 641 tCO2eq/€MM.
  - Aluminium: 4.79 → 4.38 → 4.31 tCO2eq/t.
  - Automotive: 192 → 192 → 100 gCO2eq/vkm.
  - Cement: 0.65 → 0.64 → 0.50 tCO2eq/t.
  - Coal Mining exposure: €0.2bn (2021) → €0.01bn → €0 by 2025 (phase-out).
  - Iron & Steel: 1.05 → 0.82 → 0.81 tCO2/t.
  - Oil & Gas: 64 → 64 → 55 gCO2eq/MJ (central value of 52–58 range).
  - Power Generation: 202 → 123 → 110 kgCO2eq/MWh.
  - Commercial Real Estate (Italy): 43.16 → 38.94 → 22.11 kgCO2eq/m2.
  - Residential Real Estate (Italy): 30.13 → 28.77 → 19.26 kgCO2eq/m2.

- Policies and sectoral levers:
  - Coal Mining: lending phase-out policy by 2025.
  - Oil & Gas: operations governed by specific sector rules to drive portfolio alignment with climate neutrality and shift toward low/renewable fuels.
  - Sectoral plans identify levers to meet decarbonization goals.

- Data caveats:
  - Metrics and data may change with methodology updates (NZBA/SBTi), data source evolution, and market practices.
  - Projections depend on sector assumptions, company strategies, technology progress, and government policies; data quality and availability may vary over time.

- Green Mortgages:
  - Objective embedded in the 2022–2025 Business Plan; commercial divisions mobilized to design and deliver products/services that support customers’ environmental sustainability and accelerate green housing finance.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.1.7 Greenhouse gas emission reduction targets
nodes.start_phrase: The aforementioned sectors for which 2030 emission reduction targets have been set, approved by the Bank's Board of Directors, were identified based on a materiality criterion from among the most emission -intensive sectors envisaged by NZBA.
nodes.summary: Introductory overview of Intesa Sanpaolo’s 2030 greenhouse gas reduction targets across high-emitting NZBA sectors, approved by the Board and effective from 2021 for Oil & Gas and Coal mining (coal phase-out by 2025) and from 2022 for others. Targets and baselines follow UNEP-FI Climate Target Setting Guidelines (Apr 2021), SBTi Financial Sector Guidance v1.1 (Aug 2022), PCAF methodologies, and IEA Net-Zero 2050 scenarios to align with Paris temperature goals (except Residential Real Estate). The perimeter includes medium- to long-term lending (plus short-term for Oil & Gas), Hold-To-Collect bonds for Oil & Gas, and material banking book equity. SME scope: unaffiliated sole proprietorships excluded; Agriculture includes corporate SMEs with turnover >€10m; Commercial Real Estate includes corporate SMEs (not retail SMEs); Residential Real Estate includes only private retail exposures. To avoid double counting, only defined value-chain segments are covered: primary farming operations; aluminium producers; light-vehicle production (excluding components); cement/clinker producers; crude steel producers (excluding mining/finishing); Oil & Gas upstream and fully integrated operators (excluding refineries/pipelines/downstream); power generation and integrated utilities (excluding transmission/distribution); and building-use emissions in Italy for CRE/RRE. Emission scopes considered: Agriculture, Aluminium, Cement, Iron & Steel, Power Generation (Scopes 1–2); Automotive (Scope 3 WTW); Oil & Gas (Scopes 1–3); CRE/RRE (Scopes 1–3). The SDA approach is used with sector intensity metrics: Agriculture tCO2eq/€MM revenue; Aluminium tCO2eq/t; Automotive gCO2eq/vkm; Cement tCO2eq/t; Iron & Steel tCO2/t; Oil & Gas gCO2eq/MJ; Power kgCO2eq/MWh; CRE/RRE kgCO2eq/m2. Coal mining has a phase-out policy instead of an intensity target; Oil & Gas alignment is governed by specific sector rules. Progress is monitored annually on physical and economic intensity and absolute emissions (reported in the Climate Report), with no 2024 absolute GHG cap; in 2023, methods and reference areas were updated per SBTi for Power Generation and Automotive, revising the Automotive target only.

nodes.title: Climate change mitigation and adaptation objectives at the portfolio level
nodes.heading: 3.1.7.1 Climate change mitigation and adaptation objectives at the portfolio level
nodes.start_phrase: Metrics and data may be updated over time based on developments in emission calculation methods, updates to the NZBA and SBTi Guidelines, as well as updated data sources and established market practices.
nodes.summary:
- Methodology updates: In 2023 the bank updated its methodology and reference perimeter for the Power Generation and Automotive sectors to align with SBTi. This required revising the Automotive target; the Power Generation target remained unchanged.

- Portfolio-level climate objectives, baselines, 2024 status, and 2030 targets (emissions are “financed emissions/intensity” unless noted):
  - Agriculture (tCO2e/€MM): 721 → 675 → 641 (2030)
  - Aluminium (tCO2e/t): 4.79 → 4.38 → 4.31 (2030)
  - Automotive (gCO2e/vkm): 192 → 192 → 100 (2030)
  - Cement (tCO2e/t): 0.65 → 0.64 → 0.50 (2030)
  - Coal Mining (exposure, €bn): 0.2 → 0.01 → 0 (2025 phase-out)
  - Iron & Steel (tCO2e/t): 1.05 → 0.82 → 0.81 (2030)
  - Oil & Gas (gCO2e/MJ): 64 → 64 → c. 52–58 (2030; central value tracked per footnote)
  - Power Generation (kgCO2e/MWh): 202 → 123 → 110 (2030)
  - Commercial Real Estate (kgCO2e/m²): 43.16 → 38.94 → 22.11 (2030) [achievement highly dependent on grid decarbonization]
  - Residential Real Estate (kgCO2e/m²): 30.13 → 28.77 → 19.26 (2030) [achievement highly dependent on grid decarbonization]

- Data and methodology caveats: Metrics may change over time with evolving emission calculation methods, NZBA/SBTi guidance, data sources, and market practices. Figures rely on projections and sector assumptions that can be influenced by external factors (e.g., technology progress, government policy). Data quality and availability may vary.

- Green Mortgages objective: Embedded in the 2022–2025 Business Plan. Business divisions coordinate targeted product solutions and customer support initiatives to promote environmental sustainability and drive uptake of green mortgages.

nodes.title: Objectives and metrics relative to Green Mortgages
nodes.heading: 3.1.8 Objectives and metrics relative to Green Mortgages
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group contributes to the reduction of carbon emissions and promotes access to sustainable housing solutions through the provision of loans for energy -efficient real estate projects and the improvement of existing energy performance.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines Intesa Sanpaolo’s portfolio-level climate strategy, aligned with NZBA and SBTi. In 2023, methodologies for Power Generation and Automotive were updated per SBTi; the Automotive target was revised, while the Power Generation target remained unchanged.

- Sector decarbonization targets and 2024 progress for financed emissions/exposure:
  - Agriculture (Primary farming): intensity reduced from 721 to 675 tCO2e/€MM; 2030 target 641.
  - Aluminium: 4.79 to 4.38 tCO2e/t; 2030 target 4.31.
  - Automotive: unchanged at 192 gCO2e/vkm; 2030 target 100.
  - Cement: 0.65 to 0.64 tCO2e/t; 2030 target 0.50.
  - Coal Mining: exposure cut from €0.2bn (2021) to €0.01bn; phase-out to €0 by 2025.
  - Iron & Steel: 1.05 to 0.82 tCO2e/t; 2030 target 0.81 (near achievement).
  - Oil & Gas: unchanged at 64 gCO2e/MJ; 2030 target defined as a range consistent with SBTi (central value specified by the Group).
  - Power Generation: 202 to 123 kgCO2e/MWh; 2030 target 110.
  - Commercial Real Estate: 43.16 to 38.94 kgCO2e/m2; 2030 target 22.11 (highly dependent on grid decarbonization).
  - Residential Real Estate: 30.13 to 28.77 kgCO2e/m2; 2030 target 19.26 (highly dependent on grid decarbonization).
  - Note: Metrics are subject to updates as methods, NZBA/SBTi guidance, data sources, and market practices evolve; results rely on projections and assumptions sensitive to technology and policy developments.

- Green Mortgages program:
  - Embedded in the 2022–2025 Business Plan to promote energy-efficient housing through dedicated products and services, supporting both new efficient buildings and retrofits.
  - Scope includes loans to private individuals in Italy and in countries served by the International Banks Division; internal ESG classification extended beyond Italy.
  - Intermediate goals track the share of green mortgages in annual originations and the energy performance of financed properties; performance is on track.
  - Aligned with EeMAP to standardize energy-efficiency mortgages at the EU level.
  - Cumulative disbursements: €9bn by 31.12.2024 toward a €12bn target by 31.12.2025; €4.1bn disbursed in 2024. Data compiled from accounting (Parent Company) and management systems (IBD).

- ESG integration into governance, risk, and lending:
  - CRO, CFO, and CSO coordinate ESG/climate risk identification and management, setting objectives and lending guidelines.
  - The Risk Appetite Framework includes:
    - Exposure limits for Coal Mining and Oil & Gas (Coal Mining limit aligned with 2025 phase-out).
    - Early-warning thresholds/KRIs for emissions intensity of financed activities in Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, and Iron & Steel to meet NZBA/SBTi commitments.
    - Monitoring of new mortgage disbursements by EPC to improve collateral quality and reduce transition risk.
    - Specific thresholds for Residential Real Estate disbursements with lower EPCs and in areas of very high physical risk.
    - A threshold for sovereign debt exposures deemed “high risk” under internal ESG criteria.
  - Climate Scenario Analysis informs materiality assessments and is used in regulatory stress testing and ICAAP/ILAAP to assess loan portfolio vulnerabilities.

nodes.title: Climate change actions and resources at the portfolio level
nodes.heading: 3.1.9 Climate change actions and resources at the portfolio level
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the regulatory evolution on sustainability, the Group has adopted a medium - to long -term strategy and a cross -cutting and holistic approach to ESG issues, which is based on:
nodes.summary:
- Focus on reducing carbon emissions and promoting sustainable housing via financing energy-efficient real estate and upgrades, extending internal ESG classification from Italy to the International Banks Division, with intermediate goals to increase Green Mortgage share and improve collateral energy performance; targets reported as on track.
- Green Mortgages target: cumulative €12bn by 31.12.2025; table shows a 31.12.2024 “Final balance” of €9bn, with a note clarifying that the 2024 cumulative disbursement represented in the “Final” field refers to €4.1bn. 2024 data compiled from Parent Company accounting records and IBD management systems; 2022–2023 from management software.
- Climate risk governance: medium-to-long-term ESG strategy; integration of ESG/climate in the Risk Appetite Framework with limits, KRIs, and actions; CRO, CFO, and CSO coordinate on ESG risks/opportunities, objectives, and lending strategies; fostering an ESG risk culture.
- RAF controls include: sector limits for Coal Mining (annual reduction toward 2025 phase-out) and Oil & Gas; KRIs on financed emissions intensity for Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, Iron & Steel aligned to NZBA/SBTi; monitoring of new mortgage disbursements by EPC class; thresholds for lower EPCs and high physical risk areas; thresholds on sovereign debt defined as high ESG risk.
- Climate scenario analysis used for stress tests, ICAAP/ILAAP, assessing transition and physical risks on NFC portfolios and real estate collateral via shocks to counterparty balance sheets and property energy efficiency.
- Physical risk management: PD impacts from catastrophes considered in Credit Risk Appetite; RAF indicators for exposure to RRE in high acute-physical-risk locations with remedial actions; ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing incorporates physical risk drivers.
- ESG/Climate Credit Framework: sector-level color coding/heatmap guiding credit strategy; counterparty-level ESG score (including climate preparedness for transition/physical risk) applied across divisions and extended in 2024 to financial institutions and sub-sovereigns; transaction-level sustainable lending framework. Emission reductions cannot be precisely attributed to individual portfolio actions.
- Retail green finance aligned with EPBD: products support purchase/build of efficient homes and efficiency upgrades (e.g., windows, boilers, EVs, solar/PV). Green – Mutuo Domus offers APR reduction and free energy certification for renovations; eligible for class B or ≥1-class improvement.
- Portfolio transparency and alignment: services to assess savings from energy retrofits; processes aligned with EU Taxonomy; participation in EeMAP and the Energy Efficient Mortgage Label with quarterly green vs standard portfolio reporting since 2021.
- SME/corporate green products: 
  - S-Loan with ESG KPIs and annual monitoring to drive sustainability improvements.
  - 2024 S-Loan Progetti Green for investments in renewables, energy efficiency, sustainable transport, climate adaptation, and green buildings.
  - S-Loan CER with rate incentives and bonus for energy shared to Renewable Energy Communities.
  - Energia Impresa financing lines for RES (PV, onshore wind, small hydro, purification residual gases, small biogas/biomethane) and energy efficiency.
  - Nova+ (Green, Mobility, Agritech) supporting innovation toward climate neutrality, circularity, sustainable mobility, and resilient agriculture.
  - Medium/long-term loans with SACE Green guarantee (for Italian companies up to €500m turnover) and InvestEU – Sustainability Guarantee (for SMEs/Small Mid Caps).
- Nature and resilience initiatives: Think Forestry program (from Nov 2023) with Climate Network to drive reforestation and corporate emissions management; mobilizes customers and consumers via crowdfunding (For Funding) and card-commission contributions; future tools to measure, reduce, and manage residual emissions.
- Climate adaptation support: dedicated post-disaster credit lines, subsidized loans, payment suspensions, simplified procedures; business insurance offerings extend to catastrophic events (earthquake/flood).
- International Banks Division: green products for retail/micro-business, including Green Mortgages and efficiency loans; 2024 launch of Green dedicated S-Loan at VUB, CIB Bank, and Banca Intesa Beograd.
- IMI Corporate & Investment Banking: ESG financing solutions including sustainability-linked loans/bonds/guarantees/securitisations/hedging and use-of-proceeds instruments (Green/Social/Sustainable bonds, Green convertibles, renewables project finance); ESG Advisory Team (since 2023) supports client transition strategies and tools.
- Asset management: Fideuram ISPB Asset Management SGR, Fideuram AM (Ireland), and Eurizon Capital SGR signed the 2024 Global Investor Statement to Governments on the Climate Crisis.
- Supply chain climate risk: Code of Ethics requires ethical, social, and environmental responsibility from suppliers; internal procurement guidelines define roles, responsibilities, and processes to manage purchases consistent with these principles.

nodes.title: Strategy for managing climate risks in the supply chain
nodes.heading: 3.1.10 Strategy for managing climate risks in the supply chain
nodes.start_phrase: With respect to strategies and actions that control and mitigate the climate risks which may affect its supply chain, as per its Code of Ethics, the Group is committed to promoting forms of behaviour consistent with the highest ethical standards, both nationally and internationally.
nodes.summary:
- Launch and expansion of the Think Forestry programme (Nov 2023) to help corporate clients reduce CO2 emissions and promote nature, including:
  - Partnership with Climate Network non-profit and a large-scale reforestation initiative in Italy.
  - Bank-led tree planting in multiple Italian cities and client engagement.
  - Consumer involvement via the For Funding crowdfunding platform and allocation of a portion of card transaction commissions.
  - Development of tools for clients to measure, reduce, and manage residual emissions.
- Climate adaptation support in Italy through targeted financial measures for populations affected by natural disasters: dedicated credit lines, subsidised restoration loans, payment suspensions, protection actions, and streamlined procedures.
- Business insurance offerings (“Tutela Business Manifattura” and “Tutela Business Commercio”) with optional catastrophic event coverage, including earthquake and flood.
- International Banks Division initiatives:
  - Financing for energy efficiency, circular economy, and climate impact reduction, plus ESG awareness and education.
  - Retail/micro-business products such as loans and Green Mortgages for property purchase, construction, and energy efficiency.
  - Introduction (Q3 2024) of the Green dedicated S-loan at VUB, CIB, and BIB.
- IMI Corporate & Investment Banking Division’s ESG-focused solutions:
  - Sustainability-linked instruments (loans, bonds, guarantees, securitisations, hedging) incentivizing improved ESG performance.
  - Use-of-proceeds instruments (Green loans; Green, Social, Sustainable and Green Convertible bonds) and project finance for renewables (wind, solar, biomass, hydro), supported by a circular economy credit facility.
  - ESG Advisory Team (est. 2023) providing customised advisory on strategies and transition plans.
- Asset management commitment: Fideuram ISPB AM SGR, Fideuram AM (Ireland), and Eurizon Capital SGR signed the Global Investor Statement to Governments on the Climate Crisis, urging stronger policies to limit warming to 1.5°C.
- Supply chain climate risk management:
  - Code of Ethics guiding supplier relationships on ethical, social, and environmental responsibility, fostering transparent, long-term partnerships.
  - Internal purchasing guidelines defining roles, responsibilities, and procurement processes aligned with the Code of Ethics.
- Cross-references to further details in the Sustainable finance metrics section of ESRS S4 and the Climate Report.

nodes.title: Policies to mitigate and adapt to climate change in the supply chain
nodes.heading: 3.1.10.1 Policies to mitigate and adapt to climate change in the supply chain
nodes.start_phrase: With respect to strategies and actions that control and mitigate the climate risks which may affect its supply chain, as per its Code of Ethics, the Group is committed to promoting forms of behaviour consistent with the highest ethical standards, both nationally and internationally.
nodes.summary:
- Launch of the Think Forestry programme (Nov 2023) to support customers’ environmental transition, reduce CO2 emissions, and promote nature through national forestry initiatives and Italian reforestation.
- Bank participation via tree planting in multiple cities and customer engagement; expansion through For Funding crowdfunding and allocation of a portion of credit card commissions to the project.
- Planned evolution to offer tools for measuring, reducing, and managing residual CO2 emissions for corporate customers.
- Climate adaptation support in Italy: dedicated credit lines, subsidised loans for restoring damaged properties, loan suspensions, protection measures, and simplified procedures after natural disasters.
- Business insurance products (“Tutela Business Manifattura” and “Tutela Business Commercio”) with optional catastrophic coverage (earthquake and flood).
- International Banks Division: financing for energy efficiency, circular economy, climate impact reduction, and ESG awareness initiatives.
- Retail and micro-business: loans and Green Mortgages for property purchase, construction, and energy efficiency.
- Introduction (Q3 2024) of “Green dedicated S-loan” at VUB, CIB, and BIB.
- IMI Corporate & Investment Banking: broad ESG financing toolkit (sustainability-linked loans/bonds/guarantees/securitisations/hedging) and use-of-proceeds instruments (Green/Social/Sustainable bonds, Green convertible bonds, Green loans, and renewable Project Finance).
- Establishment of an ESG Advisory Team (2023) to tailor ESG tools to clients’ strategies and transition plans.
- Asset management companies signed the Global Investor Statement to Governments on the Climate Crisis (2024).
- Supply chain climate risk management anchored in the Code of Ethics, procurement guidelines, and Green Procurement rules emphasizing life-cycle environmental criteria, energy and emissions reduction, waste and materials efficiency, and ESG risk governance.
- Supplier selection includes ESG, reputational checks, and alignment with the Group’s Environmental and Energy Policy; commitment reinforced by participation in UN-led sustainability initiatives.
- New platform (2023) integrated with Supplier Gate to automate supplier qualification, create a Global Score including ESG (supported by questionnaires and ISO 14001/50001), and provide dashboards.
- Incentivisation of higher-ESG suppliers via Global Score uplift; ESG questionnaire made mandatory for tenders in 2024 to map supplier maturity and drive improvements.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emissions metrics

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emissions metrics - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.1.12 Greenhouse gas emissions metrics
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its strategy to combat climate change in its own operations and at portfolio level, the Group measures and reports the effectiveness of its climate change mitigation and adaptation policies using the metrics below, which contribute to the achievement of its greenhouse gas emission reduction targets.
nodes.summary: Introduction to Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s greenhouse gas emissions metrics, outlining how the Group measures and reports progress toward its emission reduction targets under the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard. Defines Scope 1 (direct emissions from owned/controlled sources such as building heating and company car fleet), Scope 2 (indirect emissions from purchased energy like electricity, steam, heat, cooling), and significant Scope 3 categories (all other indirect emissions, including financed emissions, paper and office equipment production, and waste management). Positions these metrics within the Group’s climate change mitigation and adaptation policies and points to the subsequent section on gross GHG emissions for Scopes 1, 2, 3 and total.

nodes.title: Gross GHG emissions – Scope 1, 2, 3 and total
nodes.heading: 3.1.12.1 Gross GHG emissions – Scope 1, 2, 3 and total
nodes.start_phrase: This section covers, in particular, the metrics applicable to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions which apply to both own operations and the upstream and downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Section of a Consolidated Sustainability Statement detailing energy intensity denominator for high-climate-impact activities and comprehensive greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions metrics, methodologies, results, and intensity calculations.
- Energy intensity denominator (high-climate-impact sectors): net revenue of 65 million euro; other activities 51,893 million euro; total Group net revenue 51,958 million euro.
- GHG reporting framework: GHG Protocol Corporate Standard; covers Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (indirect electricity/heat/cooling; location- and market-based), and Scope 3 (significant categories 1–15).
- 2024 GHG results (tCO2e): Scope 1 = 45,280; Scope 2 location-based = 115,789; Scope 2 market-based = 16,656; Scope 3 total = 59,892,681.
- Total GHG emissions: 60,053,750 tCO2e (location-based) and 59,954,617 tCO2e (market-based).
- Geographic split (location-based total): Italy 35,128,121 tCO2e; Foreign 24,925,629 tCO2e.
- Scope 3 breakdown highlights (tCO2e): Purchased goods/services 7,179; Capital goods 6,432; Fuel and energy-related activities 25,645; Upstream transport/distribution 13,161; Waste 254; Business travel 5,959; Employee commuting 33,441; Upstream leased assets 2,419; Use of sold products 239; Downstream leased assets 3,489; Investments (financed emissions) 59,794,462. Scope 3 calculated with 26.4% primary data.
- Dominant driver: Category 15 (Investments/financed emissions) constitutes the vast majority of total GHG emissions; calculated on prudential consolidation perimeter and includes non-consolidated associates/JVs.
- Financed emissions methodology: aligned to PCAF; data source hierarchy—reported emissions (26.5%), physical activity-based, and economic activity-based proxies; attribution via exposure to counterparties vs their total liabilities; emissions data lagged to 2022.
- Residential Real Estate portfolio: estimated 2 million tCO2e (linked to the Group’s 2030 reduction target; details in Climate Report).
- Methodologies and emission factors: ABI Guidelines; electricity residual/national mixes from AIB/ISPRA/IEA/EPA; fuels from ISPRA/UNFCCC/EPA; district heating from supplier data/DEFRA/EPA/ISPRA; vehicle factors from ISPRA; lifecycle factors from Ecoinvent 3.5; GWP from IPCC AR.
- Scope 3 category methods detailed for categories 1–8, 11, 13; newly included in 2024 vs 2023: cloud services (cat. 1), employee commuting (cat. 7), upstream leased assets (cat. 8), downstream leased assets (cat. 13). Excluded as not applicable: categories 9, 10, 12, 14. Biogenic CO2 (Scope 1): zero.
- Renewable electricity procurement and Scope 2 market-based instruments: 81.3% of electricity covered by contractual instruments; 76.5% bundled (GOs, green contracts, PPAs, i-RECs), 4.8% unbundled (i-RECs for Egypt).
- GHG emission intensity (total tCO2e/net revenue): denominator net revenue used = 44,798 million euro (excludes insurance-related items to align with prudential Scope 3 cat. 15); intensity = 0.001338 tCO2e/euro (market-based) and 0.001341 tCO2e/euro (location-based). Even when considering revenue consistent only with category 15, intensity would be <0.003.
- Governance notes: country-level disaggregation applied; conservative treatment of leased/for-sale real estate; no significant subsequent events affecting GHG reporting.

nodes.title: Financed emissions
nodes.heading: 3.1.12.2 Financed emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As part of Scope 3 - category 15, in line with the methodology developed by the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF), the following priority of emission data sources has been established:
nodes.summary:
- Scope 2 contractual instruments: 81.3% of the Group’s energy purchases/sales are covered by contractual instruments; 76.5% are bundled and 4.8% unbundled.
- Renewable electricity certification: instruments used are Guarantees of Origin (GOs), “green” supply contracts, Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), and International Renewable Energy Certificates (i-RECs). Bundled instruments include GOs, green contracts, and PPAs; unbundled instruments are i-RECs used for Egypt.
- No significant events or changes affecting GHG emissions occurred between the Group’s reporting date and those of entities in its value chain.
- Financed emissions (Scope 3, category 15):
  - Data source hierarchy: reported emissions (26.5% of financed emissions as of 31 Dec 2024), physical activity-based estimates, and economic activity-based estimates using sectoral intensity and clustering by country/size.
  - Attribution method: based on the Group’s exposure (loans, debt securities, equity) relative to counterparties’ total liabilities and equity.
  - Emissions reference year: 2022, implying a two-year lag versus exposure data.
- GHG emission intensity:
  - Method: total tCO2e divided by net revenue.
  - Net revenue used: 44,798 million euro (vs. total revenue 51,958 million euro), reconciled per banking directive definitions.
  - Results: 0.001338 tCO2e/euro (market-based) and 0.001341 tCO2e/euro (location-based).
  - Revenue definition excludes insurance segment items (160, 170) to align with prudential scope; even using revenue consistent only with category 15, intensity remains below 0.003.

nodes.title: GHG emission intensity
nodes.heading: 3.1.12.3 GHG emission intensity
nodes.start_phrase: This section covers the intensity of GHG emissions, i.e. total GHG emissions in metric tonnes of CO 2eq compared to net revenue.
nodes.summary:
- Scope 2 contractual instruments and renewable energy sourcing:
  - 81.3% of Scope 2 electricity is covered by contractual instruments; 76.5% bundled and 4.8% unbundled.
  - Instruments used to certify renewable electricity: Guarantees of Origin (GO), “green” supply contracts, Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), and International Renewable Energy Certificates (i-RECs).
  - Bundled instruments are GO/green contracts/PPAs/i-RECs; unbundled are only i-RECs (for Egypt).
  - No significant post–reporting-date changes affecting GHG emissions across the value chain.

- Financed emissions (Scope 3, category 15) methodology:
  - Aligned with PCAF; data source priority: reported emissions (26.5% of financed emissions at 31/12/2024), then physical activity–based, then economic activity–based estimates (revenue × sector/geography/size emission factors from a clustering model).
  - Attribution factor based on Group exposure (loans, debt securities, equity) relative to counterparties’ total liabilities (financial liabilities and equity).
  - Emissions reference year is 2022, creating a two-year lag versus exposure data.
  - No significant post–reporting-date changes affecting GHG emissions across the value chain.

- GHG emission intensity:
  - Calculated as total GHG tCO2eq emissions divided by net revenue.
  - Net revenue used: €44,798m (vs total revenue €51,958m), reconciled to financial statements at 31/12/2024.
  - Intensity results: 0.001338 tCO2eq/€ (market-based) and 0.001341 tCO2eq/€ (location-based).
  - Net revenue definition follows the banking accounts directive; excludes insurance-related items (160, 170) to align with prudential scope and Scope 3 category 15. Using only category 15–consistent revenue would still keep intensity below 0.003.

- Internal Carbon Pricing (ICP):
  - Strategic shadow-price scheme applied to Green Banking Procurement, specifically centrally managed ICT purchases.
  - ICP factors electricity-related emissions of IT equipment into lifecycle cost; coverage includes laptops (99%), mini-desktops (100%), desktops (100%), cash-in/cash-out (100%), ATMs/MTAs (100%), monitors (35%), printers (81%).
  - Carbon price set at €57/tCO2eq in 2019; increased to €100/tCO2eq in 2023 (above NGFS €64 and within LCIA €50–160 range); based on a third-party study.
  - 2024 ICP-covered Scope 2 location-based emissions: 3,487 tCO2eq; coverage equals 3.02% of total Scope 2 location-based emissions. CapEx shadow price applied at €100/tCO2eq. No application reported for R&D shadow price, internal carbon fee/fund, or impairment testing.

- Anticipated financial effects from climate risks/opportunities:
  - Disclosure limited to information already available under Pillar 3, using phase-in for other elements.
  - Provides banking book exposures (loans, debt securities, equity not held for trading/sale), loans collateralised by immovable property, and repossessed real estate exposed to chronic and acute climate risks, broken down by NACE sector and geography.
  - Sensitive exposures presented separately for chronic-only, acute-only, and combined impacts.

nodes.title: Internal carbon pricing
nodes.heading: 3.1.13 Internal carbon pricing
nodes.start_phrase: Internal Carbon Pricing (ICP) is a scheme through which undertakings assign a monetary value to GHG emissions and integrate it (the “price”) into investment decisions and business operations.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on the Group’s Internal Carbon Pricing (ICP) scheme and disclosure of anticipated financial effects from climate-related physical risks aligned with Pillar 3.
- ICP purpose and scope: a shadow price used to internalize GHG costs in investment and operations to manage climate risks and support transition to a zero-emission model. Applied to centrally managed ICT procurement; residual non-centralized purchases are excluded.
- Application details: ICP targets Scope 2 (location-based) emissions from electricity used by IT equipment, using product certifications/supplier declarations. The carbon cost is added to lifecycle cost to inform procurement choices.
- Coverage of equipment: laptops (99%), mini-desktops (100%), desktops (100%), cash-in/cash-out devices (100%), ATMs/MTAs (100%), monitors (35%), printers (81%).
- Pricing methodology and levels: based on technical assessment of equipment energy use and environmental characteristics; informed by a third-party study and LCIA Environmental Prices. Price set at €57/tCO2e in 2019; increased to €100/tCO2e in 2023 (above NGFS €64/tCO2e), aligned with a 1.5°C pathway and within LCIA’s €50–160/tCO2e range.
- Quantified impact: 3,487 tCO2e of Scope 2 (location-based) emissions in 2024 covered by the ICP; this represents 3.02% of total Scope 2 (location-based) emissions. Table indicates application as a CapEx shadow price at €100/tCO2e; no use of R&D shadow price, internal carbon fee/fund, or impairment-testing carbon prices.
- Anticipated financial effects disclosure: limited to material physical risks per Pillar 3, using phase-in for other required information. Provides banking book exposure data (loans, debt securities, equity not for trading/sale; loans backed by real estate; repossessed real estate) to non-financial corporates, broken down by NACE sector and geography, and categorized by exposure to chronic risks, acute risks, or both.

nodes.title: Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.1.14 Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: This section covers the anticipated financial effects from material physical risks.
nodes.summary:
- Introduces the Group’s Internal Carbon Pricing (ICP) scheme as a shadow price integrated into investment and procurement decisions to manage climate-related risks and drive a zero-emission business model.
- Scope and application: ICP is applied to centrally managed ICT procurement (e.g., laptops, desktops, ATMs, printers, monitors), using product energy certifications/supplier declarations; residual decentralized purchases are excluded.
- Pricing and methodology: price set via third-party study and LCIA Environmental Prices; €57/tCO2e in 2019, increased to €100/tCO2e in 2023 (above NGFS €64/tCO2e; within €50–160 LCIA range); incorporated into lifecycle cost assessments alongside energy use.
- Coverage and emissions: ICP covers Scope 2 location-based emissions from electricity used by in-scope IT devices; 3,487 tCO2e in 2024, representing 3.02% of total Scope 2 location-based emissions; Table shows application to CapEx shadow price only.
- Anticipated financial effects disclosure: leverages Pillar 3 reporting for material physical risk exposures; focuses on banking book exposures (loans, debt securities, equity not held for trading/sale), including loans collateralised by immovable property and repossessed collateral.
- Risk segmentation: exposures classified by sensitivity to chronic (gradual) and acute (sudden) climate events, with breakdowns by NACE sector, geography, maturity buckets, credit quality (Stage 2, NPE), and related impairments for Italy and core European geographies.
- Physical risk methodology: uses external provider for asset-level mapping (collateral/counterparty sites); adopts NGFS Current Policies (RCP 6.0) as a prudent baseline scenario; notes concentration of significant physical risk in Italy and main CEE markets (Croatia, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Serbia, Hungary).
- Real estate collateral energy performance: provides EU/non-EU breakdowns of loans collateralised by residential/commercial property and repossessed assets by energy intensity (kWh/m²) and EPC label, indicating substantial portions with estimated EP scores due to certification requirements.
- ESRS E2 – Pollution materiality approach: conducts double materiality assessment (impact and financial) across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains, guided by Group policies and ESG risk governance and informed by internal/external experts.
- Impact materiality outcome: identifies negative, indirect material impacts in the downstream value chain driven by exposures to industries with significant pollution footprints.
- Financial materiality outcome: no material pollution-related risks in own operations; potential reputational risk in upstream suppliers; material credit and reputational risks in the downstream portfolio, notably related to air, soil, and microplastic pollution.
- Opportunities assessment: reviewed own operations and downstream product expansion for environmentally aligned offerings; no opportunities deemed financially material for pollution reduction at this stage.

nodes.title: ESRS E2 – Pollution
nodes.heading: 3.2 ESRS E2 – Pollution
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Scope: ESRS E2 – Pollution section of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, focused on the Group’s double materiality assessment (impact and financial) related to pollution across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains.
- Approach and governance: Assessment guided by internal policies and ESG risk governance rules, with environmental experts engaged. Methods included interviews with internal units and external stakeholders, ESG supplier questionnaires, and portfolio analysis. Impact criteria followed legal standards (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
- Impact materiality findings: Negative indirect material impacts identified in the downstream value chain due to portfolio exposures to high-pollution industries. Own operations and upstream impacts assessed but not identified as materially negative.
- Financial materiality—risks: 
  - Own operations: no pollution-related risks identified.
  - Upstream: potential reputational risk from suppliers with weak pollution management.
  - Downstream: credit and market risks (with associated reputational risk) tied to counterparties in high-pollution sectors; credit and reputational risks deemed material, especially related to air pollution, soil pollution, and microplastics.
- Financial materiality—opportunities: 
  - Own operations: reviewed initiatives to reduce pollution; none material given the business nature.
  - Upstream: no material opportunities.
  - Downstream: assessed potential to expand environmentally aligned products; none considered materially advancing pollution reduction among customers.
- Conclusion: Material risks arise primarily from downstream portfolio exposures; no material opportunities identified related to pollution management.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.2.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS E2 – Pollution within a consolidated sustainability statement, centered on a double materiality assessment (impact and financial) across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains.
- Method: Mapping of pollution-related impacts, risks, and opportunities using internal policies and governance frameworks; expert input; qualitative/quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood); supplier ESG questionnaires; portfolio exposure analysis for high-pollution sectors.
- Impact materiality results: Negative, indirect, material impacts identified in the downstream value chain due to portfolio exposures to high-pollution industries; own operations and upstream assessed but downstream dominates materiality.
- Financial materiality results: 
  - Own operations: no pollution-related risks identified.
  - Upstream: potential reputational risk from suppliers with weak pollution management.
  - Downstream: material credit and reputational risks (also linked to market risk), notably related to air pollution, soil pollution, and microplastics.
- Opportunities: Reviewed across perimeters; potential product expansion toward environmental objectives considered; no material opportunities identified for pollution reduction in portfolios or own operations.
- Policies: Alignment with UN Global Compact and Principles for Responsible Banking; recognition of finance’s role in addressing pollution and nature loss.
- New Rules on Biodiversity and Nature (prepared 2024, adopted Jan 2025): Aligned with ESRS E4; apply Group-wide; identify sensitive sectors (e.g., mining/extraction, transport); prohibit lending tied to sensitive activities in critical areas or in countries not party to key environmental accords (e.g., Montreal Protocol).
- Enhanced ESG/reputational due diligence for activities in countries not ratifying pollution-related conventions (Rotterdam, Basel, Stockholm); public transparency; governance of updates by CRO and CSO.
- Targets: Aim to integrate environmental/pollution risks into risk management and decision-making; current models/metrics evolving with a medium/long-term horizon; no specific quantitative targets yet.
- Actions: Deployment of S-Loan Progetti Green and SACE Green-guaranteed loans to support pollution prevention, control, and reduction; third-party environmental insurance for environmental damage and imminent pollution threats.
- ESG integration: Proprietary ESG scoring includes pollution-related factors (certifications, waste, pollution data) and feeds into credit frameworks and strategies.
- Stakeholder engagement: Partnerships, training, research, working groups, and awareness campaigns to promote pollution reduction and nature protection; signatory to the Finance Leadership Statement on Plastic Pollution.

nodes.title: Policies, targets and actions at portfolio level
nodes.heading: 3.2.2 Policies, targets and actions at portfolio level
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the principles of its Code of Ethics, Intesa Sanpaolo Group has joined major international initiatives such as t he UN Global Compact and the Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB), making it one of the premiere European financial groups to have joined all of the leading sustainability initiatives sponsored by the United Nations for the financial sector, within th e framework for achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.
nodes.summary:
- Context and commitments: Intesa Sanpaolo aligns with its Code of Ethics and major UN initiatives (UN Global Compact, Principles for Responsible Banking) to support the SDGs, acknowledging pollution challenges, nature preservation, and the financial sector’s role.

- New governance rules: In 2024 the Group prepared, and in January 2025 adopted, Group-wide “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature,” aligned with the E4 standard. These support own operations and sustainable lending for projects with positive environmental impacts.

- Sector and geography restrictions: The rules identify sensitive sectors with potential negative impacts on biodiversity and/or pollution (e.g., mining/resource extraction, transport). Lending is prohibited to counterparties and projects in these sectors when located in critical areas (such as protected areas or countries that have not ratified key environmental agreements like the Montreal Protocol).

- Enhanced due diligence: ESG and reputational risk assessments receive special attention for sensitive activities in countries that have not ratified major conventions addressing pollution, including the Rotterdam, Basel, and Stockholm Conventions.

- Transparency and oversight: An overview of the rules is publicly available. The CRO and CSO governance areas are responsible for updates, ensuring alignment with evolving regulations, standards, and best practices. The rules sit within the Group’s broader ESG risk management and risk appetite framework.

- Targets and methodology: The Group aims to integrate environmental (including pollution) risks into its risk management and decision-making. Current materiality assessments draw on developing models and data over a medium/long-term horizon. No specific quantitative pollution targets have yet been set; these will be refined as standards and data improve.

- Actions and instruments:
  - Financing: S-Loan Progetti Green and loans backed by SACE Green guarantees support investments that prevent, control, and reduce pollution.
  - Risk transfer: A third-party environmental insurance policy covers environmental damage, imminent pollution threats, and emergency conservation/restoration services.
  - ESG scoring: A proprietary ESG model incorporates pollution-related factors (environmental certifications, waste/pollution data from external providers) and feeds into credit processes, frameworks, and strategies.

- Stakeholder engagement: The Group fosters a culture of sustainable change through engagement initiatives, partnerships, training, research, working groups, and awareness campaigns, and is a signatory to the Finance Leadership Statement on Plastic Pollution.
