nodes.title: Customer engagement processes
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.2 Customer engagement processes
nodes.start_phrase: The Group is committed to ensuring clear and transparent access to its channels, encouraging customer awareness in economic and financial management.
nodes.summary:
- Defines a sustainability classification framework for credit products and loans across 277 categories (environmental, social, other), with eligibility based on: recognition by internal working groups, financing specific sustainable economic activities, targeting zero-emission sectors, or linking to sustainability KPIs aligned with company strategy. Classification occurs at application and is monitored throughout the loan’s life.
- Describes customer engagement practices to ensure clear, transparent access and needs-driven product development, including collaboration with industry associations (e.g., ACEPI), use of advanced listening tools and satisfaction surveys, direct dialogues with beneficiaries, and the Social Impact Roadshow 2024 to capture non-economic impacts.
- Highlights the Banca dei Territori Division’s inclusive credit solutions to address social gaps (e.g., low university attainment), using market research and focus groups; introduces Gamma Impact products for students and the unemployed with favorable terms and extended repayment; embeds continuous customer experience measurement and staff feedback to refine processes and services.
- Outlines remediation and complaint-handling channels (online, app, mail, email), emphasizing timely resolution, regulatory reporting by the compliance function, and a Code of Ethics mechanism for reporting non-compliance via a dedicated email to ensure substantive dispute resolution.
- Presents targets and initiatives to promote ESG within the 2022–2025 Business Plan, supporting companies and supply chains in assessing sustainability and developing transition plans aligned with the NRRP; details the expansion of ESG Workshops (exceeding the one-per-Regional Centre target), conducted with institutional and technical partners, and promoted across media to embed ESG as a business priority and leverage the ecological transition for innovation and growth.

nodes.title: Remediation processes and channels to submit complaints
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.3 Remediation processes and channels to submit complaints
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group maintains a constant dialogue with its customers to ensure top -tier service.
nodes.summary:
- Framework for classifying sustainable finance: 277 categories across environmental, social, and other sustainability; credit products flagged by internal working groups; lending classified as sustainable if tied to eligible activities, zero‑emission sectors, or KPI‑linked sustainability targets. Classification occurs at application and is monitored for stability over the loan’s life.

- Customer engagement and transparency: use of surveys, listening tools, and industry initiatives (e.g., ACEPI) to align products with evolving needs and improve advisory clarity; direct dialogues and feedback loops (e.g., Social Impact Roadshow 2024) to capture non‑economic impacts and drive continuous improvement.

- Inclusive credit solutions: Banca dei Territori Division develops socially oriented products to bridge gaps (e.g., low university attainment), using market research (Istat, Eurostat) and focus groups; Gamma Impact products for students and unemployed offer favorable terms and extended repayment to expand access to credit; ongoing customer experience and satisfaction monitoring across channels; staff feedback informs process and service enhancements.

- Complaints and remediation: multiple submission channels (online, app, mail, email, branch); emphasis on timely, effective resolution; compliance function provides regular (at least annual) reporting on complaint handling; Code of Ethics enables reporting of non‑compliance via a dedicated email for substantive dispute resolution.

- ESG targets and support for businesses: ESG prioritized in the 2022–2025 Business Plan; support for companies and supply chains to assess sustainability levels and develop transition plans aligned with the NRRP; expansion of ESG Workshops (exceeding one per Regional Centre) offering guidance with institutional and technical partners; broad promotion via press, website, social media, and partner channels; aim to embed ESG in decision‑making and position ecological transition as an innovation and growth opportunity.

nodes.title: Targets and metrics related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.4 Targets and metrics related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has set itself the objective of promoting ESG practices, included as a priority in the 2022 -2025 Business Plan, by raising awareness among companies and their supply chains and helping them to understand their own level of sustainability, as well as in establishing a transition plan geared towards more responsible and innovative models, in line with the ecological transition of the NRRP.
nodes.summary:
- Defines a sustainability classification framework for credit products and lending, spanning 277 categories (environmental, social, other). Loans qualify if they fund activities within classified categories, target zero-emission sectors, or are tied to sustainability KPIs aligned with company strategies. Classification occurs at application and is monitored for stability throughout the loan’s life.

- Describes customer engagement and product design practices focused on transparency and needs-based innovation:
  - Collaboration with industry bodies (e.g., ACEPI) to classify complex instruments and improve advisory.
  - Use of listening tools, market research, focus groups, and continuous satisfaction/experience surveys to refine offerings.
  - Direct consultations with beneficiaries; Social Impact Roadshow 2024 to discuss non-economic impacts.
  - Banca dei Territori Division (BdT) develops inclusive credit (e.g., Gamma Impact) for students and unemployed, with favorable terms and extended maturities; staff feedback feeds process improvements.

- Outlines remediation and complaint channels: submissions via website/app, mail, email, and branches; timely handling with annual compliance reporting; Code of Ethics provides a dedicated inbox for reporting non-compliance, aiming for effective dispute resolution.

- Presents ESG capability-building via Workshops:
  - Goal to help companies assess sustainability, set transition plans, and align with NRRP ecological transition.
  - Workshops co-developed with institutions and partners; promoted through Group and partner channels.
  - Expansion across Italy since 2021 (e.g., Brescia, Milan, Turin, Genoa, Padua, Bari, Palermo).
  - KPI: 16 ESG Workshops active as of 31.12.2024 (target 12 by 2025; no baseline value).

- Details actions and financial solutions for social inclusion and support to production:
  - S-Loan lines for SMEs/corporates:
    - S-Loan Diversity to advance women’s empowerment and gender equality.
    - S-Loan ESG to improve overall sustainable performance, including for non-profit enterprises and cooperatives.
  - Business Microcredit using the SME Guarantee Fund for start-ups, freelancers, and associations with limited credit access.
  - Business Gemma for female-led businesses and self-employed women.
  - Anti-usury loans enabled via foundations/associations under Law 108/96, using guarantees to prevent financial exclusion; results monitored monthly (exposures/benefit by region); available as personal and mortgage loans.
  - Cre.S.Co. (Credit for Community Development): partner-backed guarantee funds and subsidised loans for NPOs (including ATS), supporting socially beneficial projects and small organisations’ growth.
  - Gamma Impact via the Fund for Impact: subsidised rates and up to 30-year terms for high-potential individuals lacking access to traditional credit; approx. €110m disbursed in 2024, including:
    - Per Merito (unsecured student loans; ~€107m in 2024)
    - mamma@work (for new working mothers; ~€2m)
    - Newer products: Obiettivo Pensione, Per Crescere, Per avere Cura, Per Esempio.
  - Emphasis on measurable social impact and ongoing monitoring.

nodes.title: Actions related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.5 Actions related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group provides its customers with a wide range of medium - to long -term products with the aim of helping to find ESG solutions and supports the most vulnerable groups by promoting access to credit through specific projects and local partnerships.
nodes.summary:
- Expansion of ESG workshops in Italy: launched in 2021 (Brescia) and scaled to 16 workshops across multiple cities by 31 Dec 2024; 2025 target set at 12.
- Broad social inclusion and access-to-credit offering:
  - S-Loan lines for SMEs and corporates (Diversity and ESG) to improve sustainability and gender equality.
  - Business Microcredit Financing via the SME Guarantee Fund.
  - Business Gemma loans for female-led businesses and self-employed women.
  - Anti-usury loans guaranteed by foundations/associations under Italian Law 108/96, monitored monthly to estimate regional benefits.
  - Cre.S.Co. (Credit for Community Development): subsidised loans to NPOs via partner-backed guarantee/cost-coverage funds.
  - Gamma Impact via the Fund for Impact: subsidised, long-tenor credit for people excluded from traditional credit; ~€110m disbursed in 2024, including Per Merito (~€107m) and mamma@work (~€2m). New products include Obiettivo Pensione, Per Crescere, Per avere Cura, and Per Esempio. Impact measured with the mandatory RIM questionnaire.
- Retail customer support in housing:
  - Mutuo Giovani: up to 100% LTV, subsidised rates, fee waivers, flexibility; accessible to non-standard workers; strong market positioning.
  - Participation in Italy’s Guarantee Fund for Main Home Purchases (Sostegni-bis and extensions) to provide high LTV and competitive rates to priority borrowers (e.g., under 36, single-parent households).
- Consumer protection and governance: strict adherence to Consumer Credit Rules, automated usury and debt-to-income monitoring, robust complaints management, and controlled product development with transparent data and impact measurement.
- Financial education: “Finanza Insieme” (launched Sept 2023), a free, interactive platform with 350+ topics across Savings, Investment, Risk, Insurance, Pensions, Credit, Inheritance; modules span context, bias awareness, training exercises, and topical deep-dives.
- SME and ecosystem programs: Women Value Company (with Marisa Bellisario Foundation), Resto al Sud, Crescibusiness (ESG growth path), Imprese Vincenti, and Supply Chain Development including Sustainable Supply Chains.
- Corporate ESG enablement: group ESG training and in-person/remote ESG workshops and advisory.
- Social-impact lending governance and measurement:
  - Negative EVA impact ceiling (since 2023) to support high-social-impact loans with limited immediate economic return.
  - RIM-based impact assessment for “impact products” and NPO loans (≥€50k, ≥6 months), including outcome/impact analysis and SROI; ex-ante questionnaires active, ex-post planned/underway; feedback shared with clients and presented in meetings/roadshows.
- Support for women victims of violence: adherence to ABI agreement enabling 18-month suspension of mortgage/personal loan instalments (ISP also suspends the entire instalment); valid until 25 Nov 2025.
- Youth-focused banking: XME Conto UP! (zero-fee account for minors with free services) and Flash Up Studio prepaid card/app for students (payments, scholarships, campus services where applicable).
- Remittances: international money transfers via Western Union for migrant customers.
- IMI Corporate & Investment Banking: full suite of ESG financing (sustainability-linked loans/bonds/guarantees/securitisations/hedging) and use-of-proceeds instruments (green/social/sustainable bonds, green convertibles, renewable energy project finance); ESG Advisory Team (since 2023) supports clients’ transition plans.
- International Banks Division:
  - Bank of Alexandria (Egypt): microfinance-led inclusion strategy; ~€34m loans in 2024; client training with WFP; partnerships with NGOs, ministries, private sector; strong focus on small farmers, livestock, crafts.
  - First-home youth mortgages in six entities (CIB Bank, Eximbank, ISP Slovenia, ISP Albania, BiH, VÚB Banka): ~€263m disbursed in 2024.
  - Women/Youth in Business support (e.g., EBRD program in Serbia): ~€22m disbursed in 2024.
  - Pensioner-focused products in five geographies: ~€113m disbursed in 2024.
  - Training: webinars/workshops on circular economy, green/S-Loan financing, EU Taxonomy alignment, and sector impacts (e-mobility, food & beverage).
- Sustainable finance metrics and reporting:
  - Internal classification rules (end-2022) and reporting (from 2023) across three categories: environmental, social, and other sustainability (e.g., sustainability-linked covenants/KPIs).
  - 2024 disbursements: environmental €7.6bn; social €4.5bn (excludes disaster/urban regeneration loans); other sustainability €7.0bn.
  - 2024 stock: environmental €20.3bn; social €20.1bn; other sustainability €15.8bn; methodology notes on accounting vs operational balances.
- Investment and insurance with sustainability focus:
  - Asset Management Division policies aligned with EU SFDR: integrates sustainability risks, considers principal adverse impacts, and embeds sustainability in remuneration.
  - Coverage of products under SFDR Articles 6 (risk integration), 8 (ESG characteristics), and 9 (sustainable investment objectives).

nodes.title: Sustainable finance metrics
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.6 Sustainable finance metrics
nodes.start_phrase: For the purpose of greater internal and external transparency with respect to products and transactions deemed sustainable, the Group has decided to draw up specific rules for the classification of sustainable credit products and lending transactions, approved at the end of 2022.
nodes.summary:
- The Group established internal rules (approved end-2022) for classifying sustainable credit products, applied from 2023, covering environmental, social, and “other” sustainability categories.
- Category scope:
  - Environmental: targeted loans to Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit, and Corporate & Project Finance.
  - Social: anti-usury loans, products for vulnerable groups, Non-Profit loans, and other social loans.
  - Other sustainability: non-targeted loans with sustainability covenants/KPIs for Businesses, Non-Profit, and Corporate & Project Finance.
- 2024 loans disbursed: €7.6bn environmental; €4.5bn social (excludes disaster relief and urban regeneration); €7.0bn other.
- 2024 loan stock: €20.3bn environmental; €20.1bn social; €15.8bn other.
- Measurement approach: environmental figures use accounting balances for the Parent Company (incl. IMI C&IB) and operational balances for the IBD; social and other figures are entirely from operational balances.
- The Group emphasizes ongoing client dialogue to deliver sustainability-conscious investment, responsible lending, and insurance solutions, outlining policies, objectives, actions, and metrics across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Asset Management Division’s fiduciary duty includes integrating ESG, based on the view that high-ESG issuers support long-term performance.
- SFDR-aligned Sustainability Policy: integrates sustainability risks into investment processes and remuneration (Art. 5), considers principal adverse impacts (Arts. 4 and 7), and defines selection/monitoring methodologies.
- Product coverage spans SFDR categories: Article 6 (risk integration), Article 8 (ESG characteristics with good governance), and Article 9 (sustainable investment objectives), across all asset classes for mutual funds and portfolio management with appropriate pre-contractual disclosures.

nodes.title: Sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7 Sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance
nodes.start_phrase: The Group considers it essential to maintain an ongoing dialogue with customers, as a fundamental starting point for offering advice, services and products, in the knowledge that it plays a key role in investment assistance, prudent management of savings, and responsible lending, in addition to offering insurance protection.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Group-wide rules (approved end-2022, effective from 2023 reporting) for classifying sustainable credit products and lending into three categories: environmental sustainability, social sustainability, and other sustainability.
- Defines categories:
  - Environmental sustainability: targeted lending/products to Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit Sector, and Corporate & Project Finance classified as “environmental.”
  - Social sustainability: targeted lending/products such as anti-usury loans, offerings for vulnerable groups, loans to the Non-Profit Sector, and other social loans.
  - Other sustainability: non-targeted transactions featuring sustainability-linked covenants/KPIs for Businesses and the Non-Profit Sector, and Corporate & Project Finance.
- Reports 2024 disbursements: €7.6bn (environmental), €4.5bn (social; excludes disaster relief and urban regeneration), €7.0bn (other sustainability).
- Reports 2024 stock: €20.3bn (environmental), €20.1bn (social), €15.8bn (other sustainability).
- Explains methodology: environmental figures use accounting balances for the Parent Company (including IMI C&IB Division) plus operational balances for the IBD component; social and other sustainability figures are based entirely on operational balances.
- Introduces sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance, highlighting the Group’s client-centric advisory role across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Details Asset Management Division policies aligned with EU SFDR (Reg. 2019/2088):
  - Integrates sustainability risk into investment processes and advice; considers principal adverse impacts (Articles 4 and 7); embeds sustainability risks in remuneration (Article 5).
  - Applies Sustainability Policy across all asset classes and product types:
    - Article 6 products (integration of sustainability risks),
    - Article 8 products (promote environmental/social characteristics with good governance),
    - Article 9 products (sustainable investment objectives).

nodes.heading: 4.4.7 Sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance
nodes.start_phrase: The Group considers it essential to maintain an ongoing dialogue with customers, as a fundamental starting point for offering advice, services and products, in the knowledge that it plays a key role in investment assistance, prudent management of savings, and responsible lending, in addition to offering insurance protection.
nodes.summary:
Sustainability -conscious investment products and sustainable insurance  
 
The Group considers it essential to maintain an ongoing dialogue with customers, as a fundamental starting point for offering  
advice, services and products, in the knowledge that it plays a key role in investment assistance, prudent management of 
savings, and responsible lending, in addition to offering insurance protection. To this end, the following paragraphs outline  
policies, objectives, actions and metrics in asset management, private banking and insurance.

nodes.title: Sustainability-conscious investment products
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1 Sustainability-conscious investment products
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its fiduciary commitment to the Group’s customers and investors, the Asset Management Division (hereinafter, also “AM Division”), being a financial market participant, also has a fiduciary commitment to its clients and investors and, more generally, to stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Group-wide rules (approved end-2022, effective for 2023 reporting onward) for classifying sustainable credit products into three categories: environmental sustainability, social sustainability, and other forms of sustainability, with definitions and eligible loan types (Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit, Corporate & Project Finance; anti-usury and vulnerable-group products for social; non-targeted transactions with sustainability covenants/KPIs for “other”).
- Presents 2024 sustainable lending volumes disbursed: €7.6bn environmental, €4.5bn social (excludes loans for natural disasters and urban regeneration), €7.0bn other sustainability.
- Provides 2024 stock of sustainable loans: €20.3bn environmental, €20.1bn social, €15.8bn other.
- Explains calculation methodology: environmental figures combine Parent Company accounting balances (incl. IMI C&IB Division) and IBD operational balances; social and “other” figures are based entirely on operational balances.
- Introduces the Group’s approach to sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance, emphasizing ongoing client dialogue and responsible advice across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Details Asset Management Division policies aligned with EU SFDR (Reg. 2019/2088): integration of sustainability risk into investment processes and advice, consideration of principal adverse impacts (Arts. 4 and 7), and incorporation of sustainability risks into remuneration (Art. 5).
- Clarifies product categorization under SFDR in pre-contractual disclosures across all asset classes: Article 6 (integration of sustainability risks), Article 8 (promotion of environmental/social characteristics with good governance), and Article 9 (sustainable investment objectives).

nodes.title: Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.1 Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its fiduciary commitment to the Group’s customers and investors, the Asset Management Division (hereinafter, also “AM Division”), being a financial market participant, also has a fiduciary commitment to its clients and investors and, more generally, to stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Group-wide rules (approved end-2022, effective from 2023) for classifying sustainable credit products into three categories:
  - Environmental sustainability: targeted loans to Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit, and Corporate & Project Finance.
  - Social sustainability: anti-usury, products for vulnerable groups, Non-Profit, and other social loans.
  - Other sustainability: non-targeted loans tied to sustainability covenants/KPIs for Businesses/Non-Profit and Corporate & Project Finance.
- 2024 sustainable lending metrics:
  - Disbursements: €7.6bn environmental; €4.5bn social (excludes disaster/urban regeneration loans); €7.0bn other.
  - Stock: €20.3bn environmental; €20.1bn social; €15.8bn other.
- Measurement approach:
  - Environmental figures use accounting balances for the Parent Company (incl. IMI C&IB) and operational balances for IBD.
  - Social and “other sustainability” figures are based entirely on operational balances.
- Introduces sustainability-conscious investment and insurance approach, emphasizing ongoing client dialogue and responsible advisory across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Asset Management Division (AM Division) policies aligned with EU SFDR:
  - Integrates sustainability risks into investment processes and remuneration (Articles 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9).
  - Considers Principal Adverse Impacts (PAIs).
  - Applies to mutual funds and portfolio management that disclose under SFDR; excludes mandates with limited discretion.
- Shareholder engagement framework:
  - Commitment Policy for issuer dialogue.
  - Strategy for exercising intervention and voting rights at investee meetings.
- Governance for sustainability within AM Division:
  - Board of Directors defines and oversees the Sustainability Policy.
  - CEO/GM supported by ESG Committee; multiple committees (Risk, Sustainability) and functions (Compliance & AML, Risk Management) oversee implementation, risk monitoring, and policy adherence.
- External engagement and initiatives:
  - Signatory/member of CDP, Italian Stewardship Principles (Assogestioni), UN PRI, ICGN, IIGCC, Net Zero Engagement Initiative, NZAMI (with note on 13 Jan 2025 review and suspended reporting).
  - Ongoing participation in ESG best-practice forums and training.
- Annual review of sustainability policies by ESG & Strategic Activism with Compliance & AML to maintain alignment with evolving best practices.
- Private Banking (Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking) policies:
  - Integrates sustainability risks and PAIs into product selection, advisory, and insurance distribution; policies published internally and on the website.
  - Assesses product companies (asset managers and insurers) for sustainability risk management, PAI consideration, regulatory compliance, and adherence to ESG principles/codes (e.g., Net Zero, Stewardship Principles, Climate Action 100+, Nature Action 100), also via subsidiaries FAM and FAMI.

nodes.title: Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.2 Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.start_phrase: Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking , in line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s commitment to sustainable economic development, in accordance with the principles outlined in the Group’s Code of Ethics and aware of the importance of allocating resources according to social and environmental sustainability criteria for long -term value creation, has adopted policies on the integration of sustainability risks and information on the main adverse impacts on sustainability factors when selecting issuers, creating the financial product catalogue and providing investment advice and insurance distribution services (hereafter, these services are jointly referred to as “Advice”).
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Portfolio management mandates with prescriptive investment policies are excluded from certain sustainability processes due to limited manager discretion.
- Shareholder engagement: Activities are guided by a Commitment Policy (issuer dialogue, methods, topics) and a Strategy for exercising intervention and voting rights at investee shareholder meetings.
- Sustainability governance at Eurizon Capital SGR S.p.A.:
  - Board of Directors sets and oversees the Sustainability Policy.
  - CEO/General Manager, supported by the ESG Committee, propose integration of sustainability risks in investment, remuneration policies, and identification of principal adverse impacts; ESG Committee monitors implementation, screening strategies, portfolio processes, and external governance activities.
  - Financial, Credit and Operational Risk Committee oversees product risk exposure, including sustainability risks.
  - Sustainability Committee ensures fund management aligns with ethical principles in fund regulations.
  - Compliance & AML monitors adherence to the Sustainability Policy and regulatory controls.
  - Risk Management monitors sustainability risk of managed products.
- External engagement and initiatives: Active participation in ESG best-practice platforms, training and conferences; signatory/member of CDP, Italian Stewardship Principles, UN PRI, ICGN, IIGCC, NZEI, and NZAMI; note that NZAMI commenced a review on 13 Jan 2025, suspending implementation tracking and reporting.
- Policy review: Annual review by the ESG & Strategic Activism unit with Compliance & AML to align methodologies with evolving national/international best practices.
- Private Banking (Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking) policies:
  - Integrates sustainability risks and principal adverse impacts (PAIs) into issuer selection, product catalogue construction, investment advice, and insurance distribution; policies are available to employees and clients.
  - Counterparty due diligence covers: adherence to ESG principles/codes (e.g., Net Zero, Stewardship Principles, Climate Action 100+, Nature Action 100), governance and organization for sustainability, integration of sustainability risks into investment and remuneration, SFDR/Taxonomy-compliant product ranges and EET usage, compliance with ESMA 14 May 2024 guidelines on fund names using ESG/sustainability terms, and PAI consideration per SFDR RTS. Applied at onboarding and updated regularly within Product Governance.
- Advisory process and product alignment:
  - Collects client sustainability preferences during profiling.
  - Applies internal rules and a product classification model (primary/secondary markets) to match products with client preferences.
  - When mismatches occur, provides reasons so clients can reconsider preferences for the specific transaction.
- Private Banking sustainability governance and controls:
  - Sustainability Manager provides integrated oversight and alignment with Group initiatives.
  - Steering Committee holds a quarterly ESG session to set strategic initiatives and assess financial impacts.
  - ESG & Strategic Activism team ensures proper ESG management in asset management companies.
  - The Intesa Sanpaolo Chief Compliance Officer is responsible for implementing sustainability-risk and PAI policies in advisory and insurance distribution under a centralized internal control model.
  - Ongoing monitoring embedded in Product Oversight and Governance with metrics on product scope and consistency with client sustainability preferences.
- Targets and metrics (Eurizon, Business Plan 2022–2025):
  - AuM of UCIs under SFDR Articles 8 and 9: baseline 110 bn euro (31/12/2021); 156.6 bn euro achieved (31/12/2024); 2025 target 156 bn euro.
  - Share of AuM in Articles 8 and 9 UCIs: baseline 46% (31/12/2021); 76% achieved (31/12/2024); 2025 target 60%.

nodes.title: Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.3 Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the definition of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s 2022 -2025 Business Plan, Eurizon contributed to the Group’s expressed commitment to achieving global climate objectives, by committing to foster the transition to a low -carbon economy, starting with the evolution of its product range.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Fideuram – Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking’s and the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s ESG governance, regulatory alignment, product oversight, and advisory practices within a consolidated sustainability framework.
- Governance and compliance: establishment of internal ESG-focused structures, policies integrating sustainability risks into investment and remuneration, and centralized oversight under the Group Chief Compliance Officer; policy monitoring embedded in Product Oversight and Governance with specific metrics.
- Regulatory alignment: adherence to SFDR and the EU Taxonomy, incorporation of Principal Adverse Impacts (PAIs), compliant product documentation (including use of the European ESG Template – EET), and an internal framework to meet ESMA’s 14 May 2024 Guidelines on funds’ names using ESG/sustainability terms.
- Counterparty oversight: comprehensive sustainability due diligence of all product companies during onboarding and through regular updates, formalized within Product Governance processes.
- Client advisory integration: collection of clients’ sustainability preferences during MiFID profiling; internal product-selection rules to match those preferences; a cross-instrument product classification model and pre-trade consistency checks, with explanations and the option for clients to adjust preferences if a proposed transaction is not aligned.
- Sustainability governance: a Sustainability Manager with integrated oversight; a quarterly “Sustainability (ESG)” session within the Steering Committee to set priorities and assess financial feasibility; and an ESG & Strategic Activism team managing ESG topics across asset management companies.
- Targets and metrics (Asset Management – Eurizon): commitment to expand Article 8/9 SFDR products within total UCIs AUM—baseline 110 billion euro (46%) at 31.12.2021; final 156.6 billion euro (76%) at 31.12.2024; 2025 targets 156 billion euro (60%).
- Targets and metrics (Private Banking): monitoring the share of Article 8/9 SFDR products in total client AUM—baseline 19% at 31.12.2021; final 78% at 31.12.2024; 2025 target 70%.
- Asset Management methodologies (per Sustainability Policy, updated Nov 2024): 
  - Negative screening (SRI Binding by sector; PAI Binding by adverse impacts; ESG Binding by issuer rating; for sovereigns, carbon intensity vs GDP and FATF blacklist).
  - Positive screening (ESG integration and/or pursuit of sustainable investment objectives).
  - Stewardship/active ownership via engagement and voting.
  - Compliance monitored by Risk Management with Compliance & AML support.
- Product range and strategies: c. 156.56 billion euro in Article 8/9 funds at end-2024; most 2024 UCIs integrate ESG; key strategies include capital-protection solutions, flexible step-in equity exposure, and buy & watch bond portfolios.
- Mandates: all institutional mandates apply negative screening; extensive ESG and engagement reporting (e.g., 50 mandates worth 12.5 billion euro with ESG reports); 37 mandates for 22 non-captive clients (~9.5 billion euro) with specific restrictions/engagement support; 82 insurance/captive pension mandates (~48 billion euro) with Article 8 ESG integration.
- Private Banking actions: continued enhancement of the Group ESG Programme (launched June 2021), integration of sustainability across operations, development of ESG advisory in line with the 2022–2025 Business Plan, and adoption of a more detailed sustainability preferences questionnaire at end-2024.

nodes.title: Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.4 Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.start_phrase: In order to measure the percentage penetration of sustainability -focused assets under management, it was decided to monitor the percentage incidence of (AUM) products classified as Article 8 and 9 SFDR in the total AUM held by customers, as shown below.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Measurement and enhancement of sustainability-conscious investment products across Asset Management and Private Banking within a consolidated sustainability framework.
- Key metric: Share of customer AUM invested in SFDR Article 8 and 9 products. Baseline 19% (31.12.2021); 78% achieved by 31.12.2024; 2025 target set at 70%.
- Asset Management ESG integration:
  - Policy framework updated November 2024; methodologies to integrate sustainability risks into the investment process.
  - Approaches:
    - Negative screening: sectoral exclusions (SRI), adverse impacts (PAI), ESG risk ratings; sovereign exclusions based on carbon intensity and FATF blacklist.
    - Positive screening: ESG integration and sustainable investment objectives.
    - Stewardship/engagement: active ownership via voting and dialogue.
  - Oversight: Risk Management with Compliance & AML monitor adherence.
  - Scale and products: About €156.56bn in Article 8/9 funds at end-2024. Most 2024 UCIs (Eurizon Capital SGR, Eurizon Capital SA, Epsilon SGR) integrate ESG; strategies include capital protection, flexible “step-in” equity exposure, and buy & watch bond funds.
- Mandates and reporting:
  - Institutional mandates: all apply negative screening; ESG reports produced for 50 mandates (€12.5bn); engagement reports available on request.
  - Non-captive clients: 37 mandates for 22 clients totaling ~€9.5bn, with specific investment restrictions and engagement/corporate governance support (including Eurizon Capital Real Assets SGR and Epsilon SGR mandates).
  - Insurance and captive pension mandates: 82 mandates totaling ~€48bn with Article 8 ESG integrations.
- Private Banking actions:
  - Intensified Group ESG Programme (launched June 2021) to embed sustainability across operations amid evolving regulation and stakeholder expectations.
  - ESG advisory development aligned with the 2022–2025 Business Plan: Fideuram enhanced its advisory model to capture and manage client sustainability preferences.
  - Client profiling: MiFID-based sustainability preferences collected since 2021; a more detailed questionnaire introduced at end-2024.

nodes.title: Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.5 Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its Sustainability Policy131, the Asset Management Division has defined special methodologies for selecting and monitoring financial instruments aimed at integrating sustainability risks into the AUM Investment Process.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Sustainability-conscious investment products across Asset Management and Private Banking, with targets, methodologies, product ranges, mandates, reporting, and advisory enhancements.
- Key metric (Private Banking): Percentage of customers’ AUM in SFDR Article 8/9 products monitored.
  - Baseline (31.12.2021): 19%
  - Achieved (31.12.2024): 78%
  - Target (2025): 70%
- Asset Management ESG methodologies (per Sustainability Policy, updated Nov 2024):
  - Negative screening: sector-based SRI binding; PAI binding for adverse impacts; ESG binding via sustainability ratings for corporates; for sovereigns, carbon intensity vs GDP and FATF blacklist.
  - Positive screening: ESG integration into analysis/selection or pursuit of sustainable investment objectives, with good governance.
  - Stewardship/Active Ownership: engagement through voting and dialogue with issuers.
  - Oversight: Risk Management monitors compliance, supported by Compliance & AML.
- AUM and product offering (end-2024):
  - ~€156.56bn in Article 8 and 9 funds promoting environmental/social characteristics or with sustainable objectives.
  - Most 2024 UCI launches by Eurizon Capital SGR, Eurizon Capital SA, and Epsilon SGR integrate ESG; strategies include capital-protected products, flexible “step-in” equity exposure, and “buy & watch” bond portfolios.
- Mandates and reporting:
  - All institutional mandates apply negative screening; ESG reports produced for 50 mandates totaling €12.5bn, with optional engagement reporting.
  - 37 mandates for 22 non-captive clients (~€9.5bn): specific investment restrictions and engagement/corporate governance support (7 via Eurizon Capital Real Assets SGR; 1 via Epsilon SGR).
  - Insurance mandates and captive open pension funds: 82 mandates (~€48bn) with Article 8 ESG integration.
- Private Banking actions:
  - Intensified ESG program (launched June 2021) aligning with regulatory developments and societal expectations; integration of sustainability across business operations.
  - ESG advisory development per 2022–2025 Business Plan: since 2021, collection of client sustainability preferences via MiFID profiling; enhanced, more detailed sustainability preferences questionnaire adopted end-2024.

nodes.title: Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.6 Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.start_phrase: Regulatory developments envisaged by regulators and the civil society’s continued attention to the transition to a more sustainable economy have led the Group to further intensify its commitment, initiatives and improved approach to sustainability, confirming the focus and strategic importance of the ESG Programme launched in June 2021.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the excerpt: how the Group integrates ESG across Asset Management, Private Banking, and Insurance, with concrete targets, methodologies, product development, governance, and training.

- KPI and progress (Private Banking AUM mix): tracking the share of client AUM invested in SFDR Articles 8 and 9 products; baseline 19% (31.12.2021), 78% achieved (31.12.2024), versus a 2025 target of 70%.

- Asset Management ESG methodologies:
  - Negative screening: exclusions based on sector (SRI binding), adverse impacts (PAI binding), and ESG ratings for corporates; for sovereigns, exclusions tied to carbon intensity (per GDP) and FATF blacklist.
  - Positive screening: ESG integration and/or pursuit of sustainable investment objectives.
  - Stewardship: active ownership through voting and engagement.
  - Oversight: Risk Management monitors compliance with support from Compliance & AML.

- Asset Management portfolio and products:
  - ~€156.56bn in Article 8/9 funds at end-2024.
  - 2024 launches by Eurizon Capital SGR/SA and Epsilon SGR integrated ESG across:
    - Capital-protection products with varying horizons.
    - Flexible “step-in” strategies with staged equity exposure.
    - “Buy & watch” bond funds with decreasing duration.

- Institutional and insurance mandates:
  - All institutional mandates apply negative screening; ESG reports provided for many (50 mandates, €12.5bn), including portfolio-vs-benchmark positioning and optional engagement reporting.
  - 37 mandates for 22 non-captive clients (~€9.5bn; 7 via Eurizon Capital Real Assets SGR, 1 via Epsilon SGR) include specific investment restrictions and governance/engagement support.
  - Insurance mandates and captive open pension funds: 82 mandates, ~€48bn, with Article 8 ESG integrations.

- Private Banking ESG initiatives and offer:
  - ESG Programme (launched June 2021) intensified; sustainability preferences gathered via MiFID profiling since 2021; enhanced, more detailed questionnaire adopted end-2024.
  - 2022–2025 commercial goals to grow Article 8/9 share among total and new placements; in 2024, >85% of new products were Article 8/9.
  - Product alignment: 44 portfolio management lines brought to Article 8 (2 Fogli Fideuram, 17 Fideuram Omnia, 25 Wealth Collections).
  - “Il Mio Foglio ESG” (Article 8) expanded: clients can build bespoke portfolios from Article 8/9 strategies or choose risk-based “guided pathways” following a High Conviction, thematic ESG approach.
  - Fideuram AM Ireland: launched Fonditalia Clean Energy Solutions (Article 9) in June; introduced ETF D‑X platform (6 equity/bond solutions, 7 ISINs) classified Article 8.
  - Guided Open Architecture includes third‑party ESG solutions from leading managers.

- ESG culture and training:
  - Creation of “ESG Ambassador” role to promote sustainability, support sales/marketing, and capture client/partner needs; pilot finalized in 2024, full rollout in 2025.
  - Mid‑2024 event captured Ambassador proposals for role evolution; “Fideuram for the Environment” initiative initiated; end‑year proposal presented to top management.

- Insurance ESG governance and policies:
  - An Insurance Group Sustainability Policy defines governance, management, control, disclosure, and concrete E/S/G commitments; reviewed as regulations/context evolve and approved by the boards of all Insurance Group companies.
  - Investment Policy for ESG integration guides responsible investing, monitors risks/opportunities (e.g., climate adaptation, GHG, non‑renewable energy use), applies engagement (focus on long-term transition plans) and exclusions for non‑responsible/critical sectors; principles set by the Board and apply across the Insurance Group.
  - Non‑life: an Underwriting Policy (for Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione) establishes principles and macro-processes for underwriting in line with ESG considerations (details truncated in the excerpt).

nodes.title: Sustainable insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.2 Sustainable insurance
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s strategic objectives and the materiality that the integration of ESG factors has assumed for the financial and insurance sector, the Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group (hereinafter also referred to as the “Insurance Group”) has continued its development of environmental and social matters over the years, implementing concrete actions and initiatives aimed at increasingly consolidating internal governance and at the same time generating a concrete and material impact on its customers.
nodes.summary:
- The Division set escalating 2022–2025 targets to expand ESG offerings, aiming to increase the share of SFDR Article 8 and 9 products across total and new placements; in 2024, over 85% of new products qualified as Articles 8/9.
- Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking Asset Management SGR aligned 44 portfolio management lines to Article 8 SFDR (2 Fogli Fideuram, 17 Fideuram Omnia, 25 Wealth Collections) and expanded “Il Mio Foglio ESG” (Article 8) to let clients build custom ESG portfolios or select model portfolios using a High Conviction, ESG-thematic approach.
- Fideuram Asset Management Ireland dac broadened Article 9 and Article 8 ranges by launching Fonditalia Clean Energy Solutions (Article 9) and an ETF D-X platform with multiple equity and bond solutions (Article 8).
- Through a Guided Open Architecture, the Group complements in-house solutions with third-party ESG products from leading international managers.
- To support ESG advisory quality, the Group ran education and training initiatives and created the “ESG Ambassador” role: piloted in 2024 with full rollout planned for 2025. Ambassadors contributed proposals on role evolution, sales/marketing support, and training; the “Fideuram for the Environment” initiative was launched; end-of-year proposals were presented to top management.
- In Sustainable Insurance, the Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group strengthened ESG governance and risk management with defined roles, policies, processes, and monitoring tools aligned with evolving regulations.
- A Group-wide Sustainability Policy sets governance, management, control, disclosure frameworks, and concrete E, S, and G commitments, subject to ongoing review and Board approvals for all Insurance Group companies.
- An Investment Policy integrates ESG factors into the insurance investment process, monitoring negative impacts (e.g., climate adaptation gaps, GHG emissions, non-renewable energy use), growing ESG options, conducting issuer engagement on transition plans, and applying exclusions to critical sectors; it is Board-approved and applies across the Insurance Group.
- In non-life insurance, an Underwriting Policy for Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione establishes principles and macro-processes for risk selection (details partially provided).

nodes.title: Policies on sustainability-conscious insurance products - Insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.2.1 Policies on sustainability-conscious insurance products - Insurance
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s strategic objectives and the materiality that the integration of ESG factors has assumed for the financial and insurance sector, the Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group (hereinafter also referred to as the “Insurance Group”) has continued its development of environmental and social matters over the years, implementing concrete actions and initiatives aimed at increasingly consolidating internal governance and at the same time generating a concrete and material impact on its customers.
nodes.summary:
- ESG investment expansion in Private Banking:
  - 2022–2025 targets to increase the share and launch of SFDR Article 8 and 9 asset management products; in 2024, over 85% of new products were Article 8/9.
  - Alignment of 44 portfolio management lines to Article 8 SFDR (2 Fogli Fideuram, 17 Fideuram Omnia, 25 Wealth Collections).
  - Enrichment of “Il Mio Foglio ESG” (Article 8) with a curated ESG investment universe and guided model portfolios built on a High Conviction, thematic ESG approach.
  - Fideuram Asset Management Ireland launched the Fonditalia Clean Energy Solutions fund (Article 9) and the ETF D‑X platform (6 equity/bond solutions; 7 ISINs, all Article 8).
  - Guided Open Architecture broadened to include leading third‑party ESG products.
  - ESG culture and training: creation of ESG Ambassadors to promote sustainability and gather client/consultant feedback; 2024 pilot completed, full rollout in 2025; mid‑2024 workshops shaped role evolution, sales/marketing/training support; launch of “Fideuram for the Environment”; proposals presented to top management.

- Sustainable insurance governance and policies:
  - Group‑wide Sustainability Policy integrating ESG into governance, management, control, and disclosure, with Board approvals and periodic updates.
  - Investment Policy integrating ESG, with ongoing monitoring, issuer engagement on climate transition, and exclusion strategies for “not socially responsible”/critical sectors.
  - Non‑life Underwriting Policy (Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione) embedding ESG risk criteria; top management oversight.
  - Commitments to SDGs, PSI, UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, Equator Principles; membership in NZAOA (since 2021) and FIT (since April 2024).

- Insurance climate actions and product measures:
  - Decarbonization targets: 50% reduction in EVIC‑weighted carbon intensity by 2030 vs. 2021; net‑zero by 2050.
  - Exclusion thresholds include: unconventional weapons; ≥18% revenue from thermal coal mining/power or new coal projects; ≥10% revenue from unconventional oil & gas; issuers with low ESG ratings.
  - Active ownership: bilateral engagements with the 20 highest‑emitting portfolio issuers; focused dialogue with oil & gas to set science‑based targets, publish transition plans, align capex/strategy, cut methane, avoid unconventional/high‑carbon sources and sensitive‑area drilling.
  - Use of measurement and monitoring indicators; continuous application of exclusions and offering of SFDR Article 8/9 investment options.
  - Non‑life: emissions monitoring where data are available; participation in initiatives to advance ESG awareness and best practices.

- Insurance product offering with ESG focus:
  - Life and non‑life products primarily for Intesa Sanpaolo Group clients.
  - Life business (Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni—renamed from Intesa Sanpaolo Vita—and Fideuram Vita): Article 8‑oriented products integrating ESG; tailored solutions for families of disabled persons, minors/incapacitated (with Guardianship Judge), and non‑profit entities.
  - Non‑life (Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione): protection for people, homes, vehicles, SMEs/Corporate; features supporting sustainable mobility (e.g., EV breakdown services, distance‑based policies); coverage for catastrophic risks/natural events and renewable energy plants; support for clients’ digitalization and ecological transition.

nodes.title: Actions on sustainability-conscious products - Insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.2.2 Actions on sustainability-conscious products - Insurance
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group is committed to supporting the transition to a net -zero-emission future, strictly complying with the IPCC’s scientific indications and the objectives of the Paris Agreement and the NZAOA Protocol.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group’s ESG governance for underwriting risks, with Top Management responsible for implementing and monitoring governance per Board directives.
- Public commitments to international ESG frameworks: UN SDGs, PSI (2019), UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, Equator Principles; joined NZAOA (2021) and Forum for Insurance Transition to Net Zero (FIT) in April 2024.
- Climate strategy and targets: alignment with IPCC, Paris Agreement, NZAOA Protocol; 50% reduction in EVIC-weighted carbon intensity by 2030 vs. 2021; net-zero by 2050; focus on a just and inclusive transition.
- Investment decarbonisation levers under the ESG integration policy:
  - Exclusions: unconventional weapons; ≥18% revenue from thermal coal mining/power; new coal projects; ≥10% revenue from unconventional oil & gas; issuers with low ESG ratings.
  - Active ownership and engagement: dialogue with top 20 portfolio emitters; engagement with oil & gas and third parties on science-based targets, credible transition plans, methane reduction, avoidance of unconventional, carbon-intensive projects, and no new drilling in sensitive areas (e.g., Arctic).
  - Ongoing measurement and monitoring using specific indicators; application of SFDR Article 8 and 9 investment options and exclusions.
- Non-life portfolio: monitoring of investee emissions where data allow; participation in national/international initiatives to raise ESG awareness and spread best practices; development of new solutions and process strengthening.
- Product offering aligned with sustainability:
  - Life business (Intesa Sanpaolo Vita/Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni and Fideuram Vita): insurance, pension, and financial products primarily for Group customers; strong focus on SFDR Article 8 and tailored solutions for vulnerable groups (families of disabled persons, minors/incapacitated with guardianship) and non-profits.
  - Non-life business (Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione): protection for people, homes, vehicles, SMEs/Corporate; features for sustainable mobility (EV breakdown services, usage-based policies); cover for catastrophic and climate-related events; products safeguarding renewable energy plants; support for companies’ digital and green transition.
- ESRS G1 – Business Conduct: double materiality assessment methodology covering own operations, upstream suppliers, and downstream portfolios; engagement with internal/external stakeholders; analysis using scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood metrics.
- Impact materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: positive impacts from policies on integrity, whistleblowing, political engagement/lobbying transparency, anti-corruption/anti-bribery.
  - Upstream: positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: material indirect negative impacts linked to exposures in high-impact sectors on business ethics.
- Financial materiality and risk assessment:
  - Own operations: operational, compliance, and reputational risks, including cybersecurity and sanctions.
  - Upstream: reputational risk from suppliers lacking structured ethics controls (Code of Ethics, anti-corruption policy).
  - Downstream: credit, market, strategic, and reputational risks tied to counterparties.
- Integrated risk approach: considers geography, sector, and business type; monitors penalties for internal violations; selects suppliers on ethical/compliance grounds; performs legal compliance checks on counterparties; assesses risks across countries and activity areas for the Group, suppliers, and financed/invested entities.

nodes.title: Governance information
nodes.heading: 5 Governance information
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS 2 – General disclosures: Materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS G1 – Business Conduct within the Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Approach: Double materiality assessment covering impact materiality (inside-out impacts) and financial materiality (outside-in risks/opportunities) across own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (clients/investments).
- Methodology for impact materiality:
  - Interviews with internal teams and external experts.
  - Use of ESRS materiality metrics: scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood.
  - Own operations: evaluation of internal controls and corporate culture (ethics, anti-corruption, whistleblowing, political engagement/lobbying).
  - Upstream: ESG questionnaires to suppliers and analysis of responses.
  - Downstream: portfolio exposure analysis to high-impact industries on business ethics; consideration of investment/lending criteria.
- Impact materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts from robust policies and culture (integrity, anti-corruption/bribery, whistleblower protection, political engagement/lobbying principles).
  - Upstream: material positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: material indirect negative impacts linked to exposures in sectors with high business-ethics risks.
- Methodology for financial materiality:
  - Dual quantitative and qualitative assessment across scopes.
- Risk assessment highlights:
  - Own operations: operational, non-compliance, and reputational risks, notably cybersecurity and potential sanctions.
  - Upstream: reputational risk from suppliers lacking structured ethical governance (e.g., Code of Ethics, anti-corruption policies).
  - Downstream: credit, market, strategic, and resultant reputational risks.

nodes.title: ESRS G1 - Business Conduct
nodes.heading: 5.1 ESRS G1 - Business Conduct
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS 2 – General disclosures: Materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Section covers ESRS G1 – Business Conduct within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, focusing on a double materiality assessment.
- Defines impact materiality (inside-out impacts across own operations and value chain) and financial materiality (outside-in risks and opportunities affecting financial performance, financing, and cost of capital over different time horizons).
- Scope includes own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (clients/portfolios), assessed against the Group’s business framework, controls, and risk profile.
- Impact materiality methodology: interviews with internal teams and external experts; qualitative and quantitative analysis using ESRS criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
  - Own operations: assessed via internal controls and corporate culture (ethics, responsible practices).
  - Upstream: ESG supplier questionnaire and feedback analysis.
  - Downstream: analysis of portfolio exposures to high-impact sectors for business ethics (human rights, compliance, anti-tax evasion, AML, anti-competitive behavior), considering investment/lending criteria.
- Impact outcomes:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts from policies and strategies on integrity, whistleblower protection, political engagement/lobbying transparency, anti-corruption/anti-bribery.
  - Upstream: material positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: material indirect negative impacts from exposure to sectors with higher business-ethics risks.
- Financial materiality approach combines quantitative and qualitative assessments across scopes.
  - Own operations risks: operational, non-compliance, reputational—highlighting cybersecurity and potential sanctions.
  - Upstream risks: primarily reputational where suppliers lack robust ethics frameworks (e.g., Code of Ethics, anti-corruption policy).
  - Downstream risks: credit, market, strategic risks with associated reputational risk.
- Integrated risk management approach considers location, business type, sector, and operational structure.
  - Own operations: monitoring of penalties for regulatory/procedural violations.
  - Upstream: supplier monitoring/selection based on corporate soundness and ethical compliance.
  - Downstream: legal compliance checks before offering products/services.
- Country and sectoral contexts for the Group, suppliers, and financed/invested counterparties are factored into analyses.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 5.1.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS 2 – General disclosures: Materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Part of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement under ESRS G1 – Business Conduct, focused on double materiality assessment and corporate culture policies.
- Double materiality approach:
  - Impact materiality: Inside-out assessment across own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (clients/portfolios), using stakeholder interviews and qualitative/quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
  - Financial materiality: Outside-in assessment of risks and opportunities via qualitative and quantitative analysis across the same scopes.
- Methods and data sources:
  - Own operations: Evaluation of internal controls, ethical culture, cybersecurity, and sanctions exposure.
  - Upstream: ESG supplier questionnaire, analysis of supplier responses and ethical policies (e.g., anti-corruption).
  - Downstream: Portfolio exposure analysis to high-impact sectors on business ethics, incorporating lending/investment criteria.
- Impact materiality findings:
  - Own operations: Material positive impacts from policies promoting integrity, whistleblower protection, political engagement/lobbying transparency, anti-corruption/anti-bribery.
  - Upstream: Material positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: Material indirect negative impacts linked to exposures in sectors with higher risks in corporate culture and supplier relationship management.
- Financial materiality findings (risks):
  - Own operations: Operational risk and associated reputational risk tied to corporate culture.
  - Upstream: Reputational risk concerning whistleblowing protection and corruption/bribery issues among suppliers.
  - Downstream: Credit and reputational risks from counterparties with potential issues in corporate culture and supplier management; market and strategic risks considered.
  - Integrated risk approach considers geography, sector, business type, and operational structure; monitoring of penalties, supplier selection, and counterparty compliance checks.
- Financial materiality (opportunities): No opportunities assessed as financially material within business conduct.
- Corporate culture policies and governance:
  - Corporate culture positioned as foundational, aligned with integrity, sustainability, and social responsibility.
  - Key instruments: Code of Ethics and Internal Code of Conduct.
  - Code of Ethics:
    - Applies to all Group companies; part of sustainability management; covers stakeholder relations and key areas (human rights, labor, environment, anti-corruption).
    - Governance: Approved by the Board of Directors with Risks and Sustainability Committee support; monitoring by Chief Sustainability Officer Area and Chief Audit Officer; potential third-party assessment per UNI EN ISO 26000:2020; reporting to BoD, RSC, MCC, and Surveillance Body.
    - Alignment with leading standards (OECD Guidance and Guidelines, UN Global Compact, Istanbul Convention, EU Charter).
    - Implementation: Public availability; mandatory distribution and acknowledgment for directors, employees, collaborators; dedicated reporting channel with confidentiality and non-retaliation; constructive remediation via training for non-fraud cases.
    - Training: Mandatory, role-based programs; 2024 content update with tiered depth on compliance; ongoing awareness activities led by CSO.
  - Internal Code of Conduct: Adopted and overseen by governance/control functions; operationalizes conduct aligned with the Code of Ethics (section truncated).

nodes.title: Policies, targets and actions related to corporate culture
nodes.heading: 5.1.2 Policies, targets and actions related to corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase: Corporate culture is the foundation of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s identity and strategies.
nodes.summary:
- Part of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement focusing on corporate culture, governance, and financial materiality assessment.
- Financially material risks identified:
  - Own operations: operational risk and related reputational risk tied to corporate culture.
  - Upstream value chain: reputational risk regarding whistleblower protection and corruption/bribery.
  - Downstream value chain: credit and reputational risks from counterparties with potential issues in corporate culture and supplier management.
- Opportunities mapped in business conduct considered non-material from a financial standpoint.
- Corporate culture policies:
  - Corporate culture presented as core to strategy, integrity, sustainability, and social responsibility.
  - Code of Ethics and Internal Code of Conduct as key tools ensuring ethical, compliant, and inclusive conduct.
  - Governance and oversight: Board of Directors (with support from Risks and Sustainability Committee), Management Control Committee, Surveillance Body; monitoring by Chief Sustainability Officer and Chief Audit Officer through risk-based audits; potential independent third-party review aligned with UNI EN ISO 26000:2020.
  - Alignment with major international standards (OECD Due Diligence and Guidelines, UN Global Compact Ten Principles, Istanbul Convention, EU Charter of Fundamental Rights).
  - Non-compliance managed with proportionate measures and a constructive, training-oriented approach; protected reporting channels with confidentiality and non-retaliation.
  - Wide dissemination: publication on intranet/website; mandatory acknowledgment by directors, employees, and collaborators.
  - Training and awareness: compulsory, role-based programs; 2024 update introduces a general module plus three deep-dive levels on compliance with corporate rules.
  - Internal Code of Conduct adopted and monitored by governance/control functions, detailing expected and prohibited behaviors.

nodes.title: Policies related to corporate culture
nodes.heading: 5.1.2.1 Policies related to corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase: Corporate culture is the foundation of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s identity and strategies.
nodes.summary:
- Financial materiality assessment:
  - Own operations: operational risk and related reputational risk tied to corporate culture.
  - Upstream value chain: reputational risk linked to whistleblower protection and corruption/bribery.
  - Downstream value chain: credit and reputational risks from counterparties with potential issues in corporate culture and supplier management.
  - No financially material opportunities identified in business conduct.

- Corporate culture framework:
  - Core instruments: Code of Ethics and Internal Code of Conduct underpin integrity, sustainability, and social responsibility.
  - Governance and oversight: Code approved by the Board of Directors with support from the Risks and Sustainability Committee; monitored by the Chief Sustainability Officer area and Chief Audit Officer; reporting to BoD, RSC, Management Control Committee, and Surveillance Body; potential third-party review aligned with UNI EN ISO 26000:2020.
  - Alignment with international standards: OECD Due Diligence Guidance, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, UN Global Compact Ten Principles, Council of Europe Istanbul Convention, EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
  - Scope and adoption: Applies to all employees, directors, external collaborators, non-employee advisors, agents, and interns; subsidiaries adopt with possible stricter/localized provisions subject to Parent approval; branches may adapt to local law without altering principles.

- Training and implementation:
