  - Basis for preparation of the sustainability report.

nodes.title: Statement on due diligence in sustainability matters
nodes.heading: 5.3 Statement on due diligence in sustainability matters
nodes.start_phrase: The following table indicates where in the sustainability report information can be found on the due diligence process at KfW Group, including the way in which the main aspects and steps of the due diligence process are applied:
nodes.summary:
- Presents KfW Group’s due diligence framework for sustainability and maps each core element to specific chapters of the sustainability report:
  - Embedding due diligence in governance, strategy, business model, materiality and risk management
  - Engaging affected stakeholders across all steps
  - Identifying and assessing adverse impacts
  - Taking actions through defined policies and tools
  - Tracking effectiveness and communicating results
- Cites key instruments and topics linked to these elements, including: Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines, exclusion lists, Paris-aligned sector guidelines, 1.5°C alignment of financing, expansion of impact management and environment quota, SDG mapping, greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity actions and resilience, DEG Impact/Climate Commitments, and social topics (diversity and inclusion, remuneration, working conditions), plus value chain workers and customers (consumers, corporates).
- Explains internal controls and risk management for sustainability reporting:
  - Embedded in KfW’s group-wide internal control system and financial reporting processes, enhanced for ESRS
  - Risk identification and assessment at critical process points using a uniform matrix (financial, normative, reputational impacts and probability), documented in a risk control inventory
  - Main reporting risks: data accuracy, completeness, processing, and timeliness; mitigated via multi-stage, decentralised quality assurance and approvals (e.g., multiple-assessor verification)
  - Extension of controls to non-financial process owners via the “Restructuring sustainability reporting at KfW Group” project
  - Results integrated into group ICS rules and reported annually to the Executive Board and Board of Supervisory Directors
- Summarises ESG risk disclosures:
  - ESG risks are treated as risk drivers within existing risk types, not as a standalone category
  - Climate-related drivers primarily affect credit risk; counterparty governance affects credit and equity investment risk; internal governance breaches and information security relate to operational risk; demographic change and customer relationship quality affect equity investment risk
- Describes reinforcement of ESG risk management via a tranSForm sub-project:
  - Objective to enhance identification, assessment and management of ESG risks and meet regulatory requirements by end-2024
  - Central tool: ESG risk profile application covering banks, corporates, funds, securitisations, and countries (the latter added in H1 2024)
  - Integration of ESG risks into the group risk management cycle and instruments according to plan

nodes.title: Internal controls and risk management relating to sustainability reporting
nodes.heading: 5.4 Internal controls and risk management relating to sustainability reporting
nodes.start_phrase: Risk management in sustainability reporting is based on the established process-integrated internal control system (“ICS”) of KfW Group.
nodes.summary:
- Describes KfW Group’s sustainability reporting controls as integrated into the existing group-wide internal control system (ICS) and financial reporting processes, enhanced to meet ESRS-specific requirements.
- Explains the ICS risk assessment approach: identification, description, and evaluation via a risk matrix (damage types such as financial, normative, reputational; and probability), with hedging measures documented in a risk control inventory and informed by expert judgment and operational risk data.
- Identifies key sustainability reporting risks around quantitative data (accuracy, completeness, processing) and timeliness, mitigated through multi-stage, decentralized quality assurance and approval processes (including multiple-assessor verification) and leveraging established financial reporting controls.
- Notes that for processes owned outside Finance, risk handling requirements are formalized and published under the “Restructuring sustainability reporting at KfW Group” project.
- States that risk assessment outcomes and controls are incorporated into group ICS rules and reported annually to the Executive Board and the Board of Supervisory Directors, with further detail available in the risk report’s internal control section.
- Clarifies that ESG risks are not a standalone risk category; they act as drivers within existing risk types and are assessed through the risk inventory.
- Highlights key ESG risk drivers: climate risks mainly affect credit risk; counterparty governance affects credit and equity investment risks; KfW’s own governance breaches and information security threats relate to operational risk; demographic change and customer relationship quality impact equity investment risk.
- Outlines a dedicated ESG risk sub-project within the group-wide tranSForm program aimed at enhancing ESG risk identification, assessment, and management and meeting regulatory requirements by end-2024, without an ESRS results-based target.
- Presents the “ESG risk profile” application as the central tool capturing ESG risks of business partners (banks, corporates, funds, securitisations), with country profiles added in H1 2024, and notes the integration of ESG risks into the risk management cycle by end-2024, with further development steps to be detailed in the next section.

nodes.title: Disclosures on ESG risks
nodes.heading: 5.5 Disclosures on ESG risks
nodes.start_phrase: As is the case for all ESG risks, the ESG risks identified as material in the materiality assessment conducted in accordance with ESRS are not classed as an independent category of risk.
nodes.summary:
- Describes KfW Group’s internal controls and risk management for sustainability reporting, building on the group-wide internal control system (ICS) used for financial reporting and enhanced for ESRS-specific needs. It outlines risk identification and assessment via a standardized risk matrix (financial, normative, reputational impacts and probability), documentation in a risk control inventory, and mitigation through multi-stage, decentralized quality assurance and approval (e.g., multiple-assessor verification). Requirements for units outside financial reporting are formalized under the “Restructuring sustainability reporting at KfW Group” project, with outcomes integrated into group ICS and reported annually to the Executive and Supervisory Boards.
- Explains that ESG risks identified as material are treated as risk drivers within existing risk types rather than as a separate category. Climate-related drivers are mainly linked to credit risk; counterparty governance drivers affect credit and equity risks; internal governance breaches and information security relate to operational risk; demographic change and customer relationships affect equity risk. Further detail is referenced in the risk report.
- Details the ESG risk management sub-project within the group-wide “tranSForm” program, aiming (through end-2024) to strengthen ESG risk identification, assessment, and management, and to meet applicable regulatory requirements. The central tool is the ESG risk profile application for business partners (banks, corporates, funds, securitisations, with country profiles added in H1 2024), integrated into the risk management cycle.
- Outlines meta-measures for ESG risk management derived from national and European supervisory guidance: establishing an ESG risk profile database; integrating ESG risks into credit ratings; embedding ESG in risk and business strategies and risk appetite; collateral valuation and risk-bearing capacity; enhancing ESG stress testing; defining/reporting KPIs and KRIs; standard and ad hoc ESG reporting; integrating ESG into the credit process; expanding the ESG risk inventory; specifying operational and reputational ESG risks; assessing market price risk impacts; and increasing external transparency. Group-wide implementation with possible subsidiary-specific actions; planned detailed work packages were completed by end-2024.
- Reports completion (by end-2024) of KPIs for transition, physical, and other climate/environmental risks and related risk appetite, along with ongoing portfolio-level climate risk actions (use of ESG risk profiles and targeted ESG stress tests). Introduces a new group policy, “ESG risk management,” aligning with the 7th MaRisk amendment and the ECB Guide on climate and environmental risks; Risk Controlling will own the policy from 1 January 2025 after tranSForm concludes.
- Introduces the Environmental information chapter linked to KfW’s Strategic Objectives 2029 and the KfWplus transformation agenda, emphasizing sustainability and resilience. Identifies material environmental topics (climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, energy, pollution, biodiversity) and describes overarching targets and actions: SDG mapping of financing, 1.5°C alignment of financing activities, and an environment quota of financing above 38%. The chapter also covers sustainability policies, environmental exclusion lists, topic-specific sections (including GHG emissions, pollution, biodiversity, and material climate/biodiversity risks), and EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures.
- Provides SDG mapping methodology and status: aim to map 100% of annual new business to at least one SDG with disclosure of financing volumes per SDG; comprehensive review at transaction level; in 2024, 98.2% of new commitments were allocated, with a small portion not clearly mappable.

As KfW Group’s primary objective, sustainable promotion is at the heart of the strategic objectives 2029, in

nodes.title: Overarching environmental targets and actions - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.1 Overarching environmental targets and actions
nodes.start_phrase: Three targets are embedded in the strategic objectives 2029 with respect to the topics “climate change mitigation”, “climate change adaptation”, “energy”, “pollution” and “biodiversity” identified as material within the banking business:
nodes.summary:
Overarching environmental targets and actions
Three targets are embedded in the strategic objectives 2029 with respect to the topics “climate change mitigation”, “climate change adaptation”, “energy”, “pollution” and “biodiversity” identified as material within the banking business:
– SDG mapping of KfW’s financing activities
– 1.5° C alignment of KfW’s financing activities
– Environment quota of financing of more than 38%
KfW Group considers the targets to be in line with the orientation of the promotional policy and the focus 
on sustainable transformation in Germany and around the world. These targets and the corresponding 
actions are described in further detail below (for the “1.5° C alignment of KfW’s financing activities” target, 
see the corresponding section of this chapter).
SDG mapping of KfW’s financing activities

nodes.title: SDG mapping of KfW’s financing activities
nodes.heading: 6.1.1 SDG mapping of KfW’s financing activities
nodes.start_phrase: The United Nations adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in 2015, covering the three dimensions environmental, social and economic.
nodes.summary:
- The chapter “Environmental information” situates sustainability as a core element of KfW Group’s Strategy 2029 and KfWplus transformation agenda, highlighting climate and environmental aspects under the promotional principles of sustainability, transformation, and resilience.
- A materiality assessment identifies five key topics for the banking business: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, energy, pollution, and biodiversity. The chapter provides overarching targets, actions, and policies, and references topic-specific sections (climate/energy, pollution, biodiversity, and material climate/biodiversity risks) plus EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures.
- Overarching targets:
  - SDG mapping of 100% of annual new business (98.2% achieved in 2024), disclosing financing volumes by SDG.
  - 1.5°C alignment of financing activities (detailed in a separate section).
  - Environment quota of financing of more than 38% of annual new commitments.
- SDG mapping:
  - KfW developed its own approach due to a lack of harmonized indicators, aligning with the UN 2030 Agenda, German federal sustainability strategy, SDG Compass, UN Global Compact, and WBCSD guidance.
  - Mapping uses standard financing data, product/sector classifications, qualitative and quantitative impact indicators, and development markers; negative impacts are mitigated via E&S Appraisal, IFC Performance Standards, and exclusion lists.
  - Illustrative 2024 allocations show substantial volumes for SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities), SDG 7 (Clean Energy), SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 9 (Industry/Infrastructure), and SDG 8 (Decent Work; adjusted for mandated energy-stability transactions).
  - Topic linkages: climate/energy contributions primarily to SDG 7 and SDG 13; pollution to SDG 3, SDG 6, SDG 12; biodiversity to SDG 14 and SDG 15, with attention to the mitigation hierarchy and safeguards for indigenous peoples.
  - SDG mapping evidences intended positive contributions but does not quantify overall impact.
- Expansion of group-wide impact management:
  - The “tranSForm” program (through 2024) strengthened governance, impact management, 1.5°C alignment, GHG accounting, ESG risk integration, sustainability reporting, and data/IT.
  - From 2025, Group Development advances harmonized impact indicators (SDG-based), data quality, and automated methodologies for GHG savings (renewables, energy efficiency, transport/mobility), with phased technical implementation.
  - No planned use of biodiversity offsets or similar instruments within impact management; such aspects are handled within E&S Appraisal where needed.
- Environment quota:
  - Target set at a minimum 38% of new commitments; designed to ensure a sustained promotional volume in climate and environmental themes.
  - Eligibility criteria vary by financing type and reflect market norms of public promotional programs; the quota covers material areas of climate mitigation/adaptation, energy, and pollution.
  - Direct inclusion for programs or financings explicitly focused on climate/environment (e.g., renewables, e-mobility, carbon sinks, CCS, production of mitigation/adaptation technologies). Other project or corporate financings require demonstrated resource/emission reductions (e.g., waste, wastewater, air/noise pollution) to qualify.

nodes.title: Expansion of group-wide impact management
nodes.heading: 6.1.2 Expansion of group-wide impact management
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s strategic efforts in the area of “sustainable financing” were grouped in six sub-projects under the “tranSForm” project until the end of financial year 2024.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group outlines its impact logic from financing to intended outcomes and notes that SDG mapping clarifies contributions but cannot yet quantify sustainability impacts, prompting establishment of a group-wide impact management system.
- The “tranSForm” project (through 2024) expanded sustainable financing with goals to strengthen contributions to the SDGs and Paris climate targets and support a GHG‑neutral future in line with the Federal Government’s mandate, the Climate Action Programme 2030 and the German Sustainable Finance Strategy.
- Key tranSForm elements: governance enhancements, expansion of impact management, 1.5°C alignment of financing, development of a GHG accounting system, tighter integration of ESG risks, implementation of financial sustainability reporting, and data/IT enablement.
- A harmonised, group-wide understanding of impact and SDG-based impact indicators were established; Group Development will continue advancing impact management from 2025.
- 2024 focused on strengthening the data basis (availability and quality) for impact management and on automating existing GHG savings methodologies; centralised technical calculations are being phased in, starting with renewable energy, complementing prior methods for energy efficiency and transport/mobility. Ongoing reporting on methodological advances and indicators is planned.
- Impact measurement is the core of impact management; biodiversity offsets, mitigation actions, and local/indigenous knowledge are not planned tools, but relevant aspects are addressed via Environmental and Social Appraisal when necessary.
- An environment quota is a strategic target within the KfWplus transformation agenda: at least 38% of annual new commitment volume in the reporting year must qualify, defined as eligible new commitments over total new commitments. The self-imposed target ensures sustained climate and environmental promotional activity without stakeholder involvement in its setting.
- Eligibility criteria for the quota vary by financing type and reflect market-standard ambition and public promotional program conditions (no additional scientific input used). The quota covers material areas: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, energy, and pollution.
- Direct inclusion applies to programs with explicit climate/environment focus and to project/corporate financings for renewable energy, e‑mobility, carbon sinks, carbon capture and storage, and production of mitigation/adaptation technologies; in some programs only specific loan purposes qualify.
- Other climate mitigation or pollution-avoidance financings (e.g., waste, wastewater, air/noise control) are included only if specific reduction targets are met with proven resource reductions.

nodes.title: Environment quota
nodes.heading: 6.1.3 Environment quota
nodes.start_phrase: The promotional priority area “climate change and environment” is included as an element in the strategic KfWplus transformation agenda.
nodes.summary:
- Explains KfW Group’s impact logic from financing to outcomes, noting SDG mapping as an initial transparency step that does not yet quantify sustainability impacts.
- Describes the expansion of a group-wide impact management system under the “tranSForm” project to strengthen contributions to the SDGs and Paris climate goals, including governance, 1.5°C alignment, GHG accounting, stricter ESG risk integration, sustainability reporting, and data/IT enablement.
- Notes a harmonised impact understanding and SDG-based impact indicators, with 2024 focused on data availability/quality and technical/procedural upgrades; Group Development assumes ongoing responsibility from 2025.
- Details methodologies for measuring GHG savings (renewables, energy efficiency, transport/mobility), moving toward automated, centralised calculation; initial technical rollout in 2024 for renewables; ongoing methodological reporting planned.
- States impact measurement will not use biodiversity offsets, mitigation actions, or local/indigenous knowledge; such aspects are handled via Environmental and Social (E&S) Appraisals.
- Defines the “environment quota” as a strategic lever in KfWplus, targeting ≥38% of annual new commitments (Strategic Objectives 2029); self-imposed target to sustain high climate/environmental financing.
- Outlines eligibility criteria: direct inclusion for programmes/projects explicitly focused on climate/environment (e.g., renewables, e-mobility, CCS, carbon sinks, adaptation tech); other climate/pollution projects must show ≥15% reduction in resource use/pollution; energy efficiency must deliver ≥15% CO2eq reduction for new investments and ≥20% for replacements; business sectors ensure rule compliance and data quality; methodology unchanged year over year.
- Reports 2024 environment quota of 44% (slightly below 45% prior year, above 38% target). Headwinds: high EU reference rate and state-aid constraints dampened SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients volumes; positives: higher climate/environment shares at KfW Development Bank, Export & Project Finance, DEG, and KfW Capital’s Green Transition Facility.
- Summarises 2024 volumes/quotas by sector (EUR bn; environment quota): Group total 112.8/34.7 (44%); SME Bank & Private Clients 35.8/20.7 (58%); Customised Finance & Public Clients 41.6/1.8 (21%, with adjustments); KfW Capital 1.6/0.1 (4%); Export & Project Finance 23.9/6.6 (28%); KfW Development Bank 7.8/4.7 (60%); DEG 2.5/1.2 (48%).
- Highlights key 2024 programmes contributing to the quota, including:
  - Federal Funding for Efficient Buildings (10.0), Climate-friendly Construction (7.7), Climate Action Campaign for Corporates (1.6), Environmental Protection Programme (0.8) in SME Bank & Private Clients.
  - Development Bank financing in energy/efficiency/urban transport (2.5) and environmental protection incl. biodiversity, water/waste (1.2).
  - Municipal investment loans (0.5), Sustainable Mobility (0.3), Efficient Buildings – Municipalities (0.3), Climate-friendly Construction – Municipalities (0.2), and “Nature-based solutions” (0.2) in Customised Finance & Public Clients.
  - Export & project finance for wind/rail and other energy/mobility (5.0).
  - DEG renewable energy in developing countries (0.4).
  - KfW Capital Green Transition Facility for climate tech funds (0.1).
- Identifies “sustainable transformation” of corporates and public institutions as an overarching topic aligned with SDG contributions, the environment quota, 1.5°C alignment, and Paris-aligned sector guidelines; notes sector-specific roles (e.g., IPEX-Bank focus on renewables/mobility transition; Development Bank’s support across partner-country sectors; DEG’s tailored transformation/climate resilience work; KfW Capital’s climate tech investments).
- Clarifies target governance: environmental targets (SDG contribution, 1.5°C alignment, environment quota) are set annually with the Board of Supervisory Directors for a five-year horizon (from FY 2024), monitored via the internal control system, and adjusted as needed through annual strategic reviews.
- Lists overarching policies on climate, energy, pollution, and biodiversity, including E&S Appraisal guidelines and exclusion lists; policies are embedded in procedural rules, reviewed annually, and assigned clear responsibilities; business-sector guidelines (Development Bank, IPEX-Bank, DEG) operationalise the sustainability mission and E&S standards.

nodes.title: Additional information on KfW Group’s environmental targets
nodes.heading: 6.1.4 Additional information on KfW Group’s environmental targets
nodes.start_phrase: The strategic objectives, including the environmental targets enshrined in them (SDG contribution of KfW’s financing activities, 1.5°C alignment of KfW’s financing activities, environment quota), are defined annually with the Board of Supervisory Directors.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group designates the sustainable transformation of corporate customers and public institutions as an overarching material topic within climate and environmental management.
- Transformation efforts are aligned with the SDG contribution of financing activities, the environment quota, the 1.5°C target, and Paris-aligned sector guidelines.
- Business sector contributions:
  - Customised Finance & Public Clients and SME Bank & Private Clients: financing for renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable mobility, and environmental protection (with commitment volumes referenced elsewhere).
  - KfW Capital: “Green Transition Facility” investing via venture capital funds in start-ups and tech companies driving environmental change.
  - KfW IPEX-Bank: financing projects that enable digital and sustainable business, prioritising renewable energy and mobility transition to support 1.5°C alignment.
  - KfW Development Bank: support in partner countries for renewable energy, environmental protection, sustainable agriculture, education, and health, in collaboration with governments and local stakeholders, aiming for long-term economic, social, and environmental benefits (commitments referenced elsewhere).
  - DEG: tailored transformation support to build sustainable and climate-resilient businesses aligned with the SDGs (with further details in DEG Impact/Climate Commitments).
- Environmental targets are embedded in annually defined strategic objectives (including SDG contribution, 1.5°C alignment, and environment quota), agreed with the Board of Supervisory Directors; they apply for five years from financial year 2024 under “Strategic objectives 2029,” are reviewed annually, and monitored within the internal control system with root-cause analysis for any shortfalls.
- Overarching environmental policies cover climate, energy, pollution, and biodiversity, including E&S Appraisal guidelines and exclusion lists; topic-specific policies on climate/energy, biodiversity, and ESG risks are detailed in dedicated sections. Policies are integrated into procedural rules, reviewed annually, and have clearly assigned responsibilities in the Organisation Manual.
- Environmental and Social Appraisal (E&S) Guidelines apply internationally recognised standards; sector-specific sustainability guidelines specify E&S requirements for KfW Development Bank, KfW IPEX-Bank, and DEG.

nodes.title: Overarching policies
nodes.heading: 6.2 Overarching policies
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s overarching policies regarding the topics of climate, energy, pollution and biodiversity are presented in the following chapter.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group positions the sustainable transformation of corporate customers and public institutions as an overarching material topic, aligned with SDG contribution targets, an environment quota, a 1.5°C financing alignment, and Paris-aligned sector guidelines.
- Business sector contributions:
  - SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients: financing for renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable mobility, and environmental protection.
  - KfW Capital: “Green Transition Facility” investing via VC funds in start-ups/tech firms enabling environmental change.
  - KfW IPEX-Bank: focus on digital and sustainable projects, prioritising renewables and mobility transition.
  - KfW Development Bank: supports partner countries across renewables, environmental protection, sustainable agriculture, education, and health with long-term socio-economic-environmental impacts.
  - DEG: works with clients on tailored, climate-resilient transformation aligned with SDGs.
- Environmental targets and governance: strategic objectives (including SDG contribution, 1.5°C alignment, environment quota) are set annually with the Board of Supervisory Directors, apply as “Strategic objectives 2029” from FY 2024 for five years, reviewed annually, and monitored via the internal control system with root-cause analysis for shortfalls.
- Overarching sustainability policies: E&S Appraisal and exclusion lists complemented by topic-specific climate, energy, biodiversity, and ESG risk policies; policies are embedded in procedures, reviewed annually, and have defined responsibilities.
- E&S Appraisal framework:
  - Uses IFC Performance Standards or World Bank ESS, EHS Guidelines, ILO Core Labour Standards, and applicable national standards; sector add-ons include Equator Principles (KfW IPEX-Bank), EDFI standards (DEG), BMZ requirements/human rights strategy (KfW Development Bank).
  - Covers pollution prevention, biodiversity, labour/working conditions, community health/safety, resettlement, indigenous peoples, and cultural heritage.
  - Two-step process: screening/categorisation (A, B+, B, C; FI categories for intermediaries) followed by in-depth assessment for higher-risk projects.
  - Mitigation/offset actions are binding; regular reporting and corrective measures are required; projects with unacceptable residual impacts are not financed.
  - EU/OECD high-income investments primarily benchmark national standards; outside these, both national and international standards apply.
- Domestic promotional business guideline (SME Bank & Private Clients; Customised Finance & Public Clients): uniform E&S framework for direct and on-lending; product-level use-of-proceeds screening informs simplified vs in-depth assessment; actions set for material gaps; partners expected to have proportionate E&S procedures/ESMS; KfW conducts spot checks.
- KfW IPEX-Bank guideline: Equator Principles-based; all financings subject to E&S requirements; independent expert monitoring for category A and B+; contractual reporting; project-level grievance mechanisms and documentation.
- KfW Development Bank guideline: applies to all projects; integrates E&S and climate mainstreaming (mitigation and adaptation) from project inception; aligns with BMZ concepts; embeds sustainability in procurement; requires ESS10-compliant grievance mechanisms; supports E&S documentation via BMZ funds; conducts on-site controls and can mandate third-party monitoring; resettlement/livelihood restoration undergo separate final audits.
- DEG guideline: EDFI/IFC-based E&S due diligence with risk categorisation; project-specific ESAPs for medium/high risks; annual client reporting; internal and external annual audits of process compliance.
- Group-wide exclusion list: bars financing linked to unacceptable climate, environmental, and social risks, including radioactive materials and unbound asbestos, new nuclear power plants (except hazard-reduction for existing assets), uranium mining, upstream coal/oil/gas and associated activities, and projects threatening protected ecosystems without adequate offsets; also excludes activities banned under international conventions (e.g., ozone-depleting substances, CITES-listed species); sets qualitative conditions for palm oil, forestry (RSPO/FSC), and large reservoirs/hydropower.
- KfW Capital exclusion list: extends Group exclusions to oil/gas upstream and midstream, new oil power plants, substantial hazardous chemicals, commercial logging in semi-natural tropical rainforests, non-medical animal testing products, fur-related activities, shark fins, and whaling; compliance ensured through due diligence and contractual terms.
- DEG exclusion list: applies EDFI Harmonised Exclusion List; compliance monitored via DEG’s internal controls; aligns with Group exclusions on pollution and biodiversity.
- Monitoring and accountability across entities: binding action plans, periodic reporting, independent expert reviews where needed, grievance mechanisms, and corrective enforcement ensure ongoing compliance with environmental and social requirements.

nodes.title: Overarching policies - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.2 Overarching policies
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s overarching policies regarding the topics of climate, energy, pollution and biodiversity are presented in the following chapter.
nodes.summary:
Overarching policies
KfW Group’s overarching policies regarding the topics of climate, energy, pollution and biodiversity are presented in the following chapter. The focus is particularly on the aspects that address the material environmental topics emphasised in the “Environmental information” chapter. This comprises the guidelines on E&S Appraisals and exclusion lists. Further – topic-specific – policies on climate, energy and biodiversity and ESG risks are set out in the “Specific disclosures: Climate and energy” and “Specific disclosures: Biodiversity” sections of this chapter and the “Disclosures on ESG risks” section in the “General information” chapter. Sustainability policies and guidance are included in KfW Group’s procedural rules and are subject to an annual review including consultation with the responsible units. The fixed responsibilities for each policy and guidance are defined in the Organisation Manual.

nodes.title: Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines
nodes.heading: 6.2.1 Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Extract from KfW Group’s 2024 Combined non-financial report (Environmental information) covering exclusions, climate and energy disclosures, financed and operational GHG emissions, 1.5°C alignment and sector guidelines, DEG climate commitments, and biodiversity and pollution topics.

- Exclusion lists:
  - KfW Capital applies an exclusion list (building on KfW Group, IFC and EIF lists) to restrict activities misaligned with ethical, social and environmental standards; compliance is due-diligenced and contractually required.
  - Additional exclusions beyond Group list: upstream/midstream oil and gas (transport/storage), new oil power plants; production/trade of significant quantities of hazardous chemicals; biodiversity-related bans (commercial logging in semi-natural tropical rainforests; non-medical animal testing products, with life-sciences exceptions; fur farming/trade; shark fin and commercial whaling). Social consequences of biodiversity impacts are not separately covered.
  - DEG follows the Harmonised EDFI Exclusion List; implementation is mandatory via E&S appraisal and internal controls.

- Climate and energy: GHG accounting framework
  - First-time 2024 group-wide GHG accounting aligned with ESRS, GHG Protocol (2024 Corporate Standard) and PCAF (Part A).
  - 2024 total gross emissions (market-based): 144,592,421 tCO2e; Scope 1: 3,917; Scope 2 MB: 1,996 (LB: 11,627); significant Scope 3: 144,586,508, mostly Category 15 (investments) at 144,510,150 tCO2e.
  - GHG intensity: 6,601 tCO2e per EUR million net revenue.

- Operational (banking operations) emissions:
  - 2024 total market-based: 82,271 tCO2e across Scope 1, 2 and significant Scope 3 categories (1, 2, 6, 7).
  - German operations purchase 100% green electricity; 86.5% covered by bundled contractual instruments.
  - Emissions calculated using activity data and standard databases (ecoinvent, EEA, USEPA, DEFRA, UBA, IPCC); 7.4% of Scope 3 (excl. Cat. 15) uses primary supplier data.
  - Foreign locations included via extrapolation; results involve estimates and judgments.

- Financed emissions (banking business):
  - Calculated per PCAF across seven asset classes; coverage: 80.1% of total assets.
  - 2024 financed emissions: 144,510,150 tCO2e (Scope 1: 52.84%; Scope 2: 4.54%; Scope 3: 42.62%).
  - Emission concentration: Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply (NACE D) and Transportation and storage (NACE H) together 57.5%; Manufacturing (NACE C) 12.4%.
  - Portfolio economic intensity: 0.331 tCO2e per EUR thousand on EUR 436.8bn financing volume.
  - Data quality: average PCAF Data Quality Score 4.55; 14.1% of financed emissions based on primary reported data; plan to improve data quality and methodology.

- 1.5°C alignment targets and governance:
  - Group sustainability target split into 1) 1.5°C alignment of new financing and 2) portfolio GHG neutrality by mid-century; 2024 set as base year, first progress measurement end-2025.
  - Paris-aligned sector guidelines are the key steering tool; responsibility sits with business sector heads and subsidiary boards; Sustainability Strategy division monitors implementation.

- Paris-aligned sector guidelines:
  - Define science-based, sector-specific minimum requirements for high-emitting sectors, aligned with IEA Net Zero by 2050; balance transformative and transitional technologies while avoiding lock-in.
  - Updated since 2021: strengthened 1.5°C alignment (2022), shipping steered via Poseidon Principles, oil and gas guidelines added in Dec 2023.
  - Applied to new financing with limited exceptions (e.g., federal mandates); embedded in product design, eligibility criteria, contracts, and loan processes across business sectors. KfW Capital currently mostly out of scope but will apply if relevant.

- Actions to achieve 1.5°C alignment:
  - Group-wide GHG accounting built under the tranSForm project to track decarbonisation impacts of sector guidelines.
  - Promotion and financing programs contributing to the environment quota support the transition, subject to refinancing capacity.

- DEG Impact/Climate Commitments:
  - Three commitments (since 2022): enhance development impacts, align with 1.5°C and reduce emissions via a science-based pathway, and support client transformation; target neutral portfolio by 2040 through permanent removals (sink projects).
  - Intensity reduction pathway: average −4.2% per year from 2025 vs. 2021 baseline (413 tCO2e/EUR million), aligned with SBTi absolute contraction; applies to financed emissions from own funds.
  - 2024 actions: climate data-driven customer selection; piloting department carbon budgets (from 2025); client transformation support via CARI and DERa enhancements; investments and guarantees for carbon sink projects; digitised GHG data capture.

- Pollution:
  - Material positive impacts (financing environmental projects) and negative impacts (financing polluting sectors) identified; managed via cross-cutting targets and policies (sustainability guidelines and exclusion lists).

- Biodiversity:
  - Biodiversity roadmap (BioDiv-Roadmap) progressed in 2024 (phase 2): status quo, portfolio/materiality/regulatory/peer analyses, partnership scoping; sets action areas for 2025–2026 to develop and implement a group biodiversity strategy, expand positive-impact projects, reduce negative impacts in new business, manage risks, and begin selective biodiversity data collection.
  - KfW Development Bank focus: EUR 0.5bn in 2024 for projects with biodiversity as primary/secondary objective, OECD DAC biodiversity/tropical forest-labelled.
  - Policies in E&S appraisal: IFC Performance Standard 6 / World Bank ESS6 address habitat loss, fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological/nutrient/pollution impacts, endangered species safeguards, ecosystem services; PS7/ESS7 ensure indigenous peoples’ FPIC and social safeguards.
  - Climate-related biodiversity drivers managed via sector guidelines and exclusion lists; no additional group-specific land/ocean/deforestation policies beyond existing E&S guidelines.

- ESG risk perspective:
  - 2024 risk inventory assessed biodiversity risk drivers (e.g., ocean acidification, resource scarcity, dependency on ecosystem services, land/sea use, pollution, species exploitation, resource costs); none deemed material for the year across risk types.

nodes.title: Exclusion lists at KfW Group
nodes.heading: 6.2.2 Exclusion lists at KfW Group
nodes.summary:
- Biodiversity policy framework: KfW applies IFC Performance Standards/World Bank ESS, especially PS6/ESS6, to identify, avoid and minimize biodiversity and ecosystem service impacts (habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient and other pollution), excludes projects that would cause net reductions of endangered species, and requires prevention of invasive species and land degradation. Social dimensions are covered via PS7/ESS7 on Indigenous Peoples (free, prior, informed consent and consultation). No additional KfW-specific policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas or deforestation beyond these standards. Climate change as a biodiversity driver is addressed indirectly via climate mainstreaming, ESS6 in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline, Paris-aligned sector guidelines, and exclusion lists.

- Climate and biodiversity risk disclosures: General ESG risk management is referenced elsewhere; specific biodiversity risk resilience analysis (FY2024 risk inventory) defined drivers such as ocean acidification, resource scarcity, dependence on ecosystem services, land/sea use, water/soil pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, and rising resource costs. Potential impacts are mainly through credit and equity risks (higher PDs). A two-step assessment (sector-based screening, then counterparty ESG risk profile with mitigants) found no biodiversity risk drivers material in 2024; stakeholders were not separately included.

- EU Taxonomy context (Article 8): Outlines the EU sustainable finance framework, six environmental objectives, technical screening criteria, and phased reporting. In 2024, financial institutions disclose eligibility for all six objectives and alignment for climate mitigation/adaptation only; full alignment reporting for all objectives begins in 2025. Credit institutions disclose the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) per DDA templates, based on counterparty data, plus qualitative disclosures; banking operations are excluded. Scope is tied to NFRD/CSR-RUG, with CSRD pending transposition as of 31 Dec 2024.

- Application at KfW Group: Sustainability is core to strategy; the “tranSForm” project governs taxonomy implementation. KfW voluntarily publishes group-wide taxonomy KPIs for 2024; KfW IPEX-Bank has reported since 2021 and uses consolidated reporting at group level. KfW supports the taxonomy’s transparency aims but highlights limitations: large portions of its promotional portfolio (sovereigns, supranationals, non-EU counterparties, and SMEs outside NFRD/CSRD) fall outside mandatory screening; the taxonomy’s current focus skews toward climate-related activities; high ambition levels and data gaps depress alignment rates. Consequently, taxonomy results are not yet used to steer business sectors or financing decisions, though selected products reference taxonomy criteria (notably “substantial contribution”).

- Reporting basis and metrics: Taxonomy KPIs use IFRS gross carrying amounts, FinRep classifications for counterparties and product groups, and the regulatory consolidated group consistent with financial consolidation. The GAR measures the share of taxonomy-aligned exposures within covered assets.

nodes.title: Specific disclosures: Climate and energy - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.3 Specific disclosures: Climate and energy
nodes.summary:
Specific disclosures: Climate and energy
KfW Group sees an important role for itself in the transformation of the economy and society with the aim of improving economic, environmental and social living conditions. KfW Group wants to live up to its responsibility in the climate-friendly transformation with the aim of achieving the 1.5° C alignment of its new business. 
The Paris-aligned sector guidelines for emission-intensive sectors serve as an implementation tool for this target and are presented in this chapter as well as the measures adopted to achieve 1.5° C alignment for 
new business. In addition, DEG’s targets and activities in connection with climate and energy are briefly outlined. Before this, an introductory overview of KfW Group’s GHG emissions in 2024 is provided.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emissions
nodes.heading: 6.3.1 Greenhouse gas emissions
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from KfW Group’s Combined non-financial report (Environmental information) focusing on DEG’s climate actions, pollution and biodiversity disclosures, biodiversity strategy work, ESG risk assessment, and EU Taxonomy Article 8 reporting.
- DEG climate goals and actions:
  - Climate-friendly customer selection (avoidance): Pre-commitment climate data collection to assess Paris alignment using MDB Paris Alignment Principles and KfW sector guidelines; plan to steer direct business via carbon budgets from 2025; ongoing since 2022.
  - Management of new business (reduction): Department-specific carbon budgets for Corporates and Infrastructure to flexibly allocate portfolio and support higher emitters’ transition; defined in 2024, piloting from 2025.
  - Transformation support (reduction and adaptation): Expansion of advisory via the CARI programme; DERa expanded to include CO2e reduction and transformation effects; portfolio DERa target of 32 points by 31 Dec 2024; ongoing for all customer groups.
  - Neutralisation of remaining emissions (neutralisation): Diversified afforestation/reforestation portfolio to neutralise financed emissions; ongoing since 2022 with a 2040 carbon-neutrality goal.
- 2024 progress at DEG: Increased HR capacity for climate management/advisory; digitised portfolio customers’ GHG data collection and documentation; numerous climate-relevant Business Support measures (e.g., carbon accounting training for funds, bank GHG inventory modelling); pilot climate advisory in Nicaragua and Nigeria; EUR 1.5 million support to DEG Impulse’s CARI; additional investment in a carbon sink fund and EU guarantees to scale sink investments towards 2040 neutrality.
- Pollution disclosures: Materiality assessment recognises both positive impacts (financing environmental projects) and negative impacts (financing high-pollution industries). Measurement, prevention and minimisation are addressed through cross-cutting targets (SDG contribution, environment quota) and policies (sustainability guidelines, exclusion lists). Detailed ESRS E2 information is cross-referenced to the general “Overarching environmental targets and actions” section.
- Biodiversity focus and actions:
  - Strategic priority with “BioDiv-Roadmap” Phase 2 completed in 2024, conducting status quo, portfolio, materiality, regulatory and peer analyses, and identifying partnerships and action areas.
  - Phase 3 (2025–2026): Develop a qualitative biodiversity strategy; expand positive-impact projects; reduce negative impacts in new business; manage biodiversity-related risks per regulation; establish foundations for selective biodiversity data collection from co-financed projects; potential use of offsets and local/indigenous knowledge handled via E&S Appraisal where needed.
  - KfW Development Bank: EUR 0.5 billion in 2024 for projects with biodiversity as main/secondary objective and those labelled under OECD DAC biodiversity/tropical forest (3–5 year horizon); offsets/indigenous knowledge inclusion is project-dependent via E&S Appraisal (IFC PS/World Bank ESS).
- Policies relevant to biodiversity: E&S Appraisal applies IFC Performance Standards or World Bank ESS, notably PS6/ESS6 (and ESS1 on ecosystem services), requiring avoidance/minimisation of habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient/pollution impacts; excludes projects reducing endangered species populations; addresses land degradation and ecosystem service impacts. Social aspects via PS7/ESS7 ensure consultation and consent of indigenous peoples. No additional group policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas, or deforestation beyond those cited. Climate change as a biodiversity driver is addressed through Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists and via climate mainstreaming in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline.
- Climate and biodiversity risk assessment: ESG risk management referenced elsewhere; 2024 risk inventory analysed biodiversity-related drivers (e.g., ocean acidification, ecosystem service dependencies, land/sea use, pollution, exploitation, rising resource costs). Two-step approach: sector-based screening to flag at-risk partners, then ESG risk profiling considering mitigation. No biodiversity risk drivers were deemed material for any risk type in 2024.
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures:
  - Regulatory context: Six environmental objectives; multiple delegated acts; 2024 obligations require eligibility reporting for all six objectives and alignment reporting only for climate mitigation/adaptation; full alignment reporting for all objectives from 2025; banks disclose KPIs including the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) using counterparty data and publish qualitative disclosures (Annex XI). CSRD not yet transposed in Germany as of 31 Dec 2024; CSR-RUG still applies.
  - KfW Group application: Through the tranSForm project, KfW voluntarily publishes group-wide taxonomy KPIs for 2024; KfW IPEX-Bank continues mandatory single-entity reporting and joins consolidated reporting. KfW supports taxonomy aims but notes scope/data limitations: large portions of its portfolio (sovereigns, supranationals, SMEs outside NFRD/CSRD, non-EU counterparties) fall outside mandatory screening; sector coverage is partial; stringent criteria and data gaps yield low alignment rates. Consequently, taxonomy outcomes are not used to steer business sectors or individual financings. Select products align with certain taxonomy criteria (notably substantial contribution), e.g., Climate action campaign for corporates (293), Sustainable mobility (267–269), Green Transition Facility VC fund.
  - Reporting basis: IFRS gross carrying amounts; FinRep-based counterparty/product classifications; regulatory consolidation perimeter; GAR defined as taxonomy-aligned exposures over covered assets.

nodes.title: Actions to achieve 1.5 °C alignment for new financing
nodes.heading: 6.3.4 Actions to achieve 1.5 °C alignment for new financing
nodes.start_phrase:
As part of the “Paris alignment” sub-project of the “tranSForm” project, a methodology for accounting 
GHG emissions was established to regularly capture the group-wide GHG footprint of the financing portfolio.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group applies Paris‑aligned sector guidelines to new and extended programmes to ensure alignment with the 1.5°C goal; exceptions may occur when the Federal Republic of Germany mandates financing outside these guidelines.
- Governance and oversight: responsibility for implementing and complying with sector guidelines lies with business sector heads and subsidiary management boards; the Sustainability Strategy division centrally monitors proper implementation.
- Product and loan processes: SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients review and, if needed, adjust product/programme conditions to meet sector guidelines; compliance is embedded in factsheets and contracts as eligibility criteria, with borrowers confirming adherence.
- On‑lending controls: intermediary banks must monitor and document appropriate use of funds per contractual obligations.
- Across Customised Finance & Public Clients, KfW Development Bank, KfW IPEX‑Bank and DEG, each financing is checked and documented for applicability and compliance with sector guidelines; non‑compliant cases cannot proceed.
- KfW Capital’s equity fund‑of‑funds activity is currently outside the scope of sector guidelines but will apply them to new activities or in portfolio reviews if relevant.
- To achieve 1.5°C alignment, KfW is building a group‑wide GHG accounting system (via the “Paris alignment” sub‑project of “tranSForm”) to regularly measure and disclose the portfolio’s financed emissions, accounting for portfolio heterogeneity and improving transparency to stakeholders.
- Additional levers include environment‑quota‑contributing programmes and maintaining ample refinancing capacity to support climate and energy financing.
- DEG’s three Impact/Climate Commitments (since 2022) aim to: increase positive development impact; reduce GHGs in line with a science‑based 1.5°C pathway; and actively support client transformation for resilience and impact.
- DEG’s decarbonisation approach: shift to climate‑conscious new business and offer transformation support to existing clients; permanently remove residual emissions via sink projects from 2040 to achieve a neutral portfolio by 2040; interim targets for 2030/2035 are in development.
- Targets and methodology: reduce portfolio GHG intensity by an average 4.2% annually from 2025 (two‑thirds reduction vs. 2021), measured as tCO2e per EUR million financing cash value; applies to financed emissions per PCAF (Scope 1+2 direct, and Scope 3 cat. 15 for indirect via FIs); 2021 baseline intensity is 413 tCO2e/EUR million.
- Where sector guidelines do not yet cover relevant sectors, DEG applies the SBTi “absolute contraction” 4.2% pathway and, from 2025, department‑specific intensity targets and carbon budgets in screening and final decisions.
- Systems for GHG accounting and progress tracking were tested through 2024; from 2025, DEG will publish performance and progress per ESRS.
- Action hierarchy underpinning DEG’s plan: 1) avoid emissions, 2) reduce emissions and adapt via client transformation pathways, 3) neutralise remaining emissions from 2040, collectively targeting a 4.2% annual portfolio intensity reduction from 2025.

nodes.title: DEG Impact/Climate Commitments
nodes.heading: 6.3.5 DEG Impact/Climate Commitments
nodes.start_phrase:
With the adoption of the three Impact/Climate Commitments, DEG’s work since 2022 has focused (1) in an even more targeted manner on further increasing the positive development impacts of its customers’ 
projects on society and the environment, (2) reducing greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Paris Climate 
Agreement’s 1.5° C target in the fight against climate change using a science-based pathway and 
(3) actively supporting its customers in their transformation to strengthen their resilience and achieve even 
greater development impacts.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines DEG’s three Impact/Climate Commitments: maximizing positive development impacts, reducing GHGs in line with the Paris 1.5°C goal via a science-based pathway, and actively supporting customer transformation and resilience.
- DEG’s climate strategy centers on decarbonizing its portfolio through climate-conscious new business (avoidance), transformation support for existing clients (reduction), and permanent removal of residual emissions from 2040 via carbon sink investments to achieve a climate-neutral portfolio by 2040; an investment strategy and interim 2030/2035 targets are being developed.
- Target framework: reduce portfolio GHG intensity by an average 4.2% annually from 2025 versus 2021 (aiming for a two-thirds reduction), measured as t CO2e per EUR million financing cash value for ordinary business financed with own funds; coverage includes financed emissions per PCAF (Scope 1 and 2 in direct financing; attributable Scope 3 cat. 15 for indirect FI financing) and excludes emissions from on-lending of external funds.
- Governance and methodology: alignment with Paris-aligned sector guidelines, SBTi requirements (absolute contraction approach for mixed portfolios), and MDB Principles for Paris Alignment; department-level emission intensity targets and carbon budgets will guide early assessment and final financing decisions from 2025.
- Baseline and systems: 2021 baseline GHG intensity is 413 t CO2e per EUR million; full financed-emissions accounting established using customer data and GHG modeling; a test phase through 2024 built the GHG accounting and progress measurement systems, with ESRS-aligned performance reporting to start in 2025.
- Key actions to achieve targets:
  - Climate-friendly customer selection (avoidance): pre-commitment climate data collection and Paris alignment checks; introduce carbon budgets for direct business from 2025.
  - Management of new business (reduction): define and pilot department-specific carbon budgets (Corporates and Infrastructure) from 2025 to enable and steer higher-emitter transformations.
  - Transformation support (reduction and adaptation): scale advisory via the CARI program; integrate CO2e reduction/transformation into the DERa framework with a 2024 portfolio score target of 32.
  - Neutralisation (from 2040): build a diversified afforestation/reforestation sink portfolio to remove remaining financed emissions.
- 2024 progress highlights: expanded climate management/advisory HR capacity; digitized portfolio customer GHG data collection and integration; delivered climate-relevant Business Support (e.g., fund carbon accounting training, bank GHG inventory modeling) and pilot advisory with clients in Nicaragua and Nigeria; contributed EUR 1.5 million to DEG Impulse’s CARI; invested in another carbon sink fund and secured EU guarantees to scale sink investments toward 2040 neutrality.
- Pollution disclosure: material positive and negative impacts identified—reducing pollution via environmental financing and potential harms via financing high-pollution sectors; management via cross-cutting targets (SDG contribution, environment quota), sector sustainability guidelines, and exclusion lists, with detailed ESRS E2-1/E2-2/E2-3 information referenced elsewhere in the report.

nodes.title: Specific disclosures: Pollution
nodes.heading: 6.4 Specific disclosures: Pollution
nodes.start_phrase: In the materiality assessment, with regard to pollution as a consequence of its promotional and financing activities, KfW Group identified as material both positive (reduction of pollution through the financing of environmental projects) and negative impacts (financing of projects/companies in particularly polluting industries or industries with high pollutant emissions).
nodes.summary: This section of KfW Group’s Financial Report (Combined non-financial report > Environmental information) outlines DEG’s climate action hierarchy and KfW’s biodiversity work. It details DEG’s key measures: climate‑friendly customer selection aligned with Paris goals (ongoing from 2022, with carbon budgets for direct business planned from 2025); reduction via department‑specific carbon budgets for Corporates and Infrastructure (defined 2024, piloting 2025); transformation support through the CARI advisory program, with DERa expanded to track CO2e reduction/transition and a 2024 portfolio target of 32 points; and neutralisation of remaining financed emissions by 2040 through afforestation/reforestation sink investments. Reported 2024 progress includes enhanced HR capacity, digitised GHG data capture for portfolio clients, climate-relevant business support (e.g., carbon accounting training, bank GHG inventory modeling), pilot advisory projects in Nicaragua and Nigeria, EUR 1.5 million support to CARI via DEG Impulse, and further investment plus EU guarantees for carbon sink funds to underpin the 2040 neutrality goal. On pollution, the group recognizes both positive and negative impacts from financing; monitoring and mitigation are embedded in cross-cutting SDG and environment-quota targets, sector sustainability guidelines, and exclusion lists, with ESRS E2 disclosures referenced elsewhere. On biodiversity, KfW advanced the BioDiv Roadmap’s second phase in 2024 (status, portfolio/materiality/regulatory/peer analyses, partnerships) and set action areas; from 2025–2026 it will develop a qualitative biodiversity strategy, scale positive-impact projects, reduce negative impacts in new business, manage biodiversity-related risks, and begin selective biodiversity data collection, while offsets/mitigation and local/indigenous knowledge are addressed via E&S appraisal (IFC PS/WB ESS) and may be integrated in the strategy. KfW Development Bank’s 2024 biodiversity actions included EUR 0.5 billion for projects with biodiversity as a main or secondary objective and OECD DAC biodiversity/tropical forest labels, targeting governments and public institutions in developing and emerging economies; biodiversity targets currently sit within SDG 14/15 mapping, with a dedicated strategy forthcoming.

nodes.title: Specific disclosures: Biodiversity
nodes.heading: 6.5 Specific disclosures: Biodiversity
nodes.start_phrase: The topic of biodiversity was a particular focus of KfW Group’s strategic orientation in 2024 in the second phase of the “BioDiv Roadmap” (see the “Biodiversity actions” section of this chapter).
nodes.summary:

nodes.title: Biodiversity actions
nodes.heading: 6.5.1 Biodiversity actions
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group is developing a biodiversity roadmap until 2026.
nodes.summary:
- Biodiversity became a priority in 2024 as KfW Group completed phase 2 of its internal BioDiv Roadmap, conducting baseline, portfolio, materiality, regulatory, and peer analyses, and setting future action areas.
- No standalone biodiversity targets exist yet beyond contributions to SDG 14 and SDG 15; some biodiversity actions also count toward the environment quota.
- Phase 3 (2025–2026) will develop and implement a group biodiversity strategy, expand positive-impact projects, reduce negative impacts in new business, manage biodiversity-related risks per regulation, and build capabilities to selectively collect biodiversity data from co-financed projects; offsets, mitigation, and indigenous knowledge are considered via E&S processes.
- KfW Development Bank places a special focus on biodiversity; in 2024 it targeted about EUR 0.5 billion for projects where biodiversity is a main or secondary objective, carrying OECD DAC biodiversity/tropical forest labels, with a 3–5 year horizon; treatment of offsets and indigenous knowledge is project-dependent via E&S appraisal (IFC PS/World Bank ESS).
- Policy framework: The E&S Appraisal applies IFC Performance Standards (or World Bank ESS), especially PS6/ESS6 and ESS1, to address biodiversity threats (habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient/other pollution), require avoidance/minimization, exclude projects causing net reductions in endangered species, prevent invasives, and mitigate land degradation and ecosystem-service impacts; PS7/ESS7 ensures consent/consultation of Indigenous Peoples.
- KfW has no additional group-specific policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas, or deforestation beyond those reported; climate-biodiversity linkages are not separately required in E&S guidelines except for climate mainstreaming and ESS6 in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline; climate impacts are managed via Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Biodiversity risk assessment (2024): KfW evaluated drivers (e.g., ocean acidification, resource scarcity from biodiversity loss, dependence on ecosystem services, land/sea use, water/soil pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, rising resource costs) for impacts mainly on credit and equity risks through counterparties’ default probabilities, using sector-based screening and ESG risk profiling; stakeholders were not separately involved; result: no biodiversity risk drivers were material in 2024.

nodes.title: Specific disclosures on biodiversity in policies
nodes.heading: 6.5.2 Specific disclosures on biodiversity in policies
nodes.start_phrase:
The IFC Performance Standards (or, in KfW Development Bank, the World Bank’s Environmental and Social 
Standards), which are applied in the E&S Appraisal in certain circumstances and are enshrined in the E&S 
Appraisal guidelines (see the “Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines” section of this chapter) take account of direct influences on the loss of biodiversity and further biodiversity aspects as set out below.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines KfW Group’s biodiversity-related policies within its Environmental and Social (E&S) Appraisal, anchored in the IFC Performance Standards and, for KfW Development Bank, the World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESS).
- It highlights IFC Performance Standard 6/ESS6 (and ESS1 for ecosystem services), requiring identification, avoidance or minimisation of biodiversity risks such as habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological changes, and pollution (including nutrient pollution). Projects causing a net reduction in endangered species populations are excluded, and prevention of invasive species is required.
- The standards also address impacts on ecosystem extent and condition (e.g., land degradation) and on ecosystem services, integrating social aspects via PS7/ESS7 to ensure consent and consultation of indigenous and local communities where relevant.
- KfW Group does not maintain additional group-specific policies for land use/agriculture, oceans/seas, or deforestation beyond those already specified.
- Climate change as a direct biodiversity driver is not separately required in the E&S Appraisal guidelines, aside from climate mainstreaming and the application of ESS6 in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline; related impacts are managed through Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Readers are referred to the general “Disclosures on ESG risks” for overarching ESG risk management targets, actions, and policies.
- On strategy resilience, KfW’s 2024 risk inventory evaluated biodiversity/ecosystem risk drivers—including ocean acidification, biodiversity-related resource scarcity, dependence on ecosystem services, land/sea use, pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, and rising resource costs—and their influence across risk types.
- The principal transmission channel identified is via credit and equity investment risks if biodiversity loss increases counterparties’ probability of default. A two-step analysis screens sectors for biodiversity dependency/impact, then assesses at-risk partners’ ESG risk profiles after mitigation measures; stakeholders were not separately consulted.
- Outcome: No biodiversity risk drivers were classified as material in any risk type for financial year 2024.

nodes.title: Disclosures on climate and biodiversity risks
nodes.heading: 6.6 Disclosures on climate and biodiversity risks
nodes.start_phrase: For general information on KfW Group’s ESG risk management, including the existing targets, actions and policies in this regard, please refer to the “Disclosures on ESG risks” section in the “General information” chapter.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Environmental information within KfW Group’s Combined Non-Financial Report, focusing on biodiversity-related policies, risk disclosures, and strategic resilience.
- Policy framework: KfW applies IFC Performance Standards (or World Bank ESS for KfW Development Bank) within its E&S Appraisal, especially PS6/ESS6 (and ESS1 for ecosystem services).
- Biodiversity requirements under PS6/ESS6:
  - Identify and address threats such as habitat loss and fragmentation, invasive alien species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient and other pollution.
  - Avoid impacts where possible; otherwise minimize and mitigate.
  - Exclude projects that would cause a net reduction in endangered or critically endangered species.
  - Prevent introduction of invasive species; prevent/mitigate land degradation; manage negative impacts on ecosystem extent, condition, and ecosystem services.
- Social safeguards: Through PS7/ESS7 (Indigenous Peoples), ensure informed and willing consent and appropriate consultation of local and Indigenous communities in financing activities.
- Scope limits: No additional KfW-specific policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas, or deforestation beyond those stated.
- Climate–biodiversity linkage: E&S Appraisal guidelines have no explicit climate requirements as a direct biodiversity driver, except climate mainstreaming and ESS6 within KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline; climate-related biodiversity impacts are managed via Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Risk disclosures reference: Points readers to the general “Disclosures on ESG risks” section for broader ESG risk management targets, actions, and policies.
- Strategy resilience and risk assessment (FY 2024):
  - Assessed biodiversity/ecosystem risk drivers: ocean acidification, resource scarcity from biodiversity loss, dependence on ecosystem services, land and sea use, water/soil pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, rising resource costs.
  - Primary transmission channels: credit and equity investment risks via increased probability of default of business partners.
  - Methodology: sector-based screening of counterparties’ biodiversity dependencies/impacts; for at-risk partners, ESG risk profile assessed (considering mitigation) to determine high-risk status in relevant biodiversity categories.
  - Stakeholder input: not separately included.
  - Outcome: no biodiversity risk drivers classified as material in any risk type for financial year 2024.

nodes.title: Resilience of KfW Group’s strategy and business model regarding biodiversity risks
nodes.heading: 6.6.1 Resilience of KfW Group’s strategy and business model regarding biodiversity risks
nodes.start_phrase:
KfW Group examined whether and to what extent ESG risk drivers impact KfW Group’s overall risk profile in 
the short term in the risk inventory of financial year 2024 (see “Risk management approach of KfW (overview)” 
in the “Risk report” chapter).
nodes.summary:
- Explains KfW Group’s biodiversity-related policy framework within its Environmental and Social (E&S) Appraisal, based on IFC Performance Standards or the World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESS), especially PS6/ESS6.
- Details PS6/ESS6 requirements: identify and manage biodiversity and ecosystem-service risks (e.g., habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient and other pollution); avoid or minimize impacts; prohibit projects causing net reductions in endangered species; prevent invasive species; mitigate impacts on ecosystems (including land degradation) and on ecosystem services.
- Addresses social aspects via PS7/ESS7 on Indigenous Peoples, ensuring informed and willing consent and necessary consultations.
- States KfW has no additional group-specific policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas, or deforestation beyond those standards.
- Notes climate change as a biodiversity driver is not directly required in E&S Appraisal guidelines except for climate mainstreaming and ESS6 in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline; wider climate impacts are managed through Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Points to separate “Disclosures on ESG risks” for broader climate and biodiversity risk information.
- Summarizes 2024 biodiversity risk analysis: identified drivers (ocean acidification, biodiversity-related resource scarcity, dependence on ecosystem services, land/sea use, pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, rising resource costs); assessed impacts mainly via credit and equity risks through counterparties’ default probabilities using sector-based screening and ESG risk profiles; stakeholders not separately involved; outcome—no biodiversity risk drivers deemed material in 2024.
- Provides EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure context: purpose of taxonomy, six environmental objectives, and the delegated acts/Commission Notices setting technical screening criteria.
- Clarifies reporting scope and timing: in 2024, financial institutions disclose taxonomy eligibility for all six objectives and alignment only for climate mitigation and adaptation; full alignment reporting across all six objectives begins in 2025.
- Specifies credit-institution KPIs and templates: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) per DDA Annex VI, nuclear/gas templates per Annex XII, qualitative disclosures per Annex XI; relies on counterparty-provided information; excludes banking operations from taxonomy reporting.

nodes.title: Disclosures in accordance with Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 6.7 Disclosures in accordance with Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: Substantial financial resources are required for the transformation to a sustainable economy.
nodes.summary:
- Section context: Environmental information within a combined non-financial report detailing disclosures required under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation.
- Purpose and policy backdrop: Explains the EU’s sustainable finance agenda (2018 Action Plan; 2021 Strategy) aimed at redirecting capital toward environmentally sustainable activities through a standardized classification system (EU Taxonomy).
- EU Taxonomy scope: Defines environmentally sustainable (“taxonomy-aligned”) economic activities using technical screening criteria to increase transparency of capital flows.
- Environmental objectives covered: Six objectives—climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Regulatory and guidance framework: Details the delegated acts and notices establishing technical screening criteria and clarifications, including:
  - Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 for mitigation and adaptation,
  - Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2485 expanding activities for those two objectives,
  - Complementary Climate Delegated Act (EU) 2022/1214 including nuclear and natural gas as transitional activities,
  - Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2486 for the other four objectives,
  - Related Commission notices addressing interpretation.
- Reporting obligations and phasing (Article 8/DDA): Vary by entity type and phase in over time.
  - 2024: Financial corporations report taxonomy eligibility for all six objectives and alignment only for mitigation and adaptation.
  - 2025: Full eligibility and alignment reporting for all six objectives.
- Credit institution disclosures: Must report taxonomy eligibility and alignment of financing activities, using counterparty information; disclose the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) per DDA Annex VI and nuclear/gas-related templates per Annex XII; provide qualitative disclosures per Annex XI; exclude banking operations processes from taxonomy reporting.
- Applicability in Germany: Reporting scope tied to European corporate sustainability reporting rules; at the 31 December 2024 reporting date, the NFRD (implemented via Germany’s CSR-RUG) remains in force, with CSRD adopted but not yet transposed.

nodes.title: Legal requirements in the context of the EU Taxonomy Regulation
nodes.heading: 6.7.1 Legal requirements in the context of the EU Taxonomy Regulation
nodes.start_phrase: Substantial financial resources are required for the transformation to a sustainable economy.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the EU Taxonomy Regulation’s purpose to redirect capital toward environmentally sustainable activities via a standardized classification system and technical screening criteria.
- Outlines the six environmental objectives under Article 9: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, water and marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Summarizes key delegated acts and guidance: 2021/2139 (criteria for mitigation/adaptation), 2023/2485 (additional activities), 2022/1214 (nuclear and gas transitional conditions), 2023/2486 (criteria for the other four objectives), and related Commission Notices.
- Details Article 8 disclosure obligations and phasing: in FY2024 financial institutions report eligibility for all six objectives and alignment for mitigation/adaptation only; full eligibility and alignment reporting across all six objectives begins in FY2025.
- Specifies credit institution reporting: the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) as the main KPI per DDA Annex VI, nuclear/fossil gas templates per Annex XII, qualitative disclosures per Annex XI, reliance on counterparty data, and exclusion of banking operations processes from taxonomy reporting.
- Clarifies the regulatory reporting scope linkage to European corporate sustainability reporting: NFRD (implemented in Germany via CSR-RUG) currently applicable; CSRD published in 2022 but not yet transposed in Germany by 31 December 2024.
- Describes KfW Group’s application: sustainability embedded in strategy; group-wide “tranSForm” project for sustainable finance; voluntary publication of taxonomy KPIs for FY2024; KfW IPEX-Bank has reported since FY2021 and is using consolidated reporting at the parent level for the first time.
- Notes limitations of taxonomy coverage for KfW’s portfolio: exclusions include sovereigns, supranationals, SMEs not subject to NFRD/CSRD, and non-EU counterparties—key segments for a public promotional bank—leading to low observed alignment rates due to scope, ambition level, and data gaps.
- States that taxonomy screening currently is not used to steer business sectors or individual financing decisions; product criteria in select programs reference taxonomy “substantial contribution” (e.g., Climate action campaign for corporates, Sustainable mobility for municipalities and companies, Green Transition Facility), but taxonomy is otherwise not central to product design.
- Sets out the reporting basis: assets measured at gross carrying amounts from IFRS consolidated financial statements; FinRep definitions used for counterparty type and product grouping; reporting at the regulatory consolidated group level consistent with the commercial consolidation; GAR defined as the share of taxonomy-aligned exposures in covered assets.

nodes.title: Application of the EU taxonomy within KfW Group
nodes.heading: 6.7.2 Application of the EU taxonomy within KfW Group
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability in its actions is a particular priority and an overarching business objective for KfW Group.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group positions sustainability as a core objective embedded in its mission, policies, and risk and business strategies.
- Through its tranSForm sustainable finance project, the group is implementing internal processes to meet EU Taxonomy reporting obligations.
- For the first time, KfW Group will voluntarily publish group-wide taxonomy KPIs under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation for financial year 2024.
- KfW IPEX-Bank has reported mandatory EU taxonomy data since 2021 and, for 2024, is using consolidated reporting at the parent group level.
- The group supports a standardized taxonomy to enhance transparency and steer sustainable financing but stresses that KPIs must be meaningful and comparable.
- Large parts of KfW’s portfolio are excluded from mandatory taxonomy screening (e.g., financing to sovereigns and supranationals, SMEs not subject to NFRD/CSRD, and non-EU counterparties), which reflects its public promotional and international mandate.
- Current taxonomy scope centers on environmental/climate-relevant activities; many deserving sectors are not taxonomy-eligible, and data gaps plus stringent criteria lead to low alignment rates.
- Consequently, KfW has not used taxonomy screening to manage business lines or individual financing; product design has only selectively leveraged taxonomy criteria (notably “substantial contribution”) in specific programs and a VC fund (e.g., programme 293, programmes 267–269, Green Transition Facility).
- Taxonomy reporting basis: assets recognized at gross carrying amounts under IFRS consolidated financial statements, applying FinRep definitions for counterparty type and product grouping; scope aligns with the regulatory consolidated group, matching the commercial-law consolidation perimeter.
- The Green Asset Ratio (GAR) is defined as the share of taxonomy-aligned exposures within specified covered assets.

nodes.title: Basis for taxonomy reporting within KfW Group
nodes.heading: 6.7.3 Basis for taxonomy reporting within KfW Group
nodes.start_phrase: For taxonomy reporting, assets are recognised in gross carrying amounts on the basis of KfW Group’s consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (“IFRS”).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How KfW Group applies the EU Taxonomy in its environmental reporting and builds taxonomy KPIs for the first time at group level for financial year 2024.
- Strategic stance: Sustainability is a core objective; KfW supports a standardized taxonomy to increase transparency but stresses KPIs must be meaningful and comparable.
- Voluntary reporting: Group-wide taxonomy KPIs disclosed under Article 8 for 2024; KfW IPEX-Bank has reported since 2021 and uses consolidated reporting at parent level for the first time.
