- KfW Development Bank: Open-access grievance mechanism (email, online form, branch offices, project managers) with published criteria and reports. Projects must establish local grievance mechanisms per World Bank ESS10 and ESS2, including worker mechanisms. Process includes validity checks, preliminary review, remedial actions, and alternatives if needed; evaluation for systemic improvements. Planned inclusion of anti-retaliation measures; mechanisms are monitored and improved via training and awareness.
- KfW IPEX-Bank: Additional complaint channels (email, web form) for regulatory matters per BaFin and WpHG; acknowledgment with typical processing under two weeks; centralized coordination; option for anonymity. Sustainability-related concerns handled by the sustainability officer and Group Communications. Borrowers must maintain grievance procedures; documentation and training as needed.
- DEG: Grievance mechanism for those adversely affected by DEG-cofinanced projects; written submissions via form/email/post. Independent Expert Panel (IEP) of three external experts decides on arbitration or compliance reviews, ensures alignment with DEG guidelines and human rights policies, and monitors agreed actions. Anti-retaliation policy in place; EU Whistleblowing Directive relevant; no additional training beyond the mechanism.
- KfW Capital: Central complaints management via post or email; anonymity possible. LkSG-relevant matters routed to Compliance. Cross-entity complaint forwarding established. Due diligence checks that VC funds have whistleblowing mechanisms for employees and potentially externals (e.g., portfolio company staff).
- Governance and compliance culture: Code of Conduct anchors corporate values (ethics, integrity, collaboration, risk culture, diversity, leadership, skills). Strict adherence to laws/regulations on anti-corruption, AML/CFT, sanctions/embargoes, securities/tax compliance, data protection, and risk management. Whistleblower protections aligned with EU Directive 2019/1937 and the German HinSchG; safeguards per Section 25h KWG. Participation in Transparency International and EITI; cooperation with BMZ on corruption prevention and integrity standards.
- Cultural development: “Cultural journey” project launched in January 2024 to align culture with strategic goals and enhance employer attractiveness. Employee-inclusive design with workshops; target culture defined with leadership; implementation underway across departments, coordinated by HR and Corporate Development.

nodes.title: Promoting and further developing the corporate culture
nodes.heading: 8.1.1 Promoting and further developing the corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s Code of Conduct is at the centre of promotional activities and an expression of corporate culture.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on KfW Group’s governance and compliance framework, anchored in a group-wide Code of Conduct that promotes ethical behavior, integrity, collaboration, risk culture, diversity, effective leadership, and skills development.
- Compliance as the foundation of corporate culture: adherence to statutory, regulatory, and internal requirements covering anti-corruption and fraud, AML/CFT, sanctions/embargoes, securities and tax compliance, data protection, and risk management.
- Alignment with international and national standards: anti-bribery aligned with the UN Convention and German law; whistleblower protections per EU Directive 2019/1937 and the German HinSchG; safeguards per Section 25h KWG.
- Group-wide compliance guidelines supplemented by company-specific policies and work instructions; anti-corruption and crime prevention embedded in the sustainability program.
- External commitments and partnerships: member of Transparency International; DEG supports the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative; cooperation with BMZ and application of BMZ integrity quality criteria in international financing; rules of conduct aligned with German Federal Government and major banks.
- “Cultural journey” project (launched Jan 2024) to strengthen culture in support of strategy, increase agility, and enhance employer attractiveness; co-led by HR and Corporate Development with broad employee involvement, workshops defining target culture, and bank-wide implementation launched at the management conference.
- Governance and accountability: Executive Board holds overall compliance responsibility; subsidiary management ensures implementation; Executive Board delegates group compliance to an independent Compliance department.
- Compliance department roles under MaRisk: early identification of legal changes, decision preparation, monitoring compliance; focus areas include crime prevention, AML/CFT, sanctions, securities, tax, data protection, and MaRisk compliance.
- Designated officers within Compliance: fraud officer (leads crime prevention), money laundering officer, securities compliance officer, and data protection officer; Legal Affairs supports on legal processes; group rules on criminal offense prevention and handling gifts/invitations.
- Reporting and whistleblowing mechanisms: internal and external parties can report suspected unlawful conduct to the fraud officer or an external ombudsperson; integrated with broader complaints management.
- Incident handling: fraud officer logs and processes cases; losses recorded in Risk Controlling’s database; coordinates investigations and risk analyses; can convene a cross-functional fraud task force for exceptional cases (e.g., employee involvement with ≥ EUR 1 million potential loss or major reputational risk); informs the Executive Board; Internal Auditing reviews procedures.
- Oversight and assurance: annual audit of compliance implementation within the consolidated financial statements; audit report provided to BaFin; violations can lead to fines and sanctions; Internal Auditing also examines compliance units.

nodes.title: Strategies relating to aspects of business conduct policies
nodes.heading: 8.1.2 Strategies relating to aspects of business conduct policies
nodes.start_phrase:
The prevention of criminal acts and compliance with the Code of Conduct are the collective responsibility 
of KfW Group.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and compliance framework:
  - The KfW Executive Board holds overall responsibility for compliance; subsidiaries’ managing directors and their compliance units implement binding rules.
  - An independent Compliance department, aligned with MaRisk, leads group-wide compliance, early detection of legal developments, decision preparation, and monitoring of regulatory adherence.
  - Focus areas include prevention of criminal acts, anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing, sanctions/embargoes, securities and tax compliance, data protection, and MaRisk compliance.
  - Designated officers (fraud, money laundering, securities compliance, data protection) sit within Compliance; group-wide guidelines govern criminal offence prevention and handling of gifts/invitations.
  - Legal Affairs supports Compliance on legal procedures (e.g., searches and seizures).

- Code of Conduct:
  - Applies to all employees, managers, Executive Board members, and subsidiary management.
  - Executive and subsidiary boards maintain their own codes referencing duties to supervisory bodies.

- Reporting, whistleblowing, and incident handling:
  - Multiple reporting channels (fraud officer and external ombudsperson) are available to employees and external parties.
  - A protected whistleblowing system ensures confidentiality; the ombudsperson (bound by legal privilege) discloses identities only with the whistleblower’s consent.
  - Information and training on whistleblower protection are provided internally.
  - The fraud officer logs and processes all suspected incidents, with losses recorded in a Risk Controlling database, prepares risk analyses, coordinates investigations, and can convene a cross-functional fraud task force for exceptional cases (e.g., employee involvement with loss potential ≥ EUR 1 million or material reputational risk).
  - Executive Board is informed on case handling; Internal Auditing reviews procedural compliance.

- Audits, oversight, and consequences:
  - Annual audit of compliance implementation accompanies the consolidated financial statements; the auditor’s report is submitted to BaFin.
  - Violations may lead to fines and sanctions.
  - Compliance units are included in Internal Auditing’s regular audits; further results are referenced in the risk report.

- Anti-corruption controls:
  - Annual risk analysis under Section 25h KWG identifies and mitigates internal and external fraud/corruption risks, notably in lending/approvals, procurement, and contracting.
  - Two corruption-related cases in 2024 involved external bidders (not KfW employees); those bidders were excluded from the award process per internal rules.
  - Group-wide rules and a Code of Conduct set binding standards for accepting/giving gifts and benefits, including approval options and fixed value limits, emphasizing transparency and conflict-of-interest management.

- Training and culture:
  - Annual divisional discussions on anti-corruption are required.
  - Mandatory e-learning on criminal acts, AML/CFT, and data protection; targeted in-person training for higher-risk roles (e.g., award/approval functions and foreign branches).
  - Cultural change initiatives (“Cultural journey”) are communicated via workshops and events.

- EU Taxonomy (Article 8) disclosures:
  - Presentation of Taxonomy KPIs, including the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock and flow, with associated coverage over total assets and percentages of assets excluded from GAR numerator/denominator in line with Article 7 and Annex V.
  - Additional disclosures on trading book, financial guarantees, assets under management, and fees/commissions (with methodological notes on use of turnover vs. CapEx KPIs for counterparties and general lending).

nodes.title: Taxonomy tables pursuant to Annex VI/XII (EU) 2021/2178 (DDA)
nodes.heading: 9 Taxonomy tables pursuant to Annex VI/XII (EU) 2021/2178 (DDA)

nodes.summary:
- Section of KfW’s 2024 Combined Non‑Financial Report presenting EU Taxonomy disclosure tables pursuant to Annex VI/XII of Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 (DDA) under Article 8 for credit institutions.
- Focuses on key performance indicators (KPIs) required by the Taxonomy: the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) as the main KPI and related additional KPIs.
- GAR (stock): total environmentally sustainable assets reported as 832 (turnover-based) and 939 (CapEx-based), yielding a GAR of 0.2% on both bases; KPI coverage spans 84.1% of total assets; 37.0% of assets are excluded from the numerator and 15.9% from the denominator under Article 7 and Annex V rules.
- GAR (flow): total environmentally sustainable activities of 352 (turnover) and 446 (CapEx), each yielding 0.1%; coverage 13.8%; exclusions of 10.1% from the numerator and 0.7% from the denominator.
- Additional Article 8 items: trading book, financial guarantees, assets under management, and fees and commissions income. Financial guarantees and AuM show zero environmentally sustainable amounts; trading book disclosures reference CRR Article 94(1) and 325a(1) conditions; fees and commissions KPI (excluding lending and AuM) requires forward‑looking disclosures, targets, and methodological explanations.
- Methodology notes clarify KPI coverage as a share of total assets; use of counterparty Turnover KPI versus CapEx KPI (with general lending based on Turnover KPI); and the treatment of assets excluded from GAR numerators and denominators per Annex V.

nodes.title: Summary of KPIs to be disclosed by credit institutions under Article 8 Taxonomy Regulation
nodes.heading: 9.1 Summary of KPIs to be disclosed by credit institutions under Article 8 Taxonomy Regulation

nodes.summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures for a credit institution (KfW) in line with Annex VI/XII of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 (DDA), including required key performance indicators (KPIs).
- Summarizes the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) as the main KPI:
  - GAR stock and flow disclosed using counterparties’ Turnover and CapEx KPIs.
  - Coverage over total assets is low: about 0.2% (stock) and 0.1% (flow).
  - Shows significant portions of assets excluded from the numerator and parts of the denominator in accordance with Article 7 and Annex V, with specific percentages provided.
- Provides additional KPIs:
  - Trading book, financial guarantees, assets under management, and fees/commissions (non‑lending/AuM).
  - Values are mostly zero or minimal; notes that forward‑looking information is required for fees/commissions and that CRR conditions determine trading book applicability.
- Details the GAR calculation (Turnover basis) with a granular asset and sector breakdown:
  - Asset classes: loans and advances, debt securities (including use‑of‑proceeds instruments), equity.
  - Counterparties: financial undertakings (notably credit institutions), non‑financial undertakings, households, and local governments.
  - Identifies taxonomy‑eligible and taxonomy‑aligned amounts mapped to environmental objectives (Climate Change Mitigation, Climate Change Adaptation, Water and Marine Resources) and activity types (use of proceeds, transitional, enabling).
- Quantifies key figures:
  - Total assets: EUR 547,192 million.
  - GAR‑covered assets: EUR 460,085 million; assets not covered by GAR: EUR 87,106 million (primarily central governments/supranationals, central banks, and trading book).
  - Taxonomy‑eligible exposures: EUR 10,452 million; taxonomy‑aligned exposures: EUR 831 million (turnover‑based), with breakdowns for financial and non‑financial counterparties.
- Identifies assets excluded from the GAR numerator but included in the denominator:
  - SMEs and non‑financial corporates not subject to NFRD, non‑EU counterparties, derivatives, on‑demand interbank loans, and other asset categories.
- Reports off‑balance‑sheet exposures for undertakings subject to NFRD:
  - Minimal financial guarantees; no assets under management.
- Includes methodological footnotes:
  - Clarifies coverage metric, when Turnover vs CapEx KPI is used (general lending uses Turnover), and references to CRR Article 94/325a for trading book conditions.

nodes.title: Assets for the calculation of GAR
nodes.heading: 9.2 Assets for the calculation of GAR
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from KfW Financial Report 2024 (Combined non-financial report) presenting EU Taxonomy disclosures per Annex VI/XII of Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 (DDA), focused on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology and results.
- Scope and structure: Detailed GAR tables for assets covered in both numerator and denominator, assets excluded from the numerator but in the denominator, and assets not covered for GAR; shown for both turnover- and capital-expenditure-based KPIs; includes off-balance-sheet exposures subject to NFRD.
- Environmental objectives covered: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), with distinctions between taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned exposures and, where applicable, Use of Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- Key totals (denominator context): Total assets 547,192 million EUR; Total GAR assets 460,085 million EUR; Assets not covered for GAR 87,106 million EUR (central governments/supranationals 58,063; central banks 26,740; trading book 2,303). Assets excluded from numerator but in denominator: 202,654 million EUR (SMEs/NFCs not under NFRD 138,165; non‑EU counterparties 63,080; derivatives 7,445; on-demand interbank 519; other adjustments).
- Turnover-based KPI: Taxonomy-eligible 10,646 million EUR; taxonomy-aligned 832 million EUR. Breakdown highlights: Financial undertakings eligible 9,198/aligned 506 (mostly credit institutions); Non-financial undertakings eligible 1,448/aligned 325. Households and local governments show zero taxonomy alignment. CE/PPC/BIO amounts are small and confined to non-financial undertakings (CE 62; PPC 83; BIO 1).
- Capex-based KPI: Taxonomy-eligible 10,619 million EUR; taxonomy-aligned 939 million EUR. Financial undertakings eligible 9,080/aligned 516; Non-financial undertakings eligible 1,539/aligned 423. CE/PPC/BIO again small (CE 55; PPC 92; BIO 1).
- Instrument split: Within financial undertakings, eligibility/alignment largely in loans and advances and debt securities (including Use of Proceeds bonds); equity instruments are minimal but include a small fully aligned non-financial equity position (14 million EUR).
- Off-balance-sheet exposures: Minimal taxonomy relevance; small financial guarantees reported (turnover: 25 million EUR eligible 2; capex: 25 million EUR eligible 1), no alignment; no assets under management.
- Sectoral GAR information (turnover): NACE 4-digit breakdown for non-financial corporates (subject to NFRD) and SMEs/other NFCs, with examples across electricity production (35.11), motor vehicles (29.10), water transport (50), transport-related services (52.22, 52.23), head offices (70.10), basic metals (24.10), chemicals (20.5), etc., showing gross carrying amounts and “of which environmentally sustainable” figures, notably higher alignment in electricity production.

nodes.title: GAR sector information
nodes.heading: 9.3 GAR sector information
nodes.summary:
- This section of KfW’s 2024 Combined non-financial report presents EU Taxonomy disclosures pursuant to Annex VI/XII (EU) 2021/2178 (DDA), focusing on Green Asset Ratio (GAR) sector information and a GAR KPI stock overview.
- GAR sector information – Turnover and – Capital expenditure:
  - Provides a NACE 4‑digit sector breakdown of gross carrying amounts (in € million) and the “of which environmentally sustainable” portions across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - Splits exposures between Non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD and SMEs/other non‑financial corporates not subject to NFRD, and reports totals per sector.

nodes.title: GAR KPI stock

Use of Proceeds, equity instruments), counterparty types (financial undertakings/credit institutions, other financial corporations, non-financial undertakings, households, local governments), and “of which” tags (Use of Proceeds, transitional, enabling). Measures both taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned proportions of covered assets; indicates share of total assets covered by the GAR denominator.
- Headline results (GAR stock – Turnover and CapEx):
  - Taxonomy-eligible exposure concentrated in climate objectives: 2.3% (CCM) and 0.2% (CCA) of total covered assets; 0.0% for WTR, CE, PPC, BIO.

Within this, financial undertakings account for 50.0% (of which credit institutions 49.7%); loans and advances represent 47.3%, debt securities 2.4%, non-financial undertakings 1.0%, local government financing 4.1%, households 0.9%. Equity instruments and other subcategories are negligible (0.0%).

nodes.title: GAR KPI flow
nodes.heading: 9.5 GAR KPI flow
nodes.summary: This section of the KfW Financial Report 2024 presents EU Taxonomy disclosures (Annex VI/XII of Regulation (EU) 2021/2178) within the Combined non‑financial report, focusing on Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs by flow for Turnover and Capital Expenditure, plus off‑balance sheet KPIs. It details, as a percentage of the flow of total eligible assets at the disclosure reference date, the shares of taxonomy‑eligible and taxonomy‑aligned financing across the six environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO), with breakdowns “of which use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling.” The scope covers assets included in both the GAR numerator and denominator: loans and advances, debt securities (including use‑of‑proceeds instruments), and equity not held for trading, split by counterparty type (financial undertakings including credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings; non‑financial undertakings; households; local governments; collateral). Reported outcomes show very low taxonomy shares concentrated in climate change mitigation: for Turnover, total GAR assets are about 0.6% taxonomy‑eligible and 0.1% taxonomy‑aligned; for Capital Expenditure, about 0.7% eligible and 0.1% aligned. Other environmental objectives (adaptation, water, circular economy, pollution prevention, biodiversity) are reported as 0.0%. Eligible flow is mainly in financial undertakings—especially credit institutions—and in loans and advances, with non‑financial undertakings contributing around 0.1%; households and local governments are negligible. Most “use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” sub‑breakdowns are 0.0%. A “total new assets covered” figure of 16.4% is shown. The off‑balance sheet KPI (Turnover) covers financial guarantees and assets under management: financial guarantees are 7.8% taxonomy‑eligible and 0.6% taxonomy‑aligned (largely under climate change mitigation, with small transitional and enabling components), while assets under management are 0.0% for both eligible and aligned.

nodes.title: ESG factors in business strategy, governance and risk management
nodes.heading: 1 ESG factors in business strategy, governance and risk management
nodes.start_phrase: This chapter provides an overview of Nordea’s ESG -related business strategy, governance and risk management.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Overview of how Nordea integrates ESG factors into business strategy, governance, and risk management, with detailed E, S and G sections to follow.
- Definition and risk transmission: ESG factors can affect financial, environmental, social, or governance performance/solvency and act as risk drivers across traditional prudential risks (credit, market, business model, operational—including reputational/legal—and liquidity) and their sub-categories; these are cross-mapped to Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy.
- Double materiality approach: In line with CSRD, Nordea maps both its impacts on people and planet and the impacts of ESG factors on the bank and its counterparties.
- Materiality assessment (MA): A climate and nature-related MA, leveraging ICLAAP and a 4-level risk materiality banding, embeds climate and environmental (C&E) risk drivers.
- Key findings and capital impact: The 2024 MA indicates material exposure to multiple C&E risk drivers, mainly via counterparties; Nordea reserved additional capital in 2024 for climate-related credit risk; a CSRD-aligned Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) was also performed.
- Risk strategy and transition: Nordea’s strategy is to actively engage customers to drive sustainability transitions, mitigate identified C&E risks, and capture growth opportunities.
- Strategic pillars: Sustainability efforts center on four areas—financial strength, climate and environmental action, social responsibility, and governance and culture—linked to relevant UN SDGs and material topics.
- Business model resilience: Dependent on counterparties’ sustainability and effective risk mitigation; aims to align on-balance sheet lending and investments with the Paris Agreement via reductions in financed GHG emissions.
- Products, funding, and liquidity: ESG-related offerings support customer transition and integrate sustainability into funding and liquidity strategies, including sustainability-linked funding activities.
- Targets and implementation: Internal targets to cut operational GHG emissions by 40–50% by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050; interim portfolio targets guide net-zero steering; integration into lending/investment policies and practices.
- External frameworks and commitments: Engagement with Principles for Responsible Banking, UN Global Compact, Equator Principles, Poseidon Principles, and other industry standards.

nodes.title: ESG FACTORS IN BUSINESS STRATEGY: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: 1.1 ESG FACTORS IN BUSINESS STRATEGY: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors are the characteristics potentially positively or negatively impacting the ﬁnancial, environmental, social or governance performance or solvency of Nordea or its counterparties, across value chains or business environments.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Overview of Nordea’s ESG-related business strategy, governance and risk management, with detailed E, S and G sections to follow.
- ESG as risk drivers: ESG factors can positively or negatively affect Nordea or its counterparties and transmit primarily through traditional prudential risk categories (credit, market, business model, operational including reputational and legal, liquidity, and sub-categories), and via actions Nordea takes on material sustainability impacts. ESG ambition and risk management are cross-mapped to Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy.
- Double materiality foundation: Strategy and risk alignment are based on systematic identification and mapping of ESG factors via transmission channels to operations, business model and risk profile, using the CSRD’s double materiality concept (impacts on planet/society and on Nordea/counterparties).
- 2024 materiality assessment (MA): A climate and nature-related MA, leveraging ICLAAP and a 4-level risk materiality banding, identifies material exposure to climate and environmental risk drivers across prudential risks, mainly via counterparties. Additional capital was reserved in 2024 for climate-related credit risk. Results also informed a CSRD-aligned double materiality assessment (DMA).
- Risk strategy and positioning: Nordea aims to actively support a sustainability-based transition through customer engagement while capturing growth opportunities, with risk mitigants for identified C&E drivers. Sustainability efforts center on four areas: financial strength; climate and environmental action; social responsibility; and governance and culture, linked to relevant UN SDGs and areas of material impact through lending, investments and operations.
- Paris alignment and products: Objective to align on-balance sheet lending and investments with the Paris Agreement by reducing financed GHG emissions. ESG-related products, customer and investee engagement, and sustainability-linked funding integrate sustainability into funding and liquidity strategies.
- Targets and policies: Internal targets to reduce GHG emissions 40–50% by 2030 and achieve net zero by 2050. Interim portfolio targets support net zero steering and balance sheet alignment with policy and best practice. Commitments embedded in lending/investment policies and internal frameworks (procurement, travel, conduct) and anchored in initiatives such as PRB, UN Global Compact, Equator Principles and Poseidon Principles. Mitigations include industry credit policies, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments and monitoring of energy performance certificates.
- Biodiversity integration: 2024 position on biodiversity and nature-related impacts adopted for incorporation into strategy, governance and risk management toward 2025. Biodiversity included in business environment scanning; sector guidelines updated (with general and sector-specific expectations in agriculture, aquaculture, feed and food processing, and real estate). Capacity building, training and initial dependency/impact assessments using the WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter and ENCORE conducted. 2025 plans include enhanced, quantified biodiversity assessments across the value chain focused on the lending portfolio.
- Reporting and regulation: CSRD applies from 2024, replacing NFRD; Nordea reports under ESRS in the 2024 Annual Report and benchmarked against draft EBA ESG risk management guidelines to prepare for finalization.
- EU Taxonomy and KPIs: Disclosure of taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned exposures under Article 8, with Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs showing the share of taxonomy-aligned assets. 2024 scope includes retail exposures (per internal methodology), NFRD undertakings (financial and non-financial), local government financing, collateral obtained (real estate) and off-balance sheet exposures, with details in the Annual Report and GAR templates.
- Visual framework: Reference to a figure outlining how ESG-related objectives, targets and limits are aligned within business and risk strategies.

nodes.title: ESG FACTORS IN BUSINESS STRATEGY: INTRODUCTION - Introduction

nodes.heading: 1.1 ESG FACTORS IN BUSINESS STRATEGY: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors are the characteristics potentially positively or negatively impacting the ﬁnancial, environmental, social or governance performance or solvency of Nordea or its counterparties, across value chains or business environments.
nodes.summary: Nordea’s introduction explains how environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors act as risk drivers across traditional prudential risk categories (credit, market, business model, operational including reputational and legal/litigation, liquidity, and sub-categories) and through actions on material sustainable development impacts, with management cross-mapped to Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy. Using the CSRD’s double materiality concept, Nordea conducted a climate and nature-related materiality assessment (MA) within the ICLAAP framework and a 4-level risk materiality banding, concluding material exposure to climate and environmental (C&E) risk drivers mainly via counterparties; in 2024 it reserved extra capital for additional climate-related credit risk and performed a double materiality assessment (DMA). The risk strategy emphasizes customer engagement, risk mitigation, and alignment of on-balance sheet lending and investments with the Paris Agreement via financed emissions reductions, supported by sustainability-related funding and product offerings. Nordea’s sustainability efforts span financial strength, climate and environmental action, social responsibility, and governance and culture, with relevant UN SDGs; internal targets include a 40–50% GHG reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050, plus interim portfolio targets, embedded through PRB, UN Global Compact, Equator Principles, Poseidon Principles, and policies (industry credit policies, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments, monitoring of energy performance certificates) and internal frameworks (procurement, travel, employee conduct). In 2024 Nordea approved a biodiversity position for integration into strategy, governance and risk management by 2025, embedded biodiversity in its business environment scanning (BES), updated sector guidelines (notably for agriculture, aquaculture, feed and food processing, and real estate), conducted initial dependency/impact assessments using WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter and ENCORE, and plans in 2025 to enhance quantification across the value chain—focusing on the lending portfolio—to reduce downstream impacts and capture opportunities.

nodes.title: Reporting and EU Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 1.1.1 Reporting and EU Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: As of 2024, the CSRD applies to Nordea.
nodes.summary:
- Embedding sustainability commitments into Nordea’s internal policy frameworks (procurement, travel, employee conduct) and aligning with climate benchmarks and GHG reduction targets.
- Implementing mitigation measures beyond GHG targets, including industry credit policies, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments, and monitoring of energy performance certificates.
- Advancing biodiversity integration: a 2024-approved biodiversity position to be embedded in strategy, governance and risk management toward 2025; inclusion of biodiversity in the 2024 Business Environment Scanning; updated sector guidelines (general plus agriculture, aquaculture, feed and food processing, and real estate), with further enhancements planned in 2025.
- Building capabilities through methodologies, data foundations, trainings and internal dialogues; initial value-chain dependency and impact assessments using WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter and ENCORE; 2025 plan to quantify dependencies/impacts, focus on the lending portfolio, and drive targeted actions to reduce downstream risks and capture opportunities.
- Reporting transition to CSRD from 2024, applying ESRS and the double materiality concept; feasibility and benchmarking work to prepare for the EBA guidelines on ESG risk.
- EU Taxonomy compliance under Article 8: disclosure of taxonomy-eligible and -aligned exposures; reporting Green Asset Ratio KPIs and details in the 2024 Annual Report and GAR templates 6, 7, and 8.
- Scope for 2024 disclosures includes retail exposures, exposures to undertakings under NFRD (financial and non-financial), local government financing, collateral obtained by possession (residential and commercial properties), and off-balance sheet exposures.
- Reference to an overarching approach (Figure 1) for aligning ESG objectives, targets and limits across business and risk strategies.

nodes.title: ESG FACTORS GOVERNANCE: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: 1.2 ESG FACTORS GOVERNANCE: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea has embedded oversight of strategic steering for material ESG impacts within its Group governance model (Figure X).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Nordea’s ESG governance framework and how ESG oversight is embedded in Group governance.
- Board roles and committees:
  - Board sets purpose, values, and strategic direction for sustainability; ensures compatibility with a sustainable economy transition.
  - BOSC advises and recommends strategic sustainability priorities for Board approval.
  - BRIC oversees financial impacts of ESG, Group risk profile, and key ESG risk developments.
  - BAC oversees sustainability reporting, including regulatory disclosures and related controls.
- Group Leadership Team and executive committees:
  - Group CEO proposes strategic sustainability priorities and sets related targets.
  - SEC oversees business implementation of sustainability and facilitates operational ESG risk management.
  - RC oversees ESG-related risk strategy and policy framework; sub-committees address ESG topics within their mandates.
  - ALCO sets principles for performance management and financial planning frameworks.
  - ESG Reporting Sub-committee supports sustainability disclosures and methodologies, particularly financed emissions used in the risk appetite framework.
- Board effectiveness and capability:
  - Annual suitability assessments of individual Board members and the Board as a whole inform training.
  - 2024 trainings covered facilitated/financed emissions, customer engagement, social responsibility/just transition, Nordic energy transition, and emission removals/offsetting.
- Credit risk governance:
  - ESG-related risks in credit processes follow delegated decision-making; high ESG-risk customers are escalated to higher-level credit committees.
- Group-wide implementation:
  - ESG programme (established 2021) ensures consistent ESG integration across 1st and 2nd lines of defence and addresses regulatory change.
  - Overseen by an Operational Steering Committee co-chaired by the Chief of Staff and Head of Group Credit Risk Control; involves all business areas, Group functions, risk areas, Group Financial Management, and Risk Control.
  - 2024 focus on building the ESG Data Foundation to enable data-driven portfolio steering, enhance ESG risk management, disclosures, and management oversight.

nodes.title: ESG factors in group governance
nodes.heading: 1.2.1 ESG factors in group governance
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea has embedded oversight of strategic steering for material ESG impacts within its Group governance model (Figure X).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Nordea’s ESG governance framework and how sustainability is embedded in Group governance, strategy, and risk management.
- Board-level roles:
  - Board sets purpose, values, and oversees integration of sustainability into strategic priorities and business planning, ensuring compatibility with a sustainable economy transition.
  - Board Operations and Sustainability Committee (BOSC) develops and reviews sustainability priorities, targets, and objectives; Board approves on BOSC’s recommendation.
  - Board Risk Committee (BRIC) oversees financial impacts of ESG factors, Group risk profile, and key environmental, social, and governance risk developments.
  - Board Audit Committee (BAC) oversees sustainability reporting in quarterly and annual reports, including regulatory disclosures and the control environment.
- Executive-level roles:
  - Group CEO proposes strategic sustainability priorities and sets related targets and objectives.
  - Sustainability & Ethics Committee (SEC) oversees implementation of sustainability in business strategy and facilitates operational ESG risk management.
  - Risk Committee (RC) oversees implementation of ESG risk strategy and policy framework; its sub-committees address ESG topics within their mandates.
  - Asset & Liability Committee (ALCO) governs performance management and financial planning frameworks.
  - ESG Reporting Sub-committee (under ALCO) prepares sustainability disclosures and oversees methodologies, especially for financed emissions used in the risk appetite framework.
- Governance practices:
  - Annual suitability assessment of individual board members and the Board as a whole informs training plans.
  - 2024 Board and Group Leadership Team training covered facilitated emissions, customer engagement strategies, social responsibility/just transition, Nordic energy transition, and emission removals/offsetting.
  - ESG-related credit risk decisions follow delegated authorities, with high ESG-risk customers escalated to higher-level credit committees.
- Group-wide implementation:
  - ESG programme established in 2021 to ensure consistent implementation across first and second lines of defence and to meet regulatory changes.
  - Programme overseen by an Operational Steering Committee co-chaired by the Chief of Staff and Head of Group Credit Risk Control, involving all relevant business areas, Group functions, risk areas, Group Financial Management, and Risk Control.
  - 2024 focus on building an ESG Data Foundation to enable data-driven portfolio steering, enhance ESG risk management, improve disclosures, and strengthen management oversight.
- Reference to a figure providing an overview of the ESG-related governance model.

nodes.title: Group-wide implementation governance
nodes.heading: 1.2.2 Group-wide implementation governance
nodes.start_phrase: A Group -wide ESG programme was established in 2021 with the objective to ensure efficient and consistent implementation of ESG factors in the business and risk strategies across the 1 st and 2nd lines of defence (LoD) and delivering on relevant regulatory changes.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Nordea’s ESG governance framework, embedding oversight of material ESG impacts into group governance.
- Defines the Board’s role: sets purpose and values, integrates sustainability into strategy and business plans, and ensures alignment with a sustainable economy transition.
- Details Board committees:
  - BOSC: develops and oversees strategic sustainability priorities, targets, and objectives; recommends them for Board approval.
  - BRIC: oversees financial impacts of ESG and reviews the Group’s risk profile and key ESG risk developments.
  - BAC: oversees sustainability reporting, including quarterly/annual reports, regulatory disclosures, and the reporting control environment.
- Outlines Group Leadership Team responsibilities:
  - CEO proposes strategic sustainability priorities and sets related targets.
  - SEC: oversees implementation of sustainability in business strategy and facilitates operational ESG risk management.
  - RC: oversees ESG risk strategy and policy framework.
  - ALCO: sets principles for performance management and financial planning frameworks.
  - ESG Reporting Sub-committee (under ALCO): prepares sustainability disclosures and oversees methodologies, especially for financed emissions in the risk appetite framework; RC sub-committees provide ESG input within their mandates.
- Describes annual Board and collective suitability assessments feeding into training; 2024 training covered facilitated emissions, customer engagement, social responsibility/just transition, Nordic energy transition, and emission removals/offsetting.
- Explains ESG risk governance in credit processes: decisions follow delegated authorities; high ESG-risk exposures are escalated to higher-level credit committees.
- Presents group-wide implementation governance: an ESG programme (since 2021) spanning 1st and 2nd lines of defence, overseen by an Operational Steering Committee co-chaired by the Chief of Staff and Head of Group Credit Risk Control, involving all relevant business areas, functions, and risk units.
- Highlights 2024 programme focus on building an ESG Data Foundation to enable data-driven portfolio steering, improved ESG risk management, disclosures, and management oversight.
- References an overview figure of the ESG-related governance model.

nodes.title: ESG factors in organisational structure and reporting
nodes.heading: 1.2.3 ESG factors in organisational structure and reporting
nodes.start_phrase: ESG is an integrated component of existing processes for decision -making, risk management, escalation and reporting across the three LoDs .
nodes.summary:
- ESG is embedded into decision-making, risk management, escalation, and reporting via a three lines of defense (LoD) model.
- Responsibilities by LoD:
  - 1st LoD: Sets and implements strategic responses and mitigations for ESG impacts/risks; Chief of Staff ensures coordination.
  - 2nd LoD: Develops the Sustainability and ESG policy framework and oversees 1st LoD implementation; Head of GCRC coordinates as policy owner.
  - 3rd LoD: Provides independent assurance and advice on ESG-related risks.
- Coordination and roles:
  - Each LoD appoints an ESG coordinator/ambassador.
  - Group Sustainability coordinates 1st LoD; GCRC coordinates 2nd LoD; Group Internal Audit plans ESG assurance coverage based on risk assessment.
  - Cross-risk coordination mandated for key topics (e.g., greenwashing) and for ESG reporting aggregation to ensure consistent framework implementation.
- Competence and training:
  - Three-layer training approach: (1) general mandatory Code of Conduct e-learning plus optional ESG e-learnings and regulatory updates; (2) tailored training for roles directly working with ESG; (3) in-depth training for selected groups.
  - Group Risk prioritizes nature risk analysis and financed emissions accounting; Group Compliance completes targeted trainings on ESG regulatory requirements, terminology, and EU Taxonomy.
- Board-level ESG reporting (aggregated and quarterly):
  - Sustainability Roadmap monitoring of strategic progress and targets, including voluntary and supervisory commitments.
  - ESG Management Report: exposures by group/business area/sector/product; historical and forecast financed emissions; EU Taxonomy eligible/aligned assets; sustainable finance/funding/savings volumes; ESG data quality indicators and progress tracking.
  - Group Risk Report: risk appetite monitoring for ESG cross-risk concentrations and financed emissions per the Common Risk Taxonomy.
  - Other risk reports: financed emissions by business area, geography, industry, and customer; climate physical and nature-related risk concentration; mitigation status and coverage.
  - Embedded ESG within ICAAP (capital adequacy, stress testing, scenarios); 2nd LoD reporting on ESG embedment (e.g., Group Compliance Report).
- Remuneration alignment with ESG:
  - ESG goals integrated across variable pay plans and the long-term incentive plan; Group Pool funding and profit sharing link pay to green financing (per the Green Financing Framework) and Sustainability Roadmap goals.
  - ESG scorecards support ambitions to 2025.
  - Senior leaders’ incentives tied to progress on the Sustainability Roadmap, increased green financing volumes, and improved gender balance in senior leadership, alongside non-financial KPIs (employee engagement, customer satisfaction, risk/compliance/conduct).
  - A material portion of GLT and senior leaders’ non-financial remuneration is linked to ESG factors.

nodes.title: Remuneration
nodes.heading: 1.2.4 Remuneration
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea has integrated ESG goals in all Group’s variable pay plans, extending it from the GLT and other senior leaders across the Nordea Group to variable pay participants through introduction of ESG -related goals to the Group Pool funding mechanism and more broadly to all employees by adding green ﬁnancing, deﬁned in accordance with Nordea’s Green Financing Framework, and Sustainability Roadmap goals in the proﬁt sharing plan.
nodes.summary:
- ESG governance is embedded across decision-making, risk management, escalation, and reporting through three Lines of Defense (LoDs).
- 1st LoD: accountable for strategic ESG response and risk mitigation; coordinated by the Chief of Staff.
- 2nd LoD: develops the Sustainability and ESG policy framework and oversees 1st LoD implementation; coordinated by the Head of GCRC as framework owner.
- 3rd LoD: provides independent assurance and advice on ESG-related risks.
- ESG coordinators/ambassadors are appointed within each LoD; Group Sustainability coordinates the 1st LoD, GCRC the 2nd LoD, and Group Internal Audit coordinates ESG assurance based on risk assessment.
- Cross-risk coordination is mandated for key topics (e.g., greenwashing) and processes (e.g., aggregation of ESG reporting) to ensure consistent implementation of the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework.
- Competence building follows a three-layer training model: general mandatory ESG-integrated Code of Conduct and e-learnings; tailored training for roles working directly with ESG; and in-depth training for selected groups.
- Group Risk focuses on nature risk analysis and enhancing financed emissions accounting; Group Compliance completed mandatory ESG regulatory training, including EU Taxonomy.
- Quarterly ESG-specific Board reporting includes:
  - Sustainability Roadmap monitoring of strategic ESG implementation, targets, and commitments.
  - ESG Management Report on Group exposures, sector/product views, financed emissions (historical and forecast), EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment, sustainable finance/funding/savings volumes, and ESG data quality indicators.
  - Group Risk Report covering ESG risk appetite, cross-risk concentrations, and financed emissions across the risk taxonomy.
  - Additional risk reports on financed emissions by business area/geography/industry/customer, climate physical risk, nature-related risk concentrations, and mitigation status.
  - ESG embedded in non-ESG reports (e.g., ICAAP stress testing and scenario analysis) and 2nd LoD reporting on ESG embedment (e.g., Group Compliance Report).
- Remuneration integrates ESG goals across variable pay, Group Pool funding, and profit sharing (aligned with Nordea’s Green Financing Framework and Sustainability Roadmap); ESG scorecards are included in long-term incentives.
- Senior leaders’ ESG remuneration goals target Sustainability Roadmap progress, increased green financing volumes, and improved gender balance in senior leadership, alongside non-financial KPIs (employee engagement, customer satisfaction, risk/compliance/conduct) and financial targets—making ESG a material component of leadership pay.

nodes.title: ESG FACTORS RISK MANAGEMENT: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: 1.3 ESG FACTORS RISK MANAGEMENT: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the overall policy framework, the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework speciﬁcally addresses the integration of ESG related items into the risk management cycle.
nodes.summary:
- Introduces Nordea’s Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework for integrating ESG considerations into the risk management cycle, grounded in Group Board Directives on Sustainability and Risk and aligned with CSRD double materiality.
- Defines ESG factors as environmental, social, or governance characteristics that can affect Nordea’s or its counterparties’ financial performance or solvency across value chains and time horizons.
- Details 2024 enhancements: updates to ESG risk identification and materiality assessment (MA), cascading into risk area documents and strategy-setting guidance; outlines 2025 focus on expanding identification/management of material ESG risks and strengthening monitoring and controls.
- Clarifies governance: GBD on Sustainability embeds impact materiality in business strategy; GBD on Risk embeds financial materiality in risk management; CEO Instruction (CEOI) on ESG Factors is the entry point for ESG materiality assessments.
- Notes 2024 approvals of the CRO Protocol on ESG-related risk and the Group Accountable Executive Protocol on Sustainability Strategy, which operationalize ESG integration into risk management and strategy, cascading to 1st and 2nd lines of defence.
- Presents the ESG Factor Taxonomy (initiated in 2021 and updated annually), aligned with EU Taxonomy, GRI 300, SASB, EBA guidance, ECB guide on climate and environmental risks, CSRD and ESRS, and other sources.
- Describes the materiality assessment approach: a Group-wide taxonomy of ESG risk drivers (hazards) and transmission channels derived from literature and validated with business and risk areas to reflect Nordea’s business model.
- Summarizes 2024 climate and nature-related MA: identification and assessment of C&E risk drivers across geographies, sectors, and portfolios over short, medium, long, and very long-term horizons; acknowledges potential impact on all prudential risks individually and in cross-risk views.
- States that the broader Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) in 2024 also evaluated social and governance aspects.
- Explains transmission channels as causal chains through which ESG drivers affect Nordea directly (own operations) or indirectly (via counterparties, invested assets, third parties), distinguishing economic transmissions (micro and macro real-economy effects) from financial transmissions (e.g., increased PDs in credit risk).
- Outlines management pathways: direct effects handled via internal governance and controls; indirect effects addressed through business and risk strategies and activity-level risk management.
- Notes a gross risk approach is used for identification (pre-mitigation) and defines impact durations: short (<1 year), medium (1–5), long (5–10), very long (10+ years).

nodes.title: Policy framework
nodes.heading: 1.3.1 Policy framework
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the overall policy framework, the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework speciﬁcally addresses the integration of ESG related items into the risk management cycle.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Nordea’s Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework for integrating ESG factors into the risk management cycle, grounded in Group Board Directives on Sustainability and Risk, and aligned with CSRD double materiality.
- Defines ESG factors as environmental, social, or governance characteristics affecting Nordea’s or counterparties’ financial performance or solvency across value chains and time horizons.
- Details 2024 enhancements: updated ESG risk identification and materiality assessment (MA), broader cascade into risk area documents and strategy-setting guidance; 2025 focus on extending material ESG risk management and strengthening monitoring and controls.
- Clarifies governance: GBD on Sustainability embeds impact materiality in strategy and governance; GBD on Risk embeds financial materiality in risk management and governance.
- Positions the CEO Instruction on ESG Factors as the starting point for ESG-related materiality assessments across the Group.
- Notes 2024 approvals of the CRO Protocol on ESG-related risk and the Group Accountable Executive Protocol on Sustainability Strategy, expanding financial and impact materiality in the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) and cascading into 1st and 2nd lines of defense.
- Maintains an annually updated ESG Factor Taxonomy (since 2021) aligned with EU Taxonomy, GRI, SASB, EBA guidance, ECB climate and environmental risk guide, CSRD and ESRS, and other sources.
- Describes the materiality assessment approach: a Group-wide taxonomy of ESG risk drivers (hazards) and transmission channels, defined via literature and validated with business/risk areas for Nordea’s business model.
- Reports 2024 climate and nature-related MA identifying C&E risk drivers across geographies, sectors, and portfolios over short, medium, long, and very long-term horizons, with potential impacts across all prudential risks and cross-risk views; DMA also covers social and governance aspects.
- Explains transmission channels as causal chains affecting Nordea via its counterparties, invested assets, third parties, or own operations; distinguishes economic (micro/macro) from financial transmissions and maps them to prudential risk categories.
- Classifies effects as direct (managed via internal governance and controls) or indirect (managed via business/risk strategies) and applies a gross risk perspective (pre-mitigation), with defined impact durations: short (<1 year), medium (1–5 years), long (5–10 years), and very long (≥10 years).

nodes.title: Approach to the assessment of materiality of ESG factors
nodes.heading: 1.3.2 Approach to the assessment of materiality of ESG factors
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea has in place a Group -wide ESG Factor Taxonomy of ESG risk drivers (i.e. hazards) and a list of transmission channels.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and purpose: Introduces Nordea’s ESG Factors Risk Management approach and its integration into the overall risk management cycle through a Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework anchored in Group Board Directives (GBD) on Sustainability and on Risk, reflecting double materiality under CSRD.

- Definitions and governance: Defines ESG factors as environmental, social, or governance characteristics that can affect Nordea or its counterparties across time horizons and value chains. Clarifies governance split: GBD on Sustainability for impact materiality in business strategy; GBD on Risk for financial materiality in risk management. The CEO Instruction (CEOI) on ESG Factors is the entry point for Group-wide ESG materiality assessments.

- 2024–2025 developments: In 2024, updates enhanced ESG risk identification and materiality assessment (MA), with cascading into risk area documents and strategy-setting guidance. New protocols approved: CRO Protocol on ESG-related risks and Group Accountable Executive Protocol on Sustainability Strategy, detailing integration into risk and strategy frameworks and expanding double materiality assessment (DMA). 2025 focus will extend material ESG risk identification/management and strengthen monitoring and controls.

- ESG Factor Taxonomy: A Group-wide taxonomy of ESG risk drivers and transmission channels, first developed in 2021 and updated annually, aligned with EU Taxonomy, GRI, SASB, EBA guidance, ECB C&E risk guide, CSRD/ESRS, and other sources.

- Materiality assessment approach: Transmission channels are derived from literature and validated with business/risk areas to reflect Nordea’s business model. The 2024 enhanced climate and nature-related MA identified relevant C&E risk drivers across geographies, sectors, and portfolios over multiple time horizons (short <1y; medium 1–5y; long 5–10y; very long >10y). These drivers potentially affect all prudential risks individually and on a cross-risk basis. In parallel, the DMA added social and governance aspects.

- Transmission channels: Distinguishes economic transmissions (micro effects like operational disruptions from severe weather; macro effects like productivity shifts due to mitigation investments) that map to the broader economy, and financial transmissions that flow into Nordea’s risk profile (e.g., higher PDs in credit risk due to transition impacts). Classifies relationships into direct effects on Nordea (managed via internal governance/controls) and indirect effects via third parties/counterparties (managed via business and risk strategies). Risk identification uses a gross risk approach (pre-mitigation).

- Supporting tools: Heatmaps highlight industries and, for physical climate risks, countries/regions vulnerable to environmental factors. Used as a starting point in credit, market, and operational risk for portfolio classification and materiality assessment.

- Embedding in ICAAP/ILAAP and risk taxonomy: ESG factor materiality is assessed across all prudential risks within ICAAP/ILAAP. Where material, ESG-related risks must be embedded in the Common Risk Taxonomy and frameworks. ESG-related risks are Level 2 under credit risk; for other Level 1 risks (market, liquidity, capital/business model, operational, compliance), ESG-specific Level 3 risks are defined, including fair value market risk, financial reporting, reputational, outsourcing and third party, physical security, legal, technology, conduct and customer outcomes, governance, and people risks.

- Materiality criteria and bands: Materiality is assessed on a gross basis relative to total exposure. A four-band system determines materiality and impact:
  • Band 1: quantitative loss vs CET1; always material.
  • Band 2: quantitative loss vs CET1; requires qualitative expert judgment to determine materiality.
  • Band 3: qualitative criteria; always material.
  • Band 4: not meeting Bands 1–3; always non-material.
  Bands 2–3 rely on documented expert judgment. The assessment is reviewed annually via MA and ICLAAP.

- ESG Risk Appetite Framework (RAF): A dedicated ESG RAF defines risk statements, metrics, limits, and governance with monitoring/reporting at Group, branch, and subsidiary level. It ensures the ESG risk profile:
  • aligns with strategic sustainability objectives;
  • remains within financed emissions targets;
  • aligns with the business environment to avoid disruptive changes;
  • limits material cross-risk ESG concentrations;
  • stays within lower-level limits/controls of underlying prudential risks.

- Risk Appetite Statement (RAS): Since 2019, a Board-approved qualitative ESG RAS sets operating boundaries, requiring prudent management of material ESG exposures across all prudential risks, customer engagement to align with the Paris Agreement, and reduction of financed emissions over time.

- Metrics and limits: ESG RAF metrics exist at Levels 1–3 to control and monitor ESG-specific risks. Metric design considers:
  • consolidation/aggregation across risk areas and alignment with long/very long-term strategy and targets;
  • position within the Common Risk Taxonomy and focus on material, higher-impact ESG exposures;
  • strategic ambition, including Group commitments (e.g., financed emissions) and exclusions;
  • coherence with related metrics (e.g., tolerances for emissions restatements vs portfolio emissions trajectory).

nodes.title: ESG factors in Risk Appetite Framework
nodes.heading: 1.3.3 ESG factors in Risk Appetite Framework
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its prudent risk management, Nordea needs to ensure that risks driven by ESG factors (i.e. ESG Factor Taxonomy) are adequately managed and mitigated.
nodes.summary:
- Nordea uses ESG heatmaps to flag industries and regions potentially vulnerable to environmental and climate physical risks. These heatmaps are a starting point for deeper analysis and support credit, market, and operational risk identification, portfolio classification, and materiality assessment.

- ESG risk materiality is assessed within ICAAP and ILAAP across all prudential risks, informed by MA and DMA outputs. Where material, ESG risks are embedded in Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy and frameworks.

- Taxonomy placement: ESG-related risks are Level 2 under credit risk; for other Level 1 prudential risks (market, liquidity, capital/business model, operational, compliance), specific ESG Level 3 risks are defined, including fair value market risk, financial reporting, reputational, outsourcing/third party, physical security, legal, technology, conduct and customer outcomes, governance, and people risks.

- Materiality is assessed on a gross basis (ignoring mitigants) using a four-band scheme:
  - Band 1: quantitatively defined vs CET1; always material.
  - Band 2: quantitatively defined vs CET1; requires expert judgment to confirm materiality.
  - Band 3: qualitatively defined; always material.
  - Band 4: not meeting Bands 1–3; always non-material.
  Expert judgments for Bands 2–3 are documented; the assessment is reviewed annually in MA and ICLAAP updates.

- ESG Risk Appetite Framework (RAF) sets dedicated ESG risk statements, metrics, limits, and governance to ensure Nordea’s risk profile:
  - aligns with strategic sustainability objectives and financed emissions targets,
  - avoids disruptive business model shifts,
  - limits cross-risk ESG concentrations,
  - and stays within defined Level 2/3 limits for underlying prudential risks.

- An ESG Risk Appetite Statement (RAS), introduced in 2019 and since enhanced, mandates prudent management of material ESG risks across all prudential risks, customer engagement to align with the Paris Agreement, and progressive reduction in financed emissions.

- ESG RAF metrics (at Levels 1–3) are designed considering:
  - aggregation across the Group and links to long-term strategy,
  - relevance within the risk taxonomy and material ESG factor exposure,
  - strategic ambition, including financed emissions commitments and exclusions,
  - alignment among metrics (e.g., restatement tolerances vs. emissions trajectory).

- Metrics and limits are consistently defined and measured across units; governance for monitoring, reporting, and breach escalation is set by the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework.

- Board-approved limits and KRIs for financed emissions (loans to the public) were introduced in 2021. In 2024, Group Level 1 financed emissions limits were tightened to meet GHG targets and cascaded as Level 2 limits to business areas, based on 2019 baselines and 2030 targets, requiring year-on-year declines.

- Lending and investment strategies set limits on exposures to harmful/controversial activities. Public sector guidelines (forestry, real estate, shipping, agriculture, gambling, fossil fuels, defense, mining) define exclusions, requirements, and customer engagement expectations for Paris alignment.

- Implementation across risk types: industry credit policies embed sector guideline requirements in lending and origination; Illiquid Exposures investments apply detailed ESG analysis and a separate ESG rating in due diligence aligned with minimum requirements and long-term targets.

- Further details on ESG strategy, risk management, and governance are provided in environmental, social, and governance sub-sections.

nodes.title: Environmental, social and governance factors
nodes.heading: 2 Environmental, social and governance factors
nodes.start_phrase: Management of environmental factors is key for Nordea.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on environmental factors within Nordea’s ESG approach, defining climate and environmental (C&E) risk drivers and granular hazards (e.g., flooding) and how they affect the bank’s risk profile.
- Clear climate strategy with short- and long-term objectives for 2030 and 2050, targeting net-zero emissions by 2050 at the latest.
- Prioritization of UN SDGs: 7 (Affordable and clean energy) and 12–15 (Responsible consumption/production, Climate action, Life below water, Life on land); commitment to support customers’ transitions and reduce Nordea’s own impact via aligned internal/external policies.
- Analytical finding that lower GHG emissions intensity and quantified emissions-reduction targets correlate with lower probability of default.
- Establishment of an ESG Factor Taxonomy aligned with EBA guidance, EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852, CSRD, and best practices; environmental factors split into climate- and nature-related, each with physical and transition effects and specific hazards.
- Use of the taxonomy in annual climate- and nature-related materiality assessments (MA); 2024 enhanced MA assessed all prudential risks using a four-band process, with only compliance risk rated non-material (Band 4).
- Completion of CSRD-required Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) in Q2 2024; internal MA mapped C&E risk drivers to ESRS topics/subtopics; methodology aligned with ICLAAP thresholds and assessed across portfolios, geographies, and business areas.
- ESRS E1–E5 mapping and materiality outcomes: E1 Climate change—material; E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems—material; E2 Pollution—non-material; E3 Water and marine resources—non-material; E5 Resource use and circular economy—non-material. The nature-related scope includes biodiversity loss, ecosystem status/services, water use and discharges (including oceans), marine resources, pollution, and non-climate environmental hazards.

nodes.title: ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS
nodes.heading: 2.1 ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS
nodes.start_phrase: Management of environmental factors is key for Nordea.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Nordea’s approach to Environmental factors within ESG, covering strategy, objectives, and risk management.
- Strategy and targets: defined climate and environmental (C&E) risk drivers and granular hazards; set short- and long-term climate positions for 2030 and 2050 with a net‑zero emissions target by 2050; prioritization of climate objectives; identification of material UN SDGs (7, 12–15) to guide actions; analysis showing lower probabilities of default for companies with quantified GHG reduction targets; commitment to support customers’ transitions while reducing Nordea’s own impact; policies aligned with international and European frameworks.
- Risk management: establishment of an ESG Factor Taxonomy aligned with EBA guidance, EU Taxonomy (Regulation 2020/852), CSRD, and best practices; environmental taxonomy split into climate- and nature-related factors, each with physical and transition effects and associated hazards.
- Materiality processes: taxonomy used in annual climate- and nature-related materiality assessment (MA); in 2024 all prudential risks were assessed against C&E risk drivers using a four-band materiality process, with only compliance risk deemed non-material (Band 4); CSRD Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) conducted by Q2 2024, mapping internal C&E drivers to ESRS topics and aligning with ICLAAP thresholds; assessments consider portfolios, geographies, and business areas.
- ESRS E1–E5 mapping outcomes: Climate change (E1) – physical and transition effects material; Pollution (E2) – non-material; Water and marine resources (E3) – non-material; Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4) – transition effects material; Resource use and circular economy (E5) – non-material. Scope of nature-related changes includes biodiversity loss, species status, ecosystem extent/condition, ecosystem services, water use and discharges, marine resource extraction/use, pollution, and other non‑climate environmental hazards.

nodes.title: Business strategy, targets and objectives
nodes.heading: 2.1.1 Business strategy, targets and objectives
nodes.start_phrase: Management of environmental factors is key for Nordea.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Nordea’s approach to environmental factors within ESG, covering strategy, targets, risk taxonomy, materiality assessments, and alignment with EU/International frameworks.
- Strategy and objectives: Environmental management is central to Nordea’s business and risk profile. The bank defines climate and environmental (C&E) risk drivers and granular hazards. It has set 2030/2050 climate positions with a goal to be net-zero by 2050. Material UN SDGs identified: 7 (Affordable and clean energy) and 12–15 (Responsible consumption/production, Climate action, Life below water, Life on land).
- Risk–return linkage: Analysis indicates lower probabilities of default for companies with quantified GHG emissions reduction targets and lower emissions intensities.
- Implementation: Ambitions executed via internal/external policies aligned with international and European frameworks and benchmarks; Nordea commits to support customers in reducing impacts while also reducing its own footprint.
- ESG Factor Taxonomy: Developed in line with EBA/REP/2021/18, EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852, CSRD, and best practices. Environmental factors split into climate- and nature-related, each with physical and transition effects and granular hazards. Used as input for annual climate- and nature-related materiality assessments.
- 2024 assessments: All prudential risks assessed against C&E drivers using a four-band materiality process; only compliance risk assessed as non-material (Band 4). CSRD-required Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) completed in Q2 2024, mapping internal C&E drivers to ESRS topics and aligning with ICLAAP thresholds across portfolios, geographies, and business areas.
- Materiality outcomes (ESRS E topics): E1 Climate change—Material (physical and transition effects); E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems—Material (transition effects). Non-material: E2 Pollution; E3 Water and marine resources; E5 Resource use and circular economy.

nodes.title: ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS RELATED RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 2.1.2 ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS RELATED RISK MANAGEMENT

nodes.title: Risk identiﬁcation
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.1 Risk identiﬁcation
nodes.start_phrase: As deﬁned in the section ‘Approach to the assessment of materiality of ESG factor’, Nordea has in place a speciﬁc ESG Factor Taxonomy.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: Nordea emphasizes management of environmental factors within ESG, distinguishing between risk drivers (impacts on risk profile) and granular hazards (e.g., climate-related flooding). Environmental factors are split into climate- and nature-related elements, each with physical and transition effects.
- Strategy and targets: Nordea has short- and long-term climate objectives, prioritizing climate with a commitment to be net-zero by 2050. It aligns with material UN SDGs (7, 12–15) and supports both customer transitions and reduction of its own impact. Internal and external policies are aligned with international/EU frameworks. Nordea’s analysis links lower GHG intensity and quantified reduction targets to lower probabilities of default.
- ESG Factor Taxonomy and regulatory alignment: Nordea’s ESG Factor Taxonomy is aligned with EBA guidance, EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU 2020/852), CSRD, and best practices. It feeds into the annual climate- and nature-related materiality assessment (MA) and the CSRD double materiality assessment (DMA).
- 2024 materiality assessment (MA) and DMA: All prudential risks in Nordea’s risk taxonomy were assessed against climate and nature (C&E) risk drivers using a four-band process consistent with ICLAAP. Only compliance risk was non-material (Band 4). The DMA maps internal C&E risk drivers to ESRS topics (E1–E5) across portfolios, geographies, and business areas.
- ESRS mapping and outcomes: Climate change (E1) is material; biodiversity and ecosystems (E4) is material; pollution (E2), water and marine resources (E3), and resource use and circular economy (E5) are non-material. Climate-related drivers map to E1; nature-related degradation maps to E2–E5.
- Data adequacy and methodology enhancements (2024): 
  - Improved business loans data and customer NACE code quality.
  - Better collateral-to-EPC matching; use of PED values (Sweden) and correct EPC versions vs PED (Finland) for household alignment.
  - Inclusion of buildings post-2021 via NZEB-10% approach.
  - Enhanced identification of exposures to physical hazards (acute/chronic) with impact assessment.
  - Inclusion of exposures to Norwegian NFRD undertakings and alignment for other financial NFRD entities.
  - Disclosure of “Use of Proceeds for Households” per internal GAR; updated GAR methodology for residential real estate (gross carrying amount excluding unknown second mortgages in DK/FI).
  - Definition of Template 10 exposures as those supporting transition/adaptation under Green/Sustainability-Linked Funding frameworks but not EU Taxonomy-aligned.
  - Short-term controls to address data gaps; expectation of improved client disclosures medium/long term. Use of PCAF proxies and internal estimates for GHG accounting; methodologies governed internally with further data collection tied to disclosure ambition.
- Risk assessment by material risk type: Overview of approach and results across business model, credit, market, liquidity, and operational risks, with detail on business model risk.
- Business model risk specifics:
  - Key drivers: Concentration in lending (≈85% of income/REA) makes credit risk-linked ESG hazards (e.g., flooding, decarbonization needs) most relevant; care taken to avoid double counting.
  - Transmission: Broad channels where multiple hazards can increase credit risk (e.g., stranded assets, liability, shifting customer preferences). One overarching transmission channel identified: potential absence of an effective long-term strategy to respond efficiently to material C&E hazards.
  - Assessment methods: Literature review; quantitative analyses of NII/NCI concentration and group-wide emission targets by business area; long-term stress testing (30+ years); heatmapping from ESG factors to transmission channels impacting business model risk.

  - Disclosure of “Use of Proceeds for Households” per internal GAR methodology.
  - Inclusion of post‑2021 buildings via NZEB‑10% approach.
  - Use of PED values for Swedish households and EPC/PED alignment fixes for Finnish households to identify EU Taxonomy–aligned exposures.
  - Updated GAR methodology for residential real estate (gross carrying amount excluding unknown second mortgages in DK/FI).
  - Definition for Template 10 exposures: lending under Green and Sustainability‑Linked Funding Frameworks supporting climate transition/adaptation but not EU Taxonomy–aligned.
- Notes short‑term controls and manual data collection to address data gaps, with expectations of improved customer disclosures over time.
- Describes GHG emissions accounting using proxies (e.g., PCAF) and internal estimates under governance‑set data requirements; future disclosures to leverage existing processes.
- Presents approach to 2024 materiality assessment across key risk types (business model, credit, market, liquidity, operational), with detailed focus on business model risk:
  - Main drivers stem from lending (85% of income/REA), linking business model risk closely to credit‑relevant ESG hazards (e.g., flooding, counterparty decarbonization needs) while avoiding double counting.
  - Identifies a broad transmission channel: risk of lacking an effective long‑term strategy to address relevant climate and environmental hazards within appropriate time horizons.
  - Materiality assessment methods: literature review; quantitative NII/NCI concentration analysis and review of group emission targets/strategy shifts; long‑term (+30 years) stress testing; and heatmapping of ESG risk factors to transmission channels via credit risk.

nodes.title: Market risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.3.3 Market risk
nodes.start_phrase: Market risk for Nordea is mainly driven by climate- related transition risk drivers related to ‘regulatory changes’.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Summary of Nordea’s 2024 materiality assessment (MA) of climate- and nature-related impacts on market, liquidity, and operational risks, including risk drivers, transmission channels, methods, and outcomes.
- Market risk:
  - Main risk drivers: Predominantly climate-related transition risks from regulatory changes; lesser physical risks from extreme weather (heatwaves, droughts) and flooding.
  - Transmission channel: Fair value asset devaluation.
  - Methods: Literature review; qualitative assessment by risk controllers (portfolio composition, sectors, business models, geography across Nordics/EU/US, underlying IRR and equity risks); stress testing using NGFS Phase IV IAM-based scenarios (Delayed Transition for transition risk; Current Policies for physical risk); qualitative assessment of nature-related exposure (limited, deemed not material).
  - Outcome: Assessed as Band 2, not material, no additional capital required. Climate drivers reduce fair values but within risk appetite; effects mainly via regulatory change-induced macro shocks to interest rate risk in the liquidity portfolio and equity risk outside the Nordics in illiquid exposures. FV devaluations observed in non-traded liquidity, illiquid, and DB pension scheme portfolios. Nature-related risks immaterial due to limited exposure to vulnerable sectors.
- Liquidity risk:
  - Main risk drivers: Physical flooding (acute and chronic) and transition-driven reputational risk (greenwashing).
  - Transmission channels: Cash outflows; collateral funding impact; HQLA devaluation.
  - Methods: Literature review; four short-term stress scenarios (ILAAP); nature-related risk considered qualitatively for regulatory importance across short to very long horizons.
  - Outcome: Assessed as Band 3, no capital allocation impact. Primary impacts on HQLA and real estate–collateralized assets (e.g., mortgage bonds), with compounding water-based hazards most relevant. Liquidity ratios stay within limits in all but a very severe scenario combining transition, physical, and reputational shocks. Nature-related hazards unlikely to affect liquidity.
- Operational risk:
  - Main risk drivers: Transition- and nature-related reputational risks tied to fines and litigation; physical risks assessed as non-material.
  - Transmission channels: Increased litigation and liability (legal risk); litigation due to legal risk; changed market perception (reputational risk); failures in financial reporting (financial reporting risk).
