nodes.title: Outcome of materiality assessment for market risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.3.3.4 Outcome of materiality assessment for market risk
nodes.start_phrase: The 2024 MA concluded that market risk is assessed as Band 2 and further assessed by the respective risk controller as not material and requiring no additional capitalization.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Partial document summarizes Nordea’s climate and environment (C&E) materiality assessment (MA) across market, liquidity, and operational risk, detailing key risk drivers, transmission channels, methods, and 2024 outcomes.

- Market risk
  - Main risk drivers: Predominantly climate-related transition risks from regulatory changes; smaller impact from physical risks (extreme weather, heatwaves/droughts, flooding).
  - Transmission channel: Fair value asset devaluation (only directly relevant channel).
  - Assessment methods: Literature review; qualitative portfolio-level assessment (products/sectors, business models, geography across Nordics/EU/US, underlying risk types such as interest rate and equity); stress testing using NGFS Phase IV scenarios (Delayed Transition for transition risk, Current Policies for physical risk). Nature-related risks assessed qualitatively due to low exposure.
  - Outcome: Assessed as Materiality Band 2; deemed not material with no additional capital required. Transition risks (regulatory changes) reduce fair values but remain within risk appetite. Key impacts via macro/market shocks to interest rate risk in the liquidity portfolio and equity risk (outside Nordics) in illiquid exposures; FV devaluation observed in non-traded liquidity portfolio exposures, illiquid exposures, and defined benefit pension scheme portfolios. Nature-related risks considered immaterial.

- Liquidity risk
  - Main risk drivers: Physical flooding risks (acute and chronic); transition-related reputational risk (including greenwashing).
  - Transmission channels: Cash outflows, collateral funding impact, and HQLA devaluation.
  - Assessment methods: Focus on short-term C&E impacts, including exposure to GHG-intensive sectors and collateral values; literature review; four short-term stress scenarios (ILAAP). Nature-related risk considered from a regulatory-importance perspective (non-quantified) over short to very long horizons.
  - Outcome: Assessed as Materiality Band 3 with no capital allocation impact. C&E drivers mainly affect HQLA and real estate–collateralized assets (e.g., mortgage bonds); compounding water-based hazards are most relevant. Liquidity ratios remain within limits in all but a very severe scenario combining transition, physical, and reputational shocks. Nature-related hazards not likely to affect liquidity.

- Operational risk
  - Main risk drivers: Transition and nature-related transition risks via reputational channels, primarily from potential fines or litigation; physical risks assessed as non-material.
  - Transmission channels: Increased litigation and liability (legal risk), litigation due to legal risk, changed market perception (reputational risk), and failures in financial reporting (financial reporting risk).

nodes.title: Materiality assessment method for operational risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.3.5.3 Materiality assessment method for operational risk
nodes.start_phrase: The MA assessment for operational risk includes the following methods to evaluate climate and nature -related transition risk:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Materiality assessment (MA) of operational risk from climate and nature (C&E) factors, emphasizing transition and physical risks.
- Methodology:
  - Review of scientific, regulatory, standard-setter, and industry literature.
  - Qualitative identification of C&E hazards and mapping of critical assets/operations by geography.
  - Scenario-based analysis to determine time horizons and assess quantitative/qualitative impacts for materiality decisions.
- 2024 MA outcome:
  - Operational risk (including reputational, liability, litigation) assessed as Materiality Band 3 with no capital allocation impact.
  - 34 scenarios across 7 countries.
  - Physical risks (own operations and third-party providers) assessed as non-material.
  - Transition risks (legal and greenwashing) may materialize, notably from accusations linked to financing emission-intensive customers.
- Risk response and mitigation:
  - Since 2019: commitments include support for TCFD, and financed emissions reporting aligned with GHG Protocol and PCAF.
  - Own operations: Code of Conduct emphasizes environmental responsibility; procurement assesses environmental impacts; internal carbon reduction plan to 2030 and 2050.
  - Sector targets set for shipping, agriculture, power production, motor vehicles, fossil fuels, residential real estate, and thermal peat mining, with defined transition pathways.
- Risk appetite and portfolio steering:
  - Quantitative financed emissions limit acts as a “carbon budget” for retail and corporate lending, covering counterparties’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions, measured relative to 2019.
  - Limits cascaded to business areas; steering uses 2019 baseline, 2030 forecasts, granular emissions data, and client transition plans.
  - 2024 tightening of limits toward a 40%–50% reduction by 2030; net-zero target by 2050.
- Planning, monitoring, and governance:
  - Financed emissions integrated into the Rolling Financial Forecast to 2030, with high-level outlooks to 2050.
  - Quarterly monitoring; at least semi-annual review by senior management, including GLT.
- Data and strategy enablement:
  - Customer-level emissions data collected via the internal BES process to inform strategy, ESG risk management, stress testing, capital planning, and regulatory alignment.
  - 2024 BES insights used to enhance climate- and nature-related MA using a Group-wide ESG Factor Taxonomy (hazards, risk drivers, transmission channels, and materiality assessment).

nodes.title: Risk response and mitigation
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.4 Risk response and mitigation
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea issued a ﬁrst position statement in 2019 outlining key climate transition commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Materiality assessment (MA) of operational risk related to climate and nature (C&E), emphasizing transition risk.
- Methodology: Literature review; qualitative identification of C&E hazards and mapping of critical assets/operations; scenario-based analysis with time horizons and quantitative/qualitative impact assessment.
- 2024 MA outcome: Operational risk (including reputational, liability, litigation) rated Materiality Band 3 with no capital allocation impact; 34 scenarios across 7 countries; physical risks (own operations and third parties) deemed non-material; transition risks (legal and greenwashing) could materialize due to financing emission-intensive clients.
- Risk response and mitigation:
  - Climate transition commitments since 2019: support for TCFD; financed emissions reporting aligned with GHG Protocol and PCAF; strategies to reduce financed emissions and grow sustainable financing.
  - Own operations: Code of Conduct on environmental behavior; procurement process assesses environmental impacts; internal carbon reduction plan to 2030 and 2050.
  - Sector-specific targets: shipping, agriculture, power production, motor vehicles, fossil fuel, residential real estate, thermal peat mining; portfolios to evolve to meet long-term objectives.
  - Financed emissions limit (Risk Appetite Statement) as a carbon budget for retail and corporate lending, covering counterparties’ Scope 1 and 2, relative to 2019 baseline; cascaded to business areas; steering via 2019 baseline and 2030 forecasts using granular data and clients’ transition plans.
  - 2024 update: tightened total financed emissions limits, aiming for 40–50% reduction by 2030; net-zero by 2050.
  - Integration into Rolling Financial Forecast to 2030 with outlooks to 2050; trajectory and limit utilization monitored quarterly and discussed at least semi-annually by senior management (including GLT).

nodes.title: Climate-related transition risks
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.4.1 Climate-related transition risks
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea issued a ﬁrst position statement in 2019 outlining key climate transition commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Describes a materiality assessment (MA) approach for operational risk focused on climate and nature-related transition risks, using three methods: literature review, qualitative hazard and geographic mapping, and scenario-based analysis with time-horizon assessments.
- Reports 2024 MA outcome: operational risk (including reputational, liability, litigation) is Band 3 material with no capital allocation impact; 34 scenarios across seven countries were analyzed. Physical risks (own operations and third-party providers) deemed non-material; transition risks tied to legal exposure and potential greenwashing—especially linked to financing emissions-intensive clients—may materialize.
- Outlines climate-related transition risk responses: a 2019 position statement committing to TCFD, GHG Protocol and PCAF-aligned financed emissions reporting, and business area strategies to 2025 to engage clients, cut financed emissions, and expand sustainable finance toward a 2030 internal GHG reduction target.
- Highlights own-operations measures: Code of Conduct on environmental behavior, environmental criteria in third-party procurement, and an internal carbon reduction plan to 2030 and 2050.
- Details sector-specific climate targets for portfolios (shipping, agriculture, power production, motor vehicles, fossil fuels, residential real estate including mortgages and tenant-owner associations, and thermal peat mining) to align with long-term objectives.
- Introduces a Risk Appetite Statement-financed emissions limit functioning as a carbon budget for retail and corporate lending (Scope 1 and 2 of counterparties), measured relative to 2019 and cascaded to business areas, with allocations guided by 2019 baselines, 2030 forecasts, granular data, and client transition plans.
- Notes 2024 tightening of financed emissions limits, aiming for a 40%–50% reduction by 2030, with a longer-term net zero 2050 target aligned to broader economic transition pathways.
- Explains integration of financed emissions trajectories into the Rolling Financial Forecast to 2030 and high-level outlooks to 2050, using policy-driven sector decarbonization, client targets, and lending forecasts; monitored quarterly and discussed at least semi-annually by senior management (including GLT).
- Describes the Business Environment Scan (BES) process to collect customer-level emissions data and assess ESG impacts, supporting strategy, risk management, stress testing, capital planning, and regulatory alignment; 2024 BES insights enhanced the climate- and nature-related MA via a Group-wide ESG Factor Taxonomy covering hazards, drivers, transmission channels, and materiality assessment.

nodes.title: Climate-related physical risks
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.4.2 Climate-related physical risks
nodes.start_phrase: For climate -related physical risks, as part of the ESG Factor Taxonomy, Nordea has in place speciﬁc risk drivers which potentially could (negatively) impact Nordea.
nodes.summary:
- Climate-related physical risks: Nordea defines specific risk drivers under its ESG Factor Taxonomy, with flooding identified as the most relevant risk to 2030, especially for real estate collateral (potential collateral devaluation). The Group discloses gross exposure to acute and chronic physical hazards in Part 2, Table X. Mitigation relies on EPC data, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments, industry credit policies, monitoring of national adaptation and insurance availability, and environmental/building certifications and permits. Ongoing data development improves risk measurement, and dedicated risk appetite indicators for climate-related physical risks are included in the RAF.

- Nature-related risks: Nordea sets physical and transition risk drivers, with physical drivers including loss of tree cover and ecosystem condition/productivity, and transition drivers covering regulatory, technological, and societal changes. Some physical drivers (land, freshwater and sea use change, invasive species, water scarcity) are assessed as less relevant for Nordea’s business. Overall exposure is mainly transition-driven; credit exposure to highly vulnerable sectors is low, though aggregate exposures (e.g., real estate) can elevate total risk. Materiality is largely regulatory in nature.

- Quantification and analytics: Nordea applies an external biodiversity impact scoring (Finance for Biodiversity Foundation, 04/2023) to its lending portfolio, identifying highest biodiversity footprints in agriculture, animal husbandry, food processing & beverages, and materials. The bank is evaluating multiple biodiversity quantification approaches with commercial and academic partners, and in 2025 will continue quantifying biodiversity impacts and risks, refining data needs and understanding risk transmission to portfolios.

- Strategy, governance, and risk appetite: In 2023, Nordea published its first position on biodiversity and nature-related impacts and risks, including a Biodiversity Roadmap and commitments to embed biodiversity into strategy, governance, and risk management by 2025. Initial internal trainings have been conducted, and work has begun to extend nature-related targets in the Risk Appetite Framework. An initial 2023 risk appetite approach focuses on identifying, monitoring, and mitigating nature-related risks for large corporates in vulnerable industries.

- Existing commitments and sector policies: Nordea implements the Equator Principles for project finance and is a signatory to the Responsible Ship Recycling Standards and Poseidon Principles to address environmental and labor risks in shipping and to mitigate climate risks. In alignment with the UN Global Compact, commitments cover recycling, pollution prevention, and broader environmental safeguards. The current strategic ambition also targets mitigation of freshwater stress, resource scarcity, and water, air, and land contamination.

nodes.title: Nature-related risks
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.4.3 Nature-related risks
nodes.start_phrase: For nature -related risks, as part of the ESG framework, Nordea has deﬁned speciﬁc physical and transition risk drivers which potentially could (negatively) impact Nordea .
nodes.summary:
- Climate-related physical risks: Nordea identifies specific risk drivers within its ESG Factor Taxonomy, with flooding risk to underlying real-estate collateral highlighted as most relevant through 2030 (potential collateral devaluation).
- Disclosure: The Group’s gross exposure to acute and chronic climate-related physical hazards is reported in Part 2 (Table X).
- Risk management and mitigation: Uses EPC data, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments, industry credit policies, monitoring of national adaptation and insurance availability, and environmental/building certifications and permits; ongoing data enhancement projects improve precision.
- Governance: Specific risk appetite indicators for climate-related physical risks are integrated into the Risk Appetite Framework (RAF).
- Nature-related risks: Defined physical (e.g., loss of tree cover, ecosystem condition/productivity) and transition drivers (regulatory, technology, societal trends); certain physical drivers (land/freshwater/sea use change, invasive species, water scarcity) assessed as less relevant for Nordea.
- Exposure profile: Nature-related exposure is mainly driven by transition risks; credit exposure to highly vulnerable sectors is low, though aggregate exposures (e.g., real estate) can elevate overall risk; materiality is largely regulatory-driven.
- Quantification efforts: Applied external biodiversity impact scoring (Finance for Biodiversity Foundation, 04/2023) identifying highest-footprint sectors (agriculture, animal husbandry, food processing & beverages, materials); assessing multiple biodiversity impact methodologies; 2025 work to deepen quantification, data needs, and risk transmission to portfolios.
- Strategy and commitments: Published first Group position on biodiversity and nature-related impacts/risks (2023) with a Biodiversity Roadmap toward 2025; initiated internal training and began extending nature-related targets in the RAF.
- Standards and sector policies: Implementing Equator Principles for project finance; signatory to Responsible Ship Recycling Standards and Poseidon Principles to address ship recycling, labor conditions, environmental impact, and climate risks in shipping and project finance; aligned with UN Global Compact.
- Broader environmental focus and risk appetite: Addresses freshwater stress, resource scarcity, and pollution across media; established an initial 2023 risk appetite approach for nature-related risks focused on identifying, monitoring, and mitigating risks for large corporate counterparties in vulnerable industries.

nodes.title: Risk control and monitoring
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.5 Risk control and monitoring
nodes.start_phrase: The following section presents the risk control and monitoring per material risk type of Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy, starting with business model risk, credit risk, market risk, liquidity risk and operational risk respectively.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Nordea’s risk control and monitoring framework structured by material risk types, with this excerpt detailing business model risk and credit risk.
- Business model risk:
  - Portfolio-wide target to reduce financed emissions in the lending book by 40–50% by 2030, cascaded to material sectors; initial sector targets set in 2022 under NZBA, expanded in 2024.
  - Targets based on science- and policy-aligned benchmark scenarios, covering the majority of financed emissions and embedded in Nordea’s transition plan.
  - Public disclosure of sector targets and methodologies; business areas set medium-term financed-emission targets.
  - Ongoing monitoring via internal reporting and financed-emission forecasting; annual reporting in the Annual Report; anchored in the risk appetite framework and monitored via RFF.
- Credit risk:
  - Systematic integration of ESG into the credit process through an ESG Factor Taxonomy, applied as ESG-related credit risk drivers.
  - For corporate borrowers, ESG drivers assessed at industry and customer level; material ESG risks incorporated into credit assessments.
  - ESG rating override framework (updated in 2024) to address severe ESG impacts misaligned with ratings; linkage to findings from the 2024 materiality assessment.
  - Regular monitoring via early warning indicators that flag ESG-related issues, triggering mandatory ESG assessments and, where needed, escalation to higher-level credit committees.
  - ESG considerations influence customer selection, capital allocation, collateral valuation, and pricing; margins for green and sustainability-linked loans tied to asset/customer ESG performance.
  - Strategic loan pricing aligns with business selection, risk appetite, and risk-adjusted return targets.
  - Collateral transition-related measures include re-evaluating external shipping appraisers and quarterly sourcing/monitoring of EPC data for real estate.
  - Climate transition risk focus on high-emitting business models, assessing emissions intensity trends, quality of transition plans, and impacts on repayment capacity, aligned with Group targets.
  - Physical risk controls in real estate via insurance requirements, building regulations and adaptation measures, public early warning systems, internal market value monitoring/revaluation, and LTV limits.
  - Nature-related risk controls via counterparty certification (e.g., forestry, sustainable real estate), internal policies and programs to mitigate environmental harm, ESG-related exclusion criteria, engagement requirements, and monitoring of transition plans.
  - Application of the Equator Principles, including environmental and social impact assessments for large infrastructure and industrial project finance.

nodes.title: Business model risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.5.1 Business model risk
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea’s medium -term portfolio -wide target to reduce emissions in the lending portfolio by 40 -50% by 2030 has been cascaded to individual portfolios deemed material in regard to ﬁnanced emissions, last updated per Q3 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Outlines Nordea’s risk control and monitoring within its Common Risk Taxonomy; this excerpt focuses on business model risk and credit risk.

- Business model risk:
  - Portfolio-wide target to reduce financed emissions in the lending book by 40–50% by 2030, cascaded to material sectors; initial sector targets set in 2022 under NZBA (residential real estate, shipping, oil & gas, offshore & thermal coal & peat mining); additional sector targets developed in 2024.
  - Targets based on science- and policy-aligned benchmark scenarios that cover most financed emissions, aligning with Nordea’s transition plan.
  - Governance and transparency: sector targets published on Nordea.com and in the Annual Report; business areas set their own medium-term financed-emission targets; progress monitored via internal reporting and forecasting and disclosed annually; ambition anchored in the risk appetite framework and monitored via RFF.

- Credit risk:
  - Systematic integration of ESG through an ESG Factor Taxonomy as ESG-related credit risk drivers across the credit process.
  - Corporate borrower assessments consider industry and customer-level ESG risks; material ESG impacts are incorporated into credit ratings, with ESG rating overrides available when warranted; 2024 updates include a strengthened customer risk assessment and rating-override framework informed by the 2024 materiality assessment.
  - Ongoing monitoring via early warning indicators; ESG assessments triggered when relevant; high ESG-risk cases escalated to higher-level credit committees.
  - ESG influences business selection, capital allocation, collateral valuation, and pricing; margins for green and sustainability-linked loans tied to asset or customer ESG performance; pricing frameworks reflect risk appetite and risk-adjusted return targets.
  - Collateral and data practices include quarterly revaluation of shipping collateral via external appraisers and periodic sourcing/monitoring of EPC data for real estate valuations.
  - Climate transition risk focus on high-emitting business models, assessing emissions intensity trends, transition plan quality, and impacts on repayment capacity, aligned with group financed-emissions targets and transition plan coverage.
  - Physical climate risk in real estate mitigated through insurance requirements, adherence to building regulations and adaptation measures, policy-maker early warning systems, market value monitoring/revaluations, and LTV limits.
  - Nature-related risk managed via counterparty certifications (e.g., forestry, sustainable real estate), effective environmental policies/programmes, and internal industry credit policies with ESG-related exclusions and requirements for engagement and transition plan monitoring.
  - For large infrastructure and industrial project finance, environmental and social impact assessments are conducted under the Equator Principles.

nodes.title: Credit Risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.5.2 Credit Risk
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea continues to enhance and re -develop aspects of the credit customer ESG assessment process to systematically integrate ESG -related considerations in the credit process.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: The section outlines Nordea’s risk control and monitoring across its Common Risk Taxonomy, covering business model, credit, market, liquidity, and operational risks, with a strong focus on integrating ESG factors into frameworks, processes, targets, measurement, and governance.

- Business model risk:
  - Portfolio-wide target to reduce financed emissions by 40–50% by 2030, cascaded to material sectors; initial sector targets set in 2022 under NZBA (residential real estate, shipping, oil & gas, offshore & thermal coal & peat mining), expanded in 2024.
  - Targets aligned with science- and policy-based decarbonization pathways using benchmark scenarios that cover the majority of financed emissions; disclosed in the Annual Report and on Nordea.com.
  - Business areas set portfolio-specific financed emission targets; progress monitored via internal reporting, forecasting, and the risk appetite framework, with oversight via the RFF.

- Credit risk:
  - Systematic integration of ESG in credit processes via the ESG Factor Taxonomy as ESG-related credit risk drivers; material ESG risks treated as rating drivers with potential ESG rating overrides.
  - 2024 updates include a refined rating override framework and enhanced customer risk assessment linked to the 2024 materiality assessment.
  - Ongoing monitoring through early warning indicators requiring ESG assessments when triggered; high ESG-risk cases escalated to higher credit committees.
  - ESG influences business selection, capital allocation, collateral valuation (e.g., quarterly shipping appraiser reviews, EPC data for real estate), and pricing; margin incentives in green and sustainability-linked loans.
  - Transition risk assessment focuses on emissions intensity trends, transition plan quality, and impacts on repayment capacity, aligned to Group emission targets.
  - Physical risk controls in real estate via insurance requirements, adherence to building regulations, policy-maker early warning systems, market value monitoring, and LTV requirements.
  - Nature-related risk controls via certifications (e.g., forestry, sustainable real estate), environmental and social policies/programs, internal industry credit policies with exclusions and transition plan requirements; Equator Principles applied to large project finance.
  - 2024 developments include ESG risk definitions, semi-automated screening to flag customers for enhanced ESG assessment, dedicated ESG analysts, and use of external databases/controversy screening.

- Market risk:
  - Adoption of PCAF methodology for financed emissions in listed equity and corporate bond portfolios, improving measurement and steering across trading and banking books.
  - 2024 focus on data quality and classification expansion to include private equities and funds by sector.

- Liquidity risk:
  - ESG framework for illiquid exposures enabling proactive capital allocation, monitoring of positive/negative ESG factors, and control of current/future impacts.
  - Investment principles require minimum ESG criteria for fund managers, sector guideline protections, annual impact tracking including financed emissions, and accountability for ESG integration across the investment cycle.
  - Climate focus on reduction initiatives, avoidance, neutrality, and natural resource preservation.
  - For real assets: assessment of green building certifications, adherence to RSRS and Poseidon Principles in shipping, and presence of Net Zero targets to enhance risk management.

- Operational risk:
  - ESG embedded in the operational risk taxonomy, including reputational, liability/litigation, and ESG-related financial reporting risks.
  - Key tools: scenario analysis, Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA), Change Risk Management and Approval (CRMA), Third Party Risk Management (TPRM), and Incident Management.
  - Reputational risk management addresses ESG-driven media/stakeholder concerns; climate- and nature-related litigation risk defined to capture ESG-related legal exposures.
  - ESG-related financial reporting risk covers completeness and accuracy of ESG disclosures in financial/regulatory reporting.
  - Material operational risks influenced by ESG managed through the standard risk lifecycle and three lines of defense model.

nodes.title: Market risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.5.3 Market risk
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea is applying the PCAF methodology for measuring ﬁnanced emissions in the listed equity and corporate bond portfolios.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Nordea’s 2024 enhancements to ESG risk management across credit, market, liquidity, and operational risk.
- Credit risk: Adoption of an ESG Factor Taxonomy to define ESG credit risks; semi-automated customer screening with analyst oversight to identify material ESG impacts on creditworthiness; use of external databases to assess ESG performance and controversies, focusing on customer vulnerability and resilience.
- Market risk: Application of PCAF methodology to measure financed emissions in listed equity and corporate bond portfolios; improved capability to measure, report, and steer carbon footprints in trading and banking book holdings; 2024 focus on data quality and sector classification, extended to private equity and funds.
- Liquidity/illiquid exposures: ESG framework guiding proactive capital allocation and monitoring of positive and negative ESG impacts; principles for fund manager selection and oversight (minimum ESG criteria, legal sector guideline protections, annual progress tracking including financed emissions); emphasis on managers’ stewardship responsibilities; climate priorities include emission reduction, avoidance, neutrality, and natural resource preservation; ESG integration assessed through due diligence, holding, and exit; for real assets, checks on green building certifications, RSRS/Poseidon Principles compliance, and Net Zero targets; principles aimed at strengthening risk management.
- Operational risk: ESG embedded in the operational risk taxonomy (including reputational, liability/litigation, and reporting risks); tools include scenario analysis, RCSA, CRMA, TPRM, and incident management; management of reputational risks from ESG factors; definition of climate- and nature-related litigation risk; definition of ESG-related financial reporting risk; all managed via the risk management lifecycle and three lines of defense.

nodes.title: Liquidity risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.5.4 Liquidity risk
nodes.start_phrase: The ESG framework within the illiquid exposures portfolio allows for a proactive allocation of investment capital, monitoring and tracking several metrics and data points for ESG factors (those having both positive and negative effects).
nodes.summary:
- Credit risk management
  - In 2024, ESG risk management for corporate customers was advanced, with ESG Factor Taxonomy-based credit risk definitions established to identify ESG risks in the credit process.
  - A semi-automated screening tool, with human oversight, flags customers for enhanced ESG assessments by dedicated analysts, focusing on both vulnerability and resilience to material ESG issues.
  - External databases are used to evaluate ESG performance and identify controversies.

- Market risk
  - Nordea applies the PCAF methodology to measure financed emissions in listed equity and corporate bond portfolios, covering trading book fair-value holdings and banking book investments.
  - 2024 efforts focused on improving data quality and sector classification, extending coverage to private equities and funds.

- Liquidity risk
  - An ESG framework for the illiquid exposures portfolio enables proactive capital allocation and monitoring of multiple ESG metrics, assessing current and future impacts.
  - Clients are encouraged to become positive-impact contributors; minimum qualifying criteria for fund managers and legal sector guideline protections are required before investments.
  - Annual monitoring of ESG impacts, including financed emissions, is mandated; fund managers are expected to manage institutional capital responsibly and address ESG factors in underlying portfolios.
  - Climate priorities include reduction initiatives, carbon avoidance, neutrality, and natural resource preservation.
  - ESG integration is assessed across the entire investment cycle (due diligence, holding, exit).
  - For real assets, evaluations include green building certificates, adherence to RSRS and Poseidon Principles for shipping, and Net Zero targets.
  - These principles aim to strengthen overall risk management.

- Operational risk
  - ESG factors are embedded in the operational risk taxonomy (including reputational, liability, and litigation risks) to support identification and assessment of ESG-related operational risks.
  - Tools in place: scenario analysis, RCSA, CRMA, TPRM, and an Incident Management Framework.
  - Reputational risk from ESG issues is actively managed to prevent negative media or stakeholder attention.
  - Liability and litigation risk is defined as climate- and nature-related litigation within the Common Risk Taxonomy, complementing dispute management.
  - ESG-related financial reporting risk covers failures to provide complete, accurate, compliant ESG information in financial/regulatory reporting.
  - Material ESG-impacted operational risks are managed per the continuous risk management lifecycle and the three lines of defense model.

nodes.title: Operational risk
nodes.heading: 2.1.2.5.5 Operational risk
nodes.start_phrase: ESG factors are embedded in the operational risk taxonomy (including reputational risk and liability and litigation risk), to support the identiﬁcation and assessment of ESG related risks relevant for operational risk.
nodes.summary:
- In 2024, Nordea advanced ESG integration into credit risk management by establishing ESG Factor Taxonomy-based credit risk definitions and introducing a semi-automated customer screening tool complemented by ESG analyst reviews, leveraging external data to assess ESG performance and controversies.
- For market risk, Nordea applied the PCAF methodology to measure financed emissions across listed equities and corporate bonds, improving its capability to measure, report, and steer carbon footprints in trading and banking book portfolios, with enhanced data quality and sector classification extended to private equities and funds.
- Within liquidity risk, an ESG framework for illiquid exposures enables proactive capital allocation and tracking of ESG metrics, sets minimum qualifying criteria for fund managers, requires annual monitoring of ESG impacts (including financed emissions), and emphasizes fund managers’ accountability in addressing ESG across the investment lifecycle; climate priorities include emissions reduction, avoidance, neutrality, and natural resource preservation, with additional checks for real assets (e.g., green building certificates, RSRS/Poseidon Principles, Net Zero targets).
- In operational risk, ESG factors are embedded in the risk taxonomy (covering reputational, liability/litigation, and ESG-related financial reporting risks) and managed through tools such as scenario analysis, RCSA, CRMA, TPRM, and incident management; specific attention is given to climate- and nature-related litigation and to mitigating reputational impacts from ESG issues, all governed via Nordea’s risk management lifecycle and three lines of defense.

nodes.title: Capital & liquidity adequacy conclusion
nodes.heading: 2.1.3 Capital & liquidity adequacy conclusion
nodes.start_phrase: Capital adequacy assessment coverage for ESG -related impacts was initiated in 2020 and extended in 2021 to cover all prudential risk categories of Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: Nordea assesses ESG-related impacts on capital and liquidity across all prudential risk categories using a cross-risk view and a consistent 4-band materiality system within its ICLAAP/ICAAP framework.
- ICAAP conclusions: In 2024, capitalisation was evaluated per risk type and cross-risk. Additional capital was deemed necessary only for climate-related impacts on credit risk; no extra capital needed for other risks. Nordea maintains a strong capital position to cover this. All prudential risks except compliance and market risk are materially driven by ESG drivers; some ESG effects are already embedded in risk quantification.
- ILAAP conclusions: Environmental liquidity risks were quantified at Group level (2022, revisited 2023). In 2024, climate/nature-related hazards are most likely to affect HQLA and residential real estate–collateralised assets, with compounding chronic and acute water-related hazards most relevant. Liquidity ratios remain within limits except under very severe compounding scenarios; nature-related hazards are highly unlikely to affect liquidity. Overall liquidity buffers are sufficient for ESG-related risks.
- Stress testing program:
  - General: Annual ICLAAP includes climate-related stress tests and sensitivity analyses covering trading/banking books, liquidity, and strategic resilience.
  - Credit risk: Since 2020, short-term (3-year) transition scenarios via a GHG emissions tax show material impacts; methodologies enhanced using Scope 1–2 emissions and sector proxies. Physical risk tests since 2021 focus on Nordic drought/flooding. Long-term tests for net-zero alignment reveal high methodological uncertainty and dependence on customer/policy actions; climate-related credit risks are material in both short and long term.
  - Market risk: Short-term scenarios cover transition risk (NGFS Delayed Transition–based) and acute physical risk via an internal “Nordic flood risk on mortgage credit spreads” scenario aligned with credit/liquidity scenarios.
  - Liquidity risk (ILAAP): Short-term transition and flood scenarios indicate climate change is a material driver of asset liquidity, deposit, and off-balance-sheet risks, though impacts are assessed as low.
  - Operational risk: Transition risk drivers linked to legal and greenwashing effects are most material.
- Integration and development: From 2023, climate stress testing is embedded in ICAAP. In 2024, credit stress testing included a short-term transition scenario in a main ICAAP scenario, an expanded flood scenario, long-term portfolio projections under various transition paths, and a first-time sensitivity to biodiversity loss. Embedding aims to enhance learning and align stress testing with broader climate- and nature-related activities.

nodes.title: ICAAP
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.1 ICAAP
nodes.start_phrase: Capital adequacy assessment coverage for ESG -related impacts was initiated in 2020 and extended in 2021 to cover all prudential risk categories of Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Capital and liquidity adequacy conclusions integrating ESG/climate and nature-related risks across ICAAP/ILAAP and stress testing.
- ICAAP:
  - ESG capital adequacy assessment initiated in 2020, expanded in 2021 to all prudential risks using a cross-risk view.
  - 2024 materiality assessment evaluated each risk class for capitalisation using a 4-band materiality framework.
  - Outcome: additional capital reserved for climate-related impacts on credit risk; no extra capital needed for other risk types; strong overall capital position.
  - ESG drivers materially affect all prudential risks except compliance and market risk; some ESG impacts already embedded in risk quantification.
- ILAAP:
  - Environmental liquidity risk quantified at Group level in 2022 and revisited in 2023.
  - 2024 conclusion: climate/nature hazards most likely to affect HQLA and residential real estate–collateralised assets; chronic and acute water-related hazards most relevant.
  - Liquidity ratios remain within limits except under very severe compounding scenarios; nature-related hazards highly unlikely to affect liquidity; sufficient liquidity buffer confirmed.
- Stress testing:
  - Conducted annually within ICLAAP to gauge materiality and transmission of climate/nature impacts on trading and banking books, liquidity, and strategic resilience.
  - Credit risk: since 2020, 3-year GHG tax scenarios show material impacts on losses and REA; improved with Scope 1–2 emissions data and industry proxies. Physical risk tests since 2021 on drought/flooding; long-term net-zero alignment reveals methodological uncertainty and dependence on customer and policy actions; climate-related credit risks material short and long term.
  - Market risk: short-term transition scenario based on NGFS Delayed Transition; acute physical scenario focused on Nordic flood risk effects on mortgage credit spreads, aligned with credit/liquidity scenarios.
  - Liquidity risk: short-term transition and flooding scenarios indicate climate as a material driver of asset liquidity, deposit, and off-balance-sheet risks, but overall low potential impact; informs Group assessments.
  - Operational risk: transition-related legal and greenwashing scenarios assessed as most material.
- Integration and enhancement:
  - From 2023, climate stress testing embedded in ICAAP.
  - ICAAP 2024 included a short-term transition scenario within a main ICAAP scenario, a comprehensive flood scenario, long-term transition portfolio projections, and first-time biodiversity loss sensitivity analysis.
  - Embedding supports learning, strengthens linkage with broader climate/nature activities, and informs requirements and results.

nodes.title: ILAAP
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.2 ILAAP
nodes.start_phrase: Environmental related liquidity risk impacts were quantiﬁed in 2022 in a Group level assessment and the process was revisited in 2023.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Nordea’s capital and liquidity adequacy conclusions in relation to ESG risks, integrating findings from ICAAP/ILAAP and stress testing.
- ICAAP: ESG factors assessed across all prudential risks using a cross-risk view and a four-band materiality framework; additional capital is deemed necessary for climate-related credit risk only, with no extra capital for other risk types. Nordea’s capital position is sufficient. Most prudential risks (except compliance and market risk) are materially driven by ESG factors, with some impacts already embedded in risk quantification.
- ILAAP: Environmental liquidity risks analyzed (2022–2024). Water-related hazards (chronic and acute) could most affect HQLA and residential real estate–collateralized assets; liquidity ratios remain within limits except under very severe compounding scenarios. Nature-related hazards are unlikely to affect liquidity. Overall liquidity buffers are adequate for ESG-related risks.
- Stress testing framework: Annual climate-related stress tests and sensitivities embedded in ICLAAP/ICAAP to gauge impacts on credit, market, liquidity, operational risks, and business strategy resilience.
  - Credit risk: Since 2020, short-term transition scenarios (GHG emissions tax) show material impacts on losses and REA; methods enhanced using Scope 1–2 emissions and proxies. Physical risk tests (since 2021) focus on Nordic drought and floods. Long-term net-zero alignment tests highlight methodological uncertainty and dependence on customer and policy actions; climate-related credit risks are material in both short and long term.
  - Market risk: Short-term scenarios cover transition risk (NGFS Delayed Transition, simplified) and acute physical risk via a Nordic flood scenario impacting mortgage credit spreads, aligned with credit/liquidity scenarios.
  - Liquidity risk: Short-term transition and flood scenarios used for ILAAP indicate climate change is a material driver of asset liquidity, deposit, and off-balance sheet risks, but with low potential impact under assessed scenarios.
  - Operational risk: Transition-related legal and greenwashing risks assessed as most material.
- Ongoing enhancement: From 2023, climate stress testing integrated into ICAAP. In 2024, expanded to include a short-term transition scenario in a main ICAAP scenario, a more comprehensive flood scenario, long-term transition portfolio projections, and first-time biodiversity loss sensitivity analysis. Embedding aims to strengthen learning and alignment across climate- and nature-related risk activities and requirements.

nodes.title: Stress testing
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.3 Stress testing
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the yearly ICLAAP process Nordea performs a set of climate related stress tests and sensitivity analysis.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: Nordea’s ICAAP/ILAAP integrates ESG factors across a cross-risk view, extending since 2021 to all prudential risk categories within the Common Risk Taxonomy and using a consistent 4-band materiality classification from the ICLAAP framework.
- 2024 MA and capitalisation assessment: For the first time, each risk type was assessed both individually and cross-risk for capital needs. Conclusion: only climate-related impacts on credit risk warrant additional capital; other risk types require no extra capital. Nordea maintains a strong capital position to cover this.
- ESG risk driver influence: All prudential risks except compliance and market risk are materially driven by ESG risk drivers; several ESG impacts are already implicitly reflected in risk quantification.
- ILAAP and liquidity: Environmental liquidity risk quantified at Group level (2022, revisited 2023). 2024 conclusion: climate/nature-related hazards could most affect HQLA and residential real-estate–collateralised assets; compounding chronic and acute water-related hazards are most relevant. Liquidity ratios remain within limits except under very severe compounding scenarios; nature-related hazards are highly unlikely to affect liquidity. Overall liquidity buffers are sufficient for ESG-related risks.
- Stress testing framework: Annual ICLAAP includes climate-related stress tests and sensitivity analyses to assess impacts on trading/banking books, liquidity, and business strategy resilience.
- Credit risk stress tests: Since 2020, short-term scenarios simulate rising GHG emissions taxes over three years, showing material impacts on credit losses and REA; methodology enhanced using customer Scope 1–2 data and sector proxies. Physical risk tests (since 2021) focus on Nordic drought/flooding. Long-term tests on net-zero alignment reveal significant methodological uncertainty and dependence on customer/policy actions; climate-related credit risks are material in both short and long term (transition and physical).
- Market risk stress tests: Short-term transition scenario based on NGFS “Delayed Transition” (reduced risk factors) and an acute physical risk scenario (“Nordic flood risk on mortgage credit spreads”), aligned with credit and liquidity scenarios.
- Liquidity risk stress tests: Short-term transition and flooding scenarios indicate climate change is a material driver of asset liquidity, deposit, and off-balance sheet risks via outflows, but overall potential impacts assessed as low.
- Operational risk: Transition-related legal and greenwashing risks assessed as most material.
- Capability development and integration: From 2023, climate stress testing embedded in ICAAP. In 2024, enhancements include a short-term transition scenario within core ICAAP scenarios, a more comprehensive flood scenario, long-term portfolio projections under varied transition paths, and first-time biodiversity loss sensitivity analysis. Integration is intended to strengthen learning, governance, and alignment across climate- and nature-related activities.

nodes.title: SOCIAL FACTORS
nodes.heading: 2.2 SOCIAL FACTORS
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea sees human rights as the foundation for the work within the Group’s social responsibility strategy and fundamental to ensuring a social license to operate and continued business growth.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Nordea’s social strategy and related risk management. It positions human rights as the foundation of Nordea’s social responsibility and business growth, implemented through the ESG Policy Framework for both own operations and financial counterparties, and aligned with UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the UN Global Compact, and the Equator Principles. It highlights priority SDGs—4 (Quality Education), 5 (Gender Equality), 8–10 (Decent Work and Inclusive Growth, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, Reduced Inequalities)—and emphasizes sector-sensitive human rights requirements. Internally, Nordea’s Code of Conduct covers stakeholder impacts, customer relationships, equality and diversity, human and labor rights, and financial crime control; annual Code training is mandatory, with optional human rights training, and policies address gender balance, non-discrimination, procurement, and sanctions (the latter indirectly managing social impacts). Stakeholder engagement is detailed in the Annual Report.

On risk management, Nordea’s ESG Factor Taxonomy defines social risk drivers and maps them to ESRS topics using a decision-tree approach based on its ICLAAP materiality process, linking ESRS S1–S4 to the Common Risk Taxonomy and assessing implications for credit, operational, and compliance risks. The materiality outcomes indicate S1 (own workforce—especially working conditions) and S4 (consumers and end users—customer relationships/information) are material from a financial risk perspective, while S2 (workers in the value chain) and S3 (affected communities) are assessed as non-material.

nodes.title: Risk assessment and measurement per relevant risk type
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.2 Risk assessment and measurement per relevant risk type
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea constructed heatmaps to provide a structured methodology to identify possible social risks in the value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How Nordea assesses, measures, and mitigates social risk across credit, operational, and compliance risk types using its Common Risk Taxonomy and ESG Factor Taxonomy, and how ESRS topics map to these risks.

- Credit risk:
  - Uses heatmaps to identify social risks (human rights violations) across value chains, incorporating country-level differences in human rights protection.
  - ESRS S2 (Workers in the value chain) and S3 (Affected communities) linked to credit risk but assessed as not material.
  - Industry credit policies exclude specific human rights violations; additional criteria apply to gambling and defense sectors.
  - Mitigation: ESG screening at industry and customer level; ESG rating overrides when needed; early warning indicators include ESG triggers; enhanced scrutiny for customers with non-EU supply chains or exposed Nordic activities; reliance on business strategy, control systems, permitting/certification, KYC; social impact assessments under the Equator Principles for large project finance; employee rights issues addressed via counterparty and management risk in credit assessments.

- Operational risk:
  - Qualitative assessment deems all Level 2 social factors relevant; ESRS S2 and S3 linked but not materially impacting inherent operational risks.
  - Management through the standard operational risk management framework and tools.

- Compliance risk:
  - Qualitative assessment maps ESRS S1 (Own workforce) and S4 (Consumers and end users) as material.
  - S1 mapped to people risk (employment lifecycle, remuneration, wellbeing, capacity/competence, sustainable employment, D&I).
  - S4 data privacy subtopic mapped to data privacy risk (non-compliance with privacy, secrecy, data ethics).
  - Managed under the Compliance Risk Management Framework; product approval process includes ESG pre-screening and, when relevant, full approval with detailed risk and quality analysis.

nodes.title: Credit risk

  - Identification/assessment: Sector heatmaps used to spot potential social risks (human rights violations) across value chains, incorporating a country dimension reflecting varying national protections. ESRS S2 (Workers in the value chain) and S3 (Affected communities) linked but assessed as not material to credit risk.
  - Policy controls: Industry credit policies exclude specific human rights violations; additional criteria for customers in gambling and defence.
  - Mitigation/response: ESG social factors screened and integrated into credit assessments at industry and customer level; ESG rating overrides applied when impacts misalign with ratings; early warning indicators include ESG triggers requiring assessments; enhanced focus on customers with non‑EU supply chains or certain Nordic exposures; reliance on KYC and customer selection; social impact assessments under Equator Principles for large projects; employee relations/rights misconduct considered via counterparty and management risk in existing rating processes.

- Operational risk:
  - Scope: Includes reputational, liability, and litigation risks.
  - Assessment: All Level 2 social factors deemed relevant; ESRS S2 and S3 linked but not material to inherent operational risks.
  - Management: Handled through the regular operational risk management framework and tools referenced in environmental risk management.

- Compliance risk:
  - Assessment: ESRS S1 (Own workforce) and S4 (Consumers and end users) deemed material.
  - Mapping: S1 mapped to Level 2 People Risk (employment lifecycle, remuneration, wellbeing, capacity/competence, sustainable employment, diversity & inclusion); S4 (Data privacy) mapped to Level 2 Data Privacy (risks of non‑compliance with privacy, professional secrecy, data ethics laws/regulations).
  - Management: Governed by the Compliance Risk Management Framework; product approval process includes ESG prescreening and requires full approval with quality/risk analysis when ESG risks are relevant.

- Overall approach:
  - Consistent use of ESG Factor Taxonomy within credit, operational, and compliance risk processes.
  - Differentiated materiality conclusions by risk type: social topics not material for credit and operational inherent risks, but material for compliance (workforce and data privacy).
