Delivery through various initiatives and multi-channel access, supporting fair practices and social inclusion.

nodes.title: Significant (geographical) markets
nodes.heading: Significant (geographical) markets
nodes.start_phrase: In order to achieve the maximum possible transparency and in the interest of clearer lines of reporting, segments were defined in accordance with the IFRS 8 thresholds.
nodes.summary:
- Segment definition and reporting: Operating segments follow IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center are combined and disclosed as “Austria and other.”
- Employee footprint (31/12/2024): Total headcount 43,574 across Austria and CEE. Regional totals include Central Europe 11,187; Southeastern Europe 12,455; Eastern Europe 8,852 (Russia); Ukraine 5,690; Austria 5,390. Figures cover all Group units within the IFRS consolidation scope with more than 100 employees.
- Value chain scope per ESRS: Reporting covers own operations and upstream/downstream value chains, including products/services, business relationships, and supply chain. RBI’s model centers on deposit-taking and lending to corporate and retail clients in Austria and CEE, with additional services in leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises funding sources (customer deposits, issued bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities; sustainability-related funding/liquidity risks are considered. Customer money placed in investment and pension funds is excluded. Suppliers of goods and services for RBI’s operations are included.
- Downstream value chain: Primarily on-balance financial assets (loans and leases) and investment activities. Corporate lending is the key value chain with the greatest impact materiality; retail lending is also a key element. Exposures to sovereigns, financial institutions, and central banks are not core to the sustainability-related value chain but are disclosed where market practice (e.g., PCAF) applies. A second key downstream chain is assets under management in investment and pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without such control or look-through are excluded.

nodes.title: Definition of value chain
nodes.heading: Definition of value chain
nodes.start_phrase: According to ESRS, it is necessary to report information related to an undertaking’s own operations and its upstream and downstream value chain, including its products and services, its business relationships and its supply chain.
nodes.summary:
- Explains how significant geographical markets and operating segments are defined for reporting, aligning with IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, the Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center segments are combined and presented as “Austria and other.”
- Provides employee headcount by geography as of 31/12/2024, covering only Group units with more than 100 employees. Regional totals include Central Europe 11,187, Southeastern Europe 12,455, Eastern Europe (Russia) 8,852, Ukraine 5,690, Austria 5,390, for a Group total of 43,574.
- Defines the value chain in line with ESRS, covering own operations plus upstream and downstream activities. Describes RBI’s business model: primarily deposit-taking and lending in Austria and CEE, with additional services in leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: funding sources (customer deposits, issued bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities; sustainability-related funding and liquidity risks are considered. Customer money in investment/pension funds is excluded from upstream. Suppliers of goods and services are included as part of upstream.
- Downstream value chain: on-balance sheet lending/leasing and financial investments that finance customers/investees and drive positive or negative sustainability outcomes. Corporate lending is the most material impact area, with retail lending also important. Lending to sovereigns/financial institutions and central bank investments (primarily for liquidity) are generally not key for sustainability reporting, though disclosed where market conventions (e.g., PCAF) exist. A second downstream key chain is assets under management in investment and pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without such control or look-through are excluded.

nodes.title: Description of the upstream value chain
nodes.heading: Description of the upstream value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The upstream value chain of RBI consists of the financial liabilities that are borrowed as deposits or issued as bonds or equity.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and segmentation: To enhance transparency, operating segments are defined using IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, the Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center segments are combined and reported as “Austria and other.”
- Significant geographical markets and workforce: Employee headcount as of 31/12/2024 totals 43,574 across Austria and CEE. Regional totals include Central Europe (11,187: Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia), Southeastern Europe (12,455: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Kosovo, Romania, Serbia), Eastern Europe (8,852: Russia), plus Ukraine (5,690) and Austria (5,390). Figures cover Group units within the IFRS consolidation scope with more than 100 employees.
- Business model: RBI provides banking services to corporate and retail clients in Austria and CEE, focused on deposits and lending, and also offers leasing, asset management, pension fund business, and investment banking.
- ESRS-aligned value chain reporting: Information covers own operations and the upstream and downstream value chain, including products/services, business relationships, and supply chain.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises funding sources (deposits, bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities, with consideration of sustainability-related funding and liquidity risks. Customer investments in third-party investment and pension funds are excluded. Suppliers of goods and services for operations are also part of the upstream chain.
- Downstream value chain (financial assets): Primarily on-balance sheet lending and leasing activities. Corporate lending is the key value chain with greatest impact materiality; retail lending is an additional element. Lending to sovereigns and financial institutions and placements with central banks (mainly for liquidity) are not core to the sustainability-related value chain, though disclosed where market convention (e.g., PCAF) exists.
- Downstream value chain (assets under management): Includes investment and pension fund activities where RBI employees have direct operational control of the investment process. Third-party funds without such control or look-through capability are excluded.

nodes.title: Description of the downstream value chain
nodes.heading: Description of the downstream value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The main downstream key value chain of RBI consists of the on-balance sheet financial assets, which are lent or leased to customers and financial investment activities of RBI.
nodes.summary:
- Geographic segmentation and reporting: Operating segments are defined per IFRS 8; for the consolidated non-financial statement, “Group Corporates & Markets” and “Corporate Center” are combined as “Austria and other.”
- Workforce distribution: Headcount by geography as of 31/12/2024 totals 43,574, spanning Austria and CEE (Central, Southeastern, Eastern Europe, including Ukraine and Russia). Data covers IFRS-consolidated units with more than 100 employees.
- Value chain scope per ESRS: Reporting covers own operations and upstream/downstream value chains linked to RBI’s banking model (corporate and retail banking in Austria and CEE), plus leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises financial liabilities (deposits, bonds, equity) used to fund customer activities, with funding/liquidity sustainability risks considered; also includes suppliers of goods and services. Customer investments in investment/pension funds are excluded from upstream.
- Downstream value chain (material focus):
  - Primary: On-balance sheet financial assets (lending/leasing and investment activities), with corporate lending having the greatest sustainability impact materiality; retail lending is also key. Lending to sovereigns/financial institutions and central bank liquidity placements are not core to sustainability-related value chain, though disclosed where market practice (e.g., PCAF) exists.
  - Secondary: Assets under management in investment/pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without control/look-through are not key.
- Downstream activities deemed non-material/excluded: Cash and cash equivalents (mainly with central banks/financial institutions); trading assets/liabilities (short-term; climate market risk addressed under ESRS E1); non-consolidated associates and investees included only for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; investment property excluded (own-use property covered under in-house ecology for climate).
- Data maturity: 2024 value chain disclosures reflect available information; broader coverage expected as CSRD implementation advances.
- Stakeholder engagement (SBM-2): Key groups include shareholders/owners; customers (corporate, private, SME); employees and their representatives; regulators and supranational bodies (e.g., ECB, EIB, IFC, EBRD, MIGA, central banks); business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers); NGOs and civil society; membership organizations (e.g., WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI); the RBI Sustainability Council; and external ESG expert groups.

nodes.title: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.heading: SBM- 2: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.start_phrase: RBI defines its stakeholders as those people or groups of people that have a legitimate interest in the company through their direct or indirect business activities.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and exclusions in the downstream value chain: RBI deems several areas immaterial and excludes them from value chain reporting—cash and cash equivalents (mostly held at central banks/financial institutions), trading assets and liabilities (short-term; related market risk sustainability aspects addressed under ESRS E1: Climate change), non-consolidated associates and investees (only included for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; otherwise excluded from broader value chain considerations), and investment property (non-core; own-use property impacts covered in the Climate change chapter/in-house ecology).
- Data availability and roadmap: 2024 value chain information is limited to data readily accessible to RBI, with an expectation of broader coverage as CSRD implementation advances.
- Stakeholder engagement (SBM-2): Defines stakeholders as parties with a legitimate interest through direct or indirect business activity and identifies priority groups:
  - Shareholders/owners (private and institutional investors)
  - Customers (corporate, private/consumer, SMEs)
  - Employees and their representatives (unions, staff council; full-time, part-time, contractors)
  - Regulatory and supranational authorities (e.g., ECB, central banks, MIGA, EIB, IFC, EBRD)
  - Business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers)
  - NGOs and civil society (including proxies for “silent stakeholders” like ecosystems, biodiversity, local communities)
  - Membership organizations (WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI)
  - RBI Sustainability Council (internal and external ESG experts)
  - External ESG expert groups (third-party consultants, advisory panels)
- Period and context: Content is part of RBI Group’s 2024 Group management report.

nodes.title: General description of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: General description of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: RBI defines its stakeholders as those people or groups of people that have a legitimate interest in the company through their direct or indirect business activities.
nodes.summary:
- Clarifies which downstream value chain elements are deemed immaterial and excluded: cash and cash equivalents; trading assets and liabilities (short-term; sustainability risks addressed under ESRS E1: Climate change); investment property (non-core). Own-use property impacts are covered in the Climate change chapter’s in-house ecology section.
- Non-consolidated associates and investees are considered only for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; they are excluded from other value chain aspects.
- For 2024, value chain information is limited to data readily accessible to RBI, with broader coverage expected as CSRD implementation advances.
- Defines stakeholder engagement and identifies primary stakeholder groups: shareholders/owners; customers (corporate, retail, SMEs); employees and their representatives; regulatory and supranational bodies (e.g., ECB, central banks, MIGA, EIB, IFC, EBRD); business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers); NGOs and civil society (including proxies for ecosystems, biodiversity, and local communities); industry and membership organizations (WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI); the RBI Sustainability Council; and external ESG expert groups.
- Emphasizes integrating stakeholder views and ESG expertise into governance and business practices.

nodes.title: Frequency and formats of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: Frequency and formats of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: RBI engages with its stakeholders through various methods to ensure their interests and views are adequately considered in the company's strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- RBI engages stakeholders to incorporate their interests into strategy and business model, assess material sustainability topics, and refine sustainability management, while participating in national and international forums.
- Engagement formats and typical frequencies:
  - Conferences: annual/biannual events (e.g., sustainability summits, industry ESG forums).
  - Meetings: focused sessions with partners, regulators, and customers, often monthly/as needed.
  - Advisory sessions: quarterly or project-based with external ESG experts, partners, and internal stakeholders.
  - Training: regular, year-round education on ESG practices, financial literacy, compliance, and sustainability strategies for employees, customers, and partners.
  - Formal committees: monthly/quarterly bodies (e.g., Sustainability Council, ESG Task Force, RBI Sustainability Committee, and workforce-related committees).
  - Working groups: cross-functional/internal-external teams on ESG initiatives, climate action, and reporting.
  - Written engagement: surveys (annual), newsletters (monthly), reports, correspondence, and transparent customer complaint channels.
- Key topics include ESG integration, sustainable finance, climate change, human rights, environmental impact, regulatory compliance, financial literacy, and sustainability performance.
- Organization: a decentralized engagement model where units (ESG & Sustainability Management, Corporate Communications, Legal, Compliance, etc.) manage their own stakeholder interactions aligned to their expertise.
- Coordination: a central stakeholder dialogue database maintained by Group ESG & Sustainability consolidates inputs from all units for reporting, documentation, and monitoring.

nodes.title: Organization of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: Organization of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: RBI organizes its stakeholder engagement through a decentralized approach, where various units engage with stakeholders based on their specific areas of expertise and operational focus.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How RBI engages stakeholders to inform strategy, business model, and sustainability management, and how these engagements are organized and tracked.
- Purpose: Gather stakeholder views, assess material sustainability topics (ESG, climate, human rights, compliance), and feed results into continuous sustainability improvement; active participation in national/international forums.
- Engagement formats and typical frequencies:
  - Conferences: large formal events (annual/biannual) on sustainable finance, climate change, ESG integration.
  - Meetings: targeted discussions (often monthly/as needed) with partners, regulators, customers on ESG requirements, financial literacy, sustainability initiatives.
  - Advisory sessions: one-on-one/group input (quarterly/as needed) with external ESG experts, partners, internal teams on human rights, environmental impact, regulatory compliance.
  - Training: regular programs year-round on ESG practices, financial literacy, compliance, sustainability strategies for employees, customers, partners.
  - Formal committees: monthly/quarterly bodies (e.g., Sustainability Council, Task Force on ESG, RBI Sustainability Committee, workforce-related committees) for decision-making on ESG and people topics.
  - Working groups: cross-functional and external collaborations on ESG projects, climate action, sustainability reporting.
  - Written engagement: surveys (annual), newsletters (monthly), reports, correspondence, and customer complaint channels to collect feedback and share updates on ESG, regulatory changes, performance.
- Organization model: Decentralized execution by specialized units (ESG & Sustainability Management, Corporate Communications, Legal, Compliance), ensuring topic-relevant interactions.
- Governance and reporting: Central consolidation via a stakeholder dialogue database managed by Group ESG & Sustainability to document, monitor, and report engagement activities across the organization.

nodes.title: Purpose of stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: Purpose of stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: The purpose of RBI’s stakeholder engagement is to ensure that the interests and views of stakeholders are adequately considered in the company’s strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- Explains RBI’s purpose for stakeholder engagement: to embed stakeholder interests and views into corporate strategy and the business model.
- Details benefits of engagement: 
  - Gathers insights on sustainability, regulatory compliance, and performance.
  - Identifies and prioritizes material issues aligned with stakeholder interests.
  - Advances sustainability goals through awareness, support, and collective action.
  - Enhances transparency and accountability via open communication.
  - Fosters collaboration and partnerships to address shared challenges and share best practices.
- Describes how engagement outcomes are used:
  - Feedback is incorporated into strategy and operational practices.
  - Inputs inform initiatives in sustainability, risk management, and policy updates, helping prioritize goals.
  - Diverse perspectives support organization-wide decision-making.
  - Significant outcomes are documented and reported where feasible despite no centralized system.
  - 2024 examples include ESG risk advisory sessions with partners, Modern Slavery Statement implementation discussions, and employee/customer ESG surveys; these informed materiality assessments and sustainability strategy.
- Outlines stakeholder inclusion in due diligence and materiality assessments:
  - Engagement with shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, and NGOs through meetings, conferences, advisory sessions, and surveys.
  - Insights are integrated into strategic objectives and operational adjustments to align with expectations.
  - Materiality assessment guided by ESRS, with reference to GRI and UN Global Compact, ensuring alignment with supervisory and supranational stakeholder expectations.
- Emphasizes that integrating stakeholder input supports RBI’s long-term sustainability and success.

nodes.title: Consideration of stakeholder engagement outcomes
nodes.heading: Consideration of stakeholder engagement outcomes
nodes.start_phrase: RBI values the insights and feedback gathered from stakeholder engagements and integrates these outcomes into its decision-making processes, strategy and business model where feasible.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the purpose of RBI’s stakeholder engagement: to align strategy and business model with stakeholder interests by gathering insights, identifying material issues, supporting sustainability goals, enhancing transparency/accountability, and fostering collaboration and partnerships.
- Explains how engagement outcomes are used: feedback is incorporated into strategy and operations; informs initiatives in sustainability, risk management, and policies; supports inclusive decision-making; significant outcomes are documented and reported despite no centralized system.
- Provides 2024 examples: advisory sessions with business partners on ESG risks, discussions on Modern Slavery Statement implementation, and employee/customer ESG surveys; these informed materiality assessments and the sustainability strategy.
- Details stakeholder inclusion in due diligence and materiality: structured engagement with shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, and NGOs via meetings, conferences, advisory sessions, and surveys; insights feed into strategic objectives and operational adjustments.
- Describes the materiality assessment framework: comprehensive process guided by ESRS requirements and international standards (GRI, UN Global Compact) to reflect expectations of key stakeholders, supervisory authorities, and supranational organizations.
- Emphasizes the goal of integrating stakeholder perspectives to support RBI’s long-term sustainability and success.

nodes.title: Inclusion of stakeholders in due diligence and materiality assessment
nodes.heading: Inclusion of stakeholders in due diligence and materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: For RBI, understanding the interests and views of its key stakeholders is fundamental to aligning its strategy and business model with stakeholder expectations.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose of stakeholder engagement: to incorporate stakeholder interests into RBI’s strategy and business model by gathering insights, identifying material issues, advancing sustainability goals, enhancing transparency and accountability, and fostering collaboration and partnerships.

- Use of engagement outcomes: stakeholder feedback informs strategy and operations, shapes initiatives (sustainability, risk management, policies), supports decision-making with diverse perspectives, and is documented/reported where feasible to maintain transparency.

- 2024 engagement examples: advisory sessions with business partners on ESG risks, discussions on Modern Slavery Statement implementation, and employee/customer ESG surveys; these informed materiality assessments and the sustainability strategy.

- Due diligence and materiality assessment: structured engagement with shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, and NGOs via meetings, conferences, advisory sessions, and surveys; material topics selected per ESRS and guided by GRI and UN Global Compact; inputs from initiatives like UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and SBTi; continuous monitoring to track evolving stakeholder interests and trends.

- Governance for ESG: a Sustainability Council of external ESG experts guides strategy on economic, environmental, and social issues and anchors stakeholder concerns in policies.

- Climate and nature strategy: alignment with UNEP FI PRB; participation in international working groups (climate adaptation targets, biodiversity, pollution, human rights) and a core group shaping guidance to 2030; hosting a biodiversity day to raise awareness of nature’s economic interdependence; support for clients via tailored financial products and ongoing portfolio assessments.

- Circularity focus: event on circular economy (notably in packaging) to engage stakeholders and integrate circularity principles into business strategy; circularity identified as a key impact area under PRB commitments and target setting.

nodes.title: Overall ESG strategy
nodes.heading: Overall ESG strategy
nodes.start_phrase: RBI continuously evaluates the interests and views of its stakeholders to ensure alignment with its strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- RBI’s materiality and due diligence are strengthened by longstanding expertise and structured stakeholder engagement (surveys, workshops, and dialogues with customers, employees, rating agencies, NGOs, and sustainability experts).
- Global frameworks guide priorities: the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking serve as RBI’s core framework, complemented by participation in UNEP FI working groups and the Science Based Targets initiative to identify high-impact areas and direct strategic investment.
- Ongoing monitoring of stakeholder interests and emerging trends enables timely strategy and business model adaptations, building resilience, trust, and value creation.
- Recent stakeholder feedback validated RBI’s overall ESG strategy and business model, prompting no major changes while reinforcing integration of stakeholder insights into decisions.
- A Sustainability Council of external ESG and sustainability experts supports stakeholder dialogue and steers economic, environmental, and social policy direction.
- Climate and nature actions: RBI is the only DACH representative in an international UNEP FI core group shaping guidance to 2030; it participates in working groups on climate adaptation target setting, biodiversity, pollution, and human rights.
- RBI hosted a Biodiversity Day on 27 Nov 2024 with 100+ participants from finance, regulators, clients, and NGOs, emphasizing that over USD 44 trillion of global GDP depends on nature and translating this interdependence into actionable measures for industry and banking.
- The strategy combines qualitative and quantitative criteria, supports clients’ climate performance through tailored financial products, and continuously assesses the portfolio to align with sector-specific needs.
- Circularity is a key impact area under the PRBs; RBI organized a circular economy event (with focus on packaging) to advance sustainable practices, with insights feeding integration of circular principles into strategy and target-setting commitments.

nodes.title: Climate & nature
nodes.heading: Climate & nature
nodes.start_phrase: Since the UNEP FI´s principles for responsible banking serve as the guiding framework for RBI, RBI also participates in several UNEP FI working groups to foster its knowledge on practical implementation processes.
nodes.summary:
- RBI leverages its longstanding expertise to strengthen due diligence and materiality assessments, informed by structured stakeholder engagement (surveys, workshops, and dialogues with customers, employees, rating agencies, NGOs, and sustainability experts).
- External frameworks—including the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB) and the Science Based Targets initiative—guide impact identification, strategic focus, and investment priorities.
- Ongoing monitoring of stakeholder interests and emerging trends enables timely strategy and business model adjustments, reinforcing trust, resilience, and value creation.
- Recent stakeholder feedback confirmed RBI’s overall ESG strategy and business model; the bank remains committed to integrating stakeholder insights into decision-making.
- A Sustainability Council of external ESG experts advises on economic, environmental, and social priorities and supports stakeholder dialogue and sustainability management.
- Climate and nature: PRB serves as the guiding framework; RBI participates in UNEP FI working groups on climate adaptation target setting, biodiversity, pollution, and human rights, and acts as the sole DACH representative in a core group shaping guidance and potential 2030 requirements for signatory banks.
- RBI hosted a Biodiversity Day on 27 Nov 2024 with 100+ participants (including regulators, UN bodies, NGOs, and clients) to raise awareness of nature’s economic interdependence (USD 44 trillion of global GDP depends on nature) and highlight actionable measures for industry and banking.
- The bank’s strategy combines qualitative and quantitative criteria, offering tailored financial products to improve clients’ climate performance and conducting ongoing portfolio assessments to address sector-specific needs.
- Circularity: Recognizing its rising importance—especially in packaging—RBI convened a stakeholder event and is integrating circular economy principles into its strategy and operations; circularity is a designated PRB impact area supporting RBI’s target-setting commitments.

nodes.title: Circularity
nodes.heading: Circularity
nodes.start_phrase: RBI recognizes the growing importance of circular economy practices, particularly within the packaging industry.
nodes.summary:
- Describes RBI’s robust due diligence and materiality assessment supported by long-standing experience and structured stakeholder feedback (surveys, workshops, and dialogues with customers, employees, rating agencies, NGOs, and sustainability experts).
- Highlights the use of frameworks like the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and the Science Based Targets initiative to prioritize high-impact areas and guide strategic focus.

- Confirms recent stakeholder feedback largely validated RBI’s overall strategy and business model, with no major changes required.
- Details the establishment of an external Sustainability Council to guide strategy on economic, environmental, and social issues and embed stakeholder concerns into policies.
- Outlines climate and nature initiatives: active participation in UNEP FI working groups (climate adaptation target setting, biodiversity, pollution, human rights) and membership in an international core group (only DACH banking group representative) shaping guidance for signatory banks to 2030.
- Reports on RBI’s Biodiversity Day (27 Nov 2024) to raise awareness of nature’s economic interdependence (USD 44 trillion of GDP depends on nature) and identify practical measures for clients and stakeholders.
- Explains a strategy combining qualitative and quantitative criteria, including tailored financial products and ongoing portfolio assessments to support clients’ climate performance and sector-specific needs.
- Emphasizes circularity as a key impact area, particularly in the packaging industry, with dedicated events to define the financial sector’s role and integrate circular economy principles into strategy and operations, supporting PRB target-setting commitments.

nodes.title: Human rights
nodes.heading: Human rights
nodes.start_phrase: T h e d e v e l o p m e n t o f R B I ' s G r o u p H u m a n R i g h t s P o l i c y i n 2 0 2 3 d e m o n s t r a t e s t h e c o m p a n y ’ s c o m m i t m e n t t o f o s t e r i n g d i a l o g u e o n h u m a n r i g h t s i s s u e s .
nodes.summary:
- Human rights: RBI developed a Group Human Rights Policy in 2023 through collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute and a cross‑divisional working group, underscoring expert- and stakeholder‑driven strategy. It is also preparing a Modern Slavery Act statement with external consultants and legal experts.
- Operational integration: A cross-functional human rights working group met monthly in 2024 to embed human rights due diligence into banking processes.
- Financial inclusion: In line with UNEP FI’s Principles for Responsible Banking, RBI hosted a Financial Inclusion Summit in Prague (Sept 2024) to share best practices and align on financial education, products for vulnerable groups, and readiness for the EU Accessibility Act, featuring a UNEP FI keynote.
- Customer focus: RBI is continuously improving complaint management and customer service, using ongoing assessments of interactions and satisfaction to refine products and service strategies.
- Next steps: Continue regular stakeholder engagement and materiality assessments; monitor and adjust engagement effectiveness; and review internal ESG policies to ensure continuous improvement and alignment with best practices, strengthening trust and transparency.
- Stakeholder engagement governance: Management and supervisory bodies are kept informed of stakeholder views (shareholders, customers, employees, authorities, partners, NGOs, civil society, employee reps, membership organizations, Sustainability Council, external ESG experts) through:
  - Regular engagement and structured feedback to senior management, including customer survey insights and reporting of NGO‑raised controversies on human rights or climate/nature.
  - Sustainability Committee discussions where materiality findings and stakeholder feedback are presented to inform strategic decisions of the Management and Supervisory Boards.

nodes.title: Next steps
nodes.heading: Next steps

nodes.title: Stakeholder Engagement Governance
nodes.heading: Stakeholder Engagement Governance
nodes.start_phrase: RBI ensures that its administrative, management and supervisory bodies are informed about the views and interests of key stakeholders – including shareholders, customers, employees, regulatory and supranational authorities, business partners, NGOs, civil society, employee representatives, RBI membership organizations, the RBI Sustainability Council and external ESG expert groups – regarding sustainability-related impacts through several key mechanisms:
nodes.summary:
- Human rights: RBI developed a Group Human Rights Policy in 2023 through collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute of Fundamental and Human Rights and a cross-divisional working group, signaling a structured approach to expert- and stakeholder-informed strategy. RBI is preparing a Modern Slavery Act statement with external consultants and legal experts. In 2024, a cross-functional group met monthly to integrate human rights due diligence into banking processes.

- Financial inclusion and customer health: In line with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, RBI prioritized financial inclusion, hosting a 2024 Prague summit that aligned Sustainability, Retail, and Marketing on best practices, financial education, services for vulnerable groups, and the upcoming EU Accessibility Act, with a UNEP FI keynote linking to global expectations. RBI is continuously refining complaint management and customer service based on feedback and satisfaction assessments.

- Next steps: Ongoing stakeholder engagement and materiality assessments will guide improvements. RBI will monitor the effectiveness of these engagements, adjust as needed, and regularly review internal ESG policies to strengthen relationships, trust, and transparency.

- Stakeholder engagement governance: Administrative, management, and supervisory bodies are kept informed of stakeholder views—from shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, NGOs, civil society, employee representatives, membership organizations, the Sustainability Council, and external ESG experts—via:
  - Regular engagement (surveys, workshops, Sustainability Council meetings), with insights and any NGO controversies on human rights or climate/nature reported to leadership.
  - Sustainability Committee discussions of materiality and feedback findings.
  - Regular updates on material impacts, ESG performance, risks, and compliance.
  - Internal communications (newsletter, intranet, monthly briefings).
  - A dedicated Group ESG & Sustainability Management team and local officers to run proactive dialogue and integrate insights into strategy.

- Own workforce engagement: Structured exchanges with the Works Council (including monthly jour fixe), Works Council meetings in Austrian subsidiaries, biennial employee engagement surveys, CEO calls with anonymous Q&A, and fireside chats and consultation hours with People, Culture & Organization.

- Workers in the value chain and affected communities: RBI factors customer practices and conditions for value chain workers and communities into due diligence and strategy. Participation in the UN Global Compact Human Rights Accelerator (2023) and PRB working groups (e.g., ILO Decent Work, best practice community), along with collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute, enhances due diligence for corporate customers. Ongoing supplier assessments and monitoring help prioritize and identify significant impacts.

nodes.title: Stakeholder group: own workforce
nodes.heading: Stakeholder group: own workforce
nodes.start_phrase: RBI uses different formats to actively integrate the interests and views of its employees into its strategic framework.

- Value chain workers and affected communities: Participation in the UN Global Compact Human Rights Accelerator (2023) and PRB working groups (including ILO Decent Work and best-practice community) to strengthen human-rights due diligence for corporate customers. Collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute of Fundamental and Human Rights to establish the RBI Group Human Rights Policy. Ongoing supplier assessments and monitoring to set priorities and identify significant impacts.
- Outcome: These stakeholder formats feed insights to administrative, management, and supervisory bodies, enabling informed decision-making.

nodes.title: Stakeholder groups: workers in the value chain and affected communities
nodes.heading: Stakeholder groups: workers in the value chain and affected communities

nodes.title: Stakeholder group: consumer and end-user
nodes.heading: Stakeholder group: consumer and end-user
nodes.start_phrase: As a customer-centric organization, RBI puts the interests, views and rights of its customers and potential customers at the center of its strategy.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on the stakeholder group “consumer and end-user,” highlighting RBI’s customer-centric strategy aimed at becoming the most recommended financial services group through continuous innovation and superior customer experience.
- Integration of consumer insights into strategy via:
  - Code of Conduct ensuring respectful treatment, truthful marketing, and prioritization of consumer rights.
  - Commitment to responsible banking by signing the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
  - Multi-channel customer feedback mechanisms (surveys, digital interactions, in-branch surveys) informing product development and service.
  - Transparent, robust complaint management to enhance accountability and long-term relationships.
- Use of customer insights to design products and services that align with consumer interests and mitigate risks like over-indebtedness.
- Overview of SBM-3: identification and management of material impacts, risks, and opportunities within a complex economic, geopolitical, and environmental context.
- Explanation of the consolidated non-financial statement focusing on material sustainability topics reflecting stakeholder expectations and RBI’s impacts on economy, environment, and people (including human rights).
- Description of the 2024 double materiality assessment conducted per ESRS:
  - Impact materiality: RBI’s significant impacts on people and the environment.
  - Financial materiality: topics with actual or potential material financial effects on RBI.
  - Reference to IRO-1 for the process used to identify and assess material impacts, risks, and opportunities.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with the strategy and business model
nodes.heading: SBM- 3: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with the strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: As an internationally active banking group, RBI faces specific challenges in its efforts to realize its sustainability vision.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on the stakeholder group “consumers and end-users,” positioning RBI as customer-centric, guided by a vision to be the most recommended financial services group and a mission to turn continuous innovation into superior customer experience.
- Integration of consumer insights through: 
  - Code of Conduct ensuring respectful treatment and prohibiting misleading marketing.
  - Commitment to responsible banking via the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.

- Use of customer insights to shape product and service development, aligning with consumer interests and mitigating risks such as over-indebtedness and challenges in financial services use.
- Overview of SBM-3: material impacts, risks, and opportunities and their interaction with RBI’s strategy and business model amid economic, geopolitical, and environmental risks.
- Consolidated non-financial statement highlights 2024 material sustainability topics reflecting stakeholder expectations and detailing RBI’s impacts on the economy, environment, and people (including human rights).
- Execution of a 2024 double materiality assessment aligned with ESRS, covering:
  - Impact materiality (effects on people and the environment).
  - Financial materiality (current or future financial effects on RBI).
- Reference to IRO-1 for the methodology used to identify and assess impacts, risks, and opportunities.

nodes.start_phrase: The outcomes, including both the material topics from own operations as well as from the value chain, are shown below :
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Extract from RBI’s 2024 Group Management Report outlining double materiality findings and the management of sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) under ESRS.
- Core outcome: Most material issues are downstream in the lending and investment portfolios and assets under management; own operations and upstream suppliers are also assessed. Annual re-evaluation planned.
- Environmental (E):
  - E1 Climate change: Negative impacts from financing high‑carbon sectors; financial risks (credit, market, transition); opportunities in green financing, sustainability‑linked products, renewable/efficiency projects, and advisory. Own operations impacts across scopes 1–3; adaptation risks to buildings, asset lifespans, and energy/procurement prices; energy sourcing choices affect footprint.
  - E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Financing can drive biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation; alignment with UNEP FI PRB and regulatory expectations emphasized.
  - E5 Circular economy: Potential positives via procurement standards and efficient IT/hardware; downstream financing in real estate, transport, and energy contributes to waste and environmental strain.
- Social (S):
  - S1 Own workforce: DEI and inclusion benefits and risks (equal pay, discrimination, whistleblowing); employee development and training; health, safety, and well‑being; social dialogue and voice; secure employment, wages, work‑life balance; data privacy protection.
  - S2 Workers in the value chain: Potential human rights risks (forced/child labor, health and safety, wages, non‑discrimination) linked to financed clients and investments.
  - S3 Affected communities: Positive impacts via sector exclusions (tobacco, gambling, defense) and governance risk checks; social financings for essential services, jobs, and SME support (including women‑owned and underserved regions).
  - S4 Consumers/end-users: Privacy, cybersecurity, and resilience; responsible marketing and access to quality information; non‑discrimination; access to products and services. Identifies positive impacts, potential harms, and financial/regulatory risks.
- Governance (G1 Business conduct):
  - Culture of integrity and ethical compliance; whistleblower protection; anti‑corruption and bribery prevention/training; incidents risks; AML/CFT effectiveness; political engagement for informed policymaking; fair supplier relationships and ESG standards in procurement.
- Strategic linkages: Each topic mapped to business model responses (customer centricity, sustained growth, strong risk governance, efficiency), value chain segment (own operations, upstream, downstream), stakeholders, and time horizons.
- IRO management and methodology:
  - First ESRS‑aligned double materiality assessment conducted via workshops (Sep 2023–Jun 2024), separately for own operations and value chain, using ESRS 1 AR 16 touchpoints plus company‑specific topics.
  - Internal experts (compliance, data security, people & culture, facility management, procurement, risk, sustainable finance, subsidiaries, staff council, etc.) and ongoing external engagement (e.g., UNEP FI PRB working groups, ESG monitoring).
  - CSRD implementation team (finance and sustainability) led the process; subsidiaries perform aligned CSRD reporting.

nodes.summary:
- Focus: Impact, Risk, and Opportunity (IRO) management under IRO-1, detailing RBI’s process to identify and assess material sustainability topics for its consolidated non-financial statement.
- Methodology: A double materiality assessment aligned with ESRS, covering both impacts (positive/negative) and related risks and opportunities across RBI’s own operations and its value chain.
- Scope and timing: First ESRS-compliant assessment conducted via workshops from September 2023 to June 2024; processes run at Group level and by EU subsidiaries that publish their own CSRD reports.
- Stakeholder involvement: Internal topic experts assessed direct impacts; external stakeholders engaged through long-standing channels such as PRB working groups; continuous ESG topic monitoring informs materiality.
- ESRS touchpoints (own operations): Initial topic list based on ESRS 1 AR 16 and expanded with company-specific topics—10 total (5 environmental, 4 social, 1 governance), including sub-topics and sub-sub-topics.
- Process steps: Internal workshops to introduce ESRS and double materiality; experts reviewed and adapted topic lists; potentially significant topics were completed with department input; topics without identified touchpoints were deemed not material and documented.
- Responsible functions: Materiality analysis led by internal stakeholders across areas including Compliance; Corporate Citizenship/Donations/Volunteering; Data Security/Risk Management/GDPR; Financial Inclusion/Literacy; People, Culture and Organization; In-house Ecology/Facility Management; Lobbying/Political Engagement/Marketing; Procurement/Supply Chain; Risk Controlling; Selected Subsidiaries; Staff Council/Employee Representatives; and Sustainable Finance.
- Governance: The CSRD implementation project team—combining finance and sustainability experts—held primary responsibility for conducting the double materiality assessment.

nodes.title: Own operations
nodes.heading: Own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The initial assessment for own operations was based on the list of potentially material topics according to ESRS 1 AR 16 data points and was expanded by adding company-specific topics.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: RBI’s process for identifying and assessing material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) for sustainability disclosure, aligned with ESRS and the double materiality principle.
- Scope of disclosure: Covers topics with significant positive/negative impacts from RBI’s operations, products, services, and value chain, and the related risks and opportunities to RBI.
- Methodology: A double materiality assessment conducted via workshops from September 2023 to June 2024, performed separately for own operations and the value chain.
- Stakeholder engagement: Internal topic experts evaluated direct impacts; external stakeholders engaged through ongoing channels such as PRB working groups; continuous ESG topic monitoring influences materiality.
- Organizational coverage: Assessment conducted at RBI Group level and by EU subsidiary banks, which publish their own CSRD reports.
- ESRS touchpoints for own operations: Initial topic set based on ESRS 1 AR 16 data points, expanded with company-specific issues, covering 10 topics (five environmental, four social, one governance) including sub-topics.

- Internal responsibilities: Materiality analysis driven by ESG-experienced stakeholders across functions including Compliance, Data Security/Risk/GDPR, Sustainable Finance, Procurement/Supply Chain, People & Culture, Facility Management, Risk Controlling, Corporate Citizenship, Marketing/Lobbying, Financial Inclusion/Literacy, Staff Council, and selected subsidiaries.
