nodes.title: ESG sectoral strategies
nodes.heading: 20.3.1 ESG sectoral strategies
nodes.start_phrase: This policy collated and i ncluded sectoral policies on oil & gas, steel, and real estate and construction.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: RBI’s lending business sector policies within ESG strategies, consolidating sectoral policies for oil & gas, steel, and real estate & construction, including an oil & gas exclusion component.
- Objectives: classify clients and projects into supportive, transformative, and restrictive categories; set principles, rules, and engagement criteria; support qualitative targets addressing circular economy and climate change impacts; and define sector-specific customer/project criteria to drive decarbonization and value-chain engagement.
- Applicability and governance: mandatory for all RBI group units involved in lending; Credit Portfolio Management accountable for implementation; developed with input from Corporate Customers, Group Regulatory Affairs, Group ESG & Sustainability Management, and others.
- Regulatory alignment: EU Taxonomy Regulation; Paris Agreement; EU Climate Law (Regulation (EU) 2021/1119); ECB’s climate and environmental risk supervision guide (Nov 2020); UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking; alignment with EU/US/UK regulations.
- Transparency and access: internal policy available via a group-wide database; oil & gas exclusion policy also published externally.
- Monitoring: monthly compliance monitoring via a dashboard showing portfolio distribution across supportive/transformative/restrictive categories with EAD and RWA; access for Risk, Corporate Customers, and Sustainable Finance; deviations trigger notification to responsible units and client negotiations to resolve breaches.
- Thermal coal policy: phase-out of thermal coal financing by 2030; transformation-related business permitted under defined conditions; client acceptability threshold at 25% or less of revenues from thermal coal with a clear exit plan by 2030; applies group-wide and includes value-chain engagement guidance.

nodes.title: Business policy on thermal coal
nodes.heading: 20.3.2 Business policy on thermal coal
nodes.start_phrase: This is an exit (phase-out) policy that sets rules for the exit from thermal coal financing by 2030.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: RBI Group’s on-balance lending ESG sector policies, consolidating sector strategies and exclusions, governance, and monitoring.
- ESG sectoral strategy: Integrates policies for oil & gas, steel, and real estate & construction, including an oil & gas exclusion component.
  - Classifies exposures as supportive, transformative, or restrictive with customer/project-level criteria to drive decarbonization.
  - Supports qualitative targets on climate change and circular economy.
  - Applies to all group lending units; Credit Portfolio Management is accountable.
  - Built on EU Taxonomy, Paris Agreement, EU Climate Law, ECB climate risk guidance, UNEP FI PRB, and alignment with EU/US/UK rules.
  - Stakeholder involvement: Corporate Customers, Group Regulatory Affairs, Group ESG & Sustainability Management, among others.
  - Accessibility: internal database; oil & gas exclusion policy published externally.
  - Monitoring: monthly dashboard showing portfolio split by category with EAD and RWA; deviations trigger escalation to industry leads and client engagement.
- Thermal coal policy: Exit by 2030 with allowance for transitional financing.
  - Acceptability threshold: ≤25% revenues from thermal coal plus a clear exit plan by 2030.
  - Applies to all lending units; head of Corporate Customers responsible.
  - Based on Paris Pledge, Katowice Rulebook, UN Global Compact Principles 7–9.
  - Monthly monitoring; external statement on renewable energy focus and coal exit available.
- Tobacco policy: Defines acceptable, critical, and non-acceptable clients.
  - Acceptable producers: global, high transparency/governance, responsible labeling/marketing (health warnings, minors’ protection), and active transition with at least one reduced-risk brand per main market.
  - Acceptable distributors: ≥75% of sales from such responsible producers.
  - Applies to all lending units; head of Corporate Customers responsible.
  - Based on WHO FCTC, UN SDG 3, UNEP FI PRB Principle 2, EU Tobacco Products Directive, and Audiovisual Media Services Directive.
  - Monthly monitoring; policy available in internal database.
- Nuclear energy policy: Seeks to avoid/minimize environmental risks from nuclear activities.
  - Avoids financing/advisory/participation in nuclear energy business and funds focused on nuclear.
  - ESG-based classification and due diligence at onboarding, financing, and annual review.
  - Applies to RBI financial institutions and investment/fund/asset management entities.
  - Key stakeholders: compliance officers (sanctions/sensitive business), relationship, product and credit risk, and execution departments.

nodes.title: Business policy on tobacco
nodes.heading: 20.3.3 Business policy on tobacco
nodes.start_phrase: The policy outlines business rules for tobacco producers and distributors, categorizing customers as acceptable, critical, or non-acceptable.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: All RBI group units involved in lending must comply with internal sector policies accessible via a group-wide database. Ultimate accountability rests with the Head of Corporate Customers, with monthly monitoring of compliance.
- Climate and energy alignment: The lending policy framework references the Paris Pledge for Action, the Katowice Rulebook, and the UN Global Compact Principles 7–9. RBI emphasizes support for renewable energy and a phased exit from thermal coal, with a dedicated statement referenced.
- Tobacco sector policy: Defines client categorization (acceptable, critical, non-acceptable) for producers and distributors.
  - Acceptable producers: global scale, high transparency and governance, responsible labeling/packaging/marketing with strong health warnings and protection of minors, and a transition toward reduced-risk products, including at least one reduced-risk brand in each main market.
  - Acceptable distributors: at least 75% of sales sourced from responsible tobacco producers meeting the above criteria.
  - Applies to all lending units; monitored monthly; Head of Corporate Customers accountable.
  - Regulatory basis: WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control; UN SDG 3; UNEP FI Principles of Responsible Banking (Principle 2); EU Directives 2014/40/EU (tobacco products) and 2010/13/EU (Audiovisual Media Services).
- Nuclear energy policy: Seeks to avoid and minimize environmental risks by refraining from financing, advising, or participating in transactions that could mobilize or catalyze nuclear energy activities with lasting detrimental effects.
  - All financing requests involving nuclear activities are classified and assessed under RBI’s ESG framework.
  - Multi-department internal checks at onboarding, during financing, and through annual reviews.
  - Applies to all RBI financial institutions and investment service providers/fund or asset management companies.
  - Key stakeholders: compliance officers (financial sanctions and sensitive business), relationship management, product and credit risk, and transaction execution departments.
- Overall: Establishes ESG-driven lending standards and sector exclusions/criteria for sensitive industries, with clear accountability, transparency, and routine oversight.

nodes.title: Business policy on nuclear energy
nodes.heading: 20.3.4 Business policy on nuclear energy
nodes.start_phrase: The policy is implemented to avoid and minimize environmental risks associated with nuclear power plants.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines RBI’s internal ESG-related business policies and process frameworks governing lending and risk management:

- Cross-cutting governance and access: All group units involved in lending must comply. Policies are published in a group-wide database. Ultimate responsibility typically lies with the Head of Corporate Customers (for sector policies) and the Head of Group Compliance (for nuclear energy). Monitoring is conducted monthly for sector policies and annually for certain process frameworks.

- Renewable energy and coal phase-out: Commits lending activities to align with climate frameworks (Paris Pledge for Action, Katowice Rulebook, UN Global Compact Principles 7–9), with an explicit focus on supporting renewable energy and phasing out thermal coal. Responsibility: Head of Corporate Customers; monthly monitoring.

- Tobacco business policy: Categorizes customers as acceptable, critical, or non-acceptable. Acceptable tobacco producers must demonstrate strong transparency and governance, responsible labeling/marketing with health warnings and protection of minors, and a transition toward reduced-risk products (at least one such brand in each main market). Distributors should source at least 75% of sales from these responsible producers. Applies across the value chain and all lending units. Based on WHO FCTC, UN SDG 3, UNEP FI PRB Principle 2, and EU Directives 2014/40/EU and 2010/13/EU. Responsibility: Head of Corporate Customers; monthly monitoring.

- Nuclear energy policy: Seeks to avoid or minimize environmental risks by refraining from financing, advising on, or otherwise mobilizing business related to nuclear energy, including investment funds focused on nuclear. Financing requests are classified and evaluated under RBI’s ESG framework during onboarding, financing, and annual reviews, with multiple departments conducting internal checks. Stakeholders include compliance officers (main), relationship, product and credit risk, and transaction execution teams. Responsibility: Head of Group Compliance. Based on international nuclear safety and accident conventions (CPPNM, ENC, NARE, NS, and the Joint Convention). Available internally and accompanied by a public position statement.

- Process policy – Simplified EU Taxonomy Regulation KPI calculation framework: Integrates ESG considerations into risk management, supported by documents on ESG process flow in corporate lending, sectoral strategies, financed emissions calculations, and ESG in corporate underwriting. Applicable to risk and business-line employees, with implementation accountability in Group Financial Institutions, Country and Portfolio Risk Management. Aligned with the ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks. Each component has specific monitoring, with the overall framework reviewed annually.

nodes.title: Simplified EU Taxonomy Regulation KPI calculation framework
nodes.heading: 20.3.5 Simplified EU Taxonomy Regulation KPI calculation framework
nodes.start_phrase: The policy describes how ESG-relevant topics are to be reflected within the risk management area, and for which a stand- alone supporting document has been created.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes governance and responsibility for two key policies: a business policy on nuclear energy overseen by the head of Group Compliance, and an ESG risk framework/process policy implemented by Group Financial Institutions, Country and Portfolio Risk Management.
- Nuclear energy policy basis: aligned with international nuclear conventions (CPPNM, ENC, NARE, Nuclear Safety, and the Joint Convention on Spent Fuel and Radioactive Waste). Developed by Group Compliance in coordination with compliance officers responsible for sensitive business. Published internally and complemented by a public position statement.
- ESG risk framework scope: outlines how ESG topics are integrated into risk management, including identification, measurement, management, processes, and governance; applicable to risk staff and all business lines.
- Supporting documents for ESG framework: ESG process flow (integration in corporate lending), sectoral strategies, financed emissions calculations, and ESG in corporate underwriting.
- Monitoring: specific monitoring for each policy with annual implementation reviews across units.
- Stakeholders involved in ESG policy: Sustainable Finance, Group Corporate Risk Management, Group Risk Controlling, and Corporate Business.
- Regulatory bases: nuclear policy grounded in international nuclear conventions; ESG policy grounded in the ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks.
- Publication and access: both policies are available internally in a group-wide database; the nuclear policy also has a public-facing position statement.
- Mentions a process policy on a simplified EU Taxonomy Regulation KPI calculation framework as part of the broader ESG process landscape.

nodes.title: RBI Group ESG rulebook
nodes.heading: 20.3.6 RBI Group ESG rulebook
nodes.start_phrase: To help its customers to improve their carbon footprint and make their transformation sustainable, RBI needs to be able to assess transactions and projects on the basis of ESG criteria and advise its customers accordingly.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Provide a harmonized, group-wide framework to assess and flag transactions and customers against ESG criteria, support clients’ sustainable transformation, and prevent greenwashing.
- Scope: Applies to ESG flagging of financial products for corporate and institutional clients (including financial institutions, sovereigns, and local/regional governments) across head office, subsidiary banks, Raiffeisen Leasing, and Raiffeisen Bausparkasse.
- Governance: Policy ownership by Group Structured Finance & Investment Banking; implementation of underwriting-related elements by Group Corporate Credit Management.
- Standards and references: Based on Loan Market Association guidelines, ICMA principles, EU Taxonomy Regulation, Zertifikateforum Austria Sustainable Finance Code of Conduct, ESG target market concept (BSW, BVI, WM Daten Service), and prevailing anti‑greenwashing practices.
- Development and updates: Regularly updated; developed with broad involvement from Structured Finance, Institutional Clients, Risk, Capital Markets units, Regulatory, Group ESG & Sustainability Management, Legal, Finance, Research, Raiffeisen Certificates, Retail Bonds & Equity Trading, and ESG experts across subsidiaries, Raiffeisen Leasing, and Bausparkasse.
- Publication: Available internally via a group-wide database.
- Thematic coverage: 
  - Climate change mitigation (per EU Taxonomy)
  - Climate change adaptation (per EU Taxonomy)
  - Energy efficiency (RBI green category)
  - Renewable energy (RBI green category)
- Corporate underwriting integration: Defines ESG data required in the Risk Statement to credit decision makers; sets triggers for deeper analysis based on customer and industry environmental scores; mandates ESG risk analysis (decision authority enforces if missing); provides guidance for account, product, and risk managers on reporting and partial assessment of clients’ environmental risks.
- Regulatory alignment: Prepared in line with the ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks, EBA Guidelines on loan origination and monitoring, EBA Report on ESG risks management and supervision, and the FMA Guide for Managing Sustainability Risks.
- Controls and monitoring: ESG risk analysis embedded in the Risk Statement ensures implicit policy monitoring and alignment with relevant process stakeholders.

nodes.title: ESG in corporate underwriting
nodes.heading: 20.3.7 ESG in corporate underwriting
nodes.start_phrase: The policy describes which type of ESG-related information the corporate risk manager, via its risk statement, transfers to the credit decision maker and in which cases, dependent on a combination of customer & industry environmental score,
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Provide a group-wide ESG rulebook to assess transactions and projects on ESG criteria, support customers’ sustainable transformation, and define “sustainable customers” and “sustainable transactions.” Regularly updated to reflect market developments.
- Scope: Applies to corporate and institutional customer segments (including financial institutions, sovereigns, and local/regional governments) across head office, subsidiary banks, Raiffeisen Leasing, and Raiffeisen Bausparkasse.
- Governance: Policy ownership with Group Structured Finance & Investment Banking; Group Corporate Credit Management accountable for implementation in underwriting.
- Standards and references: Aligned with Loan Market Association guidelines, ICMA principles, EU Taxonomy Regulation, Sustainable Finance Code of Conduct of Zertifikateforum Austria, ESG target market concept (BSW, BVI, WM Daten Service), and anti-greenwashing market practices.
- Development process: Cross-functional involvement from Structured Finance & Investment Banking, Institutional Clients, Risk, Capital Markets units, Regulatory, Group ESG & Sustainability, Legal, Finance, Research, Raiffeisen Certificates, Retail Bonds & Equity Trading, and ESG experts in subsidiaries and leasing/building society entities.
- Availability: Published internally in a group-wide database for key stakeholders.
- Thematic coverage: 
  - Climate change mitigation and adaptation aligned with EU Taxonomy.
  - Energy efficiency and renewable energy included as RBI green categories.
- Integration into corporate underwriting:
  - ESG information embedded in the Risk Statement provided by the corporate risk manager to decision makers.
  - Trigger for deeper analysis based on combined customer and industry environmental scores.
  - Mandatory ESG risk analysis; decision authorities require it if missing.
  - Guidance for underwriters on reporting and partial assessment of customers’ environmental risks.
  - Key stakeholders include account managers, product managers, and risk managers across RBI units.
- Regulatory framework: Prepared in line with ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks, EBA Guidelines on loan origination and monitoring, EBA Report on ESG risks management and supervision, and FMA Guide for Managing Sustainability Risks.
- Alignment: Coordinated with all relevant process stakeholders to ensure consistent application and monitoring.

nodes.title: ESG process flow corporates
nodes.heading: 20.3.8 ESG process flow corporates
nodes.start_phrase: The policy describes how ESG risks have been included in the three lines of defense model for risk management (especially the first and second lines of defense, as the third line of defense, audit, is regulated in the respective audit policies).
nodes.summary:
- Integrates ESG risks into the three lines of defense model, emphasizing first and second lines; audit remains governed by separate audit policies.
- Defines ESG process steps for business and risk functions to incorporate ESG risks, involving account managers, back-office officers, product managers, risk managers, credit analysts, and portfolio managers.
- Assigns accountability for policy implementation to Group Financial Institutions, Country and Portfolio Risk Management.
- Aligns with key regulations: ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks, EU Taxonomy Regulation (and delegated acts), and CSRD Articles 19a/29a with Article 8 Taxonomy disclosure obligations.
- Publishes the policy internally in a group-wide database and aligns it with all relevant stakeholders.
- Establishes the RBI taxonomy rulebook as the methodology for identifying, assessing, and disclosing taxonomy-eligible and -aligned financing, ensuring compliance with technical screening criteria and minimum safeguards.
- Specifies governance and workflow: Sustainable Finance reviews flagged transactions and documentation; a dedicated taxonomy tool must be used where applicable.
- Covers both collection of disclosed counterparty KPIs for general-purpose exposures and assessment of known use-of-proceeds exposures during origination.
- Applies group-wide to head office and subsidiaries; key users include ESG experts, Risk Controlling, and Regulatory Reporting.
- Assigns implementation responsibility for the taxonomy rulebook to Group Risk Data & Regulatory Reporting; assessments occur where transactions are booked; head office provides the taxonomy tool, training, and support to subsidiaries.
- Details climate-related policies for assets under management, notably a coal sector policy:
  - Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. targets a complete phase-out of coal industry financing by 2030.
  - Ensures compliance with InvFG §30 through diligent selection and continuous monitoring; negative criteria disclosed in fund prospectuses and enforced via daily internal limits.
  - Policy applies to all investible entities across the coal value chain (mining, processing, power generation, transport, infrastructure) and covers all retail funds and portfolios; best-efforts application to third-party funds and special funds subject to investor agreements.

nodes.title: RBI taxonomy rulebook
nodes.heading: 20.3.9 RBI taxonomy rulebook
nodes.start_phrase: The RBI taxonomy rulebook outlines the regulatory requirements of the EU Taxonomy Regulation and the respective implementing and delegated acts and how these need to be implemented across RBI in order ensure regulatory compliance.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines RBI Group’s ESG risk integration within the three lines of defense model, emphasizing the roles of the first and second lines (with audit covered by separate policies). It defines end-to-end ESG process steps across business and risk functions and identifies key stakeholders, including account managers, back-office officers, product managers, risk managers, credit analysts, and portfolio managers. Group Financial Institutions, Country and Portfolio Risk Management is accountable for implementation, and the policy is aligned with ECB guidance on climate and environmental risks, published internally via a group-wide database. A central component is the RBI taxonomy rulebook, which translates EU Taxonomy Regulation requirements and related acts into internal methodology for classifying and disclosing taxonomy-eligible and -aligned financing, ensuring compliance with technical screening criteria and minimum safeguards. Sustainable Finance, supported by relevant departments, reviews transactions and documentation, using a dedicated taxonomy tool where applicable. The policy governs both the collection of counterparty KPIs for general-purpose exposures and the assessment of exposures with known use of proceeds at origination, to be applied by head office and subsidiaries—especially ESG experts, Risk Controlling, and Regulatory Reporting. RBI is subject to CSRD (Articles 19a and 29a) and Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation, with Group Risk Data & Regulatory Reporting responsible for implementing the taxonomy rulebook, supported by group-provided tools, training, and subsidiary support. The document also summarizes policies addressing climate mitigation and adaptation, highlighting a coal sector policy for assets under management at Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H., which targets a complete phase-out of coal industry financing by 2030. Compliance is anchored in InvFG requirements for prudent selection and monitoring, with continuous system-based checks, negative screening criteria disclosed in fund prospectuses, and daily enforcement via internal limits. The coal policy covers all coal-related activities (mining, processing, power generation, transport, and infrastructure) and applies to all retail funds and managed portfolios, with best-efforts application to third-party-managed funds and special funds in line with investor agreements. Overall, the section frames governance, roles, tools, controls, and regulatory alignment for ESG risk management and EU Taxonomy reporting across the group.

nodes.title: Sector policy on coal
nodes.heading: 20.3.10 Sector policy on coal
nodes.start_phrase: Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. is pursuing the systematic phase-out of all coal industry financing by 2030.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope
  - Integrates ESG risks into the bank’s three lines of defense model (focus on 1st and 2nd lines; audit covered by separate policies).
  - Provides end-to-end ESG process steps for business and risk functions.
  - Key stakeholders: account managers, back-office officers, product managers, risk managers, credit analysts, portfolio managers.
  - Implementation accountability: Group Financial Institutions, Country and Portfolio Risk Management.
  - Aligned with relevant stakeholders and published internally in a group-wide database.
  - Regulatory basis: ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks.

- RBI Taxonomy Rulebook and disclosures
  - Translates EU Taxonomy Regulation (and delegated/implementing acts) into RBI-wide requirements and methodology.
  - Governs disclosure of financing aligned with environmental objectives, technical screening criteria, and minimum safeguards.
  - Sustainable Finance (with relevant departments) reviews transactions/documentation; dedicated taxonomy tool used where applicable.
  - Covers both counterparty KPI collection for general-purpose exposures and assessment of known use-of-proceeds at origination.
  - Applies to all involved head office and subsidiary staff (notably ESG experts, Risk Controlling, Regulatory Reporting) for eligibility/alignment flagging and KPI reporting.
  - RBI subject to CSRD Articles 19a/29a and Taxonomy Regulation Article 8 disclosure obligations.

nodes.title: E1-3: Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies
nodes.heading: 20.4 E1-3: Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies
nodes.start_phrase: One key goal for the climate & environmental business strategy is to incorporate the climate targets of the Paris Agreement into RBI’s balance sheet.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Actions and resources for climate change policies within RBI’s value chain for corporate and institutional customers, aiming to embed Paris Agreement targets into the balance sheet.
- Risk and opportunity assessment: Portfolio- and counterparty-level analyses using materiality and impact assessments, financed emissions, climate stress tests, and ESG counterparty evaluations integrated into the lending process.
- Strategic steering: Translating insights into targets by industry, reallocating resources away from clients not meeting environmental/economic parameters, and using updated internal tools (strategic scorecard with higher ESG weighting, sectoral strategies).
- Client segmentation: Three clusters—restrictive (phase-out if no transition), transformative (supported with transition financing), and supportive (already sustainable); plans to set client engagement criteria and quantitative targets.
- Risk governance: Credit policy reflects minimum ESG criteria; lending incorporates ESG in a three-lines-of-defense model for corporates.
- ESG budgeting: Establishing ESG budgets at group and subsidiary levels to guide funding plans and steer KPIs (e.g., Green Asset Ratio), with plans to fully integrate ESG budgeting into the overall budget process.
- Incentives: ESG management incentive program (launched 2022, piloted in Austria) to promote sustainable lending and discourage non-ESG business; rollout to subsidiaries with system upgrades to capture ESG data.
- Funding and capital markets: Group-wide support for sustainability bond issuances, development of ESG bond frameworks for CEE subsidiaries, and promotion of ESG bond formats to broaden the investor base; no fixed completion timelines.

nodes.title: E1-3: Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies - Introduction

nodes.heading: 20.4 E1-3: Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies
nodes.start_phrase: One key goal for the climate & environmental business strategy is to incorporate the climate targets of the Paris Agreement into RBI’s balance sheet.
nodes.summary: This section outlines RBI’s approach for corporate and institutional customers to align its balance sheet with Paris Agreement targets by identifying climate-related risks and opportunities and managing sustainability risks across portfolios and counterparties. RBI conducts qualitative and quantitative assessments using materiality and impact analyses, financed emissions calculations, climate stress tests, and ESG counterparty assessments embedded in the lending process. Results inform internal steering via industry targets, reduced exposure to non-compliant clients, and enhanced tools: an updated strategic scorecard with higher ESG weighting producing scores per country and business line, sectoral strategies, and a credit policy and lending process incorporating minimum ESG criteria under a three lines of defense model. Customers are clustered as restrictive (phase-out if no transition), transformative (supported with transition finance), or supportive (already sustainable), with planned client engagement criteria and quantitative targets. ESG finance planning introduces an ESG budget for head office and subsidiaries to adjust funding plans and steer KPIs such as the Green Asset Ratio, with intent to fully integrate it into the overall budget. Incentives and funding include an ESG management incentive program (launched 2022; prototype in Austria; based on the RBI ESG Rulebook; planned group-wide rollout) and ESG wholesale funding steering to support sustainability bond issuances and ESG bond frameworks in CEE; no specific completion timelines are set.

nodes.title: Sustainable financing
nodes.heading: 20.4.1 Sustainable financing
nodes.start_phrase: Providing sustainable financing generates added value for RBI’s customers and supports a variety of societal activities that are suited to sustainable financing.
nodes.summary:
- Defines sustainable financing as financing with long-term positive environmental, climate, societal, or social impact that supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
- Establishes group-wide uniform definitions and anti-greenwashing controls through the RBI Group Policy, RBI Group ESG definitions, and a greenwashing prevention check for lending and non-lending products.
- Aligns policies with external standards: Loan Market Association guidelines, ICMA principles, EU Taxonomy Regulation, Sustainable Finance Code of Conduct of Zertifikateforum Austria, ESG target market concept by BSW/BVI/WM Daten Service, and market practices against greenwashing.
- Reports 2024 sustainable financing for corporate and institutional customers (RBI AG and CEE subsidiaries) as of 31 Dec 2024:
  - Total €12.4bn; utilized €8.6bn (69%); unutilized €3.8bn (31%).
  - Utilized breakdown by category (amount; share of total sustainable financing):
    - Sustainable real estate: €3,761m; 30%
    - Renewable energy: €1,117m; 9%
    - Energy efficiency measures: €546m; 4%
    - Sustainable mobility: €430m; 3%
    - Water supply, sewage, waste management: €117m; 1%
    - Sustainable forestry and farming: €27m; ~0%
    - Manufacturing industry: €78m; 1%
    - ESG KPI-linked loans: €1,929m; 16%
    - ESG rating-linked loans: €580m; 5%
- Reports 2024 sustainable financing for solely corporate customers:
  - RBI Group: €12.2bn total (13% of the corporate portfolio); €8.5bn utilized; €3.7bn unutilized.
  - RBI AG: €7.6bn total (17% of RBI AG corporate portfolio); €4.2bn utilized; €3.4bn unutilized.
- Notes that providing sustainable financing is an ongoing process with no fixed completion timeline.

nodes.title: Sustainable real estate
nodes.heading: 20.4.2 Sustainable real estate
nodes.start_phrase: Real estate and construction are among the key industries closely monitored by stakeholders involved in the low-carbon economy and sustainable finance.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on RBI’s sectoral strategy for sustainable real estate and construction, aligning with low‑carbon and responsible banking objectives.
- Introduction of sector-specific policy with categorization of clients/projects as supportive, transformative, or restrictive for net‑zero transition.
- ESG-based engagement criteria and Exposure at Default (EAD) portfolio targets set for construction (2025, 2030) and real estate (2025), supported by a monitoring tool that flags deviations and triggers corrective actions.
- 2024 sustainable real estate financing utilized by corporate and institutional customers: €3.8 billion (44% of RBI’s €8.6 billion sustainable financing).
- Funding side: €838 million in green building assets within RBI AG’s Green Bond portfolio as of 31 Dec 2023, representing 44% of the portfolio; eligible projects exhibit lower energy consumption vs. national averages and deliver 38,952 tCO2 annual reductions (~47 tCO2 per €1 million invested).
- Framing of renewable energy, energy efficiency, and electrification as key transition drivers per IRENA’s World Energy Transitions Outlook 2023, with emphasis on the role of financing institutions.
- Renewable energy: €1.1 billion financing utilized in 2024; green bond renewable portfolio estimated to save 960,219 tCO2 annually (~1,732 tCO2 per €1 million invested); IRENA notes ~2% potential global CO2 reduction from renewables expansion.
- Strategic steps to scale renewables: deepen track record across CEE, finance under new regulatory regimes, transfer specialist know-how to subsidiaries, add offerings like on-site battery financing, and support district heating transitions; no fixed completion timelines.
- Energy conservation and efficiency focus: investments in efficiency technologies and energy storage (e.g., BESS); IRENA attributes ~25% of global CO2 reduction potential to efficiency.
- 2024 energy efficiency financing utilized: €545.7 million; estimated annual GHG reduction of 7,323 tCO2 (~15 tCO2 per €1 million invested).

nodes.title: Energy conservation and efficiency
nodes.heading: 20.4.3.2 Energy conservation and efficiency
nodes.start_phrase: The focus is on investments related to energy efficiency measures, such as for instance manufacturing, development, installation, maintenance or repair of products or technology that reduce energy consumption as well as energy storage projects (e.g. battery energy storage systems, BESS).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of RBI’s sectoral approach to sustainable real estate and construction, including a policy that classifies activities as supportive, transformative, or restrictive for net‑zero transition, with ESG-based engagement criteria and Exposure at Default (EAD) portfolio targets (2025/2030) and a monitoring tool that flags deviations for corrective actions.

Green building assets in RBI AG Green Bond portfolio: €838 million as of 31 Dec 2023 (44% of portfolio), with projects below national average energy use and annual emissions reductions of 38,952 tCO2 (~47 tCO2 per €1 million invested).
- Renewable energy: Recognized as a key transition driver (IRENA). 2024 financing utilized: €1.1 billion; estimated savings from RBI AG renewable energy loan portfolio: 960,219 tCO2 annually (~1,732 tCO2 per €1 million). Growth actions include building track record across CEE, financing under new regulatory regimes, transferring know-how to subsidiaries, adding on-site battery financing, and supporting district heating transition (ongoing, no set timelines).
- Energy conservation and efficiency: Focus on investments that reduce energy consumption and storage (e.g., BESS). Estimated to deliver 25% of global CO2 reductions; by 2050 global energy use must drop 6% vs. 2020, requiring €300 billion/year investment in the EU by 2030. 2024 financing utilized: €545.7 million; estimated savings: 7,323 tCO2 annually (~15 tCO2 per €1 million). RBI will target clients with high-impact CapEx (e.g., green steel), leverage EU funds, and emphasize energy-efficient digital infrastructure (data centers, fiber) (ongoing).
- Electrification: Targeting sustainable mobility, grids, and utilities; expected to account for 50% of final energy use by 2050 and 19% of CO2 reductions. 2024 financing utilized: €429.6 million; estimated savings: 15,550 tCO2 annually (~319 tCO2 per €1 million). RBI is pursuing opportunities across battery production, BESS, and partnerships with automotive and utilities; lithium-ion remains dominant (ongoing).
- Hydrogen and carbon capture: Hydrogen’s role in hard-to-abate sectors, with 12% CO2 reduction potential. Objectives include one-third of industrial hydrogen being low-emission by 2030; demand projected at 15 EJ by 2030 and 63 EJ by 2050. RBI will identify clients with refurbishment CapEx needs and assess opportunities across the hydrogen value chain (electrolysis, fuel cells, pipelines, storage), steel transition, and transport (merchant hydrogen, FCEVs, refueling stations, ports) (ongoing).

nodes.title: Electrification

Plans to back early investments across the green hydrogen supply chain (electrolysis, fuel cells, pipelines, storage) and identify client refurbishment CapEx for applications in hard‑to‑abate sectors (steel transition, industrial merchant hydrogen, FCEVs, hydrogen refueling stations, ports). nodes.title: Hydrogen and carbon capture

nodes.title: Retail banking
nodes.heading: 20.4.4 Retail banking
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the climate and environmental business strategy and its first pillar, one of the key targets of retail banking is to enhance the green loan offering to RBI’s retail customers.
nodes.summary:

- Product offering and targets: 
  - Tools to assess customers’ carbon footprints.
  - Increased sales of green and social loans to private individuals and small businesses.
  - Green unsecured purpose loans for property energy-efficiency upgrades (purpose validated in approval).
  - Green mortgage loans for financing/refinancing with defined use of proceeds under the green and social loans framework.
- Ambition 2025 commitments:
  - Broaden access to green mortgages, unsecured ESG loans, and other ESG-focused products.
  - Provide resources and tools to help customers navigate their ESG transition.
  - Train retail staff on ESG principles to better advise customers.
- Greenwashing and negative impact prevention:
  - Implement ESG expert opinions and greenwashing prevention checks.
  - Maintain an exclusion list of activities the bank will not finance.
  - Ongoing employee training to spot sustainability-critical signals.
- ESG expert opinion process:
  - Evaluates ESG impacts at project and company level; informs go/no-go lending decisions.
  - Considers PRB Impact Radar industry impacts, negative impacts and mitigations, controversies/incidents, and regulatory context (EU standards).
  - For critical cases, issued by Sustainable Finance; locally by ESG experts under its guidance.
  - Standardized through an internal ESG opinion tool and training workshops for local experts.

nodes.title: Prevention of greenwashing and negative ESG impacts
nodes.heading: 20.4.5 Prevention of greenwashing and negative ESG impacts
nodes.start_phrase: To address the topics of negative ESG impacts and greenwashing prevention within sustainable finance transactions, RBI has implemented different processes, which include the ESG expert opinion and the greenwashing prevention check, as well the establishment of an exclusion list of all corporate activities in which RBI does not wish to be involved.
nodes.summary:
- Retail banking strategy aligns with climate/environment goals by expanding green loan offerings and aiming to be customers’ first choice for retail ESG products.
- Product focus includes:
  - Green unsecured purpose loans for energy-efficiency property improvements, with purpose validated in approval.
  - Green mortgage loans secured by real estate, financing/refinancing projects aligned with the green and social loan framework.
- Development of tools to assess customers’ carbon footprints and advisory support to increase sales of green and social loans to individuals and small businesses.
- Ambition 2025 retail commitments:
  - Broaden availability of green mortgages, unsecured ESG loans, and other ESG-focused retail products.
  - Provide resources and tools to help customers in their ESG transition.
  - Train retail staff on ESG principles and their relevance to retail banking.
- Greenwashing and negative ESG impact prevention measures:
  - ESG expert opinion process and greenwashing prevention checks.
  - Exclusion list of activities the bank will not finance.
  - Ongoing employee training to identify sustainability-critical sectors and activities.
- ESG expert opinion details:
  - Evaluates ESG impacts at project and company levels and offers a qualitative conclusion to inform lending decisions.
  - Considers PRB Impact Radar industry impacts, negative impacts and mitigation, controversies, and the legal/regulatory environment.
  - For critical cases, issued by Sustainable Finance; otherwise by local ESG experts under Sustainable Finance guidance.
  - Standardized via an internal ESG opinion tool and training workshops for local experts.

nodes.title: ESG expert opinion
nodes.heading: 20.4.6 ESG expert opinion
nodes.start_phrase: For ESG critical transactions, particularly projects where an ESG expert opinion has to be issued , the ESG expert opinion evaluates the ESG impact of the transaction at project and company level, and assesses its impact on the environment and social issues.
nodes.summary:
- Sets out Raiffeisen Bank International’s retail banking strategy under its climate and environmental agenda, prioritizing an expanded green loan offering and positioning RBI as the first choice for retail ESG products.
- Describes tools to assess customers’ carbon footprints and the launch of sustainability-oriented retail products, notably green unsecured purpose loans for property energy-efficiency improvements and green mortgages aligned with the bank’s green and social loan framework.
- Summarizes “Ambition 2025” retail sustainability goals: broaden green/ESG product availability, provide resources and tools to support customers’ ESG transitions, and train retail staff in ESG principles.
- Details measures to prevent greenwashing and mitigate negative ESG impacts, including an ESG expert opinion process, a greenwashing prevention check, an exclusion list of prohibited activities, and employee training to identify high-risk sectors and signals.
- Explains the ESG expert opinion: a standardized, qualitative assessment at project and company level using criteria such as PRB Impact Radar industry impact, potential negative impacts and mitigations, controversies, and regulatory context; it informs lending decisions and is issued by the Sustainable Finance unit for critical cases or by trained local ESG experts using an internal tool.
- Notes the context as part of RBI’s 2024 Group management report.

nodes.title: Greenwashing prevention check
nodes.heading: 20.4.7 Greenwashing prevention check
nodes.start_phrase: RBI has established a process to prevent greenwashing and has rolled it out across the group as part of the RBI ESG Rulebook.
nodes.summary:
- RBI has instituted a group-wide greenwashing prevention check under its ESG Rulebook, requiring defined internal steps and ESG expert involvement (bid, decision, execution phases) for all sustainable finance transactions.
- The check assesses the structure of sustainable products (green, social, sustainability-linked, etc.) using LMA guidelines, ICMA Principles, and the EU Taxonomy for qualification and (de)flagging, and is a precondition for RBI’s participation.
- Objective is to minimize greenwashing risk by adding an independent supervisory layer from RBI AG’s Sustainable Finance department.
- RBI is building ESG awareness and capabilities across RBI AG and CEE subsidiaries via Corporate and Retail ESG Ambassadors, a knowledge-sharing hub, and regular training (EU Taxonomy, ICMA bond standards, circular economy, ESG products).
- Monthly update calls and head-office support for client meetings foster consistent execution and a group standard for sustainable financing.
- In 2023 RBI held its first Climate and Environmental Business Summit (~200 participants across all business lines), aligning on the vision, actions, and next steps to implement the climate and environmental business strategy.
- Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. set a plan to phase out coal financing by 2030, with strict exclusion criteria and targets to lower portfolio coal-revenue exposure, aligned with the Paris 1.5°C goal to reduce its carbon footprint.
- The asset manager practices active ownership: proactive and responsive company engagements on ESG, and exercises voting rights (directly or by proxy) under internal principles grounded in transparent, sustainable corporate governance.

nodes.title: Raising awareness – supporting the business units in RBI AG and the subsidiary banks in Central and Eastern Europe
nodes.heading: 20.4.8 Raising awareness – supporting the business units in RBI AG and the subsidiary banks in Central and Eastern Europe
nodes.start_phrase: It is key to raise awareness of ESG-related topics in the business units, to build up ESG knowledge internally and to ensure efficient cooperation within RBI.
nodes.summary:
- RBI’s greenwashing prevention check: a mandatory, groupwide process embedded in the RBI ESG Rulebook that requires ESG experts’ involvement during bid, decision, and execution phases of all sustainable finance transactions.
- Scope and standards: applies to all sustainable products (green, social, sustainability-linked, etc.) and uses LMA guidelines, ICMA Principles, and the EU Taxonomy for defining, qualifying, and (de)flagging transactions.
- Governance and risk control: the Sustainable Finance department at RBI AG acts as an additional supervisory layer to minimize greenwashing risk; compliance is required for RBI AG and all subsidiary banks.
- ESG awareness and capability building: establishment of Corporate ESG Ambassadors across CEE subsidiaries and a Retail ESG Ambassadors network/knowledge hub to strengthen internal ESG knowledge and cooperation.
- Training and knowledge sharing: ESG Academy e-learning plus business-specific training (EU Taxonomy, ICMA bond standards, circular economy, ESG products), monthly update calls, and head office support in client meetings on sustainable financing.
- Group alignment and strategy execution: efforts to standardize sustainable finance practices across day-to-day business; 2023 Climate and Environmental Business Summit (≈200 participants) to align vision, actions, and next steps across all business lines.
- Asset management coal policy: Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. plans to phase out coal financing by 2030 with strict exclusion criteria and targets to lower portfolio coal revenue exposure, aligning with the Paris 1.5°C pathway to reduce its carbon footprint.
- Stewardship and advocacy: proactive and responsive company engagement to assess financial and ESG performance, drive CSR and sustainability improvements, and exercise shareholder rights (directly or via proxy) under transparent, sustainability-focused governance principles.

nodes.title: Actions on coal
nodes.heading: 20.4.9 Actions on coal
nodes.start_phrase: Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. has outlined a comprehensive plan to phase out coal financing by 2030.
nodes.summary:
- RBI’s greenwashing prevention check:
  - Group-wide process embedded in the RBI ESG Rulebook to prevent greenwashing in sustainable finance.
  - Mandatory precondition for all sustainable transactions across RBI AG and subsidiary banks.
  - ESG experts from RBI AG’s Sustainable Finance team involved in bid, decision, and execution phases.
  - Focus on the structure of sustainable products (green, social, sustainability-linked, etc.).
  - Uses LMA guidelines, ICMA Principles, and the EU Taxonomy for defining, qualifying, and (de)flagging transactions.

- ESG awareness and capability building:
  - Establishment of Corporate ESG Ambassadors in all CEE subsidiaries and a growing network of Retail ESG Ambassadors.
  - Knowledge-sharing hub, monthly update calls, and business-specific trainings (EU Taxonomy, ICMA bond standards, circular economy, ESG products) via RBI’s ESG Academy.
  - Head office supports subsidiaries in client engagements on sustainable finance to create a group standard for daily business.
  - 2023 Climate and Environmental Business Summit (≈200 participants) aligned all business lines on the climate and environmental business strategy and future actions.

- Actions for assets under management (Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H.):
  - Coal:
    - Comprehensive phase-out of coal financing by 2030 with key milestones by 2025.
    - Strict exclusion criteria and declining revenue thresholds for coal exposure; targets entire coal value chain and considers nation-state exposure.
    - Active stewardship: proactive and responsive company engagement, voting, and transparency improvements (focus on Scope 1 and 2) to reduce product carbon intensity.
    - Policy aligned with Paris 1.5°C pathway; highlights health, environmental, and climate risks of coal and need for ~75% emissions reduction by 2030.
  - Nuclear:
    - Systematic exit from nuclear and uranium investments, complete by 2030 with milestones by end-2025.
    - Phased divestment of equities and corporate bonds based on revenue thresholds; applies across mutual and special funds.
    - Avoids countries with expansive nuclear policies via a sovereign ESG indicator.
    - Expected outcomes: reduced nuclear exposure and increased allocation to renewables, aligning with sustainability strategy and Austria’s nuclear stance.

nodes.title: Actions on nuclear
nodes.heading: 20.4.10 Actions on nuclear
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. continued its systematic exit from financing the nuclear and uranium industry, with a complete exit planned by 2030 and certain milestones to be achieved by end of 2025.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H.’s active engagement with portfolio companies to improve transparency and data quality for carbon footprints, focusing on scope 1 and scope 2 emissions, to lower the carbon intensity of sustainable financial products.
- Outlines a comprehensive coal policy covering the full value chain (mining, processing, power generation, transport, and related infrastructure), multiple geographies, and relevant stakeholders, including nation-state coal exposure.
- Commits to phasing out all coal-related activities and financing by 2030, with significant milestones by 2025, through engagement and stricter data requirements, aligned with the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C target.
- Highlights health and environmental harms from coal (heavy metals, toxins, radioactive substances) and the need for ~75% reduction in coal-related emissions by 2030 to meet climate goals.
- Details a nuclear and uranium exit strategy: phased divestment from equities and corporate bonds, revenue thresholds for companies involved, and avoidance of countries with expansive nuclear policies via the sovereign ESG indicator.
- Applies the nuclear policy across all mutual funds and considers special mandates; affects companies in nuclear energy, uranium mining/processing/transport/infrastructure, and fund investors.
- Sets milestones by end-2025 and full nuclear-related divestment by 2030, with ongoing monitoring and assessment updates.
- Anticipates outcomes including reduced exposure to nuclear/uranium, greater allocation to renewable energy, and alignment with the firm’s sustainability strategy and Austria’s nuclear policy.

nodes.title: Actions on climate strategy
nodes.heading: 20.4.11 Actions on climate strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. conducts monitoring and management of the carbon footprint of assets in scope.
nodes.summary:
- Monitoring and management of the carbon footprint for in-scope assets by Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. (RKG), aligned with fiduciary duty.
- Active corporate engagement to assess financial/non-financial risks and drive ESG/CSR improvements, aiming for long-term performance benefits.
- Distinction between proactive engagement (opportunity and risk identification) and responsive engagement (targeted dialogue on sustainability-related controversies).
- Exercise of shareholder voting rights based on transparent, sustainable corporate governance principles.
- Annual engagement with the 20 largest GHG emitters in the portfolio, focusing on companies without Paris-aligned commitments or otherwise among top emitters.
- Scope of climate actions: investment process of RKG; assets in scope are corporate issuer holdings of self-managed retail funds.
- Interim emissions targets cover Scope 1 and Scope 2 CO2; broader climate neutrality commitment considers more GHGs but faces data limitations, especially for full emissions categories; engagement is continuous.
- Own-operations environmental actions within Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI): group-wide, locally tailored measures spanning building management, energy reduction, mobility (public transport support, bicycle storage), and employee training/information.
- High implementation rates in energy-saving and efficiency initiatives, contributing to climate protection and reducing operational costs; recurring annual measures and ongoing system efficiency upgrades.

nodes.title: Environmental actions
nodes.heading: 20.4.12 Environmental actions
nodes.start_phrase: A variety of options are available to enhance sustainability within RBI.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H.’s climate strategy actions, including monitoring and managing the carbon footprint of assets in scope (corporate issuer holdings of self-managed retail funds).
- Emphasizes fiduciary duty and active engagement with portfolio companies to both assess financial/non-financial risks and drive improvements in ESG/CSR that support long-term performance.
- Distinguishes between proactive engagement (identifying opportunities and risks) and responsive engagement (addressing sustainability-related controversies and contextual risk assessment).
- Describes the exercise of shareholder voting rights, directly or via proxy, guided by internal principles grounded in transparent, sustainable corporate governance.
- Commits to annual engagement with the 20 largest GHG emitters in the portfolio, prioritizing firms lacking Paris-aligned commitments or otherwise among top emitters.
- Interim climate targets cover scope 1 and 2 CO2 emissions; broader climate neutrality goals encompass more greenhouse gases but are constrained by current data availability; climate-related engagement is continuous.
- Details RBI’s own-operations environmental measures: building and energy management, mobility initiatives, and employee awareness programs, tailored locally yet designed for group-wide application.
- Notes recurring measures (e.g., support for public transport) and ongoing efficiency upgrades (e.g., heating and cooling systems), with high implementation rates that contribute to climate protection and cost reduction.
- Highlights promotion of low-carbon commuting and business travel (public transport, bicycle storage) and staff training/information platforms to strengthen sustainability engagement across RBI.

nodes.title: E1-4: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
nodes.heading: 20.5 E1-4: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
nodes.start_phrase: RBI’s financed emissions targets are at the first stage set for non-financial corporations.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: RBI’s E1-4 climate targets for financed emissions, primarily for the non-financial corporations lending portfolio, with early steps for retail mortgages.
- Scientific/Policy basis: Aligns with IPCC AR6 1.5°C (C1, no/limited overshoot), UNEP Emissions Gap 2023, UNFCCC NDCs, and EU NECPs. Where national pledges are less ambitious than net‑zero pathways, RBI applies net‑zero pathways.
- Scenario selection: Chooses NGFS Net Zero Orderly Transition (Phase 4), consistent with ~1.4°C, includes CO2 and non‑CO2 GHGs; country-specific data via IMF climate dashboard. Uses IAM MESSAGEix‑GLOBIOM; sector coverage includes energy, transport, buildings. Will update with future NGFS phases.
- Target-setting approach: Adopts an overarching Absolute Contraction approach (portfolio-level) over SDA due to data gaps and need for GHG-based pathways; acknowledges NGFS sectoral granularity and will further explore SDA for internal steering.
- Scope coverage: Targets currently include Scope 1 and Scope 2; applies pro‑rata assumptions where scenarios lack non‑Scope 1 guidance. Scope 3 excluded for now due to higher volatility and double counting risk; may evolve.
- Portfolio context: Assumes alignment with country macroeconomics; limited exposure to highly sensitive sectors (e.g., thermal coal, oil upstream), supporting an overarching approach.
- 2030 target for non-financial corporations lending:
  - Reduction: 27% financed emissions reduction from 2023 to 2030 (cross‑sector pathway).
  - Baseline (2023, updated methodology using PCAF database Sept 2024): 11,342,449 kgCO2e (Scope 1+2); intensity 264 tCO2e per million €.
  - 2030 target values: intensity 193 tCO2e per million €; absolute 8,279,988 kgCO2e.
  - Note: 2023 baseline recalculated; figures in the 2023 sustainability report are not comparable due to methodology updates.
- Monitoring and reporting: Will track and disclose financed emissions and intensity annually through 2030 in line with CSRD.
- Governance and process: Target setting involved Corporate Business, Risk Management, Sustainable Finance; approved by the Management Board.
- Methodological considerations and risks: Physical intensity metrics may not ensure equivalent financed emissions reductions; PCAF standards show volatility/non‑comparability; decarbonization scenarios often lack explicit non‑Scope 1 guidance.
- Retail mortgages: 2024 baseline calculation underway for residential real estate. RBI will monitor for at least one year, engage subsidiaries, validate data stability, and plans to set targets in 2025.
- Scope of attribution: Targets apply to covered emissions for the non‑financial corporations lending portfolio (referenced to Section E1‑6).

nodes.title: E1-4: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation - Introduction
nodes.source_title: E1-4: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
nodes.source_heading: E1-4: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
nodes.heading: 20.5 E1-4: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
nodes.start_phrase: RBI’s financed emissions targets are at the first stage set for non-financial corporations.
nodes.summary: RBI sets financed emissions targets for its non-financial corporations lending portfolio aligned with IPCC AR6 Category C1 (1.5°C, no/limited overshoot), using the NGFS Net Zero Orderly Transition scenario (Phase 4, 1.4°C) curated by the IMF for country-specific CO2 and non-CO2 GHG data and the MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM IAM. After assessing UNEP’s 2023 Emissions Gap Report, UNFCCC NDCs, and EU NECPs—and applying net‑zero pathways where national pledges are less ambitious—RBI adopts the overarching Absolute Contraction approach (prioritizing GHG/CO2e disclosure as a PCAF signatory) over SDA due to current sectoral data gaps, while noting NGFS provides sectoral granularity (energy, transport, buildings). Targets cover Scope 1 and 2 only (Scope 3 excluded due to volatility and double counting; pro‑rata applied for other scopes where needed). Baseline year 2023 Scope 1+2 financed emissions are 11,342,449 kgCO2e with intensity 264 tCO2e/mn €, targeting a 27% reduction by 2030 to 8,279,988 kgCO2e and intensity 193 tCO2e/mn €. RBI highlights risks that physical emissions intensity metrics may not align with financed emissions reductions and cites volatility/non-comparability in PCAF standards; portfolio lacks significant thermal coal and oil upstream exposure. Targets were set with input from Corporate Business, Risk Management, and Sustainable Finance and approved by the Management Board. The 2023 baseline was recalculated using an updated methodology (PCAF database, Sep 2024), rendering prior 2023 published figures non-comparable.

nodes.title: Retail mortgage loans
nodes.heading: 20.5.1 Retail mortgage loans
nodes.start_phrase: RBI started to calculate the baseline of the emissions for the year 2024; this includes residential real estate.
nodes.summary:
- RBI applies a portfolio-based, cross-sector decarbonization approach using country-specific data to align its lending portfolio with a 1.5°C pathway under CSRD/IPCC.
- Target set: 27% reduction in financed emissions for the non-financial corporations lending portfolio by 2030 from a 2023 base year, based on weighted exposure across sectors.
- Governance and process: Corporate Business, Risk Management, and Sustainable Finance were involved; targets approved by the Management Board; approach follows industry best practice.
- Metrics rationale: Preference for financed-emissions intensity (e.g., kgCO2e/t € or tCO2e/mn €) over physical intensity to avoid mismatches that could leave financed emissions flat or declining inadequately; notes volatility and limited comparability in current PCAF standards.
- Scope treatment: Given scenario gaps beyond Scope 1 (e.g., IEA NZE 2050), RBI applies pro‑rata decarbonization shares for other scopes; current targets cover Scopes 1 and 2, with Scope 3 excluded due to volatility and double-counting risks; sectoral approaches continue for internal steering.
- Tracking and disclosure: RBI will monitor and report financed emissions and intensity annually through 2030.
- Recalibrated 2023 baseline (updated methodology using PCAF database as of Sept 2024): Scope 1+2 financed emissions of 11,342,449 kgCO2e; intensity of 264 tCO2e/mn €; 2030 targets are 193 tCO2e/mn € intensity and 8,279,988 kgCO2e absolute financed emissions. 2023 figures in the published sustainability report are not directly comparable due to methodology updates; the 2023 baseline was recalculated for consistency with year-end 2024.
- Retail mortgages/residential real estate: 2024 baseline calculation initiated; RBI will monitor for at least one year, engage subsidiaries, and assess data drivers/uncertainties before setting targets, which are planned for 2025.

nodes.title: Assets under management
nodes.heading: 20.5.2 Assets under management
nodes.start_phrase: For Raiffeisen Capital Management the relationship of the target to the objectives is as follows: The interim targets as well as the net zero target by 2050 directly contribute to the objective, i.e. climate-neutral objective.
nodes.summary:
- Assets under management (Raiffeisen Capital Management): Sets relative climate targets aligned with a climate‑neutral objective—reduce financed emissions intensity (scope 1 and 2) by at least 25% by 2025 and 50% by 2030 from a 2019 base, and achieve net zero GHG emissions by 2050. Commits to engage with the 20 largest GHG emitters in the portfolio. Target scope covers equities and corporate bonds in self‑managed retail funds; interim targets cover CO2 scope 1 and 2 only, while the 2050 net‑zero commitment spans broader GHGs, with full category coverage limited by data availability. Financed emissions intensity was 122.97 tCO2 per € million invested in 2019 and 42.96 in 2023. Self‑managed retail fund size rose from €7.8bn (2020) to €14.7bn (2024).

- Own operations (RBI): In line with a 1.5°C pathway, targets a 42% reduction in scope 1 and 2 CO2 emissions by 2030; 2024 is the new baseline due to an expanded consolidation scope. Energy consumption and mix in 2024 (E1‑5): total 155,829 MWh, with 53% from fossil sources (including 20,745 MWh oil, 9,097 MWh natural gas, 60,775 MWh purchased fossil electricity/heat/cooling, 14 MWh coal, 1 MWh other), 9% from nuclear (15,094 MWh), and 38% from renewables (64,572 MWh purchased renewable electricity/heat/cooling, 66 MWh renewable fuels including biomass, 559 MWh self‑generated). Business travel and fleet fuel use accounted for 29,857 MWh. Renewable electricity consumption was supported by 559 MWh of self‑generation.

nodes.title: Own operations
nodes.heading: 20.5.3 Own operations
nodes.start_phrase: For own operations, the CO2 emission reduction targets are used to steer towards more sustainable business practices.
nodes.summary:
- Climate targets for Raiffeisen Capital Management’s assets under management:
  - Interim, relative emissions-intensity targets for equities and corporate bonds in self-managed retail funds: at least −25% by 2025 and −50% by 2030 vs. 2019 (scope 1 and 2), with a net-zero GHG target by 2050.
  - Engagement goal to actively engage the 20 largest GHG emitters in the portfolio.
  - Scope limitations: interim targets cover scope 1 and 2 CO2; broader GHG coverage envisaged for net zero, but full emissions categories not yet feasible due to data gaps.
  - Financed emissions intensity baseline and progress: 122.97 tCO2 per € million invested (2019) vs. 42.96 (2023).
  - AUM context for self-managed retail funds: €7.8 billion (2020) vs. €14.7 billion (2024).

- Own operations climate management:
  - Target aligned to 1.5°C: −42% CO2 emissions in scope 1 and 2 by 2030.
  - 2024 set as the new baseline due to expanded consolidation scope; therefore, no comparability with earlier years.

- Energy consumption and mix (E1-5) for own operations in 2024:
  - Total energy consumption: 155,829 MWh; significant contributor to location-based emissions.
  - Fossil energy: 90,632 MWh (53% of total), including coal 14 MWh, crude oil/petroleum 20,745 MWh, natural gas 9,097 MWh, other fossil 1 MWh; purchased electricity/heat/cooling from fossil sources 60,775 MWh.
  - Nuclear energy: 15,094 MWh (9%).
  - Renewable energy: 65,197 MWh (38%), including purchased renewable electricity/heat/cooling 64,572 MWh, self-generated non-fuel renewables 559 MWh, renewable fuels (incl. biomass) 66 MWh.
  - Fuel from business travel and fleet: 29,857 MWh.
  - Note on baselining: 2024 is the baseline year for energy due to scope expansion; prior-year comparisons are not provided.

nodes.title: E1-5: Energy consumption and mix
nodes.heading: 20.6 E1-5: Energy consumption and mix
nodes.start_phrase: Due to the expansion of RBI’s consolidation scope for reporting in 2024, this year has been set as the new baseline for energy consumption.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines Raiffeisen Capital Management’s climate objectives for assets under management, linking interim targets and a 2050 net-zero goal to a climate-neutral strategy.
- Sets relative emissions-intensity targets (scope 1 and 2): at least −25% by 2025 (vs. 2019), −50% by 2030 (vs. 2019), and net-zero GHG by 2050.
- Commits to engage with the 20 largest GHG emitters in the portfolio.
- Defines scope as equities and corporate bonds in self-managed retail funds; interim targets cover scope 1 and 2 only due to data limitations, while the net-zero ambition has broader GHG coverage.
- Reports financed emissions intensity for self-managed retail funds improved from 122.97 tCO2/€m invested (2019) to 42.96 tCO2/€m (2023); assets grew from €7.8bn (2020) to €14.7bn (2024).
- For own operations, sets a 42% reduction target in scope 1 and 2 CO2 emissions by 2030, aligned with the 1.5°C pathway; 2024 is the new baseline due to an expanded reporting consolidation scope.
- Presents 2024 energy consumption and mix for own operations (baseline year): total 155,829 MWh; 38% renewable, 53% fossil, 9% nuclear; includes 29,857 MWh from business travel/fleet and 559 MWh self-generated renewables.
- Details energy breakdown: fossil (90,632 MWh), nuclear (15,094 MWh), renewables total (65,197 MWh), with specific contributions from coal, oil, gas, purchased electricity/heat/cooling, and renewable purchases/self-generation.

nodes.title: E1-6: Gross GHG emissions of categories Scope 1, 2, and 3 as well as total GHG emissions
nodes.heading: 20.7 E1-6: Gross GHG emissions of categories Scope 1, 2, and 3 as well as total GHG emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Since 2020, RBI has calculated and published its scope 3 category 15 financed GHG emissions, i.e. the indirect downstream emissions associated with its lending and investment activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Reporting of gross GHG emissions (Scopes 1, 2, 3) and total emissions for both financed emissions (value chain/Scope 3, category 15) and own operations.
- Methodology: Calculations align with the PCAF standard (GHG Protocol–compliant) and use IFRS scope of consolidation. 2024 updates include September 2024 PCAF parameters (with inflation adjustment) and purchasing power parity for sovereigns.
- Scope expansion in 2024: 
  - Inclusion of customers’ Scope 3 emissions across all sectors in financed emissions.
  - First-time estimation for the mortgage asset class.
  - Adjusted sovereign calculations using PPP; disclosed both with and without LULUCF impacts.
- Coverage: Financed emissions calculations covered 56.7% of total assets; gaps stem from data unavailability or inapplicability of PCAF methods. Vehicle loans excluded due to immateriality.
- Data sources and quality: Customer-reported data used where available; otherwise estimated via PCAF emission factors. For corporate classes, ~31% of covered exposure used customer Scope 1–2 data; including sovereigns and households, 17% of covered exposure used customer data. Weighted PCAF data quality score ~3.6 (stable).
- Key financed-emissions results (2024):
  - Asset classes in scope: business loans, corporate bonds, commercial real estate, project finance, and (new) mortgages.
  - Scope 3 financed emissions reported for relevant classes; bank notes inherent double counting within its portfolio due to value-chain overlaps.
  - Sovereign Scope 1 financed emissions reported separately to avoid double counting with corporate portfolio: 12.93 Mt CO2e (incl. LULUCF) and 14.06 Mt CO2e (excl. LULUCF), now using PPP-based factors; high data quality.
  - Avoided emissions from electricity generation project finance reported separately with no netting against positive emissions.
- Year-over-year dynamics:
  - Covered gross carrying amount (excl. central government) rose 40.4%, mainly from adding mortgages, lifting absolute financed emissions.
  - On a comparable basis (excluding mortgages and applying 2024 parameters), customer Scope 1–2 financed emissions decreased by 20.8%.
- Distribution insights:
  - Sectoral (NACE) and country breakdowns provided; high-intensity sectors include electricity/gas, manufacturing, agriculture, and mining; top exposures include Austria, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Romania, Hungary, Germany, Luxembourg, Russia, US, Croatia.
- Own operations (2024):
  - Consolidation expanded in line with CSRD.
  - Total average emissions: 139,054 tCO2e (location-based): Scope 1 = 9,375 t (7%), Scope 2 = 21,805 t (16%), Scope 3 = 107,875 t (78%).
  - First-time disclosure of cloud and data center service emissions; granularity expected to improve.
  - Data captured via ESG Cockpit, covering >90% of employees; emphasis on energy efficiency first. Data quality graded as exact or calculated (no estimated).
