nodes.heading: 20.7 E1-6: Gross GHG emissions of categories Scope 1, 2, and 3 as well as total GHG emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Since 2020, RBI has calculated and published its scope 3 category 15 financed GHG emissions, i.e. the indirect downstream emissions associated with its lending and investment activities.
nodes.summary: RBI outlines its financed GHG emissions (Scope 3 category 15) methodology and 2024 results under the PCAF standard (GHG Protocol compliant) on an IFRS consolidation basis, expanding scope to include customers’ Scope 3 across all sectors and a first estimate for mortgages (vehicle loans excluded). Covered exposures were €113.3bn (56.7% of total assets), with PCAF asset classes totaling €85.3bn and financed emissions of 10,175 ktCO2e (Scope 1+2) and 21,818 ktCO2e (Scope 3), intensities of 119 and 197 tCO2e/€m, and a weighted data quality score of 3.6; 31% of covered corporate exposure (17% including sovereign and households) used customer-reported data. Sovereign financed emissions were 12.93 MtCO2e (incl. LULUCF) and 14.06 MtCO2e (excl.), calculated with PPP-adjusted factors and excluded from portfolio totals to avoid double counting. Avoided emissions from electricity generation project finance were 286 ktCO2e. 2023 figures were recalculated with Sept‑2024 PCAF parameters; on a comparable basis, customer Scope 1+2 fell 20.8%. Sectoral (NACE) and top-country breakdowns are provided.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emissions from own operations
nodes.heading: 20.7.1 Greenhouse gas emissions from own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The data relating to own operations is collected for RBI, which includes the subsidiary banks in Central and Eastern Europe, head office and the material Austrian subsidiaries.
nodes.summary:
- Presents a country-by-country breakdown of financed emissions, including:
  - Gross carrying amount covered by emissions calculation (€ million) for 2024 and 2023.
  - Financed emissions (thousand tCO2e) for Scope 1,2 and Scope 3.
  - Emission intensities (tCO2e per € million) for Scope 1,2 and Scope 3.
  - Weighted data quality scores (High=1, Low=5) for each scope.
- 2024 totals for financed emissions:
  - Gross carrying amount: €85,337 million (vs. €60,774 million in 2023).
  - Scope 1,2 emissions: 10,175 thousand tCO2e; intensity: 119.2 tCO2e/€m.
  - Scope 3 emissions: 21,818 thousand tCO2e; intensity: 411.1 tCO2e/€m.
  - Weighted data quality around 3.6 (Scope 1,2) and 3.5 (Scope 3).
- Notable country insights (2024):
  - Higher Scope 3 intensities: Hungary (720.7), Germany (639.7), Rest of the world (583.7), Russia (820.4).
  - Lower intensities: United States (8.4/181.6), Luxembourg (47.2/53.9), Austria (74.2/203.4).
  - Best data quality among listed: Germany (3.0/3.1); others generally 3.4–3.9.
- Own operations greenhouse gas emissions (RBI group-wide, expanded per CSRD in 2024 to include further units):
  - Total 2024 emissions (location-based): 139,054 tCO2e.
    - Scope 1: 9,375 t (7%).
    - Scope 2 (location-based): 21,805 t (16%).
    - Scope 3: 107,875 t (78%).
  - First-time disclosure of cloud and data center service emissions; data granularity expected to improve as suppliers provide more detailed breakdowns.
  - Data collected via ESG Cockpit, covering >90% of employees; performance tracked with company-specific KPIs, with emphasis on reducing consumption and improving energy efficiency.
  - Data quality framework: 1=exact, 2=calculated, 3=estimated; own operations data are exact and calculated, with no areas in category 3.

nodes.title: Total greenhouse gas emissions in detail
nodes.heading: 20.7.2 Total greenhouse gas emissions in detail
nodes.start_phrase: The net revenues amounting to € 8,701 million, which served as the basis for calculating the GHG intensity, are reported under operating income in the income statement of the consolidated financial statements.
nodes.summary:
- Provides a 2024 greenhouse gas inventory with full Scope 1, Scope 2 (location- and market-based), and detailed Scope 3 category breakdowns.
- Key figures:
  - Scope 1: 9,375 tCO2e; share under regulated emissions trading schemes not reported.
  - Scope 2: 21,804 tCO2e (location-based); 23,419 tCO2e (market-based).
  - Scope 3 total: 32,100,872 tCO2e, dominated by Category 15 Investments (31,992,997 tCO2e). Other reported categories include purchased goods and services (1,494), cloud services (51,084), capital goods (7,573), fuel- and energy-related activities (14,707), upstream transport and distribution (1,983), waste (3,288), business travel (7,967), employee commuting (19,736), and upstream leased assets (43). Downstream categories 9–14 are not reported.
  - Total emissions: 32,132,051 tCO2e (location-based) and 32,133,666 tCO2e (market-based).
- GHG intensity per net revenue: 0.004 tCO2e/€ (both location- and market-based), calculated on €8,701 million net revenues.
- Disclosure note: Financed emissions exclude the Sovereign Debt asset class to avoid double counting; these are disclosed separately under PCAF asset class reporting.
- E1-9 section outlines anticipated financial effects from climate risks/opportunities, focusing on methodology for assessing material physical risks in the banking book:
  - Prepared under the IFRS scope and aligned with EU Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 amending 2021/637, Template 5 (Climate change physical risk).
  - Reliance on counterparties’ ESG data, third-party vendors, and public registers; information not fully verified and no liability assumed for completeness/correctness.
  - Data challenges highlighted, especially in CEE: limited or unenforced Energy Performance Certificates, use of registration/headquarter addresses as proxies for non-financial corporates, internal data quality issues, and incomplete geographic coverage by data providers.
- Document context: Group management report of Raiffeisen Bank International for Financial Year 2024.

nodes.title: E1-9: Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities
nodes.heading: 20.8 E1-9 : Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-rela ted opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The assessment of the material risk positions with physical risk based on the European Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 of 30 November 2022 amending the implementing technical standards laid down in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/637 as regards the disclosure of environmental, social and governance risks - Template 5: Banking book - Climate change physical risk: Exposures subject to physical risk were prepared taking into account the IFRS scope of consolidation.
nodes.summary:
- Presents a detailed 2024 greenhouse gas inventory:
  - Scope 1: 9,375 tCO2e; no emissions from regulated trading schemes reported.
  - Scope 2: 21,804 tCO2e (location-based) and 23,419 tCO2e (market-based).
  - Scope 3: 32,100,872 tCO2e across categories, dominated by Investments (31,992,997 tCO2e); other notable items include cloud services (51,084 tCO2e), fuel- and energy-related activities (14,707 tCO2e), employee commuting (19,736 tCO2e), and business travel (7,967 tCO2e).
  - Total emissions: 32,132,051 tCO2e (location-based) and 32,133,666 tCO2e (market-based).
  - GHG intensity: 0.004 tCO2e/€ net revenue (both location- and market-based), based on €8,701 million net revenues.
  - Notes that sovereign debt emissions are excluded from financed emissions totals to avoid double counting and are reported separately per PCAF.

- Discloses anticipated financial effects from climate risks (E1-9) and outlines the approach to assessing physical and transition risks in line with EU Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 (Template 5), using IFRS consolidation scope.

- Details data sources and limitations:
  - Reliance on counterparty-provided information, third-party vendors, and public registers; limited verification possible.
  - Data gaps in energy performance (EPC availability/enforcement) across CEE countries.
  - Use of registration/headquarter addresses as proxies for non-financial corporates; incomplete geographic coverage and internal data quality constraints; threshold calibration may cause result volatility.
  - Acknowledges methodological and data-quality limitations; results may evolve.

- Explains risk segmentation and methodology:
  - Exposures broken down by region, by acute vs chronic physical risks, and identification of any climate change adaptation alignment.
  - Two assessment lenses: (1) counterparty address focusing on selected NACE sectors of non-financial corporates; (2) collateral address focusing on commercial and residential real estate exposures for non-financial corporates and households.
  - Time horizons aligned with ICAAP: short (≤3 years), medium (≤10), long (>10), grouped by remaining maturity.

- Key physical risk findings for non-financial corporates:
  - €12,124 million (33.9%) of assessed exposure subject to physical risk: €2,930 million chronic only, €7,807 million acute only, €1,387 million both; €0 million identified as covered by climate change adaptation actions.
  - Sectors in scope: A (Agriculture), B (Mining), C (Manufacturing), D (Electricity/Gas/Steam/Air conditioning), E (Water/Waste/Remediation), F (Construction), G (Wholesale/Retail/Vehicle repair), H (Transportation/Storage), L (Real estate).

nodes.title: E1-9: Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities - Introduction
nodes.source_title: E1-9: Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities
nodes.source_heading: E1-9 : Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-rela ted opportunities
nodes.heading: 20.8 E1-9 : Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-rela ted opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The assessment of the material risk positions with physical risk based on the European Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 of 30 November 2022 amending the implementing technical standards laid down in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/637 as regards the disclosure of environmental, social and governance risks - Template 5: Banking book - Climate change physical risk: Exposures subject to physical risk were prepared taking into account the IFRS scope of consolidation.
nodes.summary: RBI outlines its climate physical risk disclosure for the banking book under EU Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 amending 2021/637 (Template 5), using the IFRS scope of consolidation and relying on counterparties, third-party vendors, and public registers, with a liability disclaimer and noted data limitations (incomplete/unenforced Energy Performance Certificates in CEE, proxy use of registration/headquarter addresses for non-financial corporations, incomplete geographic coverage, internal data quality issues, and vendor threshold calibration volatility). Two tables segment exposures by region and assess physical risk at counterparty address for selected NACE sectors (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, L) and at collateral address for commercial/residential real estate exposures, with time horizons aligned to ICAAP (short ≤3 years, medium ≤10, long >10) based on remaining maturity, and splits by acute vs chronic risk and climate change adaptation alignment. For non-financial corporations in scope, €12,124 million (33.9%) is subject to physical risk, comprising €2,930 million chronic-only, €7,807 million acute-only, and €1,387 million both, with €0 million identified as covered by climate change adaptation actions; a regional table provides detailed proportions and maturity breakdowns.

nodes.title: Exposures collateralized by commercial or residential real estate subject to physical risk
nodes.heading: 20.8.1 Exposures collateralized by commercial or residential real estate subject to physical risk
nodes.start_phrase: Out of the total exposure collateralized by commercial or residential real estate under the scope of the assessment, € 4,994 million, or 12.8 per cent, was identified as subject to physical risk, of which € 0 million was sensitive to chronic risks only, € 4,993 million was sensitive to acute risks only, and € 0 million was sensitive to both chronic and acute physical risks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Assessment of physical and transition climate risks for exposures collateralized by commercial and residential real estate, covering non-financial corporates (CRE-backed) and households (RRE-backed).
- Physical risk exposure: €4,994 million (12.8% of €39,040 million gross carrying amount) identified as subject to physical climate risk.
- Risk type: Almost entirely acute physical risk (€4,993 million); no exposure sensitive to chronic-only or combined chronic and acute risks.
- Adaptation coverage: €0 million of physical-risk-sensitive exposure covered by climate change adaptation actions/alignment.
- Maturity profile of physical-risk-sensitive exposure: €892 million short-term, €885 million medium-term, €3,217 million long-term, indicating a long-term concentration.
- Regional breakdown of physical risk (gross carrying amount; exposure at material physical risk; share):
  - Central Europe: €29,687m; €4,127m; 13.9% (largest contributor; all acute; 633 ST / 637 MT / 2,857 LT)
  - Northern Europe: €6,603m; €557m; 8.4% (all acute; 155 ST / 158 MT / 244 LT)
  - Eastern Europe: €1,824m; €157m; 8.6% (all acute; 70 ST / 31 MT / 56 LT)
  - Southwestern Europe: €348m; €77m; 22.2% (all acute; 34 ST / 37 MT / 6 LT)
  - Rest of World: €519m; €60m; 11.6% (all acute; 1 ST / 8 MT / 51 LT)
  - Western Europe: €15m; €12m; 76.8% (small base; all acute; 11 MT)
  - Southeastern Europe: €18m; €4m; 21.5% (all acute; 3 MT / 1 LT)
  - Southern Europe: €26m; ~€0m identified as sensitive.
- Transition risk definition: Material transition risk identified as exposures to sectors highly contributing to climate change, aligned with EC Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 Template 1 and IFRS Group consolidation.
- High-contribution sectors (NACE): A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, L.
- Additional disclosures indicated: Breakdown of these transition-risk exposures by energy consumption ranges and EPC labels, and the share covered by climate change mitigation-aligned activities.
- Time horizons: Short, medium, and long term aligned with internal ICAAP definitions.
- Source context: Group management report of Raiffeisen Bank International for Financial Year 2024.

nodes.title: Exposures from non-financial corporations under material transition risks
nodes.heading: 20.8.2 Exposures from non-financial corporations under material transition risks
nodes.start_phrase: Sectors that highly contribute to climate change were defined based on the NACE segmentation, where highly contributing sectors are:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and results of physical climate risk assessment for exposures collateralized by commercial and residential real estate:
  - Total gross carrying amount: €39,040m; exposures sensitive to physical risk: €4,994m (12.8%).
  - Risk type split: €4,993m acute risk only; €0m chronic only; €0m both; €0m covered by climate change adaptation actions.
  - Maturity of risk-sensitive exposures: short term €892m; medium term €885m; long term €3,217m.
  - Regional highlights (risk-sensitive exposure/proportion): Central Europe €4,127m (13.9%); Northern Europe €557m (8.4%); Western Europe €12m (76.8% on a small base); Eastern Europe €157m (8.6%); Southwestern Europe €77m (22.2%); Southeastern Europe €4m (21.5%); Rest of World €60m (11.6%); Southern Europe €0m.

- Definition and measurement of transition risk (per EU Implementing Regulation 2022/2453, Template 1; IFRS Group consolidation):
  - Non-financial corporate portfolio gross carrying amount: €47,825m; assets at material transition risk: €36,313m (75.9%).
  - Of which aligned with climate change mitigation actions: €197m (0.54%).
  - Maturity of transition-risk assets: short term €22,884m; medium term €11,509m; long term €1,921m.
  - High‑contributing NACE sectors in scope: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, L.
  - For loans collateralized by commercial immovable property within the transition‑risk assets, an energy performance breakdown is provided:
    - EP score (kWh/m²): ≤100: €3,547m; >100–200: €2,797m; >200–300: €1,738m; >300–400: €703m; >400–500: €291m; >500: €510m.
    - EPC labels: A €1,764m; B €1,526m; C €895m; D €445m; E €98m; F €105m; G €60m.
  - Short/medium/long-term definitions aligned with internal ICAAP.

- Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4-2) governance and policy developments:
  - Environmental topics, including biodiversity, embedded in RBI’s risk framework.
  - RBI Group Biodiversity Policy developed in 2024, planned publication in 2025; content to include definitions, exclusion list, materiality assessment with mitigation actions, and roadmap/timeline.
  - Governance: consolidated by Group Financial Institutions and Country & Portfolio Risk Management with business lines and Group ESG & Sustainability Management; implementation in 2025 by business units with central oversight.
  - Alignment with international standards and initiatives: Nature Target Setting Framework, Global Biodiversity Framework, TNFD, SBTN, and net-zero frameworks.

- Policies for assets under management (Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H.):
  - Biodiversity policy aims to contribute to addressing the nature crisis and support a sustainable value chain.
  - Core elements: collaboration and knowledge transfer; company engagement; portfolio impact analysis; target setting and disclosure.
  - Notes challenges in data and metrics; strategy to evolve with frameworks.
  - Oversight by the Chief Sustainability Investment Officer (CSIO).

nodes.title: Resource use and circular economy
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: The section outlines RBI’s approach to resource use and circular economy across its value chain and own operations, anchored in its climate and environmental business strategy and risk framework. Sectoral strategies/policies (e.g., oil & gas, steel, real estate & construction) define supportive, transformative, and restrictive criteria, with ongoing refinement for high-CO2 and high-impact sectors. Own-operations circularity is governed by an environmental policy and supplier engagement via the Supplier Code of Conduct.

- Actions in the value chain: RBI integrates an ESG E-score into customer clustering and underwriting, giving circularity an indirect role. It provides advisory services on net-zero and circularity, and increased financing in 2024 for circularity projects (eco-efficient products, resource-efficient production, waste prevention/reduction/recycling). Waste and material KPIs have been tracked since 2016. RBI participates in the UNEP FI PRB Resource Efficiency and Circularity Target working group (since 2022) and includes circularity in its ESG questionnaire.

- Actions in own operations: Local Facility Management and Procurement, aligned with Group ESG & Sustainability, implement measures such as switching from plastic to glass, reducing paper, raising recycling rates, extending IT hardware lifecycles, and promoting reuse. IT procurement and reuse volumes are tracked quarterly, balancing technical and security constraints to reduce resource intake.

- Targets in the value chain: Circular economy is a UN PRB focal area, with initial priority on packaging and building materials. For packaging, RBI aligns with the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (70% recycling by 2030) and material-specific targets, and has set:
  - By 2030: Relevant packaging-industry customers’ post-consumer packaging waste recycled per the Directive.
  - By 2028: Circularity topics included in at least 90% of customer engagements in the packaging sector.
  RBI is guided by the EU Taxonomy for construction materials and plans to set portfolio-level targets in 2025.

- Targets in own operations: Circularity targets support overall emissions-reduction goals, focusing on material use (notably IT and business travel) and waste. Implementation is driven by an ISO 14001-certified environmental management system (since 1998) and ISO 14064-1:2019 GHG validation for head office (since 2013), overseen by the Environmental Committee and ESG/sustainability teams.

- Resource inflows (value chain): Portfolio impacts on resource intensity are analyzed using the UNEP FI impact tool; key drivers are real estate, land transport (including pipelines), and electricity/gas/steam/air conditioning supply.

- Resource inflows (own operations): Primary physical inputs include office supplies, IT equipment, and company cars; energy is a critical input covered elsewhere. Procurement emphasizes environmental and social sustainability. Purchased goods/services (including cloud) are reported in Scope 3 emissions, with all material goods recorded quarterly.

- Resource outflows: Addressed in conjunction with resource inflows per ESRS linkage, with cross-references to related chapters.

- Data, monitoring, and alignment: Ongoing KPI development (potentially adding quantitative circularity metrics in 2025), regular internal tracking, and alignment with broader climate goals and regulatory frameworks (EU directives and taxonomy).

nodes.title: Social Information
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Social information on RBI’s own workforce under ESRS, covering both employees and non‑employees.
- Strategic framing (ESRS 2 SBM‑3): The workforce is integral to RBI’s Strategic Roadmap 2024–2025; goal to be an attractive employer with a high‑performing culture.
- People and culture priorities: leadership development; fostering a collaborative, customer‑centric culture; building current and future capabilities; sustainable and fair reward and recognition; strong employer branding; meaningful careers and growth; emphasis on continuous learning and high qualification standards in a regulated industry.
- Working conditions and employee relations: focus on high employee satisfaction and secure employment; benefits extended to part‑time and temporary staff; acknowledgment that job security influences financial stability, health, stress, and work‑life balance.
- Non‑employee workforce: use of service‑contract providers and temporary agency workers; RBI defines tasks for agency temps; specific note of agency‑engaged IT staff at Raiffeisenbank a.s. (Prague) and Raiffeisen Bank Sh.a (Tirana).
- Early‑career/temporary programs: seasonal trainees (June–October, 1–4 months, pupils and students, supportive/administrative tasks without independent responsibility) and internships (up to 6 months with possible extension, enrolled students, similar supportive tasks); both offered full‑time.
- Impact lens: recognition of both positive and negative impacts of workforce practices on operations.

nodes.title: Own workforce
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope
  - ESRS-aligned disclosure on “Own workforce” covering employees and non-employees, with strategic importance embedded in RBI’s People & Culture pillar.
- Material impacts, risks and opportunities
  - Positive aims: attractive employer, high-performing culture, secure employment, fair reward, meaningful careers, continuous learning.
  - Potential negatives and financial risks: equal pay gaps, discrimination, weak whistleblowing, poor work-life balance—leading to operational disruption, fines, legal costs, turnover, productivity loss, and reputational harm.
- Working conditions and employment relationships
  - Predominantly permanent contracts; fixed-term only in defined cases (e.g., parental leave cover, initial 6-month period).
  - Use of seasonal trainees and internships; limited use of agency/contracted non-employees for projects or shortages.
  - Flexible working time, hybrid/telework and part-time options to support work-life balance; benefits extended broadly, with some country-specific limitations.
- Health, safety and wellbeing
  - Strong focus on physical and mental health, ergonomic workplaces, burnout prevention, health checks, wellness programs, psychological support (incl. post-robbery).
  - Group-wide H&S systems, risk-based monitoring, and monthly reviews by health@RBI.
- Fair pay and rewards
  - Group total rewards policy ensures market-adequate, primarily fixed remuneration with fully flexible variable pay; focus on financial stability and development.
  - Commitment to adequate wages and upcoming salary transparency project (EU Pay Transparency Directive).
- Employee voice and participation
  - Multiple engagement channels: CEO live calls, regular employee surveys and pulse checks, staff councils (45% coverage), European Works Council, employee reps on Supervisory Boards in several countries.
  - Ombudsperson (RBI AG) for confidential, neutral support and systemic insights.
  - Whistleblowing via Whispli platform for anonymous reporting; structured internal violation management.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI)
  - Group D&I policy, diversity officers in all key subsidiaries, employee resource groups (e.g., EMBRACE for LGBTQIA+), Board sponsorship, national diversity charters.
  - Programs for women’s empowerment, generation management, disability inclusion, intercultural topics; extensive leader and staff trainings on anti-harassment and inclusion.
  - Broad flexibility measures (hybrid, part-time, educational leave), dependent care supports, and country-specific work-family benefits.
- Learning, development and performance
  - Group policies for learning, talent management and performance; mandatory annual development dialogues; talent and trainee programs across countries.
  - ESG Academy and SkillUp! ESG journeys; AI Pioneer Program to accelerate AI literacy and adoption; leadership initiative on impactful conversations.
- Data protection and governance
  - HR GDPR policy and broader data protection rules; operational risk reporting of HR-related incidents; adherence to ILO principles and UN/EU human rights standards.
  - Company agreements in Austria on flexible working time and social benefits; periodic reviews.
- Targets and management approach
  - 2025 goals: maintain whistleblowing standards; sustain flexible/hybrid work; publish and implement updated D&I policy; develop engagement metrics; launch pay transparency project.
  - Women in senior leadership target of 35% achieved in 2024; annual goal setting cascaded across Group HR.
- Key metrics (2024, selected)
  - Workforce: 43,574 employees (17,146 male; 26,428 female); major countries—Russia 8,852; Ukraine 5,690; Austria 5,390; Romania 5,047.
  - Employment types: 40,847 permanent; 2,727 temporary; 2,629 part-time; turnover 18%.
  - Non-employees: 3,486 (agency and service-contract workers).
  - Collective arrangements: 41% covered by CBAs; 45% covered by worker representatives; EWC active.
  - Diversity: B-1 (63% male/37% female); B-2 (53% male/47% female); age—21% <30, 62% 30–50, 17% >50.
  - Social protection: Kosovo exceptions; otherwise broad coverage for sickness, unemployment, injury/disability, parental, retirement.
  - Disability: 1.48% of employees (per local legal definitions).
  - Development: 92% had performance/career reviews; average 34 training hours (31 male/36 female).
  - Health & safety: 100% coverage; 0 fatalities; 86 work-related accidents; recordable rate 1.11.
  - Work-life balance: 100% entitlement to maternity, paternity, carers’ leave; take-up—maternity 14%, paternity 1%, carers’ 1% male/6% female.
  - Pay: unadjusted Group gender pay gap 38% (27% unweighted country average); highest-to-median pay ratio 89.
  - Incidents: 4 discrimination cases; 63 complaints via channels; €0 fines; 0 severe human rights incidents.
- Effectiveness monitoring
  - Regular employee surveys, external work-family audit, ongoing health and safety reviews, and dedicated DEI/HR resources to track and refine measures.

nodes.title: Workers in the value chain
nodes.summary:
- Scope and focus
  - Outlines RBI’s policies, processes, and controls to protect human rights and manage impacts on workers in its value chain, primarily through lending, compliance, and ESG risk management.

- Codes and overarching policies
  - RBI Code of Conduct: commits to respect international human rights standards (UDHR, ECHR, UNGPs), avoid direct/indirect involvement in violations, and handle sensitive sectors with care (e.g., nuclear, coal, defense, gambling). Extends expectations to suppliers via a supplier Code of Conduct.
  - Group Human Rights Policy: sets responsibilities, due diligence principles, and remediation expectations; aligns with UN/EU standards (ILO, ICCPR, ICESCR, GRI); annually reviewed; can lead to terminating relationships if violations persist.

- Human rights due diligence approach
  - Risk-based, context-sensitive assessment using a traffic-light model; periodic reviews of existing relationships.
  - Prioritizes severe risks; prescribes prevention, mitigation, and where needed, remediation in line with UNGPs.

- Lending and compliance frameworks
  - Corporate Rating Manual and Counterparty Credit Policy: integrates an ESG score (social/governance include value-chain worker risks) into annual credit reviews; influences pricing, risk costs, and will be integrated into ratings; global scope across all corporate customers.
  - Business Compliance Framework: defines compliance risk appetite; uses adverse media (including human rights) and other indicators to guide measures from enhanced due diligence to rejection/termination; update planned for 2025 to incorporate human rights/ESG indicators and related remediation/approval processes.
  - ESG Risk Framework/ESG process flow: screens ESG‑critical transactions against UN Global Compact principles; requires ESG expert opinions, uses a four‑eyes control, and applies an Exclusion List referencing IUCN, RSPO, Ramsar, UNESCO, EU Ship Recycling, and Kimberley Process.

- Engagement with value chain workers (S2-2)
  - When customers have adverse social/governance scores, RBI engages customer representatives in the downstream value chain to seek countermeasures and information; no direct engagement with customers’ employee representatives.

- Remediation and grievance channels (S2-3)
  - For low/poor social or governance scores, RBI discusses and monitors corrective actions (e.g., staff councils, turnover monitoring, adverse news tracking) and may withhold additional funding if no improvement.
  - High human rights risk findings are reported to Group Compliance; actions range from collaborative improvements to relationship termination; whistleblowing channel available to value chain workers.
  - For ESG‑critical transactions with negative expert opinions, escalation to the Management Board for decision.

- Actions on material impacts and risk management (S2-4)
  - 2024 rollout of a country‑ and sector‑based Human Rights Score; lowest‑scoring third triggers actions (extra risk review, loan rejection, limit reductions).
  - High‑risk human rights due diligence: dialog‑based validation to improve customers’ human rights safeguards or exit relationships.
  - Enhanced onboarding due diligence for mining/mineral traders, especially conflict minerals; onboarding can be aborted if risks are material.
  - Ongoing semi‑automated adverse media screening in multiple languages; first line analyzes alerts and seeks client statements/mitigations for severe cases.
  - Corporate ESG Score model: annual, analyst‑led assessment of social topics (working conditions, supplier HR screening, codes of conduct, community impact, training, data protection, critical sectors); influences pricing/risk costs; sources include sustainability reports, annual reports, questionnaires, and news.
  - Country ESG score considering social standards, labor force dynamics, and technological change; planned rollout in 2H 2025.
  - ESG expert opinions embedded in limit reviews, using PRB Impact Radar and UNGC labor/human rights topics.

- Governance, responsibilities, and resourcing
  - Policy owners include Credit Portfolio Management and Group Corporate Credit Management; Compliance and ESG teams co‑develop and implement frameworks.
  - Human Rights Working Group coordinates integration of human rights into compliance/risk and complaint processes.
  - Centralized ESG competencies in Compliance; staffing includes 3 FTE for ESG/human rights due diligence and 25 FTE for ESG scoring, supported by IT development/testing resources.
  - Frameworks and manuals are internally published and updated regularly; processes include stakeholder meetings and board approvals.

- Performance and incidents
  - No serious downstream value chain human rights incidents reported in 2024.

- Targets and planned enhancements (S2-5; 2025 focus)
  - Roll out updated Business Compliance Framework incorporating social indicators; formalize remediation/approval processes for high‑risk customers.
  - Report credit limits/exposure by human rights score to the Sustainability Committee to improve portfolio steering.
  - Maintain ESG score coverage above 97% of credit‑rated corporates; reduce unanswered ESG data points below the 2024 baseline of 45%.
  - Implement credit policy measures for low social/governance scores across lending and limit applications.
  - Develop and implement human rights training and expand sustainability e‑learning.
  - Targets set internally without involving value chain worker representatives.

nodes.title: Affected communities
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: The document covers how Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) manages material impacts, risks, and opportunities relating to affected communities, with a strong emphasis on social financing as part of its strategy and business model.

- Social financing impact and volumes:
  - Definition aligned with RBI’s Sustainability Bond Framework and ICMA principles; aims to support SDGs and reduce social inequalities.
  - Corporate and institutional social financing totaled €1.698 billion (utilized €1.421 billion; unutilized €277 million) as of 31 Dec 2024, broken down into:
    - Access to essential services: €642 million (e.g., hospitals, care facilities, regional infrastructure, drinking water).
    - Training and education: €204 million (e.g., schools, kindergartens).
    - Employment generation: €575 million.
  - Retail/SME social lending in 2024:
    - New social retail loans: €766 million, 99.6% to SMEs.
    - New social loan category for private individuals launched in Albania: €3 million.
    - SME social loans new sales: ~€763 million; SME loans classified as general purpose per RBI Framework, validated by Morningstar Sustainalytics.
  - Strategic intent: increase social loan sales to private individuals and small business customers across CEE; recognize eligibility for public/EU incentives that can enhance portfolio economics and mitigate risks.

- Financial opportunity and governance:
  - ESG embedded as a business opportunity in the Group Strategic Roadmap; non-financial ESG criteria integrated into remuneration and strategic objectives; advisory focus on sustainable and socially responsible banking.

- Policies relating to affected communities:
  - General: References to group-wide Code of Conduct and Human Rights Policy.
  - Sector policies:
    - Defense: Avoid involvement in human rights abuses/controversial weapons; continuous monitoring; Group Compliance ownership; public Position Statement.
    - Gambling: Serve only reputable, transparent, regulated operators; manage AML/CFT risks; Group Compliance ownership; based on UNGC and Austrian Gambling Law; public Position Statement.
    - Tobacco: Restricts producers/distributors due to health impacts; aligned with WHO FCTC.
    - Thermal coal: Phase-out by 2030 (environment-driven, acknowledging links to health and environment rights).
    - Oil & gas, steel, real estate & construction: Merged policy (Q1 2024), primarily environmental with social references to Code of Conduct and human rights; Risk Management ownership.
  - Process policies:
    - Human rights due diligence (including remediation) aligned with value chain worker processes.
    - ESG Rulebook and greenwashing prevention (binding, group-wide; annual review):
      - Harmonized ESG definitions; customer ESG scoring; transaction classification aligned with EU Taxonomy where applicable.
      - Social finance products definitions (social loans, bonds, and other use-of-proceeds instruments) aligned with LMA/ICMA; second-party opinions may be required.
      - Scope: Corporate & Institutional Clients across RBI AG and key subsidiaries; responsibility: Group Structured Finance & Investment Banking; developed with cross-functional stakeholders.

- Asset management (Raiffeisen KAG) sectoral exclusions:
  - Controversial weapons: Excludes producers; daily monitoring; aligned with international conventions; applies to retail funds and, as far as possible, special and third-party funds; public policy.
  - Food speculation: Excludes derivatives on agricultural commodities (e.g., cereals, meat, maize, soy, sugar, cocoa, coffee) for mutual funds; rationale based on potential harm to vulnerable populations; public policy.

- Engagement, remediation, and channels:
  - For low social/governance customer scores, RBI engages clients to gather community impact information and require countermeasures.
  - Remediation processes and whistleblowing channels are referenced to group-wide frameworks.

- Actions and effectiveness:
  - Deployment of social financing across essential services, education, and employment generation; examples include hospitals, care facilities, roads/bridges, school buses, rural broadband, schools, and water supply.
  - SME social lending integrated into retail ESG and climate/environmental business strategies; ongoing with no fixed end date.
  - Human rights due diligence (country/industry risk scoring; high-risk due diligence including mining) referenced.
  - Exclusion policy enforcement: ongoing reviews for defense and gambling clients; 2024 training launched on sensitive business areas to improve policy implementation.
  - Asset management engagement: proactive and responsive ESG dialogues to enhance CSR and long-term financial performance.

- Other details:
  - No serious human rights incidents in the downstream value chain in 2024.
  - Social financing management sits within Sustainable Finance and Retail Customers governance areas.

- Targets:
  - Targets mirror those for value chain workers; set via internal planning without direct involvement of affected communities.
  - Retail ESG lending target: at least 10% of new retail loans to be ESG-relevant (green and social) by 2025; 2024 result: 11.5% share for mortgage and unsecured purpose loans to SMEs and private individuals, majority being SME social loans.

nodes.title: Consumers and end-users
nodes.summary:
- Scope and definition of consumers/end-users
  - RBI serves ~16.8 million private customers across Austria and CEE with a broad retail offering (accounts, payments, consumer finance, leasing, mortgages, investments).
  - Consumers/end-users are private individuals using products for personal (non-professional) purposes; includes prospective customers and those exposed to RBI marketing.
  - Vulnerable groups include persons with disabilities, women, elderly, migrants/refugees, people in specific geographies, and minors. EU Accessibility Act (to be implemented by June 2025) frames inclusion/accessibility requirements.

- Information-related impacts and management
  - Privacy, cyber security, and operational resilience are critical given RBI’s role as critical infrastructure; strong ISMS with policies, standards, testing (penetration, red teaming), and incident management.
  - 2024 saw increased DDoS activity and some supplier incidents; no material damage, lessons learned integrated.
  - Access to (quality) information: focus on clear, comparable, comprehensive disclosures; staff training; financial literacy initiatives; adherence to ICC Advertising and Marketing Code to mitigate negative marketing impacts.

- Social inclusion impacts
  - Non-discrimination and access to products/services underpin financial inclusion; digital and physical accessibility (branch remodeling, ATM features, multilingual interfaces, web accessibility progress) and special conditions for students/retirees.
  - Responsible marketing: transparency, clear labeling of risks/costs, GDPR-compliant communications; sector-specific rules (e.g., FMA minimum standards for building societies).

- Risks (financial and non-financial)
  - Privacy/cyber failures could lead to fines, litigation costs, trust loss, higher insurance, business loss.
  - Poor access to quality information risks regulatory sanctions, mis-selling litigation, lower uptake, higher defaults, higher service costs.
  - Social inclusion gaps risk missed market opportunities and revenue; value-chain risks considered immaterial.
  - Ongoing consumer litigation noted (e.g., FX mortgages in Poland); medium-to-long-term sustainability issues could create financial risks.

- Policy framework (selected)
  - Code of Conduct; Group Human Rights Policy.
  - Information & Cyber Security Policy (ISO/IEC 27001 aligned; PSD2, NIS, EBA, DORA).
  - Data Protection Policy (GDPR, DPA, ePrivacy) with governance and training.
  - Customer Complaint Management Policy (EBA/ESMA-aligned).
  - Retail Credit and Retail Restructuring Policies (responsible lending, transparency, non-discrimination).
  - Retail Investment Product Distribution (MiFID II appropriateness/suitability).
  - Group Marketing Policy (binding ICC Code).
  - Product Governance (Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H.) and WAG directive.
  - FMA minimum standards for Raiffeisen Bausparkasse.

- Engagement with consumers/end-users (S4-2)
  - Multi-channel complaint system with defined timelines (acknowledgment within 24 hours; resolution typically within 10 business days).
  - Regular customer satisfaction and brand health tracking across markets; campaign pretests; ESOMAR-compliant research, including for vulnerable groups.
  - Direct and indirect feedback loops for Austrian subsidiaries (KAG, Bausparkasse); escalation routes to industry boards and authorities.

- Remediation and grievance channels (S4-3)
  - Web-based complaint case management; root-cause analysis and mitigation integrated annually; Board and Supervisory Board informed.
  - GDPR breach processes: authority/customer notification within regulatory timelines; documentation and corrective actions.

- Actions and effectiveness (S4-4)
  - Security: layered technical/organizational controls, third-party security requirements, continuous monitoring, awareness programs; 321 info-security FTEs; dedicated data protection teams and officers.
  - Information quality and literacy: staff training; education initiatives (Minecraft My Finance Quests; World Phenomena Money in SK; TABI children’s account/app; Zlatka.in platform in CZ/SK/EN); transparent investment and loan information.
  - Inclusion and access: multi-channel service model, barrier-free branches/ATMs (>65% implementation for branch accessibility), WCAG-aligned web progress, multilingual ATMs; training on serving customers with impairments.
  - Responsible marketing: ICC Code adherence, consent management, clear/understandable materials; FMA standards applied for building societies.

- Targets (S4-5)
  - Data protection: DSR completion within one month (internally targeted ≤25 days); breach handling within 72 hours; strengthen processes, plain-language communication, Archer GDPR platform use, training coverage; 2024 violations immaterial and closed (mainly human error), 23 authority reports, no significant penalties.
  - Information & cyber security: annual assessment against group standards; goals to optimize cyber resilience, regulatory compliance, and 100% employee awareness training; reporting to Group Security Committee and Supervisory Board.
  - Access to information/responsible marketing: continue compliance-driven approach and local subsidiary targets; monitor complaints (e.g., KAG tracks volume and resolution time).
  - Non-discrimination/access to services: no group-wide numeric targets; subsidiaries plan timely EU Accessibility Act compliance by June 2025.
  - Complaint management: annual root-cause mitigation measures treated as rolling targets to reduce negative impacts and enhance customer outcomes.

nodes.title: Governance information
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Governance information on business conduct (G1-1: Corporate culture) centered on RBI’s Code of Conduct.
- Employee relations and ethics: Commitment to fair employment, equal treatment, zero discrimination/harassment/violence, and prohibition of modern slavery and human trafficking.
- Political neutrality and advocacy: Strict rules for corporate contributions; lobbying limited to authorized staff during legislative/regulatory processes.
- Awareness and accountability: Mandatory periodic e-learning on Code basics; all employees sign compliance statements and disclose/update conflicts of interest.
- Scope and ownership: Code applies to RBI’s own operations and its upstream/downstream business relationships; content responsibility lies with the Head of Capital Markets Compliance.
- Global standards alignment: Participation in UN Global Compact; adherence to the European Convention on Human Rights, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
- Governance and updates: Regular review and alignment with regulations and international standards via a cross-functional process (Group Compliance, ESG & Sustainability, Legal, People/Culture/Organization); subsidiaries adapt local versions; final review by the Sustainability Committee and Management Board.
- Communication: Code published in English and local languages across the Group; CEO communicates updates to all employees.
- Six ethical pillars defined: customer relations; investor relations; employee relations; compliance with laws and regulations; combating financial crime; social and environmental responsibility.
- Social and environmental responsibility: RBI recognizes its economic, social, and environmental impacts; pursues long-term profitable business while avoiding harm through due diligence; aims to elevate environmental protection and social standards as part of its sustainability strategy (responsible banker, fair partner, engaged corporate citizen).
- Context: Extract from the Group Management Report, Financial Year 2024.

nodes.title: Business conduct
nodes.summary:
- Governance and corporate culture
  - RBI Code of Conduct sets group-wide standards for ethical behavior across own operations and value chain; requires periodic e-learning and signed compliance statements, including conflict-of-interest disclosures.
  - Owned by Head of Capital Markets Compliance; regularly reviewed with Group Compliance, ESG, Legal, HR; finalized by Sustainability Committee and Management Board; communicated by CEO and published in English and local languages.
  - Aligned with UN Global Compact, European Convention on Human Rights, UN Guiding Principles, and Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
  - Six ethical pillars: customer relations, investor relations, employee relations, compliance with laws, combating financial crime, social and environmental responsibility.

- Social, environmental, and human rights commitments
  - Avoid social/environmental harm through due diligence; contribute to improved environmental protection and social standards.
  - Sensitive-industry policies (defense, nuclear, gambling); prohibition on financing controversial weapons.
  - Environmental protection focus on minimizing impacts and CO2 emissions; avoidance of projects with significant environmental harm; suppliers expected to meet the same standards.
  - Diversity & inclusion policy ensures equal opportunities and inclusive workplace.

- Responsible banking framework
  - Signatory to UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking; integrates ESG at strategy, portfolio, and transaction levels with KPIs, training, impact analysis, targets, ESG products, stakeholder engagement, and audited PRB progress reporting; supports Paris Agreement goals.

- Corporate governance
  - Adheres to Austrian Corporate Governance Code; annual compliance audit without objections.
  - Transparent stakeholder communication via Corporate Governance Report and website.

- Business conduct policies and programs
  - Anti-bribery & corruption (ABC) policy aligned with Austrian law, UK Bribery Act, US FCPA, and UN Convention; group-wide scope; targeted training for functions at risk; program overview public.
  - Whistleblowing policy with external anonymous platform and multiple channels; zero-tolerance for retaliation; confidential, independent investigations; EU Directive and Austrian WPA compliance; regular reporting to Management and Supervisory Boards; 2024 awareness campaign.
  - Group Compliance Training Policy (since 2019): mandatory, role-based annual training on Code of Conduct, ABC, fraud, conflicts, AML/CFT, market abuse; tracked and risk-based.

- Supplier management (G1-2)
  - ~13,000 suppliers, primarily IT, facilities, consulting, marketing; head office manages most supplier volume across CEE.
  - Supplier Code of Conduct mandatory in contracts (or equivalent); minimum social and environmental standards; right to terminate for significant breaches.
  - Sustainability criteria in selection; annual top-supplier survey (certifications, environmental compliance, CO2 indicators); collaboration with key suppliers to reduce emissions; fair payment terms commitment.

- Anti-corruption framework (G1-3)
  - Zero-tolerance stance; tone from the top; clear policies and procedures; robust prevention, detection, and independent investigation processes.
  - 2024 training coverage of functions-at-risk: 96%; boards trained via Fit & Proper program.
  - Periodic and ad hoc risk assessments; internal controls include conflict-of-interest disclosures, expense checks, KYC/KYE/KYBP, and compliance review of external contributions.
  - Regular management reporting; accountability with risk-based internal sanctions.

- AML/CFT
  - Board-approved, annually reviewed policy aligned with FATF and local laws.
  - Key measures: appointed AML/CFT officer; risk-based due diligence (incl. PEPs/UBOs); enhanced DD for high risk and certain countries; offshore requirements; monitoring and FIU reporting; ICS, audits; ongoing training; industry engagement; continuous enhancement.

- Tax compliance
  - Strategy guided by law, Code of Conduct, and internal policies; rejects tax evasion; complies with FATCA, CRS, QI, TPDA, DAC6, Pillar 2.
  - Strengthened tax control system in 2024; no business model presence in tax havens, with wind-down of any residuals.
  - Clear governance (CEO/CFO/Head of Group Tax; local management); training and annual risk analyses; use of whistleblowing channels; audited reporting; active engagement with authorities and industry bodies; country data disclosed per Austrian BWG.

- Incidents of corruption or bribery (G1-4)
  - 2024: zero convictions and zero fines; internal disciplinary measures applied where necessary under investigation framework.

- Political influence and lobbying (G1-5)
  - High-transparency standards; registered in Austrian, German, and EU transparency registers; adheres to relevant codes of conduct.
  - Political contributions only by Management Board under strict conditions; none made in 2024; compliance oversight named; process regularly monitored.
  - Main lobbying topics include EU financial services and regulatory initiatives (e.g., CMU, SRM, SSM, CRD/CRR, MiFID, DGS/EDIS, TLAC/MREL); 2024 activities not linked to material impacts/risks/opportunities.
  - No recent “revolving door” appointments; memberships in Austrian Economic Chamber and Federation of Austrian Industries.

- Payment practices (G1-6)
  - Commitment to fair terms and on-time payments across Austria and CEE; sample data show standard net terms (15–30 days), average payment times generally within or better than terms, and high alignment with standard terms.
  - No outstanding legal proceedings for late payments in 2024.
  - Guidance to expedite SME invoices; improvement measures underway (staff training, supplier onboarding data quality, invoice support, dedicated contacts) to raise on-time payment share.

nodes.title: Preface
