nodes.title: Responsible investment and social finance
nodes.heading: 3.2.2 Responsible investment and social finance
nodes.start_phrase:
Contribution to sustainable development through I+
financing and investment that promotes sustainable
performance in companies, addresses societal
challenges, mitigates a specific issue, or pursues
positive societal outcomes.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from Santander’s 2024 Annual Report (Sustainability chapter 3.2: Communities’ sustainable development), covering how the bank supports communities, advances responsible investment and social finance, and manages environmental, social and climate change (ESCC) risks.

- Supporting economic and social development (3.2.1):
  - Through finance and investment:
    - EUR 350.5bn for home purchases; EUR 214.2bn for other consumer goods.
    - EUR 330bn to set up or grow companies (including >530k SMEs and self-employed).
    - EUR 24.1bn in green finance raised/facilitated; EUR 88.8bn SRI assets under management.
    - EUR 1.27bn in microcredits to >1.3m microentrepreneurs.
  - Through community support:
    - 2.6m new people financially included.
    - EUR 166m invested in communities (EUR 104m for higher education, employability and entrepreneurship), benefitting 5m people.

- Responsible investment and social finance (3.2.2):
  - Social finance:
    - Tagging and reporting framework aligned with sustainable finance systems.
    - Latin America microfinance platforms (Prospera, Tuiio, Surgir) delivered EUR 1.27bn microcredit to >1.3m clients in 2024, often bundled with accounts and microinsurance.
    - Agreements with Multilateral Development Banks in Spain, Chile, Brazil and Poland; IFC social bond in Brazil to fund SMEs in underserved regions and microentrepreneurs.
  - Socially Responsible Investment (SRI) strategy and progress:
    - Wealth Management & Insurance target: EUR 100bn SRI AuM by 2025.
    - 2024 SRI AuM: EUR 88.8bn (EUR 63.5bn SAM; EUR 25.3bn third-party funds in Private Banking), +32% YoY.
    - Data governance: monthly SRI AuM calculation; quarterly reporting to Group Sustainability data office; annual limited assurance.
    - SRI definition aligned to SFDR Articles 8/9 (and equivalents outside the EU), including SFDR Article 2.17 sustainable investments and internal SFICS standards across Group-managed/advised and third-party assets.
  - Policies, governance and stewardship:
    - SAM’s SRI, Engagement and Voting policies; conflict of interest policies; SAM Board oversight.
    - Forums for SRI strategy, voting/engagement, investment & sustainability; Group ESG Wealth forum oversight.
    - Alignment with Spain’s CNMV Stewardship Code; SAM’s first SRI report published (voting and engagement).
  - SAM product and methodology:
    - Expanding SRI product range (e.g., transforming pension plans under SFDR Art. 8; launches like GO Global Environmental Solutions and Target Maturity III).
    - Engagement focus on high-emitting sectors; participation in “Global Investor Statement to Governments on the Climate Crisis.”
    - ESG approach: exclusions; proprietary, materiality-based ESG ratings across >30 key E, S, G topics; sector-weighted factors; criteria to identify SFDR Art. 2.17 sustainable investments; use of ESG data providers; enhanced training and data coverage outside the EU; structured engagement and voting with escalation.
  - Insurance and Private Banking:
    - Insurance: products protecting vulnerable groups; advancing SRI in insurers’ investments.
    - Private Banking: EUR 25.3bn SRI AuM (third-party, incl. committed capital to alternatives); advisory lists mainly SFDR Art. 8/9; added social metrics to IPB portfolio sustainability reports; client thought leadership on climate adaptation vs mitigation, circular economy, and green hydrogen; awards for Social Responsibility and Sustainability (Chile).

- Environmental, social and climate change management (3.2.3):
  - Key risks addressed: financing activities that breach policies and harm present/future generations; environmental/social harm due to inadequate stakeholder engagement or client due diligence.
  - ESCC policy commitments:
    - Support clients’ transition to a low-carbon economy, while managing social impacts (e.g., indigenous rights, health and safety, community impacts).
    - By 2030: cease investing in/providing financial services to clients with >10% revenues from coal-fired power generation; zero exposure to thermal coal mining; support international standards and treaties.
    - Application of the precautionary principle in ESCC risk analysis.
  - Sector standards and prohibitions:
    - Enhanced due diligence and standards for oil & gas, power generation/distribution, mining & metals, and soft commodities (incl. retail farming/ranching in the Amazon).
    - Prohibited: financing activities that threaten Ramsar Sites, World Heritage Sites, or IUCN categories I–IV; projects requiring FPIC that do not meet IFC PS7 without a credible plan.
    - Comprehensive E&S due diligence for CIB clients in covered sectors, including cases involving resettlement of indigenous or vulnerable groups.
  - Alignment with international frameworks:
    - UN Global Compact, UDHR, ILO, Convention on the Rights of the Child, Rio Declaration, UN Convention against Corruption, Equator Principles, and IFC Performance Standards.

nodes.title: Environmental, social and climate change management
nodes.heading: 3.2.3 Environmental, social and climate change management
nodes.start_phrase: This section outlines how we manage these IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Sustainability and Risk Management within Santander’s 2024 Annual Report, with links to Business Model, Corporate Governance, and Financial Review/Compliance.
- Private Banking ESG integration: publishing thought leadership on climate adaptation vs mitigation, circular economy, and green hydrogen; embedding ESG into portfolio management and advisory; industry recognition in 2024 for Social Responsibility and Sustainability (Chile).
- Environmental, Social and Climate Change (ESCC) policy:
  - Commitment to support clients’ transition to a low‑carbon economy; application of the precautionary principle.
  - 2030 commitments: cease services to clients with >10% revenues from coal-fired power; no exposure to thermal coal mining; support for international standards and treaties.
  - Sector standards and exclusions covering oil & gas, power generation/distribution, mining/metals, and soft commodities (with focus on Amazon-related activities).
  - Prohibited financing for projects threatening Ramsar Sites, World Heritage Sites, or IUCN I–IV areas; and projects requiring FPIC that do not comply with IFC Performance Standard 7.
  - Alignment with UN, ILO, IFC, Equator Principles, and broader human rights and anti-corruption frameworks.
- ESCC governance and due diligence:
  - ESCC assessments embedded in credit/investment workflows; Board-owned policy; risk decisions consider ESCC implications.
  - Questionnaire-based reviews for clients in covered sectors; analysis spans labor rights, supply chains, community impacts, and grievance mechanisms.
  - Red flags trigger enhanced due diligence; findings escalated to risk committees.
  - Annual ESCC assessment of CIB clients in sectors with climate alignment targets (oil & gas, power generation, automotive, steel, aviation), evaluating GHG emissions, targets, and transition risk.
  - Strengthened governance for sustainable finance; FCC controls to mitigate environmental crimes.
- Equator Principles (EP) application:
  - Signatory since 2009; internal procedure for project-related transactions.
  - Categorization (A/B/C) with corresponding due diligence responsibilities between Front Office and ESCC Risk.
  - E&S findings integrated into credit approvals; ongoing monitoring of E&S clauses and action plans; corrective measures as needed.
  - 21 EP-scope projects analyzed in 2024.
  - Community risk management focuses on resettlement, community health/safety, and indigenous peoples’ FPIC.
- Principal Adverse Impacts (PAIS) in asset management:
  - Measurement of KPIs on key sustainability factors; mitigation based on impact severity, frequency, stewardship effectiveness, and exposure.
- Community Support strategy:
  - Core pillars: higher education, employability, entrepreneurship; complemented by financial education and support for vulnerable people; delivery via donations and partnerships guided by B4SI-aligned methodologies and a humanitarian crisis response guide.
  - 2024 outcomes: ~EUR 104 million invested; 2.2 million people and businesses helped; 1,181 partnerships in 14 countries.
  - Long-term impact: >EUR 2.4 billion invested over 28 years; >3.7 million beneficiaries; progress toward EUR 400 million commitment for 2023–2026 (EUR 208.9 million allocated by 2024).
  - Education initiatives include scholarships, mobility, research, internships, and university digitalization; lifelong learning and comprehensive support for entrepreneurs and businesses across growth stages.

nodes.title: Community Support
nodes.heading: 3.2.4 Community Support
nodes.start_phrase:
This section outlines how we manage the following IRO:
Contribution to education, employability and I+
entrepreneurship, as well as to community
development through support programmes.
nodes.summary:
- Oversight of environmental and social risks in local communities under the Equator Principles, including due diligence to ensure projects manage impacts such as involuntary resettlement, community health and safety, and impacts on Indigenous peoples, requiring FPIC per IFC Performance Standard 7.
- Management of principal adverse impacts (PAIS) from asset management: disclosure and monitoring via sustainability KPIs per SAM’s PAIS procedure; when impacts arise, mitigation is guided by assessments of severity, frequency, effectiveness of dialogue, and exposure.
- Community support strategy (IRO): long-standing focus on higher education, employability, and entrepreneurship, complemented by financial education and aid to vulnerable groups; governed by a Sensitive Issues Policy, a B4SI-inspired Guide on Community Support and People Helped, and a humanitarian crisis guide.
- Education: scholarships and grants; 1,181 agreements with universities and entities in 14 countries; digital enablement via Campus Digital; collaboration platforms Universia and MetaRed (digital transformation, entrepreneurship, sustainability).
- Employability: lifelong learning and early-career access through Santander Open Academy (free, short courses with certificates) and Universia’s AI-enabled job matching; inclusion via Fundación Universia supporting people with disabilities and vulnerable groups.
- Entrepreneurship: support for SMEs and startups through Santander X and the Santander X 100 community, offering training, advice, resources, and visibility.
- 2024 outcomes and scale: around EUR 104 million allocated to education, employability, and entrepreneurship; 2.2 million people and businesses helped; over 28 years, EUR 2.4 billion invested, 3.7 million people and businesses supported; target of EUR 400 million (2023–2026) with EUR 208.9 million allocated by 2024; 1,181 partnerships in 14 countries.
- Other community programmes: EUR 62.5 million devoted to social action beyond core pillars; 2.9 million people helped; priorities include financial education, support for vulnerable people, and arts and culture, often via local NGOs and Santander foundations in several countries.
- Corporate volunteering: group-wide framework with locally tailored initiatives; 75,000 hours volunteered; examples include financial education, employability mentoring, environmental projects, emergency shelter support, and pro bono services.
- Financial education: programmes aligned with OECD principles and tailored by audience; use of social media to reach younger people; 4 million people accessed financial education content in 2024 (social counted by engagement).
- Humanitarian crisis response: structured assessment and governance to enable rapid, effective aid; 2024 actions included responses to Spain’s DANA storms, Chilean wildfires, Brazil floods, and an earthquake in China, with support to affected clients, employees, and coordination with NGOs.
- Charitable foundations: significant support via Fundación Banco Santander (Spain), including a 2024 donation of 22,167,105 Banco Santander shares to fund cultural, educational, social, and environmental projects; additional foundations in Argentina, the US, Mexico, Portugal, Poland, and the UK align with local needs and the Group’s priorities.
- Customer focus introduction: transition to Section 3.3 highlights a customer-centric, multi-channel model serving individuals, SMEs, corporates, and public entities, with the chapter focusing on individual customers, including those potentially vulnerable to product and service marketing.

nodes.title: Our customers
nodes.heading: 3.3 Our customers
nodes.start_phrase:
Our customer-centric approach is a fundamental lever for
generating sustainable value67, building a digital bank with
branches and a multi-channel offering that covers all of our
customers' financial needs.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines Santander’s community support, customer focus, and conduct governance. It highlights financial education as a core pillar of inclusion, delivered with age- and needs-based content, aligned to OECD principles, integrated into volunteering, and expanded via channels like social media; in 2024, 4 million people engaged with these initiatives. It details a formal, governed procedure for responding to humanitarian crises, assessing severity by scale and urgency, with 2024 actions covering the DANA storms in Spain, Chilean wildfires, Brazil’s floods, and China’s earthquake, including tailored support for customers, employees and families, and coordination with NGOs. On philanthropy, Fundación Banco Santander advances cultural, educational, social, and environmental projects; in 2024 the bank donated 22,167,105 shares to fund the foundation via dividends, supporting activities like managing the art collection, cultural productions, university partnerships, and the Paseo de Pereda HQ remodeling. Additional country foundations (Argentina, US, Mexico, Portugal, Poland, UK) run locally focused programs aligned to global priorities. The customer section describes a customer-centric, digital-with-branches, multichannel model across five global business segments, with this chapter focused on individual and potentially vulnerable customers. It sets out customer conduct risk management: key risks (claims/loss of customers from poor practices; harm from insufficient product information; inadequate complaint handling) and a conduct risk model approved by the compliance and conduct committee. Principles include fair treatment, responsible sales and pricing, transparency, data protection, complaint handling, fraud safeguards, financial education, and special consideration for vulnerable customers and overindebtedness prevention. Processes span product/service approval, sales oversight (suitability, advertising), and post-sales (recoveries, fraud, complaints). Governance involves a Product Governance and Consumer Protection area within Compliance and Conduct, board oversight of product approval and remuneration policies, and local/global compliance committees setting risk appetite and monitoring. In 2024 the bank advanced European Accessibility Directive implementation to improve accessibility across products, services, and channels; risk metrics were influenced by mortgage disputes in Spain and CHF mortgages in Poland, with contact centers providing responses and solutions.

nodes.title: Our customers - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.3 Our customers
nodes.start_phrase:
Our customer-centric approach is a fundamental lever for
generating sustainable value67, building a digital bank with
branches and a multi-channel offering that covers all of our

nodes.summary: Introduces Santander’s customer-centric approach as a lever for sustainable value, highlighting a digital bank with branches and a multi-channel offering across five global business segments serving individuals, SMEs, large corporations, and public entities. Notes that impacts related to corporate clients are addressed separately in section 3.2.3 of Environmental, Social, and Climate Change Management, and clarifies that the actions described are specific to Santander (not sector-wide), with cross-references to other report sections and financial statement notes.

nodes.title: Conduct with customers
nodes.heading: 3.3.1 Conduct with customers
nodes.start_phrase:
In this section we cover how Santander manages the following
IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Customer conduct, consumer protection, and financial inclusion in Santander’s 2024 Annual Report (sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2).
- Customer conduct risk and IROs: Identifies risks of losses and customer harm from inadequate practices, insufficient information, and poor complaints access; sets opportunities to improve outcomes.
- Customer conduct risk model: Approved by the compliance and conduct committee; aligns with the “Simple, Personal and Fair” culture; covers product/service design, sales, and post‑sales; emphasizes fair treatment, transparency, responsible sales/pricing, data protection, complaints handling, financial education, fraud safeguards, and attention to vulnerable customers/overindebtedness.
- Governance: Product governance and consumer protection within Compliance oversees execution; Board supervises product approval and remuneration policies; remuneration and risk committees and compliance forums set risk appetite and monitor conduct risk.
- Policies, guides, and accessibility: Group-wide policies ensure consistent implementation and communication; 2024 focus on the European Accessibility Directive to improve access to products, services, and channels, with tech and UX enhancements.
- Monitoring and metrics: Risk appetite metrics for claims/internal events to detect and manage issues; 2024 dispute impacts noted (mortgage fees in Spain, CHF mortgages in Poland) with appropriate customer responses.
- Product/service approval: Formal policy mandates transparent, fair, needs‑based design and pricing; local and corporate forums require unanimous approval and use standardized documentation and reviews across the lifecycle and channels.
- Conduct training and licensing: Mandatory refresher training for all employees; adherence to regulatory certifications (e.g., MiFID) and specialized training for sales teams.
- Pay linked to conduct: At least 40% of sales variable pay tied to quality and conduct metrics to reinforce good customer outcomes and target‑market suitability.
- Sales monitoring: Ongoing lifecycle oversight using Customer Voice (queries, complaints, surveys) and sales controls (e.g., early cancellations) to trigger improvements; 2024 actions included stronger welcome communications, call‑center sales enhancements in Mexico, and tighter campaign governance in Poland.
- Post‑sales fraud conduct: 2024 integration of conduct guidelines into the Group Fraud Policy; 2024–2026 improvement plans to unify fraud case channels, standardize taxonomies, enhance communications, and strengthen first/second line controls, with special focus on vulnerable customers; additional controls via NPS and QA.
- Complaints handling: Multi‑channel access and escalation options (e.g., Ombudsman/regulators); digital investments to speed resolution and enable self‑service; structured root‑cause analysis with action plans and senior oversight; 2024 progress across all countries, including a 19% claims reduction in Spain (ex‑sector events).
- AI in complaints: Global working group to enhance platforms; AI embedded in registration/analysis. Brazil’s “Viva Voz” scaled analysis from 3% in two days to 60% in one day (aiming 100%); Spain and Poland piloting similar tools.
- Complaint profile and outcomes: Standardized Group metrics show distribution by type (e.g., banking procedures, loans, investments, payments, insurance, others) and resolution rates, with the majority resolved in favour of the bank.
- Vulnerable customers: Group regulations (Nov 2023) on vulnerability and overindebtedness rolled out in 2024 to unify standards; indicators and a methodology under development to identify and address vulnerabilities proactively; bi‑monthly global‑local coordination and global staff training launched.
- Financial inclusion and health (3.3.2): Strategic priority to support social progress, prosperity, and entrepreneurship with tailored solutions in each market.
- Measurement approach: Uses World Bank Global Findex to size unbanked/underbanked/financially distressed populations; considers access, use, and financing; assesses involuntary exclusion via perceived barriers; applies a correction factor reflecting Santander’s market penetration to gauge addressable inclusion needs.

nodes.title: Financial inclusion and financial health
nodes.heading: 3.3.2 Financial inclusion and financial health
nodes.start_phrase:
This section outlines how we manage the following IRO:
Positive impact on customers due to the bank’s offer of I+
products and services that adapt to their needs and
expectations and promote financial inclusion and
health.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpts from Santander’s 2024 Annual Report covering customer conduct, financial inclusion and health, vulnerable customer management, complaints handling, and the start of privacy/data protection and cybersecurity.
- Customer complaints: Standardized claims metric used group-wide; breakdown of complaint types (e.g., banking procedures, loans, investments, payment methods, insurance, others) and resolution outcomes (in favour of the bank vs. customer).
- Vulnerable customers: Group regulations on vulnerable customers and prevention of over-indebtedness approved in Nov 2023 and embedded across markets in 2024. Use of indicators and a developing methodology to identify potential vulnerability and adapt services. Bi‑monthly coordination between local units and global team; global employee training rolled out.
- Financial inclusion strategy and measurement: Inclusion and financial health positioned as drivers of social progress. Market sizing of unbanked, underbanked, and financially distressed segments using World Bank Global Findex, with definitions and an adjustment for Santander’s market penetration.
- Inclusion target and progress: Ambition to reach 5 million people with inclusion measures in 2023–2025; cumulative progress shown (about 1.8 million in 2023 and 4.3 million by 2024). In 2024, roughly 1.0 million included via access initiatives and 1.6 million via finance initiatives.
- Access initiatives: Expanding access to cash and transactions via remote/underserved-area branches and third‑party partnerships (e.g., Correos Cash in Spain; retailers like Oxxo/7‑Eleven in Mexico; mobile/remote solutions in Portugal, Argentina, Poland, Uruguay). Promoting digital access (wallets, POS, programs like Cashless Poland and Chile’s Mas Lucas), basic accounts beyond regulatory minimums, and tailored support for seniors. Getnet enhances digital payments access for underbanked merchants and individuals.
- Finance initiatives: Microfinance in Latin America since 2002 supporting low-income and underbanked entrepreneurs—evolving from microcredit to broader microfinance (basic accounts, financial education, microinsurance). Efficiency gains via technology (mobile branches, faster disbursement). Mixed group/individual lending models adapted by country (greater individual lending in Peru and Colombia; growing in Brazil and Mexico).
- Additional finance-based support: Debt relief and hardship programs (e.g., Portugal’s Iris; UK tools and assistance; Spain mortgage relief). Affordable housing initiatives (Spain’s Social Housing Fund, affordable rentals; US LMI housing support). Targeted credit for groups with constrained access (SMEs at risk limits in Spain, LMI small businesses in the US, limited-credit-history entrepreneurs in Argentina, special programs in Mexico).
- Financial health: Defined as the ability to manage short-term needs and long-term goals to avoid distress. Initiatives include money-management tools, debt calculators, advisory, and financial education to complement inclusion. 2024 saw metrics set to monitor financial health, particularly for over-indebted customers.
- Privacy, data protection, and cybersecurity: Introduction of IROs related to personal data protection, cybersecurity awareness, and potential regulatory and reputational risks. Emphasis on compliance with data protection laws and Group standards amid increased data processing from digitalization.

nodes.title: Privacy, data protection and cybersecurity
nodes.heading: 3.3.3 Privacy, data protection and cybersecurity
nodes.start_phrase: This section outlines how we manage these IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Focus on financial inclusion and support for vulnerable customers:
  - Debt relief programs, payment deferrals, and credit line extensions for customers in financial distress.
  - Initiatives to improve access to basic financial services and affordable housing for low-income households.
  - Expanded physical and alternative access in underserved and remote areas (e.g., Spain, Portugal, Argentina, Poland, Uruguay), including partnerships with retailers and third parties (Correos Cash, Oxxo, 7-Eleven).
  - Promotion of digital payments where adoption is low (Cashless Poland, Mas Lucas in Chile).
  - Basic and low-fee accounts for vulnerable customers (Cuenta Life in Chile; no-fee account in Spain).
  - Tailored services for seniors (Portugal’s Here & Now; UK third‑party access; retiree products in Mexico and Argentina).
  - Participation in affordable housing initiatives (Spain’s Social Housing Fund; US Communities plan).
  - Credit access programs for SMEs and individuals with limited credit history in several markets.

- Progress on financial health:
  - Common Group approach defining financial health as the ability to meet short-term needs and long-term goals.
  - Tools and advisory to improve money management (budgeting tools, debt calculators) complemented by financial education.
  - 2024 rollout of metrics to monitor financial health, particularly for over‑indebted customers.

- Privacy and data protection:
  - Group-wide compliance framework aligned with GDPR and local laws, emphasizing data minimization and protection of confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience.
  - Governance model with corporate/local policies, DPOs/privacy champions, oversight via indicators and annual reviews.
  - Regular monitoring, incident management procedures, third‑party oversight, internal audits, centralized tooling, and ongoing training.
  - 2024 third‑party data incident: prompt notification to affected individuals and authorities, public disclosure, reinforced fraud controls, education campaigns, and containment with corrective actions implemented.

- Cybersecurity:
  - Board-approved cybersecurity framework; CISO role defined; policies aligned with international standards and updated in 2024.
  - External posture monitoring via Bitsight; 2024 score of 790 (advanced, upper quartile among peers).
  - Employee initiatives: ethical phishing, incident reporting culture, mandatory and specialized trainings for high‑risk roles and frontline teams.
  - Customer awareness and protection campaigns with high engagement (Cyber Heroes, in-branch workshops, “Everyday Cyber,” sponsorship activations, “Obvious Passwords” in Uruguay, Titania podcast); phishing reporting channel provided.
  - Active collaboration and leadership in industry and global forums (FS‑ISAC Europe chair, US Ransomware Task Force, WEF Cybercrime Atlas, IIF, EFR, EBF, DigitalEurope).

- Business conduct and corporate culture (Governance):
  - The Santander Way: values (Simple, Personal, Fair), TEAMS behaviors, leadership principles, and strong risk culture (Risk Pro).
  - Talent and culture enablers: enhanced Dojo digital learning platform, employee listening (YourVoice), and performance review model (MyContribution: 50% what, 40% how, 10% risk management).
  - Global Culture Policy to ensure coherence across the Group.

nodes.title: BUSINESS CONDUCT (Governance information)
nodes.heading: 4. BUSINESS CONDUCT (Governance information)
nodes.start_phrase: We are a global company, guided by a common culture, The Santander Way.
nodes.summary:
- Extract from Santander’s Annual Report 2024 (Governance – Business Conduct, Corporate Culture) describing “The Santander Way” as the Group’s unifying culture aligned with strategy.
- Core elements: values (Simple, Personal, Fair), corporate behaviours (TEAMS), robust risk culture (Risk Pro), and leadership principles.
- 2024 initiatives:
  - Embedded behaviours and leadership principles in talent processes and leadership development.
  - Strengthened employee upskilling and employability with tools aligned to business and market needs.
  - Evolved Dojo digital learning platform to offer personalized, role-based, continuous learning.
  - Used the YourVoice employee listening program to identify improvements and implement action plans.
  - Reinforced culture via the MyContribution performance review: 50% “what,” 40% “how,” 10% risk management.
- Governance foundation: Global Culture Policy to ensure a coherent culture across the Group.
- Leadership focus areas: promote a Group-first mindset, lead transformation, build and grow talent, model TEAMS, and drive an inclusive culture.
- Overall emphasis on maintaining a strong risk management culture integrated into everyday performance and decision-making.

nodes.title: Corporate culture
nodes.heading: 4.1 Corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase:
We are a global company, guided by a common culture, The
Santander Way.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from Banco Santander’s Annual Report 2024, Governance – Business Conduct (Section 4), covering corporate culture and ethical conduct, including conduct standards and responsible taxation.

- 4.1 Corporate culture – The Santander Way:
  - Culture foundations: values (Simple, Personal, Fair), corporate behaviours (TEAMS), leadership principles (Group first, lead transformation, grow talent, display TEAMS, drive inclusion), and a strong risk culture (Risk Pro).
  - 2024 actions: embedded behaviours and leadership principles in talent processes; boosted employee upskilling aligned to business needs; evolved Dojo digital learning platform for personalized, role‑based, continuous learning; used the YourVoice listening program to shape action plans; reinforced culture through MyContribution performance review (50% what, 40% how, 10% risk management).
  - Governance: Global Culture Policy sets common standards across all subsidiaries.

- 4.2 Ethical conduct – scope of risks and responsibilities:
  - Focus on acting responsibly toward investors, employees, society and the environment; paying taxes to support wealth distribution; preventing bribery/corruption and financial crime (e.g., AML).

- 4.2.1 Conduct standards – General Code of Conduct (GCC):
  - GCC approved by the Board; applies to all employees, management, and subsidiaries; publicly available.
  - Promotes equal opportunity, non‑discrimination, zero tolerance for harassment, respect, work‑life balance, human rights, and environmental protection.
  - Implementation:
    - Mandatory annual training (including penal responsibility, conflicts of interest, gifts/invitations), with an employee pledge.
    - #YourConductMatters awareness campaigns; guidance from Compliance; Canal Abierto whistleblowing channel; breaches sanctioned per regulation.
  - Monitoring and outcomes: GCC training completion tracked as a risk appetite metric; 99.1% completion as of Dec 2024; mandatory training tied to performance reviews; incidents linked to GCC violations are monitored.
  - Policy alignment: Conflicts of Interest Policy updated and simplified; Procurement Management Conduct Policy integrated.

- 4.2.2 Responsible taxation:
  - Tax strategy aligned with purpose and business strategy; Board approval and periodic review; risk management through the internal control model.
  - Cooperative compliance: adheres to Spain’s and the UK’s tax practice codes (since 2010), Portugal’s (since 2022), and submits an annual Tax Transparency Report to Spain’s Tax Authority (since 2015).
  - Core principles: comply with tax obligations per the spirit and intention of the law; respect transfer pricing and pay taxes per operations, risks and profits in each jurisdiction; do not provide tax advice or planning strategies when marketing/selling financial products.

nodes.title: Ethical conduct
nodes.heading: 4.2 Ethical conduct
nodes.start_phrase:
In this section we cover how Santander manages the following
IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Scope of the excerpt: Sustainability governance on ethical conduct, responsible taxation, financial-crime compliance, and ethical reporting channels within Grupo Santander’s 2024 Annual Report.

- Ethical conduct and conduct standards (GCC):
  - Group-wide General Code of Conduct approved by the Board; applies to all employees, management and subsidiary governing bodies; published on the corporate website.
  - Core values: equal opportunity, non-discrimination, zero tolerance of harassment, respect, work-life balance, human rights, and environmental protection.
  - Implementation mechanisms: mandatory annual GCC training and employee pledge; #YourConductMatters awareness campaigns; Compliance function for queries; Canal Abierto whistleblowing channel; breaches sanctioned per regulation.
  - Risk management: quarterly tracking of mandatory training completion as a risk appetite metric (99.1% completion as of Dec-2024; no remediation required); training tied to performance reviews; monitoring incidents linked to GCC violations.

- Responsible taxation:
  - Board-approved tax strategy aligned with purpose and sustainable, responsible banking; governed by an internal control-based tax risk management model.
  - Cooperative compliance: adheres to Spanish and UK codes since 2010, Portuguese code since 2022; voluntary Tax Transparency Report to Spain’s Tax Authority since 2015.
  - Principles: comply with the spirit and intent of tax law; arm’s-length transfer pricing aligned to value creation, risks and profits; do not market tax advice/planning or facilitate customer tax avoidance; transparent country-by-country disclosure; restrictions on non-cooperative jurisdictions require Board approval and enhanced oversight.
  - 2024 tax contribution: EUR 22.5bn total taxes; EUR 10.9bn paid directly (includes EUR 5.9bn income tax paid; 30.9% effective rate on cash taxes); income tax expense EUR 5.3bn (27.8% effective rate), with timing differences explained.

- Financial crime compliance (FCC):
  - Board-approved corporate FCC framework covering AML/CFT, sanctions, and since 2023 anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABC); policies and CDD/KYC aligned to domestic/international rules and updated for evolving threats.
  - Centralized oversight with technical FCC units; extensive awareness via training, intranet, campaigns, and newsletters; continuous engagement with businesses to identify and mitigate new risks.
  - Inclusion with control: unbiased FCC onboarding for “people in special situations” with appropriate due diligence; flexible remote/in-person onboarding.
  - Sector risk approach: enhanced KYC and transaction monitoring for sectors with elevated risks (corruption, trafficking, modern slavery, labor exploitation, child abuse, environmental crime).
  - ABC program: group-wide RCSA; higher exposure areas include Marketing, Sponsorships, Vendor Management, and HR; tailored training including procurement teams and board members; 166,199 employees trained in FCC; strengthened outsourcing/supplier controls with greater automation.
  - Detection and reporting: robust FIU-led systems, internal controls, and independent investigation committees; 2024 outcomes—453,175 investigations and 231,810 disclosures to authorities; FCC-related concerns can also be raised via whistleblowing channels.
  - No finalized judicial or administrative proceedings in 2024 related to corruption/anti-bribery or AML/CFT, per stated materiality criteria.

- Ethical channels (Canal Abierto):
  - Anonymous, confidential whistleblowing channel with anti-retaliation protections; local channels per subsidiary in multiple languages under common standards since 2020.
  - Minimum standards: CEO endorsement, employee communication and lessons learned, easy access and anonymity, external reporting platforms, conflict-of-interest safeguards in investigations, and regular internal audits.
  - Governance: Board-approved policy and operating procedure; Banco Santander’s channel overseen by the Chief Compliance Officer; accessible via intranet and corporate website.
  - Scope: primarily for employees; some subsidiaries open to vendors/customers; excludes standard business incidents/complaints.
  - Reportable matters include GCC breaches, unlawful acts, SOX-related issues, AML/CFT and ABC breaches, securities law violations, serious legal/administrative offenses, and conduct against corporate behaviors.
  - Case handling: diligent, independent, objective processing; typical 60-day timeline extendable by 30 days; explicit conflict-of-interest management; prohibition of reprisals.
  - Culture and oversight: GCC training includes Canal Abierto module; ongoing awareness communications; annual consolidated reporting to the Risk Supervision, Regulation and Compliance Committee and the Audit Committee; continuous improvement focus on analytics to inform governing bodies and action plans.

nodes.title: Ethical channels
nodes.heading: 4.3 Ethical channels
nodes.start_phrase: In this section we cover how Santander manages these IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Ethical channels (whistleblowing) and supplier responsibility within Santander’s Sustainability, Governance, Risk and Compliance framework.
- Ethical reporting channel (Canal Abierto):
  - Anonymous, confidential Group-wide channel to report unethical conduct; anti-retaliation explicitly enforced.
  - Local implementations across Group units in multiple languages, aligned to a 2020 Group policy with minimum standards (CEO endorsement, accessibility and anonymity, external platforms, conflict-of-interest controls, regular internal audits).
  - Governance: Board-approved policy; Banco Santander channel under the Chief Compliance Officer; procedures published on corporate site and platform.
  - Scope and use: Accessible via intranet for employees and via corporate website/platform for stakeholders; some local channels open to vendors and customers; business complaints outside scope are excluded.
  - Reportable matters include: unlawful acts; breaches of the General Code of Conduct (GCC); accounting/audit irregularities (SOX); AML/CFT, corruption and bribery; securities law violations; serious legal/administrative/EU-law infringements; conduct contrary to corporate behaviours.
  - Case handling commitments: diligent, independent, objective investigations; 60-day processing target (+30 days for complex cases); conflict-of-interest management; strict anti-retaliation.
  - Awareness and oversight: mandatory annual Code of Conduct training including Canal Abierto; ongoing communications with statistics and guidance; annual consolidated reporting by Compliance to the Risk Supervision, Regulation and Compliance Committee and the Audit Committee.
  - Monitoring and assurance: quarterly data collection on volumes, types, and measures; regular external auditor review of data integrity and traceability.
- 2024 Canal Abierto outcomes:
  - 4,437 reports received (2.1% of headcount), including 216 from third parties (163 customers, 53 vendors); increase from 3,611 in 2023 due to a wider business perimeter.
  - Categories (selected counts): GCC breaches 2,286; marketing 321; privacy/security/confidentiality 116; internal fraud 292; harassment 1,094 (per CSRD definition; 89% workplace harassment); equal opportunities/non-discrimination 132; conflicts of interest 219; other GCC 112; HR cases 1,754; other typologies 397.
  - Closed reports: 4,122; disciplinary actions: 715, including 393 dismissals (0.2% of headcount).
  - Corruption-specific: 14 reports led to 3 dismissals.
  - No judicial proceedings recorded for discrimination or violations of fundamental rights; no employee cases referring to serious human rights incidents.
  - Data scope: multiple countries and Group units (e.g., Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Spain, Mexico, Poland, Portugal, UK, US, etc., including Digital Consumer Bank subsidiaries and SCIB branches).
- Supplier responsibility and ESG in procurement:
  - Objectives (IROs): promote responsible practices with vendors, assess ESG performance, provide improvement tools; mitigate risks to operational resilience by vetting supplier solvency, reputation, and legal compliance.
  - Group-wide outsourcing and third‑party management model plus third‑party certification policy to ensure minimum standards and manage risks in resilience, solvency, reputation, and regulatory compliance.
  - Supplier ESG certification methodology to identify higher sustainability risk suppliers and calibrate controls accordingly, complementing the third‑party certification policy.
  - Capacity building: support suppliers via the UN Global Compact training programme to enhance sustainability knowledge and implementation.
  - 2024 progress: began embedding a new ESG approval methodology across the Group to strengthen sustainability in procurement.

nodes.title: Our suppliers
nodes.heading: 4.4 Our suppliers
nodes.start_phrase: In this section we cover how Santander manages these IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Ethics and whistleblowing: Quarterly monitoring and external audit of ethical channel data. In 2024, 4,437 reports were received (2.1% of headcount), including 216 from third parties; 4,122 were closed, leading to 715 disciplinary actions and 393 dismissals (0.2% of headcount). Main categories included breaches to the Group Code of Conduct, harassment (defined per CSRD; 89% workplace harassment), internal fraud, equal opportunities/non-discrimination, conflicts of interest, privacy/security, and other compliance areas (incl. AML/CTF, corruption and bribery—14 corruption reports, 3 dismissals). Increase vs. 2023 (3,611) reflects a broader perimeter. The Group reports no judicial proceedings for discrimination/fundamental rights and no serious human rights incidents involving employees.

- Supplier management and ESG: Group-wide outsourcing/third‑party certification and an ESG certification methodology to identify and control sustainability risks; support via UN Global Compact training. A new ESG approval methodology pre‑classifies suppliers by sector exposure (S&P ESG Risk Atlas) and assigns low/medium/high risk using surveys (country risk, size, environmental traits). By year‑end, 487 at‑risk suppliers were assessed; remediation plans applied as needed. Sustainability criteria are embedded in procurement (e.g., cards, electricity, vehicles) and requested in tenders with high ESG impact (ATMs, hardware, cash transport), covering carbon footprint, recycled materials, energy efficiency, accessibility, and legal compliance. A corporate tool standardizes high‑risk supplier certification and reviews risks (cybersecurity, continuity, data protection, anti‑bribery, etc.). Ethical channels for suppliers are being expanded; expert teams are being built.

- Supplier payments: EUR 11.6bn paid; 89% local suppliers (88% of volume). Average payment 15 days; 81% within legal maximum; implementing SME‑specific controls. No significant term differences and no judicial/administrative proceedings for non‑payment.

- Sustainability statement basis and scope: The report is Santander Group’s consolidated non‑financial and sustainability information under EU CSRD (Directive 2022/2464) and related regulation, aligned with Spanish law; approved 25 Feb 2024; covers 1 Jan–31 Dec 2024. Topic scopes are specified: climate/transition (CIB portfolios in thermal coal, power, O&G, aviation, steel, autos; DCB auto loans; Brazil agro; Spain/UK mortgages and real estate), Equator Principles (CIB), environmental footprint (Group-wide with defined Scope 3 exceptions), EU Taxonomy GAR (prudential group), and employee metrics (Group scope with noted exclusions).

nodes.title: SUSTAINABILITY NOTES
nodes.heading: SUSTAINABILITY NOTES
nodes.start_phrase:
2013/34/EU as regards disclosure of non-financial and diversity 
information.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt is from Banco Santander’s Annual Report 2024, Sustainability Notes (SN 1), setting out the introduction, legal basis, scope, and consolidation approach for the Group’s Sustainability statement. It confirms the statement is part of the consolidated directors’ report, approved on 25 February 2024, covers 1 January–31 December 2024, and follows the Group’s consolidated basis consistent with financial statements. It details compliance with EU sustainability reporting requirements (Directive (EU) 2022/2464, Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772), Spanish Commercial Code Art. 49 (Act 11/2018 transposing Directive 2014/95/EU), and EU Taxonomy disclosures (GAR per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178).

It specifies topic-by-topic scope:
- Environmental/transition topics: green finance (Corporate & Investment Banking), EV financing (Digital Consumer Bank auto loans), and sustainable payment card materials (selected Group companies across multiple countries).
- ESG risk management: portfolio exposure to climate-sensitive sectors (Full Group); Equator Principles (Corporate & Investment Banking).
- Paris Alignment: climate alignment coverage for CIB portfolios (thermal coal, power generation, oil & gas, aviation, steel, auto manufacturing); Digital Consumer Bank (auto loans); Brazil commercial banking (agro); Spain and UK commercial banking (residential mortgages and real estate).
- Environmental footprint: Full Group, with specified Scope 3 emissions (categories 1, 2, 4, 9) calculated for major companies in listed countries and Digital Consumer Bank geographies.
- EU Taxonomy: Green Asset Ratio based on the prudential consolidated group.
- Social information (employees): headcount (Full Group, excluding accident data for Santander Polska S.A.) and remuneration (Full Group).

The contents page signals broader report sections on business model, sustainability, corporate governance, economic and financial review, and compliance.

nodes.title: Introduction, basis of presentation of the Sustainability statement and other information
nodes.heading: SN 1. Introduction, basis of presentation of the Sustainability statement and other information
nodes.start_phrase: 2013/34/EU as regards disclosure of non-financial and diversity information.
nodes.summary:
- Nature and regulatory basis of the statement: Consolidated non‑financial and sustainability information for Banco Santander, S.A. and subsidiaries, approved by the board on 25 February 2024. Prepared in line with CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 (ESRS), Spanish Commercial Code Art. 49 (Act 11/2018 transposing Directive 2014/95/EU), and EU Taxonomy (Reg. (EU) 2021/2178). Reporting period: 1 January–31 December 2024; same consolidated basis as the financial statements with defined scope differences by topic.

- Scope overview by topic (examples):
  - Environmental: Green finance (CIB), EV financing (Digital Consumer Bank), cards in sustainable materials (main Group companies across multiple countries), ESG in risk management (Group), portfolio exposure to climate‑sensitive sectors (Group), Equator Principles (CIB), climate alignment for specified sectoral portfolios and geographies, environmental footprint (Group with defined Scope 3 coverage), EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (prudential group).
  - Social: Employees (headcount, remuneration, training, engagement; Group scope with noted exceptions), communities (SRI AuMs in Wealth; education/employability support across main geographies and foundations; other community programmes across Group markets), customers (coverage of customer base/offices/channels; NPS in main geographies; complaints for entities >1% of claims; financial health & inclusion across major markets).
  - Governance: Corporate governance and shareholder/investor communications (Banco Santander, S.A.), ethical conduct (mandatory GCC training), tax contribution (Group), financial crime compliance (main obliged entities), litigation and penalties (Group), ethical channels across multiple geographies, supplier management (payments and ESG‑risk‑evaluated suppliers across specified countries).

- Subsidiary reporting under CSRD: Within the consolidation perimeter, Santander Consumer Bank AS (Norway), Santander Bank Polska S.A. (Poland), and Stellantis Banque France (France) are obliged to report. Entities in countries where CSRD is not yet transposed are not considered obliged. No exemption used for information on upcoming events/negotiations. No additional significant post‑period events (from 1 January 2025 to report preparation) beyond those in the annual accounts.

- Value chain definition and coverage: Constructed per ESRS 1 and EFRAG guidance; split into upstream (financial authorities, product/service providers), own operations (assets, geographies, cross‑cutting functions), and downstream (Retail & Commercial Banking; Digital Consumer Bank including Openbank and SCF; CIB; Wealth Management & Insurance; Payments via PagoNxt and Cards; JVs/associates; retailers such as car dealerships).

- Information not disclosed: Partial disclosure of ESRS 2 MDR‑A (OpEx/CapEx for action plans) due to confidentiality/sensitivity; selected spend metrics provided (e.g., training, energy efficiency, community investment). No other exclusions for IP/know‑how.

- Time horizons used: Short term 1 year; medium term 1–5 years; long term >5 years, aligned with ESRS and explicitly indicated where different.

- Significant estimates and assumptions: Heavy reliance on third‑party data and estimates for GHG emissions, climate target‑setting and forward‑looking parameters; subject to methodological, data, market, technological, and regulatory uncertainties. Expect improvements in data quality/coverage; Group may update targets and methodologies. EU Taxonomy disclosures also subject to data uncertainty.

- Comparatives and methodological changes:
  - Transitional provision used under ESRS 1: no prior‑year comparatives in first year, except where required by Spanish Law 11/2018.
  - Method changes: calendar days lost now include fatalities; energy consumption recalculated by country generation mix and certified renewable electricity; Scope 1 now includes refrigerant gas leaks.
  - Scope changes: internal consumption now covers 100% of Group; compensation of Scopes 1 and 2 now for 100% of Group from 2024.
  - Scope 1 and 2 reduction targets reviewed (2020 baseline, 2030 horizon). No material restatements identified.

- Incorporation by reference: Specific ESRS requirements are fulfilled via cross‑references to the consolidated annual accounts and audit report (e.g., subsidiary list; penalties; linkage of OpEx/CapEx to accounts; tax information; serious human rights incidents for employees/affected groups/consumers; anti‑corruption/bribery fines). A CSRD content index (SN 11) maps requirements to report sections.

- ESRS phase‑in provisions applied (not disclosed in year one): 
  - ESRS 2 SBM‑1 (total revenue/revenue by significant ESRS sectors)
  - ESRS 2 SBM‑3 (potential financial effects)
  - ESRS E1‑9 (potential physical/transition risks and climate opportunities)
  - ESRS S1‑7 (non‑employee worker characteristics)
  - ESRS S1‑14 (H&S for non‑employee workers)
  - ESRS S1‑15 (work‑life balance)

- Cross‑references to datapoints from other EU legislation and their materiality/location: Includes board diversity and independence (Delegated Reg. 2020/1816), due diligence statement, involvement in fossil fuels/chemicals/controversial weapons/tobacco (with some deemed not material), and E1‑1 transition plan and Paris‑aligned benchmark considerations; mapped to relevant Sustainability Notes and sections.

nodes.title: Sustainability governance
nodes.heading: SN 2. Sustainability governance
nodes.summary:
- Presents a comprehensive cross-reference of ESRS 2 and topical ESRS datapoints that derive from other EU legislation (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3 Article 449a, EU Climate Law, EU Benchmark Regulations), indicating for each datapoint whether it is material and where it appears in the report (e.g., sections and Sustainability Notes).
- Climate (ESRS E1) disclosures highlighted as material include: transition plan to climate neutrality by 2050; Paris-alignment/transition alignment metrics; GHG emissions reduction targets; energy consumption and mix; energy intensity in high-impact sectors; gross Scope 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions and intensity; GHG removals and carbon credits; portfolio exposure to climate-related physical risks, including disaggregation by acute/chronic risks, location of significant assets at risk, and real estate energy-efficiency classes; degree of exposure to climate-related opportunities (some items phased in). These link to CRR/Pillar 3 templates and EU Delegated/Implementing Regulations and are located mainly in “Our climate transition plan” and Sustainability Notes (SN 4, SN 7.1).
- Other environmental topics (ESRS E2–E5) are largely deemed not material for the period: pollutants to air/water/soil (E2-4), water and marine resources policies and metrics (E3-1, E3-4), biodiversity and ecosystems (E4-2 incl. oceans/seas and deforestation policies), waste (E5-5, incl. hazardous/radioactive waste).
- Social standards: Employees (ESRS S1) include human rights policy commitments and due diligence (ILO core conventions), workplace accident prevention systems, grievance mechanisms, fatalities/accident days lost, unadjusted gender pay gap, CEO pay ratio, and incidents of discrimination; some datapoints (e.g., trafficking prevention) are not material. Value chain workers (S2), affected communities (S3), and consumers/end-users (S4) are mostly not material, with cross-references to customer and human rights sections where relevant.
- Governance (ESRS G1): anti-corruption and anti-bribery standards, fines, and whistleblower protection are disclosed and linked to Business Conduct and Financial Crime Compliance.
- Governance structure and oversight:
  - Board of Directors: 15 members (13 non-executive, 2 executive), 66.67% independent; gender split 40% women/60% men (reported diversity ratio 67%); broad international background; explicit responsibility for responsible banking and sustainability strategy, KPIs, and oversight.
  - Responsible Banking, Sustainability and Culture Committee (RBSCC): 5 independent directors (80% women); advises on strategy/policies for E, S, G; 2024 agenda included climate strategy/targets, ESG in credit process, green finance, own footprint and value-chain emissions, social agenda (financial inclusion, human rights), community support/Universidades, inclusive culture and women in senior roles, embedding sustainability in remuneration, supplier ESG, non-financial reporting, regulatory trends, and CSRD training.
  - Audit Committee: 5 independent directors (60% women); oversees financial and sustainability reporting processes and internal controls; 15 meetings in 2024, including joint sessions with the risk committee.
  - Risk Supervision, Regulation and Compliance Committee: 5 external directors (40% women; 3 independent); oversees financial and non-financial risks, risk appetite, culture; 18 meetings in 2024; topics included data protection, operational resilience, conduct, complaints and whistleblowing.
  - Nomination and Remuneration Committees also review sustainability-related issues (e.g., integration of sustainability targets into remuneration).
- Management committees and three lines of defence:
  - Corporate Accounting and Financial Reporting, Management and Sustainability Committee approves and validates sustainability disclosures; meets monthly.
  - Risk Control Committee offers a holistic risk view against risk appetite.
  - First line (business/functions) owns and manages risks and data for sustainability metrics; Corporate Sustainability leads strategy and coordination; Accounting and Management Control maintains internal control over sustainability information.
  - Second line (Risk; Compliance & Conduct) challenges and oversees risk management and control effectiveness.
  - Third line (Internal Audit) independently assesses adequacy and effectiveness of controls over financial and sustainability reporting and compliance with codes/policies; reports to the Audit Committee.
- Internal control over sustainability information:
  - COSO-based system evolving to cover all material topics; identifies material risks, sets controls, and addresses key challenges (assumptions/judgments, completeness/boundaries, third‑party/value-chain data, consolidation of metrics).
  - Steps toward reasonable assurance for selected sustainability metrics.
  - Control architecture outlined across control culture, risk assessment (RCSA), control activities, information/communication, and monitoring.
- Cross-cutting frameworks and policies embedding ESG:
  - Responsible Banking framework and policy; Accounting & Financial Reporting, Management and Sustainability information framework; Responsible Banking model (roles and responsibilities across the three lines).
  - Board-approved corporate frameworks include Responsible Banking, Risk, Cybersecurity, Compliance & Conduct, Financial Crime, Human Resources; key policies include Code of Conduct, Securities Markets Code, Environmental/Social/Climate Risk, Tax, Conflict of Interest, Defence Sector, AML/CFT, Remuneration, Performance Management, Succession, Culture.
- Double materiality assessment methodology:
  - Aligned with ESRS 1–2 and ERAG; phases include background and stakeholder analysis and identification of 100+ impacts, risks, and opportunities across the value chain and time horizons.
  - Tools and inputs: UNEP FI impact analysis, ENCORE database for environmental dependencies, and human rights due diligence.
  - IROs mapped to ESRS topics (AR 16), with dependencies between impacts and risks/opportunities, organizational ownership, and potential financial effects.
- Extensive cross-references guide readers to where each disclosure appears (e.g., Sustainability Notes SN 2 governance, SN 4 transition plan, SN 7.1 environmental footprint, SN 7.3 employees; report sections on climate transition plan, employees, customers, business conduct) and to CRR Pillar 3 disclosure templates for climate risk.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment – Detailed methodology
nodes.heading: SN 3. Materiality assessment – Detailed methodology
nodes.start_phrase: The Group and subsidiaries’ double materiality assessments are based on European Sustainability Regulatory Standards (ESRS) 1 and 2, and the Double Materiality Assessment Guide from the ERAG.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Extract from a sustainability and governance section of an annual report detailing the Group’s responsible banking framework, double materiality assessment methodology and results, key impacts/risks/opportunities (IROs) across ESRS topics, and the climate transition plan including financed emissions and target-setting.
- Governance and policy framework: Describes the Responsible Banking and Sustainability Policy (principles, targets incl. human rights), and the Responsible Banking Model (first/second/third lines of defence) to embed ESG. Confirms rigorous drafting/approval/monitoring standards, with approval by the Board or its committees. Lists core corporate frameworks (Responsible Banking, Risk, Cybersecurity, Compliance and Conduct, Financial Crime, HR) and policies (Code of Conduct, Securities Markets Code, Environmental/Social/Climate Risk, Tax, Conflicts of Interest, Defence sector, AML/CFT, Remuneration, Performance, Succession, Culture). Refers to website for full regulatory documents.
- Topical coverage: Signals specific regulations and management approaches for material topics and IROs: climate change, own workforce, customers/consumers, affected communities, and business conduct.
- Double materiality methodology (ESRS 1 and 2; EFRAG guidance): 
  - Phase 1 Background and stakeholder analysis using internal strategic/financial materials plus external sources (UNEP FI impact tool, ENCORE for environmental dependencies, human rights due diligence).
  - Stakeholder mapping and inputs from customers, employees, investors, regulators, NGOs, communities.
  - Phase 2 Identification: 100+ IROs categorized per ESRS AR 16, mapped to value chain, time horizons, dependencies between impacts and risks/opportunities, managerial ownership, and financial effect type.
  - Phase 3 Assessment: 32 IROs deemed material. Impacts assessed on scale, scope, irreparability, and likelihood. Risks assessed via climate risk quantification (transition/physical) aligned with EBA ESG risk guidance; other environmental risks linked to nature/biodiversity approach (ENCORE; Kunming-Montreal GBF target 15); social/governance via SASB and internal financials. Opportunities sized via projected ESG revenues vs Group revenue.
  - Phase 4 Thresholds: Materiality threshold set at 3.5/5 for impact and financial materiality; statistical rationale provided.
- Stakeholder priorities: Broad consensus on prioritizing climate action/green transition, data protection, transparency, and financial inclusion. Retail customers emphasize privacy/transparency; employees/senior management weight ESG areas evenly; investors/regulators/NGOs prioritize environmental issues. Input volumes: 9,000+ retail customers; c.200 employees; 8 investors; 8 senior managers; 3 NGOs; 2 regulators/supervisors.
- IRO register examples (linked to ESRS, value chain, time horizon, and management sections):
  - Climate (E1): Positive impacts from financing renewables/low-carbon tech and reducing own Scope 1–2; negative impacts from financing non-sustainable activities; opportunities for revenue growth across clean tech and sectoral solutions; reputational risk if climate policies/objectives are perceived as inadequate.
  - Own workforce (S1): Positive impacts via health, safety, well-being, flexible work; diversity and equal opportunity; learning and talent development; fair/market-based remuneration. Negative impacts/risks from discrimination, inadequate conditions, misconduct or conflict.
  - Consumers and end users (S4): Positive impacts via inclusive, needs-based products and financial health initiatives; cybersecurity education. Negative impacts/risks from poor disclosure, weak complaints handling, data protection breaches, inadequate treatment of vulnerable customers, and substandard conduct.
  - Affected communities (S3): Positive impacts from education, employability, entrepreneurship programs; lending to support economic growth; socially responsible investment/lending. Negative impacts from financing that breaches ESG policies or insufficient stakeholder due diligence in financing.
  - Business conduct (G1): Positive impacts from ethical culture, tax contribution, effective whistleblowing channels, responsible supply chain management. Negative impacts/risks from corruption/bribery, ineffective grievance processes, vendor solvency/reputation/compliance weaknesses, and financial crime.
- Climate transition plan (SN 4):
  - Target design: Uses physical emissions intensity for power generation, steel, aviation, auto manufacturing; absolute emissions for oil & gas. Emphasizes engagement over divestment and case-by-case judgment to avoid perverse incentives; acknowledges lack of a universal “transition finance taxonomy.”
  - Scenario basis: 2030 alignment targets anchored in IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (IEA-NZE), consistent with a 1.5°C pathway; own Scope 1–2 reduction aligned with SBTi cross-sector absolute reduction (>4.2% linear annual).
  - Coverage and baselines: CIB portfolio targets are global (core subsidiaries); SCF auto lending target covers European passenger cars across 16 units in 13 countries. Baseline years: 2019 (most sectors), 2020/2022 (auto manufacturing/auto lending), 2020 for own operations.
  - Financed emissions measurement: Applies PCAF methodologies; notes at least one-year data lag; supplements with sector-average factors for regulatory perimeters; includes equity and sovereign exposures where material.
  - Portfolio exposure: Approximately 9% of total lending (and ~18% of CIB lending) in sectors with published alignment targets (excluding thermal coal phase-out). PCAF membership since 2021.
- Cross-references: Each IRO links to relevant report sections on climate risk management, employees, customers, communities, suppliers, ethics/whistleblowing, and environmental/social risk processes, reinforcing integrated governance and accountability.

nodes.title: Our transition plan
nodes.heading: SN 4. Our transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: Target types : To help our customers’ transition to a low-carbon economy, we employ physical emissions intensity for setting targets in the power generation, steel, aviation and auto sectors.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines Santander’s transition plan and approach to setting portfolio alignment targets: physical emissions intensity for power, steel, aviation and autos; absolute emissions for oil & gas; prioritizes client engagement over divestment and evaluates cases individually to avoid unintended disincentives amid the absence of a universal transition finance taxonomy.
- Uses the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (IEA‑NZE) scenario to set 2030, 1.5°C‑aligned targets; aviation target based on expected adoption of current technologies. Own operations’ Scope 1 & 2 target follows SBTi’s cross‑sector absolute contraction (exceeding a 4.2% linear annual reduction).
- Provides scenario reference points for 2030 (e.g., power 0.19 tCO2/MWh; oil & gas −23% vs 2019; steel 1.29 tCO2e/t; aviation 60.59 gCO2e/RPK; autos 116 gCO2/vkm; own ops −42% vs 2020).
- Defines target coverage: CIB portfolio targets are global and include core subsidiaries; SCF target covers European passenger car loans and leases across 16 units (13 countries), with plans to extend to other vehicle types. Notes baseline years (2019 for initial sectors; 2020/2022 for autos) and that sectors with published targets represent ~9% of total lending and ~18% of CIB lending.
- Explains financed emissions methodology and disclosure: calculates according to PCAF, focused on high‑emitting, actionable value chain segments, with a data lag of at least one year; also estimates financed emissions for long‑term equity and sovereign debt holdings.
- Discloses financed emissions for alignment across sectors (power generation, oil & gas, aviation, steel, auto manufacturing, Brazil agriculture, European auto lending, UK/Spain mortgages and commercial real estate), including exposures, covered scopes, absolute emissions, physical and financial intensities, and PCAF data quality scores for 2020–2023.
- Details data quality and attribution: primary sources include CDP, Trucost, Asset Impact, TPI and company reports; for corporate loans, attribution uses Total Value of the Company (equity + debt) to reduce market cap volatility. Clarifies these calculations differ from EBA Pillar 3 perimeter and methods.
- States stance on internal carbon pricing: does not apply a standalone “fictitious” internal carbon price; instead integrates carbon cost assumptions in scenario analysis and transition risk tools and supports real‑economy carbon pricing. Offsets residual Scope 1 & 2 emissions via rigorously selected, independently rated carbon credits, with ongoing monitoring of the voluntary carbon market.
- Notes EU Paris‑aligned benchmarks: Santander is not excluded; exposure to undertakings excluded from these benchmarks is disclosed in Pillar 3.
- Provides EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures: reports Green Asset Ratio (GAR) of 3.04% (turnover‑based) and 3.28% (CapEx‑based); flow GAR of 2.6% and 3.4% respectively; eligibility for climate objectives at 34%. Highlights limitations—Taxonomy does not capture all transition‑supporting activities and numerator/denominator asymmetry excludes, for example, many SME and non‑European green loans.
- Assesses locked‑in GHG emissions: own direct emissions and key assets are not material sources of Scope 1 & 2; Scope 3 materiality is dominated by category 3.15 (financed emissions, >99% of Scope 3). Category 3.11 (use of sold products) is not material. Insufficient counterparty data currently prevents robust locked‑in estimates for category 3.15.

nodes.title: EU Taxonomy
nodes.heading: SN 5. EU Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase:
In 2020, the European Union adopted the Taxonomy Regulation
that sets out a list of activities that can qualify as environmentally
sustainable90 and stipulates that companies subject to the
Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD91) must disclose
how their operations align with the EU Taxonomy.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Grupo Santander’s approach to managing its environmental impact, including reducing operational CO2e emissions (scopes 1 and 2) and offsetting residual emissions through rigorously selected, certified, and independently rated carbon credits, with active monitoring of the voluntary carbon market.
- Notes Santander’s inclusion under EU Paris‑aligned benchmarks and references disclosure of exposures to undertakings excluded from those benchmarks in Pillar 3 reports.
- Explains “locked‑in” GHG emissions: direct emissions and key assets’ scope 1 and 2 are not material; scope 3 financed emissions (category 3.15) account for over 99% of total scope 3; “use of sold products” (3.11) is not material; data gaps currently prevent reliable estimation of locked‑in financed emissions.
- Outlines EU Taxonomy Article 8/CSRD reporting, focusing on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), which measures financing of Taxonomy‑aligned activities versus total balance sheet.
- Reports 2024 GAR results: 3.04% (turnover‑based) and 3.28% (CapEx‑based), while noting Taxonomy limitations that understate transition efforts (e.g., asymmetric numerator/denominator, limited data such as energy efficiency certificates in some markets, and complex DNSH/MSS evidence requirements).
- Introduces a complementary “European & symmetric” GAR to address design limitations, with 2024 results of 7.90%, aligning numerator and denominator only to European, labelable exposures.
- Provides GAR/KPI disclosures for other businesses per European Commission requirements: asset management KPI 1.59% (turnover) and 2.60% (CapEx); insurance investment KPI 1.45% (turnover) and 2.05% (CapEx); investment services KPI deemed immaterial.
- Presents a consolidated KPI across businesses: 2.99% (turnover‑based) and 3.24% (CapEx‑based), weighted by revenue shares.
- Highlights that many transition‑supporting activities are not fully captured by current Taxonomy criteria (e.g., certain hybrids), and that data and implementation challenges reduce reported alignment.
- References where to find fuller disclosures, EU taxonomy templates, and links to the bank’s green transition support and GFANZ transition planning sections.
- Introduces the Sustainable Finance and Investment Classification System (SFICS), updated from 2022 guidelines and expanded in 2024 to include socially responsible investment standards, establishing Group‑wide criteria for classifying environmental, social, and sustainable activities.
- Notes SFICS alignment with international standards and principles (EU Taxonomy, ICMA, LMA, UNEP FI, Climate Bonds, Febraban) to enable tracking, product development, and greenwashing risk mitigation.
- Details SFICS updates: a customer‑based sustainability approach complementing activity‑based criteria; expanded sector guidance (manufacturing, real estate, sustainable agriculture, etc.); new activities covering water, waste, circular economy, and biodiversity goals.
- Describes eligible product types under SFICS: dedicated‑purpose (use‑of‑proceeds) financing and sustainability‑linked financing aligned with ICMA/LMA standards, supported by an updated (2023) global framework for green, social, and sustainability funding that governs use of proceeds, selection, management, and reporting.

nodes.title: Sustainable finance and investment classification system (SFICS)
nodes.heading: SN 6. Sustainable finance and investment classification system (SFICS)
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainable finance is key to meeting our climate ambition.
nodes.summary:
- The document excerpt is from the 2024 Annual Report’s Sustainability section, focusing on the Sustainable finance and investment classification system (SFICS) and a comprehensive set of performance tables.
- SFICS overview and purpose:
  - Introduced in 2022 and updated in 2024 to include socially responsible investment standards; now a Group-wide system to classify environmental, social and sustainable assets and activities.
  - Aims to track sustainable activity, guide product development, and mitigate greenwashing risk across all business units.
  - Draws on leading market standards and principles, including the EU Taxonomy (with 2023’s four new environmental objectives), ICMA and LMA principles, UNEP FI framework, Climate Bonds Standard, and Brazil’s Febraban taxonomy.
- Key 2024 enhancements to SFICS:
  - Adds a customer-focused sustainability approach to complement the activity-based approach.
  - Expands criteria for manufacturing, real estate, sustainable agriculture, and other sectors.
  - Incorporates new environmental goals on water, waste, circular economy and biodiversity, reflecting EU Taxonomy developments.
  - Commits to ongoing evolution to better classify green and transition activities in support of customer transitions and climate ambition.
- Eligible sustainable finance products and frameworks:
  - Use-of-proceeds instruments (green, social, sustainability bonds and loans) directed to eligible environmental and social activities aligned with ICMA/LMA, Climate Bonds Standard, and the EU Taxonomy.
  - Sustainability-linked financing aligned with ICMA/LMA, with structures tied to pre-defined ESG performance targets and metrics.
  - A 2023 updated, unified Green, Social and Sustainability Funding Global Framework governs all labelled funding across the Group, replacing prior global bond frameworks; it aligns with best practice on use of proceeds, project selection, management of proceeds, and reporting, and is consistent with SFICS.
- “Our progress in figures” (SN 7) outlines the metrics and disclosures to follow:
  - Green transition: green finance volumes, environmental footprint, Scopes 1–3 and total GHG emissions, carbon-credit-backed mitigation projects, and Equator Principles reporting.
  - EU Taxonomy tables.
  - Employees: breakdowns by region, gender, management group, age, contract type; collective bargaining and social dialogue; turnover; remuneration and ratios (including senior management and long-term incentive links); leadership composition; training; and occupational health and safety.
  - Customers: customer base, engagement channels, NPS rankings by country, and complaints.
  - Financial inclusion: number of people financially included and microfinance activity.
  - Community support: contributions, outputs and outcomes.
  - Tax contribution: total taxes paid.

nodes.title: Our progress in figures
nodes.heading: SN 7. Our progress in figures
nodes.summary:
- Extract from the 2024 Annual Report’s Sustainability section, “SN 7. Our progress in figures,” summarizing performance through data tables.
- SN 7.1 Green transition:
  - Green finance: CIB contributed EUR 24.1bn in 2024; accumulated EUR 139.4bn since 2019. Metrics aligned with league tables; excludes financial inclusion; not equivalent to EU Taxonomy.
  - Environmental footprint (2024 vs 2023): total internal energy 1,012,554 MWh with 78.3% certified renewable, 17.7% fossil, 0.6% nuclear, 3.3% non-certified renewable. Electricity use up 6.4% to 856.65 GWh; renewable electricity 793.14 GWh (+1.7%); non-renewable electricity 63.52 GWh (+147.8%).
