nodes.title: Other work-related rights
nodes.heading: 6.1.7.3 Other work-related rights
nodes.start_phrase: To prevent, mitigate and remedy significant negative impacts on the company’s own workforce when it comes to inadequate handling of employee information and data, Swedbank has taken the following actions.
nodes.summary:
- Employee health and wellbeing: In Sweden, nationwide occupational health services provide prevention, remediation, and rehabilitation; in the Baltics, equivalent needs are covered by employer-provided health insurance. Group-wide wellness initiatives and the “Swedbank at Work” concept support organisational, social, and digital work environments across home markets.
- Competitive and fair pay: Transparent Salary Policy and structured salary criteria assess competence, performance, and role complexity. Annual reviews ensure alignment with standard reference salaries and legal/collective agreements. Sweden follows collective-agreement minimum wages; Baltic reference wages use external data. Equal pay for equal work is a core principle. The Group’s job architecture, which underpins pay, was reviewed in 2024.
- Learning and development: A strong learning culture with formal and on-the-job learning, LinkedIn Learning, mentoring, workshops, and team discussions. 2024 initiatives include Inspire Forward (strategic leadership), Project Management Programme, Java upskilling, and ESG capability building for corporate client executives. Effectiveness is tracked via training hours, turnover, sick leave, salary review metrics, pay gaps, equal treatment, and engagement.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI): A Group-wide DEI Policy extends to the Board and governance. A rotating Chief Diversity Officer role in executive management strengthens DEI integration. Key actions include management skills programmes on DEI, reverse mentoring, expert sessions, and salary equity mapping to prevent unfair pay differences.
- Equal pay and workforce stability: Remuneration strategy aims to attract and retain diverse talent in an inclusive environment. Ongoing salary equity mapping addresses pay gaps, supporting employee trust, retention, and business continuity.
- Employee networks and inclusion practices: Swedbank Women in Tech (open to all), LGBTQ+ network GLaS, and Young Professionals foster networking, innovation, and employer attractiveness. Flexible working hours and prayer rooms support religious practices. Participation in external DEI indices provides independent assessment. Outcomes are monitored via turnover, sick leave, pay gap, equity, and engagement indicators.
- Employee data protection and privacy: Annual GDPR reviews; a Group-wide personal data deletion project launched in 2024 continues into 2025, harmonising retention periods and documentation. Updated principles for processing employee/consultant data undergo consultation in 2025. Strong policies, internal/external audits, mandatory training, data minimisation, retention/deletion registries, strict access controls, robust security, incident response, and channels for reporting concerns ensure compliance (GDPR and local laws).
- Follow-up and governance: The People Pulse survey ran three times in 2024, covering engagement, NPS, sustainable employees, strategic direction, compensation, performance development, leadership, culture, and equal treatment; managers analyse and act on results. Sick leave (short/long-term) is monitored at market and Group levels, including by Group Risk. Annual Performance Development reviews align goals and assess performance/conduct. Quarterly, the central health and safety committee oversees work environment risks, action plans, Sustainable Employee Index, equality issues, sickness rates, and incidents.
- Metrics and targets (S1-5): Employee engagement is a strategic target measured via the Engagement Index and Sustainable Employee Index (targets >=80 for both). Equity and diversity goals include equal gender distribution (40/60 women/men) at top management and among successors, maintaining equal pay for equal work, and reducing the gender pay gap. Targets are proposed by Group HR process owners, reviewed by HR leadership, and adopted by the CEO after GEC review; employee Board representatives support oversight. Results in 2024 show high, stable engagement, with strong scores for team collaboration, learning through work, and meaningfulness; sustainable employee measures remain high, reflecting value of flexible, collaborative workplaces.

nodes.title: Follow-up on actions
nodes.heading: 6.1.7.4 Follow-up on actions
nodes.start_phrase: A number of metrics and indicators have been implemented to follow up and ensure that the actions and initiatives implemented by Swedbank lead to good results.
nodes.summary:
- GDPR and data governance: In 2024 Swedbank ran a Group-wide GDPR review covering employees, consultants, candidates, and customers, with annual cadence. It launched a multi‑year personal data deletion project (2024–2025) to harmonize and register deletion periods across systems, and updated principles for processing employees’ and consultants’ personal data, to be consulted in 2025 and revised continuously. Additional GDPR information is referenced in S4-1.

- Monitoring and follow-up: Swedbank uses defined metrics and indicators to track outcomes of actions and initiatives. The People Pulse survey ran three times in 2024, covering nine themes (engagement, NPS/commitment, sustainable employees, strategic direction, compensation, performance development, leadership, work culture, equal treatment). Managers analyze and act on team results.

- Health, safety, and absence: Sick leave (short and long term) is monitored in each home market and at Group level, including oversight by Group Risk. Management teams’ work environment risks and action plans are reviewed quarterly by the central health and safety committee. The Sustainable Employee Index is a key KPI for business area managers and is followed quarterly alongside equal opportunity issues, sickness rates, and incidents.

- Performance management: “Performance Development” supports goal setting aligned to strategy, with annual manager-employee reviews that assess performance, conduct, and development.

- Equal opportunities and data: Equal opportunity and anti-discrimination efforts are measured via the annual survey. Swedbank tracks gender and age (via personal identity numbers) but does not collect other protected characteristics (e.g., LGBTQ+, ethnicity, disability). Additional sick leave detail is referenced in note G13.9.

- Workforce metrics and targets (S1-5): Strategic workforce focus on employee engagement and a sustainable workforce. Targets from 1 Jan 2024:
  - Sustainable Employee Index ≥80
  - Engagement Index ≥80
  - Equity and diversity: achieve 40/60 gender balance (women/men) at top management and among successors to top management; maintain equal pay for equal work and reduce the gender pay gap.
  Scope covers Group employees across Swedbank’s home markets and selected international locations; some data involves assumptions and is not externally validated.

- Target-setting and governance: Process owners in Group HR propose targets based on prioritized areas and survey insights; Group HR management reviews, Head of Group HR elevates to GEC/CEO, and the CEO adopts. Targets are intended to be consistent over time; no methodological changes in the year. Employee representatives on the Board support follow-up. Results are reviewed quarterly by GEC and reported annually; targets apply to the 2024 financial year.

- 2024 results highlights: Engagement remained high and stable; strongest scores in team collaboration, learning and development, and meaningful work. Sustainable employee measures stayed high, reflecting the value of combining workplace flexibility with in-person collaboration.

nodes.title: Targets, S1-5
nodes.heading: 6.1.8 Targets, S1-5
nodes.start_phrase: One of Swedbank’s strategic targets for its own workforce is employee engage - ment.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and redress context: References earlier-described actions Swedbank has taken to provide or enable redress for any actual material consequences.

- GDPR and data protection:
  - 2024 Group-wide GDPR review to keep processes and retained personal data up to date, covering employees, consultants, candidates, and customers; performed annually.
  - Multi‑year personal data deletion project launched in 2024 and continuing in 2025 to harmonise and register deletion periods across systems and processes with ongoing management.
  - Updated principles for processing employees’ and consultants’ personal data; to be consulted in 2025 and continuously revised.
  - Additional GDPR information referenced (S4‑1).

- Follow‑up mechanisms and people metrics:
  - People Pulse survey conducted three times in 2024, covering nine areas: engagement, commitment (NPS), sustainable employees, strategic direction, compensation, performance development, leadership, work culture, and equal treatment. Managers analyse and act on results.
  - Sick leave and intentional absence tracked in home markets and Group-wide; Group Risk monitors both short‑ and long‑term sick leave.
  - Performance Development tool supports annual target‑setting, development planning, and performance assessment.
  - Quarterly oversight by the central health and safety committee; business units report top work‑environment risks and action plans. Sustainable Employee Index tracked as a key KPI; equal opportunities, sickness rates, and incidents followed up with action plans.

- Equal opportunities and anti‑discrimination:
  - Measured via the annual employee survey; Sustainable Employee Index monitored at GEC level.
  - Follow‑up on gender and age; other discrimination grounds (e.g., LGBTQ+, ethnicity, disability) not collected.
  - Additional information on sick leave referenced (note G13.9).

- Metrics and targets (S1‑5):
  - Strategic focus on employee engagement with 2024 as baseline year.
  - Targets and measures:
    - Sustainable Employee Index target ≥80.
    - Engagement Index target ≥80.
    - Equity and diversity: achieve 40/60 women/men at top management and at higher levels (successors to top management); maintain equal pay for equal work and reduce gender pay gap.
  - Scope/assumptions: targets apply Group‑wide; certain measures exclude PayEx and Franchise; pay gap target applies to home markets; assumptions used where data missing; no methodology changes in the year; measures not externally validated.
  - Target‑setting governance: Group HR process owners propose based on survey insights; reviewed by Group HR management; Head of Group HR elevates to GEC/CEO; CEO adopts. Employee representatives on the Board contribute to follow‑up. Results reviewed quarterly at GEC and annually reported.

- 2024 results highlights:
  - Sustainable Employee Index: 85 (target ≥80) vs 86 in 2023.
  - Engagement Index: 84 (target ≥80) vs 85 in 2023.
  - Gender balance:
    - Top management: 47/53 women/men (improved from 40/60 in 2023 and 33/67 in 2022).
    - Successor pool to top management: 57/43 (similar to 56/44 in 2023/2022).
  - Gender pay gap: 1.1 percentage points (improved from 1.5 in 2023 and 1.8 in 2022).
  - Survey strengths: team collaboration, learning and development through work, and sense of meaningful work; sustained high/stable work‑situation scores reflecting the value of flexible and collaborative environments.

- Workforce characteristics and methodology (S1‑6):
  - Data sources: HRMS, POL, HCM; legal entities supply missing data; completeness and consistency checks performed; headcount is end‑of‑period; Group coverage includes home markets and selected other countries; measures not externally validated.
  - Headcount 2024: 19,217 (female 11,729; male 7,488), down from 19,341 in 2023.
  - By country 2024: Sweden 11,098; Estonia 2,810; Latvia 2,200; Lithuania 2,833; other countries 276.
  - Employment types 2024: permanent 18,050; fixed‑term 1,167; temporary 649; full‑time 17,567; part‑time 1,001. Country‑level breakdowns provided.
  - Staff turnover: 1,442 in 2024 (vs 1,894 in 2023); employees who left due to voluntary/termination/retirement/death reported as 8 in 2024 (10 in 2023).

nodes.title: Characteristics of own workforce, S1-6
nodes.heading: 6.1.9 Characteristics of own workforce, S1-6

nodes.title: Collective bargaining coverage and social dialogue, S1-8

nodes.title: Training and skills development, S1-13
nodes.heading: 6.1.13 Training and skills development, S1-13
nodes.start_phrase: Employees are offered opportunities to develop and find inspiration in line with changes in the world around us and are encouraged, according to a self-leader - ship principle, to take responsibility for and drive their personal development and careers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus areas: Employee training and skills development (ESRS S1-13) and health and safety metrics (ESRS S1-14) in Swedbank’s 2024 Annual and Sustainability Report.
- Training and development approach:
  - Emphasis on self-leadership, with employees responsible for their own development and careers.
  - Performance Development (PD) is the core tool for goal setting and development aligned with Swedbank’s strategy.
  - High competence standards; mandatory Group-wide courses in ethics, safety, anti-corruption/bribery, and prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing.
  - Related references: Development and learning (S1-4), Training (S4-4), Code of Conduct (G1-1), and Financial crime.
- Training and performance review metrics and methodology:
  - Attendance ratio covers employees with main assignments, broken down by legal gender.
  - Average training hours per employee calculated by total training hours per gender divided by total employees per gender (employment figures per ESRS S1-6).
  - Data source: HR system SABA; if entity-level data missing, data requested from the entity.
  - Data quality controls for completeness (all employment types/countries) and consistency (vs prior reports).
  - Assumption: if legal-entity data missing, performance is assumed equal to the overall average/total observed.
- 2024 training and development outcomes (vs 2023):
  - Percentage attending regular performance and career development reviews: Female 91% (90%); Male 93% (91%); Other 92% (91%).
  - Reviews per employee: Female 0.91 (0.90); Male 0.93 (0.91); Other 0.92 (0.91).
  - Total number of reviews: 10,698 (2024), 6,959 (2023); combined 17,657.
  - Average training hours per employee: Female 30 (33); Male 21 (24); Total 27 (30).
  - Targets/notes: One annual review per employee required; 100% participation target for mandatory trainings; gender measured as legal male/female.
- Health and safety scope and governance:
  - Internally reported occupational accidents and work-related ill health; incidents during commute excluded.
  - Reporting follows local legislation and is logged in the Group incident system by employees/managers.
  - All employees are covered by the Group’s health and safety system; local legislation applied in each country.
  - External oversight (e.g., Swedish Work Environment Authority) and annual internal audits of work environment management.
  - Assumption: In Finland, Norway, USA, China, and PayEx (outside incident system), occupational accident frequency assumed equal to other parts of the Group.
- 2024 health and safety indicators (vs 2023):
  - Coverage by health and safety system: Own workforce 100% (100%); Non-employees 100% (100%).
  - Deaths due to occupational injuries/work-related ill health: Own workforce 0 (0); Non-employees 0 (0).
  - Registered occupational accidents: Own workforce 25 (23); Non-employees 0 (0).
  - Accident frequency (own workforce): 0.90 (0.82); Non-employees 0 (0).

nodes.title: Health and safety metrics, S1-14
nodes.heading: 6.1.14 Health and safety metrics, S1-14
nodes.start_phrase: The table presents internally reported occupational accidents in the form of occupational accidents and work-related ill health.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Summarizes Swedbank’s 2024 approach and performance on employee training/skills development (ESRS S1-13) and health and safety metrics (ESRS S1-14), including methodologies, data sources, assumptions, and key results.

- Training and skills development (S1-13):
  - Philosophy and tools: Emphasis on self-leadership and shared responsibility for career growth. Performance Development (PD) is the core process to set individual goals and development activities aligned with Swedbank’s strategy.
  - Competence standards: High competence expectations across roles; mandatory Group-wide courses on ethics, security, anti-corruption/bribery, and AML/CFT, with a 100% participation target for mandatory training.
  - Metrics and results:
    - High participation in regular performance and career development reviews (around 91–93% in 2024, broadly in line with 2023).
    - One review per employee expected annually; total reviews conducted in 2024 were 17,657 (with gender breakdowns captured).
    - Average training hours per employee declined slightly year-on-year (total 27 hours in 2024 vs 30 in 2023; women generally higher than men).
    - Gender is measured as legal gender (Male/Female).
  - Methodology and data quality:
    - Review participation ratio covers employees with main assignments, broken down by gender.
    - Average training hours calculated as total completed hours per gender divided by total employees per gender; headcount figures align with ESRS S1-6.
    - Data sourced from HR system SABA; gaps from specific legal entities are requested from local representatives.
    - Quality checks ensure completeness (all employment types/countries) and consistency (vs prior reports).
  - Assumptions: If data is missing for certain legal entities, performance is assumed to align with overall averages.

- Health and safety metrics (S1-14):
  - Scope and exclusions: Reports occupational accidents and work-related ill health occurring at or due to work; commuting incidents are excluded.
  - Reporting system: Incidents are reported per local legislation to authorities and internally through a Group incident system following a common routine.
  - Coverage and governance: 100% of employees are covered by the Group’s health and safety system in all operating countries; subject to external reviews (e.g., Sweden’s Work Environment Authority) and annual internal audits.
  - Assumptions: For Finland, Norway, USA, China, and PayEx (not fully covered by the incident system), accident frequency is assumed equal to other parts of the Group.
  - 2024 performance (vs 2023):
    - Coverage: 100% for both employees and non-employees.
    - Fatalities: 0 for employees and others (unchanged).
    - Registered occupational accidents (employees): 25 (up from 23).
    - Accident frequency (employees): 0.90 (up from 0.82).
    - Non-employee accidents: 0.

- Cross-references: Additional detail is available in Development and learning (S1-4), Training (S4-4), Code of Conduct (G1-1), and Financial crime sections.

nodes.title: Work-life balance, S1-15
nodes.heading: 6.1.15 Work-life balance, S1-15
nodes.start_phrase: All Swedbank employees are entitled to parental leave through collective agree- ments or local legislation.
nodes.summary:
- Work-life balance and parental leave: All employees are entitled to parental leave via collective agreements or local law. Swedbank emphasizes flexibility as part of its equity and diversity work, offering part-time options for returnees, flexible hours, and offsite work when roles allow.
- Parental leave metric and scope: Measures the proportion of employees entitled to parental leave who actually took it, reported by legal gender (Male/Female) as of 31 December 2024. Additional country and gender detail is referenced in note G13.9.
- Parental leave assumptions: Employees outside home markets (5% of workforce) who are on leave on 31 December 2024 are assumed to be on parental leave; within this group, 5% of women and 2% of men are assumed to have taken leave.
- Parental leave results: 2024 vs 2023 share taking leave—Female: 16% (16%); Male: 15% (13%); Total: 16% (15%).
- Remuneration indicators purpose: Disclose gender pay gaps, CEO-to-median employee pay ratio, and equal pay for equal work gaps to assess remuneration inequality within the Group.
- Methodologies:
  - Gender pay gap: Difference between men’s and women’s gross hourly wages relative to men’s wage; scope is all Group employees; positive means men earn more.
  - CEO pay ratio: CEO’s annual total remuneration relative to the median of all employees (excluding the highest paid); scope is all Group employees.
  - Equal Pay Gap: Comparison of average salary index for men and women by job level and market in home markets; positive means men earn more.
- Data sources and quality: Data drawn from HR and finance systems; missing legal-entity data gathered from entity representatives; checks for completeness and consistency against prior reports.
- Remuneration assumptions: Where entity data is missing, assume results align with other entities. Since home markets are ~95% of the workforce, the Group median total remuneration is assumed equal to the home markets’ median.
- Reported outcomes:
  - Gender pay gap (all employees), 2024 (2023): Sweden 19% (19%); Estonia 29% (29%); Latvia 29% (30%); Lithuania 32% (33%); Swedbank Group 28% (29%).
  - CEO total remuneration ratio vs employees’ median, 2024 (2023): Group 31 (32).
  - Equal Pay Gap (equal work), 2024 (2023): Sweden 1.6% (1.9%); Estonia 0.1% (1.1%); Latvia 0.2% (0.9%); Lithuania –0.2% (0%); Total (home markets) 1.1% (1.5%).
- Clarifications: Gender is measured as legal gender (Male/Female).

nodes.title: Remuneration indicators, S1-16
nodes.heading: 6.1.16 Remuneration indicators, S1-16
nodes.start_phrase: The tables presenting pay gaps provide information on the percentage difference between women’s and men’s salaries and the ratio between the remuneration of the highest paid employee and the median remuneration of all employees.
nodes.summary:
- Work-life balance and parental leave (S1-15)
  - All employees are entitled to parental leave via collective agreements or local laws.
  - Flexible work is integral to equity and diversity efforts: options include part-time after leave, flexible hours, and remote work where roles allow.
  - Measurement: proportion of employees entitled to parental leave who took it, by legal gender (Male/Female), reported as of 31 Dec 2024.
  - Assumptions: for employees outside home markets (5% of workforce), anyone on leave on 31 Dec 2024 is assumed to be on parental leave; estimated uptake in this group is 5% for women and 2% for men.
  - Results: 2024 parental leave uptake—Female 16% (2023: 16%), Male 15% (2023: 13%), Total 16% (2023: 15%). Further country/gender detail in note G13.9.

- Remuneration indicators (S1-16)
  - Purpose: show gender pay gaps, CEO-to-median pay ratio, and equal pay for equal work, to assess remuneration inequality.
  - Methodologies:
    - Gender pay gap = (men’s gross hourly wage − women’s) relative to men’s; scope: all Group employees; positive % means men earn more.
    - CEO total remuneration ratio = CEO’s annual total remuneration / median annual total remuneration of all other employees; scope: all employees.
    - Equal Pay Gap = comparison of average salary index for men vs women per job level and market; scope: home markets; positive % means men earn more.
  - Data sources and quality: HR and finance systems; missing data obtained from legal entities; checks for completeness and consistency with prior reports.
  - Assumptions: where entity data is missing, align with observed totals; Group median remuneration assumed equal to home markets’ median (home markets ≈95% of workforce).
  - Reported outcomes:
    - Gender pay gap 2024 (2023): Sweden 19% (19), Estonia 29% (29), Latvia 29% (30), Lithuania 32% (33), Group 28% (29).
    - CEO-to-median pay ratio: 31 (2023: 32).
    - Equal Pay Gap 2024 (2023): Sweden 1.6% (1.9), Estonia 0.1% (1.1), Latvia 0.2% (0.9), Lithuania −0.2% (0), Total 1.1% (1.5).

- Consumers and end-users (S4): information-related impacts
  - Materiality: handling sensitive customer information assessed as a material topic across the value chain.
  - Strategy: robust personal data protection embedded in strategy; products and services designed to meet GDPR requirements.
  - Risk management: processes to identify, manage, and mitigate data-protection risks for new/changed products, processes, and organizational changes.
  - Potential impacts: inadequate data handling can cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, customer anxiety, and financial risk.
  - Affected stakeholders: existing/prospective customers, employees and consultants (and related parties), and branch visitors.
  - Vulnerable groups: minors, elderly, individuals with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance data.

- Governance and policies for data protection (S4-1)
  - Key documents: Code of Conduct; Policy for Human Rights (aligned with UN Guiding Principles); Policy for Conduct Risk; Customer Complaint Policy.
  - Commitments: compliance with laws on fundamental rights including personal data protection; due diligence to prevent and address negative impacts in own operations and business relationships.
  - Conduct Risk Policy principles cover product design/distribution, data processing, and market conduct risks; Complaint Policy ensures effective handling and prevention of recurring issues.
  - GDPR application: processing requires a legal basis and balancing of interests vs individuals’ rights; applies to all data subjects whose data Swedbank processes; customer communications provide detailed information on processing practices.

nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.2.1 Introduction
nodes.start_phrase: Chapter S4 Consumers and end-users concerns Swedbank’s reporting related to information-related impacts for consumers and/or end-users.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Section S4 covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers and end-users, mapped in the value chain primarily downstream (consumers/end-users), with no identified impacts, risks, or opportunities upstream/own operations for this topic.
- Materiality and strategy: Protection of sensitive customer information is material to Swedbank’s business model and strategy. Trust in how personal data is handled is critical. Products and services are designed to meet GDPR requirements, with structured policies, guidelines, and processes to ensure correct, secure data handling.
- Risk management: Swedbank maintains processes to identify, manage, and mitigate risks in personal data processing, including those arising from new or changed products, processes, and organizational changes. Poor data handling could cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, customer anxiety, and financial risk.
- Stakeholders affected: Existing and prospective customers, employees (including consultants) and their related parties, and visitors to branches. Vulnerable groups identified include minors, the elderly, and individuals with disabilities; customers with health-related insurance are at particular risk due to special-category data.
- Governance and policies (S4-1): Key documents include the Code of Conduct, Policy for Human Rights (aligned with the UN Guiding Principles and due diligence), Policy for Conduct Risk (product governance, data processing, market conduct), and Customer Complaint Policy (handling and prevention of complaints). Personal data rights are embedded within Swedbank’s human rights commitments and EU GDPR guidance.
- GDPR compliance: Swedbank is responsible for processing personal data only with a legal basis and with careful consideration of individuals’ rights, applying to all data subjects, not just customers. The bank provides detailed information to consumers and end-users about how their personal data is processed.
- Overall commitment: Robust personal data protection for all individuals to maintain trust, with impacts, risks, and opportunities for this topic identified as material.

nodes.title: Strategy and business model, SBM-3
nodes.heading: 6.2.2 Strategy and business model, SBM-3
nodes.start_phrase: For Swedbank, the protection of sensitive customer information is imperative and customers must feel confident about how the Group handles personal data.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: Section S4 covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers and end-users across the value chain, identified as material in the Group’s assessment.
- Strategic importance: Protecting sensitive customer information is core to the business model and strategy. The bank designs products and services to meet GDPR requirements and operates structured policies, guidelines and processes to ensure correct, secure data handling.
- Risk management: Swedbank has processes to identify, manage and mitigate risks in personal data processing, including for new or changed products, processes and organizational changes, ensuring alignment with strategy.
- Potential impacts: Inadequate data handling can breach privacy, erode trust, create anxiety among customers, and pose financial risk to the bank.
- Affected stakeholders and vulnerable groups: Existing/prospective customers, employees and consultants (and related parties), and branch visitors may be affected. Higher-risk groups include minors, the elderly, individuals with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance due to the sensitivity of health data.
- Governance and policies (S4-1): 
  - Code of Conduct (commitments on data protection and fundamental rights)
  - Policy for Human Rights (UN Guiding Principles; due diligence to prevent and address adverse impacts in own operations and business relationships)
  - Policy for Conduct Risk (principles for product design, distribution, data processing, and market conduct)
  - Customer Complaint Policy (standards for handling complaints and preventing recurrence)
- GDPR compliance: Personal data processing requires a legal basis and careful balancing of Swedbank’s interests with individuals’ rights; protections apply to all data subjects whose data Swedbank processes, not only customers. The bank provides detailed information to end-users about how their data is processed.
- Overarching commitment: Robust personal data protection is essential to maintain customer confidence and trust.

nodes.title: Policies, S4-1
nodes.heading: 6.2.3 Policies, S4-1
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank has policies and governance documents addressing impacts, risks and opportunities related to consumers and end-users, including handling sensi - tive customer information.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and focus: Section S4 “Consumers and end-users” of Swedbank’s Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 covers information-related impacts on consumers/end-users, primarily in the downstream part of the value chain. It links to the Group’s materiality process (IRO-1) and maps impacts, risks, and opportunities for this topic.

- Materiality and strategic importance: Protection of sensitive customer information is deemed material and fundamental to Swedbank’s strategy. Extensive processing of personal data is inherent in financial services; improper handling can cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, customer anxiety, and financial risk for the bank.

- Governance framework: The topic is managed through key policies and governance documents:
  - Code of Conduct (commitments on data protection and fundamental rights)
  - Policy for Human Rights (UN Guiding Principles; due diligence across operations and relationships)
  - Policy for Conduct Risk (principles for product design, distribution, data processing, and market conduct)
  - Customer Complaint Policy (procedures to receive, resolve, and learn from complaints)
  Personal data rights are embedded within the bank’s human rights commitment and EU GDPR framework.

- GDPR-based management approach: Swedbank applies structured methods, policies, guidelines, and processes aligned with GDPR:
  - “Privacy by design” for products and services; legal basis required for all processing
  - Balancing the bank’s interests with individuals’ rights; applies to anyone whose data is processed, not just customers
  - Transparency through detailed information to end-users about data processing
  - Processes to identify, manage, and mitigate risks, including for new or changed products, processes, and organizational changes

- Stakeholders and vulnerable groups: Affected stakeholders include existing/prospective customers, employees and consultants (and related parties), and branch visitors. Higher-risk groups identified include minors, elderly people, individuals with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance due to special-category data.

- Commitment and outcomes: Swedbank emphasizes robust personal data protection to maintain and strengthen trust, recognizing both potential negative impacts and opportunities in managing consumer information responsibly.

nodes.title: Policies, S4-1 - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.2.3 Policies, S4-1
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank has policies and governance documents addressing impacts, risks and opportunities related to consumers and end-users, including handling sensi - tive customer information.
nodes.summary: Overview of Swedbank’s consumer/end-user policy framework and governance for impacts, risks, and opportunities, particularly around sensitive customer information and personal data. Key policies: Code of Conduct (values and data protection commitments), Policy for Human Rights (aligned with UN Guiding Principles; due diligence across own operations and business relationships; focus on precaution, prevention, and addressing human rights violations), Policy for Conduct Risk (principles for designing, distributing, and evaluating financial products/services, data processing, and managing market conduct risks), and Customer Complaint Policy (procedures for receiving/handling complaints and reducing future complaints). Emphasizes compliance with laws on fundamental rights and GDPR, with personal data rights integrated into human rights commitments.

nodes.title: Protection of personal data in accordance with GDPR
nodes.heading: 6.2.3.1 Protection of personal data in accordance with GDPR
nodes.start_phrase: GDPR is based on established and internationally recognised conventions and principles for the protection of human rights.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and materiality: The S4 Consumers and end-users section covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers/end-users, identified as a material topic in the downstream value chain. Protecting sensitive customer data is central to the Group’s strategy. Mishandling data can cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, anxiety, and financial risk. Affected stakeholders include customers, prospects, employees/consultants, and visitors. Vulnerable groups include minors, the elderly, people with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance.

- Governance and policies: Swedbank manages these impacts via the Code of Conduct, Human Rights Policy (aligned with UNGPs), Conduct Risk Policy, and Customer Complaint Policy. The right to personal data protection is treated as a human right. GDPR compliance underpins product/service design and data processing. Risk management follows the three lines of defence with independent controls, supported by a Data Protection Officer function. The Group does not currently track cases of failures to respect international principles in the downstream value chain.

- GDPR compliance and stakeholder information: Personal data processing requires a legal basis, with transparent information provided through websites, apps, branches, and customer meetings. Redress/compensation for data breaches follows GDPR and applicable law. The approach is aligned with SDGs, ILO, OECD, and UN guidance to promote ethical practices and human rights.

- Procedures for contact and rights (S4-2): Swedbank explains what data is collected, why, legal grounds, and processing practices, enabling customers to exercise their rights. Data handling adheres to GDPR principles: lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.

- Complaints and incident handling: Customer complaints are logged, reviewed quarterly, and used to drive improvements; cases close when repeat complaints cease. Employees receive regular information security training. In the event of non-compliance or incidents, affected individuals are notified without undue delay via direct channels or public notices if necessary. The CEO has ultimate responsibility; operational incident management lies with designated coordinators; effectiveness is tested via first- and second-line controls and benchmarking against authority guidance and case law. Customer satisfaction is monitored via regular surveys (NKI).

- Remediation (S4-3): Data Breach Guidelines govern incident response and evaluation of remedial sufficiency. Customers can escalate issues through the customer centre, branches, Data Protection Officer, complaints officer, customer ombudsman, and then to external authorities (e.g., ARN, IMY) or consumer advisory bodies.

- Data processors: A three-step due diligence process covers pre-contract assessments (technical/organizational/contractual measures), ongoing monitoring of security posture, and off-boarding to ensure return/erasure of personal data per contract.

- Actions and strategies (S4-4): Ongoing work spans regulatory compliance, risk identification, customer communication, and tool/system support. “Data protection by design and by default” is embedded in product and service development. Expected outcomes are not specified due to uncertainty; no progress metrics are provided as this is the first year of CSRD-aligned reporting.

- Training and awareness: Annual and role-based information security training is mandatory across all countries. Swedbank runs a yearly security month, regular briefings, and continuous phishing simulations. Mandatory and voluntary GDPR/data protection training aims to strengthen employee awareness and, indirectly, customer and societal understanding of personal data protection.

nodes.title: Procedures for contacts, S4-2
nodes.heading: 6.2.4 Procedures for contacts, S4-2
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank publishes information on external websites, at customer meetings and in applications about how and why the Group collects and processes cus - tomers’ personal information and data, and how customers can assert their rights.
nodes.summary:
- Bank-wide commitment to GDPR-compliant processing, customer redress for personal data breaches, and multiple contact channels (chat, mail, branches, web).
- Human Rights Policy aligned with UN SDGs, UN Guiding Principles, ILO and OECD guidelines, emphasizing privacy and data protection; no current tracking of downstream human-rights noncompliance cases.
- Governance and risk management via three lines of defence with independent controls; CEO holds ultimate accountability for personal data handling; designated incident coordinators manage operations.
- Transparent customer information on data collection, purposes, legal bases, processing and retention, with access to DPO, customer service, and authorities; tools such as register extract forms provided.
- Seven GDPR-aligned data protection principles guide all processing: lawfulness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.
- Complaint handling integrates customer feedback into improvements: complaints logged, reviewed quarterly, followed by evaluation, testing, and closure; actions routed through data breach or complaint processes as needed.
- Incident response and notification: affected individuals contacted promptly (phone/email/website); processes assessed through first- and second-line controls and by referencing regulatory guidance and case law; customer satisfaction tracked via surveys (NKI).
- Remediation (S4-3): Data Breach Guidelines define actions for incidents with significant negative impacts and require evaluation of action sufficiency; overall GDPR compliance embedded in policies and directives.

nodes.title: Procedures for remediation, S4-3
nodes.heading: 6.2.5 Procedures for remediation, S4-3

nodes.summary:
- Focus on Swedbank’s data protection and privacy practices, grounded in GDPR and broader human rights commitments (UN SDGs, UN Guiding Principles, ILO, OECD), emphasizing the right to privacy, family life, and protection of personal data.
- Governance and risk management: three lines of defence model with independent controls; CEO holds ultimate responsibility for lawful personal data handling, with operational duties delegated to incident coordinators and decision-makers; ongoing operational controls and regulatory/case-law benchmarking to identify and close gaps.
- Customer information and rights: clear, accessible disclosures across websites, apps, and customer meetings on what data is collected, legal bases, purposes, processing, retention, and contacts (including DPO); tools like register extract forms provided.
- Core data protection principles: adherence to seven GDPR-aligned principles (lawfulness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage minimisation, integrity/confidentiality, accountability).
- Complaints and feedback: centralized complaint registration, quarterly review and analysis, improvement cycle with testing and closure when issues cease; multiple contact channels (chat, phone, letters, branches); NKI surveys monitor customer satisfaction.
- Incident response and remediation: Data Breach Guidelines define actions for incidents with potential negative impacts; prompt notification to affected individuals via phone/email or public channels if direct contact isn’t possible; compensation/redress handled per GDPR and applicable laws.
- Escalation paths: if dissatisfied after internal review, customers can escalate to the DPO, complaints officer, customer ombudsman, and ultimately external bodies such as ARN, IMY, municipal consumer advisers, and the Swedish Consumer Banking and Finance Agency.
- Data processors: structured three-step due diligence—pre-contract assessment of technical/organizational measures, ongoing security monitoring, and off-boarding ensuring return/erasure of personal data per contract.
- “Privacy by design and by default”: embedded in product and service development; ongoing compliance supported by policies, instructions, and system tools.
- Training and awareness: mandatory annual and role-based information security training, annual security month, ongoing security briefings, simulated phishing; mandatory and optional GDPR/data protection training to raise employee and broader societal awareness.
- Limitations and disclosures: Swedbank does not currently track incidents of non-compliance with international human rights principles in the downstream value chain and does not measure customer awareness of its data protection work; no quantitative progress reporting yet as this is the first year aligning with CSRD; outcomes of future actions are not forecast due to uncertainties.

nodes.title: Actions and strategies, S4-4
nodes.heading: 6.2.6 Actions and strategies, S4-4

Expected outcomes are not specified due to uncertainty; no prior progress data as this is the first CSRD-adapted reporting year.

nodes.title: Training

nodes.summary:
- Focus on Swedbank’s data protection and privacy governance, grounded in GDPR and aligned with international human rights frameworks (UN SDGs, UNGPs, ILO, OECD). Redress for personal data breaches follows applicable law.
- Governance and risk management use the three lines of defence, with independent controls, ongoing compliance monitoring, and Board reporting. The CEO holds ultimate responsibility; operational incident handling is delegated to coordinators/decision-makers.
- Transparent customer communication on how and why personal data is processed, rights and legal bases, and easy access to forms, contact details, and guidance via web, branches, chat, mail, and phone.
- Data protection is guided by seven core principles (lawfulness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability).
- Complaints and remediation: structured complaint intake and tracking, quarterly reviews, follow-up and improvement loops, and defined escalation to the data protection officer, complaints officer, customer ombudsman, and external authorities (ARN, IMY, municipal advisers, and sector bodies). Incident notification to affected individuals occurs promptly through available channels.
- Procedures for remediation and incidents are set out in policies, instructions, directives, and Data Breach Guidelines, including assessment of actions’ sufficiency.
- Data processors: a three-step due diligence lifecycle—pre-contract assessment, ongoing monitoring, and off‑boarding with return/erasure—ensures GDPR-compliant processing on Swedbank’s behalf.
- Actions and strategies (S4-4): regulatory compliance, risk identification, customer communication, and “data protection by design and by default” in products/services. First year aligned to CSRD; expected outcomes not quantified due to uncertainties.
- Training: annual and role-based information security and GDPR training across all countries, a yearly security month, regular briefings, and simulated phishing; completion is monitored to ensure coverage.
- Continuous follow-up: global monitoring of EU rules and case law, annual updates to public information, integration of improvements via complaint and incident processes, and compensation for individuals harmed by data protection failures.
- Data Protection Officer: accessible to all data subjects; oversees GDPR compliance, runs impact assessments and balancing tests, and reports quarterly/annually to the Board. Personal data retention aligns with purpose and legal obligations (e.g., AML, accounting); incidents are reported to authorities when required. No serious human rights incidents related to customers were reported during the year.
- Customer ombudsman: dedicated team managing the complaint and improvement processes; adheres to Swedish FSA timelines (initial handling within 14 days, with updates if extended).
- Metrics and targets (S4-5): overarching aim to minimise the number and impact of incidents; no outcome-based targets reported. Group-wide metrics published on:
  - Enquiries and complaints to the Data Protection Officer (from individuals and supervisory authorities), showing a notable increase in 2024.

nodes.title: Follow-up
nodes.heading: 6.2.6.2 Follow-up
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank has a global monitoring system to adapt data protection processes to new regulations, practices and guidelines from the EU, and also an improvement process linked to customer complaints, which entails follow-up, evaluation and improvement measures.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Swedbank’s data protection governance, monitoring, and continuous improvement, including annual follow-up of public information, a global system to track EU regulatory changes, and integration of customer-complaint learnings into corrective actions managed via incident and complaint processes.
- Emphasis on training: ongoing follow-up to ensure employees complete information security and personal data handling training; high completion rates reported by country for 2022–2024, measured via internal systems.
- Clear accountability structure: a Data Protection Officer (DPO) within Group Compliance monitors GDPR compliance, is accessible to customers, employees and other data subjects, and reports quarterly and annually to the Board on alignment with external regulations and the bank’s risk appetite.
- Risk management processes: data protection impact assessments, balancing of interests, and product processes used to assess necessity, fairness, proportionality, and to mitigate risks to individuals’ data rights; monitoring of safeguards when new systems and processes are developed.
- Data handling principles: processing based on balancing individual rights with business needs, retention limited to necessity and extended where required by law (e.g., accounting, AML, capital adequacy, legal purposes), and reporting of personal data incidents to authorities when required by GDPR.
- Redress and accountability: individuals may receive compensation if harmed due to inadequate data protection procedures; no reported serious human rights issues or incidents related to customers during the year.
- Customer ombudsman function: dedicated unit with seven ombudsmen and two complaint analysts overseeing complaint and improvement processes; adherence to the Swedish FSA standard to process or update customers within 14 days.
- Metrics and targets: objective to minimize the number and impact of personal data incidents; no outcome-based targets or time-series effectiveness comparisons reported. Metrics include counts of enquiries and complaints to the DPO (by country) and employee training completion rates, covering 2022–2024, sourced from internal systems and not externally validated.

nodes.title: Data protection officer
nodes.heading: 6.2.6.3 Data protection officer
nodes.start_phrase: In order for Swedbank to determine whether the processing of personal data is appropriate, necessary and fair, and to identify any risks related to personal data handling, privacy and data, the Group has processes in place, such as impact assessments, balancing of interests and the product process.
nodes.summary:
- Ongoing follow-up ensures employees complete training on handling personal data.
- Swedbank operates a global monitoring system to align data protection processes with evolving EU regulations, practices, and guidelines, and runs an improvement process tied to customer complaints.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets, S4-5
nodes.heading: 6.2.7 Metrics and targets, S4-5
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank seeks to minimise the number and consequences of personal data incidents.
nodes.summary:
- Follow-up and monitoring of data protection: Ongoing checks to ensure employees complete personal data handling training; a global system tracks EU regulatory changes and feeds an improvement process tied to customer complaints; incidents and improvements are handled via established personal data incident or complaint processes. Information on personal data handling is reviewed annually, and data protection controls are embedded when new systems/processes are developed. Individuals harmed by deficient procedures may receive compensation per law and internal rules.

- Data Protection Officer (DPO) and risk processes: Swedbank uses impact assessments, balancing of interests, and product processes to ensure processing is appropriate, necessary, fair, and proportionate, with mitigations documented. The DPO within Group Compliance monitors GDPR compliance and reports quarterly and annually to the Board against external requirements and the bank’s risk appetite. Customers, employees, and other data subjects can contact the DPO.

- Data processing principles and incident reporting: Personal data processing balances individual rights with the bank’s need to process data; retention follows purpose necessity and legal requirements (e.g., accounting, AML, capital adequacy, legal) and can exceed contract duration. Personal data incidents are reported to authorities when GDPR requires. No serious human rights issues/incidents related to customers were reported during the year.

- Customer ombudsman and complaints handling: A dedicated unit (seven ombudsmen, two complaint analysts) manages complaints and improvements, adhering to Swedish FSA timelines—aim to resolve within 14 days or inform the customer within 14 days if more time is needed.

- Metrics and targets for data protection: Objective is to minimize the number and impact of personal data incidents; methods are continually improved, but no outcome-based targets or time comparisons are reported. Group Compliance defines minimum standards and oversees compliance. Metrics cover:
  - Enquiries and complaints to the DPO: Significant increase in 2024 in enquiries (128) and complaints (112) from individuals; enquiries from data protection authorities decreased in 2024 (3). Data comes from data subjects and authorities; metrics are group-wide and not externally validated.
  - Information security training: High completion rates, though lower in Sweden and Latvia in 2024 (Sweden 93.9%, Estonia 99.0%, Latvia 97.3%, Lithuania 99.1%). Measured via internal training platforms; not externally validated.

- Business conduct (G1) scope: Covers whistleblower protection, supplier relationship and payment practices, corporate culture, and anti-corruption/bribery, with impacts/risks mapped across the value chain.

- Policies and governance for business conduct: Trust and a sustainable vision guide operations. Key governance documents include the Code of Conduct and policies on Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk. Documents are available internally (public ones on the website). The Board and Group Executive Committee actively oversee culture; values permeate governance.

- Code of Conduct and culture controls: Applies to all employees/subsidiaries; included in onboarding. Annual ethics training and attestation are mandatory and tracked as KPIs. Regular employee surveys (three times yearly) support open culture and managerial follow-up. Mandatory role-based trainings are specified; ethics training addresses anti-corruption, bribery, and benefits, with guidance for real situations. Certain roles require licenses (e.g., SwedSec), with annual ethics components.

- Handling deviations, fraud, and violations: Employees are encouraged to report cultural or rule deviations. A risk-based anti-fraud framework includes preventive/detective controls and standardized processes for investigating regulatory breaches and internal fraud. High-risk processes have enhanced controls. Reports can be made to managers or the Internal Fraud unit; specialized units (Internal Fraud and HR/FM) investigate. Serious breaches can lead to employment actions (warnings, termination) based on investigation outcomes.

nodes.title: G1 Business conduct
nodes.heading: 7.1 G1 Business conduct

- Detection, reporting, and response to misconduct: Employees are encouraged to identify and report incidents that breach rules or conflict with culture and values. Swedbank maintains a risk-based anti-fraud framework with controls to detect, prevent, and report suspected fraud, and a uniform process for investigating regulatory breaches and internal fraud.
- Reporting channels and controls: Technical and manual controls are deployed in high-risk processes. Deviations can be reported to line managers (who document and handle cases) or directly to the Internal Fraud unit. nodes.title: Policies, G1-1
nodes.heading: 7.1.1 Policies, G1-1
nodes.start_phrase: Trust from customers, shareholders, employees, business partners and society at large is crucial for Swedbank’s operations.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Swedbank’s G1 Business conduct reporting covers whistleblower protection, management of supplier relationships including payment practices, corporate culture, and anti-corruption/bribery, with impacts, risks, and opportunities mapped across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream).
- Strategic basis: Emphasis on earning stakeholder trust and advancing a vision of a financially sound and sustainable society from environmental, social, financial, and ethical perspectives.
- Governance framework: A suite of policies guides business ethics and culture, including the Code of Conduct, Policy for Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk. - Training: Mandatory annual ethics training for all employees and the Group Executive Committee (including the CEO) covers anti-corruption, bribery, and benefits assessment, with practical guidance. Role-specific training is defined in internal regulations; licensed roles (e.g., Swedsec) complete annual ethics updates.
- Culture monitoring: Employee surveys conducted three times a year on strategy, leadership, and culture; managers are required to follow up on results to promote open dialogue.
- Deviations and violations: Employees are encouraged to report incidents that deviate from culture/values. A risk-based anti-fraud framework mandates controls to detect, prevent, and report suspected fraud and a uniform process for investigating regulatory breaches and internal fraud.
- Detection and reporting: Technical and manual controls target high-risk processes. Reports can be made to managers or the Internal Fraud unit, supported by systems for identifying and tracking risks and irregularities.
- Investigations and consequences: The Internal Fraud and Group HR & Facility Management units investigate cases. Serious violations may lead to employment actions (warnings or termination), decided by management based on investigative recommendations.
- Cross-references: The text points to related sections for materiality assessment (IRO-1) and governance documents (MDR-P), as well as strategy/values (SBM-1) and governance roles (GOV-1).

nodes.title: Policies, G1-1 - Introduction
nodes.heading: 7.1.1 Policies, G1-1
nodes.start_phrase: Trust from customers, shareholders, employees, business partners and society at large is crucial for Swedbank’s operations.
nodes.summary: Overview of Swedbank’s business conduct governance and culture framework. Emphasizes trust from customers, shareholders, employees, partners, and society, and aligns with the Group’s vision of a financially sound and environmentally, socially, financially, and ethically sustainable society. Lists key governance documents addressing impacts, risks, and opportunities in business ethics and conduct: Code of Conduct; Policy for Conduct Risk; Policy on Conflicts of Interest; Policy on Financial Crime Risk; Policy on Personal Account Dealing; Policy on Enterprise Risk Management; and Policy for Operational Risk. Notes availability on the intranet and public website, with details in “Swedbank governance documents, MDR-P.” Highlights ongoing oversight of corporate-culture issues by the Board of Directors and the Group Executive Committee (including the CEO), and references related sections on strategy (SBM-1) and governance roles (GOV-1).

nodes.title: Code of Conduct
nodes.heading: 7.1.1.1 Code of Conduct
nodes.start_phrase: The basic document to ensure that Swedbank has a good corporate culture is the Code of Conduct, which constitutes the Group’s ethics policy.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Governance information – G1 Business conduct in Swedbank’s Annual and Sustainability Report 2024, covering whistleblower protection, supplier relationship management (including payment practices), corporate culture, and anti-corruption/bribery across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), with identified impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Strategic context: Emphasis on trust from stakeholders and the Group’s vision of a financially sound and sustainable society; business conduct embedded in strategic direction, values, and culture.
- Governance framework: Key policies include the Code of Conduct, Policy for Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk; documents accessible internally and selected ones publicly; oversight by the Board and Group Executive Committee.
- Code of Conduct: Serves as the ethics policy for all employees and subsidiaries; defines expected behavior in transactions and relationships; integrated into onboarding.
- Training and KPIs: Mandatory annual ethics training for all staff and executives, with focus on anti-corruption/bribery and benefits; role-specific training requirements; Swedsec-licensed staff complete annual knowledge updates with ethics content; annual confirmation of Code understanding tracked as a KPI.
- Culture measurement: Employee surveys held three times a year on strategy, leadership, and culture; managers required to act on results to foster open dialogue and continuous improvement.
- Whistleblowing and incident vigilance: Employees encouraged to report deviations from rules and values; protection for whistleblowers highlighted as a material topic.
- Anti-fraud and compliance controls: Risk-based anti-fraud framework with technical and manual controls in high-risk processes; standardized processes for detecting, preventing, reporting, and investigating suspected fraud and regulatory breaches.
- Reporting and investigation process: Incidents can be reported to managers or the Internal Fraud unit; system support exists for risk/irregularity handling; investigations conducted by Internal Fraud and Group HR & Facility Management.
- Consequences and accountability: Serious violations may lead to employment actions (warnings or termination), decided by management based on investigative recommendations.

nodes.title: Mechanisms for handling deviations and violations
nodes.heading: 7.1.1.2 Mechanisms for handling deviations and violations
nodes.start_phrase: All Swedbank employees are encouraged to remain vigilant for any incidents in their daily work that may constitute a breach of the rules Swedbank is required to follow.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and focus: G1 Business conduct covers Swedbank’s approach to corporate culture, protection for whistleblowers, management of supplier relationships (including payment practices), and anti-corruption/bribery, mapped across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream) with identified impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Governance and policies: Business conduct is guided by a suite of Group policies and governance documents—Code of Conduct, Policy for Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk—aligned to Swedbank’s purpose, vision, and values. Documents are maintained on the intranet and, where public, on the external website; oversight involves the Board and Group Executive Committee.
- Code of Conduct and culture: The Code applies to all employees and subsidiaries, integrated into onboarding, with annual ethics confirmation and mandatory training. Culture and leadership are monitored via employee surveys three times a year; managers are required to follow up. Role-based and license (e.g., Swedsec) training include ethics components.
- Managing deviations, fraud, and market abuse: The bank maintains a risk-based anti-fraud framework with technical and manual controls in high-risk processes, standardized investigation procedures, and potential employment actions for violations. Market surveillance is conducted under the EU Market Abuse Regulation to detect suspicious orders/transactions.
- Bribery and corruption risk assessment: Conducted at least biennially or as needed, assessing geography and business changes. Higher risks are identified among customer-facing staff and procurement roles handling large contracts, recruitment, and consulting. Group Compliance monitors risk trends and control effectiveness.
- Supplier governance: High ethical standards are enforced through the Purchasing Instruction and Supplier Code of Conduct. Suppliers must sign the Code (or show equivalent commitments); deviations escalate to the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee. Ongoing monitoring showed ~200 additional suppliers met the Code requirement in 2024. Supplier selection must be objective, transparent, fact-based, with sustainability criteria; procurement is extensively digitized to identify and manage risks.
- Whistleblower framework: Internal and external stakeholders can report irregularities, corruption, bribery, and policy breaches via channels compliant with the EU Whistleblower Directive and Swedish law, including an anonymous, encrypted web portal managed by an external provider. Authorized, independent handlers manage cases, with conflict-of-interest safeguards. The Board receives quarterly updates on case volumes and themes; separate internal fraud processes also exist.
- Key actions and metrics (2024): 
  - 95% of employees completed mandatory ethics training (94% in 2023); training refreshed with real-life dilemmas, with bank confidentiality training planned. Completion rates reported to the Board from Q4 2024.
  - 158 whistleblower reports received (126 in 2023); continued awareness-raising planned for 2025.
  - Annual updates to governance documents; strengthened mandates for independent whistleblower channel managers.
  - No significant standalone sustainability capex/opex identified; activities integrated into operating costs.

Compliance is tracked continuously; about 200 additional suppliers met the Code requirement in 2024. Procurement is guided by objective, transparent, fact-based evaluations with multiple alternatives and embedded sustainability criteria, supported by a digitized process for risk identification and management.

- Market surveillance: In line with the EU Market Abuse Regulation, Swedbank identifies and reports suspicious transactions and orders to deter market abuse and strengthen market integrity and trust.

- Whistleblower framework: Aligned with the EU Whistleblower Protection Directive and the Swedish Whistleblower Act, the process protects against retaliation and enables internal and external parties to report irregularities, including corruption, bribery, and Code of Conduct breaches. Reports can be made openly or anonymously via an encrypted, third-party-hosted channel. Independent, authorized units manage investigations, handle conflicts of interest, and report case volumes and themes to the Board quarterly. Relevant staff receive ongoing training. Completion is followed up annually and reported to the Board from Q4 2024. Business ethics governance documents are updated annually.

nodes.title: Key actions
nodes.heading: 7.1.3.1 Key actions
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank took a number of key actions in its own operations during the year to address the risk of Swedbank being exposed to corruption and bribery.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Anti-corruption, bribery prevention, and business ethics, with governance, training, monitoring, incident handling, and payment practices.

- Key actions taken:
  - Ethics training for all employees; targeted anti-bribery/corruption training for contract owners with high-risk contracts.
  - Annual updates of governance documents on bribery and corruption; introduction of Group-wide registers for events and sponsorships.
  - Ongoing monitoring of training completion rates; quarterly reporting on developments to the Board.
  - Group-wide corruption/bribery risk assessment to be completed in Q1 2025 with a final report to the Group Executive Committee.
  - Planned roll-out of Group-wide gifts and events training for managers and customer-facing staff.
  - No separate significant operating or capital expenditures identified for sustainability action plans; costs are embedded in normal operations.

- Metrics and oversight:
  - Aim: high business ethics and good conduct in financial markets.
  - Internal processes exist to monitor corporate culture, whistleblower protection, and anti-corruption, but Swedbank does not publish measurable outcome-oriented goals or time-series comparisons.
  - Group Compliance independently monitors compliance risks, evaluates internal rules and actions, sets minimum standards, and advises operations to align with the Board’s low risk appetite and zero-tolerance stance on bribery and corruption.
  - Regular risk assessments performed; the Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and Board on effectiveness against risk appetite and regulations.
  - Supplier relationship management is monitored internally; if supplier risk exceeds appetite, it is escalated to the CEO and Board. No public outcome-oriented goals are disclosed.

- Incidents and investigations (G1-4):
  - Internal investigations are conducted for suspected rule breaches, including bribery/corruption; may lead to employment actions and police reports.
  - Operational risks identified are reported per risk procedures; HR & Facility Management and Group Compliance conduct quarterly follow-ups on suspected cases.
  - No 2024 data on employee convictions/fines for bribery/corruption due to lack of systematic follow-up; Internal Fraud unit will develop tracking for outcomes of police reports.
  - Metrics are not externally validated.

- Market surveillance under MAR:
  - STORs (notifications of suspected market abuse) monitored Group-wide and reported by country; not externally validated.
  - STOR counts: 2024: 121; 2023: 202; 2022: 57. Country breakdown in 2024: Sweden 44, Estonia 17, Latvia 55, Lithuania 5.
  - Prior increase linked to certain Baltic government agencies’ focus on specific trading patterns.

- Payment practices (G1-6):
  - Standard supplier payment terms: 30 days; average actual payment term ~31 days.
  - Average actual payment time: 27 days overall; 21 days for SMEs (suppliers with <250 employees, classified using Moody’s data).
  - Share paid within 30-day standard: 57% overall; 71% for SMEs. Share paid within current contractual terms: 71% overall; 58% for SMEs.
  - Operational approach: Baltics pay immediately after approval; Sweden pays on due date.
  - Metrics derived from internal invoice system covering ~90% of supplier invoices (Sweden and Baltic subsidiaries); not externally validated.
  - Legal proceedings relating to late payments are tracked; figure provided for SMEs, with separate overall status referenced.

nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank seeks to achieve a high level of business ethics and good conduct in the financial market.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on anti-corruption and bribery controls: group-wide ethics training for all employees, targeted training for contract owners on high-risk contracts, annual updates to governance documents, and new registers for events and sponsorships. A Group-wide bribery/corruption risk assessment will be completed in Q1 2025, with expanded training for managers and customer-facing staff to follow. Progress is reported quarterly to the Board. Sustainability-related action plan costs are embedded in operating expenses, not separately identified.

- Governance, metrics, and oversight: Swedbank aims for high business ethics with zero tolerance for bribery and corruption and a Board-set low risk appetite. Group Compliance monitors compliance risks, evaluates rule effectiveness, proposes minimum standards, and advises operations; the Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and Board. Internal processes track culture, whistleblower protection, anti-corruption, and supplier relationship management, but no public, outcome-oriented targets or time-series comparisons are published. Exceedances of supplier risk appetite are escalated to the CEO and Board.

- Incident handling and data gaps: Internal investigations address suspected rule breaches; employment actions may follow, and suspected crimes are reported to police. Operational risks identified are escalated per risk procedures. Quarterly follow-up of suspected corruption cases is conducted by HR & Facility Management and Group Compliance. Swedbank lacks 2024 data on employee convictions/fines for bribery/corruption due to no systematic follow-up; the Internal Fraud unit will build follow-up processes. Metrics are not externally validated.

- Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) surveillance: Group-wide systems support STOR (Suspicious Transaction and Order Report) monitoring and reporting by geography; data use is internal and not externally validated. 2024 saw 121 STORs (Sweden 44, Estonia 17, Latvia 55, Lithuania 5), compared to 2023: 202 and 2022: 57; the 2023 increase is linked to certain Baltic agencies’ focus on specific trading patterns.

- Supplier payment practices (G1-6): Standard supplier payment terms are 30 days; average actual payment terms are 31 days. Overall, Swedbank pays invoices in 27 days on average (21 days for SMEs). Payments within the 30-day standard: 57% overall, 71% for SMEs. Payments within agreed actual terms: 71% overall, 58% for SMEs. In the Baltics, invoices are paid immediately after approval; in Sweden, on the due date. SME status is determined via Moody’s (<250 employees). Metrics are based on internal invoice data covering ~90% of supplier invoices (including Baltic subsidiaries) and are not externally validated. Ten legal proceedings for late payments are outstanding for SMEs; none for all enterprises.

Group Compliance independently monitors compliance risks, evaluates the effectiveness of internal rules, proposes minimum standards, and advises operations. The Board sets zero tolerance and a low risk appetite for bribery and corruption; the Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and Board. - Market abuse surveillance (MAR): The bank tracks and reports STORs (suspected insider trading, market manipulation, unlawful disclosure) Group-wide using internal systems; metrics are reported by geography and are not externally validated. STORs: 121 (2024) vs 202 (2023) vs 57 (2022); 2024 breakdown—Sweden 44, Estonia 17, Latvia 55, Lithuania 5. Variations reflect, among other things, local agency focus in the Baltics in 2023.
- Payment practices (G1-6): Standard supplier payment terms are 30 days (negotiable). Average actual payment terms are 31 days; 57% of payments are within the 30-day standard, and 71% are on time per contract terms. Invoices in the Baltics are paid immediately after approval; in Sweden, on the due date. Average actual payment time is 27 days overall and 21 days for SMEs (<250 employees, identified using Moody’s data). Metrics derive from the internal invoice system covering ~90% of supplier invoices (Sweden and Baltic subsidiaries) and are not externally validated. nodes.title: Financial crime
nodes.heading: 7.2 Financial crime
nodes.start_phrase: The Financial Crime chapter concerns Swedbank’s reporting related to the Group’s work to combat financial crime.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and definition: The chapter outlines Swedbank’s approach to combating financial crime, defined as money laundering, terrorist financing, bribery and corruption, facilitation of tax evasion, and fraud. Cybersecurity is covered elsewhere.
- Value chain and materiality: It maps where financial crime impacts and risks occur across the value chain and explains that, based on a double materiality assessment (including stakeholder input and lessons from past AML shortcomings), financial crime is a material, entity-specific topic for Swedbank.
- Risk and impact: Deficiencies in prevention and controls can harm customers and society, erode trust, and lead to financial penalties and sanctions.
- Governance framework: Swedbank uses a comprehensive set of Board-approved policies, CEO Instructions, and Group directives/guidelines to set risk appetite, responsibilities, controls, and reporting across financial crime risk categories. Public and internal documents are referenced.
- Core policies:
  - Policy on Financial Crime Risk sets overarching principles for AML/CFT, sanctions, anti-corruption/bribery, and facilitation of tax evasion.
  - Three CEO Instructions cover AML/CFT, financial sanctions, and anti-corruption, supported by directives that define internal controls and compliance measures.
- Fraud management:
  - Governed by the Policy on Enterprise Risk Management and the Policy for Operational Risk.
  - Instructions on Anti-Fraud Governance require a robust, risk-based framework to detect, prevent, and report fraud against the bank and its customers.
  - External Fraud Directive standardizes governance, processes, and preventive measures against external fraud.
  - Internal Fraud Directive standardizes investigations of regulatory breaches and suspected employee fraud.
- Cross-references: Links to detailed sections on corruption incidents and prevention (G1-3, G1-4), cybersecurity (G3, 3.4), materiality processes (IRO-1), governance documents (MDR-P), and risk note (3.7).
