nodes.title: Actions and preventive measures
nodes.heading: 7.2.3 Actions and preventive measures
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank works actively to identify and prevent all forms of financial crime where Swedbank is used for illegal transactions using the proceeds from criminal activity or for transfers intended to finance terrorism.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: Swedbank’s actions and preventive measures against financial crime, including money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions breaches, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion, as well as its fraud prevention strategy, governance, and performance trends.

- Core financial crime controls:
  - Risk-based framework grounded in a robust, data-driven risk assessment.
  - Customer due diligence, customer risk assessment, ongoing transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, and regulatory reporting of suspicious activity.
  - Strong compliance culture supported by tailored training programs for all employees based on role- and risk-specific needs.
  - Continued investment in technology to enhance screening and monitoring, with heightened focus on sanctions compliance given geopolitical developments (e.g., Russia’s war against Ukraine).

- Collaboration and information sharing:
  - Active participation in SAMLIT Financial Crime Prevention with Swedish police and major banks.
  - Multiple information-sharing initiatives with law enforcement and industry peers to improve understanding, detection, and prevention.

- Fraud strategy and initiatives:
  - Three-pillar approach: prevent, detect, investigate.
  - Ongoing enhancements to product/channel security, transaction monitoring, and processes.
  - Implementation of the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s cross-industry anti-fraud package (targeted for full implementation by end of 2025).
  - Dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme to reduce customer losses and coordinate efforts across units.
  - Support for affected customers, including stopping fraud in progress, fund recovery, and handling complaints per established procedures.
  - Interbank fraud collaboration to share trends, modus operandi, best practices, and assess the impact of new measures.

- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite:
  - Low risk appetite for financial crime set through internal regulations and monitored by Group Compliance.
  - Officer for controlling and reporting obligations (OCR) within Group Compliance reports quarterly and annually to the Board on AML/CTF effectiveness and alignment with risk appetite.
  - Internal regulations define prohibited activities, high-risk scenarios requiring enhanced measures, and explicit controls for risk owners.
  - Annual, data-driven general risk assessment across customers, products, geographies, and channels; continuous monitoring via a data application.
  - Swedbank does not publish outcome-based external KPIs for these areas but conducts internal follow-up to evaluate effectiveness.

- Recent trends and outcomes (H1 2024):
  - Overall fraud volume and customer losses decreased versus the prior year, mirroring national statistics.
  - Significant decline in vishing/smishing; rise in investment fraud; other fraud types largely stable.
  - Improvements attributed to strengthened controls, product/process security, and higher societal awareness.

nodes.title: Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
nodes.heading: 7.2.3.1 Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank works actively to identify and prevent all forms of financial crime where Swedbank is used for illegal transactions using the proceeds from criminal activity or for transfers intended to finance terrorism.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Swedbank’s comprehensive approach to preventing financial crime and fraud.

- Scope and commitment: Addresses money laundering, terrorist financing, financial sanctions violations or circumventions, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion. Emphasizes regulatory, systemic, and moral obligations, including actions within Swedbank and downstream in the value chain.
- Risk-based framework: Enterprise-wide identification and assessment of financial crime risks driving controls. Core components include customer due diligence and risk assessment, transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting, and sanctions screening of customers and transactions.
- Training and culture: Strong focus on compliance culture supported by mandatory training for all employees and tailored, risk-based programs for higher-risk roles and areas.
- Technology enablement: Ongoing investment in tools and systems to enhance sanctions screening and monitoring, strengthened in response to geopolitical developments, particularly Russia’s war against Ukraine.
- Collaboration: Active participation with Swedish law enforcement and other banks, including SAMLIT Financial Crime Prevention and multiple information-sharing initiatives to improve understanding and operational effectiveness.
- Fraud strategy: Three-tier approach—prevent, detect, investigate—backed by enhanced product and channel security, reinforced transaction monitoring, and streamlined processes. A dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme coordinates efforts, targets reduced customer losses, and ensures implementation of the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s industry-wide measures (aimed for full implementation by end-2025). Support for affected customers includes stopping ongoing fraud, recovering funds, and established complaint handling for unauthorized transactions.
- Industry coordination on fraud: Joint initiatives among major Swedish banks, the Swedish Bankers’ Association, and SAMLIT to share fraud trends, modus operandi, and assess the impact of implemented measures.
- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite: Low risk appetite for financial crime formalized through internal regulations. While Swedbank does not publish measurable outcome metrics, effectiveness is followed up internally. Group Compliance independently monitors regulatory compliance risks; the AML Officer for Controlling and Reporting (OCR) within Group Compliance reports to the Board quarterly and annually. Internal rules define prohibited activities, higher-risk circumstances requiring enhanced measures, and explicit control responsibilities for risk owners.
- Data-driven risk assessment: Annual, comprehensive assessments across customers, products, geographies, and channels, with applications that allow risk owners to continuously monitor alignment with risk appetite.
- 2024 fraud trends: Overall fraud remained high but declined in H1 2024 versus the prior year; customer losses also decreased, attributed to stronger controls, processes, and greater public awareness. Notable decline in vishing/smishing; increase in investment fraud; other fraud types largely stable.

- Collaboration and information sharing: Active participation in SAMLIT (with police and Sweden’s largest banks) and other initiatives; interbank fraud collaboration via the Swedish Bankers’ Association to share trends and modus operandi.
- Fraud strategy: Three-tier approach—prevent, detect, investigate—supported by stronger product/channel security, enhanced transaction monitoring, and streamlined processes. A dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme coordinates efforts, targets reduced customer losses, and implements the industry-wide package of measures slated for full rollout by end-2025.
- Customer support: Ongoing assistance to stop active fraud, recover funds, restore accounts, and guide victims to report to police and submit unauthorized transaction claims.
- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite: Low risk appetite formalized through internal regulations; Group Compliance (including the AML Officer for Controlling and Reporting, OCR) independently monitors and reports quarterly/annually to the CEO and Board. Internal rules define prohibited activities, higher-risk scenarios, and required controls. Annual, data-driven general risk assessment covers customers, products, geographies, and channels; thresholds tied to risk appetite trigger escalations; progress in fraud prevention reported to top management.
- Outcomes and trends: Overall fraud volumes and customer losses decreased in H1 2024 versus 2023, notably for vishing/smishing; investment fraud increased; other fraud types remained stable.
- Training outcomes: High completion rates for AML/CFT training (97–98% across countries in 2023–2024). Methodological notes clarify scope (e.g., PayEx, Swedbank Fastighetsbyrå) and state metrics are not externally validated.

  - Comprehensive sector-by-sector tables for CCM/CCA/WTR and for CE/PPC/BIO, with totals.

- 2024 turnover-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.71% of covered assets; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 3.37%.
  - Alignment is largely driven by the household mortgage portfolio (households: eligible 54.47%, aligned 3.05%).
  - Non-financial undertakings: eligible ≈ 0.96%, aligned ≈ 0.30; financial undertakings: eligible ≈ 0.28%, aligned ≈ 0.02.
  - Minimal exposure to CE/PPC/BIO objectives (eligible roughly 0.12/0.02/0.01; aligned near 0.00–0.01).
  - “Of which” amounts for use-of-proceeds and transitional/enabling activities are very small; coverage of total assets in denominator ≈ 73.39%.

  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.98%; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 3.59%.
  - Households still dominate aligned share (3.05%); non-financial undertakings aligned ≈ 0.52%.
  - Very small use-of-proceeds (~0.02) and transitional (~0.13) shares; total assets coverage ≈ 73.39%.
- 2023 turnover-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.73%; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 1.36%.
  - Households aligned ≈ 1.24%; non-financial undertakings eligible ≈ 0.61%, aligned ≈ 0.12.
  - Use-of-proceeds and transitional/enabling negligible; total assets coverage ≈ 74.42%.
  - Tables for CE/PPC/BIO are largely blank/immaterial for 2023.

  - Total assets coverage ≈ 74.42%.
- Overall message: The GAR is predominantly driven by the mortgage book; taxonomy alignment increases from 2023 to 2024 in both turnover- and capex-based views, while exposures to other environmental objectives beyond climate remain very limited, and use-of-proceeds/transitional/enabling shares are minor.

nodes.title: Basis for preparation
nodes.heading: 2.1.1 Basis for preparation
nodes.start_phrase: The sustainability statement s have been prepared on a consolidated basis .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and framework: First sustainability statements prepared under ESRS, replacing prior GRI-based Integrated Report; prepared on a consolidated basis with the same perimeter as the financial statements.
- Consolidation scope: All line-by-line consolidated entities are included; controlled but not consolidated companies assessed as non-material for sustainability and excluded. Subsidiaries in several CEE countries are exempt from standalone reporting as they are covered by the parent’s statements; certain large, listed subsidiaries will publish sub-consolidated sustainability reports. UniCredit Bank Austria AG and UniCredit Bank GmbH publish 2024 reports despite pending local transposition.
- Value chain coverage: Reporting covers both upstream (primarily tier 1 suppliers/business partners) and downstream (clients, investees, business partners) segments. Focus areas include responsible sourcing, environmental and social practices, and Scope 3 GHG emissions (including purchased goods/services and other relevant categories). Disclosures include quantitative Scope 3 data and qualitative material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and related policies, actions and targets (PATs). No omissions for IP or innovation.
- Time horizons: Defined as short term (<1 year), medium term (>1–5 years), and long term (5–10+ years), aligned with strategy, risk management, financial reporting, stakeholder expectations, and TCFD.
- Data, estimation, and methodologies: For value chain metrics (notably Scope 3), primary data is used where available; otherwise, estimates are applied due to scale/complexity, limited sector-specific standards for financial institutions, tooling constraints, and counterparty data limitations. Mapping focuses on first-tier counterparties. Financed emissions estimated for non-financial corporates and households; financial institutions and government-related counterparties excluded in the first ESRS year. Methodologies follow the GHG Protocol and PCAF, using emissions factors, proxy data, and scenario analysis (baseline, delayed transition, energy disorder). Measurement uncertainty is acknowledged; assumptions and estimation methods are disclosed, data is controlled for accuracy, and aligned with financial statement assumptions. Ongoing engagement with clients/suppliers and external providers aims to improve data quality and methods over time.
- Reporting boundaries and references: Prior-period ESRS comparisons and error disclosures are not applicable before the first ESRS year. Additional legal disclosures are limited to EU Taxonomy Article 8. Certain climate-related risk identification processes (IRO-1) are incorporated by reference to the Notes, Part E.
- Governance structure (GOV-1): UniCredit adopts a one-tier model with a Board of Directors and an internal Audit Committee; complies with Italian and EU regulations, Bank of Italy rules, and obligations tied to listings in Milan, Frankfurt, and Warsaw. The Board has 14 members (1 executive CEO/General Manager; 13 non-executives). The Audit Committee comprises 4 independent non-executive directors; the chair is elected by minority shareholders. Additional committees: Governance & Sustainability (4 members), Risk (4), Nomination (3), Remuneration (3), and Related-Parties (3). The Board appoints the CEO to execute board resolutions. No employee representation is foreseen by law or bylaws. Directors are appointed via slate voting to ensure minority representation and gender balance. The Board defines an optimal qualitative/quantitative composition, publishes a theoretical profile before renewals, and discloses alignment outcomes; specific recommendations were provided ahead of the 2024–2026 renewal.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.heading: 2.1.2 Governance
nodes.summary:
- Governance structure and composition: UniCredit’s Board of Directors comprises 14 members (1 executive CEO/General Manager and 13 non-executive). The Board is supported by six committees: Audit (4 independent members; chair elected by minorities), Governance & Sustainability, Risk, Nomination, Remuneration, and Related-Parties. Committee sizes: Governance & Sustainability and Risk (4 members each); Nomination, Remuneration, Related-Parties (3 each). Directors are elected via slate voting to ensure minority representation; no employee representation is foreseen.

- Board selection, capabilities, and training: The Board defines an optimal “theoretical profile” and required qualifications, including ESG and legal/compliance expertise, and ensures gender balance. A permanent three-year induction and training program is in place, including ESG-focused sessions (e.g., 2024 session on approach, regulation, Net Zero).

- Skills matrix and diversity: All core competencies identified in the theoretical profile are represented (international markets, banking governance/business, legal/compliance, strategy, risk/control, accounting/audit, ESG, digital/technology). The Board shows strong diversity and independence (e.g., 50% women; 93% independent; broad international experience). Committee compositions meet independence and expertise requirements, with detailed gender/age/geography breakdowns.

- Strategic oversight and risk governance: The Board sets overall strategy, including the Group’s ESG strategy and KPIs, and approves the Risk Appetite Framework (RAF), which includes climate risk KPIs. The Audit Committee assesses adequacy of financial and non-financial (ESG) reporting. The Risk Committee oversees risk strategy and policies, including climate and environmental risk. The Governance & Sustainability Committee advises on non-risk ESG matters. The CEO identifies risks, proposes strategy, ensures execution of RAF and policies, and maintains internal information flows. Roles reflect non-delegable supervisory and management responsibilities and align with ESRS double materiality.

- Management bodies and ESG integration: The Group Executive Committee (GEC), chaired by the CEO, sets ESG strategy, targets and acts as the Group’s risk council; it contributed to the 2024 double materiality assessment. Managerial committees include the Group Non-Financial Risks & Controls Committee (reputational/sensitive sectors, non-financial risks) and the Group Financial & Credit Risk Committee (credit/market/financial risks including climate and environmental). Specialized functions (Group Strategy & ESG, Group Stakeholder Engagement, Group ESG, Group Risk Management with Climate Risk & Risk Governance and Climate & Environmental Credit Analysis) embed climate and ESG into strategy, risk frameworks, origination, and credit review. ESG Advisory within Group Client Solutions supports client transition strategies and ESG communications; ESG expertise is distributed across functions and geographies.

- Business conduct: The Board approves the Group Code of Conduct anchored in UniCredit values (integrity, ownership, caring). A yearly “Tone from the Top” program promotes compliance and risk awareness; 2024 topics included unfair commercial practices, financial sanctions, ESG-sensitive sectors, AML/confidential & inside information, data protection, and digital risk.

- Governance of material IROs (GOV-2): 2024 marked the first CSRD-aligned double materiality assessment. The Board reviewed outcomes in November 2024. Processes to formalize frequency and methodology of oversight are being developed, with plans to institutionalize regular reviews. Climate risk (E1) and cybersecurity risk (S4) were confirmed material following expert review.

- Incentives linking pay and sustainability (GOV-3): The 2025 Group Incentive System is a Sustainable Performance Plan with short- and long-term conditions, a bonus-pool approach, strong pay-for-performance links, and shareholder alignment (share-based, deferrals). CEO’s 2025 scorecard: 80% financial, 20% non-financial; for CEO and selected leaders, 60% of bonus is deferred with long-term conditions (2026–2028), where Sustainability (incl. climate/Net Zero) has 20% weight. Goals include ESG business penetration, DE&I progress, and Net Zero 2030 targets embedded in RAF. Objectives cascade to Group Material Risk Takers; all GMRT short-term scorecards include at least one ESG KPI from a standardized “KPI Bluebook.” Non-executive directors receive only fixed remuneration.

- Due diligence statement (GOV-4): Due diligence is embedded in strategy and operations, not a standalone process. The double materiality assessment identified material negative impacts in climate change (GHG emissions), circular economy (resource use/waste), and consumers/end-users (data breaches). Management is addressed through policies, actions, targets, and metrics.

- Internal controls over sustainability reporting (GOV-5): A COSO-aligned internal control system (updated for “Internal Control over Sustainability Reporting,” March 2023) ensures integrity, completeness, and reliability of sustainability disclosures. A Sustainability Reporting Manager was appointed for 2024. Controls include entity-level governance and process-level controls (materiality, data collection, reconciliation). Risk/control assessments, testing, documentation, and remediation are performed, with reporting to the Board and Audit Committee. Subsidiaries provide internal certifications to the Parent.

- Strategy and value proposition (SBM-1): UniCredit is a pan-European commercial bank serving ~15 million clients via 13 banks across Italy, Germany, and Central & Eastern Europe, offering tailored advisory, financing, risk management, payments, investments, and insurance. Headcount is ~75,265 across regions. The Group has no revenues from ESRS-flagged sectors (fossil fuels, chemical production, controversial weapons, tobacco). ESG goals are embedded in client, people, and shareholder strategies, with a corporate ESG offer spanning green/social financing, sustainability-linked instruments, ESG advisory, strategic partnerships (e.g., Open-es), and risk management solutions to support client transition.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 2.1.3 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit is a pan-European Commercial Bank .
nodes.summary:
- Governance and internal controls for sustainability reporting: integrated risk assessments; Sustainability Reporting Manager reports to the Board and Audit Committee; subsidiaries provide internal certifications; defined roles, periodic updates, and remediation tracking.
- Business overview and markets: pan-European commercial bank serving ~15 million clients across Italy, Germany, Central and Eastern Europe; headcount distribution provided; no operations in ESRS-designated controversial sectors.
- ESG product offering and targets: corporate green/social financing, sustainability-linked solutions, ESG advisory, strategic partnerships (e.g., Open-es), transition risk management tools; individual products for energy-efficient home renovation and inclusive finance plus an ESG AUM catalogue; penetration targets for 2025–2027 of 15% ESG lending, 15% sustainable bonds, 50% ESG investment products.
- ESG strategy and enablers: principles-based approach aligned to Group values; goals aligned to net-zero; strategic levers (Championing Social, Enhanced Client Support via Net Zero plan, Beyond Climate, Evidencing Accountability); enablers (expanded ESG offering, lean governance, robust risk framework, empowered culture).
- Business model and value creation: client-centric model across four regions with three product factories (Corporate, Individual, Payment Solutions); payments ambition reinforced by a Mastercard partnership and expanded digital portal; value creation leveraging five capitals.
- Value chain mapping: upstream (capital providers, technology/data suppliers, regulators); downstream (retail, corporate, wealth clients; fintech/payment partners, asset managers and insurers); UniCredit’s intermediary role enabling capital flow, risk management, and economic activity.
- Stakeholder engagement and materiality: structured engagement with clients, employees, investors/shareholders, regulators, communities using NPS and multiple feedback tools; proactive policy engagement on sustainable finance; enhanced dialogue with NGOs (e.g., ESG Day); double materiality assessment informing strategy with Board oversight; strong human rights commitment.
- Climate and environmental management: double materiality inside-out/outside-in lens; integration of climate risk into models, provisioning (ECL), scenario analysis and ICAAP with resilience across time horizons; net-zero commitments (own emissions by 2030, financed emissions by 2050); sector policies restricting financing of thermal coal and high-impact oil & gas; advisory to support client transition; operational targets on renewable electricity, energy/water efficiency, circularity, mobility, and responsible sourcing.
- Nature-related and circular economy initiatives: portfolio-level impact and dependency assessments on biodiversity, pollution, water, and waste using recognized tools (e.g., ENCORE, TNFD) and heatmaps; participation in Finance for Biodiversity Pledge and UNEP FI Nature Guidance; membership in Ellen MacArthur Foundation; monitoring Water Usage Effectiveness in data centers; furniture reuse; client awareness on water and waste.
- Social topics: people strategy focused on wellbeing, DE&I, skills and development, fair employment, social dialogue, and industrial relations (including EWC); only positive material impacts/opportunities identified for own workforce; value-chain worker protections (human rights focus, UK Modern Slavery Act compliance).
- Communities and customers: commitments to financial inclusion and health (UNEP FI PRB), 2025 youth targets; tailored solutions for vulnerable groups; broad financial education initiatives; strengthened data privacy and cybersecurity; responsible marketing aligned with IAP/UPA and regulatory reviews (e.g., CONSOB).
- Business conduct and integrity: cultural transformation anchored in values; whistleblowing policy with protections; supplier standards (ILO and environmental policy); anti-bribery and corruption framework (Global Rules, Italian L.D. 231/01, Code of Conduct).
- Material IROs: detailed tables of impacts, risks, and opportunities across ESRS topics (E1–E5, S1–S4, G1), covering emissions (Scopes 1–3), green finance opportunities, physical climate credit risk, water and biodiversity, resource use and waste, workforce wellbeing/DE&I/training, human rights in the value chain, financial inclusion, privacy/cyber risks and reputational/operational risks, supplier practices, and anti-corruption; each with value-chain location and time horizons.
- IRO identification process: top-down ESRS-based double materiality at Group level, contextual analysis, extensive stakeholder engagement, gross impact assessment prior to mitigation, alignment with due diligence; no entity-specific IROs identified for the period.

nodes.title: Impact, risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.1.4 Impact, risk and opportunity management
nodes.start_phrase: The process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities was based on a top -down approach: UniCredit Holding identified a list of material IROs which has been shared with Legal Entities, and compared to their list, in order to guarantee coherence along the entire Group.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Sustainability Statements), presenting the continued “List of Material Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs)” aligned to ESRS topics, and the IRO-1 methodology for identifying and assessing them.

- ESRS S4 – Consumers and end-users:
  - Privacy:
    - Opportunity: Build long-term customer relationships via strong, safe ICT systems (downstream, medium-term).
    - Negative impact (potential): Customer data breaches and poor cybersecurity (downstream, medium-term).
    - Risks: Operational losses from unauthorized data access/cyberattacks; reputational risk from failing to protect data and meet user needs (own operations).
  - Privacy, Freedom of expression, Access to quality information:
    - Positive impact (potential): Business model transformation through digitalization, new tech, cloud, and AI (downstream, medium-term).
    - Opportunity: Market share expansion and retention via digital/innovative solutions (downstream, medium-term).
    - Opportunity: Stronger loyalty through optimized privacy, data security, and quality information (downstream, short-term).
    - Positive impact (actual): More informed customer decisions via transparent, neutral, fair advice and feedback mechanisms (downstream, medium-term).
  - Social inclusion/responsible marketing:
    - Opportunity (actual): Better client and shareholder relationships through clear, transparent communication (downstream, short-term).
  - Non-discrimination/access to products and services:
    - Positive impact (actual): Improved satisfaction and user experience by meeting expectations (downstream, medium-term).

- ESRS G1 – Business conduct:
  - Corporate culture:
    - Positive impacts (actual): Promote fair competition and reduce aggressive tax practices/evasion (upstream, medium-term); maximize value creation and distribution to stakeholders (across, medium-term).
  - Protection of whistle-blowers:
    - Positive impact (actual): Strengthen ethical culture across management, employees, partners (own operations, medium-term).
  - Supplier relationships and payment practices:
    - Positive impact (actual): Solid supplier relations and adherence to terms (upstream, medium-term).
    - Opportunity (actual): Higher quality purchases via a more sustainable, certified supply chain (upstream, medium-term).
  - Corruption and bribery:
    - Positive impact (actual): Prevention/detection through training for employees, top management, and stakeholders (upstream).
    - Risk: Money laundering, sanctions violations, bribery/corruption, KYC failures (across, medium-term).
    - Opportunity: Reputation enhancement by investing in innovative anti-corruption tools (both operations and value chain, medium-term).

- IRO-1 – Process to identify and assess material IROs:
  - Approach: Top-down, Group-led list shared with legal entities for coherence; focus on core banking activity while covering all entities in the Sustainability Statement perimeter.
  - Double materiality: Internal/external context analysis, mapping dependencies/resources/geographies, stakeholder mapping.
  - Stakeholder engagement: Questionnaires, workshops, forums, interviews, surveys; external perspectives integrated.
  - ESRS alignment: Screened ESRS 1-AR 16 matters; reconciled topics/sub-topics; tagged each impact by location (own ops/value chain), time horizon (short/medium/long), and strategic actors (e.g., employees, customers, shareholders).
  - Assessment principles: Considered gross impacts before mitigation; did not net positive against negative impacts; integrated due diligence outcomes for negative impacts (referenced GOV-4).

nodes.title: Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: IRO-1 - Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities was based on a top -down approach: UniCredit Holding identified a list of material IROs which has been shared with Legal Entities, and compared to their list, in order to guarantee coherence along the entire Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Sustainability Statement outlining material Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs) under ESRS, with a focus on consumers/end-users (S4), business conduct (G1), and the Group’s CSRD‑aligned double materiality process.

- Material IROs – S4 Consumers and end-users:
  - Privacy and cybersecurity: opportunities from strong ICT, data security and client loyalty; risks of data breaches, cyber attacks, operational and reputational impacts.
  - Freedom of expression and access to quality information: positive impacts from digitalisation, cloud and AI; opportunities to expand market share and retention through innovative digital services; improved client loyalty via privacy/data security and transparent, fair advice enabling customer feedback.
  - Social inclusion/responsible marketing: opportunities from clear, transparent communication; positive impacts on customer satisfaction and experience; better access to products and services.

- Material IROs – G1 Business conduct:
  - Corporate culture and fair competition: positive impacts from responsible tax practices; value creation and distribution to stakeholders.
  - Whistle-blower protection: positive cultural impacts across own operations.
  - Supplier relationships/payment practices: positive impacts from solid relationships and on-time payments; opportunity to improve purchased product/service quality via sustainable, certified supply chains.
  - Anti-corruption and bribery: positive impacts from prevention/detection and training; risks across AML/sanctions/bribery/KYC; opportunity to enhance reputation through innovative monitoring/prevention tools.

- IRO identification and assessment process (IRO‑1):
  - Top‑down, Group‑led list aligned to core banking activities; applied across all entities.
  - Context analysis and stakeholder mapping; reconciliation with ESRS topics and assignment of location (own operations/upstream/downstream), time horizon, and stakeholders.
  - Stakeholder engagement: internal (ESG, Reporting, Risk, Compliance, Top Management, Board) and external (employees, clients, investors, NGOs, academics, regulators, ESG raters) via interviews, surveys, workshops and desktop analysis.
  - Impact scoring: severity (scale, scope, irremediability for negatives) and likelihood; numerical 1–4 scoring; human rights negatives weighted for severity; materiality threshold set to focus on most relevant impacts; aggregation to sustainability matters by maximum score.
  - Risk/opportunity financial materiality: magnitude and likelihood (1–4); risks assessed by Group Risk Management (quantitative for climate; qualitative with data inputs for other E/S/G); opportunities assessed by Top Management (qualitative brand/competitiveness plus quantitative net profit potential); thresholds capture low‑probability/high‑impact and already‑present risks.
  - Integration: sustainability risks embedded in overall risk management (Risk Appetite, ICAAP, credit/market strategies, liquidity, models, provisioning, controversial sector policies, business continuity, reputational and litigation); opportunities integrated into product/financing innovation and strategic offerings in ESG.
  - Governance and controls: consistency/completeness checks, ESRS 2 compliance, legal entity feedback, Top Management confirmation, Board approval.

- Inputs and tools:
  - Internal: strategy, risk inventory, policies, Annual/Statutory/Integrated Reports, budget and planning frameworks.
  - External: ESG ratings/indices, EU regulations, media; Datamaran analytics; peer benchmarking; PRB, WEF Global Risks Report 2024, S&P Yearbook 2023, UNEP FI Impact Radar, OECD Guidelines.
  - Note: 2024 is first CSRD‑aligned double materiality cycle; not comparable to prior year.

- Environmental topics overview:
  - Climate change: recognition of Scope 1, 2, 3 emissions; support for green transition via financing energy efficiency, renewables, decarbonisation products/services, green tech start‑ups, and potential carbon trading; links to Notes on climate/environmental risks and scenarios.
  - Pollution, water, biodiversity, circular economy: screening shows low significance from own operations; limited exposure in construction/agriculture; no sites in/near biodiversity‑sensitive areas; opportunities for efficiency, recycling/reuse, dematerialisation and water monitoring/compliance.
  - Value chain assessment: sector heatmap of loan portfolio for nature‑related impacts/dependencies; negative impacts from financing high‑impact sectors largely non‑material except E5 (circular economy); environmental compliance/creditworthiness risks deemed non‑material; opportunities to scale green/sustainable financing.
  - Stakeholder engagement: ESG Day and external reviews (NGOs, academics, investors, clients) to validate environmental IROs.

nodes.title: Climate Change:
nodes.heading: Climate Change :
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit acknowledges that its activities and business generate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, both directly through its ow n energy consumption (Scope 1 and 2) and indirectly across its upstream and downstream activities (Scope 3).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: UniCredit’s 2024 Sustainability Statement within the Consolidated Report describes how sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) are identified, assessed, managed, and embedded across the Group’s risk and strategy frameworks, aligned with ESRS and CSRD requirements.

- Embedding sustainability in risk management:
  - Sustainability-related risks prioritized via financial materiality and stakeholder input.
  - Full integration into Risk Appetite, ICAAP, credit and market risk strategies, liquidity, credit models and provisioning, and non-financial risk controls (controversial sectors, business continuity, reputational risk, litigation).

- ESG opportunities and strategic integration:
  - Material opportunities centered on ESG-driven product and service innovation, particularly financing solutions.
  - Positioning ESG offerings to meet market demand and support environmental and social objectives, targeting long-term value creation.

- Governance and assurance of the process:
  - Top Management applied a structured, control-focused approach to ensure consistency with Standards.
  - Verification of topic completeness, stakeholder coverage across the value chain, and cross-checks with prior years.
  - Compliance review with ESRS 2 and topical standards; feedback from all Legal Entities considered.
  - Final list of material IROs presented to the Board of Directors.

- IROs identification inputs:
  - Internal: business strategy, activities, client solutions, Annual/Statutory/Integrated Reports, ESG policies, Group Inventory Risk, ESG ratings/indices, regulations, media.
  - External: Datamaran scan of 100+ ESG topics, peer benchmarking, PRB, WEF Global Risks Report 2024, S&P Yearbook 2023, UNEP FI Impact Radar, OECD Guidelines.
  - Ongoing stakeholder engagement through multiple channels.

- IROs assessment approach:
  - Use of ICAAP, management control, strategic planning, business model considerations, and budgeting.
  - 2024 marks first CSRD-aligned double materiality process with deeper financial materiality; results not comparable to prior year.

- Climate change:
  - Recognition of direct (Scope 1–2) and indirect (Scope 3) emissions.
  - Actions: financing energy efficiency and renewables; enhancing awareness and commitments.
  - Opportunities: green project financing, decarbonization products/services for clients, support for green tech start-ups, potential entry into carbon trading.
  - Cross-references to consolidated accounts for climate/environmental risk and scenario compatibility disclosures.

- Other environmental topics (pollution; water and marine resources; biodiversity and ecosystems; resource use and circular economy):
  - Operational screening indicates the Bank’s own activities are not highly impactful; no sites near biodiversity-sensitive areas.
  - Factors assessed: travel-related pollution, water management, resource/raw material use, waste, ecosystem contamination/biodiversity loss (limited relevance from small exposure to construction/agriculture).
  - Opportunities: cost savings via efficiency, recycling/reuse, dematerialization, and water monitoring/compliance.
  - Conclusion: environmental impacts and related risks from own operations are not significant; no significant biodiversity transition/physical/systemic risks identified.

- Client and portfolio perspective:
  - Sector-level heatmap of the loan portfolio to gauge nature-related risks via impacts and dependencies.
  - Negative impacts from financing polluting, water-intensive, resource-heavy, waste-generating, and biodiversity-affecting sectors—assessed as non-material except for E5 (circular economy), which is material.
  - Positive influence through client engagement and awareness-raising.
  - Opportunities to expand green/sustainable financial products and services supporting natural capital.
  - Risks from counterparty non-compliance with environmental laws and potential credit deterioration in sensitive sectors—assessed as non-material.

- Stakeholder engagement:
  - ESG Day held to gather stakeholder perspectives on environmental IROs.
  - External stakeholders (NGOs, academics, investors, clients) reviewed identified IROs to ensure a comprehensive assessment.

nodes.title: Pollution; Water and Marine resources; Biodiversity and ecosystems; Resource use and circular economy:
nodes.heading: Pollution; Water and Marine resources; Biodiversity and ecosystems; Resource use and circular economy :
nodes.start_phrase: Beyond climate, UniCredit has conducted a thorough screening of its operations and site locations to assess actual and potent ial impacts, risks and opportunities related to other environmental factors: pollution, water consumption, biodiversity and waste m anagement.
nodes.summary:
- Embedding sustainability-related risks into UniCredit’s enterprise-wide risk management, covering Risk Appetite, ICAAP, credit/market/liquidity strategies, risk models and provisioning, controversial sector policies, business continuity, reputational risk, and potential litigation.
- Prioritizing ESG opportunities via double materiality, focusing on innovation in products and services and integrating these into strategic financing offerings to drive long-term value.
- Robust governance and controls over the double materiality process: top management oversight, completeness and consistency checks across value chain stakeholders, cross-year comparisons, ESRS 2 compliance verification, and Board of Directors approval.
- Methodology for identifying, assessing, and managing IROs: internal sources (reports, policies, Group Inventory Risk, ESG ratings/indices, regulations, media) and external sources (Datamaran, peer benchmarking, PRB, WEF Global Risks 2024, S&P Yearbook 2023, UNEP FI Impact Radar, OECD Guidelines), with stakeholder engagement; assessment anchored in ICAAP, management control, strategic planning, business model and budget. First CSRD-aligned double materiality cycle (not comparable to prior year).
- Environmental topics:
  - Climate: acknowledgment of Scope 1–3 emissions; financing energy efficiency and renewables; developing decarbonization products/services, supporting green tech start-ups, exploring carbon markets; references to climate risk notes in the consolidated accounts.
  - Pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity, resource use/circular economy: operational screening finds limited significance; no sites near biodiversity-sensitive areas; opportunities in resource efficiency, recycling/reuse, dematerialization, and water monitoring; sector-level heatmap of loan portfolio for nature-related risk exposure. Negative impacts identified in financed sectors are generally non-material except E5 (circular economy); counterparty compliance and credit risks deemed non-material. Stakeholder input gathered via ESG Day and external consultations.
  - Outcome of double materiality: all environmental topics are material except pollution.
- Business conduct: assessment of internal culture, anti-corruption/bribery controls, supplier relationships and payment practices, whistleblowing, and KYC. Opportunities to strengthen reputation through advanced anti-corruption tools and more sustainable, certified supply chains; key risks include fraud, AML, sanctions breaches, bribery/corruption, and KYC failures.
- ESRS disclosures: IRO-2 maps material topics to reported policies, actions, targets, and metrics; only data points for material (sub-)topics are disclosed. A content index outlines general basis for preparation, specific circumstances, governance, due diligence, internal controls over sustainability reporting, strategy and business model, stakeholder views, material IROs (IRO-1), IRO-2, and policies, with page references.

nodes.title: Business Conduct:
nodes.heading: Business Conduct:
nodes.start_phrase: To identify impacts related to business conduct matters, UniCredit has conducted an in -depth analysis of its internal structure, policies, and business model.
nodes.summary:
- Reports results of UniCredit’s double materiality assessment, noting all environmental topics are material except pollution.
- Details a Business Conduct assessment covering corporate culture, anti-corruption/bribery controls, supplier relations and payment practices, and whistleblowing adherence, evaluated by location, activity, sector context, and transaction structure.
- Identifies opportunities: enhancing reputation via innovative anti-corruption monitoring tools; improving procurement quality through a more sustainable supply chain and prioritization of certified products meeting environmental criteria.
- Flags key risks: fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations, bribery and corruption, and KYC compliance failures.
- Explains ESRS IRO-2 approach: topics and (sub-)sub-topics derived from the DMA; only material policies, actions, targets, and related metrics/data points are reported.
- Introduces the Sustainability Statement 2024 structure reflecting double materiality results.
- Provides a content index with page references for: basis of preparation; specific circumstances; governance roles and oversight; integration of sustainability in incentives; due diligence statement; controls over sustainability reporting; strategy, business model and value chain; stakeholder interests; material impacts/risks/opportunities and strategic interaction; processes to identify/assess IROs; ESRS disclosure coverage; and policies to manage material sustainability matters.

nodes.summary:
The excerpt summarizes UniCredit’s 2024 Sustainability Statement within its Consolidated Report, focusing on the outcomes of a double materiality assessment and the structure of ESRS-aligned disclosures.

Key points:
- Double materiality results: All environmental topics are deemed material except pollution.
- Business conduct assessment: An in-depth review of internal structures, policies, and business model considered corporate culture, anti-corruption and anti-bribery practices, supplier relations and payment terms, whistleblowing procedures, and contextual factors (location, sector, transaction structures). 
  - Opportunities: Strengthening reputation via innovative anti-corruption tools; improving procurement quality through a more sustainable supply chain and prioritization of certified products meeting minimum environmental criteria.
  - Risks: Potential fraud, money laundering, sanctions breaches, bribery and corruption, and KYC compliance failures.
- ESRS disclosure approach (IRO-2): Using the DMA to identify material topics, sub-topics, and sub-sub-topics; reporting only data points tied to material policies, actions, targets, and metrics. The ESG sections reflect these results in the 2024 Sustainability Statement.

  - Due diligence statement
  - Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting
  - Strategy, business model, value chain
  - Stakeholder interests and views
  - Material impacts, risks, opportunities and their link to strategy/business model

nodes.title: List of disclosure requirements complied with
nodes.heading: IRO-2 List of disclosure requirements complied with
nodes.start_phrase: Through the DMA process, key topics, sub -topics and sub -sub topics were identified, and based on these (sub -) sub-topics, material aspects were determined for each IRO.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, Sustainability Statements (Consolidated report on operations), presenting the outcome of the double materiality assessment (DMA) and the IRO-2 content index mapping to ESRS disclosure requirements for the 2024 Sustainability Statement.
- Double materiality results: All environmental topics are material except pollution. Business conduct assessment covered internal culture, anti-corruption/bribery, supplier relationships and payment practices, and whistleblowing adherence, considering location, sector context and transaction structures.
- Business conduct risks and opportunities: Opportunities include reputational enhancement via innovative anti-corruption tools and higher-quality, sustainable procurement favoring certified products. Key risks identified include fraud, money laundering, sanctions breaches, bribery/corruption, and KYC failures.
- Reporting approach (IRO-2): Using DMA outputs, UniCredit identified topics, sub-topics and sub-sub-topics, then reported only data points (DPs) tied to material policies, actions, targets, and metrics. The following ESRS-aligned sections include page references for transparency.
- General disclosures index: Basis of preparation (BP-1, BP-2), governance roles and oversight (GOV-1 to GOV-5), strategy and business model (SBM-1 to SBM-3), materiality processes (IRO-1, IRO-2), and policies to manage material sustainability matters (MDR-P).
- Environmental disclosures index:
  - ESRS E1 Climate change: Mitigation and adaptation, transition plan, policies, actions, targets, energy consumption/mix, Scopes 1–3 and total GHG emissions, removals/carbon credits, internal carbon pricing, and anticipated financial effects (phased-in).
  - ESRS E3 Water and marine resources: Water consumption and withdrawal with related policies, actions, and targets.
  - ESRS E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Transition plan and integration in strategy, policies, actions, targets, and anticipated financial effects (phased-in).
  - ESRS E5 Resource use and circular economy: Resource inflows/outflows and waste, with related policies, actions, and targets.
- Social disclosures index:
  - ESRS S1 Own workforce: Working conditions (secure employment, adequate wages, social dialogue, freedom of association, collective bargaining, work-life balance), equal treatment/opportunities (gender equality and equal pay, training/skills, disability inclusion, anti-violence/harassment, diversity), privacy, metrics and incidents/complaints.
  - ESRS S2 Workers in the value chain: Child and forced labour—policies, engagement, remediation, actions, and targets.
  - ESRS S3 Affected communities: Economic, social, cultural rights (housing, food), security-related impacts, civil and political rights—policies, engagement, remediation, actions, and targets.
  - ESRS S4 Consumers and end users: Information-related impacts and social inclusion—policies, engagement, remediation, actions, and targets.
- Governance disclosures index:
  - ESRS G1 Business conduct: Corporate culture and policies, whistleblower protection, supplier management and payment practices, anti-corruption and bribery (prevention/detection and incident reporting), with governance roles and IRO processes cross-referenced.
- DPs from other EU legislation (IRO-2 Par. 56): Table identifies materiality and phase-in status for specific DPs, including:
  - Governance composition (board gender diversity, independence) and due diligence statement.
  - Activity involvement (fossil fuels, chemical production, controversial weapons, tobacco).
  - Climate-related DPs (transition plan to climate neutrality by 2050, energy consumption/mix/intensity, GHG scopes and intensity, removals/credits, portfolio exposure to physical risks, asset location and real estate energy classes, and opportunities—some phased-in).
  - Water: Water policy/materiality limited to water; oceans/seas and certain water efficiency metrics deemed not material.
  - Biodiversity/resource use: Certain policies on sustainable land/seas, deforestation, and waste categories not material.
  - Social: Risks of forced/child labour under S1 not material; human rights policy commitments and ILO due diligence requirements material.

nodes.title: All the datapoints deriving from other EU legislation
nodes.heading: IRO-2 - All the datapoints deriving from other EU legislation
nodes.start_phrase: IRO-2 Par. 56 - DPs that derive from other EU legislation
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Part of UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, Sustainability Statements, detailing ESRS IRO-2 datapoints derived from other EU legislation and the Group’s minimum disclosure requirements on policies and actions.
- ESRS IRO-2 mapping: Comprehensive list of disclosure requirements across governance, strategy/business model, environment (E1–E5), social (S1–S4), and governance (G1), indicating whether each datapoint is material, not material, or subject to phase-in.
- Key environmental items marked material: transition plan to climate neutrality by 2050; Paris-aligned benchmark exclusions; GHG reduction targets; Scope 1–3 and total GHG emissions and intensities; energy consumption/mix and energy intensity (high-impact sectors); GHG removals and carbon credits.
- Climate risk/opportunity disclosures: portfolio exposure to climate-related physical risks, disaggregation by acute/chronic risks, location of significant assets at material physical risk, real estate energy-efficiency classes, and exposure to climate-related opportunities—flagged as material and subject to phase-in.
- Environmental items not material: PRTR-listed pollutant emissions (E2-4), oceans/seas topics (E3-1), certain water KPIs (recycled/reused water, water consumption intensity), parts of biodiversity/deforestation (E4-2), and specific waste metrics (non-recycled, hazardous/radioactive).
- Water: Water and marine resources policy is material for water only; dedicated policy under E3 is material.
- Governance and strategy: Board gender diversity and independence disclosures; due diligence statement; involvement in sensitive sectors (fossil fuels, chemicals, controversial weapons, tobacco) flagged within SBM-1.
- Social (own workforce and value chain): Material items include human rights policy commitments and due diligence (ILO Conventions 1–8), unadjusted gender pay gap, CEO pay ratio, discrimination incidents, non-respect of UNGPs/OECD guidelines; significant risk of child/forced labor in the value chain, and related policies and incident reporting (S2–S4).
- Social items not material: certain health and safety KPIs (fatalities, accident rates, days lost), trafficking prevention, grievance mechanisms, and forced/child labor risks within own operations.
- Anti-corruption and ethics: Material disclosures on adherence to the UN Convention against Corruption, whistleblower protection, fines for violations, and anti-corruption/anti-bribery standards (G1).
- Policies and actions (MDR-P): Overview of Group policies addressing material topics identified through double materiality, with linkages to IROs.
- Smart office workplace global policy: Sets principles for planning/occupancy of major offices to drive space and energy efficiency, employee well-being, and Net-Zero alignment; defines KPIs, applicability triggers (e.g., office opening/relocation/refurbishment), and Group Real Estate oversight.
- Civil nuclear sector policy: Standards for identifying in-scope subjects/activities and conducting Reputational and ESG Risk Assessments for civil nuclear activities, including NPP operations, ancillary services, waste processing, and non-commercial research.
- Coal sector policy: Standards and risk assessment for clients/transactions related to coal-fired power generation and thermal coal mining, including operators, subcontractors, suppliers, and traders.
- Governance of sensitive sector policies: Approved by the Group Non-Financial Risks and Controls Committee; applicable across UniCredit S.p.A. and Group entities per the Operational Risk Oversight model; policy summaries available on the company website.

nodes.title: Minimum disclosure requirement on policies and actions
nodes.heading: Minimum disclosure requirement on policies and actions
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit’s policies represent the tangible expression of our commitment to ESG principles.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, Sustainability Statement, covering the Minimum Disclosure Requirement on Policies and Actions (MDR-P) for managing material sustainability matters identified via double materiality. Policies are positioned as the operational expression of the Group’s ESG commitments and link to material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs).

- Smart office workplace global policy:
  - Purpose: Guide planning and occupancy of major offices to enable efficient, sustainable real estate investments and a modern, ergonomic workplace.
  - ESG goals: Reduce operational CO2 emissions, support Net-Zero alignment; sets space-efficiency KPIs and energy efficiency measures.
  - Scope: All regions, all Group legal entities; applies to head offices and larger corporate offices (≈100+ employees).
  - Triggers: Office opening, lease extension, relocation, major refurbishment, or significant workforce size changes.
  - Oversight: Adoption monitored by Group Real Estate with local real estate functions.

- Civil nuclear sector regulation:
  - Purpose: Establish standards to manage risks in the civil nuclear sector.
  - Mechanism: Defines in-scope subjects/activities and a process with roles and responsibilities for Reputational and ESG Risk Assessment.
  - Scope: Corporate customers owning/operating NPPs; operators of non-commercial civil nuclear activities; and any financing/support tied to NPP lifecycle activities (engineering, construction, maintenance, upgrades, decommissioning, ancillary services, key components, fuel storage, safeguards), nuclear waste processing, and civil non-commercial nuclear research (e.g., fusion/ITER, medical R&D).
  - Governance: Sensitive sector guidelines approved by the Group Non-Financial Risks and Controls Committee; apply to UniCredit S.p.A. and Group entities per the Operational Risk Oversight model; summary available on the website.

- Coal sector regulation:
  - Purpose: Set standards to address risks in the coal sector.
  - Mechanism: Defines in-scope subjects/activities and the process, roles, and responsibilities for Reputational and ESG Risk Assessment.

- Water infrastructure (large dams) policy: Risk standards for owners/operators and financing of large dams and related hydropower assets across build, maintenance, upgrade, and decommissioning; recognizes biodiversity, community, and climate impacts and role in net-zero and energy transition; governed by the same Group committee.
- Statement on natural capital and biodiversity: First comprehensive framework linking climate and biodiversity; commits to sustainable financing, reducing operational impacts, avoiding activities in protected areas, and combating deforestation; references Equator Principles, IFC PS, World Bank EHS, Finance for Biodiversity Pledge; published as a positioning paper.
- ESG product guidelines: Group-wide methodology for ESG product classification and reporting to prevent greenwashing/social washing; aligned with EU Taxonomy, ICMA, ISDA, LMA, EU Transition Finance guidance, SFDR, MiFID II, and ESMA fund naming guidance; requires local implementation and verification processes; central ESG function supports structuring and conducts ex-post checks; internal policy with public abstract.
- Human rights commitment: Group-wide adherence to international standards (UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR, ILO, UNGPs, OECD, UNGC, PRI, IFC PS, WB EHS, UNEP FI PRB, EPs, WEPs, UNDRIP); promotes equal opportunities, decent work, social dialogue, fair wages, and training; approved June 2024 by Group Non-Financial Risk Committee; monitored via existing Group policies (reputational risk, whistleblowing, anti-harassment); communicated internally and to stakeholders for feedback.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion global policy: Establishes principles to foster inclusive culture, prevent discrimination, and enhance employee well-being and performance; aligned with applicable laws; applies to all entities and employees with defined responsibilities and consequence management for third-party misalignment.

nodes.title: Human rights commitment:
nodes.heading: Human rights commitment :
nodes.start_phrase: The human rights commitment outlines UniCredit's dedication to upholding human rights across its key stakeholder groups, including employees, customers, suppliers, and communities.
nodes.summary:

  - Objectives: prevent, manage, and reduce human rights impacts; promote equal opportunities, secure and quality employment, fair wages, social dialogue, collective bargaining; enhance well-being, training, transparent performance reviews, and career development.
  - Foundations: aligned with key international standards (UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR, ILO conventions, UNGPs, OECD Guidelines, UN Global Compact, UN PRI, IFC Performance Standards, WBG EHS Guidelines, UNEP FI PRB, Equator Principles, Women’s Empowerment Principles, UNDRIP, Declaration on Human Rights Defenders).

nodes.title: Diversity, equity and inclusion global policy:
nodes.heading: Diversity, equity and inclusion global policy :
nodes.start_phrase: The objective of the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Global Policy is to set out the principles by which UniCredit enhances i nclusion throughout the whole organisation, aiming to ensure that our policies, procedures, and behaviours promote diversity, equity and inclusion and create an environment where individual differences are valued.
nodes.summary:
- ESG governance and deal oversight: A central ESG function supports legal entities in structuring social/green/transitional/ESG-linked deals in line with market standards and performs periodic ex-post checks. The related policy is for internal use with an abstract on the institutional website.
- Human Rights Commitment: Group-wide commitment covering employees, customers, suppliers, and communities to prevent, manage, and reduce human rights impacts. It promotes equal opportunities, quality employment, fair wages, social dialogue, employee well-being, training, and transparent career development. It is grounded in major international frameworks (UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR, ILO core conventions, UNGPs, OECD Guidelines, UNGC, PRI, IFC PS, World Bank EHS Guidelines, UNEP FI PRB, Equator Principles, Women’s Empowerment Principles, UNDRIP, and the Declaration on Human Rights Defenders). Approved by the Group Non-Financial Risk Committee chaired by the CEO in June 2024; effectiveness monitored via existing Group policies (reputational risk, whistleblowing, anti-harassment). Communicated internally and on the website with stakeholder feedback informing improvements. Local best practices may be developed and shared across the Group.
- Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) Global Policy: Sets principles to embed inclusion across the organization, ensuring policies and behaviors promote diversity, equity, and inclusion. Aims to prevent discrimination, enhance equal opportunities, secure employment, well-being, flexible work, and forward-looking training. Applies to all employees and legal entities, aligned with applicable laws; sets expectations for third parties with consequence management. Progress disclosed through Sustainability Statements and an annual DEI report (internal and external).
- Group Remuneration Policy: Defines compensation principles aligned with long-term strategy and sustainability, linking pay to risk-adjusted performance and discouraging excessive risk-taking, including sustainability risks. Supports equal opportunities, fair pay, inclusion, and work-life flexibility. Applies Group-wide (including external distribution networks and Material Risk Takers) with local adaptations as needed. Annually proposed by the Remuneration Committee, defined by the Board, and approved by the AGM.
- People & Culture Policy Framework: Central reference for HR rules, programs, and processes across UniCredit S.p.A., Group legal entities, and foreign branches (updated version forthcoming). Ensures consistent people management, regulatory compliance, professional skills development, and alignment with strategic goals.
- Recruiting Process Regulation: Establishes transparent, consistent, legally compliant hiring aligned with UniCredit values and Code of Conduct; ensures fair, unbiased treatment of candidates. For internal use and implemented by People & Culture and line managers; references relevant Italian and supervisory regulations.
- Training and Education Guidelines: Central reference for learning policies (currently for UniCredit S.p.A., to be extended Group-wide), aligned with Banca d’Italia Circular 285 clarifications. Ensures consistent capability building so employees have the skills needed for their responsibilities. Published on the intranet with involved stakeholders in policy development.

nodes.title: Group remuneration policy:
nodes.heading: Group remuneration policy :

- Human Rights Commitment:

  - Standards referenced: UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR, ILO core conventions, UNGPs, OECD Guidelines, UN Global Compact, UN PRI, IFC Performance Standards, World Bank EHS Guidelines, UNEP FI PRB, Equator Principles, Women’s Empowerment Principles, UNDRIP, and the Declaration on Human Rights Defenders.
  - Governance: Approved by the Group Non-Financial Risk Committee chaired by the Group CEO (June 2024). Effectiveness monitored via existing group policies (e.g., reputational risk, whistleblowing, anti-harassment).

  - Transparency: Progress reported via Sustainability Statements and an annual DEI report (internal and external).

- Group Remuneration Policy:
  - Purpose: Principles and standards for compensation aligned with long-term strategy and sustainability; links pay to risk-adjusted performance; discourages excessive and sustainability-related risk-taking.

  - Applicability: Across the organization, including external distribution networks; fully applied to Material Risk Takers with local adaptations.

- Training and Education Guidelines:
  - Role: Central reference for People & Culture rules, programs, and processes at UniCredit S.p.A., to be extended groupwide.
  - Alignment: Meets Banca d’Italia Circular 285 requirements; ensures consistent management and that personnel have skills necessary for their responsibilities.

nodes.title: Training and education guidelines:

- Context: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Sustainability statements) detailing Group-wide policies, commitments, and frameworks that govern ESG, human rights, people management, customer protection, and data privacy.

nodes.title: Global policy against harassment, sexual misconduct, bullying and retaliation:
nodes.heading: Global policy against harassment, sexual misconduct, bullying and retaliation :
nodes.start_phrase: The policy, aligned with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Group's values, outlines UniCredit’s commitment to fost ering a respectful and professional workplace free from harassment, sexual misconduct, bullying, and retaliation.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines UniCredit’s global policy against harassment, sexual misconduct, bullying, and retaliation, aligned with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Group values. Emphasizes prevention, detection, enforcement, and monitoring; support and protection from retaliation for reporters (including third parties); equal treatment and dignity; and awareness of how behavior may be perceived. Applies across all Group entities and employees, internally and externally, and promotes diversity, inclusion, and employer attractiveness.
- Presents UniCredit’s annual Modern Slavery Act and human trafficking statement (published since 2016), detailing measures to mitigate risks in business operations and the supply chain. Aligns with the UK Modern Slavery Act 2015 (Section 54), ILO core conventions, ICESCR, ICCPR, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, and UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking. Covers commitment to international norms, integrity-focused internal policies, supplier due diligence and ongoing assessments, and employee training on human rights. Latest statement approved by the Board and signed by the CEO in June 2024, applying to UniCredit S.p.A. and UniCredit Bank AG.
- Describes the Group privacy policy establishing a uniform approach to personal data protection for employees and clients across all legal entities. Provides a framework for compliance with GDPR 2016/679 and local laws, supported by business advisory, monitoring, and education to ensure trust and data protection. Clarifies Data Controller accountability, supported by the Data Protection Officer’s advice.
- Details Customer Protection rules for offering banking products and services, setting principles and standards to meet external regulatory obligations. References key EU regulations and guidelines: Consumer Credit Directive (2008/48/EC), Mortgage Credit Directive (2014/17/EU), Payment Accounts Directive (2014/92/EU), PSD2 (2015/2366/EU) for transparency, Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive (2014/49/EU), and EBA product oversight and governance guidelines (EBA-GL-2015). Policy approved by the Group Compliance Officer; applies to all Group companies, products, customer types, and channels; implementation monitored via intranet tools and processes.

nodes.title: Statement on Modern Slavery Act and human trafficking:
nodes.heading: Statement on Modern Slavery Act and human trafficking :
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit statement demonstrates its commitment on promoting the respect for human rights, and it must be read in conjunction with human rights commitment.
nodes.summary:
- UniCredit outlines a Global Policy against harassment, sexual misconduct, bullying, and retaliation, aligned with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Group values. It focuses on prevention, detection, enforcement, and continuous monitoring; supports and protects reporters (employees and third parties) from retaliation; promotes equal treatment and dignity; requires employees to consider how their behavior is perceived; applies internally and externally across all Group entities and employees; and reinforces diversity, inclusion, and employer attractiveness.

- The Statement on the Modern Slavery Act and human trafficking reaffirms UniCredit’s human rights commitment and details measures to mitigate slavery and trafficking risks in operations and supply chains. It references UK Modern Slavery Act 2015 (section 54), ILO Fundamental Conventions, ICESCR, ICCPR, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, and UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking. Published annually since 2016, it covers adherence to international norms, integrity-focused internal policies, supplier minimum requirements and due diligence (pre‑engagement and ongoing), and employee training. The latest statement was approved by the Board and signed by the CEO in June 2024 for UniCredit S.p.A. and UniCredit Bank AG.

- The Group privacy policy sets a unified Group-wide framework for protecting personal data of individuals (employees, clients, and certain individuals linked to corporates), ensuring compliance with GDPR 2016/679 and local regulations. It is supported by business advisory, monitoring, and education, with accountability resting on the Data Controller (via delegated functions) and guidance from the Data Protection Officer.

- Customer Protection rules establish principles and standards for offering banking products and services in line with EU sectoral regulations, including the Consumer Credit Directive (2008/48/EC), Mortgage Credit Directive (2014/17/EU), Payment Accounts Directive (2014/92/EU), PSD2 (2015/2366/EU) for transparency, Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive (2014/49/EU), and EBA guidelines on product oversight and governance (EBA-GL-2015). Approved by the Group Compliance Officer, they apply to all Group companies, all product forms, all customer segments, and all channels, with implementation monitored via intranet tools and processes.

nodes.title: Customer Protection rules:
nodes.heading: Customer Protection rules :
nodes.start_phrase: The Customer Protection rules relating to the offer of banking products and services define principles and standards for mana ging the obligations arising from the regulatory requirements set forth in the external sectorial regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Sustainability statements) detailing key Group policies and procedures on human rights, conduct, customer protection, privacy, tax, whistleblowing, and anti-corruption.
- Global policy against harassment, sexual misconduct, bullying and retaliation: Commitment to a respectful, safe workplace; prevention, detection, enforcement, and monitoring; protection and support for reporters (employees and third parties) against retaliation; applies across all Group entities and behaviors inside/outside the workplace; promotes diversity and inclusion and employer attractiveness.

- Customer Protection rules: Principles and standards for offering banking products/services in compliance with EU sector regulations (Consumer Credit, Mortgage Credit, Payment Accounts, PSD2 transparency, Deposit Guarantee, EBA product governance); approved by the Group Compliance Officer; applies to all Group companies, products, customer types, and channels; implementation monitored via intranet processes.
- Code of Conduct: Available online; rooted in values (Caring, Ownership, Integrity); sets conduct standards for employees and third parties across key compliance risks (client interests, antitrust, market integrity, AML/CTF, sanctions, anti-bribery/corruption, data protection); Board-approved, Group-wide; top management responsible for culture and enforcement; references additional Italian Model 231/2001 Code of Ethics where applicable.
- Group tax strategy policy: Compliance with all applicable tax laws, transparency with tax authorities, timely payment of taxes, avoidance of double taxation, and maintenance of tax efficiency; cooperative relationships with authorities (e.g., Italy’s Cooperative Compliance since 2016); robust monitoring system; Board-approved, communicated Group-wide, periodically reviewed; Tax Function oversees implementation and updates.
- Whistleblowing procedure: Protects whistleblowers and prohibits retaliation in line with EU Directive 2019/1937; encourages reporting via defined channels; covers illegal/unfair/unethical conduct, regulatory breaches (including EU law), and internal rule violations; may exceed local legal requirements; CEO-approved; aligned with the Code of Conduct and anti-harassment policy; available online.
- Global anti-bribery and anti-corruption policy: Zero-tolerance stance; sets principles to identify/prevent bribery and corruption; communicates expectations internally and externally; establishes a Group-wide ABC framework; aligns with UK Bribery Act, FCPA, Sapin II, and OECD Anti-Bribery Convention.
