nodes.title: Anti-fraud policy:
nodes.heading: Anti-fraud policy :
nodes.start_phrase: The objective of the anti-fraud policy is to ensure that the internal and external fraud risks are adequately identified, understood, and assessed.
nodes.summary:
- Group-wide policy governance: A CEO-approved policy applies to all UniCredit Group legal entities, governing bodies, employees, tied agents, and temps across all activities, with stricter local laws taking precedence.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a fraud management system for identifying, assessing, and governing internal/external fraud risks; defines roles and responsibilities; aligns with EU Directive 2015/2366; implemented by Group Security and applicable to UniCredit S.p.A. and all Group entities.
- Supplier qualification and third-party risk: Aligned with ILO Fundamental Conventions and UN Global Compact; sets pre-sourcing screening criteria to ensure compliance, sustainability, and financial soundness; manages corruption, reputational, and economic risks by excluding non-qualified suppliers; promotes ethical and sustainability standards; maintains a qualified suppliers list for Procurement-led sourcing.
- Screening methodology: Uses external risk-provider scores and Procurement/Compliance checks (anti-corruption, adverse media); where scores are unavailable, relies on supplier questionnaires including environmental and social aspects; requires periodic reviews and continuous monitoring for incidents or score changes.
- Procurement scope: Supplier qualification applies when Group Procurement centrally manages negotiations/purchases; acknowledges some categories/thresholds are handled outside Procurement.
- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles and minimum requirements for end-to-end management of expenditures and investments (demand-to-pay); classifies expenditures (P&L impact) vs. investments (long-term, multi-year utility).
- Roles and responsibilities: Group Cost Management oversees Group-level expenditure approvals, monitors Group and UniCredit S.p.A. non-HR costs, manages Group ICT demand, and supports the Projects & Expenses Committee (PEC); Group Procurement centrally manages purchasing to optimize costs.

nodes.title: Supplier qualification process:
nodes.heading: Supplier qualification process :
nodes.start_phrase: Aligned with International Labour Organization's (ILO) Fundamental Human Rights Conventions and the UN Global Compact princip les, the supplier qualification process defines the criteria and methods of third -party screening prior to the involvement of the supplier in a possible sourcing action for the purchase of goods/services as part of the activities managed by Procurement.
nodes.summary:
- Group-wide policy governance and scope: CEO-approved policy applies to all UniCredit Group legal entities, governing bodies, employees, tied agents and temporary staff across all business activities, with mandatory compliance to local laws; where local rules are stricter, they prevail.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a Group-wide fraud management system to identify, understand and assess internal and external fraud risks; clarifies roles and responsibilities in fraud governance; incorporates EU Directive 2015/2366 requirements; Group Security is responsible for implementation.
- Supplier qualification process: Aligned with ILO Fundamental Conventions and UN Global Compact; sets criteria and methods for third-party screening before sourcing. Objectives include selecting compliant, sustainable and financially sound suppliers; managing third-party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational, economic); promoting ethical and sustainability principles; and maintaining a list of qualified suppliers for Procurement-led sourcing. Screening uses external risk scores plus Procurement/Compliance checks (anti-corruption, negative news); when scores are unavailable, uses questionnaires including environmental and social aspects; includes periodic reviews and continuous risk monitoring.
- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles and minimum requirements to manage expenditures and investments from demand to pay. Clarifies classifications (expenditures affecting P&L vs multi-year investments). Roles: Group Cost Management (steers approval process, monitors Group and UniCredit S.p.A. NHR costs, manages ICT demand and Projects & Expenses Committee activities) and Group Procurement (centralized purchasing for cost optimization).

nodes.title: Expenditure regulation:
nodes.heading: Expenditure regulation :
nodes.start_phrase: This global policy has the purpose to define principles and minimum requirements necessary to manage expenditures and investm ents, from demand to pay.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: A Group-wide policy, approved by the CEO, applies to all UniCredit legal entities, governing bodies, employees, tied agents, and temporary staff, to be implemented in line with local laws, adopting the stricter local requirements where applicable.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a fraud management system for all Group entities to identify, assess, and proactively mitigate internal and external fraud risks; defines roles and responsibilities; aligns with EU Directive 2015/2366; Group Security oversees implementation.
- Supplier qualification: Aligned with ILO Core Conventions and UN Global Compact principles; sets third‑party screening criteria before sourcing; aims to select compliant, sustainable, and financially sound suppliers, manage third‑party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational, economic), promote ethical and sustainability standards, and maintain a qualified supplier list for Procurement-led sourcing.
- Supplier screening mechanics: Centralized by Group Procurement for centrally managed purchases; uses external risk provider scores, anti‑corruption and adverse news checks by Procurement/Compliance; relies on questionnaires (including environmental/social aspects) when data are unavailable; includes periodic reviews and incident/risk score change monitoring.
- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles/minimum requirements for managing expenditures and investments from demand to payment; distinguishes P&L expenditures from multi‑year investments.
- Roles in spending: Group Cost Management steers Group-level approvals, monitors Group and UniCredit S.p.A. NHR costs, manages Group ICT demand, and PEC activities; Group Procurement centrally manages purchases to optimize costs.
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure: Presents methodology and KPIs for Taxonomy eligibility/alignment, enhancing transparency and supporting the transition to a low‑carbon economy; focuses on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- GAR results: 2024 Turnover-based GAR is 1.36% on €547bn total GAR assets (vs. 1.16% on €551bn in 2023), mainly driven by climate change mitigation exposures; acknowledges data gaps due to reliance on counterparties subject to NFRD.
- Calculation perimeter and exclusions: Includes only undertakings with mandatory NFRD disclosures; excludes exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers; uses only counterparty KPIs (no use‑of‑proceeds within Article 8 templates); T‑1 templates published but not fully comparable due to perimeter changes.
- Methodology for corporates and guarantees: Uses weighted averages of financing activities and counterparties’ Taxonomy-aligned activity shares; sources NFRD reports via an external provider; applies parent company KPIs where relevant; if CCM/CCA breakdown is missing, values are included in total columns, which may exceed component sums.
- Mortgages to households: For collateralized loans, assesses “Acquisition” perimeter under Delegated Regulation 2021/2139; excludes “Renovation” and motor vehicles due to data limitations; identifies “green loans” using Energy Performance Certificate and Primary Energy Demand data for eligibility KPIs.

nodes.title: Environmental information
nodes.heading: Environmental information

nodes.summary:
- Group-wide policy governance: A CEO-approved policy applies across all UniCredit legal entities, covering governing bodies, employees, tied agents, and temporary staff. It must comply with local laws, with more restrictive local requirements taking precedence.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a fraud management system to identify, assess, and proactively address internal and external fraud risks, clarifying roles and responsibilities. It incorporates requirements from EU Directive 2015/2366, applies to UniCredit S.p.A. and all Group entities, and is implemented by Group Security.
- Supplier qualification: Aligned with ILO Fundamental Conventions and UN Global Compact principles, the process screens third parties before sourcing. Objectives include selecting suppliers on compliance, sustainability, and financial criteria; managing third-party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational, economic); promoting ethical and sustainability principles; and maintaining a qualified supplier list. Group Procurement leads when purchases are centralized; some categories/thresholds sit outside Procurement.
- Supplier screening methods: Uses external risk scores plus Procurement/Compliance checks (anti-corruption, adverse news). If external scores are unavailable, uses supplier questionnaires covering environmental and social aspects. Qualifications are periodically reviewed, with ongoing monitoring for incidents or risk score changes.
- Expenditure regulation: A global policy governs expenditures and investments from demand to pay. Expenditures affect P&L; investments are long-term with multi-year utility. Key roles: Group Cost Management (approval steering, cost monitoring, ICT demand, Projects & Expenses Committee) and Group Procurement (central purchasing and cost optimization).
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure: Presents eligibility/alignment KPIs and the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) to enhance sustainability transparency and support transition to a low-carbon economy. Only undertakings subject to NFRD are included; exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals are excluded. Use-of-proceeds information is not included in Article 8 templates.
- GAR results: Turnover-based GAR is 1.36% on total GAR assets of €547bn, up from 1.16% on €551bn at year-end 2023, driven mainly by climate change mitigation exposures.
- Calculation approach: Portfolio segmented by asset class with differing methods as required. T-1 templates are published, but comparisons are not meaningful due to a changed 2024 perimeter.
- Methodology for corporates and guarantees: KPIs are a weighted average of financing activities and counterparties’ Taxonomy-aligned activity shares. NFRD entities include those meeting criteria directly or indirectly; where a counterparty contributes to a parent’s KPIs, the parent’s KPIs are used. If counterparties do not split KPIs by objective (e.g., CCM vs CCA), values are recorded in TOTAL columns, which may exceed the sum of components.
- Household collateralized loans: Focuses on the “Acquisition” perimeter (excludes “Renovation” and motor vehicles due to data gaps). “Green loans” are identified using EPC and PED data per Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 for eligibility.

Applies when purchases are centrally managed by Group Procurement; some categories/thresholds are outside Procurement’s scope.

- Environmental information – EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure:
  - Purpose: Transparency on sustainability and support for low-carbon transition through Taxonomy eligibility/alignment KPIs.

Use-of-proceeds info not included; only counterparty KPIs considered. T-1 templates provided, but year-on-year comparability is limited due to a changed disclosure perimeter.

    - Loans collateralized to households: Focus on “Acquisition” perimeter under Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 (excludes “Renovation” and “Motor vehicles”); identification of “green loans” based on top-performing buildings using EPC and PED data for Eligibility KPIs.

- Anti-fraud policy: aims to identify, assess and manage internal/external fraud risks; defines Group-wide fraud management system, roles and responsibilities; incorporates EU Directive (EU) 2015/2366 requirements; Group Security responsible for implementation.
- Supplier qualification process: aligned with ILO Core Conventions and UN Global Compact; sets screening criteria and methods to assess suppliers on compliance, sustainability and financial soundness; manages third-party risks (corruption, reputational, economic) by excluding non-qualified suppliers; promotes ethical and sustainability principles; maintains qualified supplier lists for sourcing; primarily managed centrally by Group Procurement (not all purchases fall under Procurement); risk screening via external providers plus Procurement/Compliance checks on anti-corruption and adverse news; questionnaires used by exception; periodic reviews and ongoing risk monitoring.
- Expenditure regulation: global policy defining principles and minimum requirements to manage expenditures and investments from demand to payment; applies to all disbursements across the Group; distinguishes expenditures (P&L impact) vs investments (multi-year utility); roles include Group Cost Management (steering approvals, monitoring Group and UniCredit S.p.A. NHR costs, managing ICT demand, PEC activities) and Group Procurement (centralized purchasing for cost optimization).
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 environmental disclosures:
  - GAR (green asset ratio) Turnover-based is 1.36% on €547bn total GAR assets in 2024 (vs 1.16% on €551bn in 2023), mainly driven by climate change mitigation activities.
  - Methodological scope: includes only undertakings under NFRD mandatory reporting; excludes central governments, central banks and supranationals; uses counterparties’ actual reported KPIs; use-of-proceeds data not included, so only counterparty KPIs considered; T-1 templates published but not comparable due to scope changes.
  - Financial and non-financial corporates and financial guarantees: KPIs based on weighted average of financing activities and counterparties’ Taxonomy-aligned activity share; data gathered via external provider; NFRD scope includes direct and indirect (via parent) reporters, using parent KPIs where applicable; when CCM/CCA split is missing, values reported in TOTAL column.
  - Loans collateralized to households: focuses on “Acquisition” perimeter (excludes “Renovation” and “Motor vehicles” green-loan identification constraints); eligibility uses EPC and PED; alignment for assets built before 31 Dec 2020 with documented EPC=A; Italy only Top-15% approach for pre-2020; NZEB approach for assets built after 31 Dec 2020; conservative DNSH physical risk assessment aligned with Pillar 3 Template 5, no adaptation plans considered.
  - Motor vehicles to households: eligible if loans finance vehicle purchases; aligned only if financing low-emission vehicles.
  - Assets under Management: perimeter based on Group external reporting of collective investment funds; numerator is weighted average of portfolio-level Taxonomy-aligned proportions using underlying holdings’ actual KPIs via external provider; total AuM includes all asset classes, while “of which” figures include only equity and debt (so totals can exceed components).
  - New business flow: calculated as transaction-level delta stock between year-end 2024 and year-end 2023 to capture new originations.
  - Nuclear and gas-related activities: eligibility, non-eligibility and alignment disclosed per amended Disclosures Delegated Act (Art. 8(6)-(8)); computed using latest available KPIs for NFRD-subject non-financial counterparties.

nodes.title: Motor vehicles to households

nodes.summary:
- Outlines UniCredit’s methodology for EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment KPIs within the Sustainability Statement, applying conservative assumptions and external data sources.
- Real estate exposures: considers only documented EPC=A for assets built before Dec 31, 2020; applies a Top-15% energy performance approach for Italian counterparties (pre-2020) and the NZEB (Nearly Zero Energy Building) approach for assets built after Dec 31, 2020; NZEB and Top-15% data collected by region via an external provider.
- Do No Significant Harm (DNSH) assessment integrates physical climate risk analysis aligned with Pillar 3 Template 5 thresholds and climate data; excludes adaptation plans and other mitigating actions.
- Motor vehicles to households: eligibility covers loans for vehicle purchases; alignment limited to loans for low-emission vehicles.
- Asset Under Management (AuM) KPIs: perimeter based on collective investment fund volumes disclosed in Group results; numerator is a weighted average share of Taxonomy-aligned activities at portfolio level using underlying holdings’ actual KPIs from an external provider; total AuM includes all asset classes, while “of which debt” and “of which equity” include only those categories, so totals may exceed the sum of those components.
- New business flow: measured as transaction-level delta stock between Dec 31, 2024 and Dec 31, 2023 to capture new originations.
- Additional disclosures on nuclear energy and fossil gas per Article 8(6)-(8) of the amended Disclosures Delegated Act (effective Jan 1, 2023); KPIs computed using the most recent data for non-financial corporate counterparties subject to the NFRD.

nodes.title: New Business

- Real estate/housing: pre-31 Dec 2020 assets counted only with documented EPC A; for Italian counterparties, applies Top-15% approach for pre-2021 assets; for assets built after 31 Dec 2020, applies the NZEB (Nearly Zero Energy Building) approach; data on NZEB and Top-15% sourced from an external provider.
- Integrates physical climate risk into the DNSH assessment, aligned to Pillar 3 Template 5 thresholds and climate data; excludes adaptation plans or other mitigations to remain conservative.
- Motor vehicles to households: eligibility includes loans for vehicle purchases; alignment limited to loans for low-emission vehicles.
- Asset under Management (AuM) KPIs: scope based on collective investment funds disclosed in Group results; numerator is a weighted average share of Taxonomy-aligned activities at aggregated portfolio level using underlying holdings’ actual KPIs; data collected via an external provider. Total AuM covers all asset classes, while “of which” breakdowns include only debt and equity, so totals can exceed the sum of those components.
- New Business flow: measured as transaction-level delta stock between 31 Dec 2024 and 31 Dec 2023, capturing only new originations.

nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, Sustainability statements, providing EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures for credit institutions, including methodologies and detailed quantitative KPIs (GAR stock and flow, off-balance sheet KPIs), with Annex VI templates.

- Methodology highlights:
  - Real estate alignment: For assets built before Dec 31, 2020, only documented EPC=A counted; for Italy, Top-15% energy performance approach applied; for assets built after Dec 31, 2020, NZEB (Nearly Zero Energy Building) approach used. Regional NZEB and Top-15% data sourced from an external provider. Conservative stance (only adequate documentation considered).
  - DNSH assessment: Integrates analysis of physical climate risks aligned with thresholds and climate data used in Pillar 3 Template 5; excludes adaptation plans or other mitigating actions for conservatism.
  - Household vehicles: Eligible exposures are loans for motor vehicle purchases; aligned exposures limited to low-emission vehicles.
  - Assets under Management (AuM): Perimeter based on collective investment funds disclosed in Group external communications. Alignment calculated via weighted average of portfolio-level Taxonomy-aligned proportions using external provider data on underlying holdings’ KPIs. Total AuM includes all asset classes; “of which debt/equity” only includes those classes, so totals can exceed the sum of components.
  - New business (flow): Determined via transaction-level delta stock between Dec 31, 2024 and Dec 31, 2023 (new originations only).
  - Nuclear and gas: Eligibility, non-eligibility, and alignment disclosed per Article 8(6)-(8) of the amended Disclosures Delegated Act (effective Jan 1, 2023); KPIs calculated for NFRD-subject non-financial counterparties using most recent data.

- Summary KPIs (as presented):
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: Total environmentally sustainable assets €7,432m; 1.36% turnover-based and 1.91% CapEx-based; coverage over total assets 68.99%; 56.10% of assets excluded from the numerator; 31.01% excluded from the denominator.
  - GAR flow: €2,208m; 2.19% turnover-based and 3.42% CapEx-based; coverage 26.94%.
  - Additional KPIs: Financial guarantees €291m (5.81% turnover-based; 10.73% CapEx-based). AuM €3,225m (9.22% turnover-based; 14.12% CapEx-based).

- Detailed GAR composition (turnover- and CapEx-based):
  - Comprehensive breakdowns by counterparty type (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households, local governments), instrument (loans, debt securities including UoP, equity), and environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO), including use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling categories.
  - Households: Large eligible exposure primarily through residential mortgages; aligned portions include eligible building loans and low-emission vehicle loans.
  - Exclusions and coverage: Significant portions excluded from GAR numerator or denominator per Article 7 (e.g., SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD, non-EU non-NFRD counterparties). Assets not covered for GAR include central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, and trading book items.

- Comparative view 2024 vs 2023:
  - Increase in Taxonomy-aligned amounts and ratios year over year (e.g., total aligned under turnover approach rising from €6,396m in 2023 to €7,432m in 2024; higher CapEx-based alignment).
  - Expanded off-balance sheet disclosures with higher eligible/aligned figures for financial guarantees and AuM.

- Data sourcing and conservatism: Reliance on external providers for building performance benchmarks and AuM portfolio KPIs; strict documentation requirements and exclusion of mitigation/adaptation plans emphasize conservative alignment measurement.

nodes.title: GAR sector information - Turnover based
nodes.heading: 2 GAR sector information - Turnover based
nodes.start_phrase: (€ million)
nodes.summary:
- Focus: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures within UniCredit’s Sustainability Statement of the 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, as at 31.12.2024.
- Content type: Detailed, turnover-based sector breakdown (in € million) and related KPI percentages for assets in scope of GAR, following EU Taxonomy/NFRD/EBA templates.

What the tables cover
- GAR sector information – Turnover based:
  - Granular breakdown by NACE Rev. 2 four‑digit sectors for non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD.
  - For each sector: gross carrying amount and “of which environmentally sustainable” amounts mapped to the six EU Taxonomy environmental objectives:
    - Climate Change Mitigation (CCM)
    - Climate Change Adaptation (CCA)
    - Sustainable use and protection of Water and Marine Resources (WTR)
    - Transition to a Circular Economy (CE)
    - Pollution prevention and control (PPC)
    - Protection and restoration of Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO)
  - A total column consolidates environmentally sustainable amounts across all objectives.
  - Coverage spans manufacturing (chemicals, cement, metals, electronics, machinery, vehicles), utilities (electricity production/transmission/distribution, gas, steam), water and waste (water supply, waste collection/treatment, recovery), construction and civil engineering (buildings, roads, rail, utilities, water projects), transport (rail, road services, water), telecommunications and IT, real estate (buy/sell, rental and operating, management), professional and research services, leasing, and selected social care activities.
  - Illustrative sectors with notable environmentally sustainable amounts include:
    - Electricity: production, transmission and distribution (D35.x), showing significant CCM alignment and some contributions to other objectives.
    - Water and waste: water collection/treatment/supply (E36.00) spanning CCM, CCA, WTR; waste collection and treatment (E38.11/E38.21) with strong Circular Economy components.
    - Transport and infrastructure: rail construction and services (F42.12; H49.10/H49.20) and utility projects for electricity/telecom (F42.22) showing CCM alignment.
    - Manufacturing: basic iron and steel (C24.10), cement (C23.51), selected electrical/electronic equipment (C26–C27), machinery for paper production (C28.95), and motor vehicles (C29.10) with CCM and some CCA entries.
    - Real estate: rental/operating of own or leased real estate (L68.20) with material CCM/CCA totals.
    - Leasing of cars and light vehicles (N77.11) contributing to CCM.

- GAR KPI (stock) – Turnover based – Percentages:
  - Presents the proportion of total covered assets funding Taxonomy‑relevant (eligible) and Taxonomy‑aligned activities for CCM, CCA and WTR, including “of which” categories (use of proceeds, transitional, enabling, as applicable).
  - Breakdown by counterparty segments:
    - Financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financials, management companies, insurance undertakings)
    - Non‑financial undertakings
    - Households (including loans collateralised by residential property, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans)
    - Local governments (housing and other)
    - Collateral obtained (residential and commercial real estate)
  - Headline indications:
    - Total GAR assets represent about 20.2% of total covered assets, with c.1.32% Taxonomy‑aligned for CCM, including identified use‑of‑proceeds, transitional and enabling portions.
    - Small but positive shares are reported for CCA and WTR eligibility/alignment.
    - Households show a sizable eligible share driven by mortgage exposure, with a measurable aligned component via use‑of‑proceeds.
    - Non‑financial corporates contribute to both eligible and aligned CCM shares; financial undertakings add smaller aligned portions mainly via securities and equity holdings.

Purpose and use
- Demonstrates UniCredit’s exposure to Taxonomy‑eligible and aligned activities at detailed sector level, quantifying environmentally sustainable financing by objective and aggregating to KPI percentages, in line with EU GAR disclosure requirements.

  - Total taxonomy-eligible assets: 20.46% of total covered assets; taxonomy-aligned: 1.36%.
  - Coverage of total assets in the GAR perimeter: 68.99%.
  - Key contributors: households (eligible 17.28%, aligned 0.51%, largely residential mortgages), non-financial undertakings (eligible 1.56%, aligned 0.63%), and financial undertakings (eligible 1.60%, aligned 0.21%). Use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling shares are generally small.

nodes.summary:
- Section context: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, Consolidated report on operations – Sustainability statement, presenting EU Taxonomy reporting.
- Focus of content: Detailed disclosure of Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs:
  - Stock (Capex-based) metrics as a percentage of total covered assets for 31.12.2024 and 31.12.2023.
  - Flow (Turnover-based) metrics for 2024 as a percentage of the flow of total eligible assets.
- Scope and structure:
  - Breakdowns by EU Taxonomy environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), and Biodiversity & Ecosystems (BIO).
  - Classification into Taxonomy-eligible versus Taxonomy-aligned exposures, with “of which” sub-categories for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Portfolio segmentation: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (residential mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local government financing, and collateral real estate taken into possession.
- 2024 stock highlights (Capex-based):
  - Total Taxonomy-eligible exposures around 21% of total covered assets; Taxonomy-aligned around 1.9%.
  - Approximately 69% of total assets are covered by the GAR denominator.
  - Households, especially residential mortgages, represent the largest share of eligible exposures (~17% of total covered assets), with a notable eligible share in building renovation loans.
  - Non-financial corporates contribute a smaller but material portion of eligible and aligned exposures; financial undertakings show modest aligned shares.
- 2023 stock comparison:
  - Total eligible around 19.7% and aligned around 1.78%, with coverage of total assets also circa 69%, indicating a year-on-year increase in eligible and a slight increase in aligned exposures.
  - Similar portfolio and objective breakdowns provided for comparability.
- 2024 flow highlights (Turnover-based):
  - New origination/movements show CCM as the main driver (c.13% eligible; c.2.1% aligned).
  - Additional aligned contributions from CCA and WTR are present but smaller.
  - By segment, financial undertakings and non-financial corporates contribute to both eligible and aligned flows; households add notably to eligible flows primarily via mortgages.
- Overall purpose: To evidence UniCredit’s alignment with the EU Taxonomy, quantify the share of assets financing environmentally sustainable activities, track progress year-on-year, and distinguish between eligible and fully aligned financing across objectives and portfolio segments.

- Context: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Consolidated report on operations, Sustainability statements) detailing EU Taxonomy disclosures for off-balance-sheet exposures as of 31 December 2024.
- Scope and KPIs: Reporting of “5 KPI off-balance sheet exposures” for:
  - Financial guarantees (FinGuar KPI)
  - Assets under management (AuM KPI)
- Measurement bases and views:
  - Stock and Flow perspectives
  - Turnover-based and Capex-based calculations
  - Percentages shown relative to total eligible off-balance-sheet assets
- Environmental coverage: All six EU Taxonomy environmental objectives
  - Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO)
- Classification detail:
  - Split between Taxonomy-eligible and Taxonomy-aligned proportions
  - Further “of which” breakdowns: use of proceeds, transitional, enabling
- Key results (totals across all objectives):
  - Stock, Turnover-based:
    - FinGuar: 22.64% eligible; 5.81% aligned (of which: use of proceeds 0.61%, enabling 2.17%; transitional negligible)
    - AuM: 26.83% eligible; 9.22% aligned (of which: use of proceeds 1.15%, enabling 4.55%)
  - Stock, Capex-based:
    - FinGuar: 26.61% eligible; 10.73% aligned (of which: use of proceeds 1.06%, enabling 4.46%)
    - AuM: 31.88% eligible; 14.12% aligned (of which: use of proceeds 1.32%, enabling 6.44%)
  - Flow, Turnover-based:
    - FinGuar: 26.07% eligible; 9.91% aligned (of which: use of proceeds 0.22%, enabling 4.25%)
    - AuM: no data reported
- Notable observations:
  - Climate Change Mitigation is the principal driver of eligibility/alignment; other objectives (WTR, CE, PPC, BIO) contribute marginally.
  - Transitional activities are negligible or not present in the reported splits.
  - The “enabling” and “use of proceeds” portions represent a subset of aligned exposures.

nodes.title: Additional disclosure on Nuclear and Gas related activities
nodes.heading: Additional disclosure on Nuclear and Gas related activities
nodes.start_phrase: The undertaking carries out, funds or has exposures to research, development, demonstration and deployment of innovative electricity generation facilities that produce energy from nuclear processes with minimal waste from the fuel cycle
nodes.summary:
- Section of UniCredit’s 2024 Consolidated Report (Sustainability statement) providing “Additional disclosure on Nuclear and Gas related activities” tied to the EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – Stock.
- Confirms the bank carries out, funds, or has exposures to multiple nuclear energy activities, all marked YES: R&D and deployment of innovative nuclear generation with minimal waste (4.26); construction and safe operation of new nuclear installations and safety upgrades using best available technologies (4.27); safe operation and safety upgrades of existing nuclear installations, including for district heating, industrial processes, and hydrogen production (4.28).
- Confirms exposures to fossil gas-related activities, all marked YES: construction/operation of electricity generation using fossil gaseous fuels (4.29); construction/refurbishment/operation of combined heat/cool and power generation using fossil gas (4.30); construction/refurbishment/operation of heat/cool generation using fossil gas (4.31).
- The disclosures indicate portfolio exposures (carrying out, funding, or other exposures) relevant for GAR reporting rather than an assessment of taxonomy alignment.
- Positioned within the ESG/Sustainability reporting to enhance transparency on nuclear and fossil gas-related exposures.

nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Consolidated report on operations – Sustainability statements) detailing EU Taxonomy disclosures.
- Focus: Quantitative disclosure of taxonomy-eligible but not taxonomy-aligned activities and taxonomy non-eligible activities, presented for both Turnover- and CapEx-based KPIs, with split between Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA).

Main points
- Taxonomy-eligible but not aligned (Turnover-based):
  - Total: €103,459,542k (18.97% of the KPI denominator)
  - CCM: €103,355,206k (18.95%); CCA: €104,336k (0.02%)
  - Minimal amounts reported under Delegated Regulation sections 4.28–4.31; no amounts for 4.26–4.27.
  - “Other” eligible-not-aligned activities dominate: €102,970,074k (18.81% total; €102,865,738k CCM; €104,336k CCA).

- Taxonomy-eligible but not aligned (CapEx-based):
  - Total: €103,465,539k (18.97%)
  - CCM: €103,129,476k (18.91%); CCA: €336,063k (0.06%)
  - Small amounts under sections 4.28–4.31; none for 4.26–4.27.
  - “Other” eligible-not-aligned activities dominate: €103,134,232k (18.84% total; €102,798,280k CCM; €335,952k CCA).

- Taxonomy non-eligible economic activities:
  - Turnover non-eligible total: €435,471,160k (79.54%)
  - CapEx non-eligible total: €432,656,600k (79.02%)
  - “Other” non-eligible category represents nearly all non-eligible amounts; only negligible figures recorded against specific sections (e.g., small amounts in 4.28 and 4.30).

Key takeaways
- A large majority of the denominator is taxonomy non-eligible (~79%).
- Around 19% is taxonomy-eligible but not aligned, primarily contributing to climate change mitigation; adaptation shares are minimal (≤0.06%).
- Disclosures are broken down by specific sections (4.26–4.31) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, with most activity concentrated in the “other” categories rather than specific listed sections.

nodes.summary: Introduction to UniCredit Group’s 2024 Transition Plan for climate change mitigation, detailing adoption to convert Net Zero commitments into actions and alignment with Net Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA) and Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ), meeting CSRD E1 climate requirements. The plan targets becoming a Net Zero Bank by 2050, with 2030 intermediate financed-emissions targets for six NZBA-identified, carbon‑intensive sectors, set per NZBA principles, international standards, best practices, and 1.5°C pathways. Targets apply Group‑wide via a centralized framework to ensure consistency and synergy, covering own emissions (Scope 1 and 2, market‑based) and financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) in line with the Paris Agreement. UniCredit is not excluded from EU Paris-aligned benchmarks; further target details are referenced in section E1‑4.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase:
In line with the effort sustained in the previous year s, in 2024 UniCredit Group adopted a Transition Plan to support the achievement of our Net Zero
targets for f inanced and own emissions , and to convert our commitments into actions.
nodes.summary:
- EU Taxonomy non-eligible activities: Most turnover and capex in the KPI denominators are classified as “other taxonomy non-eligible” (≈79.5% of turnover; ≈79.0% of capex), with immaterial amounts in rows tied to specific Delegated Regulation sections.
- Climate strategy and transition plan (E1-1): UniCredit adopted a Group-wide Transition Plan in 2024 aligned with NZBA, GFANZ and CSRD E1, targeting Net Zero by 2050 and 2030 interim targets across six high-emitting sectors. Scope 1–2 (market-based) Net Zero by 2030; financed emissions (Scope 3, Cat. 15) aligned to Paris Agreement. Bank is not excluded from EU Paris-aligned benchmarks.
- Decarbonisation levers:
  - Own emissions: renewable electricity sourcing, space optimization, energy efficiency, and heating system transformation.
  - Financed emissions: sector-specific engagement, portfolio rebalancing, and support for transition technologies and projects.
- Sector strategies and examples:
  - Oil & Gas: client engagement on transition plans; shift financing toward alternative fuels; reduce most carbon-intensive activities; support hydrogen, biofuels, CCUS; sponsorships (World Hydrogen Congress) and membership (European Clean Hydrogen Alliance); financing biofuels/biomethane via infrastructure funds.
  - Power Generation: finance shift from fossil to renewables (wind, PV) via project finance; industry participation (Solar Association in CZ/SK; Climate & Sustainable Leaders).
  - Automotive: support electrification and value-chain opportunities (EV batteries, infrastructure); financing EV-only plant expansion for Mercedes-Benz in Hungary; “In Motion” value-chain approach.
  - Steel: signatory to Sustainable Steel Principles; support hydrogen/electrification pathways; MLA and lender to SACE-covered green loan for Salzgitter’s SALCOS project (DRI + EAF with green power/H2; targeted 95% emissions cut by 2033).
  - Shipping: align with IMO 2023 GHG strategy; finance next-gen vessels and retrofits; ongoing client engagement pending clearer global rules and fuel availability.
  - Commercial Real Estate: prioritize energy-efficient assets and retrofits; collect EPCs; financed Coima P39 (Nearly Zero Energy Building) in Milan; launched “One4Planet Green Buildings” loan in Italy.
  - Residential Real Estate: emphasize need for government incentives; launched “Mutuo Sostenibilità Energetica” mortgage in Italy (incl. EPC simulation; €83.3m disbursed by Dec 2024); new partnerships.
- Resources and enablement:
  - Group Net Zero program since 2022; cross-functional (ESG, Finance, Risk, Business, Digital), ~150 staff.
  - ICT upgrades for data pipelines, client transition-plan assessment, dashboards, deal/portfolio impact simulations, and tagging of transition finance; non-material ICT spend.
  - Group-wide training (Net Zero basics, client plan assessment, credit implications, transition finance); local expert teams and certified programs (e.g., Germany’s Sustainable Finance Experts).
- Business integration and governance:
  - Embedding Net Zero into planning, risk, and business processes; targets set at Group level, broken down and cascaded by division.
  - Net Zero KPIs included in Risk Appetite Framework; remuneration of Top Management linked to Net Zero KPIs.
  - Sector policies tightened to cease financing of most controversial carbon-intensive activities and phase out legacy exposure; ongoing policy updates.
  - Transition Plan approved by CEO, reviewed by Board (Feb 2024); 2030 targets similarly approved before disclosure.
- Implementation progress (2024):
  - Target setting: initial 2030 targets for Oil & Gas, Power, Automotive; added Steel (Jan 2024), Shipping and Commercial Real Estate (Jul 2024); 2022 baseline for Residential.
  - Monitoring: new process delivering periodic Net Zero impact reports to business; coverage expanded from initial sectors to Steel in 2024, with Shipping and Real Estate to follow by early 2025.
  - Risk management: Net Zero embedded in policies, RAF KPIs, credit strategies, and credit process; client clustering (leaders/aligning/laggards) with tailored engagement; greater use of green/transition finance.
  - Client transition-plan assessment: cross-industry questionnaire aligned to GFANZ, CDP, CA100+; scoring 0–100 into developed/early-stage/absent plans; piloted in 2024; plan to use external experts.
  - Products/services: green and sustainability-linked financing; public-program partnerships (KfW, EIF); internal definition of transition finance (EU Commission recommendations) codified in ESG Product Guidelines; third-party certification of client transition plans required for transition finance; ESG advisory supports origination and structuring.
  - Tools and partnerships: embedded assessment and steering tools; joined Open-es (with Cerved ESG scoring) to support client decarbonisation.
- Stakeholder dialogue:
  - Active in NZBA working groups; policy engagement via IIF, AFME, EBF on transition finance and planning.
  - Local collaborations (e.g., WWF Austria) to enhance sustainable product integration.
  - ESG Day 2024 with 13,000+ participants; launched “Skills for Transition” training program across six countries to upskill workforces for the green transition.
- Policies (E1-2): Climate policies address double materiality—impacts (Scopes 1–3), risks (notably credit risk from physical and transition factors), and opportunities (green investments/products, new markets). Smart Office Workplace policy drives operational footprint reduction; sector policies (Civil Nuclear, Coal, Defense, Mining, Oil & Gas, Tobacco, Water infrastructure) manage financed emissions and risk; ESG Product Guidelines define classification/reporting and guard against greenwashing.
- Actions and resources (E1-3) for own operations:
  - 2024 GHG inventory: Scope 1 = 24,412 tCO2e; Scope 2 market-based = 16,702 tCO2e (location-based = 100,830 tCO2e); Scope 3 (excl. Cat. 15) = 285,848 tCO2e; perimeter change limits comparability.
  - Continuous focus on space optimization, renewable electricity sourcing, energy efficiency in premises/data centers, and heating decarbonisation.

nodes.title: Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.2 Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.start_phrase: For the disclosure o f Climate change IROs, reference is made to Notes to the consolidated accounts, Part E - Information on risks and related hedging policies, Section 2 -Climate and environmental risks .
nodes.summary:
- ESG capabilities and training
  - Strengthening ESG advisory across client engagement, including local ESG Expert teams in Italy to support origination/structuring of ESG deals.
  - Germany’s Sustainable Finance Experts training (externally certified) for relationship managers and other roles.
  - Group-wide Net Zero training covering fundamentals, client transition plan assessment, engagement strategies and credit implications, and transition finance; new courses planned as sector scope expands.

- Stakeholder dialogue and industry engagement
  - Active participation in NZBA working groups; engagement with policymakers/regulators via IIF, AFME, and EBF on climate goals, transition finance, and planning.
  - Local collaborations, e.g., UniCredit Bank Austria with WWF Austria to expand sustainable investment options.
  - ESG Day 2024 (“A challenged future: choosing the path ahead”) with 13,000+ participants; session on managing sustainability trade-offs; launch of the “Skills for Transition” workers’ stream delivering funded training in six countries (IT, DE, BG, CZ, SK, RO).

- Climate impact, risks, and opportunities framework (E1-2)
  - Double Materiality coverage of impacts (Scopes 1–3 upstream/downstream), risks (credit risk from acute/chronic climate events and collateral devaluation), and opportunities (green investments, new ESG products/services, green tech financing, new markets).
  - Policies: Smart Office Workplace policy (space/energy optimization); sector policies (Civil Nuclear, Coal, Defense, Mining, Oil & Gas, Tobacco, Water infrastructure) to manage financed emissions and counterparty stability; ESG Product Guidelines for classifying/reporting ESG offerings and financing energy efficiency/renewables/adaptation.
  - Climate risk disclosures referenced in Notes, Part E, Section 2.

- Actions and resources (E1-3)
  - Own operations emissions 2024: Scope 1 24,412 tCO2e; Scope 2 market-based 16,702 tCO2e (location-based 100,830); Scope 3 (excl. cat. 15) 285,848 tCO2e; perimeter change limits comparability.
  - Operational decarbonization: first Italian bank corporate PPA to power Verona data centers; Smart Office Workplace Policy; smart energy controls, insulation, LEDs; optimized HVAC/lighting algorithms; energy management guidelines (since 2022) for set-points/schedules; conversion of fossil heating to heat pumps/district heating; self-produced renewables.
  - Investment and budgeting: ~€30m cash-out in 2024 for real estate decarbonization; ~€60m multi-year budget planned. Ongoing levers: space optimization, energy efficiency, heating transformation, renewable electricity and district heating/cooling, onsite generation.
  - Resourcing: ICT and HR are critical; financial resources mainly CapEx (intangible assets and PPE lines).

- Financed emissions progress toward 2030 targets (2023 data)
  - Oil & Gas: in-scope lending €4.7bn; financed emissions 10.2 MtCO2e (−52% vs 2021 baseline 21.4); target −29% vs 2021 (15.2 MtCO2e). Reduction driven by deleveraging non-strategic/Russian clients; possible temporary increases due to metric volatility and transition support.
  - Power Generation: lending €9.8bn; intensity 107 gCO2e/kWh (−49% vs 2021; below 2030 target 111). Shift toward “pure” renewables and green loans (~€5.5bn); potential temporary intensity uptick as traditional players transition.
  - Automotive: lending €2.0bn; intensity 116 gCO2/vkm (−28% vs 2021); 2030 target 95. Driven by financing EV projects and OEM production mix shift.
  - Steel: lending €1.9bn; intensity 1.50 tCO2/tSteel (+3% vs 2022 1.45); alignment score −0.17 (better than IEA/MPP benchmarks). Supporting low-carbon steel projects; target 1.11 by 2030.
  - Shipping: lending €2.5bn; portfolio intensity −1% vs 2022 (Passenger 14.0 gCO2e/GT-nm; Merchant 9.3 gCO2e/dwt-nm); 2030 target −30% vs 2022. Focus on financing efficient newbuilds and retrofits; larger impact expected from 2025 onward.
  - Commercial Real Estate: lending €30.6bn; intensity 43.4 kgCO2e/m2 (−2% vs 2022 44.2); 2030 target −44%/−55% vs 2022. Drivers: higher share of better-performing buildings in DE/AT and grid decarbonization in DE.
  - Residential Real Estate: baseline disclosed for 2022; intensity 35.8 kgCO2e/m2 in 2023 (−1.4% vs 36.3). Continued client support; government incentives seen as critical enablers.

- Metrics and targets (E1-4)
  - Own operations: Net Zero Scope 1 and 2 (market-based) by 2030 at Group level; base year revised to 2024. Segmentation of premises by control; non-controlled assets reported in Scope 3. Levers: renewable sourcing, space optimization, energy efficiency, heating transformation. Internal working group and staff engagement established.
  - Financed emissions: ambition for Net Zero by 2050; interim targets set for six sectors (Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, Steel, Shipping, Commercial Real Estate); coal phase-out by 2028 with limited green financing exceptions.
  - Sectors excluded for low materiality: Aluminum, Cement, Aviation (each <1% of carbon-intensive exposure, lending <€1bn; total excluded sectors kept <3% of carbon-intensive portfolio). Agriculture under monitoring pending policy/methodology/data maturity.
  - Target-setting methodology: cross-functional process; internal modeling aligned with SBTi, PCAF, IEA, and NZBA guidance; on-balance sheet lending in scope; baselines confirmed; scenarios selected for 1.5°C alignment, credibility, geographic detail, and customizability.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.3 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: With regard to the relationship with policy objectives, pl ease refer to MDR -P – Policies adopted to manage material sustainability matters section .
nodes.summary:
- Focus on financed emissions and real estate portfolio decarbonisation:
  - Commercial Real Estate (Italy, Germany, Austria): emissions intensity fell from 44.2 to 43.4 kgCO2e/m2 in 2023 (-2%), driven by better building energy performance and German grid decarbonisation. 2023 in-scope lending €30.6bn. 2030 target: -44% to -55% vs 2022, contingent on regulatory and grid developments.
  - Residential Real Estate (mortgages to households in Italy, Germany, Austria): emissions intensity decreased from 36.3 to 35.8 kgCO2e/m2 in 2023 (-1.4%). No 2030 target yet due to regulatory uncertainty; ongoing support to clients and call for government incentives.

- Resources and financing for climate plan execution:
  - ICT and HR resources are critical to the transition plan; misallocation poses feasibility risks.
  - Related CapEx primarily in ICT recorded under intangible assets and PPE (referenced to notes in consolidated accounts).

- E1-4 climate targets and approach:
  - Own operations Net Zero: Scope 1 and 2 (market-based) by 2030; base year revised to 2024; emissions from non-controlled premises reported as Scope 3. Levers include renewable sourcing, space optimisation, energy efficiency, and electrification of heating (heat pumps/district heating). Internal working group and staff engagement established.
  - Financed emissions Net Zero: NZBA-aligned ambition to 2050. Sectoral targets disclosed for Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, Steel, Shipping, Commercial Real Estate; baseline disclosed for Residential Real Estate. Coal phase-out by 2028 with limited green financing exceptions. Sectors excluded for low materiality: Aluminium, Cement, Aviation (<1% exposure each); Agriculture monitored pending methodology and policy evolution.
  - Methodology: Cross-functional design using SBTi, PCAF, IEA and NZBA guidance; targets based on on-balance sheet lending; scenarios from IEA NZE 2050 and CRREM v2.01; sector-specific metrics aligned to market practice.

- Sector baselines, progress and 2030 targets (highlights):
  - Oil & Gas (Scope 3 Cat. 11; absolute financed emissions): baseline 2021 21.4 MtCO2e; 2023 10.2 MtCO2e (-47% YoY); 2030 target -29% vs 2021.
  - Power Generation (Scope 1; gCO2e/kWh): baseline 2021 208; 2023 107; 2030 target 111 (EU trajectory; convergence approach).
  - Automotive (Scope 3 Cat. 11 TTW; gCO2/vkm): baseline 2021 161; 2023 116; 2030 target 95 (approx. -41% vs 2021).
  - Steel (Fixed System Boundary incl. Scope 1,2,3 Cat. 1 & 10; tCO2/t steel): baseline 2022 1.45; 2023 1.50; 2030 target 1.11; alignment score from -0.69 (2022) to -0.17 (2023), aiming 0 by 2030.
  - Shipping (Scope 1 and Scope 3 Cat. 3 Well-to-Wake): passenger 14.1→14.0 gCO2e/GT-nm; merchant 9.5→9.3 gCO2e/DWT-nm; 2030 target -30% vs 2022.
  - Commercial Real Estate (operational; kgCO2e/m2): baseline 2022 44.2; 2023 43.4; 2030 target range 24.8–19.9 (-44% to -55%) per CRREM v2.01.
  - Residential Real Estate (operational; kgCO2e/m2): baseline 2022 36.3; 2023 35.8; monitoring without target.

- Data foundations and sector methodologies:
  - Oil & Gas: full value chain focus; Scope 3 Cat. 11; PCAF attribution using EVIC; commodity traders included above materiality thresholds.
  - Power: Scope 1 intensity using IEA emission factors by technology; European benchmark.
  - Automotive: TTW intensity based on new vehicle sales mix.
  - Steel: Sustainable Steel Principles Fixed System Boundary; portfolio tailored IEA trajectory adjusted for 47% scrap charge.
  - Shipping: intensity metrics differentiated for passenger vs merchant; client data plus public sources; targets aligned to IEA NZE.
  - Real Estate (CRE and RRE): EPC-based operational emissions with proxies where data missing; high estimated data share expected to improve with evolving regulations.

- E1-5 energy consumption and mix (own operations, 2024):
  - Total energy 437,667 MWh; 61.9% renewable (271,020 MWh), 38.1% fossil (166,647 MWh); 0% nuclear.
  - High climate impact sectors within Group (Construction, Real Estate entities): 3,020 MWh total, 61.6% fossil, 38.4% renewable.
  - Energy data validated by an assurance provider; “net revenues” corresponds to consolidated operating income.

- E1-6 GHG inventory (own and financed emissions, 2024):
  - Scope 1: 24,412 tCO2e; Scope 2: 100,830 tCO2e (location-based) / 16,702 tCO2e (market-based).
  - Significant Scope 3 total: 97,473,496 tCO2e, dominated by Investments (category 15) 97,187,648 tCO2e; other notable items: Purchased goods/services 175,259 (of which cloud/data centers 174,579), Capital goods 40,644, Upstream leased assets 25,357, Downstream leased assets 31,011, Business travel 3,237, Employee commuting 10,162.
  - Total GHG: 97,598,738 tCO2e (location-based) / 97,514,610 tCO2e (market-based).
  - Country split provided for Scopes 1,2,3; GHG intensity per net revenue: 4,021.28 (location-based) and 4,017.82 (market-based) tCO2e/€m (denominator: €24,270m operating income).
  - 91% of electricity procured from renewables in 2024; instruments include Guarantees of Origin and a corporate PPA for Verona data centers.
  - Methodologies and emission factors: GHG Protocol, DEFRA, IEA, AIB, I-REC, Green‑e, CEPI, Eurostat; expanded Scope 3 category coverage and CSRD-aligned perimeter limit historical comparability.
  - Scope 3 categories excluded as not material for a financial institution: 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14.
  - Financed emissions (Scope 3 Cat. 15) estimation via PCAF: NFC perimeter €176.9bn exposure (82.8% of NFC GCA), 16% actual/84% estimated emissions; households perimeter €69bn residential mortgages (82% of group exposure), 27% actual physical intensity. Exclusions for now: financial institutions (€144bn GCA) and sovereigns (€139bn GCA) due to data limitations; plan to enhance coverage.

- E1-7 Removals and GHG mitigation projects financed; E1-8 Internal carbon pricing: no data disclosed.

- E3 Water and marine resources:
  - No standalone water policy yet; water considerations embedded in sector policies and “sensitive sectors” framework.
  - Policies (e.g., Mining Industry, Water Infrastructure/Large Dams) include assessments of water-related environmental and social impacts and reputational risk controls.

nodes.title: E3 - Water and marine resources
nodes.heading: 2.2.3 E3 - Water and marine resources
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit’s commitment to addressing water -related issues is steadily taking shape, although it has not yet materialized into a dedicated policy to cover the material impact resulting from the DMA , relating to Fostering awareness and commitments related to water consumption, withdrawal by UniCredit clients .
nodes.summary:
- Focus on UniCredit’s sustainability disclosures related to financed emissions and water resource management within the 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts.
- Emissions methodology: combines reported company data with estimates based on Eurostat emission intensity (tons CO2 per euro of added value) by NACE code and country; refined using ISPRA/ETS registry data and sectoral averages where statistically sound; recalibrated to intensity per euro of revenue and applied to company revenues.
- Scope 3 financed emissions for non-financial corporates: calculated for exposures to sectors with high climate impact totaling €176.9bn (82.8% of GCA for non-financial corporates); 16% based on actual data and 84% on estimates; asset classes include loans and advances, debt securities, and equity.
- Scope 3 category 15 (households/residential mortgages): estimated using PCAF and the Net-Zero residential mortgages initiative; perimeter includes Italy, Germany, and Austria residential mortgages only (leasing and other CEE&EE entities excluded); €69bn exposure covered (82% of Group residential mortgage GCA), with 27% physical intensity data coverage and 73% estimated.
- Exclusions from financed emissions: financial institutions (€144bn, 22.6% of total GCA) due to low Scope 1–2 and volatile Scope 3 data; sovereigns (€139bn, 21.8% of total GCA) due to lack of reliable data/estimation approaches; commitment to expand coverage as data improves.
- E1-7 (removals and GHG mitigation via carbon credits) and E1-8 (internal carbon pricing): no data disclosed.
- Water and marine resources (E3): no dedicated Group-wide policy yet for client-related water consumption/withdrawal impacts, but six “sensitive sectors” have enhanced rules; sector policies integrate water management and environmental standards, including a Water Infrastructure (Large dams) policy and a Mining Industry policy addressing environmental and social impacts such as biodiversity loss and water contamination, with attention to reputational risk.

nodes.title: Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.2.3.1 Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit’s commitment to addressing water -related issues is steadily taking shape, although it has not yet materialized into a dedicated policy to cover the material impact resulting from the DMA , relating to Fostering awareness and commitments related to water consumption, withdrawal by UniCredit clients .
nodes.summary:
- Financed emissions methodology and scope
  - Uses both reported company emissions and estimated emissions aligned with market best practices (Eurostat intensity by NACE and country, refined with ISPRA/ETS registry and sectoral averages), recalibrated from added value to revenue, then applied to company revenues.
  - PCAF methodology applied for corporate exposures and Scope 3 category 15 (household residential mortgages).
  - Coverage and figures: €176.9bn of exposures in high climate-impact sectors (82.8% of Non-Financial Corporations’ GCA); 16% based on actual data, 84% estimated; asset classes include loans, advances, debt securities, and equity.
  - Household mortgages scope limited to Italy, Germany, Austria; €69bn exposure covered (82% of Group residential mortgage GCA); 27% physical intensity based on actual data, 73% estimated.
  - Exclusions: no financed emissions calculated for financial institutions (€144bn; 22.6% of total GCA) and sovereigns (€139bn; 21.8%) due to data limitations; intent to enhance coverage over time.

- GHG removals and internal carbon pricing
  - E1-7 (removals/carbon credits) and E1-8 (internal carbon pricing): no data to disclose.

- Water and marine resources (E3)
  - Policies: No standalone water policy yet; water considerations embedded in sectoral policies and “sensitive sectors” rules.
    - Examples: Water Infrastructure (Large dams) policy; Mining Industry policy addressing contamination risks; Oil & Gas policy bans upstream in ultra-deep water (>1,500m); Civil Nuclear policy with focus on groundwater and water.
    - ESG Product Guidelines define “Green” loans aligned to the EU Taxonomy (including water and marine resources objective).
    - Adherence to Equator Principles; application of IFC Performance Standards and World Bank EHS Guidelines covering water efficiency, pollution prevention, biodiversity.
  - Actions and resources: Strengthened sustainability governance; expanded C&E risk work beyond climate to include water, biodiversity, pollution, waste.
    - 2024 nature-related assessment to identify industries with highest impacts and dependencies, using 18 KPIs and sources such as Exiobase, GLOBIO, Natura 2000, ENCORE, guided by TNFD; portfolio heatmap produced.
    - C&E client questionnaire may be enhanced to deepen nature-related assessment.
  - Targets: No specific water/marine targets; relies on Equator Principles/World Bank standards for wastewater, ambient water quality, and conservation.

- Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4)
  - Strategy: Integrating biodiversity within broader C&E risk/opportunity framework; early-stage assessments of industry impacts/dependencies with data gaps acknowledged.
  - 2024 analysis of Natural Capital and Biodiversity across UniCredit countries to identify nature-positive business opportunities; working groups to be established.
  - Policies: No dedicated biodiversity policy yet; ESG Product Guidelines include EU Taxonomy objective on biodiversity/ecosystems.
  - Commitments: Provide sustainable financing, reduce own operational impacts, avoid operations in protected biodiversity areas, combat deforestation and degradation; publication of a Statement on Natural Capital and Biodiversity in 2024.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 2.2.3.2 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank has currently no target on water and marine resources because it applies the rules included in other standards of conduct as follows .
nodes.summary:
- UniCredit’s sustainability reporting outlines use of a Climate & Environmental (C&E) questionnaire to assess credit counterparties’ exposure to climate and broader environmental risks, using qualitative, quantitative, and forward‑looking indicators; plans to enhance it with more nature‑related factors.
- No standalone targets for water and marine resources (E3-3); instead, the Bank applies Equator Principles, World Bank/IFC EHS Guidelines on wastewater, ambient water quality, and water conservation for applicable projects.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems strategy (E4-1): integrates identification of C&E risks and opportunities (climate, biodiversity, energy, water, pollution, waste) into the business model; in 2024 conducted an initial assessment to identify industries most exposed to nature‑related risks and dependencies, noting data gaps and ongoing monitoring of evolving standards and data availability.

- E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems:
  - Strategy and assessments:

  - Policies and principles:
    - No dedicated biodiversity policy yet; ESG Product Guidelines classify “Green” loans aligned with EU Taxonomy, including objective 6 (protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems).
    - Statement on Natural Capital and Biodiversity published in 2024.
    - Sector policies embed biodiversity safeguards: Mining, Oil & Gas (incl. unconventional/Arctic), Civil Nuclear, and Water Infrastructures (large dams).
    - Rainforest Commitment restricts financing linked to deforestation, illegal logging, and other high-risk forest practices; broader commitments on Human Rights and exits from tobacco/deforestation-linked activities.
    - Currently no agriculture or sustainable ocean policies; potential future internal guidelines under evaluation.
  - Actions, engagement, and governance:
    - Signatory to the Finance for Biodiversity Pledge; contributor to climate–nature nexus papers and “Finance for Nature Positive” discussion led by FfB Foundation and UNEP FI.

    - Engagement with NGOs and civil society to refine ESG positioning; participation in EU-level policy discussions; member of IIF Sustainable Finance Nature Expert group; joined TNFD Forum.

    - Training: internal biodiversity program launching in 2025; external client training via Skills for Transition (began Nov 2024).

    - Ambitions: scale internal and client training; establish working groups to evaluate biodiversity-related business opportunities supporting clients’ transitions.
  - Targets:

- E5 Resource use and circular economy:
  - Policies:

  - Actions and partnerships:
    - Awareness-building for clients on circularity and waste.
    - Circularity embedded in the Statement on Natural Capital and Biodiversity and in the Natural Capital Framework as a Net Zero enabler.
    - Membership in the Ellen MacArthur Foundation to access expertise and cross-sector networking.
    - Active in UNEP FI’s climate–circularity nexus working group; contributed to guidance published July 2024; participating in Phase 2 for sector deep-dives.

nodes.heading: 2.3.2 S2 - Workers in the value chain
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit is aware of the importance of human rights, including in its relationship with its value chain.
nodes.summary: Overview of UniCredit’s approach to S2 (Workers in the value chain): the Group has no dedicated policy for value chain workers but relies on its Human Rights Commitment, which applies to clients and their workers as indirect stakeholders, promotes ethics and human rights (including child and forced labor), and is monitored through existing processes and an ESG Dashboard tracking social KPIs and a PRB Financial Health and Inclusion tool. UniCredit identifies sensitive sectors with additional internal rules and a monitoring cycle, uses an Impact Measurement Model to assess social dimensions in lending, and applies an “outside-in” approach via annual double materiality analysis and stakeholder engagement to manage reputational risks. A 2023 Statement on Modern Slavery and Human Trafficking complements this framework. There are currently no specific engagement processes, grievance channels, actions, or targets dedicated to clients’ workers (S2-2 to S2-5).

nodes.title: Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.1 Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.summary:
- Compensation metrics (S1-16): Explains methodology for calculating the gender pay gap at legal-entity and country level based on gross hourly pay (including variable components); states figures are not externally assured. Provides country-by-country gender pay gap results ranging from 13.7% (Bosnia and Herzegovina) to 36.3% (Russia), with other notable gaps including Italy 20.0%, Germany 29.2%, Austria 30.4%, Bulgaria 33.5%, Czech Republic 27.5%, Hungary 24.2%, Romania 27.3%, Serbia 30.1%, Slovenia 17.9%, and Croatia 20.6%. Discloses CEO-to-median employee total compensation ratio of 1:137 (as of December 2024) and details the calculation approach, including total remuneration and fair value of equity instruments per Consob Table n.1; not externally assured.

- Incidents, complaints, and severe human rights impacts (S1-17): Reports 7 incidents of discrimination, 52 complaints through workforce channels, and 1 complaint to OECD National Contact Points. Notes 60 reports investigated under anti-harassment/DE&I policies with 7 disciplinary sanctions; no costs recognized for discrimination incidents in 2024; no severe human rights incidents; metrics not externally assured.

- Workers in the value chain (S2): Acknowledges importance of human rights in the value chain but no dedicated policy for value chain workers; relies on the Group Human Rights Commitment. Describes monitoring via ESG Dashboard, sector-specific provisions for sensitive sectors, tools linked to the Principles for Responsible Banking on Financial Health and Inclusion, an Impact Measurement Model to assess social impacts in lending, and a reputational “outside-in” approach through annual double materiality and stakeholder engagement. References a Modern Slavery and Human Trafficking Statement. States there are no specific engagement processes, remediation channels, actions, or targets specifically for clients’ workers, as they are not considered direct stakeholders.

- Affected communities (S3-1): Outlines policies and practices to support communities, including funding for education, health, and community programs; improving access to credit and financial literacy with emphasis on youth and vulnerable/low-income groups. Identifies opportunities via strategic partnerships, volunteering, inclusion initiatives, third-sector product offerings, and enhanced reputation/market position. Confirms the Human Rights Commitment applies to communities and is aligned with UNGPs, ILO principles, and OECD Guidelines; reports no non-compliance cases. Highlights cultural, arts, music, and sport initiatives, emergency responses, and the UniCredit Foundation’s focus on education to improve youth prospects across Europe.

nodes.title: Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.1 Impact risk and opportunity management
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit’s relationship with affected communities is highlighted by existing policies which address material impacts and opp ortunities resulted from the DMA process:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts Sustainability Statements, covering ESRS social disclosures S2-5, S3 (Affected communities), S3-1 to S3-5, and S4-1 (Consumers and end-users), with metrics, policies, actions, and engagement.
- S2-5 (Workers in the value chain): UniCredit sets no specific targets for client workers as they are not a direct stakeholder group; no direct actions toward them.
- S3-1 (Policies for affected communities): Frameworks and commitments to human rights (UNGPs, ILO, OECD Guidelines); no cases of non-compliance. Policies aim to: 
  - Deliver positive socioeconomic impacts via education, health, community development, and improved access to credit/financial literacy, especially for youth and vulnerable/low-income groups.
  - Leverage opportunities through community partnerships, financial inclusion initiatives, employee volunteering, expanded social-impact product offerings, and reputational benefits with socially conscious stakeholders.
- Community strategy and governance: Stakeholder Engagement (Group) and Territorial Relationship (local) teams manage ongoing, initiative-dependent community engagement; feedback gathered via events and targeted outreach, prioritizing vulnerable groups.
- S3-2 (Engagement processes): Continuous involvement of communities, structured NGO engagement to inform policy updates and targets (e.g., Net Zero), participation in surveys/roundtables, and proactive disclosure; employees get at least one paid volunteer day annually.
- Flagship initiatives and events:
  - ESG Day (Nov 14, 2024): 13,000+ participants across 10 locations, pan-European format addressing environmental-social trade-offs and client transition support.
  - Skills for Transition: Fully funded social program in six countries to upskill youth (incl. NEETs) and companies for the green transition, aligning with just transition and education goals.
  - Fondazione per la Scuola Italiana: Founding member support to modernize Italian schools, reduce educational gaps, and catalyze private co-investment.
- Community products and social financing: 
  - Inclusive offerings for low-income/vulnerable clients (discounted/basic accounts), special accounts for Ukrainian refugees, MicroCredito di Libertà for women survivors of gender-based violence (100% guaranteed social microcredit for essential needs).
  - Social Financing categories: Inclusive Financing (microcredit), Impact Financing (measurable social outcomes), Social Housing (affordable access), and high social-impact loans (non-profits, religious bodies, health/social infrastructure).
  - Microcredit model supports micro-entrepreneurs/start-ups end-to-end with partnerships and capability-building.
- Cultural support: Strategic partnerships with leading institutions (e.g., Filarmonica della Scala, Arena di Verona, Bavarian State Opera, Albertina Museum), art residency prizes (biodiversity, urban regeneration, ecological issues), expanded UniCredit Art Collection digital platform with inclusive Learning Centre, public conservation projects, and heritage access initiatives.
- UniCredit Foundation (UCF): Focus on School, Job, University; engages employees and prioritizes underserved communities.
  - International partnerships: Multi-year programs with Junior Achievement (10 countries, youth 10–19) and Teach For All (6 countries; teacher recruitment/training; community-centered approach).
  - Grassroots programs: 26 NGO projects via Calls for Education across 10 countries targeting secondary school retention, university attainment, and employability.
  - Edu-Fund Platform: Up to €14m (2024–Apr 2025) for scalable education programs; Research Educational Lab to broaden interdisciplinary research; continued scholarships/research grants; employee engagement via Gift Matching, Rest-Cent, Summer School & Volunteering.
- Territorial initiatives and philanthropy:
  - Carta Etica Project: 0.2% of ethical card spending allocated to solidarity projects; >€39m since 2005, supporting 1,300 initiatives (e.g., Caritas “Pepe,” Sant’Egidio, AIL).
  - Local co-designed projects, fundraising via ilmiodono.it, ecosystem activation with partners (Elis, AICCON, Cantieri ViceVersa).
- Financial education (Banking Academy, Italy focus): Social inclusion through training on banking/finance, sustainability/ESG, entrepreneurship, export, digital tools, and economic violence; ~600 volunteer colleagues/former colleagues (UniGens); award-winning skills-based volunteering.
  - Money Talks (IV ed.): ~44,000 beneficiaries; 89% average knowledge acquisition; live talks, local labs, and video lessons, with a focus on women.
  - Road to Social Change (IV ed.): 24,800+ beneficiaries; live talks, on-demand content, ESG assessment, Social Change Manager certification; sector focus (fashion, ceramics, food, tourism, cosmetics).
  - Startup Your Life (VII ed.): 24,500+ students, 415 schools; financial and entrepreneurial PCTO courses, GREENCOMP/ENTRECOMP skills, competitions with national finals and ESG workshops.
  - ITS Startup Your Life (II ed.): Tailored financial/entrepreneurial content for ITS Academies with volunteer-led lessons.
  - Save4Young (V ed.): With Skuola.net; 190,000+ students engaged since 2020; 2024 average +45% literacy gain (+91% on payment cards); articles, web game, ESG videos, updated survey.
  - In-formati: Free courses for individuals/SMEs, customized curricula via 15-course catalog, delivered by volunteers.
  - Con Me al Centro (III ed.): Free digital training for aspiring micro-entrepreneurs (esp. women), from self-assessment to business planning with university/association partners.
  - Finance4Future (I ed.): Gen Z-focused video series with Giffoni Innovation Hub and student ambassadors, linked to Banking Academy content.
- S3-3 (Remedy and grievance): No specific community remediation channels yet; Global Anti-Retaliation Policy in place for employees/third parties.
- S3-4 (Actions and effectiveness): Ongoing social strategy across social finance, community contributions, and people support; effectiveness tracked through feedback, surveys, interviews, satisfaction, workshops, and awareness campaigns across countries.
- S3-5 (Targets): No formal targets yet for advancing positive community impacts/material opportunities due to measurement gaps.
- S4-1 (Consumers and end-users): Policies recognize the sector’s societal role; material impacts/risks/opportunities include:
  - Impacts: Digital transformation (ICT, cloud, AI), customer data protection/cybersecurity, transparent and fair advice, enhanced customer experience and satisfaction.
  - Risks: Operational (data breaches, cyberattacks), reputational (failure to meet needs or protect data).
  - Opportunities: Strong, secure ICT enabling long-term customer relationships, market share growth, and retention via innovative digital solutions.

nodes.start_phrase: Since the measurement of the positive impacts on the communities generated by our activity has not yet been measured by the B ank, we currently do not have targets related to advancing positive impacts and managing material opportunities .
nodes.summary:
- Focus on UniCredit’s Banking Academy, designed primarily for Gen Z (1997–2012), addressing topics from payment tools and financial planning to sensitive issues like economic abuse and gender bias in money management.

- Extensive partnerships with regulators, sector experts, trade associations, research institutions, high schools, universities, non-profits, and territorial institutions to broaden reach and credibility.
- Engagement of Competence volunteers (employees and former employees/UniGens) delivering live lessons, fostering intergenerational knowledge transfer and promoting a more inclusive future.
- Impact financing (social lending) to enterprises and organizations aiming for measurable, positive social outcomes alongside economic returns, targeting key social needs in communities.
- Metrics and targets (S3-5): the bank has not yet set targets for advancing positive impacts or managing related opportunities due to the absence of measured positive community impact data.
- Consumers and end users (S4): policies acknowledge the bank’s broader social role and address material impacts, risks, and opportunities.
  - Impacts: drive a sustainable transformation via digitalization, new technologies, cloud, and AI; safeguard against data breaches; ensure transparent, neutral, fair advice; enhance customer satisfaction and experience.
  - Risks: operational (data breaches and cyberattacks) and reputational (failure to meet needs or protect data integrity).
  - Opportunities: build long-term customer relationships through robust ICT; grow market share and retention via digital/innovative solutions.

- Tax strategy: Compliance-focused, cooperative stance with authorities, rejection of aggressive tax planning, and risk-managed processes.
- Whistleblowing and anti-retaliation: Multiple confidential channels for employees/third parties, privacy safeguards, training, and annual reporting to Boards.
- Supplier management and payment practices: Central supplier qualification with 100% socio-environmental screening; adherence to ILO and Environmental Policy; average invoice payment 19 days across countries, aligned to local standards; no significant late-payment legal cases.
- ABC program and outcomes: Comprehensive controls/tools, due diligence, training (100% coverage of at-risk functions), governance and reporting; no confirmed corruption/bribery incidents or fines in 2024.

nodes.start_phrase: The UniCredit group has zero tolerance for acts of corruption and prohibits them in any form, whether direct or indirect.
nodes.summary:
- Section from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Sustainability Statement) detailing the Group’s anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABC) program and payment practices.
- ABC framework:
  - Comprehensive internal regulations for risk areas (public officials, gifts and hospitality, third-party engagement, donations/sponsorships/memberships, HR, M&A).
  - Tools for documenting/approving gifts and hospitality above thresholds and for due diligence on third parties and beneficiaries; creation of an anti-corruption register of external suppliers; automated due diligence within a decentralized process.
  - Independent second-level controls by a dedicated compliance function; regular reporting of compliance risk assessments and internal audit reviews to internal control committees.
  - Governance and oversight: Group Anti-Corruption Officer and a specialized team within Compliance to advise, implement policies, review cases, and support investigations; annual compliance reporting to the Board and ad hoc reporting to top management; whistleblowing channels available.
  - Training: mandatory web-based training for all employees; 100% coverage of functions at risk; additional workshops/info sessions; induction training for new board and top management members includes ABC. ABC policies published internally; policy excerpt with guidelines available on the website.
- Metrics and outcomes:
  - Zero tolerance stance; effectiveness monitored by the Internal Control System.
  - 2024: no confirmed incidents of corruption or bribery and no related fines.
- Payment practices (G1-6):
  - Scope limited to invoices in Other administrative expenses and Other operating expenses; sampling used for some entities with a 90% confidence level due to data constraints.
  - Standard supplier payment terms followed by country (30 days in Germany, Austria, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Czech Republic, Croatia, Hungary, Romania; 60 days in Italy, Bulgaria, Serbia, Slovenia); average payment time of 19 days.
  - Expense mix: ICT services ~60% of relevant administrative expenses; marketing, consulting, and logistics ~22%; remaining ~18% individually not material (includes capitalized expenses and Other Operating Expenses).
  - No relevant pending legal proceedings related to late payments.
